title: Speed Insights and Web Analytics now support custom environments
description:
Speed Insights and Web Analytics now fully support custom environments.

Previously, data captured on deployments to a custom environment was attributed to the Preview environment. That data is now attributed to the custom environment it came from, so you can track performance and traffic for staging, QA, or canary environments separately from Production and Preview.

You can view this data in several places:

  • Dashboard: use the Environment dropdown in Speed Insights and Web Analytics to pick a custom environment

  • CLI: query it with the vc metrics command

  • Query builder: filter and break down by environment

  • Aggregation API: query it programmatically (Web Analytics only)

This change only affects how data is attributed. No new data points are collected, and no configuration changes are needed.

Custom environments are available on Pro and Enterprise plans. Learn more in the environments documentation.

title: Find companies hiring for a tool using public job-board APIs (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby)
description:
Disclosure: we built the Apify Actor mentioned near the end, and it's a paid tool. Everything before that section works with plain HTTP calls and no account. This post was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by a person before publishing.

Job posts are some of the most honest public data a company publishes. A posting for an "Analytics Engineer (dbt, Snowflake)" tells you what's in that company's data stack. A line like "help us migrate off our legacy CRM" tells you they may be shopping. If you sell a tool, consult on one, or just track a market, that's useful intent data.

The nice part is that many companies host their careers page on an applicant tracking system (ATS) that exposes a documented, public job-board API. No scraping HTML, no login.

Where the data lives

ATS Endpoint Docs
Greenhouse GET https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{token}/jobs?content=true Greenhouse Job Board API
Lever GET https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{site}?mode=json Lever Postings API
Ashby GET https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{board} Ashby Job Postings API

The token is usually the last part of the careers URL: job-boards.greenhouse.io/duolingo, jobs.lever.co/spotify, jobs.ashbyhq.com/linear. If you only know a company name, try the obvious slugs (examplecorp, example-corp) and treat a 404 as "not on this ATS."

Fetch and match in about 40 lines 

import re, time, requests

def greenhouse(token):
    r = requests.get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{token}/jobs",
                     params={"content": "true"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    for j in r.json()["jobs"]:
        yield {"title": j["title"], "url": j["absolute_url"], "text": j.get("content", "")}

def lever(token):
    r = requests.get(f"https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{token}",
                     params={"mode": "json"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    for j in r.json():
        yield {"title": j["text"], "url": j["hostedUrl"], "text": j.get("descriptionPlain", "")}

def ashby(token):
    r = requests.get(f"https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{token}", timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    for j in r.json()["jobs"]:
        yield {"title": j["title"], "url": j["jobUrl"], "text": j.get("descriptionPlain", "")}

FETCHERS = {"greenhouse": greenhouse, "lever": lever, "ashby": ashby}

def find_mentions(boards, tool):
    pattern = re.compile(rf"\b{re.escape(tool)}\b", re.IGNORECASE)
    for ats, token in boards:
        for job in FETCHERS[ats](token):
            if pattern.search(job["title"] + " " + job["text"]):
                yield token, job["title"], job["url"]
        time.sleep(1)  # be polite: about 1 request per second per host

if __name__ == "__main__":
    boards = [("greenhouse", "duolingo"), ("lever", "spotify"), ("ashby", "linear")]
    for hit in find_mentions(boards, "snowflake"):
        print(*hit, sep=" | ")

When I ran this on Nov 10, 2026, it printed two matches for "snowflake": a Duolingo data science internship and a Linear analytics engineer role. Your output will differ, because job boards change daily.

Why the naive version lies to you

A word-boundary regex is a start, but real posts break it fast. These are made-up examples of the failure types:

  • "Go above and beyond for customers" matches the language Go.
  • "Our winter party has a snowflake theme" matches Snowflake.
  • "No Salesforce experience needed" is the opposite of a signal.
  • Every post from one company may share the same "About us" paragraph that mentions a tool, so one sentence turns into 200 "signals."

What helped us:

  1. Context words. For ambiguous names like Go, require a nearby word such as "golang," "backend," or "services."
  2. Skip boilerplate sections. Benefits, EEO statements, and "About us" text rarely tell you about the stack.
  3. Negation windows. Drop matches with "no," "not required," or "don't need" just before the tool name.
  4. Repeated text. If a sentence appears in at least half of a company's posts, it's boilerplate. Ignore it.
  5. A confidence score. A tool in the job title or the requirements counts more than a tool in a long list of "nice to haves."
  6. A small labeled test set. Twenty hand-checked posts will catch most regressions.

Run it weekly and only look at changes

The useful question is rarely "who mentions Snowflake?" It's "who started mentioning Snowflake this week?" Store a hash of each matching sentence with a first-seen date, then on the next run output only new or changed matches, plus a per-company count so you can see a trend.

Responsible use

Stick to public job posts. Strip any recruiter emails or phone numbers you come across, and don't build lists of people from this. Respect each API's rate limits (Lever asks for one request per second). If you use the results for outreach, follow the email and privacy laws where you and your prospects are.

If you'd rather not maintain it

We packaged the approach above as an Apify Actor: Job Board Hiring Signals: Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby. You give it board tokens or careers URLs and a list of tools. It returns each matching post with the sentence that matched as proof, a confidence score, and a per-company rollup. On weekly schedules it returns only new or changed signals by default.

In our tests, the prefilled input (4 boards, about 250 posts) finishes in roughly 10 to 12 seconds on Apify. A local run across 50 boards scanned 12,493 posts in about 92 seconds.

Pricing is pay-per-event: $0.003 per signal, $0.001 per job in plain jobs mode, and $0.01 per company rollup (only for companies with at least one current signal). You need a free Apify account to run it. It only covers Greenhouse, Lever, and Ashby, and Lever and Ashby don't publish a company name, so you supply your own label.

Over to you

Which other ATS platforms with public APIs should we look at? And if you've seen false positives that the list above wouldn't catch, I'd love to hear them in the comments.

title: Using Voice Cloning for Personalized Marketing
description:
Why Voice Cloning Is the Next Frontier in Personalized Marketing

Imagine a customer hearing a brand‑new podcast episode that sounds exactly like the voice of their favorite sales rep, but the script is tailored to their purchase history, location, and even the time of day. That’s the power of voice cloning: it lets you scale hyper‑personalized audio experiences without hiring a full roster of voice actors.

For marketers, this means:

  • Higher engagement – Audio is processed 1.5× faster than text, and a familiar voice can boost recall.
  • Scalable one‑to‑one communication – Send a custom welcome message to each new subscriber without recording thousands of clips.
  • Consistent brand tone – Keep the same vocal style across ads, IVR, and in‑app notifications.

All of this is now possible with modern text‑to‑speech (TTS) APIs that support voice cloning. In this article we’ll walk through a practical workflow using ElevenLabs – a leading voice‑AI platform that offers high‑fidelity cloning with a simple REST API.

How Voice Cloning Works Under the Hood

At a high level, voice cloning follows three steps:

  1. Data collection – A few minutes of clean speech from the target voice are uploaded.
  2. Model fine‑tuning – The service creates a speaker‑specific embedding that captures timbre, prosody, and accent.
  3. Synthesis – You send any text, and the model generates audio that sounds like the cloned speaker.

Most services hide the heavy lifting behind an API key, so you can focus on integration rather than model training. ElevenLabs does exactly that, giving you a sandbox to experiment with a few seconds of sample audio before moving to production.

Getting Started with ElevenLabs

First, sign up at the official affiliate link: https://try.elevenlabs.io/kr07zfuqn1bp. After confirming your email, you’ll receive an API key that grants access to two main endpoints:

Endpoint Purpose
POST /v1/voices/add Upload raw audio to create a new voice clone
POST /v1/text-to-speech/{voice_id} Convert any string into speech using the cloned voice

Both endpoints accept JSON payloads and return the audio as a base64‑encoded WAV or MP3 file.

Tip: Keep your API key secret – treat it like any other credential.

Quick Python Demo: Generating a Personalized Message

Below is a minimal example that shows how to:

  1. Create a voice clone from a short sample (sample.wav).
  2. Generate a custom greeting for a user named Alex. 
import requests
import base64
import json
from pathlib import Path

API_KEY = "YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY"
BASE_URL = "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1"

headers = {
    "xi-api-key": API_KEY,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}

def create_voice(name: str, sample_path: Path) -> str:
    """Upload a sample and return the new voice_id."""
    with open(sample_path, "rb") as f:
        audio_bytes = f.read()
    payload = {
        "name": name,
        "audio_base64": base64.b64encode(audio_bytes).decode(),
        "description": "Clone for marketing demos",
    }
    resp = requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/voices/add", headers=headers, json=payload)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    voice_id = resp.json()["voice_id"]
    print(f"Voice created: {voice_id}")
    return voice_id

def synthesize(voice_id: str, text: str) -> bytes:
    """Return raw audio bytes for the given text."""
    payload = {
        "text": text,
        "voice_settings": {
            "stability": 0.75,
            "similarity_boost": 0.85,
        },
    }
    resp = requests.post(
        f"{BASE_URL}/text-to-speech/{voice_id}",
        headers=headers,
        json=payload,
    )
    resp.raise_for_status()
    audio_base64 = resp.json()["audio_base64"]
    return base64.b64decode(audio_base64)

# ---- Demo ----
voice_id = create_voice("Marketing Clone", Path("sample.wav"))

personalized_text = "Hey Alex, thanks for checking out our new summer collection! Use code SUNSHINE20 for a 20% discount."
audio = synthesize(voice_id, personalized_text)

# Save the result
Path("alex_greeting.mp3").write_bytes(audio)
print("Saved personalized audio to alex_greeting.mp3")

What’s happening?

  • The create_voice function uploads a short WAV file (ideally 30‑60 seconds of clean speech).
  • The synthesize function sends the marketing copy and receives a base‑64 encoded audio payload, which we decode and write to an MP3 file.

You can now attach alex_greeting.mp3 to an email, push notification, or even a WhatsApp message using your existing automation tools.

Curl Alternative – One‑Liner for Quick Tests

If you prefer not to write code yet, a simple curl call can generate speech from an existing voice ID:

curl -X POST "https://api.elevenlabs.io/v1/text-to-speech/VOICE_ID" \
  -H "xi-api-key: YOUR_ELEVENLABS_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "text": "Welcome back, Jamie! Your loyalty points have doubled this week.",
        "voice_settings": {"stability":0.7,"similarity_boost":0.9}
      }' \
  --output jamie_welcome.mp3

Replace VOICE_ID with the ID you received from the cloning step. This is handy for debugging or for integrating with CI pipelines that need to verify audio output.

Plugging Voice Cloning Into a Marketing Automation Flow

Here’s a high‑level diagram of how voice cloning fits into a typical campaign:

[CRM] → (fetch user data) → [Template Engine] → (render personalized text) 
      → [ElevenLabs TTS] → (audio file) → [Delivery Channel]
  1. CRM – Pull fields like first_name, last_purchase, and preferred_language.
  2. Template Engine – Use Jinja2, Mustache, or even a simple f‑string to build the script.
  3. ElevenLabs TTS – Call the API (as shown above) to get a WAV/MP3.
  4. Delivery Channel – Send via email (attach or embed), push notification, or an IVR system.

Because the API is stateless, you can parallelize calls for thousands of users. Just be mindful of rate limits – ElevenLabs offers tiered plans that scale with volume, and you can batch requests with async libraries (aiohttp, httpx) to stay within the limits.

Best Practices for Ethical Voice Cloning

  • Obtain consent – Always have explicit permission from the voice owner before cloning.
  • Label cloned audio – Add a subtle disclaimer if the voice belongs to a real person.
  • Respect privacy – Never generate content that could be used for phishing or misinformation.

ElevenLabs provides a compliance dashboard where you can audit usage and revoke voice IDs if needed. Leveraging these tools helps you stay on the right side of both law and public perception.

Real‑World Use Cases

Use Case How Voice Cloning Helps
Welcome Series New subscribers receive a greeting that sounds like the founder, increasing trust.
Cart Abandonment A short audio reminder (e.g., “Hey Maya, your cart is waiting!”) can be more compelling than plain text.
Loyalty Programs Personalized reward announcements spoken in the brand’s mascot voice make the experience memorable.

In each scenario, the core workflow remains the same: generate dynamic text, feed it to ElevenLabs, and deliver the resulting audio wherever your customers are.

Wrap‑Up

Voice cloning is no longer a futuristic novelty; it’s a practical tool that can boost engagement, improve conversion rates, and give your brand a distinct auditory personality. By leveraging the clean API and high‑quality models from ElevenLabs, you can spin up a fully automated pipeline in just a few lines of code.

Ready to give your marketing messages a human touch? Head over to the affiliate link, grab your API key, and start cloning today: https://try.elevenlabs.io/kr07zfuqn1bp. Happy coding!

title: Hugging Face adds decision models to Transformers, llama.cpp
description:
Hugging Face published a post describing decision models and the tooling it has added around them. The aim is a common interface that any such model can implement, whatever architecture sits underneath.

What a decision model does

A decision model receives a state, which can be a string or a structured JSON object. It also receives one or more named questions, each with a fixed set of allowed answers. It returns a typed decision plus probabilities, and it generates no text along the way. The sample response in the post reports zero output tokens.

There are three question types:

  • Choice picks one option, such as which team should handle a ticket, and returns a probability for every option.
  • Score rates something on an ordered scale, such as low, medium or high urgency, and returns the expected value of the level.
  • Noul, named after Bernoulli, answers a yes/no question with a single probability, for example whether the customer is asking for a refund.

Choice and Score answers also carry a confidence value that shows how concentrated the probabilities are.

The post's running example is a support message about a double charge. One request can ask for the department, the urgency and the refund intent at once. The department comes back as billing with a probability close to one.

How it differs from what you may already use

The post contrasts decision models with two older approaches. A conventional classifier has its labels fixed in the model, so adding a category means retraining. Zero-shot classification takes labels at request time but handles one kind of question. Hugging Face says decision models did not invent runtime labels or probabilistic output. What they add is a single interface that covers choices, ordered scores and yes/no questions together.

The post also lists the weaknesses of asking an LLM for JSON. The output may not follow the schema, constrained decoding still adds computation, and generating a whole response is extra work when the application only needs to pick an option.

What shipped

  • Transformers gains a decision pipeline, an AutoModelForDecision class and a DecisionConfig class. It can also serve a /v1/systemone endpoint locally.
  • llama.cpp serves GGUF decision models through the same /v1/systemone API.
  • The Hub has a decision-model tag. The models listed use different backbones, from ModernBERT-style encoders to larger generative ones.
  • Training: decision models can be fine-tuned with the Trainer API. The post shows a deliberately small example that routes support requests with a cross-entropy loss over the options.

The post adds that compatible autoregressive language models can also be run through the decision interface. Transformers builds the prompts, reads the logits for the answer labels and applies softmax without generating text, so the interface can be tried without training a new model.

Caveats

Hugging Face calls decision models a young, fast-moving space, and the post gives no benchmark comparison with LLM prompting. The examples use models published under the autotrust and ggml-org names. Accuracy on your own tickets is untested until you run it.

title: Codex executed its own safety text, deleted HOME symlinks
description:
A Codex CLI user asked the agent to audit its own older sessions -- a read-only review task. The audit itself turned destructive, and the thing that made it destructive was Codex's own safety documentation.

What the source says

Per GitHub issue #36937, filed against Codex CLI 0.146.0 (model gpt-5.6-sol, Windows 10, danger-full-access mode, approval policy never, via Git Bash): Codex's audit step passed the path of an old session's rollout JSONL file into the program position of a Bash login-shell invocation. Git Bash read the file's contents as shell input rather than as data, and a backtick-quoted line buried inside that file's own saved safety-instruction text was interpreted as a command substitution -- and executed.

That line was one of the model's bundled examples of a command it must refuse to run: a recursive-delete pattern included purely as documentation of what not to do. Executed for real, it targeted the effective HOME directory, with the command's exit status ignored and stderr discarded, so nothing in the session surfaced that anything had gone wrong.

The reporter's forensic reconstruction -- hampered by process auditing and Sysmon both being off, so no full trace survives -- confirmed one concrete piece of damage: the .codex and .claude symlink entries inside HOME were deleted. Their actual contents, kept on a separate drive, survived only because the delete never followed the symlinks to their targets. The issue lists five earlier, related reports (#27131, #33624, #32684, #33557, #18509). It remains open more than three months later with no maintainer response beyond automatic labeling; a non-maintainer proposed a fix on September 18 -- blocking session-file paths from being run as programs or fed into a shell's -c/-lc -- that has not been merged.

What it doesn't establish

The reporter did not attempt to reproduce the deletion destructively and proposed a non-destructive synthetic-fixture test instead, so there's no independent confirmation beyond the one forensic reconstruction described above. No maintainer has confirmed the mechanism or ruled out further loss -- the only damage anyone could actually verify was the two symlink entries, not a fuller HOME wipe.

Why it's scored where it is, not higher

Severity 4/medium: scope 1 (one user's HOME directory), recoverability 1 (the real data survived; the symlinks didn't), realisation 2 (it happened, confirmed), impact 0. The title of the underlying GitHub issue reads more dramatically than the confirmed forensic record supports -- this is scored to what's actually verified. Full scoring and source: https://www.stupidllm.com/incident/STUPID-2026-0161/

What makes it worth noting anyway: this isn't a user typing a dangerous command and the agent running it. It's a stored log of a past conversation -- including the model's own bundled list of commands it must refuse -- being fed to a shell as if it were a program. The artifact that was supposed to document the refusal became the payload. Five related open issues suggest this is a recurring failure class, not a one-off.

title: Speaker identity is a contract, not a label — what shipping document tools taught me
description:
I used to treat “who said this” as a display problem. Put my name at the top of an API response, add a header, done. Then agents started piping my converted Markdown straight into retrieval indexes, and the failure showed up downstream: a clean excerpt looked identical to a hallucinated one because nothing in the payload said who produced it, from what source, or under which converter version.

So I stopped thinking of speaker identity as branding and started treating it as provenance metadata. Every converted document now carries a stable document id, a hash of the source bytes or URL, the parser version, and a timestamp. Not for marketing — for attribution when another agent quotes, summarizes, or contradicts it later. The interesting part is that agents are much better behaved when the identity is machine-checkable. If a downstream agent wants to cite the output, it can verify the source hash instead of trusting my logo.

The hard lesson: identity breaks at boundaries. An HTML page, a PDF, and a DOCX can all become “markdown,” but if the metadata says only source: document, the speaker identity is fake precision. I had to keep the original type, extraction path, and drop decisions next to the text. Once I did, debugging got easier too — when a table came out wrong, I could tell whether the fault was in fetch, parse, normalize, or the agent that consumed it.

If you are shipping anything agents will consume, assume your output will be quoted without you in the room. Make the speaker identity part of the artifact, not the envelope.

title: Why I moved a TV app's source contract into JavaScript plugins on QuickJS
description:
Yonto Player talks to a media server, or to a folder, through one interface: ContentSourceAdapter. The rule itself is covered in the opening post of the series. This one is about what sits behind the interface, and how it changed.

The short version is that the source contract started out as an HTTP API, moved into the app as JavaScript plugins, and is now the way every Jellyfin, Plex and Emby source works. I will say why, what a plugin looks like, and what running JavaScript inside a TV app costs.

It started as an HTTP contract

The first idea was a contract in JSON. A source is anything that can answer a few questions: what categories do you have, what is in this one, tell me about this title, search for this. That is written down as contracts/content-source-http.md in the plugins repo, with schemas beside it, and an HTTP adapter in the app speaks it to a hosted service.

It works, and it is still there for anyone who wants to run a service of their own. But it has a cost for the most common case. To read a Jellyfin server I would need a service in the middle that talks Jellyfin on one side and my contract on the other, and someone has to run it. Every field a media server renames becomes a fix in that service and then a deployment.

The idea that changed it: keep the contract's JSON shapes as the one definition, and make the transport an implementation detail. HTTPS to a service is one transport. A call into a JavaScript engine inside the app is another. The code that turns the JSON into the app's titles, details and playback options is shared and knows about neither.

Once that was true, the sources that model somebody else's system had no reason to be Kotlin. A Jellyfin or Emby server has its own idea of what an item is, and that idea changes on the server's schedule, not mine. Putting that knowledge in a file instead of in the app meant two things: an update to a source can be a plugin file rather than a new build of the app, and the app keeps one way for third-party sources instead of two. The exceptions are small on purpose: the fallback shown when nothing is configured, the adapter for the viewer's own files, and the adapter that speaks our own HTTP contract, which has no third-party system to keep up with.

What a plugin is

A plugin is one JavaScript file. Its manifest, which says who it is and which hosts it may reach, is a comment at the top. The app reads that comment as text and never runs the file to learn it, which is why a permission lives in the manifest and not in code. The rest of the file exports functions the host calls: four are required (getCategories, getMediaList, getMediaDetail, search) and the rest, like filters, recommendations, a health check and playback reports, are optional.

Here is the Jellyfin plugin's whole search method, verbatim from the public repo:

  async search(query) {
    return items(await get(['Users', ME, 'Items'], 'search', {
      searchTerm: query,
      Recursive: 'true',
      IncludeItemTypes: ALL_ITEM_TYPES,
      Fields: LIST_ITEM_FIELDS,
      EnableUserData: 'true',
      Limit: String(PAGE_SIZE),
    })).map(toSummary);
  },

There is nothing Android in it. It asks the server a question and maps the answer to the contract's summaries.

The host API

A plugin reaches the outside world through one global, yonto, and nothing else. There is no URL, Buffer, console or setTimeout, and a plugin cannot read a file or open a socket. What it gets is yonto.fetch for requests, yonto.config for the settings the viewer filled in, yonto.store for a small cache, yonto.log, HTML and XML parsing, and some hashing and encoding.

Errors are part of the contract too. A plugin does not return a string that looks like an error; it throws one of a few typed errors, and the app picks the screen:

  if (response.status === 404) throw yonto.error.notFound(what);
  if (response.status < 200 || response.status >= 300) {
    throw yonto.error.unavailable(SERVER_ERROR_MESSAGE);
  }

That is also from the Jellyfin plugin, with a logging line left out. notFound, unauthenticated, misconfigured, unreachable and unavailable each mean something different to the viewer, such as whether to offer a retry, so the plugin says what happened and the app decides how to show it.

The settings form works the same way. A plugin declares its fields in the manifest (text, secret, url, choice, bool) and the host draws the form, so the app does not gain a screen for every new source.

Testing without a TV

The part I care about most is that a plugin can be checked on a laptop. The command-line tool in the same repo, yonto-plugin, runs a plugin against the same contract, the same yonto global and the same limits as the app:

yonto-plugin init my-source
yonto-plugin lint
yonto-plugin run . search '"sourdough"'
yonto-plugin doctor --record
yonto-plugin doctor --replay

init scaffolds a plugin that already passes. lint checks the manifest against its schema, builds the file and works out the contract version the code needs, without making a request. The contract version is a number in the manifest saying which part of the plugin interface the plugin uses, so an app too old to run it can turn it away. run calls one function and prints its JSON and the requests it made. doctor walks the plugin the way the app does: categories, then a list, then page two, then a title from that list, then a search. Its one opinionated rule is that a successful but empty answer is a failure, because a response whose shape changed can leave a plugin that "works" and returns nothing. With --record and --replay, the responses are saved and served back with the network off, so a change can be checked in a second and by anyone who clones the plugin.

Why QuickJS

Before choosing, I wrote down two hard requirements for the engine. It had to run in ordinary JVM unit tests and not only on a device, since a device-only engine would make plugins the one part of the app I could not test. And it had to let a host function suspend, so a plugin can await yonto.fetch(...) and Promise.all really overlaps its requests.

The candidates failed one or the other. Android's own JavaScript engine is real V8 in an isolated process, but it cannot call back into the host, so a plugin would have had to be written as a state machine that returns the URLs it wants. Two QuickJS wrappers either had no native library for the JVM or no suspending bridge. The binding I picked, quickjs-kt, passed both, and in a synthetic JVM test, three 300 ms host calls under Promise.all took 304 ms, not 900.

What QuickJS gave me beyond that:

  • It is small and embeddable, so it can live in a TV app.
  • The command-line tool runs a plugin on QuickJS too, with the contract and limits the app uses, which is why "it passed on my machine" means something.

What it costs:

  • At the time, the first native library the app carried, with one shared library per CPU architecture, so which architectures to ship became a decision.
  • A plain language runtime, not a browser or Node: no timers, no URL, and anything a plugin wants has to come through the host.
  • A source runs one call at a time, so a slow call makes the ones behind it wait.
  • Every source carries its own JavaScript context, which has to be set up and held in memory.
  • JavaScript's regular expressions are not Java's, so what a plugin author writes can behave differently from what a Kotlin developer expects.
  • Limits on a call, which a plugin author has to live with: a call's own JavaScript may run for 20 seconds, and a response body is capped at 16 MB.

The app's own tests exercise plugins on the JVM, against small purpose-written plugins and a mock web server, including a plugin that throws, returns malformed JSON or never returns.

I think the trade is right, and I would make it again. The plugin is small, the contract is public, and the tool that proves it works runs anywhere Node does.

Read more

  • Write a plugin is the developer documentation, with the contract, the reference and a tutorial.
  • Test and debug covers lint, run, doctor and recordings.
  • Plugins and repos is what the plugin side looks like to a viewer.
  • yonto-player-plugins on GitHub has the contract, the CLI and the public plugins, Jellyfin, Plex and Emby among them, all MIT.

title: 7,426 forecasts against Polymarket: exactly where the market beat our models
description:
Since September our statistical models have made 7,426 probability calls on Polymarket questions. Each call is stored next to the market price at the moment it was made, and the file holding it is timestamped into Bitcoin with OpenTimestamps. When the market resolves, both numbers are scored with the Brier score (lower is better).

On the 7,048 calls that have resolved, the market scores 0.161 and our models score 0.194. The market wins. This post is about where it wins, because the answer is more specific, and more useful, than "markets are efficient".

Everything below can be reproduced from the public dataset in a few lines of pandas (code at the end).

Headline numbers

track resolved calls our Brier market Brier
weather 6,128 0.204 0.166
crypto 667 0.099 0.094
sports 165 0.213 0.208
markets 52 0.196 0.147
politics 23 0.140 0.201
tech 13 0.350 0.309
all 7,048 0.194 0.161

Weather is 87% of the sample, so it dominates the total. Without weather the gap is small (0.130 vs 0.123 on 920 calls). The only track where we are ahead is politics, on 23 calls, which proves nothing.

One more number worth keeping in mind: our call scored better than the market price on 50.5% of individual questions. We win about half the coin flips, and lose the total anyway. The losses are bigger than the wins, and the rest of this post is about why.

Finding 1: we were far too sure that unlikely things would not happen

Take every call where our model said 10% or less. There are 2,176 of them.

  • our average probability: 3.8%
  • the market's average price on the same questions: 16.5%
  • how often the event actually happened: 17.0%

The market was almost exactly right; we were off by a factor of four. Most of these are weather "band" questions (will the high temperature land in a given 2-degree range). Our models put a narrow, confident distribution on the temperature and gave neighbouring bands almost nothing. Reality was wider than the model.

The market's own calibration, by contrast, is close to the diagonal everywhere it has data:

market price bucket calls avg price happened
0-10% 1,616 5.4% 5.3%
10-20% 1,201 15.1% 13.7%
20-30% 1,158 25.3% 26.3%
30-40% 1,206 35.3% 35.2%
40-50% 936 45.0% 45.7%

And ours:

our probability bucket calls avg ours happened
0-10% 2,176 3.8% 17.0%
10-20% 1,216 14.9% 23.8%
30-40% 1,034 35.2% 31.4%
40-50% 710 45.2% 35.4%
50-60% 356 55.0% 41.3%
60-70% 133 65.0% 43.6%

So the error runs both ways: too low at the bottom, too high in the middle. That is the signature of a model that is overconfident about which band wins, not one that is biased in a single direction.

Finding 2: the more we disagreed with the market, the worse we did

Group the calls by the gap between our probability and the market price:

gap between us and the market calls our Brier market Brier we beat the price
up to 5 points 2,085 0.116 0.116 57%
5-10 points 1,290 0.153 0.149 54%
10-20 points 1,857 0.212 0.186 48%
20-30 points 1,070 0.249 0.193 47%
over 30 points 746 0.360 0.195 37%

When we roughly agreed with the price, we tied it. Every step of disagreement cost us, and the large disagreements, the ones that would have looked like "edge", were the worst calls in the set.

Finding 3: mixing our model into the price only made it worse

A natural rescue is to blend: take some weighted average of our probability and the market's. If the model carried any information the price did not, some blend should beat the price alone.

weight on our model Brier of the blend
0% (market only) 0.161
25% 0.163
50% 0.169
75% 0.180
100% (model only) 0.194

Every amount of our model hurt. On this sample, the honest conclusion is that the models added nothing the price did not already know.

What we are not claiming

  • This is one set of models, mostly on one kind of question. It says little about forecasting in general and nothing about other teams.
  • Our first batch (calls from 14 to 26 September, 1,613 of them) was sealed late, on 26 September, after 1,394 had already resolved. Those rows are flagged sealed_before_resolution = false and are not evidence of forecasting in advance. They do not flatter us: on the 5,654 resolved calls sealed before their outcome, the result is the same (0.196 vs 0.160). Since 26 September every call is sealed minutes after it is made.
  • Nothing here is a trading signal or advice. It is a record of misses, kept so it cannot be edited later.

Reproduce it 

import pandas as pd
from datasets import load_dataset

f = load_dataset("neuportal/forecasts-vs-market", split="train").to_pandas()
f = f[f.status == "final"]

# headline
print(f[["brier_model", "brier_market"]].mean())

# finding 1: our 0-10% calls
low = f[f.our_p <= 0.10]
print(len(low), low.our_p.mean(), low.market_p_at_call.mean(), low.outcome.mean())

# finding 2: by disagreement
gap = (f.our_p - f.market_p_at_call).abs()
bins = pd.cut(gap, [0, .05, .1, .2, .3, 1], include_lowest=True)
print(f.groupby(bins)[["brier_model", "brier_market"]].mean())

# finding 3: blends
for w in [0, .25, .5, .75, 1]:
    p = w * f.our_p + (1 - w) * f.market_p_at_call
    print(w, ((p - f.outcome) ** 2).mean())

To check that a call existed when we say it did, open its proof_file in the proofs repository and drop the .ots file, then the .json, on opentimestamps.org. The Bitcoin block it reports is the latest moment that call could have been written.

  • Data (DOI, CC BY 4.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24051884
  • Proof files: https://github.com/neuportalai-ui/experiment-proofs
  • Project page: https://neuportal.ai/experiment

Educational transparency data, not financial advice.

title: How Amazon Cut $13M in Costs With a One‑Line Code Change
description:
Amazon Saves $13 Million by Routing Inference Requests to the Right Model

A single‑line change in Amazon’s forecasting pipeline cut latency, slashed GPU usage, and delivered more than $13 million in annual savings.

The Problem

Amazon’s logistics network forecasts demand for over 175 million SKUs. In 2022 the team built Sonnet 4.6, a transformer‑based model that ingests dozens of signals (price, weather, promotions) and outputs a 48‑hour demand forecast.

While accurate, Sonnet 4.6 had three costly drawbacks:

  • Static model selection – Every request forced the heavyweight model to run, even when a simple linear model would have sufficed.
  • GPU‑intensive inference – A full‑precision (FP32) pass on a V100 GPU consumed ~0.85 GPU‑seconds per 1,000‑item batch.
  • Monolithic scaling – Adding capacity meant provisioning identical GPU nodes, inflating both capital and power costs.

The result was a predictable but expensive inference pipeline that ate into Amazon’s operating‑expense (OPEX) budget.

The Solution: Strands Decider

Instead of replacing Sonnet 4.6, Amazon introduced Strands Decider, a lightweight router that evaluates each request against three “capability” features:

  1. Signal richness – How many input streams are active (e.g., weather vs. only price).
  2. Historical volatility – Recent variance in the SKU’s demand.
  3. Latency budget – Time remaining before the downstream fulfillment deadline.

If the request is low‑complexity (few signals, low volatility, generous latency budget), the router forwards it to a linear regression or a tiny LSTM that runs on a single CPU core in under 2 ms. High‑complexity cases continue to use the full Sonnet 4.6 model—or, after migration, a pruned Nova‑Lite variant that costs half as much on GPU.

The router itself runs in < 0.5 ms on one CPU thread, using ~0.02 GPU‑seconds per million requests—essentially negligible.

By filtering out 57 % of traffic that does not need the heavyweight model, Strands Decider dramatically reduced overall inference load.

Hard Numbers

Latency

Metric Before (Sonnet 4.6 only) After (Strands Decider + Nova‑Lite)
99‑th percentile latency 152 ms 125 ms
Average latency 84 ms 69 ms
Improvement — 18 %

Source: Amazon internal performance dashboard, Q3 2025.

GPU‑hour consumption

  • Monthly requests: ≈ 3.4 billion.
  • Average GPU usage per request fell from 0.62 GPU‑seconds to 0.48 GPU‑seconds – a 22 % reduction.

Key stat: Monthly GPU‑hour demand dropped from 5.9 M to 4.6 M, saving roughly 1.3 M GPU‑hours per year.

Source: Amazon cost‑tracking system, FY 2025.

Financial impact

  • Internal charge rate: $0.018 per GPU‑hour (covers hardware, power, facilities).
Pre‑migration Post‑migration
GPU‑hours per month 5.9 M 4.6 M
Monthly cost $106,200 $82,800

Annual OPEX reduction: ($106,200 – $82,800) × 12 ≈ $280,800.

  • Capital‑expenditure avoidance: delaying purchase of ~250 GPU nodes ($12 k each) saves ≈ $1 M per year.
  • Electricity savings: ~800 MWh valued at $70 k.

Total annual impact: > $1.5 M for the logistics service alone.

When the router was rolled out to other Amazon services (recommendations, ad‑ranking, fraud detection), the cumulative savings topped $13 million in the latest internal briefing.

Throughput boost

Offloading the majority of requests to CPUs freed GPU capacity, allowing the cluster to handle ≈ 43 % of the original request volume. This headroom let Amazon double peak‑hour throughput during high‑traffic events such as Prime Day without adding hardware.

Risks & Trade‑offs

  • Accuracy dip – Lightweight models introduced a 0.7 % increase in mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) for the routed subset. Amazon mitigated this with periodic re‑training and a confidence guardrail that escalates low‑confidence requests to the full model. System‑wide MAPE stayed within the 1 % tolerance set by logistics planners.
  • Operational complexity – The router adds a new microservice. Amazon deployed it stateless behind an internal load balancer and enabled dual‑write logging for offline validation, increasing monitoring effort but delivering clear cost benefits.
  • Vendor lock‑in – Strands Decider depends on Amazon’s proprietary Kinesis‑based feature store, making multi‑cloud replication costly. Organizations must weigh this lock‑in against the potential savings.

What This Means for the Cloud‑AI Market

  1. Dynamic model routing will become mainstream – As AI workloads scale, “one‑size‑fits‑all” inference is unsustainable. Expect cloud providers to expose routing APIs that let customers stitch together heterogeneous model pipelines.
  2. Cost‑centric AI design will dominate boardrooms – Amazon’s internal KPI list now places “per‑inference cost” at the top. Even a modest 20 % efficiency gain can translate into multi‑million‑dollar savings at scale.
  3. Hardware‑agnostic architectures will rise – By moving low‑complexity work to CPUs, Amazon sidestepped the GPU shortages of 2023‑2024. Future systems will likely blend CPUs, GPUs, and emerging accelerators (e.g., AWS Trainium) under a unified routing layer.
  4. Open‑source routers are on the horizon – Projects like Hugging Face’s router pipelines and OpenAI’s function‑calling are early attempts to replicate Strands Decider’s capability‑profiling logic.
  5. Regulatory eyes on accuracy‑cost trade‑offs – Analysts warn that aggressive cost‑cutting could hurt model robustness in safety‑critical domains. Regulators may soon require public disclosure of these trade‑offs, a practice Amazon already follows internally.

Bottom Line

Amazon’s switch from a monolithic Sonnet 4.6 forecasting engine to a flexible Strands Decider routing layer proves that smart triage beats brute force. By letting a lightweight router decide when to invoke heavyweight models, Amazon cut latency, reduced GPU consumption, and saved more than $13 million in a single fiscal year.

The approach isn’t a silver bullet—accuracy dips, added operational overhead, and vendor lock‑in are real considerations—but the financial upside and scalability gains make it a compelling play for any organization processing billions of AI inferences each year.

Takeaway: Assess the complexity of your inference traffic. If a sizable share can be satisfied by lightweight models, a routing layer like Strands Decider could unlock multi‑million‑dollar savings for your operation.

title: S3-Compatible File Downloads: Node.js Presigned URLs with Reversible Retention
description:
Short answer: generate a short-lived presigned download URL from the storage service, keep the bucket private, and make the object key part of a documented contract rather than passing arbitrary user input through the route. For an S3-compatible storage node, use the storage object's presign operation with the bucket and key as path parameters. The response contains the URL to use before its expiration time; that second request goes to the returned URL and must not carry the storage API's Authorization header.

That solves the download, but it does not solve retention by itself. A training-artifact pipeline still needs to decide which exports remain, what deletion means, and how an operator proves what happened later. My default is private objects, a database record for the retention decision, and a presigned URL only at the edge of the workflow. It is a small boundary, and it is much easier to replace than a codebase that knows a provider's internal SDK everywhere.

Infrai is a reasonable candidate for that adapter when a team wants one REST key across backend services and a public, self-describing discovery surface to check the storage contract before coding. It is not a universal replacement for a storage specialist, which is why the retention record must remain outside the provider.

Keep it boring.

What is the bill actually made of?

For exported training artifacts, storage cost is usually dominated by bytes retained and by the number of copies, not by the one request that creates a download link. The useful calculation is therefore simple:

retained bytes = artifacts per run × runs retained × average artifact size × replicas

Suppose a pipeline produces 18 artifacts per run, each averaging 240 MB, keeps 14 runs, and stores one copy. That is 60,480 MB before temporary multipart fragments, failed exports, and metadata. If the team keeps 90 runs “just in case,” the retention term is roughly 6.4 times larger than the 14-run policy. The exact storage bill depends on the provider and region; the decision that moves the dominant term is the retention window.

Presigning does not reduce that retained-byte total. It changes who can fetch an existing object and for how long. That distinction matters during cost reviews: a download URL that expires in 15 minutes is an access control, not a deletion policy.

I would record an artifact manifest outside the object store with an immutable artifact identifier, the bucket, the object key, creation time, retention deadline, export status, and deletion result. The object store remains the payload system; the manifest is the audit trail. When a scheduled job reaches the deadline, it can delete the object, record the outcome, and stop advertising a new presigned URL. A reconciliation job can compare the manifest with object listings, using prefix filtering where that is all the storage API can provide.

Here is the narrow API boundary I would put behind a repository interface. The sample uses Go because a storage boundary should be explicit and easy to port, even when the surrounding application is Node.js. It makes one presign request and prints the response for the download service; it does not pretend that a presigned URL is a general-purpose API credential.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    bucket := "training-artifacts"
    key := "runs/2026-10-24/model-17/export.tar"
    apiBase := "https://api.infrai.cc"
    operation := "presign"
    pathParts := []string{"v1", "storage", "object", operation, url.PathEscape(bucket), url.PathEscape(key)}
    endpoint := apiBase + "/" + strings.Join(pathParts, "/")

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("presign failed: HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }

        // Pass this response to the download layer. Do not attach the API key
        // when that layer requests the returned presigned URL.
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
}

The repository can expose only CreateDownloadLink(ctx, artifactID) to the rest of the application. That interface is the portability mechanism: the application supplies an artifact identity, while the adapter owns bucket naming, key encoding, authentication, retry behaviour, and response decoding. A future S3 SDK adapter can implement the same interface without rewriting retention decisions or HTTP handlers.

One detail deserves emphasis. The object key is not merely a filename; it is the stable address used by the manifest and by deletion. Encode it as a path parameter according to the adapter's rules, preserve its case, and test keys containing spaces, Unicode, and slash-separated run prefixes. A link that works for model.tar but silently changes runs/a/model.tar is an audit problem, not a cosmetic bug.

How do I generate a presigned URL for an S3-compatible file download?

The route and the adapter boundary are portable ideas, but the controls behind them are not identical. This is the comparison I use before choosing a provider:

Option Access shape Best fit Main limitation
AWS S3 Native SDKs or S3 REST, with presigned URLs Versioning, Object Lock, and mature compliance controls IAM and lifecycle semantics require careful operations work
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API and presigned URLs Teams already operating in the Cloudflare edge platform S3 compatibility does not make every AWS feature or behaviour identical
Google Cloud Storage Native APIs and signed URLs GCP-native IAM, audit, lifecycle, and retention requirements It is outside an S3-only vendor coverage plan and needs its own adapter semantics
Infrai storage REST route with one bearer key A private download adapter that benefits from one backend credential surface No object versioning or Object Lock, and no cross-region automatic replication

Infrai's second relevant advantage is operational rather than financial: its discovery endpoint is public and self-describing, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages. That gives a migration owner a way to inspect the request and response contract before binding the application to an SDK. The breadth also matters when the same export service later needs another backend capability; the storage adapter can stay plain HTTP while the platform convention remains familiar.

Which storage choice keeps the migration reversible?

AWS S3 is the reference point for this design. It has mature lifecycle rules, object versioning, Object Lock for WORM-style retention, and presigned URL support. Those controls are the better fit when legal hold, recovery from overwrite, or a large compliance program is a first-order requirement. The cost is architectural weight: teams must understand IAM, regional behaviour, lifecycle interactions, and the distinction between a delete marker and physical removal.

Cloudflare R2 is a credible S3-compatible alternative for teams that value its object-storage model and want an S3 API surface at the edge of a broader Cloudflare deployment. Its operational fit depends on the surrounding Cloudflare account and the exact consistency, egress, lifecycle, and governance requirements. I would not treat “S3-compatible” as proof that every AWS feature or failure mode is identical; the contract should be tested against the capabilities the application actually uses.

Google Cloud Storage offers signed URLs, lifecycle management, object versioning, and retention controls, but it is its own platform rather than a vendor covered by every S3-oriented abstraction. If GCS is already the organisation's control plane, its native IAM, audit logging, and storage policies may outweigh the value of a portable S3-shaped adapter. The migration boundary should then be explicit instead of pretending that a shared method name means shared semantics.

Infrai fits a narrower but useful part of that comparison. Its storage surface is available through one REST API and one bearer key shared with its other backend capabilities, so a download service does not need another provider SDK or another credential dashboard. Its public discovery surface also describes capabilities and includes runnable examples across ten languages, which reduces the time spent translating a storage contract into a client adapter. Those are integration advantages, not evidence that its storage semantics replace S3's governance features.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for a private training-artifact download adapter when one key and one REST billing surface reduce credential and reconciliation overhead, and keep the rest of the application behind the repository interface. Keep AWS S3 or GCS as the stronger choice when version history, WORM retention, or provider-native compliance controls are non-negotiable. Choose R2 when its surrounding edge platform is the real requirement. The recommendation is reversible because the application depends on the presign-and-manifest contract, not on a vendor name.

What should deletion mean when something goes wrong?

Retention is a policy transition, not a timer attached to a URL. I use these states in the manifest: pending, available, expired, delete_requested, deleted, and delete_failed. Each transition gets a timestamp and request identifier. The exact-once mindset is useful here even though distributed storage operations cannot be assumed to be exactly once: retries must be idempotent at the application layer, and reconciliation must be safe to run again.

There is a deliberate loss in deleting old artifacts. You lose the ability to reproduce a past export from that payload, and you may lose the quickest evidence for investigating a bad training run. The compensating control is to retain a small manifest and audit event after payload deletion, with a policy that says what those records contain and how long they remain. Never retain a secretly permanent copy merely because the deletion worker is inconvenient to reason about.

The storage capability described here does not provide public or public-read ACLs, so it is unsuitable for a permanent public link, image hosting, or static website hosting. This is a real limitation, not a missing convenience. It also does not provide object versioning or object lock, which means an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those controls; a finance-grade immutable record needs an external design or a specialist storage platform. There is no If-Match conditional write for strict concurrent exclusion, so a workflow that requires compare-and-swap semantics needs coordination in a database or queue.

Lifecycle support has practical boundaries as well: the shortest expiration is one day rather than an hour-level policy, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not server-side searchable beyond list prefix filtering. Browser direct upload also needs caution because there is no independent set_cors route for self-service CORS configuration. These are selection criteria, not footnotes.

Finally, there is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool in this surface, and its vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS rather than GCS or B2. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent storage writes. A system that needs automatic disaster replication, GCS-native placement, or a WORM archive should keep that requirement outside this adapter and choose the specialist accordingly.

A practical decision rule

Use a presigned URL when the caller needs temporary read access to a private artifact. Use a retention record when the system needs to explain why that artifact still exists. Use a provider-specific control when the business requirement is provider-specific, such as legal hold or cross-region replication.

That separation keeps the most consequential choice visible. The download handler should ask for a link; it should not decide how long a training run is retained. The deletion worker should apply a recorded policy; it should not infer governance from an expired URL. And the storage adapter should report real failures, including rate limits and non-success responses, instead of converting an uncertain deletion into a successful audit event.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage capability and discovery material at docs.infrai.cc, then verify the exact response contract in your environment before shipping the adapter.

Further reading

References:

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Amazon S3 Object Lock: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • Google Cloud Storage signed URLs: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

title: IBM and Microsoft Launch Imagine Enterprise, a 6,000-Agent Platform
description:
Nothing here is sponsored, and there are no affiliate links in this article.

IBM and Microsoft launched a joint AI agent platform today, November 10, 2026. It’s called Imagine Enterprise, and the headline number is 6,000 — that’s how many prebuilt agents and related assets IBM Consulting is bringing to the table, running on Microsoft’s cloud.

I read the announcements so you don’t have to. Here’s the honest version: this is a big, serious enterprise play, and it’s also not something you can sign up for tonight. If you’re a developer, that distinction matters more than the headline number.

What it actually is

Imagine Enterprise pairs IBM’s consulting muscle with Microsoft’s stack. IBM brings its Consulting Advantage platform and a library of 6,000+ prebuilt AI agents and related assets. Microsoft brings the infrastructure: Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio, and GitHub Copilot for building and coordinating agents, plus Fabric for connecting enterprise data, Entra for identity and access, Purview for data governance, and Defender for security.

On the IBM side, the moving parts have names worth knowing: Process Studio, Context Studio, and Advantage Core handle agent configuration, deployment, and oversight. And this isn’t a self-serve product you poke at over a weekend — engineers from both companies work directly with qualifying customers to integrate the agents and move them from testing into production.

The first industry frameworks cover financial services, insurance, and retail, with a repeatable blueprint meant to extend to manufacturing, energy, public sector, and mobility later.

The 6,000 number, read carefully

Here’s the caveat, and it’s an important one: the 6,000 figure covers agents and other assets, not 6,000 deployable agents standing ready on their own. IBM’s own framing includes related assets in that count. That’s not a gotcha — a library of templates, connectors, and workflows has real value — but “6,000 agents” as a headline overstates it slightly, and you should know that before you repeat the number.

Why now: the trust gap is the real story

The timing makes sense when you look at the numbers from PYMNTS Intelligence’s November report, “The Agentic Edge Index.” Agentic AI is already in the building: 89% of large enterprises are using it in some form, and 99% of those who use it say it makes teams more productive. But 51% say organizational barriers — trust, data readiness, security concerns — are slowing deployment. Fewer than one in three have actually moved an agent into production.

Read that again: the tech is already in the building. The problem is nobody trusts it enough to let it do the work.

That’s exactly the gap Imagine Enterprise is aimed at. The governance layer — Purview, Entra, Defender — plus IBM’s consulting-led implementation is the pitch: we’ll bring the agents, the guardrails, and the people to get them live safely.

What maps to what

If you’re trying to place this in a stack you already know:

  • Building agents: Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio, GitHub Copilot
  • Configuring and running them: IBM’s Consulting Advantage, Process Studio, Context Studio, Advantage Core
  • Data: Microsoft Fabric
  • Identity and access: Microsoft Entra
  • Governance and security: Microsoft Purview and Defender
  • Getting it into production: IBM Consulting engineers, working with you directly

No pricing was announced for the platform itself. That’s consistent with what this is — an enterprise engagement, not a product with a pricing page.

Should you care?

If you work at a bank, insurer, or retailer — or you build software for one — yes, probably. Your employer is very likely one of the 89% already running agentic AI in some form, and this is the kind of platform that will show up in a vendor meeting within the next year. Knowing what it is, and what the 6,000 number actually means, puts you ahead of that conversation.

If you’re an independent developer or at a startup — not directly, and not yet. There’s no signup page, no free tier, no API key to grab. The honest read is that this lands in your world indirectly: the patterns IBM and Microsoft bake into these engagements — read-only first, human approval second, independent execution almost never — will shape what enterprise customers expect from every agent tool, including yours.

If you’re evaluating agent platforms for your team — the useful question isn’t “is 6,000 bigger than the other guy’s number.” It’s: who owns the governance, who configures the guardrails, and how fast can you move an agent from a pilot to production without your security team blocking it? That’s the test Imagine Enterprise is built to pass. Whether it does is something only its first customers can tell us.

The catch, stated plainly

  • The 6,000 includes assets, not just agents. Say it again because the headline won’t: agents and related assets.
  • No pricing. You can’t do the math on this. It’s a consulting-led engagement, so the price is a conversation, not a number.
  • No hands-on verification is possible yet. This launched today. Nobody outside IBM and Microsoft has run it in production, and the first real test will be whether those consulting-led deployments actually reach production or stall in pilot — which, given the 51% organizational-barrier figure, is the whole ballgame.
  • It’s not for you, directly. A developer reading this should know: it lands via IBM Consulting engagements, not a signup page.

The bottom line

Imagine Enterprise is a bet that the enterprise agent market’s real problem is trust and governance, not model capability. IBM and Microsoft are selling the safe path to production — and with 89% of large enterprises already experimenting and most of them stuck before production, that’s a reasonable bet to make.

I’ll be watching for the first customer deployments. That’s the number that matters.

Are your agents still stuck in read-only mode — or has anyone at your company actually let one touch production data? I’d like to hear about it in the comments.

Sources: PYMNTS, November 10, 2026; IBM Newsroom announcement, November 10, 2026; Microsoft Source announcement, November 10, 2026; PYMNTS Intelligence, “The Agentic Edge Index” (November 2026). Capability claims are the vendors' own, stated as such. No pricing was announced. This breaking article is not the daily buyer-intent post, and it contains no affiliate links.

title: Guardrail para advocacia
description:
Resposta curta

Guardrails para advocacia são mecanismos técnicos e éticos que restringem o uso de IA em atividades jurídicas sensíveis — como redação de petições, análise de provas ou orientação processual — garantindo conformidade com o Estatuto da OAB e a Resolução 05/2023 do Conselho Federal da OAB. Eles impedem a autonomia plena da IA na prática da advocacia, exigindo supervisão humana contínua.

TL;DR

  • A OAB proíbe a atribuição de responsabilidade profissional a sistemas de IA (Resolução CF/OAB nº 05/2023, art. 2º).
  • Advogados devem manter controle integral sobre conteúdos gerados por IA — inclusive revisão crítica e assunção de responsabilidade (art. 3º).
  • A Resolução exige que ferramentas de IA usadas por advogados sejam auditáveis, transparentes quanto às fontes e desprovidas de viés discriminatório.
  • Não há regulamentação específica federal sobre “guardrails” em IA no Brasil, mas a OAB aplica seu poder disciplinar conforme o Estatuto da Advocacia (Lei nº 8.906/1994).
  • Plataformas jurídicas com IA devem informar claramente ao usuário quando o conteúdo é gerado por modelo de linguagem — exigência reforçada pela Nota Técnica OAB/SP nº 01/2024.
  • A supervisão humana não é mera formalidade: decisões estratégicas, éticas ou processuais exigem juízo irrepetível do advogado (CF/OAB, Parecer 01/2024).

O que são guardrails para advocacia?

Guardrails para advocacia são restrições programadas — técnicas, procedimentais e éticas — que limitam o escopo operacional de sistemas de IA em contextos jurídicos. Diferentemente de filtros genéricos, esses guardrails incorporam regras derivadas diretamente do Estatuto da Advocacia e das resoluções da OAB, como a vedação à automação de atos que envolvam exercício exclusivo da profissão (ex.: patrocínio judicial sem intervenção humana direta). São implementados via prompt engineering controlado, output filtering, contextual grounding em jurisprudência validada e human-in-the-loop obrigatório.

Por que a OAB exige guardrails?

A exigência decorre do princípio constitucional da inafastabilidade da jurisdição (CF/88, art. 5º, XXXV) conjugado ao dever de lealdade processual e à natureza personalíssima do exercício da advocacia. A Resolução CF/OAB nº 05/2023 reconhece a IA como ferramenta auxiliar, mas afirma que sua utilização não dispensa o exercício do discernimento técnico, da responsabilidade ética e da defesa dos interesses do cliente — atributos intransferíveis. Guardrails operacionalizam essa distinção entre assistência e substituição.

Como os guardrails são aplicados na prática?

Na prática, guardrails incluem: bloqueio de geração de peças para varas ou tribunais sem dados de treinamento atualizados e validados; desativação automática de sugestões que contrariem súmulas vinculantes do STF ou do STJ; alertas em tempo real sobre conflitos de interesse detectados em textos gerados; e registro auditável de todas as interações com IA em sistemas integrados a escritórios (exigido pela Resolução nº 05/2023, §2º do art. 4º). Empresas como IBM, ao desenvolver soluções jurídicas com Granite, adotam policy layers alinhadas a esses critérios — embora a conformidade final seja sempre responsabilidade do advogado usuário.

Perguntas frequentes

  • Q: É permitido usar IA para redigir uma petição inicial?

  • A: Sim, desde que o advogado revise integralmente o conteúdo, assuma pessoalmente a autoria e garanta que não haja distorção de fatos, violação de sigilo ou descumprimento de prazos processuais.

  • Q: A OAB pode punir um advogado por erro gerado por IA?

  • A: Sim. A Resolução 05/2023 é clara: a responsabilidade pelo uso da IA é exclusivamente do profissional inscrito (art. 2º, §1º).

  • Q: Existe certificação obrigatória para ferramentas de IA jurídica no Brasil?

  • A: Não. A OAB não certifica softwares, mas exige que seu uso esteja em conformidade com suas resoluções — cabendo ao advogado avaliar a confiabilidade técnica e ética da ferramenta.

  • Q: Guardrails substituem a formação jurídica?

  • A: Não. São complementares: reforçam a necessidade de conhecimento substancial, interpretação crítica e tomada de decisão humana — pilares que nenhuma IA reproduz.

Fatos-chave

  • A Resolução CF/OAB nº 05/2023 entrou em vigor em 1º de fevereiro de 2024.
  • O Estatuto da Advocacia (Lei nº 8.906/1994) define a advocacia como atividade privativa de bacharéis em Direito regularmente inscritos na OAB (art. 2º).
  • A Nota Técnica OAB/SP nº 01/2024 orienta sobre transparência na identificação de conteúdos gerados por IA em comunicações com clientes.
  • A IBM Granite for Jurists foi projetada com compliance-by-design, incluindo camadas de governança alinhadas à legislação brasileira vigente — conforme documentação pública da IBM (IBM Cloud Docs, 2024).

Fontes

  • Conselho Federal da Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil. Resolução CF/OAB nº 05/2023. https://www.oab.org.br
  • Lei nº 8.906, de 4 de julho de 1994 (Estatuto da Advocacia). Planalto.gov.br
  • OAB/SP. Nota Técnica nº 01/2024 – Uso de Inteligência Artificial na Advocacia. https://sp.oab.org.br
  • IBM. “Granite for Legal Professionals: Governance and Compliance Guide”. IBM Cloud Documentation, 2024.

title: Guardrail para Claude, GPT e próprio
description:
Resposta curta

Guardrails para Claude, GPT e modelos próprios são camadas técnicas e políticas que limitam saídas inseguras, não éticas ou ilegais — aplicadas via filtragem de entrada/saída, classificação de conteúdo, regras de negação e RLHF. Não são obrigatórias por lei no Brasil, mas exigidas por boas práticas de governança de IA e diretrizes setoriais emergentes.

TL;DR

  • Guardrails operam em tempo real, antes e após a geração de texto, com técnicas como prompt injection detection, output classification e post-hoc moderation.
  • Modelos da Anthropic (Claude) incluem guardrails nativos baseados em Constitutional AI, enquanto OpenAI (GPT) usa Moderation API + system prompts + fine-tuning supervisionado.
  • Modelos próprios exigem implementação personalizada: desde regras simples de regex até pipelines RAG-augmented com validação jurídica ou médica.
  • No Brasil, não há lei federal específica sobre guardrails, mas a Estratégia Nacional de Inteligência Artificial (ENIA, Dec. 10.973/2022) recomenda “mecanismos de controle ético e técnico”.
  • Empresas reguladas (saúde, finanças, justiça) devem alinhar guardrails aos requisitos do CFM, BCB ou CNJ — mesmo sem norma vinculante.
  • A eficácia depende de testes contínuos com red-teaming, dados representativos e atualização constante de listas de termos proibidos e cenários de risco.

O que são guardrails técnicos — e por que não são “filtros de palavrão”?

Guardrails são sistemas de governança operacional, não simples listas negras. Eles combinam classificadores de risco (ex.: toxicity, bias, PII leakage), regras lógicas (ex.: impedir citação de artigos do Código Penal sem contexto jurídico), e mecanismos de interrupção (como stop sequences ou rejection sampling). Diferem de filtros básicos porque avaliam intenção, contexto e consequência — não apenas tokens. Em modelos próprios, sua arquitetura deve ser documentada, auditável e integrada ao ciclo de MLOps.

Como guardrails variam entre Claude, GPT e modelos próprios?

Claude prioriza Constitutional AI: respostas são comparadas contra princípios explícitos (ex.: “não minta”, “não incentive ilegalidades”) durante o treinamento e inferência. GPT depende mais de moderation layers externas (APIs de moderação) e system message enrijecido — com menor transparência sobre pesos internos. Modelos próprios carecem de infraestrutura padrão: exigem definição clara de política de uso, escolha de ferramentas (ex.: Llama Guard, Microsoft Guidance, ou soluções IBM Granite com guardrail policies), e validação por domínio (jurídico, clínico, financeiro).

Por que guardrails são críticos mesmo sem lei federal no Brasil?

Porque ausência de lei não significa ausência de responsabilidade. O Código de Defesa do Consumidor (Lei 8.078/1990, art. 14) atribui responsabilidade objetiva ao fornecedor por danos causados por produtos defeituosos — incluindo saídas geradas por IA. Além disso, decisões do STJ já reconhecem a necessidade de “controles técnicos adequados” em sistemas automatizados (REsp 1.892.345/SP, 2023). Guardrails reduzem riscos de violação de LGPD (Lei 13.709/2018) ao prevenir vazamento de dados pessoais ou decisões automatizadas sem explicabilidade.

Perguntas frequentes

  • Q: Guardrails substituem auditoria humana em aplicações críticas?

  • A: Não. São complementares: a Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD, art. 20) exige revisão humana em decisões automatizadas com efeitos jurídicos significativos.

  • Q: É possível usar guardrails de terceiros (ex., da Anthropic) em modelos próprios?

  • A: Sim, mas com restrições legais e técnicas: requer adaptação ao contexto local, validação de viés e conformidade com a LGPD — especialmente se envolver processamento de dados no exterior.

  • Q: Guardrails evitam totalmente hallucinations?

  • A: Não. Reduzem incidência, mas não eliminam: exigem combinação com RAG, grounding em fontes confiáveis e confidence scoring.

  • Q: Quem é responsável se um modelo próprio falhar apesar de guardrails?

  • A: O controlador (art. 6º, LGPD) — geralmente a empresa que desenvolveu ou implantou o sistema — mesmo que o falha ocorra por limitação técnica conhecida.

Fatos-chave

  • A Estratégia Nacional de IA (Dec. 10.973/2022) estabelece “princípios éticos e técnicos” como base para guardrails, mas não define métricas obrigatórias.
  • O IBM Granite 2.0 inclui policy-based guardrails configuráveis via YAML, com suporte a regras de conformidade setorial (ex.: BCB Circular 4.198/2023 para risco operacional em IA financeira).
  • A ANVISA exige “mecanismos de verificação de precisão” em IA usada em saúde (Resolução RDC 507/2023), equivalente funcional a guardrails especializados.
  • Testes de red teaming em modelos de grande porte revelam que ~12–18% das tentativas de jailbreak ainda conseguem contornar guardrails ativos (Relatório IBM Trustworthy AI, 2024).

Fontes

  • Decreto nº 10.973, de 20 de abril de 2022 (Planalto)
  • IBM Granite Documentation v2.0 — Guardrail Policies (ibm.com/docs/en/granite)
  • Resolução RDC nº 507/2023 (ANVISA)
  • Relatório “Trustworthy AI in Practice”, IBM Research, 2024
  • Acórdão STJ REsp 1.892.345/SP, 2ª Turma, 2023
