title: Why Cursor's agent waits for input without telling you, and the fix
description:
Originally published at taskhold.com.

Short answer: Cursor plays its Completion Sound and shows a system notification when an agent needs approval or finishes, but stays quiet while you're viewing that agent's chat. Turn both on under Settings > General > Notifications. The CLI has its own notifications setting, and hooks fire only when a run stops. For questions about the work, have the agent post them to a shared board such as Taskhold's live board.

You hand Cursor's agent a long task, switch to your browser, and come back to find it stopped on an approval card a few minutes in. Or it finished and nothing told you. This guide covers when Cursor alerts you and when it stays quiet, the settings and hook that close the gaps in the editor and the CLI, and how to get the agent's questions onto your phone.

For the same problem in other agents, see Claude Code waiting for input and Codex CLI waiting for approval. To try answering a blocked agent from a browser, open the live board demo.

Why there was no alert

The Cursor editor has two settings for this, Completion Sound and System Notifications, under Cursor Settings > General > Notifications. Cursor's docs have no page for them; what follows is how Cursor staff described them on the Cursor forum in June and September 2026:

  • Completion Sound plays when an agent finishes its turn and when an approval needs your attention, for local agents and their subagents. Approvals and finished turns share one toggle and one sound.
  • The sound plays only when Cursor is in the background or you're viewing a different agent. While you're looking at the chat that shows the approval card, it stays quiet. Staff called this working as designed.
  • Some forum users report the sound not playing even with Cursor in the background. Staff asked them for the Cursor version and whether it was a local agent, a subagent or a cloud agent, so include those if you report it.

Hooks don't fill the gap on their own. Cursor's hooks reference lists no event that fires while the agent waits for approval or for an answer; the stop event fires only when the agent loop ends.

Stuck on "Waiting for subagent"

A parent agent that says "Waiting for subagent" next to a subagent marked "Stopped" is a different problem from a missed approval, and a known one. Cursor staff said on the forum in August and September 2026 that the Stopped label is in most cases a display issue, with the subagent still running behind it, and that they were tracking it without a timeline. Reports cover versions up to at least 3.19. What staff and users suggest:

  • Give it time first. Staff warn that interrupting can spawn a duplicate subagent and burn extra tokens. A "Loading Chat" tab is expected while the run is going, so watch the parent card instead.
  • If you're sure it has hung, send "Continue" to the parent agent or run Developer: Reload Window from the command palette. Staff confirmed both clear it.
  • Check for a subagentStart hook. One user saw the Stopped label only with that hook registered and lost it after removing the hook; staff haven't confirmed the link.
  • Check whether work is still happening: a growing git diff means the subagent is alive, whatever the card says.

Cards that stay on "Starting up" after the work finished are a related report, and Stop All may not clear them. Start a new chat if one gets in your way.

Fix 1: turn on the sound and system notifications

  1. Open Cursor Settings > General > Notifications and turn on Completion Sound and System Notifications.
  2. On macOS, check System Settings > Notifications > Cursor and allow notifications, and make sure a Focus mode isn't holding them.
  3. If you work with the agent's chat open on screen, expect silence for approvals in that chat. Glance at it, or move to another agent's chat while you wait.

Fix 2: Cursor CLI notifications

The Cursor CLI (agent) has its own setting. Since April 2026 it sends a desktop notification when a turn finishes or the agent is blocked on you (an approval, a question, sudo) in iTerm2, Ghostty, Warp, Kitty and Terminal.app. It passes through tmux and screen, mutes itself while you're focused on it, and approval notifications include the pending command. Turn it on in /config, or in ~/.cursor/cli-config.json:

{
  "version": 1,
  "notifications": true
}

Merge the key into your existing cli-config.json. Only permissions can be set per project; this one is global.

Fix 3: a hook for when a run ends

A stop hook runs when the agent loop ends and receives a status of completed, aborted or error. That covers a run that finished or died while you were away, though not a run paused on an approval. Save this as ~/.cursor/hooks/notify-stop.sh and make it executable with chmod +x:

#!/bin/bash
status=$(jq -r '.status')
osascript -e 'on run argv' -e 'display notification ("Agent run ended: " & item 1 of argv) with title "Cursor"' -e 'end run' "$status"
# For your phone instead: curl -s -d "Cursor agent: $status" https://ntfy.sh/<your-topic>
echo '{}'

Needs jq. On Linux, replace the osascript line with notify-send 'Cursor' "Agent run ended: $status".

Register it in ~/.cursor/hooks.json. User hooks run from ~/.cursor/, so the path is relative to it:

{
  "version": 1,
  "hooks": {
    "stop": [
      { "command": "./hooks/notify-stop.sh", "timeout": 10 }
    ]
  }
}

Cursor reloads hooks.json on save. The Hooks tab in Customize and the Hooks output channel show whether it ran and any errors.

The CLI runs stop hooks too. To have the same hook put the result on a shared task instead, see Cursor hooks with Taskhold.

Fix 4: fewer approvals to wait on

Settings > Agents > Approvals & Execution sets the run mode. Allowlist runs only the actions you've allowed without asking. Auto-review runs allowlisted calls, sends other shell commands to a sandbox where possible and passes the rest to a classifier, so you're asked only about calls it blocks and the agent still wants to make. Run Everything never asks, and Cursor describes it as accepting the risk. Fewer prompts means fewer waits, at the cost of less review.

Cloud agents and your phone

Cursor for iOS (iPhone and iPad on iOS 26 or later, on paid plans) starts and follows Cursor's cloud agents. Per Cursor's release notes for the week of August 31, 2026, cloud agents push a notification to your phone or browser when an agent asks a question or needs your approval, and no longer for each finished turn. With My Machines, a cloud agent's tool calls run on your own computer while the agent loop stays in Cursor's cloud. Android is planned.

Where Taskhold fits

Taskhold handles the other kind of stop: a question about the work, from Cursor or any other agent. With the workflow rule in .cursor/rules, the agent calls taskhold_block with one specific question instead of waiting in the chat. When the answer is a choice, it passes two to four options, marks the one it recommends and says what it will do if nobody answers.

  • The question appears as a card under Needs you on the live board and on the Needs you page (/dashboard/needs-you), laid out for a phone. Tap an option or type a reply.
  • Phone alerts can send the question to you by web push, ntfy or email. They're opening to accounts in stages.
  • The agent reads your answer with taskhold_updates, and can take the next task while it waits. 
If you need a decision from me, call taskhold_block on the task with one
specific question. When it's a choice, pass 2 to 4 options, the one you
recommend, and what you'll do if I don't answer. Then take the next todo
and check taskhold_updates between steps for my reply.

Add to .cursor/rules next to the Taskhold workflow rule from the Cursor setup page.

  • Approval cards still need an answer in Cursor. Taskhold carries questions about the work, not tool approvals.
  • Taskhold doesn't wake an agent that has stopped. The agent reads your reply the next time it calls taskhold_updates.
  • Setup is on the Cursor page, and the whole loop is in answering a blocked coding agent. If the taskhold tools never appear, see Cursor MCP server not connecting.

FAQ

Why doesn't Cursor play a sound when the agent asks for approval?

Cursor mutes the approval sound while you're viewing the chat that shows the approval card. The sound plays when Cursor is in the background or you're in another agent's chat, and only with Completion Sound turned on.

Is there a Cursor hook for when the agent needs input?

Not in Cursor's hooks reference as of October 31, 2026. The stop hook fires when the agent loop ends, with a status of completed, aborted or error, so it can alert you about finished or failed runs but not about a pending approval.

How do I get Cursor CLI notifications?

Turn on notifications in /config, or set "notifications": true in ~/.cursor/cli-config.json. The CLI then notifies you when a turn finishes or the agent is blocked on an approval, a question or sudo, in iTerm2, Ghostty, Warp, Kitty and Terminal.app.

Sources

  • Cursor docs: hooks (events, hooks.json, stop), checked 2026-10-31
  • Cursor docs: CLI configuration (notifications), checked 2026-10-31
  • Cursor docs: CLI changelog (desktop notifications, April 2026), checked 2026-10-31
  • Cursor docs: run modes, checked 2026-10-31
  • Cursor docs: Cursor for iOS, checked 2026-10-31
  • Cursor docs: release notes (cloud agent push notifications), checked 2026-10-31
  • Cursor forum: Cursor staff on the approval sound and focus (September 2026), checked 2026-10-31
  • Cursor forum: Cursor staff on muting while focused (June 2026), checked 2026-10-31

Related

  • Cursor task list over MCP: watch every task live
  • Cursor hook: show on the board when agent stops
  • Answer a blocked coding agent from your phone
  • Cursor MCP server not showing tools: the fix
  • Claude Code waits for input silently: the fix
  • Codex awaiting approval with no alert: the fix

About Taskhold

Taskhold is a hosted task list shared by a person and their AI coding agents over MCP. Agents break tasks into steps and report progress, and the person watches a live board. $12/month or $120/year per person, 7-day trial with a card, no free plan. Made by Great Work LLC.

To try it, add the MCP server https://taskhold.com/api/mcp to your agent. It connects with no sign-up, and the first time the agent uses Taskhold it gives you a link to start the trial.

  • Pricing: https://taskhold.com/#pricing

title: Designing Connected Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Systems with RFID, BLE, IoT and AI
description:
Building connected systems for pharmaceutical manufacturing presents an interesting engineering challenge.

Unlike many conventional industrial environments, pharmaceutical facilities must consider operational visibility alongside data integrity, traceability, controlled access and regulatory expectations.

A connected manufacturing architecture may need to collect information from RFID readers, BLE gateways, environmental sensors, production equipment and enterprise applications.

The challenge is not simply collecting this information. It is creating reliable data flows that support operational decision-making.

Let's examine the major components.

  1. Device and Identification Layer

The first layer consists of devices that identify assets, materials and personnel or collect environmental information.

Typical components include:

RFID tags and readers.

BLE beacons and receivers.

Temperature sensors.

Humidity sensors.

Differential pressure sensors.

Industrial gateways.

Equipment monitoring devices.

Each technology has different characteristics.

RFID is useful for automated identification and inventory workflows.

BLE can support location intelligence for compatible devices.

Environmental sensors provide readings from controlled environments.

Selecting the appropriate technology requires considering range, accuracy, interference, installation conditions and maintenance requirements.

  1. Edge Computing Layer

Industrial environments cannot always depend on every device communicating directly with centralized cloud infrastructure.

Edge gateways provide an intermediate processing layer.

They can help with:

Device connectivity.

Protocol conversion.

Local data collection.

Event buffering.

Data synchronization.

Preliminary data validation.

This architecture can improve resilience and support environments where network connectivity is intermittent.

Edge infrastructure should also include appropriate authentication, encryption, access restrictions and device management.

  1. Data Integration Architecture

A pharmaceutical facility may already use MES, ERP, LIMS and QMS platforms.

Adding RFID, BLE and IoT devices creates additional data sources.

The integration layer must determine how information moves between these systems.

A simplified architecture might look like this:

Physical devices → Edge gateways → Integration middleware → Operational databases → Analytics and enterprise applications

For example, an RFID reader may capture a material identification event.

The edge gateway receives the event and forwards it through an integration service.

The integration layer associates the identification with relevant inventory information.

The resulting event can then be made available to authorized applications.

This approach helps avoid treating each device as an isolated information source.

  1. Building Useful Event Data

Raw device readings are not always meaningful on their own.

Consider an RFID event:

Tag identifier.

Reader identifier.

Timestamp.

Location.

Event type.

Additional contextual information may be required before the event becomes operationally useful.

A material movement event, for instance, needs to be associated with the correct inventory record and relevant business process.

Similarly, BLE location information requires appropriate location mapping and accuracy considerations.

Good data architecture should define consistent identifiers, timestamps, event formats and validation rules.

  1. Applying AI Analytics

Once operational information is collected and structured, analytics can help identify patterns.

Potential applications include:

Equipment utilization analysis.

Production bottleneck identification.

Inventory trend analysis.

Unusual movement detection.

Workforce distribution analysis.

Environmental trend monitoring.

AI models should be evaluated using relevant operational data and clearly defined performance measures.

In regulated environments, model outputs should not automatically replace established quality decisions or validated process controls.

Human review and appropriate change management remain important.

  1. Security and Data Integrity

Security should be incorporated throughout the architecture.

Important considerations include:

Device authentication.

Role-based access control.

Encrypted communication.

Audit logging.

Data retention policies.

Backup and recovery.

Network segmentation.

Software change control.

Data integrity verification.

Pharmaceutical organizations should also determine which systems are subject to applicable validation requirements.

  1. Measuring Deployment Performance

A connected manufacturing project should have measurable objectives.

Possible indicators include:

Area

Example measurement

Inventory

Inventory record accuracy

Assets

Average equipment search time

Production

Work-in-progress visibility

Workforce

Area occupancy visibility

Environment

Alert response time

Integration

Data synchronization reliability

These measurements help determine whether the architecture is delivering operational value.

Conclusion

Connected pharmaceutical manufacturing requires a carefully designed combination of device infrastructure, edge computing, enterprise integration and intelligent analytics.

RFID, BLE and environmental sensors provide valuable operational information, but their usefulness depends on reliable data architecture and integration with established manufacturing workflows.

For an example of a pharmaceutical-focused AIoT approach, explore PharmaFlux AI's manufacturing intelligence platform.

The key engineering principle is simple: build connected systems around operational requirements, data integrity and reliable integration rather than deploying technology without a clearly defined purpose.

title: Day 25/75: Maximum Subarray Sum With Kadane's Algorithm - Java DSA
description:
Day 25/75: Maximum Subarray Sum With Kadane's Algorithm

75 Day DSA in Java Challenge

I had an int[] of one company's daily profit and loss, one value per trading day, plenty of them negative. The report needed the best contiguous stretch: the run of consecutive days whose profit summed to the largest total. This is LeetCode 53, Maximum Subarray, dressed up in a real task.

The brute force that timed out

My first solution tried every window. Pick a start, walk every end, sum the days between, keep the largest total.

static int maxSumBrute(int[] a) {
    int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    for (int start = 0; start < a.length; start++) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int end = start; end < a.length; end++) {
            sum += a[end];
            best = Math.max(best, sum);
        }
    }
    return best;  // O(n^2): every window summed from scratch
}

Correct, and instant on a single year of ~250 days. Then the same report ran across a 4,000-symbol universe on every refresh. The nested loops are O(n^2) per array, and across thousands of arrays the refresh timed out.

Where the time actually went

The inner loop is the problem. With start fixed at 0, I sum the window [0..end] for every end. Then start moves to 1 and I recompute nearly the same sums again. Consecutive starts overlap massively, and I reused none of that work. Every window was summed from scratch.

So the real question is not "check all windows faster." It is: what single value can I carry forward so I never re-sum a range? That value is the best-sum window ending at the current day.

Kadane: one running value, one decision per day

Walk left to right holding maxEndingHere, the largest sum of any window ending exactly at the current index. Each day there is one choice: extend yesterday's window by adding today's value, or start a fresh window at today. Keep whichever is larger.

static int kadane(int[] a) {
    int maxEndingHere = a[0];
    int maxSoFar = a[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
        maxEndingHere = Math.max(a[i], maxEndingHere + a[i]);
        maxSoFar = Math.max(maxSoFar, maxEndingHere);
    }
    return maxSoFar;  // O(n), one pass
}

A second variable, maxSoFar, records the best window seen anywhere, because the optimal window ends on some day and maxEndingHere is the best window ending on each one.

Why "reset when negative" is the same rule

If the window ending yesterday summed to something negative, carrying it into today only lowers today's value -- a positive plus a negative is smaller than the positive alone. So the instant maxEndingHere + a[i] loses to a[i] on its own, the past is a liability and you drop it. A negative running prefix never helps anything downstream. That is exactly the "reset the running total when it goes negative" phrasing you will see elsewhere, just expressed as a Math.max.

The base case that bit me

My first attempt seeded both variables at 0 and looped from index 0. It passed everything until an all-negative array such as {-8, -3, -6, -2}, where the correct answer is -2 (the least-bad single day) because the window must be non-empty. A zero seed reports 0, an empty window, which is wrong here. Seed both with the first element and loop from index 1:

  • int best = a[0]; int endingHere = a[0];
  • for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++)

If your variant is allowed to return 0 for an empty window, that is a different problem with a different base case. The two are easy to confuse because most random inputs contain a positive number that never exposes the bug.

Recovering the actual window, not just the sum

The brute force gave me the bounds for free; Kadane needs a little bookkeeping. Track a tentative start that jumps to the current index on every reset, plus bestStart/bestEnd that you snapshot whenever maxEndingHere beats maxSoFar.

static int[] maxSubarrayWithBounds(int[] a) {
    int maxEndingHere = a[0], maxSoFar = a[0];
    int start = 0, bestStart = 0, bestEnd = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (a[i] > maxEndingHere + a[i]) {
            maxEndingHere = a[i];
            start = i;                 // reset the window's left edge
        } else {
            maxEndingHere = maxEndingHere + a[i];
        }
        if (maxEndingHere > maxSoFar) {
            maxSoFar = maxEndingHere;
            bestStart = start;
            bestEnd = i;
        }
    }
    return new int[]{maxSoFar, bestStart, bestEnd};
}

Same single pass, same O(n), three extra integers. For the report I needed the dates, so this is the version that shipped.

Takeaway

The brute force was not buggy -- it answered "best contiguous-sum window" perfectly. It just could not do it cheaply, because it treated every window as unrelated to the one before it. Kadane's insight is that the best window ending today is one comparison from the best window ending yesterday: extend it, or reset it the moment the running sum turns negative. Seed on the first element so the empty window cannot sneak in, and O(n^2) collapses to a single O(n) sweep.

title: Tkinter TclError: Image Doesn’t Exist (Fix)
description:
Say you add a picture to a Tkinter window and run the program. Python stops with this:

  File "bug.py", line 9, in <module>
    tk.Label(second, image=logo).pack()
_tkinter.TclError: image "pyimage1" doesn't exist

The message is confusing. You never typed the name pyimage1. Tkinter picked it when it created your PhotoImage. Below are the three causes of this exact error, plus one related error, each with a fix. I reproduced and tested every example with Python 3.14.

What the Error Means

When you create a PhotoImage, Tkinter hands it to Tk and names it something like pyimage1. The error means you asked Tk for an image with that name, and Tk doesn't have one. Either the image belongs to a different window, or it got deleted. Ask yourself three questions:

  1. Am I making more than one tk.Tk() window? That's Cause 1. 2. Am I destroying the main window and then opening a new one? That's Cause 2. 3. Is my PhotoImage sitting in a local variable inside a function? That's Cause 3.

Cause 1: More Than One tk.Tk() 

import tkinter as tk

first = tk.Tk()
second = tk.Tk()                         # a second root window
logo = tk.PhotoImage(file="icon.png")    # created for the first root

tk.Label(second, image=logo).pack()      # used in the second root: TclError
second.mainloop()

Each tk.Tk() starts its own Tk interpreter, and an image belongs to just one of them. If you don't say which window an image is for, it goes to the first one you made. Here logo belongs to first. The label lives in second, and second can't see it.

Use exactly one tk.Tk() in your whole program. Every other window should be a tk.Toplevel. It runs inside the main window’s interpreter, so images are shared:

import tkinter as tk

root = tk.Tk()
second = tk.Toplevel(root)               # an extra window that shares the same interpreter
logo = tk.PhotoImage(file="icon.png")

tk.Label(second, image=logo).pack()
root.mainloop()

Cause 2: The Image Belonged to a Window That Was Destroyed 

import tkinter as tk

root = tk.Tk()
logo = tk.PhotoImage(file="icon.png")    # created for the first root
root.destroy()

root2 = tk.Tk()                          # a new root
tk.Label(root2, image=logo).pack()       # the old image no longer exists: TclError
root2.mainloop()

The image was made for the first root window. Destroy that window and its images go with it. The new root can't use the old image, even though the Python variable logo is still there. You'll see this in programs that close a login window and then open the main window as a second tk.Tk().

Cause 1’s fix works best here too. Keep a single root, and hide or swap its contents. Stuck with a second root? Make the image after that root exists, and pass master so Tk knows who owns it:

import tkinter as tk

root = tk.Tk()
root.destroy()

root2 = tk.Tk()
logo = tk.PhotoImage(file="icon.png", master=root2)
tk.Label(root2, image=logo).pack()
root2.mainloop()

Cause 3: Nothing Kept the Image Alive 

import tkinter as tk

root = tk.Tk()


def show():
    logo = tk.PhotoImage(file="icon.png")
    label = tk.Label(root, image=logo)
    label.pack()
    return label


label = show()
root.update()
print("images Tk still has:", root.tk.call("image", "names"))     # no pyimage1 in this list
label.configure(image=label.cget("image"))                       # uses the deleted image: TclError
root.mainloop()

logo is a local variable. When show() returns, Python throws the PhotoImage away and Tk deletes the image. The label still points at the name pyimage1, so using it again fails. Does your picture just not show up, with no error? Check this first.

I printed the images Tk still had at that point. Yours is gone. Only Tk’s four built-in icons are left:

images Tk still has: ('::tk::icons::information', '::tk::icons::error', '::tk::icons::warning', '::tk::icons::question')

Give the image something to hang onto. Store it on the widget itself, and it lives as long as the widget does:

import tkinter as tk

root = tk.Tk()


def show():
    logo = tk.PhotoImage(file="icon.png")
    label = tk.Label(root, image=logo)
    label.image = logo                   # the reference that keeps the image alive
    label.pack()
    return label


label = show()
root.update()
print("images Tk still has:", root.tk.call("image", "names"))     # pyimage1 is in this list
label.configure(image=label.cget("image"))
root.mainloop()

Now the reference holds it. pyimage1 stays in the list and nothing breaks:

images Tk still has: ('pyimage1', '::tk::icons::information', '::tk::icons::error', '::tk::icons::warning', '::tk::icons::question')

A Debugging Trick: Ask Tk Which Images Exist

Don't guess. Ask Tk. This one line prints every image the interpreter holds right now, so you can see whether yours survived:

print(root.tk.call("image", "names"))

If your pyimageN isn't in the list, the image was deleted (Cause 2 or 3). If it is in the list but the error still says it doesn't exist, the widget sits in a different window (Cause 1).

A Related Error: Too Early to Create Image 

import tkinter as tk

logo = tk.PhotoImage(file="icon.png")    # RuntimeError: no default root window yet

window = tk.Tk()
tk.Label(window, image=logo).pack()
window.mainloop()

This one has its own message.

RuntimeError: Too early to create image: no default root window

An image needs a window to live in, and Tkinter won't make one without it. Window first, image second:

import tkinter as tk

window = tk.Tk()
logo = tk.PhotoImage(file="icon.png")
tk.Label(window, image=logo).pack()
window.mainloop()

Which Cause Is It?

What you see Cause Fix
image "pyimage1" doesn't exist, and the code has two tk.Tk() Cause 1 One tk.Tk(), extra windows as tk.Toplevel
The error appears after you close one window and open another Cause 2 Reuse one root, or create the image after the new root with master=
The image is created inside a function, or the picture just does not show Cause 3 Keep a reference: label.image = logo
Too early to create image Related Create the window before the image

The Rule, Stated Once

A PhotoImage belongs to one window’s interpreter. It lives only while Python holds a reference to it. So use a single tk.Tk(), create images after it, and keep each image in a variable that lasts as long as the widget.

Does your window freeze instead? See Why Your Tkinter App Freezes (Not Responding) and How to Fix It. If you want to learn Tkinter from a first window to full projects, start with Tkinter in Python, and if Python itself is new to you, Python for Beginners. Here's another error that looks like a missing-attribute mystery: PySerial: module ‘serial’ has no attribute ‘Serial’.

Download the code: the broken and fixed versions of all four are on GitHub, in Python-projects/Troubleshooting/tkinter-image-doesnt-exist. Open each one from inside its own folder, since it reads icon.png from wherever you run it.

title: UnboundLocalError: Variable Referenced Before Assignment
description:
Say you write a small function and run it. Python stops and prints this:

UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value

It feels wrong. You did create count, right at the top of your file. On Python 3.10 and older, the same error reads local variable 'count' referenced before assignment. Same error, same causes. I tested every example below on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.14. All three print the newer wording. I couldn't test anything older.

What the Error Means

Before a function runs, Python reads the whole body and decides which names are local. The rule is short. Assign to a name anywhere in the function, and that name is local everywhere in it, from the first line to the last. Read it before the assignment has run and there's no value yet. That's your UnboundLocalError.

Reading a Global Is Fine

Only assigning causes trouble. This function just reads count, so Python happily uses the global one:

count = 5


def show():
    return count + 1


print(show())

It prints 6. Add an assignment to count inside the function and things change. Python makes it local, and the global disappears from view. Every cause below is a version of that.

The Six Causes

1. count = count + 1 Inside a Function 

count = 0


def add():
    count = count + 1
    return count


print(add())

The line count = count + 1 assigns to count, so count is local in add(). Then the right-hand side reads that local one, which has no value yet. The best fix is to skip the global entirely. Pass the value in and return the new one.

count = 0


def add(count):
    return count + 1


count = add(count)
print(count)

There's a quick fix too. Put global count inside the function and Python knows you mean the global variable. It works. But now the function changes something outside itself, and that gets hard to follow as your program grows:

count = 0


def add():
    global count
    count = count + 1
    return count


print(add())

2. total += n 

total = 0


def add(n):
    total += n
    return total


print(add(5))

total += n is shorthand for total = total + n. So it assigns to total and makes it local. Most people hit the error this way, since += doesn't look like an assignment. Pass the running total in and return the new one:

total = 0


def add(total, n):
    return total + n


total = add(total, 5)
print(total)

3. The Variable Is Only Assigned Inside an if 

def describe(score):
    if score >= 50:
        result = "pass"
    return result


print(describe(80))
print(describe(10))

describe(80) works, so the bug is easy to miss. Try describe(10). The if is skipped, result never gets assigned, and the return blows up. Give the variable a value on every path:

def describe(score):
    if score >= 50:
        result = "pass"
    else:
        result = "fail"
    return result


print(describe(80))
print(describe(10))

4. You Use It Above the Line That Assigns It 

def show():
    print(name)
    name = "Emre"


show()

The assignment to name is on line two, so name is local from line one. The print runs first, before there's any value. Move the assignment up, or pick a different name for what you want to print.

def show():
    name = "Emre"
    print(name)


show()

5. The Variable Is Only Assigned Inside a Loop 

def last_item(items):
    for item in items:
        last = item
    return last


print(last_item([1, 2, 3]))
print(last_item([]))

Give it a list with items and last gets a value. Give it an empty list and the loop body never runs, so last stays unassigned. Set a starting value before the loop:

def last_item(items):
    last = None
    for item in items:
        last = item
    return last


print(last_item([1, 2, 3]))
print(last_item([]))

You'll see this one in real programs a lot. The empty case is the one nobody tests.

6. An Inner Function Changes an Outer Variable 

def counter():
    n = 0

    def inc():
        n += 1
        return n

    return inc


tick = counter()
print(tick())

Inside inc(), n += 1 makes n local to inc(). It isn't the n from counter(). When the variable lives in an enclosing function, you need nonlocal, not global:

def counter():
    n = 0

    def inc():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n

    return inc


tick = counter()
print(tick())
print(tick())

Things That Count as Assignment Without Looking Like It

Four more statements make a name local to the whole function, and none of them has an equals sign. Read the name above any of them and you get the same error. I tested each one. Each raised UnboundLocalError:

Statement What to do
import os inside the function, below a use of os Move the import to the top of the file
for i in range(3): below a read of i Use a different loop variable
with open(...) as f: below a read of f Use a different name for the file
except ... as err: and then err used after the block Copy what you need out of the exception first

The except case catches most people off guard. Python deletes the exception variable on purpose when the except block ends. So touching it afterwards fails:

def run():
    try:
        1 / 0
    except ZeroDivisionError as err:
        pass
    print(err)             # Python deletes err when the except block ends


run()

While you're still inside the block, copy what you need into another variable:

def run():
    message = None
    try:
        1 / 0
    except ZeroDivisionError as err:
        message = str(err)     # copy what you need before the block ends
    print(message)


run()

It prints division by zero.

Which Cause Is It?

The line that fails Cause Fix
x = x + 1 or x += 1 in a function The name becomes local Pass it in and return it, or global x
A return or print of a variable set inside an if A path never assigns it Assign on every path
A use that comes above the assignment Used before assigned Move the assignment up
A variable set only inside a for or while The loop may not run Set a starting value first
x += 1 in an inner function Local to the inner function nonlocal x

The Rule, Stated Once

Assign to a name anywhere in a function and it's local to the whole function. So give it a value before you read it. If you really mean a variable from outside, say so with global (module level) or nonlocal (enclosing function). Even better, pass values in and return them.

New to Python? Start with Python for Beginners and Python modules. For more Python errors with a clear fix, try ModuleNotFoundError After pip install, Tkinter TclError: Image Doesn’t Exist and Why Your Tkinter App Freezes.

Download the code: the broken and fixed versions of all six causes are on GitHub in Python-projects/Troubleshooting/unboundlocalerror. Run any file with python bug.py from inside its folder.

title: Day 25/75: Product of Array Except Self - No Division, Two Sweeps - Python DSA
description:
Day 25/75: Product of Array Except Self

75 Day DSA in Python Challenge

I shipped a revenue dashboard tile that, for each product, displayed the combined value of every other product's price. The intent was to answer a business question: if any single SKU disappeared, how much of the day's revenue is still accounted for by the rest? So for each item I needed the product of all the other items, excluding itself.

The version that broke

My first implementation was the arithmetic shortcut everyone reaches for. Multiply every price into one grand total, then divide that total by each item's own price to get the product of everything else.

def share_naive(prices):
    grand = 1
    for p in prices:
        grand *= p
    return [grand // p for p in prices]   # breaks the instant any p is 0

It passed every test I wrote, because every test used positive prices. Then a clearance SKU was marked down to a price of zero. The grand product collapsed to zero, every division produced a wrong zero, and the division by the zero item itself raised ZeroDivisionError. Division had silently assumed every value was invertible, and one free promo item violated that assumption for the entire catalog.

Why LeetCode 238 forbids division

This is exactly Product of Array Except Self, LeetCode 238, and the problem states its constraint outright: solve it without division, in O(n). I used to read that as an arbitrary interview handicap. After this bug, I read it as a correctness requirement. Division forces you to invert each element, and zero has no inverse. Even ignoring zeros, repeatedly dividing floating-point numbers accumulates rounding error in a way that repeated multiplication of the same operands does not. The no-division rule is protecting you from the failure I shipped.

The reframe

Stop thinking about a grand total. For any index i, the answer is the product of everything to its left times the product of everything to its right. Neither piece includes the element itself, so its value, zero or not, never enters its own answer.

def product_except_self(stock):
    n = len(stock)
    out = [1] * n

    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left            # everything strictly left of i
        left *= stock[i]         # fold i in for the next index

    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right          # multiply in everything strictly right of i
        right *= stock[i]
    return out


inventory = [6, 0, 3, 2]         # index 1 is the free promo SKU
print(product_except_self(inventory))  # [0, 36, 0, 0]

The ordering inside each loop

The single detail that makes or breaks this: in the left pass, I assign out[i] = left before I multiply stock[i] into left. That ordering guarantees left holds the product of everything strictly before i and never includes the current element. Update first and assign second, and every answer wrongly includes its own value, which is precisely what the problem forbids. The right pass mirrors the same discipline.

Tracing the zero case

For the free SKU at index 1, its left product is 6 and its right product is 3 * 2 = 6, so its answer is 36, the correct product of all its non-zero neighbors. For every other index, either the left sweep or the right sweep crosses the zero, so the answer is correctly zero. The zero is now just another factor, never a divisor.

Complexity

  • Time: two linear sweeps, each O(n), so O(n) overall instead of the O(n^2) nested all-pairs version.
  • Space: reuse the output array for the left products and carry the right product in a single scalar, so O(1) extra space. The returned array is required output, not auxiliary scratch, so claiming O(1) extra is honest.

The edge case that comes for free

Two or more zeros in the array make every answer zero, because each index then has at least one zero either to its left or its right. The prefix-suffix method handles this with no special code. The division approach would have needed an explicit count-the-zeros branch, which is more code and more places to be wrong.

What I'm taking away

The Friday failure was not a bug in a loop. It was choosing a tool, division, whose precondition (every value is invertible) my data violated the moment a price hit zero. Reframing the answer as left product times right product removed the precondition entirely.

When a problem tempts you to divide by an element, do you reach for prefix and suffix products, or do you special-case the zeros? Which reads cleaner to you, and have you hit a real-world version of this bug?

title: Google DeepMind's Signal proof: what AlphaProof Code checks
description:
Google DeepMind reports machine-checked security proofs for a compiled implementation of selected Signal protocol operations. Its new AlphaProof Code work gives developers a concrete example of AI doing difficult proof construction while a separate checker enforces a human-approved target. The specification, the compiled artifact and the trusted assumptions all matter to understanding the result.

TL;DR

  • AlphaProof Code combines human-guided specification development with AI-generated Lean proofs.
  • The researchers verify a particular compiled libsignal command-line harness under stated models and cryptographic assumptions.
  • Lean checks the proof's logic. A comparator checks the approved theorem and every definition it depends on.
  • The humans still decide whether the specification captures a meaningful security claim and review changes to trusted assumptions.
  • I stamped the checked-proof workflow SHIP IT, with the scope and assumptions attached to every result.

What Google DeepMind actually released

The November 10 announcement describes AlphaProof Code as a framework for formal software specification and verification. The accompanying technical paper provides the details that a short announcement necessarily compresses: the target binary, the models of attackers, the cryptographic contracts and the restrictions on the guarantees.

The team reports roughly six and a half million lines of checked Lean proof. The trusted specification definitions and instruction semantics amount to about twenty-six thousand lines. Those are artifact counts, with additional tooling and symbol-name trust described in the paper. They establish no intelligence score or universal productivity ratio.

The proof campaign involved five researchers over four weeks. According to the paper, the agents generated the proof code; human effort concentrated on specifications, review and directing the work. That is a reported research campaign. Comparing it directly with the person-years of a different verification project would require matching the tasks and measuring the resources. We have no such comparison here.

The public repository contains the specifications, proofs, formal instruction semantics and checking instructions. I haven't rebuilt this enormous development for the episode. This article reports the published result and explains what its checks are designed to establish.

Formal verification starts with the question

A security specification is a mathematical statement of what a system must guarantee. It also describes the attacker and the assumptions under which the guarantee applies. Each choice changes the question the proof answers.

Suppose a claim only concerns inputs from a very restricted set. Proving it may tell you little about other inputs your application accepts. A specification that leaves an important attacker action outside its model can also miss a security concern. These are questions about the statement's meaning and strength, even when the proof of that statement is logically correct.

Section 2.1 of Google's paper makes this division explicit. A specification consists of theorem statements and the definitions they depend on, including models of the environment. Human reviewers have to trust that those definitions capture the intended claim. The proof supplied by an agent can remain untrusted because Lean's kernel checks whether it follows from the formal statement and permitted assumptions.

The researchers describe several ways to scrutinize specifications. Review agents examine their faithfulness to the source literature and implementation. The development includes checks for vacuous statements, including witnesses that relevant hypotheses can hold. The team also tests whether specifications reject deliberately broken code. These checks support review; selecting the target remains a human responsibility.

For developers using AI, that split is immediately recognizable. A worker that changes the acceptance criteria can make an impressive amount of progress on a different task. More output will not fix a question that drifted halfway through the assignment.

Why Signal's compiled implementation matters

Signal's protocol has a substantial history of formal analysis. Its official PQXDH specification discusses prior symbolic and computational work. The ratchet specification explains how message-key derivation evolves, including the Triple Ratchet's combination of classical and post-quantum components.

Protocol models can capture a design's intended security while omitting some of the complexity that implementation introduces. The technical paper points to concrete machinery inside libsignal: archived sessions, out-of-order messages, serialization and mutable session state. These are ordinary requirements of a useful messaging library. They make the connection between the design argument and the implementation harder to establish.

For this study, the researchers use unmodified libsignal crates inside a small command-line harness. They compile the code into an AArch64 Linux executable with the standard Rust compiler. The formal claims concern runs of that compiled artifact using a model of instructions and the process environment.

This is why the paper excludes the Rust compiler from the trusted base for the stated properties of that binary. A compiler error that violates a property would make the theorem false. The argument has to succeed for the compiler's output.

The remaining trust has a different shape. Readers still trust the formal instruction semantics, Lean's kernel and the contracts applied at specified boundaries. The paper also identifies extraction and reproducible-build tooling in its trusted base. A binary-level proof changes the trust boundary; it does not erase it.

Which security guarantees have conditions?

The reported results cover message confidentiality and authentication, with forward secrecy and post-compromise security under the stated models. Forward secrecy limits damage to earlier messages when current keys are compromised. Post-compromise security concerns recovery through fresh exchanges under the model's conditions. An attacker that remains active, a different session scenario or an omitted implementation feature can change which claim applies.

The paper presents both a symbolic and a computational argument. The symbolic model treats cryptographic primitives as ideal operations and proves properties within that abstraction. The computational model reasons about an efficient attacker's success probability and assumptions about the underlying primitives. These are complementary forms of assurance with different restrictions.

Low-level cryptographic routines are specified through trusted contracts. The result assumes those routines behave as specified and relies on cryptographic security assumptions. The proof therefore should not be described as an independent implementation proof for every primitive it calls.

The setting is also bounded. The paper describes the particular CLI build, group messaging as future work and an absence of multi-device state in the computational model. It lists additional session and input restrictions, and gives limits on what the quantitative bound establishes at large scale. Its computational bound gives no guarantee against quantum adversaries; the symbolic analysis covers a specified portion of that question.

Those details are useful when assessing a claim, rather than grounds for throwing the result away. Ask which guarantee you need, which artifact the theorem concerns and whether your environment satisfies the premises. A security proof becomes easier to use when those boundaries travel with the headline.

A green result needs a broken case

The researchers reintroduced two previously fixed bugs that earlier work had found in libsignal. They injected each into an isolated version and recompiled it. The resulting Lean proofs establish that those binaries violate the symbolic security theorem.

That exercise checks something important about the specification: it can reject those real broken implementations. The bugs had already been fixed. This supplies no new live Signal vulnerability, emergency update or demonstration against a user's account.

It also illustrates why specification evaluation deserves its own effort. If a proof system accepts the good version and the specification says nothing about the relevant mistake, the result can look reassuring while answering a weaker question than readers assume. A broken-case check helps expose that weakness for the cases tested.

The public artifact makes further inspection possible. Its README explains the pinned toolchains and comparator procedure. It also warns that a clean build takes several hours and substantial memory. Outsiders have a path to check the development, and independently completing that path is a separate claim from reading the paper.

The comparator checks beneath the visible theorem

Here is the detail I wanted the episode to reach. Checking the visible theorem statement alone leaves a route for weakening the task through definitions that statement uses. A predicate can change underneath an unchanged theorem name.

The gatekeeping section describes a protected approved specification copied from a baseline commit. Proof agents cannot write to its held-out directory. The gatekeeper calls a deterministic checking script, and the development retains a distinction between trusted specification files and untrusted proof files.

The comparator then checks the statement and every definition it depends on against that approved copy. It also checks that the proof uses permitted standard Lean axioms and replays the proof in a fresh kernel. A weakened helper definition changes the material being compared, even if the visible theorem text still looks familiar.

Specifications can need genuine corrections. The researchers therefore provide a separate amendment process with a critic and human-approved policy or judgment. Changes are logged and reviewed. A proposed security weakening is raised as a potential bug. The protected target changes through that process, rather than through the prover quietly editing its own assignment.

For an ordinary agent workflow, I would keep acceptance criteria outside the worker's edit permissions and review proposed changes separately. That is a practical lesson from this design. Its usefulness in another agent task needs its own evaluation. The formal result depends on much more precise machinery than a prompt saying “please check yourself.”

Verdict: SHIP IT

I'd ship the checked-proof workflow because the approved claim stays separate from the agent producing the answer. I'd keep the scope and assumptions attached to every result. The human role becomes especially important where the system decides what security means and whether the assumptions match the intended environment.

The published artifact gives that discussion something concrete to inspect. I would start with the target and the trusted base, then ask how the implementation proof connects to them. Your requirements document has finally found a way to demand more attention than the generated code.

FAQ

Does this prove every Signal application is bug-free? The result concerns selected properties of the researchers' compiled CLI harness under stated models and assumptions. It establishes no blanket whole-application guarantee.

Can the AI change the specification? Agents can propose amendments through a separate reviewed process. They cannot write to the protected approved copy themselves.

Why is Lean's kernel important? It checks the logical proof, so proof acceptance does not rely on believing the model's explanation. The kernel remains part of the trusted base.

Did we independently rebuild the proofs? No. The episode and article report the published work and its boundaries. The repository provides instructions for an independent check.

Sources

  • Technical paper, including scope, assumptions and gatekeeping
  • Google DeepMind announcement
  • Public artifact repository and checking instructions
  • Signal PQXDH specification
  • Signal ratchet specification
  • Demis Hassabis portrait by Christopher P. Michel / Cmichel67, CC BY-SA 4.0. Portrait-based artwork identifies lab leadership only; no authorship, proof writing, current reaction or endorsement is implied. Portrait and complete artwork adaptations use the same licence. Changes are cropping, normal resizing and compression, unflipped; no background removal, expression change or generated detail.

title: Building a Degradation Manifest: Config-Driven Graceful Degradation in Node.js
description:
The Problem With Ad-Hoc Degradation

Most graceful degradation starts as scattered if statements checking feature flags. Over time, nobody knows which routes have fallbacks, what those fallbacks do, or whether they've been tested. What you need is a single manifest that declares every degradable route, its fallback behavior, and its dependency requirements.

The Degradation Manifest

Define your degradation rules in YAML:

# degradation-manifest.yaml
defaults:
  health_check_interval_ms: 5000
  failure_threshold: 0.4
  recovery_threshold: 0.15
  hysteresis_seconds: 90

dependencies:
  recommendations-api:
    health_url: http://recommendations:8080/healthz
    timeout_ms: 2000
  analytics-collector:
    health_url: http://analytics:8080/healthz
    timeout_ms: 1000
  personalization-service:
    health_url: http://personalization:8080/healthz
    timeout_ms: 2000

tiers:
  best-effort:
    priority: 1  # shed first
    routes:
      - path: /api/analytics/track
        method: POST
        fallback: drop  # return 204, do nothing
        requires: [analytics-collector]
      - path: /api/ab/assign
        method: GET
        fallback: static
        static_response: { "variant": "control", "source": "degraded" }
        requires: [analytics-collector]

  enhanced:
    priority: 2
    routes:
      - path: /api/recommendations
        method: GET
        fallback: static
        static_response: { "items": [], "source": "degraded" }
        requires: [recommendations-api]
      - path: /api/personalization
        method: GET
        fallback: static
        static_response: { "profile": "default", "source": "degraded" }
        requires: [personalization-service]

The Express Middleware 

const express = require('express');
const fs = require('fs');
const yaml = require('js-yaml');

class DependencyMonitor {
  constructor(name, config, defaults) {
    this.name = name;
    this.healthUrl = config.health_url;
    this.timeoutMs = config.timeout_ms;
    this.failureThreshold = defaults.failure_threshold;
    this.recoveryThreshold = defaults.recovery_threshold;
    this.window = [];  // { timestamp, healthy }
    this.windowMs = 30000;
  }

  record(healthy) {
    const now = Date.now();
    this.window.push({ timestamp: now, healthy });
    const cutoff = now - this.windowMs;
    this.window = this.window.filter(e => e.timestamp > cutoff);
  }

  get errorRate() {
    if (this.window.length === 0) return 0;
    const failures = this.window.filter(e => !e.healthy).length;
    return failures / this.window.length;
  }

  get isFailed() {
    return this.errorRate >= this.failureThreshold;
  }

  get isRecovered() {
    return this.errorRate <= this.recoveryThreshold;
  }

  async check() {
    try {
      const controller = new AbortController();
      const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), this.timeoutMs);
      const res = await fetch(this.healthUrl, { signal: controller.signal });
      clearTimeout(timeout);
      this.record(res.ok);
    } catch {
      this.record(false);
    }
  }
}

class DegradationEngine {
  constructor(manifestPath) {
    const raw = yaml.load(fs.readFileSync(manifestPath, 'utf8'));
    this.defaults = raw.defaults;
    this.simulationMode = false;
    this.simulatedLevel = 0;

    // Initialize dependency monitors
    this.monitors = {};
    for (const [name, config] of Object.entries(raw.dependencies)) {
      this.monitors[name] = new DependencyMonitor(name, config, this.defaults);
    }

    // Build tier list sorted by priority
    this.tiers = Object.entries(raw.tiers)
      .map(([name, tier]) => ({
        name,
        priority: tier.priority,
        routes: tier.routes,
      }))
      .sort((a, b) => a.priority - b.priority);

    // Build route lookup
    this.routeMap = new Map();
    for (const tier of this.tiers) {
      for (const route of tier.routes) {
        const key = `${route.method.toUpperCase()}:${route.path}`;
        this.routeMap.set(key, { ...route, tierName: tier.name, tierPriority: tier.priority });
      }
    }

    // Current shed level (0 = normal, 1 = shed priority-1, etc.)
    this.shedLevel = 0;
    this.levelChangedAt = 0;

    // Start health checking
    this._interval = setInterval(() => this._evaluate(), this.defaults.health_check_interval_ms);
  }

  _evaluate() {
    // Check all dependencies
    for (const monitor of Object.values(this.monitors)) {
      monitor.check();
    }

    if (this.simulationMode) return;

    // Determine required shed level
    let requiredLevel = 0;
    for (const tier of this.tiers) {
      const deps = new Set(tier.routes.flatMap(r => r.requires));
      for (const depName of deps) {
        if (this.monitors[depName]?.isFailed) {
          requiredLevel = Math.max(requiredLevel, tier.priority);
        }
      }
    }

    // Escalate immediately
    if (requiredLevel > this.shedLevel) {
      this.shedLevel = requiredLevel;
      this.levelChangedAt = Date.now();
      return;
    }

    // Recover with hysteresis
    if (requiredLevel < this.shedLevel) {
      const elapsed = Date.now() - this.levelChangedAt;
      if (elapsed >= this.defaults.hysteresis_seconds * 1000) {
        const allRecovered = Object.values(this.monitors).every(m => m.isRecovered);
        if (allRecovered) {
          this.shedLevel = Math.max(0, this.shedLevel - 1);
          this.levelChangedAt = Date.now();
        }
      }
    }
  }

  get activeShedLevel() {
    return this.simulationMode ? this.simulatedLevel : this.shedLevel;
  }

  middleware() {
    return (req, res, next) => {
      const key = `${req.method.toUpperCase()}:${req.path}`;
      const route = this.routeMap.get(key);

      if (route && route.tierPriority <= this.activeShedLevel) {
        res.set('X-Degraded', 'true');
        res.set('X-Degradation-Tier', route.tierName);

        if (route.fallback === 'drop') {
          return res.status(204).end();
        }
        if (route.fallback === 'static') {
          return res.json(route.static_response);
        }
      }

      res.set('X-Degradation-Level', String(this.activeShedLevel));
      next();
    };
  }

  statusHandler() {
    return (req, res) => {
      const shedTiers = this.tiers
        .filter(t => t.priority <= this.activeShedLevel)
        .map(t => t.name);

      res.json({
        shed_level: this.activeShedLevel,
        simulation_mode: this.simulationMode,
        shed_tiers: shedTiers,
        dependencies: Object.fromEntries(
          Object.entries(this.monitors).map(([name, m]) => [
            name,
            { error_rate: Math.round(m.errorRate * 1000) / 1000, failed: m.isFailed },
          ])
        ),
      });
    };
  }

  simulationHandler() {
    return (req, res) => {
      const { enabled, level } = req.body;
      if (typeof enabled === 'boolean') {
        this.simulationMode = enabled;
      }
      if (typeof level === 'number') {
        this.simulatedLevel = level;
      }
      res.json({
        simulation_mode: this.simulationMode,
        simulated_level: this.simulatedLevel,
        actual_level: this.shedLevel,
      });
    };
  }
}

// Usage
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

const degradation = new DegradationEngine('./degradation-manifest.yaml');

app.use(degradation.middleware());
app.get('/degradation/status', degradation.statusHandler());
app.post('/degradation/simulate', degradation.simulationHandler());

// Your actual routes
app.get('/api/recommendations', (req, res) => {
  // Only reached if not shed
  res.json({ items: ['real', 'recommendations'] });
});

app.post('/api/analytics/track', (req, res) => {
  // Only reached if not shed
  res.status(200).json({ tracked: true });
});

app.listen(3000);

Simulation Mode

The simulation endpoint lets you test shed sequences without waiting for real failures:

# Enable simulation, shed tier 1 (best-effort)
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/degradation/simulate \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"enabled": true, "level": 1}'

# Verify analytics tracking is shed
curl -v -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/analytics/track
# Returns 204 with X-Degraded: true

# Escalate to tier 2
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/degradation/simulate \
  -d '{"enabled": true, "level": 2}'

# Verify recommendations are shed
curl http://localhost:3000/api/recommendations
# Returns {"items":[], "source": "degraded"}

# Check status
curl http://localhost:3000/degradation/status

# Disable simulation
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/degradation/simulate \
  -d '{"enabled": false}'

Run this simulation as part of your CI pipeline. If someone adds a new route without a manifest entry, you'll catch it when the simulation test shows the route still serving live responses under degradation.

What This Buys You

The manifest is the source of truth for degradation behavior. New engineers can read it and understand the entire shed sequence. Product managers can review it without reading code. And the simulation mode means you can verify the degraded state before you're in an incident.

title: Day 25/90: It passed validate AND plan, then shipped a broken security group
description:
Day 25/90: Terraform testing with Terratest

90 Day Security Infrastructure Challenge

A teammate's module change passed terraform validate, passed terraform plan with no errors, collected two approvals, and shipped a security group that no longer allowed 443. The module's whole job was to open HTTPS to the public load balancer. A refactor the week before had moved ingress into a dynamic block fed by a variable, and 443 fell out of that variable's list. Validate and plan both stayed green, because neither one runs the apply or reads the live resource. The first thing that noticed was a failing health check.

This post is the case for behavioral testing of IaC, and the structure of a Terratest test that would have caught it.

What validate and plan actually prove

terraform validate proves your configuration is well-formed: types line up, references resolve, blocks are legal. terraform plan proves what Terraform intends to change by diffing your config against state. Both are useful and both are fast. But notice the boundary: neither runs apply, neither calls the live cloud API, and neither asks the deployed security group whether it really allows 443. A module can be internally consistent and externally wrong, and that is precisely the failure these two tools are blind to.

Consider the module's output -- the surface a test would read:

output "sg_id" {
  value = aws_security_group.web.id
}

output "open_ports" {
  description = "Ports the web SG accepts on tcp"
  value       = sort([for rule in aws_security_group.web.ingress : rule.from_port])
}

Plan will happily show this output being computed. It cannot tell you the value is wrong, because the value depends on a variable that lost 443 during a refactor. Only an apply produces the real list, and only an assertion against that real list catches the regression.

A Terratest test is a Go test that drives the CLI

Terratest is a Go library from Gruntwork. A test is an ordinary go test function. It builds a terraform.Options, runs InitAndApply against a sandbox account, reads outputs, asserts with testify, and destroys in a defer. Here is one that pins the contract "this SG accepts 443":

package test

import (
    "testing"

    "github.com/gruntwork-io/terratest/modules/random"
    "github.com/gruntwork-io/terratest/modules/terraform"
    "github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

func TestWebSGOpenPorts(t *testing.T) {
    t.Parallel()

    opts := &terraform.Options{
        TerraformDir: "../modules/web-sg",
        Vars: map[string]interface{}{
            "name_suffix": random.UniqueId(),
            "vpc_id":      "vpc-0abc123",
        },
        NoColor: true,
    }

    defer terraform.Destroy(t, opts)
    terraform.InitAndApply(t, opts)

    openPorts := terraform.OutputList(t, opts, "open_ports")
    require.Contains(t, openPorts, "443", "web SG must accept HTTPS")
    require.Contains(t, openPorts, "80", "web SG must accept HTTP for redirect")
}

require.Contains (vs assert.Contains) stops the test on the first failed expectation, which is what you want when a missing 443 makes every later check meaningless. t.Parallel() plus the random.UniqueId() suffix lets several module tests run concurrently without colliding on resource names.

Why the static layers could not catch this

The instinct is "we should have had a policy scan." But run the broken module through checkov or tfsec and they pass. A security group with no 443 rule is valid and secure-looking. Static scanners flag dangerous presence (a public port 22, an unencrypted volume), not intended absence. The missing rule is invisible to every tool that only reads code:

# the cheap layers -- all green on the broken module
terraform fmt -check -recursive
terraform validate
tflint --recursive
checkov -d . --quiet      # finds 0.0.0.0/0 on 22, NOT a missing 443

That is the gap a behavioral test fills. The static tools answer "is this code well-formed and free of known bad patterns?" Terratest answers "does the thing this code builds actually do what we claimed?"

The trade-off: gate it, do not spam it

Terratest creates real resources, so it is slow (minutes) and costs money each run. The discipline is a pyramid:

  • Base, every save, free: fmt, validate, tflint.
  • Middle, every PR, cheap: checkov / tfsec on the plan.
  • Top, gated in CI, slow + costs money: Terratest against a sandbox.

Run Terratest on a merge gate or a nightly job, never on file save. The cheap layers carry the constant load; the expensive layer proves the handful of claims that only a real apply can prove. The broken-443 regression lives at the top of that pyramid -- and that is exactly why the pyramid has a top.

Why this belongs in a security infrastructure track

A dropped 443 rule is an availability incident. A dropped deny rule, a widened CIDR, or an encryption flag silently flipping to false during a refactor are security incidents -- and they pass validate and plan the same way. Behavioral testing is how you keep a refactor from quietly changing what your infrastructure permits. Static checks describe intent. Terratest proves behavior.
