title: SaaS Image Thumbnails: Object Storage, CDN, or Upload Resizing with Node.js
description:
Short answer: for a beginner SaaS serving authenticated game reports, keep originals and generated thumbnails as separate objects, and create the thumbnail in a backend worker after upload. It is the easiest path to predictable large-file throughput. Add an image CDN only when you truly need on-the-fly, edge URL transformations. Resizing synchronously inside the upload request is the option I would avoid first.

The mental model is simple: the upload request stores bytes, a worker transforms bytes, and the read path serves a known object key. That before/after split keeps a slow resize from holding an authenticated customer request open.

A report page's delivery contract

Start with object storage. Put originals under a stable prefix such as reports/original/ and write outputs under reports/thumb/. Your database can store both keys, dimensions, and a generation status. A report page then reads a thumbnail object directly through your authenticated backend, while the original remains available for export.

This is deliberately boring. Boring is useful when a game studio is shipping its first customer portal and the files are large enough to expose every timeout you forgot to measure.

It failed fast.

That sentence is the design goal for the upload path: a bounded request, a visible queue state, and a retryable job rather than a mysterious spinner.

An upload-triggered worker gives you a clean sequence:

  1. The API accepts metadata and streams the original to storage.
  2. A notification starts a worker with the bucket and object key.
  3. The worker downloads the original, resizes it, and writes a deterministic thumbnail key.
  4. The API reports pending until that key exists, then returns ready.

The result is deterministic behavior without depending on public bucket hosting. Keep the customer-facing read endpoint authenticated; do not assume a storage bucket can act like a public image host.

Ship it.

Which architecture keeps image thumbnails predictable for a small SaaS?

Path Large-file behavior Thumbnail flexibility Operational cost Good fit
Object storage plus worker Upload and transform are decoupled; retries are isolated Fixed sizes you generate ahead of time One worker and a queue/notification Beginner SaaS with predictable report views
Image CDN transformation Original upload is simple; edge work happens on reads Many URL-driven sizes and formats CDN rules, cache behavior, and vendor limits Public or high-volume image delivery
Resize during upload One request can produce the final asset Only the sizes coded into the request Long requests and harder retry handling Tiny files with one guaranteed size

Cloud object stores such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Cloudflare R2, and Backblaze B2 are strong references for the first path: they are built around durable object reads and writes, with lifecycle controls for cleanup. An image CDN is a different product category. It earns its place when clients need arbitrary transformations at edge URLs, not merely because the word “CDN” sounds faster.

S3 is the broad compatibility baseline. R2 can be attractive when its regional model and egress terms match your traffic. B2 is a sensible alternative for teams already using Backblaze. None of those names removes the need to design the worker and the authenticated read path.

The catch is important: storage alone does not provide on-the-fly image transformation. Choose a separate image CDN/service when that URL contract is a hard requirement. Conversely, a CDN adds cache invalidation and transformation policy to your system; that is real machinery for a small authenticated app.

The smallest useful Node.js boundary

The upload boundary should be short and explicit. Here is a TypeScript sketch that reads a generated thumbnail through an Infrai-backed implementation; the same boundary can sit behind an S3-compatible adapter. Infrai's practical advantage here is a plain REST API: any runtime that can send HTTP can use the same bearer-key contract without installing an SDK. Its one key / one bill model across backend capabilities means the report service does not need a separate credential or invoice for every adjacent tool, which can simplify a small team's operational review. In other words, Infrai offers one key, one bill for the adjacent backend calls. One platform also covers several backend capabilities with shared conventions, so switching vendors behind the adapter does not require changing application code. I've kept the base URL in configuration, and the key never contains customer-controlled path separators.

type ThumbnailArgs = {
  baseUrl: string;
  apiKey: string;
  bucket: string;
  key: string;
};

export async function getThumbnail(args: ThumbnailArgs): Promise<Uint8Array> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY ?? args.apiKey;
  const safeKey = args.key.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9/_-]/g, "_");
  const url = `${args.baseUrl}/v1/storage/object/get/${args.bucket}/${safeKey}`;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      },
    });

    if (response.ok) return new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer());
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      throw new Error(`thumbnail fetch failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? "0");
    const delayMs = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }

  throw new Error("thumbnail rate limit persisted after retries");
}

For writes, the idempotency key matters because a client may retry after a lost response. The worker should use the same idea for its output key: thumb/{width}x{height}/{originalKey}. A second delivery then overwrites the same deterministic object instead of creating a new variant. The read example above keeps retry handling explicit for HTTP 429 and surfaces other response bodies instead of pretending every status is success.

For automatic work, configure a bucket notification to enqueue the object event. Keep the notification handler tiny: validate the event, enqueue a job, acknowledge it. Image decoding belongs in the worker process, where you can cap memory and record duration, output bytes, and failures in your existing metrics.

The boundaries are part of the choice

Do not use this storage-first design for a public image host that needs permanent anonymous URLs. The available storage capability has no public-read ACL behavior, so public_url is not a delivery contract. Put a CDN or a service designed for public image delivery in front instead.

It is also a poor match for strict write-once retention. There is no object versioning or WORM lock here, and there is no If-Match conditional write for enforcing concurrency by itself. A financial audit archive needs an external immutability and coordination layer. Browser-direct uploads also require a CORS configuration path; if your deployment cannot configure that policy, proxy uploads through your backend.

Lifecycle cleanup starts at a one-day granularity, and metadata is not a server-side query index beyond prefix listing. Plan a database index for report ownership and a queue for deletion. Cross-region replication and cross-cloud batch migration are separate design work, not assumptions to hide in a storage abstraction.

The REST approach is useful when you want one HTTP contract from TypeScript, Python, or a worker written in another language, without installing a storage SDK. Infrai is one example of that style: its storage routes use a single bearer key and the same HTTP shape across capabilities. That convenience is a fit when consolidating backend calls matters; it does not turn object storage into an image CDN.

Your mileage may vary on the worker boundary. If thumbnails are always tiny and generated once, doing the resize inline can be acceptable. Measure p95 upload time and worker memory before moving that work into the request path.

A practical decision rule

Choose object storage plus a backend-triggered worker when customers are authenticated, originals are private, and the application can name the thumbnail sizes it needs. Choose an image CDN when clients need arbitrary edge transformations or anonymous cacheable URLs. Choose upload-time resizing only when the file size and one-size output are both tightly bounded.

That rule keeps the first release understandable and leaves room to add a CDN later. Start with the path you can observe: upload latency, queue age, resize duration, thumbnail bytes, and read errors. Then let those measurements, rather than a vendor feature checklist, decide when the architecture should grow.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429
  • https://docs.cloudflare.com/images/image-transformations/

title: Stop Reaching for java.util.Stack: ArrayDeque for Stacks and Queues
description:
Day 25/90: Queue & Stack -- Why I Stopped Using java.util.Stack

90 Day Java Challenge: Zero to Production

I inherited a service that ran a depth-first walk over a dependency graph, built around a java.util.Stack. It worked. But profiling a slow request showed time spent inside synchronized methods -- on a path that only ever ran on one thread. The stack was paying for locks nothing needed.

The inheritance that costs you

java.util.Stack extends Vector. Every Vector method is synchronized, so push, pop, and peek each grab a monitor lock on every call. Single-threaded, that lock is never contended -- it is pure overhead.

The worse part is the inherited API. Because a Stack is a Vector is a List, every List method is public on your "stack":

import java.util.Stack;

Stack<String> stack = new Stack<>();
stack.push("a");
stack.push("b");

stack.add(0, "bottom");   // insert at the BOTTOM of a stack
String mid = stack.get(0); // random access into a stack
stack.remove("a");         // delete a non-top element

A stack should make exactly one promise -- last in, first out, touched only at the top. java.util.Stack hands callers a dozen ways to break it. The type meant to enforce the discipline is the type that violates it.

ArrayDeque: one class, both shapes

The Java docs recommend ArrayDeque over Stack for a stack, and over LinkedList for a queue. It is array-backed, unsynchronized, and does not extend List. The Deque interface gives you both shapes from one object.

As a stack, use push / pop / peek -- all operating on the front:

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push("first");
stack.push("second");
stack.push("third");

System.out.println(stack.pop());   // third  (last in, first out)
System.out.println(stack.peek());  // second (top, not removed)

As a queue, use offer / poll / peek -- add at the back, remove from the front:

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer("first");
queue.offer("second");
queue.offer("third");

System.out.println(queue.poll());   // first  (first in, first out)
System.out.println(queue.peek());   // second (head, not removed)

Same class. The only difference is which methods you call. If push and offer feel vague, the explicit names addFirst / pollFirst and addLast / pollFirst say which end you mean.

The null contract: signal vs throw

Deque exposes two parallel method families that differ in how they report failure:

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

Deque<String> q = new ArrayDeque<>();

System.out.println(q.poll());  // null -- empty, no exception
System.out.println(q.peek());  // null -- empty, no exception

q.remove();                    // throws NoSuchElementException

offer / poll / peek return null or false when the operation cannot proceed. add / remove / element throw. Use the returning forms when empty is an expected state your loop handles; use the throwing forms when empty means a bug you want loud. And note: ArrayDeque rejects null elements outright (it throws NullPointerException on insert), precisely so a null from poll always means "empty."

ArrayDeque vs LinkedList, and PriorityQueue

Both implement Deque, so why prefer ArrayDeque? Memory layout. ArrayDeque keeps elements in a contiguous, growable circular array -- cache-friendly, zero per-element allocation. LinkedList allocates a two-pointer node per element, scattered across the heap, paying a cache miss on every link traversal. For ordinary stack and queue work, ArrayDeque is faster and lighter. Reach for LinkedList only when you need List indexing alongside deque behavior.

When you want elements out in priority order instead of LIFO or FIFO, use PriorityQueue -- a heap that polls smallest-first:

import java.util.PriorityQueue;

PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
pq.offer(5);
pq.offer(1);
pq.offer(3);

System.out.println(pq.poll());  // 1
System.out.println(pq.poll());  // 3
System.out.println(pq.poll());  // 5

Only the polling is ordered -- iterating a PriorityQueue gives you heap order, not sorted order.

The takeaway

java.util.Stack is a class to retire. It carries Vector's locks and Vector's API into a place that wanted neither. ArrayDeque covers both stack and queue cleanly, beats LinkedList on speed and memory, and lets you choose your failure mode. Yesterday was maps and their ordering contracts; today the container's order is the whole point -- so picking the structure is just picking the order you actually want.

title: Day 25/90: The fetch that "succeeded" on a 404
description:
Day 25/90: The fetch that "succeeded" on a 404

90 Day JavaScript Challenge: Zero to Production

The bug report was short: a user's saved settings kept silently resetting. The UI said "Saved!" every time. The data was not saved.

I traced it to a route rename. We had moved an endpoint, and one caller still hit the old path, so its request came back as a 404. The part that should have raised an alarm did nothing. Here is the function:

async function updateProfile(profile) {
  const reply = await fetch("/account/profile", {
    method: "PUT",
    body: JSON.stringify(profile),
  });
  return reply.json();
}

No missing await, no missing return. The bug is an assumption I had carried for years: that fetch throws on a 404. It does not.

fetch rejects on network failure, not on error status

This is the rule that fixes everything once it clicks. fetch rejects its promise only when the network itself fails: DNS resolution failed, the connection dropped, the request was blocked, the host was unreachable. If the server answers at all, the promise resolves, even when the answer is a 404 or a 500.

Think of it as two separate questions:

  • Did the server reply? That is what fetch answers.
  • Did the request succeed? That is what response.ok answers.

A 500 is a completed, successful round trip that carries an error in its status line. fetch reports the round trip. So in my code, reply resolved fine, reply.json() parsed the error body, and the function returned garbage as if it were real data.

Check response.ok before touching the body

response.ok is true only for statuses 200 through 299. response.status gives the exact code. Read them before you read the body:

async function updateProfile(profile) {
  const reply = await fetch("/account/profile", {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(profile),
  });
  if (!reply.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Profile update rejected: ${reply.status}`);
  }
  return reply.json();
}

Now a 404 becomes a thrown error a caller can catch. Notice the Content-Type: application/json header too. Without it, many servers will not parse your JSON body, which is its own silent failure waiting to happen.

The body stream is read-once

The response body is a stream. You can consume it exactly once. This trips people in the error path: you read the error as text to log it, then try to parse it as JSON, and you get TypeError: body stream already read.

const reply = await fetch(url);
const text = await reply.text();
const json = await reply.json(); // throws: body already consumed

Pick one read per response. In an error path, prefer .text(), because error responses are frequently HTML or a bare string and would throw a second, more confusing error if you tried .json() on them.

Timeouts and cancellation with AbortController

fetch has no built-in timeout. A request that never answers hangs forever. AbortController is the escape hatch. You pass its signal into fetch, and calling abort() rejects the fetch promise with an AbortError:

async function getJson(url, timeoutMs = 5000) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeoutMs);
  try {
    const reply = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
    if (!reply.ok) {
      const body = await reply.text();
      throw new Error(`HTTP ${reply.status}: ${body.slice(0, 120)}`);
    }
    return await reply.json();
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

The clearTimeout in finally is not optional. Without it, a fast response leaves a live timer that fires later and aborts nothing useful, or worse, in a reused controller, aborts the next request. Always pair the timer with a cleanup that runs no matter how the request ends.

The takeaway

fetch tells you the server replied. It does not tell you the request succeeded. Those are different questions, and the gap between them is exactly where a 404 disguises itself as a success. Build a wrapper that checks response.ok, reads the body once, sets the right headers, and times out, and you close that gap for every call in your app at once.

title: Day 25/420: Dataclasses and value objects -- value equality, hashability, and immutability for free
description:
Day 25/420: Dataclasses and value objects

420 Day Python Production Track

Two things bite me whenever I represent a small factual value as a plain class or dict: two equal values don't compare equal, and the value gets mutated under code that was still using it. Today I'll show both with an RGBColor, then fix them with @dataclass(frozen=True).

The two-line bug 

class RGBColor:
    def __init__(self, r, g, b):
        self.r = r
        self.g = g
        self.b = b

teal = RGBColor(0, 128, 128)
also_teal = RGBColor(0, 128, 128)

print(teal == also_teal)   # False

Same three channels, and == is False. Python's default __eq__ compares identity -- "is this the same object in memory" -- not contents. Two colors with equal channels are two different objects, so they're not equal. The instant teal lands in a set of "colors already used in this palette," the dedup logic silently fails and you ship duplicates.

It gets worse when the value is mutable and shared:

def darken(color, amount):
    color.r = max(0, color.r - amount)   # mutates in place
    color.g = max(0, color.g - amount)
    color.b = max(0, color.b - amount)
    return color

brand = RGBColor(0, 128, 128)
shadow = darken(brand, 40)
print(brand.r, brand.g, brand.b)   # 0 88 88  -> the brand color moved too

darken looks like it returns a new color. It returns the same object it mutated, so brand -- which the rest of the theme is still referencing -- just changed. A value is a fact you pass around; it should not be editable by whoever happens to hold it.

The fix: one decorator 

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RGBColor:
    r: int
    g: int
    b: int

    def __post_init__(self):
        for name, value in (("r", self.r), ("g", self.g), ("b", self.b)):
            if not 0 <= value <= 255:
                raise ValueError(f"{name} out of range 0-255: {value}")

    def darkened(self, amount):
        clamp = lambda v: max(0, v - amount)
        return RGBColor(clamp(self.r), clamp(self.g), clamp(self.b))


teal = RGBColor(0, 128, 128)
print(teal == RGBColor(0, 128, 128))        # True  -> value equality
print(len({teal, RGBColor(0, 128, 128)}))   # 1     -> hashable, dedups by value

shadow = teal.darkened(40)
print(teal)     # RGBColor(r=0, g=128, b=128)  -> unchanged
print(shadow)   # RGBColor(r=0, g=88, b=88)    -> a new object

frozen=True generates three behaviors:

  • Value __eq__. Equal channels compare equal, so the palette set collapses duplicates.
  • __hash__. The color can be a set member or dict key. A mutable object can't be -- if it changed, its hash would go stale and the set would lose it.
  • Immutability. Assignment is blocked, so a shared value can't be edited under you. 
try:
    teal.r = 255
except Exception as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__)   # FrozenInstanceError

darkened returns a new RGBColor instead of mutating -- the same way str.lower() gives you a new string. Sharing is safe again because nobody can change what they're holding.

Validate in __post_init__

The dataclass writes __init__ for you. To add invariants, implement __post_init__: the generated init assigns the fields, then calls it. The range check above means an out-of-range channel can never be constructed -- not from a test, not from parsed config, not from JSON. One place, every path.

The mutable-default trap

A field default cannot be a mutable object. This raises ValueError at class definition time:

# @dataclass
# class Palette:
#     colors: list = []   # ValueError: mutable default

The dataclass refuses because one list would be shared across every instance. Use field(default_factory=...):

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Palette:
    name: str
    colors: tuple = field(default_factory=tuple)

p = Palette("ocean")
print(p.colors)   # ()  -> fresh per instance, not shared

I use tuple, not list. On a frozen object, frozen=True only blocks reassigning the field; a list default would still let callers mutate its contents in place. A tuple keeps the whole value immutable.

Value object vs entity

The question that decides whether to freeze: if two instances have identical fields, are they the same thing?

  • RGBColor, Coordinate, Money, a date range: yes, interchangeable -> value object -> frozen dataclass, compared by value.
  • User, Order, Account: no -- two accounts with the same balance are still different accounts -> entity -> stable id, compared by id.

A value object is what; an entity is who. When a thing is fully described by its contents, make it a frozen dataclass and stop hand-writing equality, hashing, and immutability.

What value type in your codebase is still a bare dict that probably shouldn't be?

title: Polyglot AI Architecture: Keep Your .NET App, Add a Python RAG + Agent Service (gRPC, Qdrant, LangGraph, Langfuse — Real Code)
description:
Your enterprise app is .NET. Your UI is ExtJS. Now product wants RAG, agents, and evals — and the entire AI ecosystem in 2026 ships in Python first. You don't want to rewrite anything. A polyglot architecture is the answer: keep .NET as your trusted system-of-record and security boundary, run the AI workload as a separate Python service, talk over a clean typed contract, and observe both sides end-to-end.

This is a real recipe — diagram, code, deployment, and operational playbook — for shipping that pattern in production. Full version with the architecture diagram is on the original post (link at the end).

The architecture at a glance 

ExtJS web UI ──► .NET API Gateway ─REST/gRPC─► Python RAG/Agent service
                 (ASP.NET Core)                (FastAPI + LangChain + LangGraph)
                 auth · rate limit             ingestion · retrieval · orchestration
                 contract · security
                                                   │              │
                                                   ▼              ▼
                                             Qdrant vector DB   LLM provider
                                             (Docker)           (Azure OpenAI / OpenAI)

Observability spans every arrow:
  Langfuse       → LLM traces, prompts, evals, token cost
  OpenTelemetry  → end-to-end traces across .NET + Python + Qdrant + LLM

Five components, two languages, one observability fabric.

1. Why polyglot, and why now

Three forces pull against each other inside every enterprise stack in 2026:

  1. Your business logic is in .NET. Years of domain models, validation, RBAC, audit trails, integrations. None of it needs to move.
  2. Your UI is ExtJS / WinForms / WPF / Razor. It works. Rewriting it is a multi-quarter project that adds zero AI value.
  3. The AI ecosystem ships Python first. LangChain, LangGraph, llama-index, vLLM, Ragas, DSPy — Python releases land months before .NET ports (if they exist at all).
Option Outcome
Rewrite the AI stack in .NET (Semantic Kernel only) Slow to adopt new techniques; smaller library surface; locked to .NET release cycles.
Rewrite the business app in Python Throws away years of trusted code; ~100% new bugs; 12+ months.
Polyglot — keep .NET, add Python alongside Best tool per layer; clean security boundary; both stacks evolve independently.

Polyglot is the only route that respects existing investment and lets you adopt the AI ecosystem at full speed. It means: single product, single front door; .NET owns the contract (authN/Z, rate-limiting, versioning, audit); Python owns the AI workload (RAG, embeddings, orchestration), never exposed to the internet; and the boundary is a typed contract — REST+OpenAPI or gRPC+.proto.

2. What each layer is for

  • ExtJS UI — keep it. It's an HTTP client. Add a chat drawer that calls the existing .NET API. The fact that AI runs in Python is invisible to the browser.
  • .NET API Gateway — the security boundary. Authentication, authorization (RBAC, row-level), rate limiting, contract versioning, audit logging, outbound gRPC to Python (Polly), PII redaction before the prompt leaves your network, quota/billing. The Python service is never exposed to the internet.
  • Python RAG/Agent service — the workhorse. Ingestion (chunk → embed → upsert), retrieval (semantic + optional BM25 hybrid + rerank), prompt construction, pluggable LLM calls, LangGraph multi-agent orchestration, streaming, evals.
  • Qdrant — the vector DB. Sub-100 ms ANN up to ~10M vectors on one node, filters, payload indexing, open source, identical in dev and prod. (pgvector / Weaviate / Pinecone are alternatives.)
  • LLM provider — pluggable. Azure OpenAI for compliance, OpenAI direct for speed, Anthropic/Bedrock for Claude. Abstracted behind one interface so you swap providers without touching .NET.
  • Observability — not optional. Langfuse for LLM-native tracing; OpenTelemetry for end-to-end distributed tracing.

3. The request flow, end to end

  1. Browser → POST /api/v1/assistant/query with bearer token.
  2. .NET Gateway validates the JWT, checks claims (tenant_id, roles), records the audit event, runs the rate-limit check, redacts PII, then proxies (gRPC) to Python.
  3. Python RAG service embeds the query, searches Qdrant filtered by tenant_id, retrieves top-8 chunks, builds the prompt, calls the LLM with streaming, optionally invokes LangGraph agents, and streams tokens back.
  4. Langfuse records the prompt, retrieved chunks (with scores), the LLM call (model, latency, tokens, cost), and any eval score.
  5. OpenTelemetry records one trace: gateway-auth → rate-limit → grpc-call → embed → qdrant-search → llm-call → response-stream, all sharing one trace_id.
  6. Total round trip in the reference build: 1.4 s to first token, 4.1 s to complete.

4. The .NET API Gateway (Program.cs) 

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(o => {
        o.Authority = builder.Configuration["Auth:Authority"];
        o.Audience  = builder.Configuration["Auth:Audience"];
    });
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

// Tenant-aware token-bucket rate limiting
builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(o => {
    o.GlobalLimiter = PartitionedRateLimiter.Create<HttpContext, string>(ctx => {
        var tenant = ctx.User.FindFirst("tenant_id")?.Value ?? "anonymous";
        return RateLimitPartition.GetTokenBucketLimiter(tenant, _ => new() {
            TokenLimit = 100, TokensPerPeriod = 20,
            ReplenishmentPeriod = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10), QueueLimit = 0,
        });
    });
});

// Typed gRPC client to Python, with retries + circuit breaker
builder.Services.AddGrpcClient<RagService.RagServiceClient>(o => {
    o.Address = new Uri(builder.Configuration["Rag:GrpcUrl"]!);
})
.AddPolicyHandler(HttpPolicyExtensions.HandleTransientHttpError()
    .WaitAndRetryAsync(3, n => TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200 * n)))
.AddPolicyHandler(HttpPolicyExtensions.HandleTransientHttpError()
    .CircuitBreakerAsync(5, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)));

// OpenTelemetry — traces propagate to Python via W3C headers automatically
builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry().WithTracing(t => t
    .SetResourceBuilder(ResourceBuilder.CreateDefault().AddService("api-gateway"))
    .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation().AddHttpClientInstrumentation()
    .AddGrpcClientInstrumentation().AddOtlpExporter());

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAuthentication(); app.UseAuthorization(); app.UseRateLimiter();

app.MapPost("/api/v1/assistant/query", async (
    AssistantQueryRequest req, HttpContext ctx,
    RagService.RagServiceClient rag, ILogger<Program> log) =>
{
    var tenantId = ctx.User.FindFirst("tenant_id")?.Value;
    var userId   = ctx.User.FindFirst("sub")?.Value;
    if (tenantId is null || userId is null) return Results.Unauthorized();

    var sanitized = PiiRedactor.Redact(req.Query); // last place under your control
    var grpcReq = new QueryRequest {
        Query = sanitized, TenantId = tenantId, UserId = userId, TopK = req.TopK ?? 8,
    };
    var resp = await rag.QueryAsync(grpcReq, deadline: DateTime.UtcNow.AddSeconds(30));
    return Results.Ok(new AssistantQueryResponse(
        resp.Answer,
        resp.Citations.Select(c => new Citation(c.SourceId, c.Score)).ToList(),
        resp.TraceId));
}).RequireAuthorization();

app.Run();

Worth noticing: tenant-aware rate limiting keyed by tenant_id (not IP); automatic W3C traceparent propagation so FastAPI's OTel middleware continues the same trace; Polly retries + circuit breaker; and PII redaction before the wire.

4.2 The gRPC contract (rag.proto) 

syntax = "proto3";
package rag.v1;

service RagService {
  rpc Query (QueryRequest)  returns (QueryResponse);
  rpc Ingest (IngestRequest) returns (IngestResponse);
  rpc StreamQuery (QueryRequest) returns (stream StreamToken);
}

message QueryRequest  { string query = 1; string tenant_id = 2; string user_id = 3; int32 top_k = 4; }
message QueryResponse { string answer = 1; repeated Citation citations = 2; string trace_id = 3; }
message Citation      { string source_id = 1; float score = 2; }
message StreamToken   { string text = 1; bool done = 2; }

Both sides generate code from this file. No type drift, no JSON-string guesswork.

5. The Python RAG / Agent service (FastAPI) 

# app/main.py (abridged)
qdrant = QdrantClient(url=os.environ["QDRANT_URL"])
embeddings = AzureOpenAIEmbeddings(azure_deployment="text-embedding-3-small", api_version="2024-10-21")
llm = AzureChatOpenAI(azure_deployment="gpt-4o", api_version="2024-10-21", temperature=0, streaming=True)
vectorstore = Qdrant(client=qdrant, collection_name="docs", embeddings=embeddings)

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
FastAPIInstrumentor.instrument_app(app)  # OTel auto-instrumentation

@app.post("/v1/query", response_model=QueryResponse)
async def query(req: QueryRequest) -> QueryResponse:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("rag.query") as span:
        span.set_attribute("tenant_id", req.tenant_id)
        # Retrieval — Qdrant filtered by tenant for HARD isolation
        docs = await asyncio.to_thread(
            vectorstore.similarity_search_with_score, query=req.query, k=req.top_k,
            filter={"must": [{"key": "tenant_id", "match": {"value": req.tenant_id}}]})
        citations = [Citation(source_id=d.metadata["source_id"], score=float(s)) for d, s in docs]
        context = "\n\n".join(f"[{d.metadata['source_id']}]\n{d.page_content}" for d, _ in docs)
        chain = ({"context": lambda _: context, "query": RunnablePassthrough()}
                 | prompt | llm | StrOutputParser())
        answer = await chain.ainvoke(req.query, config={"callbacks": [lf]})
    return QueryResponse(answer=answer, citations=citations, trace_id=trace_id)

The tenant filter in retrieval is mandatory. Without it, your RAG service leaks documents across tenants.

5.2 The LangGraph agent — planner / tool-user / critic 

# app/agent_graph.py (abridged)
def build_agent_graph(llm, vectorstore):
    g = StateGraph(AgentState)
    g.add_node("plan", plan)        # LLM -> JSON list of tool calls
    g.add_node("execute", execute)  # run sql_query / vector_search tools
    g.add_node("draft", draft)      # synthesise an answer, cite each fact
    g.add_node("critique", critique)# check accuracy / hallucination -> 'OK' or issues
    g.add_node("finalise", finalise)
    g.set_entry_point("plan")
    g.add_edge("plan", "execute"); g.add_edge("execute", "draft"); g.add_edge("draft", "critique")
    g.add_conditional_edges("critique",
        lambda s: "finalise" if "OK" in s["critique"] else "draft",
        {"finalise": "finalise", "draft": "draft"})
    g.add_edge("finalise", END)
    return g.compile()

The plan → execute → draft → critique → finalise loop is a classic agentic pattern; the conditional edge lets it iterate until the answer passes self-review (with a max-iteration guard in real code). Ingestion is just chunk → embed → upsert, with the same tenant_id on every chunk so retrieval filters enforce isolation.

6. Wiring it with Docker Compose 

services:
  gateway:
    build: ./gateway
    ports: ["8080:8080"]              # ONLY the gateway is reachable from outside
    environment:
      Rag__GrpcUrl: "http://rag:50051"
      OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: "http://otel-collector:4317"
    depends_on: [rag, otel-collector]
  rag:
    build: ./rag
    expose: ["50051", "8000"]         # NOT published to host — internal network only
    environment:
      QDRANT_URL: "http://qdrant:6333"
      AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY: "${AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY}"
      LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY: "${LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY}"
    depends_on: [qdrant, otel-collector]
  qdrant:
    image: qdrant/qdrant:latest
    expose: ["6333"]
    volumes: ["qdrant-data:/qdrant/storage"]
volumes: { qdrant-data: {} }

Only the gateway is exposed; Qdrant, the RAG service, and the collector live on the internal Docker network with expose: (not ports:). In Kubernetes: one LoadBalancer for the gateway, ClusterIP for the rest, NetworkPolicies blocking all egress from the RAG namespace except to the LLM provider and Langfuse.

7. Observability — OTel + Langfuse answer different questions

OpenTelemetry — "where is the latency?" One trace for a query:

api-gateway: POST /api/v1/assistant/query        [1420 ms]
├── auth.validate-jwt                              [3 ms]
├── rate-limit.acquire                             [0.4 ms]
├── grpc.call rag.RagService/Query             [1410 ms]
│   └── rag-service: rag.query                  [1395 ms]
│       ├── rag.retrieve -> qdrant.search        [180 ms]
│       └── rag.generate -> azure-openai.chat   [1190 ms]

You see immediately: the LLM took ~85% of wall-clock, Qdrant ~12%, gateway single-digit ms.

Langfuse — "why did the model answer wrong?" The exact prompt (with retrieved chunks), the completion, tokens in/out, cost in USD, model version, and the citations with their scores. When a user says "the bot said our return policy is 60 days, it's 30," you open Langfuse, see that an outdated PDF chunk was retrieved at score 0.78 above the current policy at 0.74 — a concrete, reproducible bug. OTel tells you when something is slow; Langfuse tells you when something is wrong.

Evals — the closed loop 

# tests/eval_rag.py (abridged) — run nightly in CI
scores = {
    "faithfulness":      faithfulness.score(results),
    "answer_relevancy":  answer_relevancy.score(results),
    "context_precision": context_precision.score(results),
}
if scores["faithfulness"] < 0.85:
    raise SystemExit("Faithfulness regression — block deploy")

Change a prompt, swap a model, or tweak chunking, and you catch quality regressions before they ship.

8. What this architecture buys you

Concern How polyglot helps
Existing .NET investment Zero rewrite; the gateway is plain ASP.NET Core
Existing ExtJS UI Untouched; AI arrives as new endpoints
Velocity on AI features Python ships at the speed of LangChain releases
Security & compliance One auth boundary, one audit log, PII redaction at the edge
Multi-tenancy Tenant filter enforced in Qdrant AND in .NET claims
LLM provider switch One Python class; .NET never knew
Debugging OTel for latency, Langfuse for quality, linked by trace_id
Scaling Each service scales independently

9. When NOT to do this

  • Greenfield AI-only product — go pure Python; the polyglot tax is pure overhead with no .NET legacy.
  • Tiny app, single instance — use Semantic Kernel in-process and ship.
  • No observability budget — Langfuse + OTel are not optional here.
  • Hard real-time (<200 ms total) — the gRPC hop + LLM call combine to ~1 s minimum.

10. A 2-week integration plan

Week 1 — boundary: add the ASP.NET Core gateway endpoints (stubbed); wire ExtJS to a chat drawer; author rag.proto and generate both clients.
Week 2 — AI workload: stand up FastAPI + Qdrant in Compose; wire the LangChain RAG chain; add Langfuse + OTel with trace propagation; write 20 eval queries and run them nightly.

After two weeks you have a real, observable, production-shaped polyglot AI stack — and the rest is content, prompts, and evals, which is exactly where you want to spend time.

The mental model: two services, one trust boundary. The .NET side is your enterprise; the Python side is your AI lab. They meet at a contract narrow enough to maintain, typed enough to test, observable enough to debug. Keep the contract narrow, treat observability as a feature, and version everything (prompts, models, gRPC).

This is a condensed version. The full article — with the complete code, the full request-flow walkthrough, and the architecture diagram — is on PrepStack:

→ Polyglot Architecture for Enterprise AI — .NET API Gateway + Python RAG/Agent Service

title: Cómo obtener la tasa oficial del BCV en tu sistema (y los 5 errores que te hacen cobrar mal)
description:
Si tienes una tienda, un sistema administrativo o un punto de venta en Venezuela, tarde o temprano necesitas la tasa oficial del BCV dentro de tu código: para mostrar precios en bolívares, para facturar o para conciliar pagos móviles. El Banco Central no tiene una API, así que todo el mundo termina haciendo lo mismo: leer la página de bcv.org.ve.

Nosotros lo mantenemos en producción para cobrar todos los días. Estos son los detalles que no se ven en el primer intento y que, si los pasas por alto, te hacen cobrar con la tasa equivocada.

1. La tasa de mañana se publica hoy

El BCV publica la tasa por la tarde, y la publica con la Fecha Valor del siguiente día hábil. Si a las 6:00 pm consultas la página y guardas lo que ves con la fecha de hoy, acabas de guardar la tasa de mañana como si fuera la de hoy, y todo lo que cobres esa noche sale con la tasa equivocada.

La regla es simple: guarda cada tasa con su Fecha Valor, nunca con la fecha en que la leíste. En la página, la fecha está en el atributo content de un <span> debajo del bloque del dólar:

<span … content="2026-11-05T00:00:00-04:00">…</span>

Usa el atributo (2026-11-05), no el texto en español.

2. Fines de semana y feriados

El viernes por la tarde sale la tasa del lunes. Entonces, ¿qué tasa vale un sábado? La de Fecha Valor más reciente que no sea posterior a ese día: la del viernes. Para cualquier fecha pasada, la tasa vigente es la de esa fecha o la anterior más cercana. Y para lo que se cobra hoy, decide tú si usas la vigente de hoy o la más reciente ya publicada (nosotros cobramos con la más reciente ya publicada), pero que sea una decisión, no un accidente.

3. Nunca uses float 

0.1 + 0.2        // 0.30000000000000004
893.2173 * 25.5  // puede darte un céntimo de más o de menos al redondear

Con montos pequeños no se nota; con cien facturas al día, sí, y el cuadre de caja nunca da. Multiplica con decimales exactos:

// PHP: bcmath
$bolivares = bcadd(bcmul('25.50', '893.217300', 6), '0.005', 2); // 22777.04

# Python: Decimal
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP
(Decimal("25.50") * Decimal("893.217300")).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), ROUND_HALF_UP)  # 22777.04

En JavaScript, trabaja en enteros con BigInt (céntimos por millonésimas) o usa una librería de decimales. En la base de datos, columnas DECIMAL(18,6), nunca FLOAT.

4. La coma decimal y el punto de miles

La página muestra 1.234,56 (punto de miles, coma decimal). El error clásico es hacer parseFloat("893,21730000") y obtener 893. Primero quita los puntos y después cambia la coma:

$tasa = str_replace(',', '.', str_replace('.', '', '893,21730000')); // "893.21730000"

5. El certificado TLS de bcv.org.ve

El navegador abre la página sin problema, pero curl y PHP fallan con un error de certificado. Al momento de escribir esto, el servidor del BCV envía un certificado intermedio que no corresponde: el navegador busca el correcto por su cuenta y tus scripts no.

La tentación es poner verify => false. No lo hagas: desactivas la protección justo en el dato que usas para cobrar. Descarga el intermedio correcto (Sectigo), guárdalo en tu proyecto y confía solo en él:

Http::withOptions(['verify' => base_path('certs/sectigo-intermedio.pem')])->get('https://www.bcv.org.ve/');

curl --cacert certs/sectigo-intermedio.pem https://www.bcv.org.ve/

Si el BCV cambia de certificado, la consulta va a fallar de forma visible, que es justo lo que quieres.

Y además: el diseño cambia sin aviso

Leer HTML ajeno se rompe cuando el BCV rediseña su página. Dos consejos:

  • Si no encuentras el bloque esperado, lanza un error; nunca guardes un 0 ni la tasa de ayer en silencio.
  • Consulta varias veces por la tarde (por ejemplo, cada hora de 5 a 10 pm) hasta que aparezca la de mañana, y no vuelvas a pedirla cuando ya la tienes.

Si prefieres no mantener esto

Todo lo anterior lo resolvimos en una API pequeña: la tasa del dólar y del euro con su Fecha Valor, la de mañana en cuanto el BCV la publica, consultas por fecha y un webhook opcional que te avisa cuando sale una tasa nueva. Cuesta $3 al mes y los primeros 14 días son gratis: API de la tasa BCV.

curl https://orbitave.com/api/v1/rates/usd-ves -H "Authorization: Bearer $BCV_API_KEY"

Los ejemplos completos en PHP, Node y Python (consulta, conversión sin float y el receptor del webhook con su firma) están en GitHub, con licencia MIT, y te sirven aunque leas la tasa por tu cuenta: vdleon30/api-tasa-bcv.

¿Te topaste con otro detalle de la tasa BCV que no esté aquí? Cuéntalo en los comentarios.

title: I built the fastest e2e framework
description:
That's Playwright's TodoMVC example, 24 tests, same machine, same npx playwright test. Left: 3.65 s. Right: 1.05 s.

I built Flashwright, a fork of Playwright that keeps its API intact while making it blazingly fast!

You can find below benchmarks for nine frameworks on one suite, 18 Playwright scenarios head to head and what I did to make it faster.

Swap it in 

npm i -D @playwright/test@npm:flashwright-test
npx playwright install chromium
npx playwright test

Nine frameworks, one suite

Tool 1 worker 4 workers
Flashwright 2.41 s 1.54 s
Bun test + Bun.WebView 4.39 s 2.80 s
Playwright 4.63 s 3.12 s
Selenium + Mocha 5.48 s 2.77 s
Puppeteer + Jest 6.29 s 2.98 s
Nightwatch 6.45 s 3.38 s
WebdriverIO 10.57 s 4.91 s
Cypress 17.29 s 17.37 s (one spec at a time without Cypress Cloud)
TestCafe 22.55 s 9.28 s

TodoMVC is tiny, so this is mostly measuring the framework. On a slow app the gap could be a smaller.

Playwright's own benches

At least 2× everywhere, 2.86× on average. Whole test command, median of 15 alternating runs, headless Chromium, warm session off (CI mode). Test code untouched.

Scenario Workers Playwright Flashwright Speedup
TodoMVC (24 tests) 1 3670 ms 1011 ms 3.63×
TodoMVC 4 1812 ms 734 ms 2.47×
Click + assertion (15 tests) 1 1611 ms 402 ms 4.01×
Suite with real failures 1 4334 ms 1154 ms 3.76×
Shop app (setup project, 40 ms API) 1 6297 ms 2967 ms 2.12×

Strip out app and server time and Flashwright spends 3–4.5× less than Playwright on framework overhead. Reproduce: node bench/matrix.mjs 15.

Where the time went

Most of a "fast" e2e test isn't your test. It's setup, waiting, and starting over.

Warm context, fresh tab. Playwright opens a new browser context per test, so V8 compiles your app again and again. We keep one context per worker and give each test a new tab, then reset cookies, storage, routes, permissions, downloads, clock, the lot, before the next test. Want Playwright isolation back? isolation: 'strict'.

Waits that listen. Auto-wait used 20–500 ms backoff. We re-check as soon as the page moves. If nothing on the page can still change the DOM (no timers, requests, navigation, animation, workers), failing assertions bail immediately. That failure suite: 4334 ms → 1154 ms.

Input without frame tax. Clicks and hovers don't wait for animations to finish. Hit-target checks still block clicks on the wrong element.

Start work before you need it. Workers and browsers spin up while the CLI reads config. Idle spares hold the context the next test wants. After a failure, a spare is already warm. Slow tests from last run go first when you've got parallelism.

Cheaper cold start. V8 code cache on our bundles, lazy load what this run doesn't need, fewer round trips per action, leaner page scripts.

Screenshots. Faster PNG encode (same pixels). toHaveScreenshot() baselines stay byte-identical to Playwright.

Designed for agentic workflows

Agents don't run the whole suite once. They edit, run one test, edit, run again. Outside CI we keep a warm session: runner, workers, and browsers stay up for five minutes after the last run, contexts reset, renderers warm.

Run, 1.5 s after the previous Playwright Flashwright + warm session
One TodoMVC test 673 ms 240 ms 76 ms (8.9×)
TodoMVC suite, 4 workers 1804 ms 728 ms 508 ms (3.6×)

Fresh processes each run so config and env changes still land. FLASHWRIGHT_SESSION=0 kills it. CI keeps it off.

MCP: playwright mcp --adaptive-settle returns when the page is done, not after a fixed 500 ms. One save-through-API click: 1014 ms → 234 ms.

Dial it back to Playwright when you need to

Defaults favor speed. Per project, file, or describe:

export default defineConfig({
  testOrder: 'file',
  use: {
    waitForAnimations: true,
    failFastWhenIdle: false,
  },
});

test.use({
  instantAnimations: true,
  blockResources: ['image', 'font', 'media'],
});

More knobs (isolation: 'strict', workersPerProcess, locatorPolicy: 'test-id', etc.) and measured effects are in the README.

Compatibility

I ran it against Playwright 1.64.1 on the same box: tests/page 2616/2616 on Chromium, playwright-test / mcp / electron / extension parity, library parity except two internal bookkeeping tests that see recycled contexts, stress 1100/1100 in 20 s vs 49 s.

Links

  • Repo and benches: https://github.com/xcodebeast/flashwright
  • https://flashwright.dev/
  • npm: flashwright-test, flashwright, flashwright-core

If you throw it at a real suite, tell me the before/after. Especially anything that diverges from Playwright. GitHub issues are open.

title: Building an Accessible Architecture Diagram Viewer with Archify, React, and Tailwind CSS
description:
Building an Accessible Architecture Diagram Viewer with Archify, React, and Tailwind CSS

At 2:47 AM, a screen reader user reported they couldn't close your architecture diagram modal—focus was trapped behind the overlay, and the only way out was refreshing the page. Worse, your performance monitoring showed 340ms of layout thrashing every time someone opened a large diagram. These aren't edge cases. They're production failures that stem from treating a diagram renderer as a simple <div> insert when it's actually a complete document with motion, export controls, and its own interaction model.

I evaluated tt-a1i/archify as an external integrator to solve one specific problem: displaying a motion-enabled, self-contained architecture diagram inside a React application without breaking screen reader navigation or forcing repeated layout recalculation. Archify's useful boundary is its generated HTML artifact. The diagram owns rendering, animation, and export. The host application owns routing, permissions, loading state, and the accessible shell around the artifact. Keeping those responsibilities separate prevents a diagram renderer from becoming a second application framework inside your product.

The production failure mode

A common implementation animates diagram container width and height from JavaScript. Every frame, the browser recalculates layout, repaints the viewport, and composites layers. On diagrams with 40+ nodes, this creates visible jank—especially when users resize the preview or change zoom levels.

The second failure is silent but more destructive: a hand-rolled modal often leaves focus behind the overlay. A screen reader user continues navigating the page while the diagram appears open. Pressing Escape may close the visual layer without returning focus to the trigger. The user is now lost in the DOM with no audible indication of where they are.

The following component uses Radix Dialog for focus trapping, Escape handling, focus restoration, and ARIA semantics. Archify's generated HTML is passed as srcDoc, appropriate when the artifact comes from a trusted build step. The iframe receives a meaningful accessible name and a restrictive sandbox. If the diagram needs scripts, allow-scripts is sufficient—avoid adding allow-same-origin unless the artifact genuinely requires it.

import * as Dialog from "@radix-ui/react-dialog";
import { X } from "lucide-react";

type ArchitecturePreviewProps = {
  title: string;
  description?: string;
  html: string;
};

export function ArchitecturePreview({
  title,
  description = "Interactive architecture diagram preview",
  html,
}: ArchitecturePreviewProps) {
  return (
    <Dialog.Root>
      <Dialog.Trigger asChild>
        <button
          type="button"
          className="rounded-md bg-slate-900 px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium text-white
                     shadow-sm transition hover:bg-slate-700 focus:outline-none
                     focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500
                     focus-visible:ring-offset-2"
        >
          Open diagram
        </button>
      </Dialog.Trigger>

      <Dialog.Portal>
        <Dialog.Overlay className="fixed inset-0 z-40 bg-slate-950/70 data-[state=open]:animate-fade-in" />

        <Dialog.Content
          aria-describedby="architecture-preview-description"
          className="fixed inset-4 z-50 flex flex-col overflow-hidden rounded-xl
                     border border-slate-200 bg-white shadow-2xl outline-none
                     sm:inset-8 lg:inset-12"
        >
          <div className="flex items-start justify-between gap-4 border-b border-slate-200 p-4">
            <div>
              <Dialog.Title className="text-base font-semibold text-slate-950">
                {title}
              </Dialog.Title>
              <Dialog.Description
                id="architecture-preview-description"
                className="mt-1 text-sm text-slate-600"
              >
                {description}
              </Dialog.Description>
            </div>

            <Dialog.Close asChild>
              <button
                type="button"
                aria-label="Close diagram preview"
                className="rounded-md p-2 text-slate-500 hover:bg-slate-100
                           hover:text-slate-900 focus:outline-none
                           focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-blue-500"
              >
                <X aria-hidden="true" size={18} />
              </button>
            </Dialog.Close>
          </div>

          <div className="diagram-frame min-h-0 flex-1 bg-slate-50 p-3">
            <iframe
              title={`${title} architecture diagram`}
              srcDoc={html}
              sandbox="allow-scripts"
              loading="lazy"
              className="h-full w-full rounded-lg border border-slate-200 bg-white"
            />
          </div>
        </Dialog.Content>
      </Dialog.Portal>
    </Dialog.Root>
  );
}

The critical detail isn't the modal styling—it's the ownership model. Radix manages interaction state and focus. The iframe isolates Archify's document and prevents diagram styles from leaking into the host application. Tailwind handles the stable shell without requiring JavaScript measurements.

Configuration as an explicit build boundary

Generate the diagram before deployment or in a controlled server-side job, then supply it to the React component as an artifact. A small configuration file makes this boundary reproducible:

# archify.config.yaml
input: ./architecture/system.md
output: ./public/diagrams/system.html
theme: slate
motion:
  enabled: true
  durationMs: 420
  prefersReducedMotion: true
export:
  formats:
    - html
    - svg
  width: 1920
  height: 1080
security:
  sandbox: allow-scripts

The exact command depends on the repository's CLI surface, but the architectural intent remains stable: source content transforms into a self-contained HTML deliverable, and the React application consumes that deliverable rather than reconstructing the diagram at runtime.

CSS micro-interaction without layout thrashing

Use transforms and opacity for interaction feedback. Reserve container queries for responsive behavior inside the component rather than reading element dimensions in JavaScript.

@keyframes fade-in {
  from {
    opacity: 0;
    transform: translateY(0.35rem) scale(0.99);
  }

  to {
    opacity: 1;
    transform: translateY(0) scale(1);
  }
}

@keyframes diagram-pulse {
  0%,
  100% {
    box-shadow: 0 0 0 0 rgb(59 130 246 / 0);
  }

  50% {
    box-shadow: 0 0 0 0.35rem rgb(59 130 246 / 0.12);
  }
}

@container (min-width: 48rem) {
  .diagram-frame {
    padding: 1.25rem;
  }

  .diagram-frame iframe {
    animation: diagram-pulse 2.8s ease-in-out 1;
  }
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .diagram-frame iframe,
  [data-state="open"].data-\[state\=open\]\:animate-fade-in {
    animation: none;
  }
}

In a Tailwind v4 project, register the animation utility in the application stylesheet if it isn't already available:

@theme {
  --animate-fade-in: fade-in 180ms ease-out both;
}

This avoids the tempting but expensive pattern of updating inline width and height on every pointer event. The browser can usually composite transforms without recalculating the entire document layout.

Practical trade-offs

An iframe adds a document boundary and makes cross-document communication less convenient. That's a worthwhile cost when Archify exports a complete HTML experience with its own motion and controls. A direct React renderer would provide tighter state integration, but it would also couple the application to diagram internals and increase the chance of CSS, focus, and lifecycle conflicts.

A trusted srcDoc artifact is also a security boundary only when its generation pipeline is controlled. Don't interpolate user-authored HTML without sanitization. If diagrams are user-generated, sanitize before storage and consider serving them from a separate origin with a restrictive Content Security Policy.

The resulting architecture is deliberately modest: Archify produces the visual artifact, the iframe isolates it, Radix owns modal accessibility, and Tailwind styles the host shell. That separation addresses the real failure modes—layout thrashing and broken focus navigation—without turning a diagram preview into an unmaintainable custom UI subsystem.

The hardest operational dilemma here is deciding when the iframe boundary becomes more costly than direct integration. If your diagrams need bidirectional state sync with the host application—live editing, real-time collaboration, or deep keyboard navigation across diagram nodes—the document boundary starts working against you. At that point, you're building a tightly coupled diagram editor, not a viewer, and the architecture needs to change accordingly.

How are you handling architecture diagram rendering in production applications? Have you hit the layout thrashing ceiling, or are you dealing with something worse—focus traps, memory leaks from unmounted SVG, or accessibility complaints you can't reproduce? I'd like to hear what broke and how you fixed it.

title: GSoC 2026 Mentor Summit: Resilient OSS Communities
description:
by Stephanie Taylor, Google Summer of Code Program Lead

Last weekend, we hosted our annual Google Summer of Code Mentor Summit in Munich, Germany, welcoming 185 attendees representing 133 open source projects across 36 countries. The past year has presented unique challenges for open source communities, particularly with the surge of AI-generated pull requests placing additional strain on maintainers.

The 183 open source organizations participating in GSoC 2026 were at the forefront of these shifts. Each organization establishes its own AI guidelines and governance, and many continue to refine their policies as the technology evolves. Throughout the year, we have actively engaged with our communities to better understand these challenges and support them in identifying effective solutions.

Unsurprisingly, the Mentor Summit’s unconference format (where attendees create the schedule) featured numerous sessions on managing AI within both GSoC and the broader open source ecosystem. While many mentors arrived weary after a demanding season, the event fostered a strong sense of shared purpose. Discussions moved beyond common obstacles to highlight notable successes, with several organizations reporting their most impactful GSoC season yet, driven by dedicated contributors who are now transitioning into active maintainer roles.

Organizations shared a variety of strategies to address AI-assisted contributions, specifically targeting automated pull requests and supporting contributors in understanding underlying system architectures alongside AI-generated code.

Resilience emerged as a central theme of this year's summit. Open source communities have navigated dynamic shifts over the past two decades. The continued vitality and importance of open source in 2026 reflects a forward-looking mindset: one grounded in experimentation, adaptation, and continuous improvement.

For our GSoC team, the Mentor Summit underscored the remarkable collaboration across open source. Observing mentors from diverse projects exchange practical tools, workflows, and insights highlights the value of gathering community leaders to strengthen the broader ecosystem.

A huge thanks to all of the GSoC Mentors and Organization Administrators who joined us in Munich, as well as the more than 1,800 mentors worldwide who guided our 2026 contributors. Google Summer of Code wrapped up its 22nd year this week thanks to the dedication and leadership of this global community.

title: How to test docs code examples that need API keys (without leaking secrets)
description:
Code examples that need credentials are difficult to test in a clean documentation scan. A valid run may depend on access the scanner should not assume it has. But a missing key does not automatically mean the documentation is broken: a reader who cannot tell where to put their key has a documentation problem.

A practical approach is to split credential-dependent examples into layers:

  • Check syntax.
  • Test request construction and response parsing offline.
  • Run the live call separately with an authorized test-mode or sandbox account.

Use a clearly named environment variable, explain how readers obtain and provide their own value, and report skipped live calls as gaps in coverage.

Make the credential boundary clear

An API example may promise several things at once: that a package installs, a client can be configured, a request has the right shape, a key is accepted, an account has access, and a response can be parsed. A failed live call does not immediately show which promise failed.

A clean documentation check may not have a key. A forked pull request may run without repository secrets. A sandbox account may also be unavailable or lack a needed permission. Those conditions should be visible in test results, but they do not automatically establish that the example is wrong.

Start by showing readers exactly how the credential enters the example. This complete Python program reads a fictional Acme SDK credential without embedding or printing a key:

import os

api_key = os.environ.get("ACME_API_KEY")
if api_key:
    print("A key is configured")
else:
    print("Set ACME_API_KEY to run the live example")

ACME_API_KEY and the Acme SDK are fictional names. The program reports only whether a value is present. If you use a placeholder such as YOUR_API_KEY or <API_KEY>, explain which value replaces it and where the reader supplies it. A realistic-looking fake key can be mistaken for a real credential and is harder to distinguish from one.

State whether the value is a test-mode key, which environment variable the example reads, and which account or permission the live call requires. A placeholder alone does not explain how to configure the example.

Test what you can offline

Separate local work from the external call. Depending on the SDK, client construction can be local even when the client eventually needs credentials. Request building and parsing a recorded response can often be tested without contacting the service. If the SDK validates or contacts the service during construction, treat construction as part of the live boundary.

The test layers answer different questions:

Layer What it establishes What it does not establish
Syntax only The selected source parses Imports, behavior, authentication, or service access work
Offline stub or recorded fixture Local request and response handling work for the tested case The real service accepts the key or currently returns that response
Live sandbox call The tested account and service path work at that time Every account, permission, or production condition works

Make the offline test meaningful: build the same request shape as the live client, return a representative response, and assert the fields the documentation promises. Keep fixtures sanitized and free of real credentials and private customer data.

For example, this single file uses only the Python 3.12 standard library. It starts a local HTTP stub, sends a request, parses a canned JSON response, checks the result, and shuts the server down. It contacts no external API. Save it as offline_example.py:

import json
import os
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


class StubHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path != "/v1/greeting":
            self.send_error(404)
            return

        body = json.dumps({"message": "Hello from the stub"}).encode("utf-8")
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

    def log_message(self, format, *args):
        pass


def fetch_greeting(base_url):
    api_key = os.environ.get("ACME_API_KEY", "offline-placeholder")
    request = Request(
        base_url + "/v1/greeting",
        headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + api_key},
    )
    with urlopen(request, timeout=5) as response:
        return json.load(response)


def main():
    server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), StubHandler)
    thread = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
    thread.start()
    try:
        host, port = server.server_address
        result = fetch_greeting(f"http://{host}:{port}")
        assert result["message"] == "Hello from the stub"
        print(result["message"])
    finally:
        server.shutdown()
        thread.join()
        server.server_close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it with:

python3 offline_example.py

It prints:

Hello from the stub

The default value is an offline placeholder. The stub does not validate it, so the example does not prove that a service accepts any credential. A recorded fixture is another offline option: load a representative, sanitized response and assert the parsing result. A fixture can exercise parsing; a local stub can also exercise request construction and status handling. Neither replaces a live authentication check.

Skip live tests clearly

When the key is absent, make the live test’s skip visible. This shell script exits successfully with a clear message and makes no network request:

if [ -z "${ACME_API_KEY:-}" ]; then
  printf '%s\n' 'SKIP: ACME_API_KEY is not set'
  exit 0
fi

printf '%s\n' 'Credential is present; run the authorized live test here'

Replace the final message with your project’s live-test command after configuring an authorized sandbox. A successful job that skipped the live call is not evidence that the call passed.

For a pytest suite, this complete test file demonstrates the skip condition without making a real API call. Save it as test_live_example.py:

import os

import pytest


@pytest.mark.skipif(
    not os.environ.get("ACME_API_KEY"),
    reason="ACME_API_KEY is required for the authorized live test",
)
def test_live_configuration_is_present():
    assert os.environ.get("ACME_API_KEY")

When the variable is absent, pytest reports a skip. When it is present, this demonstration checks only that a value exists; replace the body with an authorized sandbox call and assertions to verify live behavior. Do not print the key in failure messages, command traces, HTTP logs, or test artifacts.

Set CI up around trust

Store the sandbox credential in the CI platform’s secret store and map it to a job-level environment variable for the live job. A practical workflow has an offline job for ordinary changes and a live job or step that runs only when the authorized secret is available. Report a skip when it cannot run.

GitHub’s secrets documentation says secrets cannot be referenced directly in an if: conditional. Map the secret to a job-level environment variable, then check that variable in the step condition. With the exception documented for GITHUB_TOKEN, secrets are not passed to runners for workflows triggered from forks. Keep syntax and offline tests available there, and arrange the live check in an authorized context rather than making it a required check on fork pull requests.

Mask sensitive values in logs, and check shell tracing, HTTP debugging, exception messages, and uploaded artifacts as well as normal test output. Never deliberately print keys.

Triage results by what they show

A needs-credentials finding says the scan cannot establish a live result without credentials. It is not, by itself, a docs-bug classification. Human review may still find a documentation problem, such as a placeholder readers cannot map to the required configuration.

A sandbox response of 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden needs investigation. It can result from a missing or invalid key, insufficient account permissions, or a setup mismatch. Check the authorized account, permissions, endpoint, and documented setup; preserve sanitized evidence without recording the key.

Keep the coverage outcome explicit:

  • Offline checks passed and the live test passed.
  • Offline checks passed and the live test was skipped because no credential was available.
  • Offline checks passed and the live test failed with an authentication or service response.
  • Syntax failed before either behavioral layer could run.

These outcomes call for different reviews. If a release requires live verification, arrange an authorized run before treating that requirement as met.

DocsAlive detects certain secret reads and placeholders, classifies credential-dependent blocks, and does not run them with customer-provided test credentials.

Disclosure: I'm on the DocsAlive team; this article is adapted from our guide at https://docsalive.com/guides/credentials-docs-examples-testing/ and was drafted with AI assistance, then checked by us.

title: vLLM Prefix Caching: One Timestamp Dropped My Hit Rate From 89% to 3%
description:
On Tuesday my support bot's time to first token roughly tripled, and nobody had touched the model, the GPU, or vLLM.

The only change in the deploy was one helpful line at the top of the system prompt:

Current date and time: 2026-10-27T14:03:22Z

That line cost me almost all of my vLLM prefix caching. The server's stats line went from a prefix cache hit rate around 89% to around 3%. Every request was now prefilling a 2,400-token system prompt from scratch, because the timestamp at token 8 made every request look brand new to the cache.

This post explains the mechanism: how vLLM prefix caching decides what counts as "the same prefix", why one changed token near the top throws away everything after it, and how I order prompts now.

TL;DR

  • vLLM prefix caching (Automatic Prefix Caching, APC) reuses KV cache blocks only for an exact token prefix. Matching content further down the prompt doesn't count.
  • The prompt is split into fixed-size blocks (16 tokens by default). Each block's hash includes the hash of the block before it, so one changed token invalidates that block and every block after it.
  • A timestamp, request ID, user name, or shuffled tool list near the top of the prompt drops your hit rate to roughly zero, even if 99% of the text is identical.
  • Fix: put static content first (instructions, tool schemas, few-shot examples), volatile content last, and coarsen anything time-based to the granularity you actually need.
  • Check it with a tokenizer diff: find the first divergent token between two real requests and divide by the block size. That number is how many blocks can be reused.

What does vLLM prefix caching actually cache?

vLLM prefix caching stores the KV cache blocks computed during prefill and reuses them when a new request starts with the exact same tokens. It doesn't cache text, embeddings or responses. It caches the attention keys and values for full blocks of tokens.

vLLM's PagedAttention already stores KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like pages in virtual memory. Prefix caching gives each full block an identity so that a later request can point at an existing physical block instead of computing it again.

On my setup (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, one GPU, recent vLLM where prefix caching is on by default), the relevant knobs look like this:

vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --block-size 16

The flag is explicit here so the intent is obvious to the next person. The block size is the number that matters for everything below.

Why does one changed token break the whole prefix cache?

Because block hashes are chained. A block's identity is not "these 16 tokens". It is "these 16 tokens, following exactly this history".

Simplified, the hashing works like this:

BLOCK = 16

def block_hashes(token_ids, extra_keys=None):
    parent = None
    hashes = []
    for start in range(0, len(token_ids), BLOCK):
        block = tuple(token_ids[start:start + BLOCK])
        if len(block) < BLOCK:
            break  # partial blocks are never cached
        h = hash((parent, block, extra_keys))
        hashes.append(h)
        parent = h  # the next block inherits this block's identity
    return hashes

extra_keys covers things like a LoRA adapter ID or multimodal inputs, so two requests with identical text but different adapters don't share KV.

This isn't a lazy implementation choice. It falls out of how attention works. The key and value vectors at position 500 depend on every token at positions 0 through 499, because each layer's hidden state at position 500 has attended to all of them. If token 8 changes, the KV for token 500 is genuinely different math. Reusing it would give you wrong outputs, not just slow ones.

So the chain is the correctness guarantee. And it means the cache only ever matches from the start.

How many blocks did my timestamp actually cost?

All of them. My system prompt was about 2,400 tokens: instructions, eight tool schemas as JSON, and four few-shot examples. With a block size of 16, that's 150 full blocks.

Where the timestamp sits First divergent token Reusable blocks
Top of system prompt ~8 (after chat template header) 0 of 150
End of system prompt ~2,390 149 of 150
In the user message after the system prompt 150 of 150

At the top, block 0 differs between any two requests that land in different seconds. Block 0's hash changes, which changes block 1's parent, which changes block 1's hash, and so on down the chain. 150 blocks recomputed per request.

The 3% residual hit rate I saw was requests that happened to arrive within the same second, plus multi-turn conversations re-reading their own earlier turns.

How do I find what's breaking my prefix cache?

Diff the token IDs of two real requests, not the strings. Strings hide the problem: chat templates inject headers, whitespace normalizes differently, and JSON serialization can reorder keys before you ever see the text.

This is the script I keep around now:

from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct")
BLOCK = 16

def ids(messages, tools=None):
    return tok.apply_chat_template(
        messages, tools=tools, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True
    )

def first_divergence(a, b):
    for i, (x, y) in enumerate(zip(a, b)):
        if x != y:
            return i
    return min(len(a), len(b))

a = ids(request_1["messages"], request_1.get("tools"))
b = ids(request_2["messages"], request_2.get("tools"))
i = first_divergence(a, b)

print(f"diverge at token {i}")
print(f"reusable blocks: {i // BLOCK} of {len(a) // BLOCK}")
print("context:", repr(tok.decode(a[max(0, i - 10):i + 10])))

Grab two logged requests from different users a few minutes apart and run it. If the divergence index is small, the context line shows you the exact culprit.

When I ran it after fixing the timestamp, it caught a second problem I hadn't noticed.

What else silently breaks prefix caching?

Anything that varies per request and sits before your large static content. The ones I've hit or seen in other people's code:

  1. Timestamps with seconds. The classic. Most prompts need the date, not the second.
  2. User name or account tier in the first line. "You are helping Dana, a Pro customer" means every user has a private cache. Fine for a chatbot with long conversations, terrible for a high-volume classifier.
  3. Tool schemas built from a set or a dict merged in a different order. This was my second bug. Tools were assembled from two plugin registries, and the merge order depended on which registry finished loading first. Same tools, different token sequence, about half the time.
  4. Retrieved RAG passages placed before the instructions. Retrieval output changes every request. If it comes first, your long instruction block never gets reused.
  5. Per-request IDs or trace tags pasted into the prompt "for debugging".
  6. Random few-shot sampling. Rotating examples per request is a valid technique, but it costs you the cache from the first rotated example onward.

None of these throw errors. Responses stay correct. You just pay full prefill on every request and wonder why latency climbs under load.

How should I order a prompt for vLLM prefix caching?

Order it from most stable to least stable. The cache rewards you for every token of shared prefix and gives you nothing for shared content after the first difference.

The layout I use now:

STATIC_SYSTEM = load("instructions.md")           # never changes per deploy
TOOLS = sorted(all_tools, key=lambda t: t["name"])  # deterministic order
FEWSHOT = load("examples.md")                     # fixed set

def build_messages(user_msg, user, retrieved):
    system = (
        STATIC_SYSTEM
        + "\n\n" + FEWSHOT
        + f"\n\nToday's date: {date.today().isoformat()}"  # day, not second
    )
    context = "\n\n".join(p.text for p in retrieved)
    return [
        {"role": "system", "content": system},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Customer: {user.name} ({user.tier})\n\n"
                                    f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {user_msg}"},
    ], TOOLS

Three changes did the work:

  • Date moved to the end of the system prompt, coarsened to the day. The whole system block now matches for everyone, all day. At midnight the last block or two change, and that's it.
  • Tools sorted by name. Deterministic serialization, same token IDs every time.
  • User identity and retrieval moved into the user turn. They still reach the model; they just stop poisoning the shared prefix.

After the deploy, the hit rate went back to the high 80s and TTFT returned to where it had been before Tuesday.

Does this apply to hosted APIs too?

Yes, the same prefix rule applies to hosted prompt caching. Anthropic's prompt caching matches an exact prefix up to the cache_control breakpoints you set, and OpenAI's automatic caching also matches on the prompt prefix. Neither can reuse anything after the first difference, for the same attention reason as vLLM.

The difference is that hosted APIs cache less finely than vLLM's 16-token blocks and add minimum lengths, so a volatile line near the top costs you the same way, just billed per token instead of shown in TTFT.

Things to check before you blame the cache

Not every low hit rate means a prompt-order bug:

  • Eviction under memory pressure. Cached blocks live in free KV memory and get evicted when running requests need the space. A high-concurrency spike can lower hit rate even with perfect prompts.
  • Different LoRA adapters don't share blocks, by design.
  • Short prompts. Anything under one full block never gets cached at all.

If the token-diff script shows a late divergence and the hit rate is still low, look at memory and concurrency next.

So why did one timestamp kill my vLLM prefix caching?

vLLM prefix caching only reuses KV cache blocks that match an exact token prefix, and each block's hash includes the hash of the block before it. A timestamp near the top of the system prompt changed block 0 on every request, which changed the identity of all 150 blocks after it, so the server recomputed the full 2,400-token prefix on every call and the hit rate fell from about 89% to about 3%. The fix is to order prompts from most stable to least stable: static instructions, sorted tool schemas and fixed examples first, then a day-level date, with user identity and retrieved context in the user turn. Then verify by diffing the token IDs of two real requests and checking where they first diverge.
