title: How to stop duplicate payment callbacks from double-crediting orders (Indonesia QRIS & virtual accounts)
description:
A customer pays, the order becomes paid, and your webhook endpoint loses its connection before the acknowledgement reaches the provider. The provider sends the notification again. Nothing unusual has happened to the payment, but your application now has another opportunity to credit the customer.

This is the failure sequence I would start with when reviewing a QRIS or virtual account integration. It is a hypothetical example, not a reported production incident. Its value is that every component can behave reasonably while the combined system still produces a duplicate credit.

The design question is simple: which durable record prevents a second delivery from causing a second business effect?

Separate the delivery from the payment

A webhook delivery is a message about a payment. It is not itself a new payment, and its arrival time does not establish the order of payment events.

Keep separate identifiers for the merchant order, provider transaction, and notification event where available. Scope provider identifiers to the integration and merchant account unless the documented contract guarantees a wider uniqueness scope.

An event identifier helps detect repeated messages. A provider transaction reference helps identify the money movement. An order identifier ties that movement to your business obligation. These keys answer different questions; replacing them all with one orderId makes reconciliation harder.

For QRIS and virtual accounts, also confirm how the approved integration maps instructions to orders. Do not assume that a QR instruction is reusable or that a virtual account identifies exactly one invoice. A reusable account number alone is an unsafe deduplication key.

Put the invariant in the database

The invariant for a single-payment order is: one accepted payment can create at most one order credit. For split payments or other models, define a different explicit invariant before writing the handler.

A memory cache cannot enforce this across restarts and multiple workers. A database query followed by an unconditional insert also leaves a race: two workers can both observe that no credit exists.

Use database constraints and a transaction around the business mutation. A useful minimal design includes a webhook inbox, a payment allocation record, an order credit ledger, and an outbox for downstream fulfilment. Give each its own uniqueness rule. The inbox can have a unique event key; the order credit should have a unique business key such as (order_id, credit_kind).

The payment allocation also needs a constraint preventing the same scoped provider transaction from being assigned to two orders. Otherwise, order-level protection can still allow one payment to fund two purchases.

Authenticate first, then commit the decision

Verify the provider's documented webhook authentication before trusting the payload. Preserve raw request bytes if signature verification requires them. Validate the merchant account, order mapping, amount, currency, and payment status against your records.

Do not invent a universal signature header, success status, or acknowledgement body. Those are integration contracts. The following Node-style pseudocode deliberately hides them behind adapter functions:

async function webhook(req, res) {
  const event = adapter.verifyAndNormalize(req.rawBody, req.headers);
  // Adapter rejects unauthenticated or malformed input.

  await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const fresh = await tx.inbox.insertIfAbsent(event);
    // Uses a stable, scoped event ID if the contract provides one.
    if (!fresh) return;

    const order = await tx.orders.lockForUpdate(event.orderId);
    const decision = validatePaymentForOrder(event, order);
    if (!decision.accepted) {
      await tx.exceptions.record(event, decision.reason);
      return;
    }

    if (order.creditPosted) {
      // Different payment references need review, not another credit.
      await tx.payments.recordObservation(event, order);
      return;
    }

    await tx.allocations.claimUniquePayment(event, order.id);
    await tx.ledger.insertUniqueOrderCredit(order, event);
    await tx.orders.markPaid(order.id, event.paymentRef);
    await tx.outbox.insertUnique({
      key: `fulfil:${order.id}`,
      type: "FULFIL_ORDER",
      orderId: order.id
    });
  });

  adapter.sendDocumentedAcknowledgement(res);
}

These helpers imply actual SQL constraints, row locking, and conflict handling, not merely application checks. validatePaymentForOrder must reject ineligible states and unverified success claims. An allocation conflict must roll back the transaction and enter a durable investigation path; it must never fall through to a credit.

When no stable event ID exists, store delivery observations without pretending a generated local ID detects duplicates. Payment allocation and order credit constraints remain the business protection. A payload hash alone is not a reliable payment identity.

Acknowledgement is a durability boundary

Return the documented acknowledgement once the event and its disposition are durable. An authenticated amount mismatch can be recorded for investigation without accepting it as a valid credit. Invalid authentication should follow the integration's rejection procedure.

If the transaction fails, do not send a success acknowledgement claiming the work was stored. Use the provider's documented error behavior and your recovery process. Conversely, if the commit succeeds and the response disappears, the next delivery should find durable evidence and receive the normal acknowledgement without another credit.

Keep slow fulfilment outside the webhook transaction. The outbox closes the gap between committing the order and scheduling that work. Its consumer still needs idempotency: a worker can perform an action and crash before recording completion. Pass the stable fulfilment key to an idempotent downstream operation, or provide a recovery procedure for uncertain side effects.

Do not erase a second real payment

Two callbacks with the same transaction reference may describe one payment. Two distinct transaction references for one order may describe two payments. Suppressing both as “already paid” would hide money that finance needs to account for.

Record the additional payment observation and reconcile it through the approved query or reporting process. An extra payment does not authorize another fulfilment, and it should not trigger an automatic refund based only on an unfamiliar callback.

Similarly, an old pending notification must not downgrade a verified paid order. Refunds and reversals belong to explicit lifecycle transitions with their own ledger adjustments. A status field that accepts whichever message arrived last is not a payment state machine.

Test the spaces between successful steps

I would make the test harness pause at the commit boundary, then kill the connection before the acknowledgement. Replay the same verified event and inspect the ledger, order, outbox, and acknowledgement together.

Also send concurrent deliveries to separate workers. Deliver two different event IDs for the same transaction. Send an older pending event after success. Try a second transaction for the same order, an amount mismatch, and a reused transaction reference against another order.

The expected result is more precise than “the endpoint returned success”: one valid order credit, one intended fulfilment, preserved evidence for exceptions, and no silent state regression.

Finally, make missing callbacks recoverable. A reconciliation job should compare provider records with local payments and orders, then route verified differences through the same guarded transition logic. Separate provider-pending payments, missing notifications, and failures to apply a received notification in operational views. They require different investigations.

A useful support record contains scoped references, amount, currency, event and receipt timestamps, verification outcome, and processing disposition. Keep secrets and full customer banking details out of ordinary logs.

For a compact checklist to use during implementation review, PAYJN's guide to handling duplicate payment webhook events covers acknowledgement, order credit protection, and conflicting notifications.

title: Implementing Game Receipt Uploads in 2026: Object Storage CORS Beyond Presigned PUT
description:
For a game receipt that must remain available for audit, the important constraint is who controls the first network hop. Short answer: route the upload through your application backend unless you have verified bucket CORS for every browser origin and request header; a presigned PUT authorizes storage, but it does not exempt the browser from CORS preflight.

That choice adds a hop. It also puts content validation, size limits, authentication, and the durable object key in one place. For small avatars and receipt images, I prefer that boring failure domain over a browser path whose authorization can be valid while the browser still refuses to send a byte.

No bytes moved.

The incident pattern is easy to misread: the application successfully obtains a signed URL, a command-line client can upload to it, and the browser reports a CORS error. The invariant is that storage authorization and browser permission are separate checks. The signature answers whether storage will accept a request. Preflight asks whether JavaScript at one origin may make that cross-origin request with a particular method and set of headers.

Why can a browser direct upload to object storage fail before a presigned PUT?

A browser may send an OPTIONS preflight before the signed PUT. It does this when the request isn't CORS-safelisted, which is common when an upload uses PUT or application-selected headers. The browser checks the preflight response against the page origin, requested method, and requested headers. If those don't match the bucket's CORS policy, the actual upload never starts. A valid signature can't repair that mismatch because the two decisions happen at different layers.

This explains the maddening split between a successful command-line test and a failed web page. A command-line HTTP client doesn't enforce the browser's same-origin policy. Testing only with such a client proves that the signature and storage request can work; it does not prove that https://game.example or https://eu.game.example is permitted to issue it.

Treat the browser's network trace as an evidence chain. Consider a receipt screen loaded from https://eu.game.example that asks an application endpoint for a signed upload, then intends to send PUT with Content-Type: image/png to storage. The signed-URL request can finish normally. Next, the browser constructs an OPTIONS request carrying the page origin, PUT as the requested method, and content-type as a requested header. If the storage response does not authorize that exact combination, developer tools may display a CORS-policy message beside the preflight while showing no subsequent PUT. Looking at the signature expiry, object key, or upload body at that point wastes incident time: storage has not evaluated those parts of the intended write. Start with the network waterfall, separate the preflight from the write, and record the precise page origin. Only after an accepted preflight followed by a rejected PUT should the runbook move on to signature scope or storage authorization.

That ordering matters.

The request should stay minimal if direct upload is used. Don't add headers casually after signing, and make the method, content type, and allowed origin part of the test matrix. US and EU deployment labels aren't CORS identities by themselves — exact origins are. A regional frontend at a different scheme, host, or port is another origin even when both deployments belong to the same game.

For the storage abstraction considered here, the bucket model mentions cors_rules, but self-service configuration isn't exposed in the supported workflow. That boundary determines the recommendation. It is not evidence that presigned URLs are generally unsuitable; it means this particular direct-browser design depends on a control the application team cannot reliably own.

Assign ownership at every trust boundary

Access control and delivery simplicity pull in opposite directions. Browser-to-storage removes a backend data hop, but it makes bucket CORS part of the application's release surface. Backend-mediated upload costs bandwidth and capacity on the application tier, but it gives the service one enforcement point and keeps storage credentials and vendor behavior out of browser code.

Option Delivery path Control point Best fit The catch
Backend-mediated upload Browser to app to private storage Application validates identity, type, size, and key Small audit artifacts and teams that want one runbook The app carries every uploaded byte and must be capacity-planned
Direct Amazon S3 integration Browser to S3 Application plus native bucket policy and CORS configuration Teams prepared to own an S3-specific contract Provider-specific policy and signing behavior enter application code
Direct Cloudflare R2 integration Browser to R2 Application plus native provider configuration Edge-oriented systems already operating R2 directly The team owns that direct integration and its browser test matrix
Direct Alibaba Cloud OSS or Tencent COS integration Browser to the selected service Application plus the selected provider's controls Regional stacks standardized on OSS or COS Switching providers means revisiting the direct contract
Stable storage abstraction Backend to a private object API Application owns admission; the abstraction owns provider selection Systems that value a fixed application contract It is not suitable when the browser must upload directly and the team needs self-managed CORS

Infrai fits the last row when the useful property is one plain REST API and one key across backend capabilities: S3, R2, OSS, or COS can sit behind the storage contract without forcing application code to change. That is a sound operational reason to use it for backend-mediated receipt ingestion. It is not a reason to force it into direct browser delivery.

Ownership beats hope.

Keep the stored object private. This storage does not offer public-read, and public_url remains null, so it isn't a fit for permanent public image links or static-site hosting. An avatar display path should obtain time-limited access through the application rather than treating the original audit file as a public asset. Separating an audit original from a derived display avatar also leaves room for scanning and transformation without rewriting the evidence object.

Enforce the evidence boundary in Go

The following server accepts the browser upload on the application's own origin, limits it to 8 MiB, verifies an allowlisted detected media type, derives the object key from the bytes, and performs one authenticated private write. The content hash matters: retrying identical content targets the same key, while changed content cannot silently replace the earlier object under that key. This is an idempotency reflex, not an optimization.

The handler uses exactly one storage route. It sends the platform credential only to the private API, never to a presigned URL, and it retries 429 responses using Retry-After when supplied. Set STORAGE_API_BASE to the API base in deployment; keeping it in configuration also makes the fixed contract visible at the boundary.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const maxReceiptBytes = 8 << 20

var allowedTypes = map[string]bool{
    "application/pdf": true,
    "image/jpeg":      true,
    "image/png":       true,
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/receipt-upload", uploadReceipt)
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

func uploadReceipt(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPut {
        http.Error(w, "method must be PUT", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
        return
    }

    body, err := io.ReadAll(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxReceiptBytes))
    if err != nil || len(body) == 0 {
        http.Error(w, "receipt is empty or exceeds 8 MiB", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }
    mediaType := http.DetectContentType(body)
    if !allowedTypes[mediaType] {
        http.Error(w, "receipt type is not allowed", http.StatusUnsupportedMediaType)
        return
    }

    sum := sha256.Sum256(body)
    key := "receipt-" + hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
    if err := putPrivateObject(r.Context(), key, mediaType, body); err != nil {
        log.Printf("receipt store failed: %v", err)
        http.Error(w, "receipt could not be stored", http.StatusBadGateway)
        return
    }

    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)
    fmt.Fprintf(w, `{"object_key":%q}`, key)
}

func putPrivateObject(ctx context.Context, key, mediaType string, body []byte) error {
    base := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("STORAGE_API_BASE"), "/")
    bucket := os.Getenv("RECEIPT_BUCKET")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if base == "" || bucket == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("storage configuration is incomplete")
    }

    endpoint := base + "/storage/object/put/" +
        url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + url.PathEscape(key)
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPut, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", mediaType)
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 64<<10))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("storage returned %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(responseBody)))
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry limit reached")
}

Run this behind the same site origin as the game client, authenticate the player before the handler, and associate the returned object key with the receipt record in a database transaction. The example deliberately does not trust the browser's Content-Type; it detects the bytes. In production, also apply authorization, malware scanning, and per-account quotas appropriate to the threat model. OWASP's upload guidance is the right checklist for those controls.

There is still a transaction boundary between object storage and the receipt record. Don't pretend otherwise. A practical reconciliation job can find database records awaiting an object write and retry the same content-derived key, while an expiry policy handles abandoned objects later. Because lifecycle expiry has a minimum of one day here, it cannot provide hour-level cleanup.

Write that into the runbook.

Which requirements disqualify this receipt design?

This design is for bounded files where backend bandwidth is acceptable. Stick with a direct S3, R2, OSS, or COS integration when removing the application data hop is more important and your team can configure, test, and monitor the provider's CORS rules. The acceptance test must run in a real browser from every production origin; a successful command-line PUT is not enough.

Choose a different retention system when the receipt must be immutable under a regulatory WORM policy. This storage has no object versioning or object lock, and an accidental overwrite cannot be recovered. It also has no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database coordinator. Content-addressed keys reduce the overwrite risk in this example, but they do not create a legal retention guarantee.

The same caution applies to geography. There is no automatic cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration tool in this storage abstraction, and its vendor coverage excludes GCS and B2. If the audit policy requires autonomous US/EU replicas, make replication an explicit external workflow or select a provider whose native retention and replication controls satisfy the policy. I'm not sure which choice fits without the actual retention period, residency rule, expected upload rate, and maximum file size; those four values should settle the architecture review.

The runbook test is short: submit an allowed file, retry the identical bytes, reject an oversized body, reject a disguised type, and verify the database points to the hash-derived private object. For a direct path, add successful and denied preflights from each exact origin. Those checks exercise the boundary that matters instead of merely proving a URL was signed.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: AI-Assisted Development Cost Reduction 2026: Real Savings & Pitfalls
description:
Originally published at nlocoding.com

Revolut slashed its AI inference costs by up to 90% within a year by switching from Anthropic Claude to self-hosted Z.ai GLM models. Lead-time productivity jumped 70% and coding-time productivity rose 60% in the same overhaul.[1]

AI-assisted development cost reduction is measurable—and urgent

AI-assisted development cost reduction 2026 isn't a boardroom fantasy. Deloitte reports that 28% of organizations saw AI-driven revenue growth, a leap from 20% just earlier in 2026.[2] That’s not just a handful of tech unicorns. The pressure is on: as token costs spike, 89% of enterprises pulled back on AI deployments, and nearly half shifted workloads to contain costs.[5] AI can save big—but it can also bleed your budget dry if you’re not watching the right line items.

90%AI inference cost reduction at Revolut in under 1 year

Most organizations get AI cost reduction wrong: hidden expenses derail savings

AI tools like GitHub Copilot and Cursor advertise massive productivity gains—Cursor's 30,000 Nvidia engineers now produce three times as much code after going AI-assisted.[3] But the sticker price never tells the whole story. Hidden costs lurk: infrastructure, self-hosting, and token usage fees can eat any savings before you notice.

IBM found that 79% of executives report productivity gains from AI, but only 29% can measure ROI with confidence.[4] If your dashboard only shows monthly subscriptions and not the spike from a busy sprint, you’re flying blind. The actionable fix? Track both direct tool costs and secondary infrastructure bills—otherwise, you’ll fall into the same trap as nearly nine out of ten enterprises who had to scale back.[5]

⚠️Common Mistake: Ignoring infrastructure and token costs means you risk burning through your budget even if headline tool prices look low.

The data shows that self-hosting AI models can cut costs dramatically

Revolut’s decision to replace Anthropic Claude with self-hosted GLM models from Z.ai didn’t just trim costs—it decimated them. The company reduced AI inference expenses by up to 90% in less than a year, while boosting lead-time productivity by 70% and coding-time by 60%.[1]

This isn’t the usual SaaS trick of squeezing a few percent here and there. Self-hosting, if you have the engineering muscle, can transform your entire cost structure. But here’s the reality: self-hosting means you own the risk, the ops, and the security headaches. It’s not for everyone. If you’re paying cloud fees and running at scale, running your own models is worth a hard look—just don’t kid yourself about the complexity.

💡Pro Tip: If internal expertise is thin, hybrid strategies—using managed AI for experimentation and self-hosting for production—can yield savings without full-on ops chaos.

AI-native firms save clients 30–50% on development in 2026

AI-native development companies claim 30–50% client savings compared to traditional hiring.[6] That’s not just about replacing humans with bots—developers using GitHub Copilot complete coding tasks 55% faster, with AI saving 30–60% of coding time.[6] The question is, where do those savings come from?

It’s not about firing your engineers. The real advantage is automating repetitive tasks, speeding up code reviews, and catching bugs before they become six-figure disasters. But the human layer remains: AI is a productivity multiplier, not a replacement. The firms that win are the ones who build teams that work with AI, not around it.

50%Development cost savings for AI-native firms vs. traditional

AI tool pricing in 2026: what you pay—and what you miss

AI coding tools in 2026 come with a buffet of free and paid plans. Cursor starts free, with Pro at $20/month, Pro+ at $60, and Ultra at $200. Teams pay $40/user/month for Standard and $120 for Premium.[7] GitHub Copilot’s Pro is $10/month, Business is $19, and Enterprise is $39 per user per month.[7] Claude Code, bundled with Claude Pro, is $20/month. Devin Desktop’s Pro plan is $20/month.[10] Pricing is transparent—but usage-based fees can cascade quickly.

Here’s what most people miss: the real price is not in the monthly license, but in unpredictable consumption. As Cloudera reported, 89% of enterprises scaled back AI deployments due to volatile token costs, not because of subscription sticker shock.[5]

Tool Free Tier Pro/Entry Price Team/Business Price
Cursor Yes $20/month $40–$120/user/month
GitHub Copilot No $10/month $19–$39/user/month
Claude Code No $20/month —
Devin Desktop Yes $20/month —

Productivity gains are real, but cost predictability isn’t

Nvidia’s 30,000 engineers using Cursor now produce three times as much code as before adopting AI-assisted workflows.[3] That is a seismic shift in developer output, the kind that changes product timelines, hiring needs, and even company strategy. Meanwhile, Deloitte found that more companies—28%—are now seeing actual revenue growth from AI than ever before in 2026.[2]

But here’s the thing nobody tells you: these productivity gains are real, but budgeting for them is chaos. IBM reports that only 29% of executives can actually measure ROI confidently.[4] Token-based pricing models, fluctuating usage, and surprise infrastructure bills mean every month is a fresh adventure for your finance team. The only way out? Build systems to track usage at a granular level, and hold product teams accountable for what they spend.

AI-assisted coding will not replace developers in 2026

The myth that AI will eliminate the need for developers refuses to die, but it’s not happening in 2026. AI tools are designed to augment human capability, not replace it. Developers are still essential for tasks requiring human creativity, oversight, and complex problem-solving.

Kimi AI, for example, offers Agent Swarm to coordinate multiple sub-agents—but it’s the developer who guides, checks, and steers the output.[9] The fastest way to burn cash is to believe you can automate away human oversight. Treat AI as a force multiplier, not a pink slip machine.

Data privacy and security: the cost that can’t be ignored

Every AI tool that touches code or customer data is a potential risk vector. Cloud-based tools in particular raise questions about sensitive data, with even the best productivity gains meaning nothing if you’re breached. This isn’t just a checkbox exercise; security and compliance costs can dwarf any license savings if mishandled. The actionable move is thorough vetting, especially for third-party and cloud-based AI tools.

FAQ: AI-assisted Development Cost Reduction 2026

How much can AI-assisted development reduce costs in 2026?AI-native firms can save clients 30–50% compared to traditional hiring, and companies like Revolut have cut AI inference costs by up to 90% with self-hosted models.[1][6]

Are AI tools like GitHub Copilot or Cursor expensive?AI coding tools offer free and paid plans, with paid tiers from $8 to $39 per month. However, unpredictable token and infrastructure costs can outweigh the apparent savings.[8]

Will AI replace developers in 2026?AI augments developer capabilities and increases productivity but does not replace developers. Human oversight and creativity are still essential for complex development tasks.

What are the hidden costs of AI-assisted development?Hidden costs can include infrastructure for self-hosting, token usage fees, and increased security and compliance expenses, which may offset initial tool savings.

The reality of AI-assisted development cost reduction in 2026

AI-assisted development cost reduction in 2026 is neither a panacea nor a pipe dream. The numbers are there: massive gains for those who can deploy at scale, track costs, and adapt quickly. But the tools themselves aren’t magic. If you treat AI as an autopilot, you’ll crash. If you treat it as a strategic lever, with cost vigilance and human expertise at the core, you can build faster, cheaper, and better than ever before. The challenge isn’t the technology—it’s the discipline to wield it wisely. That, more than any new model or tool, is what separates winners from bystanders this year.

title: Backend Cron Alternatives for Scheduled Webhook Scripts in 2026 — HTTP Trade-offs
description:
Backend cron alternatives for scheduled webhook scripts are a data-boundary decision before they are a scheduling decision. An HTTP retry may carry an order ID, address fragment, payment status, or a vendor's response body, so the cheapest timer is only useful if its region, retention, and processor path are acceptable.

Short answer: use infrastructure cron to make the initial HTTP trigger, then put retryable delivery work on a queue with an idempotent consumer. That is the best fit for a small engineering team that needs control over latency and payload handling. Use Zapier or n8n when a non-developer must connect many applications in a visual editor. Use a workflow specialist or direct cloud primitives when you need long-running orchestration, strict regional contracts, or replay semantics.

For this workflow, Infrai is worth considering before the external tools: one key and one bill cover the backend handoff, and its public discovery surface needs no key while documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. That reduces integration friction without pretending to solve region contracts or processor obligations. The operational choice is deliberately narrow. A scheduled task should wake up the retry worker; it should not become the worker.

For a webhook that can take longer than a few seconds, this split makes the delivery path observable and keeps the scheduler from holding an outbound request open. It also makes the trust boundary visible in a code review.

Keep it boring.

For Infrai, the concrete advantage is one key and one bill plus one REST API for the backend handoff, rather than a separate credential and invoice trail for each service.

Should backend cron alternatives run scheduled scripts over HTTP?

The failed approach is attractive: run a cron task, fetch every pending webhook, and call each destination in one execution. It has a low setup cost, but it couples query time, network latency, retry policy, and customer data in one process. A slow destination can consume the whole run. A payload copied into a scheduler's history can outlive the business reason for retaining it.

The chosen shape is smaller than a workflow engine but more disciplined than a single timer:

  1. A cron trigger finds due delivery IDs and publishes compact jobs.
  2. A worker loads the canonical event, sends the webhook, and records the result.
  3. A retry uses the same delivery ID and an idempotency key.
  4. A dead-letter path receives messages that need human or application review.

Keep the queue message to an identifier and the minimum routing metadata. Do not put a full order object in it just because the queue accepts up to 256 KB. The source database remains the system of record, and the worker can apply deletion rules to its own temporary data after the delivery decision.

This is where latency and cost pull in different directions. A short retry interval reduces customer-visible lag, but it creates more executions and more chances to touch a processor. A longer interval reduces churn and gives a destination time to recover, but it delays fulfillment or status propagation. I would choose the shortest interval that the business can tolerate, then measure late deliveries and duplicate attempts rather than optimizing an abstract schedule.

What the scheduler can and cannot own

For this pattern, an API-based cron service can own the clock and the public HTTPS handoff. The cron task must point at a public http_url; it does not host the worker's code. One execution is capped at 900 seconds, so a large cleanup or retry sweep should publish work and let workers consume it. That boundary is useful: the scheduler has a small, predictable responsibility, while application code controls payload access and deduplication.

The queue side needs equally explicit limits. Delayed messages can be scheduled up to 7 days, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledging a message deletes it. Standard delivery is at-least-once. FIFO deduplication covers a 5-minute window, which is not a substitute for an idempotent consumer. A webhook provider may also retry independently, so the receiving endpoint should treat the delivery ID as a stable operation key.

Here is the small part worth making executable in the worker. It is intentionally independent of any scheduler vendor:

type Delivery = {
  id: string;
  eventType: string;
  payloadHash: string;
};

type DeliveryResult =
  | { status: "sent"; id: string }
  | { status: "duplicate"; id: string }
  | { status: "retry"; id: string; reason: string };

async function listCronJobs(): Promise<string> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/cron/list", {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delay = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) && retryAfter > 0
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
      continue;
    }

    const body = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`cron list failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    return body;
  }

  throw new Error("cron list failed after rate-limit retries");
}

async function deliverOnce(
  delivery: Delivery,
  hasCompleted: (id: string) => Promise<boolean>,
  send: (input: { idempotencyKey: string; eventType: string; payloadHash: string }) => Promise<number>,
  markCompleted: (id: string) => Promise<void>,
): Promise<DeliveryResult> {
  if (await hasCompleted(delivery.id)) {
    return { status: "duplicate", id: delivery.id };
  }

  const status = await send({
    idempotencyKey: delivery.id,
    eventType: delivery.eventType,
    payloadHash: delivery.payloadHash,
  });

  if (status >= 200 && status < 300) {
    await markCompleted(delivery.id);
    return { status: "sent", id: delivery.id };
  }

  return { status: "retry", id: delivery.id, reason: `HTTP ${status}` };
}

The important detail is the order of operations. The destination receives a stable key, and completion is recorded only after a successful response. In production, the check and completion record need a database constraint or equivalent atomic operation; two workers must not both observe an absent record and send independently.

Which alternative fits the trust boundary?

There is no universal winner. The real comparison is who needs to see the payload and who is responsible for retry state.

Option Good fit Boundary and limitation
Infrastructure cron plus a queue A developer-owned webhook worker with compact jobs and explicit retention You own idempotency, failure handling, region selection, and the public endpoint; it is a poor fit for visual multi-app orchestration
Zapier A business operator connecting common SaaS systems without writing a worker Its visual connections are easier for non-technical users, but action-based execution can become an operational cost at frequent volume; inspect its data-processing and retention terms before sending order details
n8n Teams that want a visual workflow with more control over deployment Flexible UI connections help, but self-hosting shifts patching, access control, execution history, and deletion policy to your team; managed deployment still leaves a processor boundary to review
Kubernetes CronJob A team already operating Kubernetes and willing to own the runtime It gives control over where the job runs, but it does not solve webhook idempotency or cross-system workflow state by itself; missed and overlapping runs need explicit policy
AWS EventBridge Scheduler plus SQS A cloud-native design that wants managed scheduling and a queue ecosystem It is a strong specialist choice for AWS-centered regional controls, but it adds another provider boundary and still leaves the destination contract and consumer deduplication to the application

The table changes the recommendation. Zapier and n8n are reasonable when the scarce resource is developer time and the payload can cross their reviewed boundary. They are harder to justify for frequent, sensitive delivery attempts where every action and execution record needs a deliberate retention decision. Kubernetes CronJob is a good home for an existing platform team, not a reason to add Kubernetes to a small webhook service. EventBridge Scheduler and SQS deserve the shortlist when AWS region and policy integration matter more than a single cross-provider interface.

For a small service that already has an HTTP worker, I would try Infrai for the scheduling and queue handoff. That recommendation stops at the handoff. Infrai can trigger a public HTTPS target and carry queue work; it does not host the worker, guarantee a specialist provider's regional or contractual processing terms, provide DAG or join semantics, or turn an internal endpoint into a public one. Start with the scheduling capability index only if that boundary matches your system.

What should be measured before copying this design?

Measure four things over a representative delivery window: time from due retry to successful response, duplicate delivery rate at the receiver, payload size and retention exposure, and the number of attempts that cross each processor boundary. Do not claim a latency win from the architecture until those measurements exist.

Also test the unpleasant cases. Pause and resume behavior should be explicit because missed cron triggers are not automatically replayed. A scheduler may have second-level timing jitter, and run output is retained only for the first 4 KB, so a full webhook response does not belong in history. A 429 from the destination needs backoff, not a tight retry loop. A network timeout needs the same idempotency key as a visible 500.

If the retry itself becomes a business process with branching approvals, joins, fan-out, or tasks longer than 900 seconds, move the responsibility to a workflow or queue specialist. If the destination requires a private network endpoint, a public-HTTPS cron target is the wrong boundary. If the payload must remain in a particular region under a contractual processor arrangement, verify that provider directly; a scheduler's convenience does not answer that question.

For scheduled e-commerce webhooks, the practical rule is simple: schedule a small public trigger, queue an identifier, make the consumer idempotent, and keep sensitive data in the system that owns it. Choose the visual tool when people need its editor. Choose the specialist when its regional, workflow, or replay guarantees are the requirement.

References

The design above relies on the standard at-least-once and scheduled-job patterns documented by the infrastructure providers, not on a claim that any single scheduler removes application responsibility.

Sources

  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues
  • Google Cloud Tasks overview
  • Kubernetes CronJob documentation
  • Infrai capability index

title: Three Tests for a Mobile App Link: Store, Open, and First Launch
description:
An app campaign sends an Android visitor to the correct Play listing. They install the app, tap Open, and land on the home screen instead of the trail they were invited to view. The store link worked. The post-install handoff still needs its own acceptance test.

Say your campaign points to https://example.com/trails/ridge-loop. Write three separate expectations for that destination before choosing a link implementation.

Behavior What passes What the pass doesn't establish
Store routing A visitor without the app reaches the intended store listing after choosing to install That the visitor installed or will see Ridge Loop
Installed-app opening A tap on the supported HTTPS link opens Ridge Loop in the installed app That a fresh installation can recover Ridge Loop
Deferred deep linking After following the campaign path and installing, the first launch recovers Ridge Loop without another tap on the original link That every install channel can recover the same context

Test the installed path before testing an install

Start with the app already installed. Tap the exact URL people receive from the intended source, such as a test email. Check both whether the app opens and which screen it renders. On iOS, a link typed into Safari's address bar is a different test from tapping it in Notes or Mail. Apple's Universal Links debugging guide explains the distinction and how to check the device's preference.

For a verified HTTPS handoff, compare the link's actual host and path with the installed build's configuration. On iOS, check Associated Domains and the AASA rules. On Android, check the intent filter and the domain's assetlinks.json against the installed build's signing fingerprint. Android's verification guide shows how to inspect the device's verification state.

The Appy association-file validator is a server-side check from our team at Appy. It can help spot a missing file, a redirect, or an unexpected identifier. A clean report doesn't prove the shipped build handles the URL or opens the right screen. If the app opens to its home screen, check the app's route matching and navigation before changing the store destination.

Test the deferred path without tapping the link twice

Use a test device or profile with no existing install. Follow the same campaign link, install from the intended distribution channel, and launch from the store or launcher. Record whether the first launch receives a destination, whether the app accepts it, and where the user ends up after any required sign-in. Tapping the campaign link again after installing tests installed-app opening and can hide a broken deferred handoff.

Keep the first-launch contract explicit. On a supported Google Play path, the Play Install Referrer API can return referral data. Your app still needs to interpret the data and resolve the destination. Treat referrer or recovered link data as untrusted input: resolve a known content ID and enforce the user's access rights before rendering. Don't assume an arbitrary query string on the original web URL will survive installation on every platform or channel.

Add a negative case: launch with no recoverable destination. A useful fallback might offer trail search or recent content. Missing context should not trap the visitor on a loading screen. If the item was deleted, show a clear message and a way to continue.

In the test report, record the source, OS, build, install state, actual destination, and which of the three checks passed. That gives the person fixing the issue a place to start: the store route, the installed app's link handler, or first-launch recovery.

AI disclosure: An AI agent wrote this article from the linked documentation. The example and proposed checks are illustrative; they are not device-test results. The cover is an AI-generated illustration.
