title: The Death of the Prompt: Why Autonomous Agents Are the Real Paradigm Shift in Python Development
description:
We’ve all been there. You spend hours meticulously engineering a prompt. You add a few "few-shot" examples, inject some XML tags to keep the output formatted, and wrap it in a clean Python script using the OpenAI SDK. It works brilliantly for the exact test case you wrote. Then, you hand it to a user, they type something slightly unexpected, the model hallucinates, your regex parser crashes on unescaped JSON, and your morning is ruined.

Welcome to the ceiling of prompt engineering.

For the past few years, the software engineering world has treated Large Language Models (LLMs) like high-tech oracles: you ask a question, and you hope you get a pristine answer. But as developers attempt to build complex, production-ready AI applications, a glaring limitation has become impossible to ignore. Chains and static prompts are fundamentally reactive. They follow a rigid, developer-defined path from A to B. If a step fails, if data is missing, or if the user injects a novel curveball, the chain snaps.

The industry is undergoing a massive epistemic shift. We are moving away from reactive prompt processing and toward proactive execution via Autonomous Agents.

In this deep dive, we are going to tear down the theoretical foundations of autonomous agents, contrast them with the sequential chains you might already be building, and write the Python code to build a self-correcting agentic loop from scratch.

The concepts and code demonstrated here are drawn directly from the comprehensive roadmap laid out in the ebook AI Autonomous Agents with Python, you can access the free github repo with all the code examples, exercises MIT Licensed and see the ebook details link.

The Core Problem: The Fragility of the Chain

To understand why autonomous agents are taking over software architecture, we have to look at what came before. In Book 7 of our architectural progression, we mastered chains—predefined sequences of steps, often involving multiple LLM calls, data transformations, and tool usages designed to solve bounded problems.

When you build a sequential chain, you are acting as an absolute micro-manager. You write code that dictates:

  1. First, take the user input and summarize it.
  2. Second, take that summary and pass it to a translation API.
  3. Third, save the translated output to a database.

The flow is completely rigid. It is a traditional if/else control flow wrapped around a probabilistic reasoning engine.

[User Input] ---> [Step 1: Summarize] ---> [Step 2: Translate] ---> [Step 3: Save] ---> [Output]

What happens if Step 1 returns a poorly formatted summary because the input text was too chaotic? The chain breaks. What happens if Step 2 requires an unexpected intermediate step—like fetching external context from a vector database because the summary lacked domain specifics? The chain breaks.

A chain lacks two things that define true software engineering resilience: dynamic planning and self-correction.

The Self-Driving Analogy

Think about traveling from Point A to Point B.

  • A Simple Prompt Call is like asking a static map application for directions. It gives you a single fixed route. If a road closes moments later, the map can't react. You (the human) have to manually intervene.
  • A Sequential Chain is like programming an old GPS device: "Drive 10 miles on Highway 101. Then, turn right onto Elm Street." If there is a massive accident on 101, the GPS is completely helpless unless the developer hardcoded a rigid contingency for every square mile of asphalt.
  • An Autonomous Agent is the self-driving car. It is given a high-level goal: "Get me to Point B safely." It calculates an initial route, constantly monitors external sensors (observes), recalculates when it hits traffic (orients and decides), and dynamically steers around obstacles without human intervention.

An Agent, in the context of Python and LLMs, is a goal-oriented control system that uses an LLM as its reasoning engine. It navigates uncertainty, manages external state, and utilizes a diverse set of tools without requiring you to script every single micro-decision.

Anatomy of Autonomy: The OODA Loop

For an LLM to transcend its role as a static text-generator and become a true Agent, it must operate within a perpetual control structure. The industry standard model for this is derived from the OODA Loop (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act), originally developed by military strategist John Boyd.

Let’s break down how these four phases map directly into a Python application architecture:

1. Observe (Input Gathering)

The loop begins by gathering all relevant data points. This includes the initial high-level user goal, the raw results from the last executed tool, and any changes in the external environment. The Observation phase is purely about ingestion—receiving raw data from the outside world.

2. Orient (Contextualization and State Assessment)

This is the most critical phase. The Agent does not simply look at raw data; it contextualizes it within its mission, its memory, and its current state. It compares the observation to the overall goal, queries its long-term memory for past experiences, and synthesizes a rich, contextualized prompt for the LLM.

3. Decide (Plan Generation and Tool Selection)

Here, the LLM acts as the core strategist. Based on the synthesized context, the LLM generates an internal monologue (often via Chain-of-Thought prompting), selects a specific external tool, and formats the exact parameters required for that tool.

4. Act (Execution)

The Action phase is where the Python environment takes over. The agent framework intercepts the structured instruction generated by the LLM, validates it, and executes the corresponding external Python function or API call. Once execution finishes, the results are fed right back into the Observe phase, restarting the loop.

Building a Basic Agentic Loop in Python

Let's move away from theory and write some code. Below is a foundational simulation of the OODA loop in Python using the OpenAI SDK.

Instead of asking the LLM to write an answer in one massive, single-turn prompt, we are going to give it a multi-step research objective and force it to iteratively determine if the goal is met.

import os
import time
from openai import OpenAI
from typing import List, Dict, Any

# Initialize the OpenAI client
try:
    client = OpenAI()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error initializing OpenAI client: {e}")
    exit()

# Define the primary goal for the agent
PRIMARY_GOAL = (
    "Research the capital city of Brazil and the year it was officially founded. "
    "Once both facts are confirmed, generate a single, concise summary sentence."
)

# System prompt enforcing structured JSON output for state control
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a highly focused, autonomous research agent. Your sole purpose is to fulfill the PRIMARY_GOAL.
You operate in an iterative loop. Based on the current STATE and the ACTION_HISTORY, you must decide your next step.

Your output must always be a JSON object with two keys:
1. "next_action": A string describing the precise next research step required to move closer to the goal. 
2. "goal_achieved": A boolean (true or false). Set to true ONLY when the PRIMARY_GOAL is fully satisfied and the final synthesis is complete.

If "goal_achieved" is true, the "next_action" must contain the final summary sentence.
"""

ACTION_HISTORY: List[Dict[str, str]] = []
CURRENT_STATE = "Goal initialized. Starting research."

def run_agentic_loop(goal: str, max_iterations: int = 5) -> str:
    global CURRENT_STATE
    global ACTION_HISTORY

    iteration = 0
    goal_achieved = False

    print(f"--- AGENT INITIATED ---")
    print(f"GOAL: {goal}")
    print("-" * 30)

    while not goal_achieved and iteration < max_iterations:
        iteration += 1
        print(f"\n[Iteration {iteration}/{max_iterations}]")

        # A. OBSERVE & ORIENT
        context_messages = [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"PRIMARY_GOAL: {goal}"},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"ACTION_HISTORY (Past Steps): {ACTION_HISTORY}"},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"CURRENT_STATE: {CURRENT_STATE}"}
        ]

        # B. DECIDE
        try:
            response = client.chat.completions.create(
                model="gpt-3.5-turbo",
                messages=context_messages,
                response_format={"type": "json_object"}
            )
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error during decision phase: {e}"

        # C. PARSE DECISION
        try:
            decision_json = eval(response.choices[0].message.content)
            next_action = decision_json.get("next_action", "Error: No action defined.")
            goal_achieved = decision_json.get("goal_achieved", False)
        except (SyntaxError, TypeError) as e:
            print(f"Error parsing JSON output: {e}")
            break

        # D. ACT
        ACTION_HISTORY.append({
            "iteration": str(iteration),
            "decision": next_action
        })

        print(f"DECISION: {next_action}")

        if goal_achieved:
            CURRENT_STATE = f"Goal successfully completed. Final Answer: {next_action}"
            print(f"\n*** GOAL ACHIEVED ***")
            return next_action
        else:
            # Simulate execution of the action (Tool Call simulation)
            execution_prompt = f"Execute the following research task precisely: '{next_action}'. Provide the factual result only."

            execution_response = client.chat.completions.create(
                model="gpt-3.5-turbo",
                messages=[
                    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a factual execution engine. Respond only with the requested fact."},
                    {"role": "user", "content": execution_prompt}
                ]
            )

            execution_result = execution_response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
            CURRENT_STATE = f"Previous Action Result: {execution_result}. Now evaluate the remaining steps needed for the goal."
            print(f"RESULT: {execution_result}")

            time.sleep(0.5)

    if not goal_achieved:
        return f"Agent failed to achieve goal within {max_iterations} iterations."

# Execute the simulation
final_summary = run_agentic_loop(PRIMARY_GOAL)
print("\n" + "="*50)
print(f"FINAL OUTPUT: {final_summary}")
print("="*50)

Why This Code Changes Everything

Look closely at what is happening here. The LLM isn't spitting out a massive block of text in one go. Instead, it is generating control signals.

  1. In Iteration 1, it decides to find the capital of Brazil.
  2. The execution layer captures that result ("Brasília") and feeds it back into the CURRENT_STATE.
  3. In Iteration 2, the LLM reads that state, realizes it has the capital but lacks the founding year, and updates its strategy to query the founding year.
  4. Finally, it synthesizes the whole thing and flips goal_achieved to true.

This is the foundational shift: The LLM's output is no longer the final product; the LLM's output is the next command.

Advanced Architecture: The Self-Correcting Validation Agent

In a real-world enterprise environment, agents need to interact with external tools and handle failure gracefully. What happens when a tool returns an error? A traditional chain throws a stack trace and dies. An autonomous agent observes the failure, diagnoses it, and calls a correction tool.

Let’s implement a more advanced script using Pydantic and LangChain core tools to simulate a proposal validation agent that automatically fixes formatting errors.

import time
from typing import Dict, Any, List
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from langchain_core.tools import tool

# 1. Pydantic Schemas for Structured Communication
class ProjectProposal(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(description="The concise and descriptive title of the project.")
    description: str = Field(description="The detailed description, adhering to length requirements.")

class AgentDecision(BaseModel):
    action: str = Field(description="The next tool to use: 'validate' or 'correct'.")
    context: str = Field(description="Summary of the current state and why this action was chosen.")

# 2. Tool Definitions
@tool
def validate_project_rules(proposal: ProjectProposal) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Checks if the proposal adheres to strict length rules."""
    title_len = len(proposal.title)
    desc_len = len(proposal.description)

    MIN_TITLE, MAX_TITLE = 10, 50
    MIN_DESC = 100

    errors = []
    if not (MIN_TITLE <= title_len <= MAX_TITLE):
        errors.append(f"Title length ({title_len}) must be between {MIN_TITLE}-{MAX_TITLE}.")
    if desc_len < MIN_DESC:
        errors.append(f"Description length ({desc_len}) is too short. Minimum is {MIN_DESC}.")

    if errors:
        return {"status": "FAILURE", "report": errors}
    else:
        return {"status": "SUCCESS", "report": "Proposal meets all criteria."}

@tool
def generate_correction_plan(current_proposal: Dict[str, str], error_report: List[str]) -> ProjectProposal:
    """Simulates an LLM generating a corrected proposal based on errors."""
    print(f"\n[Tool: Planning Correction] Fixing input based on errors: {error_report}")
    time.sleep(0.3)

    original_title = current_proposal['title']
    original_desc = current_proposal['description']

    # Correction strategy
    new_title = original_title[:50] if len(original_title) > 50 else original_title + " (Revised)"
    new_desc = original_desc + " " + "This extra text ensures the description meets the minimum length requirement for project approval."

    return ProjectProposal(title=new_title, description=new_desc)

# 3. Decision Maker Simulation
def mock_llm_decision_maker(current_state: Dict[str, Any]) -> AgentDecision:
    if current_state['status'] == 'GOAL_MET':
        return AgentDecision(action='terminate', context="Goal reached.")
    if current_state['status'] in ['INITIAL', 'CORRECTED']:
        return AgentDecision(action='validate', context="Checking rules against current proposal.")
    if current_state['status'] == 'FAILED_VALIDATION':
        return AgentDecision(action='correct', context="Validation failed. Generating correction.")
    return AgentDecision(action='terminate', context="Unknown state.")

# 4. The Agentic Loop
def run_validation_agent(initial_proposal: Dict[str, str], max_iterations: int = 3) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    state = {
        "status": "INITIAL",
        "current_proposal": initial_proposal,
        "history": [],
        "iteration": 0
    }

    print(f"--- Agent Initialized. Goal: Validate & Fix Proposal. ---")

    while state["iteration"] < max_iterations:
        state["iteration"] += 1
        print(f"\n[Iteration {state['iteration']}] Status: {state['status']}")

        decision = mock_llm_decision_maker(state)
        print(f"   -> Decision: {decision.action.upper()} | Context: {decision.context}")

        if decision.action == 'validate':
            try:
                proposal_obj = ProjectProposal(**state["current_proposal"])
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Parsing error: {e}")
                break

            validation_result = validate_project_rules(proposal_obj)

            if validation_result["status"] == "SUCCESS":
                state["status"] = "GOAL_MET"
                print("   -> Validation SUCCESS.")
            else:
                state["status"] = "FAILED_VALIDATION"
                state["last_errors"] = validation_result["report"]
                print(f"   -> Validation FAILED: {validation_result['report']}")

        elif decision.action == 'correct':
            corrected = generate_correction_plan(state["current_proposal"], state.get("last_errors", []))
            state["current_proposal"] = corrected.model_dump()
            state["status"] = "CORRECTED"
            print(f"   -> Correction Applied.")

        elif decision.action == 'terminate':
            break

    return state

# Execute with bad input
initial_bad_proposal = {
    "title": "A Way Too Long Project Title That Completely Breaks The Maximum Character Limits Imposed By Corporate Governance",
    "description": "Too short."
}

final_state = run_validation_agent(initial_bad_proposal)

if final_state['status'] == 'GOAL_MET':
    print("\n[Final Validated Output]")
    print(ProjectProposal(**final_state['current_proposal']).model_dump_json(indent=2))

The Magic of Self-Correction

Notice what happened in the script above. The agent received a proposal that failed validation. Instead of crashing, the state machine captured the error report, pivoted to a correction tool, altered the data payload, and looped back to re-validate.

This is the exact mechanism that separates a toy script from an enterprise-grade AI system. The agent uses its error log as short-term memory to alter its subsequent actions.

Common Pitfall: The Context Window Trap

Before you go off and build agents that run for 500 iterations, we need to address a silent killer in agent design: Context Window Overload.

In our simple scripts, we passed the entire ACTION_HISTORY back to the LLM on every single loop. For a 3-step script, this is fine. But imagine an autonomous coding agent trying to debug a massive repository over 150 iterations.

  1. Cost Explosion: Every single API call sends a massive, ballooning payload of past logs. Your token costs will scale quadratically.
  2. Latency Spikes: Processing a 100k+ token context window on every turn slows your agent down to a crawl.
  3. Context Degradation: As history gets too large, models suffer from "attention dilution." They start forgetting instructions given in the system prompt at the very beginning of the run.

The Solution: RAG for Agent Memory

Production-grade agents do not pass raw history. They treat their memory like a database:

  • Long-Term Memory (LTM): Raw action logs and past experiences are stored in a Vector Database or structured SQL store.
  • Selective Retrieval: During the Observation phase, the agent queries its own memory store using the current goal and state, pulling only the relevant past insights into the active context window.

By keeping the working memory lean, you ensure your agent can run indefinitely without degrading its reasoning capability.

Conclusion: The Agentic Future

The transition from prompt engineering to agent engineering represents a maturation of our industry. We are no longer just writing text transformations; we are building autonomous control systems.

By wrapping LLMs in an OODA loop, equipping them with Pydantic-validated tools, and giving them the capacity for iterative self-correction, we unlock software that can reason through uncertainty, handle messy real-world data, and execute multi-step objectives without constant human babysitting.

The prompt is dead. Long live the agent.

Let's Discuss

  1. Where do you draw the line between deterministic code and agentic reasoning? At what point does letting an LLM make autonomous decisions become a security or reliability risk in your architecture?
  2. Have you encountered context window degradation in your own LLM applications? What memory management or state-compression patterns have you found most effective for long-running workflows?

title: Front End Observability: Why Your window.onerror Reports Say "Script error." (and How to Fix Them)
description:
A practical guide to browser error monitoring with window.onerror, covering the cross-origin blind spot, resource failures that never bubble, and error reports that die when the tab closes. Includes tests and Angular wiring.

It's late on a Friday. Support forwards a screenshot: a customer's checkout page is blank. You open your error dashboard, and there it is, forty times since lunch:

Script error.
  at  (line 0, column 0)

No file, no stack, no line. Just a message that tells you nothing.

You have window.onerror wired up. You followed a tutorial. So why is the one thing you needed missing?

If you want more write-ups on browser error monitoring and front end observability, follow me here on Medium. I publish practical, copy-pasteable pieces like this one every week.

By the end of this article you will know exactly what window.onerror hands you and what it hides. You will build a small, tested error monitor in TypeScript that catches runtime errors, failed resources, and rejected promises, and delivers them reliably. And you will find out why that dashboard shows line 0.

Keep that line 0 question in mind. We'll answer it near the end.

Why does window.onerror give you so little?

Before touching code, let's set up the problem. Browsers expose three separate failure channels, and most tutorials only cover one.

Per MDN's documentation for the Window error event, the error event fires on window when a resource fails to load or can't be used, for example when a script throws. MDN also notes that it only fires for script errors thrown synchronously, such as during initial load or inside event handlers. A rejected promise with no handler fires a different event, unhandledrejection.

Here's the map:

Failure                          What you listen for
-------------------------------  -------------------------------------
Sync exception (script/handler)  window "error"  (ErrorEvent)
Failed <img>/<script>/<link>     "error" in CAPTURE phase (plain Event)
Unhandled promise rejection      window "unhandledrejection"

If you only set window.onerror, you cover the first row and nothing else. And as you'll see, even that row has traps.

Before we get into the examples, a quick note: The code snippets provided here are meant purely for understanding the concept. Some syntax shown may reflect patterns from earlier Angular/React versions. Always refer to the official documentation for the most current API and syntax.

Next up: the version of this that almost every project starts with, and why it quietly fails.

What does a basic window.onerror handler actually receive?

Quick version (beginner)

window.onerror takes a function with five arguments. Here is the classic setup:

// src/naive-monitor.ts
window.onerror = (message, source, lineno, colno, error) => {
  void fetch('/api/errors', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ message, source, lineno, colno }),
  });
};

export {};

Trigger an error from your app:

// src/main.ts
import './naive-monitor';

const user = JSON.parse('{}') as { profile?: { name: string } };
console.log(user.profile!.name);

In Chrome, your endpoint receives something like this:

{
  "message": "Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')",
  "source": "http://localhost:5173/src/main.ts",
  "lineno": 4,
  "colno": 22
}

Message text varies by browser, and so does the exact line and column in bundled code. That works. It runs. It also has four problems.

Real-world version (pitfalls)

  1. It's a single slot. Assigning window.onerror replaces whatever was there. If a third-party widget or another monitoring script installed a handler first, you just deleted it. If one installs after you, it deletes yours.
  2. No stack. You sent the first four arguments and dropped error, which usually holds the Error object and its stack.
  3. fetch during page teardown can be cancelled. Errors that happen as the user leaves are exactly the ones you lose.
  4. Resource failures and promise rejections are invisible. A 404 on a script or an unhandled await never reaches this handler.

There's a fifth trap that bites people who copy handlers from old snippets. MDN documents that for onerror on Window, returning true cancels the default behavior, so the error won't appear in the console, though the current script still stops executing. A handler that ends with return true makes development miserable because your own errors vanish from DevTools.

Under the hood (internals, trade-offs)

MDN notes that onerror on Window and WorkerGlobalScope is the only event handler property that receives more than one argument, for historical reasons. That asymmetry only applies to the property. If you use addEventListener('error', ...), you get a single ErrorEvent object whose properties (message, filename, lineno, colno, error) match those five arguments. The return-true rule does not apply there either.

That's the first reason I'd pick addEventListener every time: it composes with other code, and it has one argument shape.

Have you ever shipped a global handler and discovered months later that another script had overwritten it? Tell me what happened in the comments, I'm collecting war stories.

So why was your dashboard stuck on "Script error."? That's the failed first attempt, and it's next.

Why does the message say "Script error." with line 0?

Quick version (beginner)

When a script from a different origin throws, the browser deliberately hides the details from your handler. It does this so a page can't peek at error text from another site's code. You get a generic message and zeroed location.

Here is a page that reproduces it. Save it as index.html:

<!-- index.html -->
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <title>Cross-origin error demo</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script>
      window.addEventListener('error', (event) => {
        console.log(JSON.stringify({
          message: event.message,
          filename: event.filename,
          lineno: event.lineno,
          colno: event.colno,
          hasError: event.error !== null,
        }));
      });
    </script>
    <script src="http://localhost:4000/widget.js"></script>
  </body>
</html>

Serve widget.js from a second origin (a different port counts) with a line like null.boom; in it. The console prints:

{"message":"Script error.","filename":"","lineno":0,"colno":0,"hasError":false}

That's your line 0.

Real-world version (pitfalls)

The fix needs both sides to cooperate. The script tag needs the crossorigin attribute, and the server hosting the script must answer with a matching CORS header.

<!-- index.html (changed line only matters: crossorigin) -->
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <title>Cross-origin error demo</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script>
      window.addEventListener('error', (event) => {
        console.log(JSON.stringify({
          message: event.message,
          filename: event.filename,
          lineno: event.lineno,
          colno: event.colno,
          hasError: event.error !== null,
        }));
      });
    </script>
    <script src="http://localhost:4000/widget.js" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
  </body>
</html>

And the response header on the CDN or asset server:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

Now the output becomes:

{"message":"Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'boom')","filename":"http://localhost:4000/widget.js","lineno":1,"colno":6,"hasError":true}

The classic pitfall: you add crossorigin but the CDN doesn't send the header. In that case the browser refuses to load the script at all, which is worse than a vague error. Roll it out with your CDN config first, then the attribute.

The Sentry write-up on reporting window.onerror covers this same cross-origin behavior and is a good companion read.

Under the hood (internals, trade-offs)

The browser treats the error as "muted" when the script isn't same-origin or CORS-approved. It's a privacy rule, not a bug, so there's nothing a handler can do after the fact. The only fix is at the delivery layer: serve your own bundles from the same origin, or serve them with CORS enabled and mark the tags with crossorigin.

Third-party scripts you don't control (ad tags, chat widgets) will stay muted unless their vendor sends CORS headers. Decide whether you want to filter those out of your dashboards, because "Script error." with no location is unactionable noise. I would drop them or tag them as low priority rather than alert on them.

That explains the screenshot. But fixing it leaves a lot of failures still unseen. Let's rebuild the monitor.

How do you catch resource errors and rejected promises too?

Quick version (beginner)

Use addEventListener for runtime errors, pass true as the third argument to catch resource errors, and add a separate unhandledrejection listener. This version is small and complete:

// src/monitor-v2.ts
const post = (data: Record<string, unknown>): void => {
  navigator.sendBeacon(
    '/api/errors',
    JSON.stringify({ ...data, pageUrl: location.href }),
  );
};

window.addEventListener(
  'error',
  (event) => {
    if (event instanceof ErrorEvent) {
      post({
        kind: 'runtime',
        message: event.message,
        source: event.filename,
        lineno: event.lineno,
        colno: event.colno,
        stack: event.error?.stack,
      });
    } else if (event.target instanceof HTMLElement) {
      post({
        kind: 'resource',
        tag: event.target.tagName,
        src: event.target.getAttribute('src'),
      });
    }
  },
  true,
);

window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', (event) => {
  post({ kind: 'promise', message: String(event.reason) });
});

export {};

Add a broken image and a floating promise to a test page:

<img src="/missing.png" alt="" />
<script type="module">
  import './src/monitor-v2.ts';
  Promise.reject(new Error('payment API timed out'));
</script>

Your endpoint receives, among others:

{"kind":"resource","tag":"IMG","src":"/missing.png","pageUrl":"http://localhost:5173/"}
{"kind":"promise","message":"Error: payment API timed out","pageUrl":"http://localhost:5173/"}

Real-world version (pitfalls)

Why the true? Resource load failures fire an error event on the element itself, and that event doesn't bubble. Your window listener would never see it in the bubbling phase. The capture phase runs on the way down, before the target, so a capturing listener on window sees every element's error event. MDN also says the event is an ErrorEvent for script errors and a plain Event otherwise, which is why the code branches on instanceof ErrorEvent.

Here's what most developers get wrong: they log event.reason as-is. A rejection reason can be anything, a string, an object, undefined. Always check instanceof Error before reading .stack.

Under the hood (internals, trade-offs)

Capture-phase listeners on window also see errors that other code already handled with try/catch? No. A caught exception never becomes an error event, so you only see what the page failed to handle. Resource errors are different: there's no try/catch around an <img>, so every failed image, script, and stylesheet reports. That can be loud. A single bad CDN path across a list of 200 thumbnails produces 200 events, which is why the next step matters.

Notice the trade-off: catching more means collecting more, and more means cost and noise. Next we add guard rails.

How do you make window.onerror monitoring safe for production?

Quick version (beginner)

Three things turn a toy into something you can ship: deduplicate repeats, cap reports per session, and never let the reporter itself throw. Here's the full module:

// src/error-monitor.ts
export type ReportKind = 'runtime' | 'resource' | 'promise';

export interface ErrorReport {
  kind: ReportKind;
  message: string;
  source?: string;
  lineno?: number;
  colno?: number;
  stack?: string;
  pageUrl: string;
  userAgent: string;
  release: string;
  timestamp: number;
}

type PartialReport = Pick<ErrorReport, 'kind' | 'message'> &
  Partial<Omit<ErrorReport, 'kind' | 'message'>>;

export interface MonitorOptions {
  endpoint: string;
  release: string;
  maxReportsPerSession?: number;
  send?: (endpoint: string, body: string) => void;
  target?: EventTarget;
}

export interface ErrorMonitor {
  reportError: (error: unknown) => void;
  uninstall: () => void;
}

export function defaultSend(endpoint: string, body: string): void {
  const blob = new Blob([body], { type: 'application/json' });
  if (typeof navigator.sendBeacon === 'function' && navigator.sendBeacon(endpoint, blob)) {
    return;
  }
  void fetch(endpoint, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body,
    keepalive: true,
  }).catch(() => undefined);
}

export function installErrorMonitor(options: MonitorOptions): ErrorMonitor {
  const send = options.send ?? defaultSend;
  const limit = options.maxReportsPerSession ?? 20;
  const target: EventTarget = options.target ?? window;
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  let count = 0;
  let reporting = false;

  const report = (partial: PartialReport): void => {
    if (reporting || count >= limit) return;

    const key = [
      partial.kind,
      partial.message,
      partial.source ?? '',
      partial.lineno ?? 0,
      partial.colno ?? 0,
    ].join('|');
    if (seen.has(key)) return;
    seen.add(key);

    reporting = true;
    try {
      count += 1;
      const payload: ErrorReport = {
        ...partial,
        pageUrl: location.href,
        userAgent: navigator.userAgent,
        release: options.release,
        timestamp: Date.now(),
      };
      send(options.endpoint, JSON.stringify(payload));
    } catch {
      // The reporter must never throw, or it would report itself forever.
    } finally {
      reporting = false;
    }
  };

  const reportError = (error: unknown): void => {
    report({
      kind: 'runtime',
      message: error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error),
      stack: error instanceof Error ? error.stack : undefined,
    });
  };

  const onError = (event: Event): void => {
    if (event instanceof ErrorEvent) {
      const error: unknown = event.error;
      report({
        kind: 'runtime',
        message: event.message,
        source: event.filename,
        lineno: event.lineno,
        colno: event.colno,
        stack: error instanceof Error ? error.stack : undefined,
      });
      return;
    }
    const el = event.target;
    if (el instanceof HTMLElement) {
      report({
        kind: 'resource',
        message: `Failed to load <${el.tagName.toLowerCase()}>`,
        source: el.getAttribute('src') ?? el.getAttribute('href') ?? undefined,
      });
    }
  };

  const onRejection = (event: PromiseRejectionEvent): void => {
    const reason: unknown = event.reason;
    report({
      kind: 'promise',
      message: reason instanceof Error ? reason.message : String(reason),
      stack: reason instanceof Error ? reason.stack : undefined,
    });
  };

  target.addEventListener('error', onError as EventListener, true);
  target.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', onRejection as EventListener);

  return {
    reportError,
    uninstall: () => {
      target.removeEventListener('error', onError as EventListener, true);
      target.removeEventListener('unhandledrejection', onRejection as EventListener);
    },
  };
}

Use it from your entry file:

// src/main.ts
import { installErrorMonitor } from './error-monitor';

installErrorMonitor({ endpoint: '/api/errors', release: '1.0.0' });

Real-world version (pitfalls)

Each guard rail earns its place:

  • The reporting flag stops recursion. If building or sending a report throws, that exception would fire another error event, which calls the reporter again. Without the flag you can melt a tab.
  • The dedupe key collapses the 200 broken thumbnails into one report. The trade-off is that you lose counts. If you need "how many users hit this", count on the server by key, or send the count with the first report.
  • The session cap protects your endpoint from a render loop that throws 60 times a second.
  • release is the field you'll thank yourself for. Without it you can't tell whether yesterday's fix worked.

Under the hood (internals, trade-offs)

Why sendBeacon first? The browser queues a beacon so it survives page unload, which is when fetch often gets cancelled. When sendBeacon returns false (queue full) or doesn't exist, the fallback is fetch with keepalive: true, which has the same survive-unload intent. One caveat: a beacon with a JSON Blob type sent to another origin triggers a CORS preflight. Keep your error endpoint same-origin, or set up CORS on it.

The target option exists for one reason: testing. We'll use it in a moment.

Here's a quick pause: have you ever been unable to reproduce a production error because the report arrived without a stack or release tag? What was the one missing field that would have saved you? Reply in the comments, I read them all.

Next teaser: how do you prove this thing works without breaking your own test runner?

How do you unit test window error handlers?

Quick version (beginner)

Install Vitest and jsdom:

npm install --save-dev vitest jsdom

// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    environment: 'jsdom',
  },
});

Now the tests. They dispatch real ErrorEvent and Event objects at document, so we exercise the same code path the browser uses:

// src/error-monitor.test.ts
import { afterEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { installErrorMonitor, type ErrorMonitor, type ErrorReport } from './error-monitor';

describe('installErrorMonitor', () => {
  let monitor: ErrorMonitor | undefined;
  const send = vi.fn<(endpoint: string, body: string) => void>();

  const install = (maxReportsPerSession?: number): void => {
    send.mockClear();
    monitor = installErrorMonitor({
      endpoint: '/api/errors',
      release: '1.4.2',
      send,
      target: document,
      maxReportsPerSession,
    });
  };

  const lastReport = (): ErrorReport => {
    const call = send.mock.calls[send.mock.calls.length - 1];
    return JSON.parse(call[1]) as ErrorReport;
  };

  afterEach(() => {
    monitor?.uninstall();
    document.body.innerHTML = '';
  });

  it('reports runtime errors with location and release', () => {
    install();
    document.dispatchEvent(
      new ErrorEvent('error', {
        message: 'boom',
        filename: 'app.js',
        lineno: 10,
        colno: 5,
        error: new Error('boom'),
      }),
    );

    expect(send).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    const report = lastReport();
    expect(report.kind).toBe('runtime');
    expect(report.lineno).toBe(10);
    expect(report.release).toBe('1.4.2');
    expect(report.stack).toContain('boom');
  });

  it('reports failed resources caught in the capture phase', () => {
    install();
    const img = document.createElement('img');
    img.setAttribute('src', '/missing.png');
    document.body.appendChild(img);

    img.dispatchEvent(new Event('error'));

    const report = lastReport();
    expect(report.kind).toBe('resource');
    expect(report.message).toBe('Failed to load <img>');
    expect(report.source).toBe('/missing.png');
  });

  it('reports unhandled promise rejections', () => {
    install();
    const event = Object.assign(new Event('unhandledrejection'), {
      reason: new Error('nope'),
    });
    document.dispatchEvent(event);

    expect(lastReport().kind).toBe('promise');
    expect(lastReport().message).toBe('nope');
  });

  it('deduplicates identical errors', () => {
    install();
    const make = (): ErrorEvent =>
      new ErrorEvent('error', { message: 'same', filename: 'a.js', lineno: 1, colno: 1 });
    document.dispatchEvent(make());
    document.dispatchEvent(make());

    expect(send).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });

  it('stops after the per-session limit', () => {
    install(2);
    for (let i = 0; i < 5; i += 1) {
      document.dispatchEvent(new ErrorEvent('error', { message: `err ${i}` }));
    }

    expect(send).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
  });
});

Run them:

npx vitest run

Expected output (timings will differ):

 ✓ src/error-monitor.test.ts (5 tests)

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  5 passed (5)

Real-world version (pitfalls)

Why dispatch on document instead of window? Test runners commonly watch window for uncaught errors and fail the run when one appears. Dispatching a synthetic error at the real window can look like a genuine crash to the runner. A stand-in target keeps the test about your logic. The capture-phase test works because document sits above the img in the event path.

Under the hood (internals, trade-offs)

These tests don't prove the browser delivers events the way jsdom does. They prove your branching, dedupe, and limits. For the delivery side, add one end-to-end check with a real browser tool against a page that really throws. Cheap tests for logic, one expensive test for wiring: that's the split I'd keep.

Now the part most Angular readers are waiting for.

How do you connect this to Angular's ErrorHandler?

Quick version (beginner)

Angular routes errors from templates, lifecycle hooks, and event handlers it manages to its own ErrorHandler, and by default that logs to the console. Because Angular catches those errors first, they often never reach window.onerror. So wire your monitor into ErrorHandler:

// src/app/monitoring-error-handler.ts
import { ErrorHandler, Injectable, InjectionToken, inject } from '@angular/core';

export const REPORT_ERROR = new InjectionToken<(error: unknown) => void>('REPORT_ERROR');

@Injectable()
export class MonitoringErrorHandler implements ErrorHandler {
  private readonly report = inject(REPORT_ERROR);

  handleError(error: unknown): void {
    this.report(error);
    console.error(error);
  }
}

// src/main.ts
import { ErrorHandler } from '@angular/core';
import { bootstrapApplication } from '@angular/platform-browser';
import { App } from './app/app';
import { REPORT_ERROR, MonitoringErrorHandler } from './app/monitoring-error-handler';
import { installErrorMonitor } from './error-monitor';

const monitor = installErrorMonitor({ endpoint: '/api/errors', release: '1.0.0' });

bootstrapApplication(App, {
  providers: [
    { provide: REPORT_ERROR, useValue: (error: unknown) => monitor.reportError(error) },
    { provide: ErrorHandler, useClass: MonitoringErrorHandler },
  ],
}).catch((error: unknown) => monitor.reportError(error));

// src/app/app.ts
import { Component, signal } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  template: `
    <button (click)="explode()">Break something</button>
    @if (clicks() > 0) {
      <p>Clicked {{ clicks() }} times</p>
    }
  `,
})
export class App {
  protected readonly clicks = signal(0);

  protected explode(): void {
    this.clicks.update((n) => n + 1);
    const user = JSON.parse('{}') as { profile?: { name: string } };
    console.log(user.profile!.name);
  }
}

Click the button and your network tab shows a POST to /api/errors:

{"kind":"runtime","message":"Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')","stack":"TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')\n    at App.explode ...","pageUrl":"http://localhost:4200/","userAgent":"Mozilla/5.0 ...","release":"1.0.0","timestamp":1790000000000}

(The stack is truncated here for readability, yours will be full.)

Real-world version (pitfalls)

Notice the module doesn't import Angular, and the handler doesn't import the monitor. The token is the seam. That keeps the monitor reusable in React or plain JavaScript, and it keeps the Angular piece trivially testable:

// src/app/monitoring-error-handler.spec.ts
import { ErrorHandler } from '@angular/core';
import { TestBed } from '@angular/core/testing';
import { MonitoringErrorHandler, REPORT_ERROR } from './monitoring-error-handler';

describe('MonitoringErrorHandler', () => {
  it('forwards errors to the reporter', () => {
    const captured: unknown[] = [];

    TestBed.configureTestingModule({
      providers: [
        { provide: REPORT_ERROR, useValue: (error: unknown) => captured.push(error) },
        { provide: ErrorHandler, useClass: MonitoringErrorHandler },
      ],
    });

    const handler = TestBed.inject(ErrorHandler);
    const error = new Error('template blew up');
    handler.handleError(error);

    expect(captured).toEqual([error]);
  });
});

ng test

Executed 1 of 1 SUCCESS

(The exact summary line depends on the runner your CLI version generates. The test itself uses only describe, it, and expect, so it works with either of the common runners. The console.error call will print the test error to the log, which is expected.)

For React, the same idea applies. Error boundaries catch render-phase errors, and those need a class component for the boundary itself, so check react.dev for the current boundary and root error callback options, then call monitor.reportError from there.

Under the hood (internals, trade-offs)

Do you need both layers? Yes. The framework handler sees what the framework swallows. The window listeners see everything else: third-party scripts, failed assets, code outside the framework, and the bootstrap itself. Dedupe makes it safe if the same error reaches both.

One last gap. Reports now arrive, but the stacks point into minified bundles.

How do you read minified stack traces from window.onerror?

Your lineno and colno describe the file the browser ran, which is the bundle. Without source maps, "line 1, column 48213" is useless.

The usual setup: generate source maps at build time, upload them to your error backend (or keep them private on your own server), and don't serve them publicly if your code is sensitive. In Vite, hidden generates maps without adding the reference comment to the bundle:

// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    sourcemap: 'hidden',
  },
});

For Angular, the builder has a matching hidden option under sourceMap in angular.json, so confirm the exact shape on angular.dev for your CLI version.

The release field from our payload is what ties a report to the right map. A map from build 1.0.0 will mislabel frames from 1.0.1.

When shouldn't you build this yourself? If you need grouping across thousands of error variants, alerting, release health, and session replay, use a hosted tool. This module is the right size for small apps, internal tools, and for understanding what those tools are doing under the hood. It's also a good way to learn the browser's failure channels so you can configure any vendor SDK properly.

What was behind line 0 all along?

Back to your Friday screenshot. The counter said "Script error." because a script from another origin threw, and the browser muted it. Your handler was fine. The delivery was the problem: the script tag lacked crossorigin, and the host lacked the CORS header.

Add both, and the next report carries a file, a line, a column, and a stack. Add the capture listener and the promise listener, and failed images and floating promises show up as well. Add the beacon and the limits, and you stop losing the last error before a tab closes.

The lesson I'd take from this: window.onerror isn't wrong, it's just one of three channels, and the rest of the work is delivery and noise control.

If this changed how you think about error reporting, share it with the teammate who owns your monitoring setup. They'll thank you after the next Friday incident.

Bonus tips

Beginner: Search your codebase for window.onerror = and return true. Both are worth a second look.

Intermediate: Use window.reportError(error) inside a catch block when you want to log a handled error through the same global channel. Check the MDN compatibility table before relying on it in older browsers.

Advanced: Track a "same error, different release" counter server-side using the dedupe key plus release. A fix that doesn't move that number didn't fix anything.

Recap

  • window.onerror passes five arguments and is a single slot. addEventListener('error', ...) composes and gives you one ErrorEvent.
  • Returning true from onerror hides the error in the console.
  • "Script error." with line 0 means a muted cross-origin script. Fix it with the crossorigin attribute plus a CORS header.
  • Resource errors don't bubble, so listen in the capture phase. Rejected promises need their own unhandledrejection listener.
  • Dedupe, cap, and guard against recursion in the reporter. Send with sendBeacon, fall back to fetch with keepalive.
  • Wire your framework's error handler into the same reporter, and test the logic with synthetic events.

Further reading: the MDN page on the Window error event, an archived copy of the older onerror documentation, the Sentry post on reporting window.onerror, the Fiverr engineering guide to front end error monitoring, and this LinkedIn write-up on capturing and reporting JavaScript errors with window.onerror.

title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation for System Design, With Worked Examples
description:
System design estimation is a way to turn an ambiguous product description into approximate traffic, storage, bandwidth, and capacity requirements. The goal is not to predict an exact production number. It is to expose the order of magnitude, make assumptions visible, and identify which part of the design deserves attention first.

A useful estimate follows a repeatable sequence: define the workload, calculate average and peak requests per second, split reads from writes, estimate data growth, calculate network throughput, and translate the results into design choices. The arithmetic should be simple enough to explain aloud and detailed enough for another engineer to challenge.

Note: Treat every number in the worked examples as an explicit hypothetical input, not a benchmark or a universal industry default. Replace assumptions with measured product analytics, load tests, payload samples, and retention requirements when sizing a real system.

The estimation method: assumptions before formulas

Start by describing what the system does. “A social feed” is not a workload; “two million daily active users each request twenty feed pages and publish half a post per day on average” is a workload you can calculate.

Write down the assumptions before doing arithmetic:

  • Users and activity: daily active users (DAU), actions per user, and whether actions happen evenly or in bursts.
  • Operation mix: reads, writes, uploads, downloads, background jobs, and internal fan-out.
  • Payload sizes: average request, response, record, and file sizes. Keep ingress and egress separate.
  • Retention: how long records, events, files, and derived data remain available.
  • Traffic shape: observed peak-to-average ratio, seasonal events, regional time zones, and retry behavior.
  • Capacity target: the utilization or headroom the system should retain during normal and degraded operation.

Ask which values are known, which are estimates, and which are deliberately conservative. If a prompt does not provide a value, choose a round assumption, say why it is plausible for the scenario, and show how the result changes if it is wrong. In an interview, this is part of the answer—not a detour before the answer.

The conversions worth keeping close

A day contains 86,400 seconds. For quick mental arithmetic, 100,000 seconds is a convenient approximation, but use 86,400 when showing a worked calculation. The approximation makes the result about 13.6% lower than the exact division, so it is useful for a first pass, not a substitute for checking a decision near a capacity boundary.

Time interval Seconds
1 day 86,400
30-day month 2,592,000
365-day year 31,536,000

For traffic, remember the order of magnitude: one million requests per day is 1,000,000 ÷ 86,400 = 11.57 requests per second, or roughly 12 average requests per second. Ten million per day is about 116/s; one hundred million per day is about 1,157/s.

Be precise about data units. Decimal units use powers of 10: 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes and 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes. Binary units use powers of 2: 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes, 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes, and 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes. NIST documents the distinction between SI and IEC binary prefixes. NIST: Definitions of the SI units — binary prefixes

Use one convention throughout a calculation. In the examples below, storage totals use decimal GB and TB; file sizes use MiB where binary units are more natural. State the convention rather than switching between MB and MiB as if they were identical.

Core formulas for system design estimation

These formulas provide a starting model. They do not capture every system cost, but they expose the main quantities that influence an initial architecture.

Average and peak request rate 

requests_per_day = DAU × requests_per_user_per_day
average_RPS      = requests_per_day ÷ 86,400
peak_RPS         = average_RPS × peak_to_average_factor

RPS means requests per second. QPS means queries per second; teams sometimes use the terms interchangeably, but define whether a “request” is an external API call, a database query, or an internal operation. One external request can fan out into several internal calls.

Do not assume one peak factor fits every product. Calculate it from observed time-bucketed traffic when possible: peak interval rate divided by the average rate for the same interval definition. If no telemetry exists, state a scenario assumption and test alternatives. A factor of 3 in an example means “we are modeling a peak three times the average,” not “all systems peak at 3×.”

Calculate read and write rates separately. A read-heavy product may need to serve a large volume of repeated data, while a write-heavy product may need sustained ingestion, ordering, durability, or downstream processing. A combined RPS figure can hide the real constraint.

Storage growth 

new_data_per_day = writes_per_day × average_record_size
logical_storage  = new_data_per_day × retention_days
physical_storage = logical_storage × copy_factor

Add indexes, metadata, compaction space, snapshots, backups, and derived data separately. A copy factor is a simplified planning input, not a universal statement about how a managed database or object store implements durability. Compression also changes the stored size; estimate it from representative data rather than assuming a fixed saving.

Network bandwidth 

bytes_per_second = requests_per_second × average_payload_bytes
bits_per_second  = bytes_per_second × 8

Calculate ingress and egress independently. Use the relevant request or response size for each path. Add protocol overhead, encryption, retries, fan-out, and retransmission where they materially affect the estimate. For large files, a small request count can still produce substantial bandwidth.

Server count 

required_instances = ceil(peak_RPS ÷ sustainable_RPS_per_instance)

If the capacity target is below full utilization, use ceil(peak_RPS ÷ (sustainable_RPS_per_instance × target_utilization)). The per-instance rate must come from a representative load test or a defensible capacity measurement for the actual workload, software, instance type, and latency target. Do not copy a generic “requests per server” number into a design and present it as fact.

Worked example 1: a read-heavy feed

Assume a feed service has 2 million daily active users. Each user loads twenty feed pages per day and creates half a post per day on average. Model peak traffic at four times the daily average. Assume each post record occupies 1,000 bytes and each feed response transfers 12,000 bytes. These are illustrative inputs.

1. Calculate reads.

reads/day = 2,000,000 users × 20 reads = 40,000,000
average read RPS = 40,000,000 ÷ 86,400 = 462.96 ≈ 463
peak read RPS = 463 × 4 ≈ 1,852

2. Calculate writes.

posts/day = 2,000,000 × 0.5 = 1,000,000
average write RPS = 1,000,000 ÷ 86,400 = 11.57 ≈ 11.6
peak write RPS = 11.57 × 4 = 46.3

The workload is roughly 40 reads for every write. That ratio does not prove a cache is required, but it tells you the read path deserves more attention than the write path in the first design pass.

3. Estimate response bandwidth.

peak egress = 1,852 responses/s × 12,000 bytes
             = 22,224,000 bytes/s
             ≈ 22.2 MB/s ≈ 178 Mbps

This is application response payload only. It excludes transport overhead and any media served separately. If feed responses include images, model image delivery as a separate path rather than hiding it inside an average API response.

4. Estimate post storage.

new logical data/day = 1,000,000 posts × 1,000 bytes = 1 GB
one year              = 1 GB/day × 365 = 365 GB
three-copy scenario   = 365 GB × 3 = 1.095 TB

The 1.095 TB figure excludes indexes, metadata, backups, and media. It is not a complete database capacity plan.

Design implications: investigate caching or precomputing frequently requested feed data, and consider read replicas only if measured database read pressure justifies them. Keep writes on a simpler path initially unless ordering, fan-out, or consistency requirements change the picture. Separate media delivery from feed API responses, and validate the assumed read distribution: a highly personalized feed may not benefit from the same cache strategy as a feed of mostly shared content.

Worked example 2: a write-heavy event log

Assume 500,000 daily active devices each emit 200 events per day. Each stored event, including its basic metadata, averages 600 bytes. Model peak ingestion at five times the average and retain events for 30 days. Use a three-copy scenario for a first storage estimate.

1. Calculate event volume and ingestion rate.

events/day = 500,000 × 200 = 100,000,000
average write RPS = 100,000,000 ÷ 86,400 = 1,157.4
peak write RPS = 1,157.4 × 5 = 5,787

2. Calculate storage.

logical data/day = 100,000,000 × 600 bytes = 60,000,000,000 bytes
                 = 60 GB/day
30-day logical storage = 60 GB × 30 = 1.8 TB
three-copy scenario = 1.8 TB × 3 = 5.4 TB

The 5.4 TB estimate excludes indexes, compression effects, retention gaps, backups, and temporary compaction space. If event payloads vary substantially, calculate by event class or use a measured size distribution instead of relying on one average.

3. Check ingress bandwidth.

peak ingress = 5,787 events/s × 600 bytes
              = 3,472,200 bytes/s
              ≈ 3.47 MB/s ≈ 27.8 Mbps

The request rate is more revealing than the raw bandwidth in this example. The system must accept and durably process nearly 5,800 small events per second at the modeled peak, even though the byte rate is modest.

Design implications: consider an append-oriented ingestion path, batching, and a durable queue or log when producers and consumers need decoupling. Partitioning can distribute sustained write volume, but the partition key must avoid concentrating one hot tenant or event type on a single partition. Define ordering requirements before choosing a partition strategy: global ordering is much more restrictive than per-device or per-aggregate ordering. Use retention and compaction policies that match the actual query and audit requirements.

Worked example 3: a file upload service

Assume 100,000 daily active users upload two files each per day. The average file is 8 MiB. Model upload peaks at eight times the average. Assume each uploaded file is downloaded three times on average, downloads peak at four times their average, and files are retained for 30 days. For a simplified capacity scenario, count three stored copies.

1. Calculate upload traffic.

uploads/day = 100,000 × 2 = 200,000
average upload RPS = 200,000 ÷ 86,400 = 2.31
peak upload RPS = 2.31 × 8 = 18.52

The request rate looks small. The payload size changes the capacity picture.

2. Calculate upload bandwidth.

peak ingress = 18.52 uploads/s × 8 MiB
             ≈ 155.3 MB/s ≈ 1.24 Gbps

The conversion uses 8 MiB = 8,388,608 bytes and decimal MB for the final rate. This is a payload estimate, not a provisioned network target; protocol overhead and burst shape still matter.

3. Calculate storage.

data/day = 200,000 × 8,388,608 bytes
         = 1.678 TB/day (decimal)
30-day logical storage = 1.678 TB × 30 ≈ 50.33 TB
three-copy scenario = 50.33 TB × 3 ≈ 150.99 TB

4. Estimate download egress.

downloads/day = 200,000 uploads × 3 = 600,000
average download RPS = 600,000 ÷ 86,400 = 6.94
peak download RPS = 6.94 × 4 = 27.78
peak egress = 27.78 × 8 MiB ≈ 233 MB/s ≈ 1.86 Gbps

Design implications: this is a data-transfer and storage problem, not simply an API request-count problem. Consider direct-to-object-storage uploads using short-lived, scoped upload authorization so application servers do not proxy every file byte. Use asynchronous processing for malware scanning, metadata extraction, and thumbnail generation when those tasks do not need to block the upload response. A CDN may reduce origin egress for repeatedly downloaded files, subject to access control and cache policy. Confirm whether “three copies” is actually how the chosen storage service bills or exposes durability; do not multiply managed storage by three if its documented storage model already accounts for redundancy.

Compare the three estimates

Example Peak primary operation Data growth Main pressure to investigate
Read-heavy feed ~1,852 reads/s; ~46 writes/s 1 GB/day logical posts Read path, cacheability, feed fan-out
Write-heavy event log ~5,787 writes/s 60 GB/day logical events Sustained ingestion, partitioning, retention
File upload service ~18.5 uploads/s; ~27.8 downloads/s ~1.68 TB/day logical files Ingress/egress bandwidth and object storage

The examples are not directly comparable capacity benchmarks: their workloads, payloads, and assumptions differ. Their purpose is to show how the same method reveals different constraints.

Sanity checks before you trust the result

Run these checks before turning estimates into an architecture:

  1. Recalculate from the other direction. Multiply average RPS by 86,400 and confirm that it returns the daily request count within rounding error.
  2. Check units at every step. Requests/s × bytes/request gives bytes/s. Multiply by eight only when converting bytes to bits. Do not label MB/s as Mbps.
  3. Separate external and internal work. If one request causes five database queries or three downstream calls, estimate those operations separately.
  4. Check peak and average consistency. Apply a peak factor to the same time unit and traffic category. Do not multiply a peak rate by a daily count again.
  5. Test the assumptions. Recalculate with half and twice the assumed activity, payload size, or retention. If the design changes sharply, the assumption needs measurement.
  6. Keep logical and physical storage distinct. State whether the estimate includes copies, indexes, backups, compression, and derived data.
  7. Look for missing workload dimensions. Concurrent connections, background jobs, retries, batch windows, and hot-key skew can matter even when average RPS looks modest.

Turn estimates into design decisions

An estimate is useful only when it changes a question or decision. Use the numbers to identify what to investigate—not to select a database or cache by formula alone.

  • Caching: consider it when reads repeat, data has an acceptable freshness window, and measured origin work is expensive. A high read/write ratio is a clue, not proof that every response is cacheable.
  • Replication: separate read scaling, availability, and durability requirements. Replicas add operational and consistency considerations; they are not a universal response to high RPS.
  • Partitioning: investigate it when write volume, storage growth, or data ownership exceeds a single partition's tested limits. Choose a key based on access patterns and skew, not only on even-looking IDs.
  • Queues and logs: use them when ingestion and processing need independent scaling, buffering, replay, or failure isolation. They add delivery semantics and operational complexity.
  • CDNs and object storage: consider them when large or repeated file transfers dominate bandwidth or application-server work. Access control and cache invalidation remain part of the design.
  • Capacity and headroom: use representative load tests to estimate sustainable per-instance throughput at the latency and error-rate targets that matter. Then calculate instance count with the formula above and add failure or deployment headroom explicitly.

For an interview, narrate the assumptions, show the arithmetic, identify the largest constraint, and explain what you would measure next. For a real design, record the inputs, source, confidence, and owner beside the estimate. A useful next step is to put the assumptions and capacity implications into a technical design document, where reviewers can challenge the numbers before they become infrastructure commitments.

Use the System Design Cheat Sheet as the companion reference while practicing these calculations. The cheat sheet is the primary resource for this topic; this article explains the reasoning behind the estimates and how to connect them to architectural choices.

References

  • Definitions of the SI units: The binary prefixes — National Institute of Standards and Technology

This article was originally published on Letinix.

title: My Store Turned Into Wingdings for Exactly One Reason, and It Was 3,410 Bytes
description:
On 7 November 2026 I added analytics to my store and rewarded myself by breaking the entire site's text. Every word on every page rendered as garbled symbols in my browser. The build was fine. The files were fine. The words were fine, somewhere underneath whatever my browser had decided they were.

The site is a small store built with Astro, deployed on Vercel. The change that morning was tiny and boring: install Vercel Analytics, drop the component into the base layout, deploy. The kind of change you make between sips of tea.

Then I opened the store and it looked like the text had been fed through a paper shredder and reassembled by an enemy.

What I checked first (all wrong)

I checked the content files. Clean. I checked the build output locally. Clean. I rebuilt. I stared at fonts, because garbled text feels like a font problem the way a cough feels like a lung problem. It usually isn't, but the feeling is strong.

Here is what I had not checked: the actual bytes of the page my browser received.

The analytics component injects an inline script into the <head>. My layout had the <meta charset> tag sitting after other elements, and the injected script landed before it. In the served HTML, the charset declaration ended up at byte offset 3,410.

That number is the whole story.

Why 3,410 bytes is a death sentence for a charset tag

When a server sends an HTML page without declaring the character encoding in the Content-Type response header, the browser has to guess. The HTML spec gives it a prescan step: it reads the beginning of the byte stream looking for a charset declaration.

The catch is the size of that beginning. The prescan only looks at roughly the first 1,024 bytes.

My charset tag was at byte 3,410. From the browser's point of view, it did not exist. So the browser fell back to a guessed encoding, guessed wrong, and rendered UTF-8 text through the wrong lens. Every multi-byte character smeared into symbols. The page was never broken. It was being read in the wrong language by a reader following its own rules correctly.

And my response headers carried no charset either, so there was no second chance. The meta tag was the only witness, and it was standing 3,410 bytes away from the only place witnesses get heard.

The fix, which is embarrassing in its size

Move the charset meta to be the first element inside <head>. Before the title. Before everything.

One line, relocated. Redeploy. In the new served HTML the charset sat at byte offset 44, comfortably inside the prescan window, and the store read like a store again. The checkout page returned 200, the text was clean, done.

Total code changed: the position of one tag. Total time spent suspecting my content, my fonts and my build before looking at the byte offsets: considerably longer, and I'd rather not be precise about it, which tells you everything.

What this one cost me in dignity, and what it taught me

Encoding bugs wear a perfect disguise. They look exactly like content bugs. The words are what's visibly wrong, so you interrogate the words, and the words are innocent, and they stay innocent no matter how many times you rebuild them.

The debugging rule I now follow, learned at byte 3,410: when text renders wrong, check how the bytes are being read before checking what the bytes say. View source. Count where the charset declaration actually sits in the served document, not where you placed it in your template, because frameworks, injectors and "helpful" components rearrange furniture in your <head> without asking. My template had the tag in a perfectly reasonable position. The served page had it somewhere else entirely. The template is a promise; the served bytes are the truth.

This applies to anything that injects into your head section: analytics, tag managers, A/B testing scripts, consent banners. Every one of them pushes your own tags further from byte zero. Most of the time it costs nothing. The day your headers don't declare a charset, it costs you your whole site's legibility, and the bill arrives looking like a content problem.

Your smallest cause?

I'm collecting these now, the bugs where the cause-to-symptom ratio is most insulting. Mine: one misplaced tag, 2,386 bytes past the limit, every word on a live store unreadable.

What's yours? The one-character typo that ate a weekend, the config line that took down the thing it was supposed to protect. Smallest cause, biggest symptom. I want to feel better, and also worse.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Kubernetes FinOps: finding the money you waste on oversized requests and idle nodes
description:
The cloud bill for your Kubernetes cluster went up again. You add nodes because new pods sit in Pending with "Insufficient cpu". Then you open a dashboard and the nodes are using 20 percent of their CPU.

Both things are true at the same time, and the reason is simple. The scheduler doesn't place pods based on what they use. It places them based on what they request. If every team asks for four times what their service needs, the cluster fills up on paper while the hardware sits mostly idle, and you pay for every one of those empty cores.

This article walks through finding that gap, closing it safely, and cleaning up the idle capacity that builds up around it.

Why requests, not usage, drive your bill

Every container can declare resource requests:

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: 2Gi

The scheduler treats those numbers as reserved. A node with 4 CPUs can hold four pods that each request 1 CPU, even if each of them actually uses 0.1. A fifth pod goes Pending, the cluster autoscaler adds a node, and the bill grows.

So the money is decided by requests. Usage only tells you how much of that money was wasted.

Requests usually get set once, early, by someone guessing. Nobody wants their service to be the one that ran out of memory, so the guess is generous, gets copied into the next Helm chart, and never gets revisited.

Step 1: Measure the gap

Start with a quick look from the command line. This needs metrics-server, which most managed clusters ship with:

kubectl top nodes
kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep -A 8 "Allocated resources"

kubectl top nodes shows real usage. The "Allocated resources" section of describe node shows how much of the node is requested. A node at 90 percent requested and 25 percent used is the pattern you are looking for.

For the whole cluster, Prometheus with kube-state-metrics gives you the same comparison per namespace. Requested CPU:

sum by (namespace) (
  kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="cpu"}
)

CPU actually used:

sum by (namespace) (
  rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container!=""}[5m])
)

And the same for memory, requested against the working set:

sum by (namespace) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="memory"})
sum by (namespace) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!=""})

Put requested and used side by side in one table and sort by the difference. In most clusters, a handful of namespaces account for most of the waste. Start there.

Step 2: Right size from real data, not from a guess

Right sizing means setting requests close to what the workload really needs, with sensible headroom. The key word is real: look at at least a week of history so you catch daily peaks and the weekly batch job.

For CPU, the 95th percentile over a week is a good starting point for the request:

quantile_over_time(0.95,
  rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace="shop", container="api"}[5m])[7d:5m]
)

For memory, look at the peak instead, because running out of memory gets the container killed rather than slowed down:

max_over_time(
  container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="shop", container="api"}[7d]
)

A few rules that keep this safe:

  • CPU request around the p95 of usage. CPU is compressible. If a pod needs more for a moment and the node has spare cycles, it gets them.
  • Memory request at the observed peak plus 20 to 30 percent headroom, and set the memory limit to the same value or a bit higher. Memory is not compressible. A container over its limit is OOM killed.
  • Change one service at a time and watch latency, restarts and OOM kills for a few days before moving on.
  • Watch out for startup spikes. JVM and some Node.js apps use far more CPU while starting. If startup gets slow after a cut, that's the reason.

Let the Vertical Pod Autoscaler do the math

If you don't want to write the queries yourself, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler can recommend requests from observed usage. It's an add on you install into the cluster. Run it in recommendation only mode so it never touches running pods:

apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api-vpa
  namespace: shop
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: "Off"

After it has watched the workload for a while:

kubectl describe vpa api-vpa -n shop

The Target value under the recommendation is what it would set. Treat it as a strong suggestion, compare it with your own percentiles, and apply it through your normal deployment process. One caution: don't let VPA change CPU or memory automatically on a workload where the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales on the same metric. The two will fight.

Step 3: Turn off what nobody is using

Oversized requests are the biggest leak. Idle resources are the second, and they are often easier to fix.

Dev and staging environments running all night. A staging namespace that nobody touches between 8 PM and 8 AM and all weekend is idle for roughly two thirds of the week. Scaling those deployments to zero outside working hours is one of the fastest savings you can get. A small CronJob running kubectl scale deployment --all --replicas=0 -n staging in the evening, and a matching one in the morning, is enough to start. Tools like kube-downscaler do the same with annotations.

Forgotten volumes. Persistent volumes outlive the apps that created them, and you keep paying for the disks:

kubectl get pv | grep -E "Released|Available"

A Released volume is no longer bound to any claim. If its reclaim policy is Retain, the disk still exists in your cloud account. Check what's on it, snapshot it if needed, and delete it.

Load balancers nobody uses. Every Service of type LoadBalancer usually creates a separate cloud load balancer with its own hourly price:

kubectl get svc -A | grep LoadBalancer

Old test services and services that should sit behind your shared ingress show up here more often than you'd expect.

Abandoned namespaces. Preview environments and experiments from months ago keep running quietly. List namespaces with their age and ask the owners of anything old whether it still needs to exist.

Step 4: Make the nodes follow the pods

Right sizing frees up space on nodes, but you only save money if the cluster actually removes nodes afterwards.

The Cluster Autoscaler removes a node when the pods on it can be moved elsewhere and the node has been underused for a while. A few things commonly block that:

  • Pods with the annotation cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false"
  • Pods using local storage, like emptyDir volumes, which the autoscaler won't evict by default in many setups
  • PodDisruptionBudgets that allow zero disruptions
  • Bare pods that aren't managed by a Deployment, StatefulSet or other controller

If your nodes never scale down, check those first.

On AWS, Karpenter goes a step further with consolidation. It removes empty nodes and also replaces several underused nodes with fewer or cheaper ones:

disruption:
  consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
  consolidateAfter: 1m

That snippet goes in the NodePool spec. Combined with right sized requests, consolidation is where the savings finally show up on the bill.

Use spot capacity for workloads that can handle interruption. Stateless services with several replicas, CI runners and batch jobs are good candidates. Spot capacity can be much cheaper than on demand, at the cost of being reclaimed at short notice, so keep databases and single replica services on regular nodes.

Step 5: Show each team what it costs

Waste comes back if nobody can see it. The most lasting fix is to make cost visible per team.

OpenCost, a CNCF project, runs in the cluster and breaks down cost by namespace, deployment, label and more, using your cloud provider's pricing. Install it, make sure every workload carries a team or app label, and share a simple weekly report: what each team requested, what it used, and what that cost.

You don't need chargeback or hard budgets to see results. In most teams, seeing "you requested 40 CPUs and used 6" next to a dollar figure is enough to start the right conversation.

A simple order to do this in

  1. Measure requested vs used per namespace.
  2. Pick the three biggest gaps and right size them from a week of data.
  3. Scale dev and staging to zero out of hours.
  4. Clean up released volumes, unused load balancers and abandoned namespaces.
  5. Make sure nodes actually scale down, with consolidation if you have it.
  6. Put cost per team in front of the teams.

Each step is small on its own. Together they often cut a large share of the compute bill without touching a single line of application code.

Takeaway

In Kubernetes, you pay for what you request, not for what you use. Measure the gap between the two, right size from real usage with headroom for memory, switch off what sits idle, and make sure your nodes shrink when your pods do. Then make the numbers visible, so the gap doesn't quietly grow back.

I'm Amit Shukla, a software engineer working across DevOps, cloud and applied AI. Behind the Stack is where I write up the things I learn the hard way, with working code and honest tradeoffs.
