title: AWS Tagging Strategy: Name, Owner and Environment Tags for Every Resource
description:
By now I have IAM, a budget, CloudTrail and CloudWatch. One more habit makes all of them easier to use: tags. When the bill rises or something looks odd, tags tell you what the resource is, who owns it and what it is for.

What tags are

  • A tag is a key and value pair attached to a resource, such as Environment = dev.
  • Most AWS resources support tags, and you can have up to 50 tags per resource.
  • Tags are labels for people and tools. They do not change how the resource works.

A simple starting set

Key Example value Why
Name web-server-1 Shows in the console list
Environment dev, test, prod Separate workloads
Owner robin Who to ask
Project blog-site Group related resources
CostCenter learning Split the bill

What tags are used for

  • Cost allocation: activate cost allocation tags in Billing, then filter Cost Explorer by tag.
  • Access control: IAM policies can allow or deny actions based on tags (ABAC).
  • Automation: scripts can find resources by tag, such as all Environment = dev instances to stop at night.
  • Search: Tag Editor and Resource Groups find resources across Regions.

Good to know

  • Tag keys and values are case sensitive, so Owner and owner are different.
  • Tags are not retroactive in Cost Explorer. Cost allocation tags only show costs from the time you activate them.
  • Tag policies in AWS Organizations help keep names consistent.
  • Do not put secrets or personal data in tags.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open EC2 or S3 and select a resource you created.
  2. Add the tags Name, Environment, Owner and Project.
  3. Open Resource Groups & Tag Editor and use Tag Editor to search by Environment = dev across Regions.
  4. Open Billing and Cost allocation tags, then activate Project.
  5. After a day, filter Cost Explorer by the Project tag.

Common mistakes

  • Inconsistent keys, such as env, Env and Environment.
  • Tagging only some resources, so reports have gaps.
  • Forgetting to activate cost allocation tags.
  • Storing sensitive data in tag values.

Key takeaways

  • Tags answer what, who and why for every resource.
  • Pick a small standard set and use it everywhere.
  • Activate cost allocation tags to see costs by tag.
  • Keep tag names consistent.

Tomorrow I'll look at how to see all of this from a single place: AWS Organizations and account structure.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

title: Batch your lookups: 14x the requests/s from the same Postgres
description:
I had a service that needed one user per request. It did what everybody does: one SELECT … WHERE key = $1 per request. On my laptop that stopped at about 18,000 requests per second. Sixty-four clients, a thousand clients, four thousand clients: 18,000.

Postgres was not busy. Every request paid a full round trip for one row, and on this laptop each round trip also went through Docker Desktop's port forwarding. The round trips were the limit, and they were more expensive here than they would be on a Linux host.

When I sent the requests that happened to be waiting at the same moment as one query, the same database answered 252,000 requests per second with 4,096 clients, and the p99 dropped from 271 ms to 28 ms.

This post is about keeping the call simple and letting something else do the batching. Disclosure: the library in my numbers is mq-bridge, which I wrote. The pattern itself is much older. In GraphQL, this is DataLoader, so I compare against one. I also compare against pipelining in the driver, which removes the waiting without changing the query.

The setup

  • A Postgres table with 1 million users. Each request fetches one of them by primary key.
  • N client tasks in the same binary. Each one sends its next request when the last one is answered. This is a closed loop: the latencies are what these clients saw, not what a fixed arrival rate would see. The HTTP section below has an open-loop run.
  • The baseline is sqlx 0.9 with a pool of 64 connections and one WHERE path = $1 per request.
  • Everything runs on one MacBook (M1, 8 cores, 8GB RAM), Postgres 17.6 in Docker Desktop.
  • Every number is the median of three runs.
  • The benchmark checks every answer against its key, so a fast wrong answer doesn't count.

The code is in
mq-bridge/benches/lookup/caller.

The code

All versions return the same struct:

#[derive(sqlx::FromRow, serde::Deserialize)]
struct User { path: String, id: i64, name: String, tier: String }

This is the baseline:

let user: User = sqlx::query_as("SELECT path, id, name, tier FROM users WHERE path = $1")
    .bind(&key)
    .fetch_one(&pool)
    .await?;

And this is the batched version, as the caller sees it:

let user: User = users.call([("path", &key)]).await?;   // Option<User> if it may be missing

One call in, one answer out. The batching SQL lives in a route, set up once at startup:

let users = Caller::from_str(r#"
batch_size: 256
concurrency: 4
input:
  middlewares:
    - lookup:
        from:
          sqlx:
            url: "postgres://localhost:55432/bench"
            table: users
            max_connections: 8
            lookup_query: "SELECT path, id, name, tier FROM users WHERE path IN (${payload:path})"
        into: $
    - parallel: { max_in_flight: 16 }
"#, "users").await?;

Calls that arrive together are read as one batch, and lookup answers the whole batch with one query. On Postgres it runs IN (${payload:path}) as path = ANY($1), so every batch size shares one prepared statement.

parallel keeps up to 16 batches in flight. The lanes share one pool of 8 connections, so at most 8 queries wait for Postgres at once. concurrency: 4 only covers handing the answers back to the callers. The lookups run in the input, so parallel is what overlaps them.

What happened

requests/s one query per request batched, 16 in flight factor
1 client 3,095 3,245 1.0x
16 clients 16,002 21,113 1.3x
64 clients 17,849 49,253 2.8x
256 clients 18,075 138,141 7.6x
1,024 clients 18,038 206,690 11x
4,096 clients 18,289 252,161 14x
p50 / p99 one query per request batched, 16 in flight
1 client 0.30 / 0.64 ms 0.30 / 0.55 ms
1,024 clients 54 / 99 ms 4.6 / 14 ms
4,096 clients 222 / 271 ms 16 / 28 ms

One query per request flattens out at 64 clients. Adding clients after that only makes the queue for the connection pool longer, which is why its latency grows with every row of the table.

With a single client, batching changes nothing. A batch of one is one query, and it costs about 0.3 ms either way.

parallel is what keeps it going. Without it, each batch waits for the previous one, and the route stops at about 60,000. Lanes only start for batches worth a query of their own, so the extra lanes cost little at 16 clients: 21,000 with them, 22,000 without.

The batches are only as full as the number of requests waiting at that moment. That is the ceiling for this kind of traffic, and it is why the single-request numbers stop around 14x.

And pipelining?

The problem is the waiting, and a driver can stop waiting without touching the SQL. tokio-postgres pipelines queries that are issued concurrently on one connection: it sends the next query before the previous answer is back. The sqlx pool doesn't do that; each connection runs one query at a time. I ran the same one-query-per-request load on 16 and on 64 tokio-postgres connections, round robin.

requests/s one query per request pipelined, 16 connections pipelined, 64 connections batched, 16 in flight
1 client 3,095 3,401 3,213 3,245
16 clients 16,002 26,085 23,482 21,113
64 clients 17,849 38,367 31,850 49,253
256 clients 18,075 47,641 37,502 138,141
1,024 clients 18,038 56,255 44,431 206,690
4,096 clients 18,289 55,109 47,882 252,161

Pipelining helps, by 2–3x, and with 16 clients it is the fastest of all. Fewer connections did better than more, because each pipeline gets deeper. Then it levels off around 55,000, with a p99 of 375 ms at 4,096 clients. Pipelining removes the waiting, not the work: Postgres still executes and answers one statement per key. Batching sends one statement for up to 256 keys.

If you can't change the query, pipelining is the cheaper fix. If you have many concurrent requests, batching goes further.

And DataLoader?

I ran async-graphql's DataLoader on the same 64-connection pool: max_batch_size 256, delay 0, one WHERE path = ANY($1) per batch. Its cache is off, as in the route. This post is only about combining requests.

requests/s one query per request DataLoader batched, 16 in flight
1 client 3,095 585 3,245
16 clients 16,002 9,476 21,113
64 clients 17,849 37,348 49,253
256 clients 18,075 109,165 138,141
1,024 clients 18,038 191,580 206,690
4,096 clients 18,289 222,924 252,161
p50 / p99 one query per request DataLoader batched, 16 in flight
1 client 0.30 / 0.64 ms 1.9 / 2.7 ms 0.30 / 0.55 ms
1,024 clients 54 / 99 ms 4.3 / 19 ms 4.6 / 14 ms
4,096 clients 222 / 271 ms 14 / 85 ms 16 / 28 ms

DataLoader does the same thing and lands in the same place. From 1,024 clients up, the route was 8–13% ahead, and DataLoader's p99 at 4,096 clients was higher, 85 ms against 28 ms.

Below that, the difference is mostly how this DataLoader waits. Even with delay 0, async-graphql collects a batch behind a Tokio timer, which fires on the next millisecond tick. That costs about 1.5 ms per batch, and it is why it does 585 requests/s with one client. A DataLoader that only yields would not pay that. So I would not read the low-client rows as "batching in a route is faster than DataLoader". They show that waiting for a timer is expensive when nobody else is coming. I did not test other implementations, such as the dataloader crate.

How each batch asks Postgres mattered more than I expected. One = ANY($1) with an array is one prepared statement for every batch size. IN ($1, …, $n) is a different statement for each n. At 64 clients, the same DataLoader with an IN list did 27,000 instead of 37,000.

If you write Rust and have one database, a Loader is about fifteen lines and nearly as fast. What a route adds is that the batching is configuration instead of code: the same lookup works against MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB, ClickHouse or HTTP, and the same Caller is available from Python, Node and C.

On ClickHouse the effect is the same. A point lookup there reads a whole granule. In a short file-to-file run against 1 million rows (ClickHouse 25.8 in Docker), one query per message did about 1,100 rows/s and batches of 1,000 keys did about 19,500, roughly 17x.

Behind an HTTP endpoint

The same lookup behind an HTTP endpoint (mq-bridge's http input → lookup → response, oha as the client), one lookup per request on a pool of 64 against batched with 16 lanes. At 20,000 requests/s offered, the batched route kept up with a p99 of 7.9 ms. One lookup per request managed about 12,400 and fell behind, with waits of almost two seconds.

Numbers
Load (HTTP, local) per request: req/s per request: p99 batched: req/s batched: p99
1 client 2,513 0.89 ms 2,645 0.64 ms
64 clients 10,974 10 ms 31,752 4.2 ms
20,000 req/s offered 12,391 1,894 ms 19,989 7.9 ms
40,000 req/s offered 12,201 3,451 ms 36,539 430 ms

At 40,000 req/s offered, the batched route was past its limit as well.


Caveats

This all ran on one laptop. The clients, mq-bridge and Postgres fought over the same 8 cores.

The 18,000 queries/s ceiling includes Docker's port forwarding on macOS. A pool of 192 connections did not raise it. With a faster path to the database that number goes up, and every factor in this post goes down. Over a real network it goes the other way: each round trip gets more expensive, and one query per request falls further behind.

The baseline and the DataLoader use 64 connections, pipelining 16 or 64. The batched route uses 8. Another driver or pool size would move the numbers. I only tested primary-key lookups with small rows, on Postgres 17.6; I did not test Postgres 18.

Most cells varied by less than 5% between the three runs, a few by up to 16%.

Try it 

cd benches/lookup
docker compose up -d --wait
export PGUSER=bench PGPASSWORD=bench   # the compose database's credentials
cd caller && cargo run --release        # args: requests per cell, variants, runs (default 50000, all, 3)

It prints the tables above for your machine, plus a few more variants. The HTTP runs are described in benches/lookup/README.md. Let me know what kind of numbers you have.

title: CSS sprite sheet animation: getting steps() right
description:
Put the sheet on an element as a background, size the element to one frame, and animate background-position across the sheet with a steps() timing function. For 8 frames of 64 × 64 in one row:

.sprite {
  width: 64px;                 /* one frame */
  height: 64px;
  background: url("walk.png") 0 0 no-repeat;
  animation: play 0.8s steps(8) infinite;   /* 8 frames at 10 fps */
}

@keyframes play {
  to { background-position: -512px 0; }     /* 8 x 64px: the whole sheet */
}

<div class="sprite" role="img" aria-label="Character walking"></div>

Every snippet ran in Chromium 156, reading computed background-position every 5 ms; not Safari or Firefox.

Why steps(N) ends at the full sheet width

Duration is frames over frame rate. The end position trips people up: the last frame sits at -448px (7 × 64), so that looks like the stop. But steps(8) is steps(8, end) — 8 equal holds, the last jump at the end — so the to value never shows. Ending at -512px lands the holds on 0, -64, -128 … -448.

The classic bug mirrors it: end at -448px with steps(8) and every step is 56px, so the first frames look fine and the last show two halves.

The jump-none form is the other correct answer, and I write it by hand even though a forward loop looks identical:

.sprite {
  animation: play 0.8s steps(8, jump-none) infinite;
}

@keyframes play {
  to { background-position: -448px 0; }     /* 7 x 64px: the last frame */
}

A sheet with more than one row

One steps() walks in a straight line; a grid must go across, drop, and go across again. Use one keyframe per frame with steps(1), which holds each value until the next:

.sprite {
  width: 64px;
  height: 64px;
  background: url("walk-grid.png") 0 0 no-repeat;   /* 4 columns x 2 rows */
  animation: play 0.8s steps(1) infinite;
}

@keyframes play {
  0%    { background-position: 0 0; }
  12.5% { background-position: -64px 0; }
  25%   { background-position: -128px 0; }
  37.5% { background-position: -192px 0; }
  50%   { background-position: 0 -64px; }
  62.5% { background-position: -64px -64px; }
  75%   { background-position: -128px -64px; }
  87.5% { background-position: -192px -64px; }
}

Each percentage is frame index over frame count, with no 100% keyframe on purpose, so the last frame holds to the end. Uneven timing is free — keyframes 10% apart held frame 8 for 240 ms.

Nobody types that for 40 frames. The GIF to sprite sheet tool and its sprite sheet maker both write this block, or the steps(N) version for a single row, from a Copy CSS button.

For a full grid, two animations on separate axes do the same job:

.sprite {
  width: 64px;
  height: 64px;
  background: url("walk-grid.png") 0 0 no-repeat;
  animation:
    across 0.4s steps(4) infinite,    /* one row: 4 frames */
    down   0.8s steps(2) infinite;    /* 2 rows, each lasting one "across" */
}

@keyframes across { to { background-position-x: -256px; } }
@keyframes down   { to { background-position-y: -128px; } }

Same eight positions at the same times in my test — but not with empty cells, which play as blanks.

Scaling up without blur

Multiply four numbers by one whole number — width, height, background-size, end position — and add image-rendering: pixelated. At 4×:

.sprite {
  width: 256px;                /* 64 x 4 */
  height: 256px;
  background: url("walk.png") 0 0 / 2048px 256px no-repeat;   /* sheet size x 4 */
  image-rendering: pixelated;
  animation: play 0.8s steps(8) infinite;
}

@keyframes play {
  to { background-position: -2048px 0; }
}

background-size is the forgotten one. Without it the 512px sheet sits in a 256px box stepping 256px at a time, so I got frames 1–4, then 5–8, then nothing. MDN defines pixelated as nearest-neighbour scaling to the nearest whole multiple.

Making it responsive

Percentages instead of pixels. background-size: 800% makes an 8-frame row eight elements wide at any width. Positions measure from the far edge: 100% puts the last frame in the box, not one past it — jump-none again.

.sprite {
  width: round(down, 100%, 64px);   /* largest whole multiple of the frame that fits */
  max-width: 256px;
  aspect-ratio: 1 / 1;
  background: url("walk.png") 0 0 / 800% 100% no-repeat;   /* 8 frames wide */
  image-rendering: pixelated;
  animation: play 0.8s steps(8, jump-none) infinite;
}

@keyframes play {
  to { background-position: 100% 0; }
}

round() keeps the scale whole: 192px in a 200px column, exactly 3×, where plain width: 100% gave 3.125× and mixed 3- and 4-pixel art pixels. It shipped in current browsers in May 2024; otherwise set a pixel width per breakpoint. For a grid, use background-size: 400% 200% and offsets of column ÷ (columns - 1).

Play once, reverse, pause on hover 

/* Shared keyframes that stop on the last frame */
@keyframes play-to-last {
  to { background-position: -448px 0; }     /* (8 - 1) x 64px */
}

/* Play once and hold the last frame */
.sprite.once {
  animation: play-to-last 0.8s steps(8, jump-none) 1 forwards;
}

/* Backwards, 8 down to 1 */
.sprite.reverse {
  animation: play-to-last 0.8s steps(8, jump-none) infinite reverse;
}

/* There and back: 1 to 8, then 8 to 1 */
.sprite.ping-pong {
  animation: play-to-last 0.8s steps(8, jump-none) infinite alternate;
}

/* Freeze while the pointer is over it */
.sprite.pause-on-hover:hover {
  animation-play-state: paused;
}

/* Still until hovered or focused */
.sprite.play-on-hover {
  animation-play-state: paused;
}
.sprite.play-on-hover:hover,
.sprite.play-on-hover:focus-visible {
  animation-play-state: running;
}

Add forwards to the classic steps(8) rule and the sprite finishes on -512px, one frame past the sheet: an empty box under no-repeat, a snap to frame 1 without it. That is why these rules use jump-none. Hover does not exist on touch, so put play-on-hover on a focusable element — hence :focus-visible.

Respect reduced motion 

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .sprite {
    animation: none;
    background-position: -192px 0;   /* frame 4, the one that reads best as a still */
  }
}

animation: none alone leaves frame 1 showing, which is not always the best still. In a ping-pong, frames 1 and 8 each hold twice at the turns — usually a natural pause.

Canvas, for per-frame timing or many sprites

CSS runs out when game logic picks the frame, when durations change at run time, or when one element per sprite gets silly. The canvas version is the 9-argument drawImage: source rectangle from the sheet, destination on the canvas.

<canvas id="stage"></canvas>

<script>
const canvas = document.getElementById("stage");
const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");

const FRAME_W = 64, FRAME_H = 64, COLS = 4;      // a 4 x 2 grid sheet
const durations = [100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 300];   // ms per frame
const total = durations.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);

const scale = 3;
const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
canvas.width = FRAME_W * scale * dpr;
canvas.height = FRAME_H * scale * dpr;
canvas.style.width = FRAME_W * scale + "px";
canvas.style.height = FRAME_H * scale + "px";
ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = false;   // after resizing, which resets the context

const sheet = new Image();
sheet.src = "walk-grid.png";

function frameAt(ms) {
  let t = ms % total;
  for (let i = 0; i < durations.length; i++) {
    if (t < durations[i]) return i;
    t -= durations[i];
  }
  return 0;
}

let start, last = -1;
function tick(now) {
  start ??= now;
  const i = frameAt(now - start);
  if (i !== last) {
    last = i;
    const sx = (i % COLS) * FRAME_W;
    const sy = Math.floor(i / COLS) * FRAME_H;
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
    ctx.drawImage(sheet, sx, sy, FRAME_W, FRAME_H, 0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
  }
  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
}
sheet.decode().then(() => requestAnimationFrame(tick));
</script>

The frame comes from elapsed time, not from counting requestAnimationFrame calls, so speed does not follow the refresh rate. My run drew at about 30 fps: 100 ms frames changed 0–33 ms late, the 300 ms hold lasted 317 ms. The durations array maps onto the duration field in the JSON atlas the tool exports. One trap: resizing a canvas resets imageSmoothingEnabled.

What goes wrong

  • Frames slide sideways. No steps(), or a later animation shorthand that drops the timing function, resetting it to ease.
  • Half of two frames. The step size is not the frame width (448 ÷ 8 is 56), or the sheet has gaps, making the stride frame plus gap.
  • Blurry. Missing image-rendering: pixelated, a fractional scale, or a PNG smoothed before it reached the browser.
  • Uneven pixels. Frames that are not a whole number of screen pixels wide: a percentage width, transform: scale(1.37), a parent in vw. At 77.3px a 2px outline rendered 1px.
  • Too big for a phone. Decoded, a 100-frame row of 256px frames is about 26 MB, and iOS caps a canvas at 4,096 × 4,096.

Sprite sheet, GIF or video?

Sheet (PNG) GIF Animated WebP / APNG
Colour Full 256 colours Full
Transparency Full alpha On/off Full alpha
Pause, reverse, play once Yes No No
Code needed The CSS above An <img> An <img>

Control is the reason to pick a sheet: a GIF plays when it loads, and CSS cannot pause it or stop it for reduced motion. GIF transparency is all or nothing too, so shadows get a hard fringe. File size I will not promise either way — export both and look. If nobody interacts with it, an animated WebP is simpler; past a few seconds, use video.

The full version, with every measurement and the browser sources, is at CSS sprite sheet animation on giftospritesheet.com.

title: Your Outbox Can Still Deliver Twice
description:
A receiver commits its work. The reply disappears. The sender sees a timeout and sends the same event again.

An outbox can preserve the event through that sequence. It cannot, by itself, tell the receiver that the work already happened.

Here is a small reproduction with two SQLite databases and ten tests. The unsafe receiver adds two rows for one event. The receiver with an inbox adds one row and returns its stored receipt on the second delivery.

This continues the previous example about recovering a lost response. That example kept a mutation and its operation receipt in one database. This time the handoff crosses between two separate databases.

Three commits to keep separate

Imagine a service that accepts a report request and hands it to a worker service. The fixture models a completed worker effect by inserting a row into report_runs; it does not generate a file or call an external API.

Step Durable state What can still be unknown?
Producer commits Report request and outgoing event exist together Whether the receiver has seen the event
Receiver commits Local effect and inbox receipt exist together Whether the sender received the reply
Sender records the receipt The matching outbox row is marked delivered Nothing about later work outside this fixture

The transactional outbox explanation from AWS describes the first boundary: save the business change and outgoing intent in the same database transaction, then publish separately.

There is still a gap between the second and third rows of the table. If the receiver commits but its reply is lost, the sender must be able to deliver the event again.

Make the receiver remember the event

The inbox key in this example is:

(source, workspace_id, event_id)

The event ID identifies one intent. The producer creates it once, persists it in the outbox, and reuses it for delivery retries. Two genuinely new requests can have identical payloads and still need different event IDs.

For a new key, the receiver inserts the local effect and its receipt in one transaction. For an existing key, it compares the payload and returns the saved receipt. A reused key with a changed payload is refused.

The transaction starts before the inbox lookup. With SQLite's BEGIN IMMEDIATE, this fixture acquires the write transaction before doing the read-then-write decision. SQLite allows only one simultaneous writer. A concurrent duplicate waits for the first transaction, then sees its receipt. The primary key remains a database constraint on event identity.

This is a deliberately small SQLite design. Another database needs its own concurrency argument; copying an existence check into two ordinary concurrent transactions is insufficient.

Reproduce the missing reply

The test injects a failure after the receiver has committed and closed its connection:

def lose_reply(event):
    consume(receiver, event)
    raise TimeoutError("receiver committed; reply lost")

The first delivery leaves the sender's outbox row pending. A fresh dispatch reads the same persisted event and sends it again. With the unsafe control, that creates a second effect. With the inbox, it returns the original receipt and leaves the effect count at one.

The send callback runs outside the producer transaction. The sender opens a new transaction only after receiving a receipt that identifies the event it sent. This keeps the example from holding a producer write lock across the simulated remote call.

Run the fixture

Save the complete file below as outbox_inbox.py and run:

python outbox_inbox.py

It requires Python 3.12 or later, uses the standard library, and creates disposable databases under a test-db folder beside the file. Each test closes its connections and removes its own temporary subdirectory.

The ten tests passed locally with Python 3.12.14 and SQLite 3.53.1. They test these outcomes:

Injected condition Assertion
Outbox insertion fails Neither the report request nor its outgoing event commits
Reply is lost, without an inbox Retrying creates two local effects
Reply is lost, with an inbox Retrying returns a stored receipt; one effect remains
Inbox receipt insertion fails The receiver's effect also rolls back
Sender cannot save the acknowledgement The receiver stays committed; retry replays its receipt
Two relays read the same pending event One fresh receipt and one replay, with the same receipt ID
Same event key, changed payload Refusal, without another effect
Same event ID in distinct trusted scopes Separate receipts for each source/workspace key
Two new requests with identical payloads Two distinct event IDs and two effects
Reply identifies an unrelated event The outgoing row stays pending

The concurrent test places a barrier after both relays have read the pending row. It therefore tests a duplicate delivery, rather than relying on thread timing to happen to create one.

Complete runnable example and all ten tests

"""Two local SQLite databases; no broker, network, MCP transport or external effect.

Python 3.12+. Run: python outbox_inbox.py
"""
from contextlib import closing, contextmanager
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
from pathlib import Path
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from threading import Barrier
import json
import sqlite3
import tempfile
import unittest
import uuid


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Event:
    source: str
    workspace_id: str
    event_id: str
    payload: str

    @property
    def key(self):
        return self.source, self.workspace_id, self.event_id


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Receipt:
    key: tuple[str, str, str]
    receipt_id: str
    replayed: bool


class PayloadMismatch(Exception):
    pass


class BadReceipt(Exception):
    pass


def connect(path):
    db = sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=5, autocommit=True)
    db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return db


def one(db, sql, args=()):
    with closing(db.execute(sql, args)) as cursor:
        return cursor.fetchone()


@contextmanager
def transaction(path):
    with closing(connect(path)) as db:
        try:
            db.execute("BEGIN IMMEDIATE").close()
            yield db
            db.execute("COMMIT").close()
        except BaseException:
            if db.in_transaction:
                db.execute("ROLLBACK").close()
            raise


def initialize(producer, receiver):
    with closing(connect(producer)) as db:
        db.executescript("""
        CREATE TABLE report_requests (
            id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, workspace_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            report_name TEXT NOT NULL
        );
        CREATE TABLE outbox (
            seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
            source TEXT NOT NULL, workspace_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            event_id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, payload TEXT NOT NULL,
            delivered INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
        );
        """).close()
    with closing(connect(receiver)) as db:
        db.executescript("""
        CREATE TABLE report_runs (
            id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
            source TEXT NOT NULL, workspace_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            event_id TEXT NOT NULL, report_name TEXT NOT NULL
        );
        CREATE TABLE inbox (
            source TEXT NOT NULL, workspace_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            event_id TEXT NOT NULL, payload TEXT NOT NULL,
            receipt_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            PRIMARY KEY (source, workspace_id, event_id)
        );
        """).close()


def payload_for(report_name):
    if not isinstance(report_name, str) or len(report_name) not in range(1, 81):
        raise ValueError("report_name must contain 1..80 characters")
    return json.dumps({"format": "csv", "report_name": report_name},
                      sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))


def request_report(producer, workspace_id, report_name):
    # Trusted, already-authorized context in this fixture. This is a NEW intent.
    event = Event("report-service", workspace_id, str(uuid.uuid4()),
                  payload_for(report_name))
    with transaction(producer) as db:
        db.execute("INSERT INTO report_requests VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                   (str(uuid.uuid4()), workspace_id, report_name)).close()
        db.execute("""INSERT INTO outbox
            (source, workspace_id, event_id, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)""",
                   (*event.key, event.payload)).close()
    return event


def insert_run(db, event):
    body = json.loads(event.payload)
    if (not isinstance(body, dict) or set(body) != {"format", "report_name"}
            or body["format"] != "csv"
            or payload_for(body["report_name"]) != event.payload):
        raise ValueError("unsupported payload; use the fixture serialization")
    with closing(db.execute("INSERT INTO report_runs "
            "(source, workspace_id, event_id, report_name) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
            (*event.key, body["report_name"]))) as cursor:
        return f"receipt-{cursor.lastrowid}"


def consume(receiver, event):
    with transaction(receiver) as db:
        old = one(db, """SELECT payload, receipt_id FROM inbox
            WHERE source = ? AND workspace_id = ? AND event_id = ?""",
                  event.key)
        if old:
            if old["payload"] != event.payload:
                raise PayloadMismatch(event.key)
            return Receipt(event.key, old["receipt_id"], True)
        # The modeled effect and its deduplication receipt commit together.
        receipt_id = insert_run(db, event)
        db.execute("INSERT INTO inbox VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
                   (*event.key, event.payload, receipt_id)).close()
        return Receipt(event.key, receipt_id, False)


def consume_without_inbox(receiver, event):
    # Deliberately unsafe control: every delivery adds a local effect.
    with transaction(receiver) as db:
        return Receipt(event.key, insert_run(db, event), False)


def next_event(producer):
    with closing(connect(producer)) as db:
        row = one(db, """SELECT source, workspace_id, event_id, payload
            FROM outbox WHERE delivered = 0 ORDER BY seq LIMIT 1""")
        return Event(**dict(row)) if row else None


def dispatch_one(producer, send):
    event = next_event(producer)
    if event is None:
        return None
    # No producer transaction is held across this external-call seam.
    receipt = send(event)
    if (not isinstance(receipt, Receipt) or receipt.key != event.key
            or not isinstance(receipt.receipt_id, str) or not receipt.receipt_id):
        raise BadReceipt("acknowledgement does not identify the sent event")
    with transaction(producer) as db:
        with closing(db.execute("""UPDATE outbox SET delivered = 1
            WHERE source = ? AND workspace_id = ? AND event_id = ?
            AND payload = ?""", (*event.key, event.payload))) as cursor:
            if cursor.rowcount != 1:
                raise BadReceipt("outbox intent changed or disappeared")
    return receipt


class HandoffTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        base = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "test-db"
        base.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        self.temp = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="handoff-", dir=base)
        self.folder = Path(self.temp.name).resolve()
        assert self.folder.is_relative_to(base.resolve())
        self.addCleanup(self.temp.cleanup)
        self.producer = self.folder / "producer.sqlite"
        self.receiver = self.folder / "receiver.sqlite"
        initialize(self.producer, self.receiver)

    def sql(self, path, statement):
        with closing(connect(path)) as db:
            db.execute(statement).close()

    def count(self, path, table, where="1"):
        # All table/where arguments below are fixed test constants.
        with closing(connect(path)) as db:
            return one(db, f"SELECT count(*) FROM {table} WHERE {where}")[0]

    def pending(self):
        return self.count(self.producer, "outbox", "delivered = 0")

    def send(self, event):
        return consume(self.receiver, event)

    def test_producer_failure_rolls_back_business_and_intent(self):
        self.sql(self.producer, """CREATE TRIGGER reject_outbox
            BEFORE INSERT ON outbox BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'injected'); END""")
        with self.assertRaises(sqlite3.IntegrityError):
            request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.producer, "report_requests"), 0)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.producer, "outbox"), 0)

    def test_unsafe_receiver_applies_twice_after_lost_reply(self):
        request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        def lose_reply(event):
            consume_without_inbox(self.receiver, event)
            raise TimeoutError("receiver committed; reply lost")
        with self.assertRaises(TimeoutError):
            dispatch_one(self.producer, lose_reply)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 1)
        dispatch_one(self.producer,
                     lambda event: consume_without_inbox(self.receiver, event))
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 2)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 0)

    def test_inbox_recovers_lost_reply_with_one_local_effect(self):
        event = request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        def lose_reply(sent):
            self.send(sent)
            raise TimeoutError("receiver committed; reply lost")
        with self.assertRaises(TimeoutError):
            dispatch_one(self.producer, lose_reply)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 1)
        receipt = dispatch_one(self.producer, self.send)
        self.assertTrue(receipt.replayed)
        self.assertEqual(receipt.key, event.key)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 1)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "inbox"), 1)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 0)

    def test_receiver_receipt_failure_rolls_back_effect(self):
        request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        self.sql(self.receiver, """CREATE TRIGGER reject_receipt
            BEFORE INSERT ON inbox BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'injected'); END""")
        with self.assertRaises(sqlite3.IntegrityError):
            dispatch_one(self.producer, self.send)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 0)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "inbox"), 0)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 1)
        self.sql(self.receiver, "DROP TRIGGER reject_receipt")
        self.assertFalse(dispatch_one(self.producer, self.send).replayed)

    def test_sender_ack_failure_replays_committed_receipt(self):
        request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        self.sql(self.producer, """CREATE TRIGGER reject_ack
            BEFORE UPDATE ON outbox BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'injected'); END""")
        with self.assertRaises(sqlite3.IntegrityError):
            dispatch_one(self.producer, self.send)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 1)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 1)
        self.sql(self.producer, "DROP TRIGGER reject_ack")
        self.assertTrue(dispatch_one(self.producer, self.send).replayed)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 1)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 0)

    def test_two_relays_deliver_same_pending_event_concurrently(self):
        request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        barrier = Barrier(2, timeout=5)
        def simultaneous_send(event):
            barrier.wait()  # Both relays have already read the pending row.
            return self.send(event)
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
            futures = [pool.submit(dispatch_one, self.producer,
                                   simultaneous_send) for _ in range(2)]
            receipts = [future.result(timeout=10) for future in futures]
        self.assertEqual({r.replayed for r in receipts}, {False, True})
        self.assertEqual(receipts[0].receipt_id, receipts[1].receipt_id)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 1)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "inbox"), 1)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 0)

    def test_same_identity_with_changed_payload_is_refused(self):
        event = request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        self.send(event)
        with self.assertRaises(PayloadMismatch):
            self.send(replace(event, payload=payload_for("monthly")))
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 1)

    def test_receipts_are_scoped_to_source_and_workspace(self):
        event = request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        events = [event, replace(event, workspace_id="team-b"),
                  replace(event, source="other-trusted-service")]
        receipts = [self.send(item) for item in events]
        self.assertEqual(len({r.key for r in receipts}), 3)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 3)
        for item in events:
            self.assertTrue(self.send(item).replayed)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 3)

    def test_new_intents_with_identical_payload_are_not_deduplicated(self):
        first = request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        second = request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        self.assertEqual(first.payload, second.payload)
        self.assertNotEqual(first.event_id, second.event_id)
        self.assertEqual(dispatch_one(self.producer, self.send).key, first.key)
        self.assertEqual(next_event(self.producer), second)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 1)
        self.assertEqual(dispatch_one(self.producer, self.send).key, second.key)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 2)
        self.assertIsNone(dispatch_one(self.producer, self.send))

    def test_unrelated_receipt_does_not_acknowledge_the_event(self):
        request_report(self.producer, "team-a", "weekly")
        def wrong_receipt(event):
            return Receipt((event.source, event.workspace_id, "different-id"),
                           "receipt-from-another-event", False)
        with self.assertRaises(BadReceipt):
            dispatch_one(self.producer, wrong_receipt)
        self.assertEqual(self.pending(), 1)
        self.assertEqual(self.count(self.receiver, "report_runs"), 0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    print(f"Python {sys.version.split()[0]}; SQLite {sqlite3.sqlite_version}",
          flush=True)
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

What the receipt actually proves

Here, a receipt means the receiver committed a report_runs row and the corresponding inbox row. It does not mean an email was sent, a payment settled, a social post appeared, or a generated report reached storage. Those effects are absent from the fixture.

Moving send_email() inside the receiver's SQLite transaction would not make the email roll back with the database. For another external handoff, the receiving API needs an appropriate idempotency or reconciliation contract of its own.

There are a few other boundaries worth keeping explicit:

  • Identity is trusted context here. The source and workspace fields are fixtures, not an authorization system. A real receiver must derive or validate that context from its authenticated caller before consulting the inbox. A receipt is not permission to act.
  • Creating an intent is separate from retrying delivery. Calling request_report() again creates a new request. Deduplicating a retried client request at that earlier entry point is a separate boundary, covered by the previous article.
  • Payload comparison is narrow. The producer uses one serialization for this small report schema. This is not a general JSON canonicalization scheme. The receiver compares the persisted payload on replay and rejects a changed one.
  • Retention is part of correctness. Deleting an inbox receipt while its event can still be replayed makes that delivery look new. Define the replay window and restore procedure before pruning receipts.
  • Deduplication does not impose business ordering. Event B can arrive before event A. Version checks, ordering rules and stale-event handling are separate decisions.

The fixture also omits relay leases, backoff, retry budgets, poison-event handling, monitoring and transport authentication. Its five-second SQLite busy timeout is a test setting, not a throughput claim. It does not simulate a power failure or prove a particular broker's delivery guarantees.

The useful result is narrower: a retried event can produce one modeled local effect when the receiver commits that effect and its deduplication receipt together. The outbox keeps an intent available for delivery; the receiver's transaction makes a repeated delivery recognizable.

Which failure boundary would you test first in your own worker: a lost reply after commit, a failed acknowledgement write, or two relays delivering the same event? Leave the sequence in the comments—especially what durable state each side can inspect after the timeout.

title: ClickHouse Cloud Executable UDFs GA: Native Code, Network Access, and Query-Level Metrics
description:
LLM observability has a data problem hiding inside a measurement problem. Teams collect prompts, completions, model names, latency, and trace identifiers, but token-usage fields are not always present—particularly when responses are streamed, proxied, or generated by self-hosted models. Without reliable usage data, it becomes harder to explain model costs, compare workloads, and identify prompts that consume tokens without improving answer quality.

One traditional solution is to export traces, run tokenization or evaluation in a separate service, and load the results back into the analytics database. That works, but it creates another pipeline to operate and another place where data can become stale.

ClickHouse Cloud's executable user-defined functions (UDFs) offer another approach: run custom code from SQL, close to the data being analyzed. In an October 5, 2026 announcement, ClickHouse made executable UDFs generally available across its AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure offerings. The release adds a Native runtime for compiled languages, broader outbound network access, infrastructure-as-code support, and query-level metrics for UDF execution.

The accompanying example project demonstrates two complementary workloads: a compiled Rust function that counts LLM tokens and a network-enabled Python function that asks an external model to grade a sample of completions.

The architectural shift is useful, but the details matter. Compiled Native UDFs and network-enabled Python UDFs are different execution paths. Teams should not assume that every runtime has network access or that moving code into a database makes its resource consumption free.

Why it matters

LLM observability depends on more than the usage numbers returned by a model provider. Some responses omit token counts, and provider-reported totals may not reveal how much of the input came from system instructions, retrieved documents, user prompts, or generated output.

That breakdown can be valuable. If a retrieval pipeline suddenly doubles the amount of context it supplies, token costs may increase even when the number of model calls remains unchanged. If a system prompt grows over time, the cost may accumulate across thousands of requests.

ClickHouse's example uses a synthetic dataset in which approximately 30% of spans lack usage information. This is a result from the company's demonstration dataset, not a universal measurement of all production LLM traffic. The example then counts tokens from the recorded text and compares its estimates with provider-reported usage where available.

The second problem is quality. Token counts explain part of the bill, but not whether a completion was useful. A separate model can grade a sample of responses, producing structured scores and verdicts that can be aggregated by application, model, or feature.

Putting these computations closer to the trace data allows engineers to connect usage, cost, and quality through familiar SQL queries. It also makes resource accounting more important: CPU-heavy tokenization and network-bound model evaluation have very different performance characteristics.

What ClickHouse announced

The general-availability release introduces several capabilities for executable UDFs in ClickHouse Cloud:

  • Native runtime: Upload compiled binaries for supported languages, including Rust, Go, C++, and JavaScript compiled with Bun.
  • Outbound network access: Network-enabled UDFs can call public endpoints, subject to the configured runtime and service capabilities.
  • Azure availability: Executable UDFs are available across ClickHouse Cloud on AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure.
  • Memory limits and deterministic functions: Configure per-process memory limits and mark functions deterministic when identical inputs are guaranteed to produce identical outputs.
  • Cloud API and Terraform: Manage UDFs through the Cloud API and supported Terraform resources, including per-service version pinning.
  • Execution metrics: ClickHouse 26.6 and later adds UDF-specific profile events and asynchronous metrics that help expose child-process costs alongside query telemetry.

The distinction between runtimes is important. The Native runtime is intended for compiled, self-contained code; the network-enabled example in ClickHouse's article uses Python. The announcement describes outbound network access as generally available, but it does not mean a Native binary can automatically make external API calls. Check the current runtime documentation before choosing an implementation.

This is an excerpt. The full article continues with:

  • Network-enabled UDFs: useful, but not free
  • Per-query metrics make UDF costs visible
  • What the token-counting benchmark tells us
  • What data and AI engineers should do
  • Limitations and open questions
  • Key takeaways

Read the full article on AI Data Legends → — with diagrams, code and sources.

Originally published on AI Data Legends. Each post here is an excerpt; the full articles live at aidatalegends.com.

title: A Free React Curriculum — 131 Chapters, From `useState` to Custom Renderers
description:
Most React tutorials stop at the same place: useState, useEffect, props, maybe context. Then they stop.

The real questions come after that. Why does my component re-render? What happens during the commit phase? How does hydration work? What is a custom renderer?

I found a curriculum that answers those. It's on KandZ Tuts, and it's 131 chapters, organized as a single progression from your first component to React's internal architecture.

Here's the breakdown.

Foundations (1–14)

What React is, Node.js and package managers, creating a project with Vite, project structure, JSX syntax and rules, embedding JavaScript expressions, functional components, importing and exporting, props, default props, the children prop, event listeners, passing handlers as props, and the synthetic event object.

State (15–24)

useState, updating primitive state, updating state from previous state, updating objects and arrays in state, conditional rendering with if/ternary/logical AND, rendering lists with map, and the importance of keys.

Forms (25–29)

Controlled inputs, textareas and selects, handling multiple inputs with one handler, form submission and preventDefault, and uncontrolled inputs with useRef.

Effects and Data (30–34)

useEffect, dependency array rules, cleanup functions, fetching API data, and handling loading and error states.

Custom Hooks and Context (35–41)

Extracting reusable logic, the prop drilling problem, createContext, providing and consuming context, useReducer, and combining context with useReducer.

Refs, Memoization, and Modern Hooks (42–57)

useRef for DOM access and mutable values, useMemo, useCallback, React.memo, useImperativeHandle, useLayoutEffect, useDebugValue, useTransition, useDeferredValue, useId, useSyncExternalStore, useOptimistic, useActionState, useFormStatus, and the use hook.

Routing and State Libraries (58–70)

React Router (route elements, outlets, dynamic params, programmatic navigation, protected and nested routes), TanStack Query (setup, useQuery, useMutation, cache invalidation), Redux Toolkit (provider, slices, actions, reducers, middleware, thunks), and Zustand.

Styling and Forms (71–75)

CSS Modules, Tailwind CSS, styled-components and Emotion, React Hook Form, and Zod integration.

Advanced Patterns (76–87)

Code splitting with React.lazy, Suspense, error boundaries, render props, higher-order components, compound components, control props, portals, React Testing Library, user interaction testing, MSW, and Playwright.

SSR and Frameworks (88–95)

SSR vs SSG, React Server Components architecture, Server Components vs Client Components rules, Server Actions, Next.js App Router, layouts and loading UI, streaming SSR and progressive hydration, and micro-frontends with Module Federation.

Production and Accessibility (96–100)

ARIA attributes, keyboard navigation and focus management, XSS prevention, React DevTools profiling, and production builds.

React Internals (101–109)

Fiber architecture and reconciliation, the commit phase vs render phase, double-pass rendering and Strict Mode, the concurrent rendering scheduler and priorities, automatic batching, memory leak prevention, synthetic event pooling and delegation, hydration mismatch errors, and progressive and selective hydration.

Advanced Frameworks (110–114)

SSG with React frameworks, Incremental Static Regeneration, Partial Prerender, React Server Functions and the wire format, and the Taint APIs.

Applied React (115–120)

i18n and localization, XState state machines, WebSockets, offline-first apps with service workers, monorepos with Turborepo and Nx, and building reusable component libraries with Storybook.

Beyond the Browser (121–130)

React Native core, React Native navigation and native modules, Electron and Tauri, React Three Fiber, WebGL and Canvas, React Konva, the Web Audio API, Web Components integration, custom Babel/SWC plugins, and custom React renderers with react-reconciler.

Chapter 131: The Complete Cheatsheet

Why the Internals Section Matters

Chapters 101–109 are the reason to read this curriculum.

Most resources stop at "here's how useEffect works." This one goes into how React actually renders—Fiber, reconciliation, the commit phase, the concurrent scheduler, automatic batching, hydration mismatches.

That's what lets you diagnose a performance problem instead of guessing at useMemo. It's the difference between using React and understanding it.

The use Hook and React 19

Chapters 54–57 cover the hooks that define modern React: useOptimistic, useActionState, useFormStatus, and the use hook.

These are not footnotes. They are how React 19 handles async forms, optimistic updates, and reading promises in render. A curriculum that skips them is teaching React from two years ago.

Beyond the Browser

Chapters 121–130 are unusual. Most React curricula stop at the web. This one covers React Native, Electron, Tauri, React Three Fiber, React Konva, the Web Audio API, and custom renderers.

If you've wondered how React renders to a canvas, a native mobile view, or a 3D scene, this is where that gets explained.

Who This Is For

  • Beginners: Start at Chapter 1 and read in order.
  • Experienced React developers: Jump to Chapter 57 (the use hook), Chapter 101 (Fiber), or Chapter 108 (hydration mismatches) if those are gaps.
  • Developers moving beyond the web: Start at Chapter 121.

The Link

React — KandZ Tuts

Free, no signup, 131 chapters.

If you've been writing React for years but never understood what the scheduler does, or you're starting from scratch and want a path that doesn't stop at useEffect, this is the most complete free curriculum I've found.

What React topics do you wish had better free resources? Let me know in the comments.

title: Fylgja CSS 2.3: Popover Defaults, Design Tokens 2025.10, and 24 New UI Components
description:
Fylgja CSS 2.3 is here, bringing updates to @fylgja/base 2.2, @fylgja/tokens 2.3, and
@fylgja/utilities 2.2 under a single guiding theme: getting more out of the modern web platform.
Popovers now look and behave right out of the box with native anchor positioning, design tokens
adopt the first stable community specification, and Fylgja UI expands from 31 to 55
ready-to-use components.

Update with:

npm install fylgja@latest

Here's a closer look at what's new.

Popovers that are ready to use in @fylgja/base

Non-dialog popovers, such as menus, dropdowns, and tooltips, now get the same elevated surface styling
as dialogs out of the box: background, text color, corner radius, and elevation shadow, paired with
tighter padding and none of the awkward browser-default borders. Every layer is exposed as a CSS
custom property (--popover-bg, --popover-color, --popover-radius, --popover-padding, and
--popover-shadow), making it easy to restyle any overlay without touching a selector.

In browsers supporting CSS anchor positioning, auto and hint popovers automatically anchor to the
button that opened them. You can place them anywhere around the trigger using --popover-position
(which accepts any valid position-area value) and fine-tune spacing with --popover-offset. Meanwhile,
manual popovers retain their centered default. The new Menu and
Tooltip components in Fylgja UI are built directly on these primitives.

Base also picked up a few smaller refinements:

  • Search clear button: The native clear button in search inputs now scales with font size and inherits the text color. Customize it via --search-clear-size, --search-clear-gap, --search-clear-color, and --search-clear-icon.
  • Fieldset error highlighting: In the optional theme (@fylgja/base/theme.css), the legend of any fieldset containing an invalid field now colors with --form-error-color, so the entire field group reads as invalid at a glance.
  • Print styles for disclosures: Print stylesheets now expand closed <details> elements, ensuring accordion and disclosure content isn't lost on paper.
  • Emoji fallbacks: A dedicated --family-emoji custom property isolates emoji fallbacks, so you can swap or reuse them independently.
  • Menu list reset: The list reset for [role="list"] and lists inside <nav> now covers <menu> elements as well.

A better system font stack

The system font stack in @fylgja/base no longer relies on system-ui. While convenient, system-ui
resolves inconsistently across operating systems, notably on Windows, where it often falls back to fonts
like Yu Gothic UI that mangle Greek letters and Chinese punctuation.

The refreshed stack now leads with -apple-system and BlinkMacSystemFont to preserve native typography
on Apple devices, while allowing other operating systems to pick fonts that naturally match the user's
locale. The monospace stack also picked up SF Mono, Monaco, Cascadia Mono, and Liberation Mono as
reliable fallbacks.

Design Tokens 2025.10 in @fylgja/tokens

Tokens now ship in the Design Tokens 2025.10 format, the first stable release of the
Design Tokens Community Group specification. The new
tokens/fylgja.resolver.json is a compliant Resolver document, allowing any modern design tool or
pipeline to consume Fylgja's aspect ratios, borders, radii, colors, easings, font sizes, shadows,
spacing, and z-index layers directly, without proprietary plugins or custom intermediaries.

import tokens from "@fylgja/tokens/tokens/fylgja.resolver.json" with { type: "json" };

Values are strongly typed, and composite tokens like shadows keep their structured properties rather
than being flattened into plain strings. (Note that sizes utilizing calc(), clamp(), or ch units are
omitted from this JSON export, as the specification cannot express them yet; they remain available across
our CSS and SCSS packages as usual.)

This release also resolves a scoping issue in the full CSS bundle (@fylgja/tokens/css/index.css).
Colors and shadows were previously declared on :root, preventing local overrides like --hue,
--chroma, or --shadow-color on an element from taking effect. They are now scoped per element,
matching the behavior of individual files like colors.css. Dark mode shadows from shadows.dark.css
are now properly applied in the bundle as well.

Toggles for popover invokers in @fylgja/utilities

Our toggle utilities (toggle-rotate, toggle-flip, toggle-turn, toggle-hide, and toggle-show)
have always responded to aria-expanded. However, native popovers opened via commandfor or
popovertarget manage state without toggling ARIA attributes.

These utilities now also track the state of a popover that immediately follows its invoker button.
This means UI accents like a rotating chevron in a dropdown button work purely in CSS, with zero JavaScript
required.

We've also shipped two key bug fixes:

  • Restored scroll-mask in minified builds: Lightning CSS folds animation-timeline into the animation shorthand when minifying. No browser accepts that syntax, so the fade mask never ran. While this remains an open issue in Lightning CSS, Fylgja now keeps animation-timeline in a separate CSS rule so the minified files Fylgja ships work out of the box, and your own build stays safe when it minifies with Lightning CSS, as Vite and Astro do.
  • Screen reader text wrapping: Text styled with .sr-only is now prevented from wrapping inside its 1px box, resolving an issue where certain screen readers would announce adjacent words without spaces.

Fylgja UI grows to 55 components

When we introduced Fylgja UI, we noted the obvious gaps: tabs, tooltips,
popovers, steppers, and more. Over the past few months, 24 new components have joined the collection,
closing nearly all of those gaps. Like the rest of the library, each component is built on clean,
semantic HTML with native platform behaviors, completely free, and ready to copy and paste:

  • Navigation: Tabs, a Stepper, a responsive Navbar, and an Action List.
  • Overlays: A Menu and Tooltip, both powered by the new popover defaults in Base, including hint popovers and interestfor for tooltips.
  • Actions: A floating Speed Dial and a Button Corner Shape showcasing the emerging CSS corner-shape property.
  • Feedback: An Alert, a shimmer Skeleton loader, a Callout, and a collapsible Callout Collapse.
  • Forms: A Form Field with native form validation styling, and a keyboard-accessible Multiselect built on checkboxes and focusgroup (available as a list or chips).
  • Sliders: A CSS-only Compare Slider to reveal image comparisons, driven entirely by a native range input.
  • Layout: A responsive Bento Grid alongside three footer layouts: Inline, Classic, and Brand.
  • Data display: A responsive Gallery and a structured Timeline.
  • Typography: A brand-new category featuring Heading Group, Heading Underline, and Heading HR.

Missing a component you'd love to see? Open an issue on the
site repository.

Published with provenance

Every package is now published through GitHub Actions with npm provenance, giving you verifiable proof
that what you install was built directly from our public repository source.

Before you upgrade

There are two small changes to keep in mind, both related to the font stack in @fylgja/base:

  • system-ui removal: If your project specifically relies on system-ui, you can restore it in your own stylesheet with --family-system: system-ui;.
  • $font-family Sass variable removed: The legacy $font-family Sass variable has been removed. It was never wired up to --family-system under the hood, so setting the --family-system custom property directly is the recommended way to configure your fonts.

For the full breakdown of changes, check out the changelogs for @fylgja/base, @fylgja/tokens, and
@fylgja/utilities.

As always, if something does not work the way you expect, feel free to
open an issue on GitHub. We look forward to seeing what you
build with 2.3!

Happy coding!

title: Fivetran Managed Data Lake Write Credentials: Letting Engines Write to Iceberg and Delta Safely
description:
Fivetran says Managed Data Lake Write Credentials are now generally available, letting query engines run DDL and DML against lake tables. Engines authenticate via OAuth2 client credentials—one Client ID and Secret per destination—so each gets a distinct identity against the hosted catalog. For teams running a dual-format Iceberg and Delta lake, the real question is how to scope write access tightly enough that an engine can delete rows or drop a table without broad bucket permissions, while Fivetran retains sole authority over metadata and schema evolution. This article explains how Fivetran strikes that balance, and what to set up before you rely on it.

Why it matters

For data engineers, the practical consequence is that permission management collapses into a single policy layer. Fivetran's catalog returns per-user access rules through the Iceberg REST protocol, so an organization defines governance once rather than re-encoding it for every engine. In Fivetran's post, Snowflake's Spitzer describes this as one policy definition and one catalog access point feeding all connected engines simultaneously. Engineers no longer maintain separate ACLs per query tool.

For AI and data engineers who provision write paths, the writable catalog credentials are visible only to Destination or Account Admins in the Fivetran dashboard. That means a data scientist spinning up an ad-hoc Spark session receives read-only access by default; only an admin can mint the short-lived, directory-scoped S3 credentials that unlock DDL and DML against a specific table's storage. The engine never holds standing broad bucket permissions, and because Fivetran retains sole authority over metadata publication, a stray schema edit in one engine cannot desynchronize what another engine reads.

What happened

Fivetran announced its Managed Data Lake service, which pulls data through more than 750 connectors and lands it in commodity object-storage buckets such as S3, ADLS, and GCS. The pipeline normalizes, compacts, and deduplicates records before writing them in both Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake open table formats, granting warehouse-grade ACID transactions on top of a lake. Alongside the core ingestion path, Fivetran introduced a write-credentials mechanism: short-lived tokens that let external compute engines execute DDL and DML directly against the lake's data files while Fivetran retains sole authority over metadata updates. According to Fivetran, this decoupling of storage from compute lets customers query and modify data through engines such as Databricks, Snowflake, or Starburst without Fivetran mediating every write.

The managed data lake write credentials feature supports destinations on S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, OneLake, and Google Cloud Storage. It includes native catalog integrations for AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, and Apache Polaris. Fivetran manages schema evolution and performance optimization on the backend, allowing engine-side writers to use vended credentials for standard SQL or Python operations.

This is an excerpt. The full article continues with:

  • Managing write access
  • Before you turn it on
  • What data and AI engineers should do
  • Limitations and open questions
  • Key takeaways

Read the full article on AI Data Legends → — with diagrams, code and sources.

title: An RTL checklist for bilingual English/Arabic websites
description:
We build a lot of English/Arabic sites for businesses in the UAE, and the same right-to-left (RTL) issues come up on almost every project. Here's the checklist we run before launch.

1. Set direction and language on the root 

<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">

Set both per page, not with JavaScript after load. Screen readers, search engines and the browser's text shaping all rely on lang, and dir controls layout from the first paint.

2. Use logical CSS properties

Replace physical properties with logical ones so one stylesheet works in both directions:

/* instead of margin-left / padding-right / left */
.card { margin-inline-start: 1rem; padding-inline-end: 1.5rem; }
.badge { inset-inline-start: 0; }
.text { text-align: start; }

Flexbox and grid already follow dir, so most layouts flip for free once the physical properties are gone.

3. Mirror icons that imply direction, not all icons

Arrows, "next/back" chevrons and progress indicators should flip. Logos, play buttons, checkmarks and phone icons should not.

[dir="rtl"] .icon-directional { transform: scaleX(-1); }

4. Handle numbers and mixed text

Phone numbers, prices and English brand names inside Arabic sentences can render in the wrong order. Wrap them:

<bdi>+971 50 000 0000</bdi>

and use dir="ltr" on inputs for phone numbers and emails.

5. Pick a proper Arabic font

System fallbacks often look uneven next to a Latin brand font. Choose an Arabic family with matching weights, and bump line-height slightly (around 1.7) because Arabic glyphs need more vertical room.

6. Give each language its own URL

/en/... and /ar/... (or a subfolder per language) with hreflang tags lets Google index both versions instead of treating one as a duplicate:

<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://example.com/en/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="ar" href="https://example.com/ar/" />

Avoid auto-translation plugins that serve both languages on the same URL.

7. Test the real flows in RTL

Forms, validation messages, sliders, date pickers and WhatsApp/contact buttons are where RTL bugs hide. Click through every one in Arabic on a phone before launch.

We're Oxedge, a small web design studio in Dubai. If you want to see how we approach bilingual projects, our notes on web design in Dubai cover the process end to end.
