title: Fixing the Front Door
description:
Originally posted October 30, 2026 on elijahpaul.io.

TLDR

Telegram onboarding has been the biggest pain since launch. We're swapping it out. Meanwhile, the people already inside are building on top of Hot Bot.

The Front Door Is Broken

Lots of people have been approved for days and still see "not approved" when they check through Telegram.

We tested it. The likely culprit: connecting Telegram from inside the X app instead of an external browser.

The workaround for now:

  1. Open the link in an external browser.
  2. If that still fails, verify with your wallet instead.

Not good enough. So we're replacing the onboarding flow entirely.

My words, mid-morning: "it was a bigger pain than we thought it would be."

Approving by Hand

Until the new flow lands, we're in the replies.

Approved. Invited. Added to the group. One by one, all day.

Team no sleep, but making sure everyone is looked after.

The Room Inside

Favorite thing about the Hot Bot community: everyone's working together to make it.

Strategies. MCP setups. Ideas for new features.

Absolute euphoric feeling vs being stranded in the Cold War of the PvP bundlers.

Built On Top

One of our users, @0xJohnB, built an anti-rug dashboard that reads his Hot Bot team through our MCP API.

Strategies, trades and activity in one view, next to his own anti-rug checks. Read-only by design.

Running on a Raspberry Pi 5 at home.

That's the point of exposing the stack. Cooking with gas.

Paper First

We push most users to trade on paper first. On purpose.

Get a feel for Hot Bot without losing money. Then give us feedback.

Subscriptions cover our costs. Proper software business.

Red Day

Whole market was down today.

Avg day in crypto. We ride.

Long on vision. Relentless on daily execution. 🔥🤖

Elijah Paul, @elijahintek

Co-founder of Hot Bot. Scottsdale, AZ

God calls us to serve others. I try to live that in business and in life.

First posted on elijahpaul.io

title: Your setTimeout Didn't Break — Chrome Killed It
description:
The log said the sync was scheduled. Two minutes later, nothing had run. No error, no rejected promise, no missed callback warning — just a line that promised future work and a database that never changed.

Here is the excerpt that ended a week of blaming my own debounce logic:

[10:41:02] change detected
[10:41:02] sync scheduled in 120000ms
[10:41:32] service worker terminated (idle)

The timer did not fail. The process that owned it was shut down, and a setTimeout cannot outlive its process.

The short version

  • setTimeout is a handle in the worker's heap. Terminate the worker and the handle is gone.
  • MV3 kills an idle background worker after about 30 seconds, no matter what is pending.
  • Persist the due time, not the timer, and re-arm it when the worker wakes.

Three suspects that were innocent

The debounce. The code coalesced rapid changes into one sync two minutes later. It worked in tests because I kept clicking things, which kept the worker alive. In production, users typed once and walked away.

A stale closure. I rewrote the callback twice looking for a captured variable. The closure was fine. It simply never executed.

Storage quota. I added error handling around chrome.storage and saw nothing, because nothing was written. The write happened inside the callback that never ran.

The pattern behind all three: I was debugging JavaScript semantics when the failure was in the execution model.

What MV3 actually guarantees

Chrome keeps a background service worker alive while it is handling events. When the event queue goes quiet for roughly 30 seconds, the worker is terminated. A single event may run for up to five minutes, but pending timers do not count as activity.

That means a timer longer than the idle window is a coin flip. It survives only if something else — a message, a click, an API call — keeps waking the worker before the reaper arrives. In a quiet extension, nothing does.

Fix 1: store the deadline, arm an alarm

This is the default answer and it covers most features:

const KEY = 'pending-sync-at';
const ALARM = 'pending-sync';

async function scheduleSync(delayMs: number) {
  const dueAt = Date.now() + delayMs;
  await chrome.storage.local.set({ [KEY]: dueAt });
  await chrome.alarms.create(ALARM, { when: dueAt });
}

chrome.alarms.onAlarm.addListener(async (alarm) => {
  if (alarm.name !== ALARM) return;
  const stored = await chrome.storage.local.get(KEY);
  if (!stored[KEY]) return;
  await chrome.storage.local.remove(KEY);
  await runSync();
});

chrome.runtime.onStartup.addListener(() => void recover());

Two details matter. alarms.create({ when }) takes an absolute timestamp, so a worker restart does not shift the deadline. And the alarm handler clears the stored key before running the work, which prevents a duplicate run if the alarm fires twice.

Fix 2: run the delay where the user already is

If the sync only matters while a tab is open, move the debounce into the content script. The page owns that timer, the worker is not involved, and closing the tab cancels work that no longer has a reason to exist. This is not a workaround; it is the right lifetime for UI-scoped work.

Fix 3: keep the worker warm (and accept the cost)

A message every 20 seconds keeps the idle timer from expiring. It also burns battery, keeps a process alive for no user benefit, and is the first thing a Chrome Web Store reviewer asks about. I have used it for a short migration window. I would not ship it as architecture.

Fix 4: move the plumbing into the build

If the codebase has dozens of timer call sites, rewriting each one by hand is how regressions multiply. vite-mv3-sw-compile-persist rewrites long setTimeout/setInterval calls into alarm-backed wrappers at build time and restores marked state on wake. It requires Vite 8+, the storage permission and alarms when long timers are present; destructured variables and anonymous callbacks that capture locals are not recoverable, so the source still needs some discipline.

One more nuance: extension API calls reset the idle timer, so a worker that is making a request is not necessarily idle. Do not rely on that as a design, but it explains why a timer sometimes survives a burst of activity and dies in a quiet minute.

With and without the plugin

The before/after from the plugin's README is the whole argument:

Without vite-mv3-sw-compile-persist

let count = 0;

chrome.action.onClicked.addListener(async () => {
  const stored = await chrome.storage.session.get('count');
  count = (stored.count as number) ?? 0;
  count++;
  await chrome.storage.session.set({ count });
});

chrome.alarms.create('cleanup', { delayInMinutes: 5 });
chrome.alarms.onAlarm.addListener((alarm) => {
  if (alarm.name === 'cleanup') cleanup();
});

With vite-mv3-sw-compile-persist

let count = 0;

chrome.action.onClicked.addListener(() => {
  count++;
});

setTimeout(cleanup, 5 * 60_000);

The second version is the code you meant to write. The plugin adds restore, dirty tracking, a debounced flush and alarm-backed timers at build time — no runtime import, no wrapper API.

Repository: vite-mv3-sw-compile-persist

If this saved you the afternoon I lost, a star on the repo is a fair trade — and it helps the next person find the explanation before the workaround.

What is the longest delay your extension promises, and what happens to that promise when the worker dies at second 30?

title: 6 Planning Patterns for AI Agents and When Each One Fits
description:
TL;DR for devs

  • Start from the task, not from a popular reasoning pattern.
  • Use a fixed workflow for predictable steps; consider model-generated plans when tasks vary.
  • Other patterns: plan then execute, ReAct-style tool use, routing to specialists, parallel work, and draft-evaluate-revise.
  • A plan is a proposal, not a guarantee, so validate actions and results.
  • Set stopping conditions (max steps, time limits) and let code handle exact arithmetic and rules.

Fixed workflows, plan-then-execute, ReAct, routing, parallel work and draft-evaluate-revise

Ask an AI assistant to “research three project management tools, compare their pricing, and recommend one for a five-person team.” A one-sentence answer may sound confident, but the task involves several pieces: identify suitable products, find current pricing, compare plans, consider the team’s needs, and present a recommendation with caveats.

This is where planning patterns can help. They give an agent a structure for turning a goal into manageable steps. They can also make an application easier to debug: you can see what steps were attempted, what information was used, and where the process failed.

Planning does not make an agent infallible. A model may misunderstand the goal, skip an important step, or rely on poor data. Developers need to choose a pattern that fits the task and add checks around tools and outputs. In this beginner-friendly guide, we’ll cover practical reasoning patterns, use a research example, and show a simple Python approach to a predictable plan.

What Is Planning in an AI Agent?

Planning is the process of deciding what actions may be needed to reach a goal. An agent may decompose a request into subtasks, select tools, gather results, and decide whether it has enough information to finish.

For a research task, a plan might be:

  1. Identify the team’s requirements from the user’s request.
  2. Find three candidate products.
  3. Visit or query reliable sources for current pricing.
  4. Compare plans that support five users.
  5. Summarize trade-offs and state what could not be verified.

This plan is useful because it exposes the work behind the final recommendation. It also gives developers opportunities to validate inputs and constrain the agent. The system can require that pricing come from a source and include an “as of” date, for example.

The OpenAI guide to building agents describes orchestration as handling multiple steps, tool use, handoffs, guardrails, and context. Anthropic’s Building Effective Agents distinguishes predefined workflows from more flexible agents. That distinction matters: not every task needs a model to invent its own sequence.

Start With the Task, Not a Reasoning Trend

A common mistake is to choose a popular pattern first and then try to fit a problem into it. Start by examining the task:

  • Are the steps predictable?
  • Does the next step depend on information returned by the previous one?
  • Can independent parts run at the same time?
  • What mistakes would matter most?
  • Does a human need to approve the outcome?
  • How will the system know it is finished?

If the steps are fixed, ordinary code may be the best planner. For example, an invoice-processing workflow could validate the invoice, retrieve the supplier record, check required fields, and route it for review in a fixed order. A model could help extract information from the document, but the application can control the sequence.

Use a model-driven plan when the request varies enough that a fixed path is awkward, or when the agent must adapt based on retrieved information. Keep the model’s options bounded: define available tools, approval rules, and a clear stopping point.

Pattern 1: A Fixed Workflow

A fixed workflow follows steps selected by the developer. It is a strong fit for repeatable processes, such as generating a weekly report or checking an application form.

A report workflow might be:

  1. Retrieve the latest sales data.
  2. Calculate totals and percentage changes in code.
  3. Ask the model to explain the results in plain language.
  4. Validate the required sections exist.
  5. Return a draft for review.

The benefit is predictability. If the task always follows the same route, the application can control the order and handle each failure explicitly. The trade-off is flexibility: a fixed workflow may be less convenient when users ask for a task that requires a different sequence.

Pattern 2: Plan, Then Execute

In a plan-and-execute pattern, the model first proposes a series of steps. The application or another model call then carries them out, often with tools. This is useful when tasks vary but can still be decomposed into a list of actions.

For the software comparison, the agent may propose gathering product candidates, retrieving pricing, comparing user limits, and composing a recommendation. The application can inspect the plan before execution. It could reject steps that use unapproved sources, ask for clarification about budget, or require confirmation before creating an account.

A plan is not inherently trustworthy. It may omit a necessary step or include one the application cannot perform. Validate each action against an allowlist and make tool results visible to the final synthesis.

Pattern 3: ReAct-Style Tool Use

A ReAct-style loop alternates between reasoning about the next step and taking an action, such as calling a search tool. The agent observes the result and decides what to do next.

A simplified loop is:

Goal → choose next action → call tool → inspect result
     → choose another action or provide final answer

This can be more adaptive than planning every step up front. If the first search finds that a product has changed its pricing page, the agent can adjust its next query. But the loop can also be less predictable. It may make unnecessary calls or keep searching after it has enough evidence.

For a production system, set limits on iterations, tool types, time, and cost. Log each tool request and result. Define conditions for asking the user a question or handing the task to a person.

Pattern 4: Routing and Specialists

A router classifies a request and sends it to a suitable workflow or specialist. A support system might route billing issues to a billing process and technical questions to a troubleshooting process.

Routing can make instructions clearer and reduce the number of tools available to each path. It can also misclassify requests. Include an “uncertain” route, test borderline examples, and make it easy to hand a case to a human.

Specialists should have a distinct role. If two agents have the same tools and instructions, splitting them may only add complexity. Use specialists when the task genuinely needs different policies, tools, or expertise.

Pattern 5: Parallel Work

Some tasks can be divided into independent subtasks. For example, one process can collect pricing, another can compare collaboration features, and a third can check deployment options. The application can then combine the results.

Parallel work can reduce waiting time or provide multiple perspectives, but it does not guarantee accuracy. The combined output needs a synthesis step that resolves disagreements and checks that sources support claims. Running several copies of a model on the same question can also multiply cost without adding useful diversity.

Use parallelization when the subtasks are genuinely independent and the results can be merged through a clear contract. Keep outputs structured enough for the application to compare.

Pattern 6: Draft, Evaluate, Revise

For tasks where quality can be checked against criteria, an agent can produce a draft, evaluate it, and revise it. A writing assistant might draft a report, check whether every claim has a source, and revise gaps.

This pattern works best when the evaluator has concrete criteria. “Make it better” is vague. “Every pricing claim must include a current source; include at least two trade-offs; mark missing data as unknown” is easier to check.

Even a separate evaluator model can make mistakes. For factual claims, use deterministic checks or verify against source material where possible. Avoid endless critique loops by setting a maximum number of revisions and a fallback when the draft still fails.

A Simple Python Example: A Predictable Research Plan

For a beginner project, you can represent the stages in ordinary Python rather than asking a model to generate an open-ended plan. Here, the research functions are placeholders; a real app would connect them to approved data sources.

from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass
class Product:
    name: str
    monthly_price_per_user: float | None
    source_url: str | None


def compare_tools(team_size: int, products: list[Product]) -> list[dict]:
    if team_size < 1:
        raise ValueError("team_size must be at least 1")

    comparisons = []
    for product in products:
        total = (
            product.monthly_price_per_user * team_size
            if product.monthly_price_per_user is not None
            else None
        )
        comparisons.append({
            "name": product.name,
            "team_monthly_cost": total,
            "source_url": product.source_url,
            "price_verified": product.source_url is not None,
        })
    return comparisons

The code handles a repeatable calculation, while a model can help interpret the user’s criteria and explain trade-offs. Notice that missing prices remain None instead of being guessed. This is a small example of a useful division of labor: models can help with language and flexible interpretation; ordinary code can perform exact calculations and enforce rules.

Make Plans Observable and Testable

A plan should help the developer understand what happened. Store or trace the steps at a level appropriate to your privacy policy: the selected tool, validated arguments, outcome, and reason for stopping. You do not need to expose private internal reasoning to users to make a system observable. A concise action log can explain that the agent checked three official pricing pages and found one plan without a public price.

Build test cases for:

  • Clear requests with enough information.
  • Ambiguous goals that should trigger a question.
  • Missing or conflicting tool results.
  • A tool failure or timeout.
  • Unsupported steps in a proposed plan.
  • Requests that should require approval.
  • Plans that exceed the allowed step limit.

Evaluate the result, not just the plan text. Did the agent use reliable sources? Did it calculate correctly? Did it stop when enough evidence was available? Did it distinguish verified facts from assumptions?

Frequent Planning Mistakes

Overplanning simple tasks

If a task takes one function call, a long agent loop adds latency and failure opportunities. Use a direct call or fixed function when it is enough.

Treating a plan as a guarantee

A plan is a proposal. It can change, fail, or be based on incorrect assumptions. Validate actions and results.

Giving the agent too many choices

A huge tool list makes selection harder and expands the testing surface. Offer only tools relevant to the current task.

Forgetting stopping conditions

Specify maximum steps, time limits, and conditions that trigger a final answer, clarification, or human handoff.

Using a model for exact arithmetic

Let code handle totals, dates, eligibility, and other deterministic rules. The model can explain results but should not be the source of exact calculations when a program can compute them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does every AI agent need to make a plan?

No. A simple agent may choose a tool and answer in one turn. Planning is useful when a task has multiple steps or dependencies, but it adds overhead and should be used when it improves the outcome.

Is chain-of-thought the same as a plan?

No. A plan is an actionable structure for completing a task. An application can show a concise plan or action summary without exposing private internal reasoning. Focus on observable actions and verifiable results.

Should I use a fixed workflow or a model-generated plan?

Use a fixed workflow when the steps are predictable. Consider a model-generated plan when the task varies and the model needs to choose among bounded options. Many systems combine both.

How do I keep an agent from looping?

Set maximum tool calls, timeouts, and explicit completion conditions. Detect repeated calls where possible and provide a clear fallback when the agent cannot finish.

Can multiple agents improve planning?

They can help when specialists have distinct roles or when independent perspectives are valuable. They also add coordination, latency, and cost. Start with one agent and split only when the workflow benefits from separation.

Conclusion

Planning patterns help an AI agent organize multi-step work, but no single pattern is best for every task. Fixed workflows offer control, plan-and-execute supports flexible decomposition, tool-use loops adapt to new results, and parallel or evaluator patterns can help with independent subtasks and quality checks.

Choose the simplest approach that fits the task. Keep the agent’s tools and decisions bounded, use ordinary code for exact rules, set clear stopping conditions, and evaluate the full outcome. A useful plan is not the one that looks most sophisticated; it is the one that reliably helps the system reach a verifiable result.

References

  • OpenAI: Building agents
  • OpenAI: Orchestration and handoffs
  • Anthropic: Building effective agents

I write about building AI agents and full-stack AI apps. Follow me for the next one, and tell me in the comments: Which planning pattern does your current agent use, and is it more complex than the task needs?

title: Marketplace Reconciliation: Long Background Jobs, Queue Workers, and Cron Timeouts
description:
Short answer: make the cron trigger enqueue a small, idempotent reconciliation task, then let workers process checkpointed chunks instead of trying to finish the payment-provider scan inside one 15-minute execution.

That decision keeps the failure boundary visible. A scheduler starts a run. A queue delivers bounded work. A database records what was applied. The worker can stop after one chunk and continue from a durable cursor, which is much easier to test than a long loop that only knows it ran for 14 minutes.

This is the shape I use for notebook-to-prod transitions and eval-driven systems: the run identity, input revision, and progress marker are data, not assumptions hidden in process memory. Prompt-cost awareness matters here too. If reconciliation also creates an explanation or classification, store that output per payment chunk so a retry does not silently spend tokens twice.

How should a background job queue handle long-running worker tasks after a cron trigger?

Start with a stable run ID for the intended business interval, such as 2026-08-09, and split the provider result set into deterministic chunks. A chunk might contain payment IDs from a stored range or a page token captured in the run record. Do not make “the next ten minutes” the checkpoint: after a timeout, a retry cannot tell which side effects committed during that interval.

The worker should claim (run_id, chunk_id) transactionally, apply each payment update with the same idempotency key, and commit the result before it advances the cursor. If that key already exists, the operation becomes a no-op. Queue delivery can still happen twice; correctness belongs in the consumer and its storage layer.

Keep it boring.

A small Python model makes the state transition concrete:

import sqlite3


def open_database(path="reconciliation.sqlite"):
    database = sqlite3.connect(path)
    database.execute(
        "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS chunks ("
        "run_id TEXT NOT NULL, chunk_id INTEGER NOT NULL, "
        "status TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (run_id, chunk_id))"
    )
    database.execute(
        "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS reconciled_payments ("
        "run_id TEXT NOT NULL, payment_id TEXT NOT NULL, "
        "PRIMARY KEY (run_id, payment_id))"
    )
    return database


def reconcile_chunk(run_id, chunk_id, payment_ids, database_path):
    with open_database(database_path) as database:
        row = database.execute(
            "SELECT status FROM chunks WHERE run_id = ? AND chunk_id = ?",
            (run_id, chunk_id),
        ).fetchone()
        if row and row[0] == "done":
            return "already_done"

        database.execute(
            "INSERT OR REPLACE INTO chunks "
            "(run_id, chunk_id, status) VALUES (?, ?, 'done')",
            (run_id, chunk_id),
        )
        # Apply each provider result using (run_id, payment_id) as its key.
        # The real payment update belongs inside this transaction boundary.
        for payment_id in payment_ids:
            database.execute(
                "INSERT OR IGNORE INTO reconciled_payments "
                "(run_id, payment_id) VALUES (?, ?)",
                (run_id, payment_id),
            )
    return "processed"

The example is intentionally an adapter-free state machine. A Node.js service can use the same fields and transitions; changing language should not change the retry contract. The example creates both tables for clarity, while a production migration, not the worker startup path, should own schema creation and make the composite keys explicit.

One detail deserves extra care: publishing the next chunk and committing the current one are separate effects. If the process dies between them, a run can be marked done with no follow-up message. A periodic reconciler can find a committed chunk whose successor is absent and publish that successor using the same run identity. It must use an outbox or an equivalent uniqueness constraint, so recovery itself is idempotent.

Where does the 15-minute limit belong in the architecture?

Put it around the scheduler invocation, not around the whole business operation. The cron handler validates its request, creates the run row, and enqueues chunk zero. It should return quickly. The worker receives one bounded message, records its outcome, and schedules or exposes the next chunk for delivery.

Measure chunks from real provider latency before setting their size. A payment page that is safe in a local notebook can become unsafe when the provider slows down, the database is locked, or an explanation model adds token latency. Leave headroom for acknowledgement and commit work. Shorter chunks increase queue traffic and bookkeeping; larger chunks increase duplicate work and recovery time. There is no universal best number.

The queue message should carry identifiers and a compact cursor, not the entire payment export. Keep the source snapshot in application storage and bind the cursor to its revision. This prevents a retry from reading a different dataset and reporting a result that cannot be reproduced. It also makes eval-driven testing practical: feed the same snapshot twice and assert that the second delivery changes no reconciliation record or model-cost record.

Which failure modes should the worker make boring?

At-least-once delivery means duplicate messages are normal. A unique database key is stronger than an in-memory set, because the latter disappears when the process restarts. A timeout is also normal: retry the unfinished chunk, not the entire nightly run.

The dangerous case is a remote side effect without a matching durable identity. For each payment, send or store an idempotency key that survives retries. If the provider supports such keys, use the provider's documented contract; if it does not, record the attempted operation and reconcile the provider's final state before retrying. Do not infer “paid” from a worker acknowledgement.

Consider a run with three chunks. Chunk zero updates the local ledger and commits, then the worker process exits before it publishes chunk one. A naive retry of the whole run may ask the provider about the same payments again, overwrite a manually corrected status, and charge for a second explanation request. A cursor-only design has the opposite problem: it may advance past a payment whose remote call completed but whose local commit did not. The durable identity solves neither uncertainty automatically; it gives the retry a place to ask the provider for final state and a unique key with which to record the answer. The recovery reconciler then sees that chunk zero is committed, sees that chunk one is missing, and publishes exactly one successor. If chunk one is delivered twice, both deliveries converge on the same (run_id, chunk_id) record. This is the useful level of detail to exercise in an eval harness: inject exits at each boundary, assert the final ledger, and separately count provider calls and model tokens.

The operational signals should answer three questions: which run is stuck, which chunk is being retried, and whether the provider state agrees with the local state. Log run ID, chunk ID, payment count, attempt count, elapsed time, and a redacted provider request ID. Keep secrets and payment details out of logs. A single alert on “queue depth is high” is not enough; a small queue with one poisoned chunk can be more urgent.

Failure signal Durable evidence Action
Worker timeout Chunk is still started Retry only that chunk after checking remote state
Duplicate delivery The composite idempotency key exists Return success without applying it again
Missing successor Current chunk is done, next message is absent Let the reconciler publish one successor
Provider disagreement Local and remote status differ Quarantine the payment for review

I treat an HTTP 409 from the application's idempotency layer as a successful duplicate, while an authentication failure or a provider rate-limit response needs a different retry policy. That distinction is a useful test case, not a reason to bury all errors under one catch-all retry. Your mileage may vary on backoff values because provider quotas and business deadlines differ, but the state transitions should stay fixed.

What should be checked before shipping the nightly run?

First, replay the same chunk and verify that payment state, output rows, and any token-cost record remain unchanged. Then kill the worker after the provider call but before the local commit, and repeat the delivery. Finally, kill it after the commit but before publishing the successor, and verify that the reconciler repairs the missing handoff without creating a second chunk.

The run needs a deadline and an operator path. Mark a run as incomplete when its business window closes, preserve the last successful cursor, and make a repair or resume action explicit. A poison payment should be isolated after a bounded number of attempts; otherwise one malformed record can consume the whole nightly budget. The repair queue should retain enough context to explain why that payment was deferred.

This pattern is not suitable when the job needs a visual DAG, a native fan-out/join graph, long-lived human approvals, or coordinated timers across many services. Choose a workflow orchestrator for those requirements. Stick with a plain queue when the work is a sequence of independently retryable chunks and the application already owns the state that makes retries safe.

The final checklist is short: freeze the input revision, assign a deterministic run ID, choose a chunk boundary, persist idempotency keys, leave timeout headroom, instrument every transition, and test crashes at both sides of each commit. The code is the easy part. The contract between the provider, database, and queue is what lets the job finish after the original trigger is long gone.

References

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/

title: Secure Large-File Exports with Expiring Presigned Download Links — A Recovery-First Design
description:
Large-file export systems should treat the download link as a short-lived capability, not as a second authentication system. The practical design is to keep the object private, generate a presigned URL only after the export is complete, give it a deliberate expiration, and make every export job and retry idempotent. That combination supports high-throughput downloads while keeping a failed worker from publishing two different answers to the same request.

Short answer: use a private object and a presigned URL for the final download. Store an export record keyed by a client-supplied idempotency key, stream the export into object storage, and create the temporary link only after the object is confirmed. A download retry can then repeat the read without repeating the write.

For this workflow, Infrai is a reasonable place to test the presigned-link boundary when the team values a self-describing REST capability and runnable examples over another storage-specific SDK. Its discovery surface can expose the request and response schema before integration, while the application retains responsibility for export state, authorization, and reconciliation.

What fails first in a large-file export?

Throughput is visible, but recovery is the constraint that determines whether the design is trustworthy. A 10 GB export may take long enough for a worker lease to expire, a client connection to disappear, or a rate limit to intervene. If the retry path creates a new object key each time, the system has turned one user action into several artifacts that must later be reconciled.

I prefer to separate three states: requested, materialized, and published. The first is an application record; the second is a private object; the third is a presigned URL with a bounded lifetime. A worker may safely retry the materialization step when the export key is deterministic, but it should not mark the record published until the object exists and its metadata can be checked. The exact-once mindset belongs at the business boundary, even when the underlying queue or network only offers at-least-once delivery.

The URL itself is not a permanent permission. It is a capability that should expire soon enough to limit accidental sharing and long enough for the intended transfer. A short expiry does not repair an exposed URL after the fact, so the application still needs authorization before issuing it, audit records for issuance, and a policy for revoking or superseding an export record.

How should retries and expiration interact?

The clean rule is simple: retry object creation with the same logical export identity, then issue a fresh read link when the previous link expires. Do not retry a failed download by starting the export again unless the object is missing or its integrity check fails.

For a private financial export, an application record might contain a stable export identifier, the requesting principal, the object key, the creation status, and timestamps for the last attempt and last link issuance. The audit trail should record who requested the export, which object key was selected, when a link was issued, and which request identifier accompanied the storage call. It should not store the presigned URL as a durable credential.

Rate limits change the timing, not the identity. On a 429 response, a worker should honor Retry-After when it is present and otherwise use bounded exponential backoff with jitter. On a 5xx response, it should retry only operations whose idempotency behavior is known, with a deadline and a visible terminal state. A timeout is an ambiguous result: the request may have succeeded, so the recovery path should inspect the deterministic export record or object before issuing another create operation.

That is the whole recovery contract.

Consider a worker that loses its connection immediately after the storage service accepts the export write. The worker cannot distinguish rejection from success by looking only at its socket, and starting again with a fresh random key makes the ambiguity worse: two apparently valid exports can now represent one debit report, one statement period, or one user request. A deterministic key lets the retry consult the application record and then the object metadata before it attempts another write, while a separate publication transition prevents a partially materialized object from being handed to a browser. This is where a few additional database fields earn their keep; they make reconciliation a query instead of an overnight investigation, and they let support explain why a link expired without retaining the link itself.

The same discipline applies to the client. A browser can request a new presigned URL after expiration, but it should not send the storage provider's authorization header to the returned URL. The application authorizes the link-issuance request; the signed URL authorizes the object read for its limited lifetime. Keeping those credentials separate is a small detail with a large blast radius.

How do you implement a file export with a temporary download link?

The storage capability used here is the presign operation for a private bucket and an export key. Its inputs include the bucket, object key, and expiration duration. The application should keep the bucket private and use signed access; a public URL is the wrong abstraction for a user export.

The following Go helper makes the API call explicit while leaving the request body to the live capability schema. The body is read from PRESIGN_REQUEST_JSON, so the expiration field is supplied exactly as the current schema defines it rather than guessed from an incomplete example. It also retries 429 responses with Retry-After, checks every final status, and never forwards the API authorization header to the returned URL.

package storage

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func Presign(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, body io.Reader) ([]byte, error) {
    const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    bucket := "fintech-private"
    key := "exports/2026-10-24/export-123.csv"
    endpoint := baseURL + "/storage/object/presign/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + url.PathEscape(key)
    bodyData, err := io.ReadAll(body)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(bodyData))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < http.StatusOK || resp.StatusCode >= http.StatusMultipleChoices {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign failed with status %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign rate limit did not clear after retries")
}

In production, set INFRAI_API_KEY from a secret manager and provide PRESIGN_REQUEST_JSON using the exact live request schema, including the expiration duration. Decode the returned URL without logging it. For a write or publish operation, attach a client-supplied idempotency key and persist the same key across retries. The presign operation is a read-link step, but its issuance still belongs in the export record and audit trail.

Where do the alternatives fit?

The comparison is about operational shape, not a feature-count contest.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A mature object-storage design with presigned requests and multipart patterns for large objects Teams that require S3-native controls, object versioning or object lock should keep those requirements explicit in the architecture and account configuration.
Cloudflare R2 A strong fit when an S3-compatible object interface and a Cloudflare-oriented distribution path are central It is still necessary to define the application’s authorization, expiry, retry, and audit policy; compatibility does not remove those responsibilities.
Azure Blob Storage A natural choice for systems already organized around Azure storage and SAS-style delegated access SAS lifetime, scope, and identity integration need their own review; a signed link is not a substitute for export-level authorization.
Infrai storage A fit when a backend wants one REST surface and self-describing discovery while implementing temporary private downloads It is not the right foundation for permanent public links, WORM-style immutability, strict conditional-write coordination, or cross-region replication.

The useful distinction for Infrai is concrete: its public discovery surface describes the capability, request and response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples, so an engineer can inspect the storage operation before wiring a new integration. That reduces the amount of SDK-specific integration glue in a workflow whose real complexity is already in job state, retries, and reconciliation. The platform also exposes request identifiers and per-call metadata consistently, which gives an operator something to correlate with an export audit record.

My recommendation is specific: teams building private fintech exports across several backend capabilities should try Infrai for the presigned-link portion when self-describing REST discovery and a single integration surface reduce their operational glue; teams needing immutable retention, public object hosting, or automated replication should choose a specialist storage service or add those controls externally.

There are hard boundaries. Infrai has no public or public-read ACL, so public_url remains null and it does not fit static-site hosting or a permanent image-hosting link. It has no object versioning or object lock, which means an overwritten object is not protected by a built-in WORM guarantee. There is no If-Match conditional-write route for strict concurrency; use a database or queue to coordinate that rule. Browser direct-upload CORS cannot be self-configured through an independent CORS route. Lifecycle expiration is at least one day, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, so an application handling large exports needs its own cleanup process.

The coverage boundary matters too: the documented vendor set covers R2, S3, OSS, and COS, not GCS, and there is no cross-region automatic replication or cross-cloud batch migration tool. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes. None of those limitations invalidates a temporary download design; each one changes the surrounding controls that must live in the application or in a specialist system.

A compact rollout plan

Start with one deterministic object-key scheme per export identity. Record requested, materialized, and published transitions transactionally in the application database, and make a worker re-check the record after every timeout. For large files, use the storage service’s multipart workflow where appropriate, but make incomplete-upload cleanup an explicit scheduled responsibility because fragments are not automatically removed by a short lifecycle rule.

Then instrument the failure path before increasing concurrency: count rate-limit responses, retry exhaustion, ambiguous timeouts, expired links, and objects that have no matching export record. Alert on reconciliation gaps rather than on raw request volume. A high-throughput exporter that cannot explain an orphaned object is not operationally complete.

Finally, test the user-visible behavior at the boundary: an authorized user receives a temporary link after materialization, a link can expire without deleting the private object, a repeated request returns the same export identity, and a failed worker can resume without publishing a second artifact. This is the part worth carrying into a design review because it stays true even when the storage provider changes.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage capability documentation and verify the current request schema before implementing the client.

Sources

  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • Azure Blob Storage shared access signatures

title: Teaching Agents to Explore
description:
Teaching Agents to Explore

When I build with coding agents, the agent writes most of the code and most of the tests. The tests pass. But that green checkmark means less than it used to.

The same agent wrote both, from one picture of how the feature should work. So the tests mostly check that picture. Nobody asks whether the picture is right.

So after an agent builds something, I ask it to explore what it built. That is usually when it starts questioning its own assumptions.

I wanted to know whether this habit really works, so I ran an experiment on two buggy APIs. The short answer: a coding agent can explore well, and a written mission helps most where bugs hide in state and in data you have to follow across the system. Exploring finds bugs that reading and guessing can't, with evidence for every claim.

I turned what I learned into a skill any coding agent can use. The skill, the experiments and every result are in a public repo.

Use the skill

The skill works with any agent that supports the open Agent Skills format, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI.

In Claude Code, install it with:

/plugin install exploratory-testing --marketplace mahdavipanah/exploratory-testing-skill

For other agents, use the skills CLI:

npx skills add mahdavipanah/exploratory-testing-skill

Then start your software and ask the agent to explore it:

Explore the orders API you just built. It runs on localhost:3000, and the docs are in docs/api.md.

The skill makes the agent work like a tester. It will:

  1. Check that the environment is what it seems.
  2. Map the system: its entities, its states, and everything it can vary.
  3. Write down the rules that must never break, like "money is never created or lost", then rank the risks.
  4. Write three to five short missions, called charters, and use its whole budget on them.
  5. Follow the data after every change, try every action in every state, and test both sides of every boundary.
  6. Back every claim with the command and its output.

You get a report that keeps bugs, behaviour that needs your decision, and open questions apart. Every bug comes with the request and the response that prove it.

For an API, a shell and curl are enough. For a web UI, give the agent a browser it can drive, such as Playwright, Google's Chrome DevTools MCP or Vercel's agent-browser.

What is exploratory testing?

James Bach defined exploratory testing as simultaneous learning, test design, and test execution. You try something, look at what happened, and let that decide what you try next.

Elisabeth Hendrickson's book Explore It! explains why you need both tests and exploring. Tests check that the software does what we intended. Exploring asks a different question: what other risks are there? An agent's own tests only ask the first one.

Exploring isn't random clicking. Hendrickson gives each session a charter, with a simple template: Explore (target) with (resources) to discover (information).

Jonathan and James Bach's session-based test management puts each charter in a time box, with notes. James Whittaker's tours add themes, such as following one piece of data through every path. Together they turn curiosity into a method you can hand to an agent.

Why agents need a method

Agents are good at the mechanics. Simon Willison points out that a coding agent's defining ability is running the code it writes.

Agents also fix exploratory testing's oldest weakness: it is hard to show what was tested, and hard to repeat it. An agent logs every command and every response.

But left alone, agents explore badly. Maaret Pyhäjärvi tested this on a to-do app with 73 known problems. An unguided AI prompt found 5% of them, autonomous Playwright agents 16%, and a skilled human tester 62%.

The researchers behind GUITester name one reason: agents care more about finishing the task than about reporting what looks wrong. Hendrickson tells of a job candidate who listed a few test ideas and declared he was done. He didn't get the job. One of my agents did the same thing.

The experiment

I gave Claude Opus 5.5, running in Claude Code, two practice APIs:

  • Restful-booker, Mark Winteringham's deliberately buggy hotel-booking API. It is famous, so the model may remember its bugs.
  • claimdesk, a small expense-claims API no model has seen. A separate agent built it and planted 15 bugs, and their list stayed sealed until the scoring was done.

Every agent got the API docs, curl, 80 requests, and one rule: report only what you saw and reproduced. Only the mission changed:

  • A got one line: "Find bugs in this API."
  • B got four charters I wrote.
  • C wrote its own charters.
  • D got the skill.
  • M got only the docs, no API, and had to predict the bugs.

Each one ran five times, in separate sessions, in random order. On claimdesk, a separate agent matched every finding to the bug list without knowing which agent wrote it. A second scorer agreed with 96 of 100 of its decisions.

Agent Restful-booker: known problems found claimdesk: planted bugs found Wrong findings, both APIs
A, no mission 35% 68% 0 of 113
B, charters written for it 46% 71% 0 of 135
C, its own charters 39% 63% 0 of 105
D, the skill 48% 72% 1 of 133
M, docs only, predicting 50% 71% 219 of 380

On Restful-booker, a mission helped: B and D found clearly more than A. On claimdesk, all four exploring agents found about two-thirds of the bugs. That API is small and its docs state every rule, so even "find bugs" covered most of it.

Writing its own charters worked most of the time. But one run of C wrote five good charters, used only 37 of its 80 requests, and stopped. That's Hendrickson's job candidate.

The surprise was M. Without touching the API, it found as many known bugs as the explorers. On Restful-booker it remembered them. On claimdesk, the bugs sat exactly where the docs made promises.

But M got there by guessing. On claimdesk, three out of four of its guesses were wrong. The exploring agents reported one wrong finding in 486.

What only exploring finds

On both APIs, some bugs were found only by exploring. No prediction named any of these:

  • Restful-booker answers one documented response format with status 200 and an error message as the body.
  • It labels its XML responses as HTML.
  • It turns 30 February into 2 March without a word.
  • One update that sets the dates to null breaks a booking for good: every later read returns status 200 with a JavaScript error as the body.
  • A date sent with a timezone offset is saved as a different day.
  • claimdesk's default page size is 10, but its docs say 20. Every exploring run caught it; no prediction did.
  • A rejected claim can't be resubmitted, although the docs say it can.
  • Ordinary amounts lose a cent: 19.99 is saved as 19.98.
  • An unknown sort value crashes the server.

You can't find these by reading. They live in what the system actually returns: its defaults, its arithmetic, its headers, and the state that earlier requests leave behind. Hendrickson's advice applies to agents too: when the map and the territory disagree, trust the territory.

Reading the code doesn't replace exploring either. I had Claude review Restful-booker's source first, and it found 30 problems. The exploring agents then found 9 more, one of them on a line the review had read.

Two problems from the review were never found by exploring. Reading and exploring find different bugs, so use both.

What a mission adds

A mission helped most with bugs hidden in state and in data you have to follow. In claimdesk, removing an item from a claim updated the claim itself, but not its total in the list or the amount finance paid later.

B's charter said to follow one claim through every view, and B found this bug in all five runs. The skill says to follow the data after every change, and D found it in four. A, with no mission, never found it.

A mission can also hide things. B's charters pointed it at views and lifecycles, so B found a bug that let a user remove an item from someone else's claim in only one run of five. A and D found it every time.

The misses followed patterns, and each one became a rule in the skill:

  • Agents test one path and generalise. On Restful-booker, they saw an id ignored when creating a booking and assumed it was ignored everywhere. In an update, it silently moves the booking to another id. Only D, told to send fields like ids on every write path, found that.
  • They check one side of a boundary. One agent saw a date included at one edge and called an inverted filter correct.
  • They trust the docs. When the docs and the API agreed on a wrong status code, most agents filed it as a question.
  • They stop early.

What stays human

Two jobs stay with you. The first is deciding what counts as a bug. Agents lean on the docs and park real problems as questions. Someone has to decide whether a 200 should be a 201, or whether a case-sensitive search is intended.

The second is the sandbox. An exploring agent reads whatever the system sends back, and a page or a response can carry instructions aimed at it. Anthropic calls prompt injection one of the biggest security challenges for browser agents.

Within those limits, the split works well. The agent brings stamina, evidence and repeatability. You bring judgement about what matters. Exploring stops being a phase someone schedules and becomes the step after every change.

Before you trust the green checkmarks, ask your agent to explore.

title: Node.js Realtime Chat Room History Backfill — A Reversible Join Boundary
description:
Short answer: For a Node.js realtime chat room, backfill history from your database before subscribing, then deduplicate the overlap by message ID. Persist each message before publishing it; this makes presence and message freshness observable while keeping the transport replaceable.

The safest design for showing who is online in a shared workspace is to backfill the last messages from your database, then subscribe to the room for newer events. Put a stable message ID on every event. That ordering makes the join boundary auditable and keeps the realtime provider replaceable.

This is an architecture decision record for a B2B SaaS team chat. The important metric is presence accuracy: a user should not see an apparently current room that silently missed a message while the join request was in flight. The bill matters too, because every retained log line and every high-cardinality label becomes an operating choice, but it is not the decision rule.

Infrai fits the transport-adapter evaluation step when a team wants a self-describing REST contract: its public discovery surface exposes schemas and runnable examples, so an engineer can inspect a capability before binding application code to it. That helps with migration work, while the database, message IDs, and presence policy remain under application control.

What must remain true at the join boundary?

Three invariants define the implementation. The database is the durable history. The realtime channel is a delivery path for events newer than the backfill boundary. The client treats the message ID as an idempotency key for display, so an intentional overlap is harmless.

The sequence is deliberately asymmetric:

  1. Read a bounded page of recent messages from the database.
  2. Record the newest message ID or timestamp in that page as the join boundary.
  3. Subscribe to the room.
  4. Fetch or accept events after the boundary, then merge by message ID.

The overlap is useful. If the provider delivers an event that was also included in the history page, the client discards the duplicate. A gap is harder: no amount of client-side sorting can recover a message that was never read or delivered.

Presence deserves the same discipline. “Online” should describe a current presence signal for the room, not the existence of a recent chat message. Keep presence state scoped to the workspace and expire it according to the product’s session policy. Do not infer it from message traffic; a quiet user may still be connected, and an automated sender may produce traffic without representing a person at a keyboard.

How should a Node.js realtime chat room backfill history on join?

Persist first, backfill from the database, subscribe second, and deduplicate by message ID. This gives the application a stable contract even when the transport changes. A four-case test matrix should cover a concurrent insert, reconnect, delayed event, and duplicate delivery.

Which transport fits a replaceable implementation?

The comparison below is intentionally about boundaries rather than feature checklists. Ably and Pusher are managed realtime products with their own channel abstractions. Socket.IO is a library and protocol layer that you operate with your own server and deployment model. Infrai exposes realtime capabilities through a plain REST surface; its discovery endpoint is public and describes request schemas and runnable examples, which lowers the cost of evaluating a new capability without making it the source of truth for chat history.

Option Useful boundary for this room Main trade-off Best fit
Ably Managed pub/sub and presence concepts Application still owns durable history and vendor-specific integration choices Teams that want a managed global messaging layer
Pusher Channels Managed channels with client-facing event delivery History and join correctness remain application responsibilities Small teams prioritizing a quick hosted channel integration
Socket.IO Self-operated connections with a familiar event model Operations, scaling, and delivery behavior stay with the team Systems that need control over the server and deployment
Infrai realtime REST-based channel creation, retrieval, and publishing behind one API surface The application must still define the database boundary, deduplication, and presence policy Teams evaluating a capability through a self-describing contract

The table does not make these interchangeable at the wire level. Replaceability comes from keeping that wire level behind an application interface. The interface should expose loadRecent(room, cursor), subscribe(room, boundary), and publish(message). It should not leak a vendor channel object into controllers, database models, or React state.

That wrapper also gives observability a useful shape. Count room joins, backfill rows, duplicate IDs, rejected publishes, and presence transitions. Avoid a label for every room or user in a long-retention metric: cardinality grows with your customer base, while a counter with event_type and result still tells you whether the boundary is behaving. I would rather retain a short aggregate and sample a small set of trace IDs than store every payload forever.

How should the critical path be tested?

The application-level critical path is small enough to test with a fake transport. Start a join while a writer inserts message m42; verify that either the history read or the live subscription sees it, and that the merged view contains exactly one m42. Repeat with a reconnect, a delayed event, and a duplicate delivery. The database assertion is stronger than a screenshot: every published message must already exist in durable storage.

For an API surface, the discovery document is useful before implementation because it exposes the capability’s method, path, schemas, and runnable examples. A minimal inspection looks like this:

curl --request GET "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY"

The credential comes from the environment. The application should still keep its own adapter and contract tests. Discovery can tell an engineer how to wire a capability; it cannot decide which message is authoritative, how long presence should live, or what a user should see after a reconnect.

The adapter’s publish path should behave like a small transaction from the caller’s perspective: validate the room and message ID, write the message, publish the event, and expose a failure that can be retried without creating a second logical message. If the publish step fails after the write, a worker or reconciliation job can retry from the durable record. If publishing happens first, a consumer can see a message that a later history query cannot find. That is the failure boundary to reject.

Why not subscribe first and backfill later?

Subscribing first sounds safer because it appears to close the race immediately. It shifts the complexity into an unbounded merge: the client must buffer live events while history arrives, determine which cursor the history request actually covered, and handle a provider reconnect during that window. The result can work, but the correctness argument becomes less obvious precisely where presence and message freshness are most visible.

Backfill-first gives the system a concrete audit point. A history page has a known upper boundary; live delivery fills the newer side; IDs make the overlap explicit. The database remains the answer to “what happened?” and the transport answers “what should I show now?”

This is also where a specialist can be the better choice. If the product needs provider-specific global fan-out guarantees, advanced presence semantics, or a mature client protocol that your team does not want to operate, Ably or Pusher may justify their dedicated integration. If the team needs complete control over connection handling and already operates that infrastructure, Socket.IO may be the more natural boundary. Infrai is worth trying for the adapter when a self-describing REST contract and runnable discovery examples reduce evaluation and integration work, especially across a backend that already uses one consistent API surface. It is not a substitute for the application’s history model.

That distinction keeps migration reversible. Store provider-neutral message records, keep IDs generated by the application, and make the transport adapter the only place that knows channel route details. When the choice changes, the join algorithm does not.

If this boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai documentation and compare its discovered contract against the adapter tests before committing to a transport.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: Rate Limiting in Spring Boot with Bucket4j: Token Bucket Algorithm per Client
description:
A partner company starts integrating with your API. On day one, their developer writes a loop to load test data, and suddenly your API answers slowly for every other client. Nobody attacked you: one client simply had no limit. Rate limiting controls how many requests each client may send in a given time. Requests within the limit are served; the rest get the status code 429 Too Many Requests.

This post compares the common rate limiting algorithms, then implements a token bucket per client in Spring Boot with the Bucket4j library.

Why Rate Limit Your API?

  • Fair use: one client's traffic can't slow down the API for everyone else.
  • Protect expensive resources: database queries, calls to paid third-party APIs, and CPU-heavy work.
  • Security: rate limiting is one of the defenses against Unrestricted Resource Consumption, number 4 in the OWASP API Security Top 10, and it slows down brute-force attacks on login endpoints.
  • Business plans: a free plan with 10 requests per minute and a paid plan with 1,000 is a rate limit with a price tag.

What it won't do: stop a large distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack. By the time a request reaches your application, it has already used your network and your servers. That protection belongs at the network level, in a CDN or a cloud firewall.

Rate Limiting Algorithms Compared

  • Fixed window: count the requests per client in each calendar minute and reset the counter when the minute ends. It's simple and cheap, but a client can send the full limit at 12:00:59 and again at 12:01:00, twice the limit within two seconds.
  • Sliding window log: store the timestamp of every request and count those in the last 60 seconds. It's exact, but it stores one entry per request.
  • Sliding window counter: combine the counts of the current and the previous window, weighted by time. It's a cheap and close approximation of the sliding log.
  • Leaky bucket: requests enter a queue that is processed at a constant rate. It smooths the traffic, but bursts wait in the queue or are dropped when it's full.
  • Token bucket: a bucket holds tokens; each request takes one, and tokens are added back at a fixed rate. It allows short bursts up to the bucket's capacity while keeping the average rate under control.

The token bucket is the most widely used, because real clients are bursty: a mobile app opening a screen sends five requests at once, then nothing for a minute.

How the Token Bucket Works

Imagine a bucket with a finite capacity. A refiller adds tokens at a fixed rate, and tokens that arrive when the bucket is full are discarded. Every request takes a token out. When the bucket is empty, the request is rejected until the refiller adds more tokens.

Two numbers define the limit: the capacity (the largest burst a client can send) and the refill rate (the long-term average).

Add Bucket4j to Your Project

Bucket4j is a Java rate limiting library based on the token bucket algorithm. The Java 17 build of version 8.21:

<dependency>
  <groupId>com.bucket4j</groupId>
  <artifactId>bucket4j_jdk17-core</artifactId>
  <version>8.21.0</version>
</dependency>

Or with Gradle:

implementation 'com.bucket4j:bucket4j_jdk17-core:8.21.0'

Older tutorials use the artifact bucket4j-core and the methods Bandwidth.classic(...) and Refill.intervally(...), which are deprecated in current versions. This post uses the current builder API.

A bucket with a capacity of 10 tokens, refilled with 10 tokens every minute:

Bucket bucket = Bucket.builder()
    .addLimit(limit -> limit.capacity(10).refillIntervally(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
    .build();

Bucket4j offers two ways to refill:

  • refillIntervally(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)) waits until the whole minute has passed, then adds all 10 tokens at once. A client that sends 10 requests in the first 15 seconds must wait 45 seconds for the next one.
  • refillGreedy(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)) adds tokens gradually, one every 6 seconds. Clients get a steadier flow, and the 11th request only waits a few seconds.

The Example: A Random Quote API

The API returns a random quote about software. A repository reads the quotes from a text file, a service picks a random one, and a REST controller exposes it:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/v1")
public class QuoteController {

  private final QuoteService quoteService;

  public QuoteController(QuoteService quoteService) {
    this.quoteService = quoteService;
  }

  @GetMapping(value = "/quotes/random", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
  public Quote getQuote() {
    return quoteService.getRandomQuote();
  }
}

A client such as Postman gets a quote:

Real clients, though, are programs. In B2B integrations, developers on the client side often send hundreds of requests per minute while they test their implementation. That's the traffic we want to limit.

The Rate Limit Interceptor

A Spring MVC HandlerInterceptor runs before the controller. If its preHandle method returns false, the request never reaches the controller, which makes it the right place for the limit. The controller doesn't need to know that rate limiting exists.

We give each client its own bucket. In this example, the client is identified by its IP address. With API keys or OAuth2, the client ID is a better key.

@Component
public class RateLimitInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {

  private static final long CAPACITY = 10;
  private static final Duration REFILL_PERIOD = Duration.ofMinutes(1);

  // One bucket per client IP. Buckets of clients that stay idle for 10 minutes are removed.
  private final Cache<String, Bucket> buckets = Caffeine.newBuilder()
      .expireAfterAccess(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
      .maximumSize(100_000)
      .build();

  @Override
  public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Object handler) {
    String clientIp = request.getRemoteAddr();
    Bucket bucket = buckets.get(clientIp, ip -> newBucket());

    ConsumptionProbe probe = bucket.tryConsumeAndReturnRemaining(1);
    if (probe.isConsumed()) {
      response.addHeader("X-Rate-Limit-Remaining", Long.toString(probe.getRemainingTokens()));
      return true;
    }

    long waitMillis = TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(probe.getNanosToWaitForRefill());
    response.setStatus(HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS.value()); // 429
    response.addHeader("Retry-After", Long.toString((waitMillis + 999) / 1000)); // seconds, rounded up
    response.addHeader("X-Rate-Limit-Retry-After-Milliseconds", Long.toString(waitMillis));
    return false;
  }

  private Bucket newBucket() {
    return Bucket.builder()
        .addLimit(limit -> limit.capacity(CAPACITY).refillIntervally(CAPACITY, REFILL_PERIOD))
        .build();
  }
}

What each part does:

  • buckets.get(clientIp, ip -> newBucket()) returns the client's bucket, or creates a new one on the client's first request. The cache is thread-safe, so two simultaneous first requests from the same client can't create two buckets.
  • The cache comes from the Caffeine library. A plain HashMap would keep a bucket for every IP that ever called your API, and memory would grow forever. Here, buckets of idle clients expire after 10 minutes, which is longer than the refill period, so expiry never resets an active limit.
  • tryConsumeAndReturnRemaining(1) takes one token if there is one. The probe says whether it succeeded, how many tokens are left, and how long the client must wait otherwise.
  • The response headers tell the client where it stands. Retry-After is the standard HTTP header, in seconds, which clients and proxies understand. X-Rate-Limit-Remaining and X-Rate-Limit-Retry-After-Milliseconds give more detail.

With Spring Boot 3 or 4, the servlet classes come from jakarta.servlet. On Spring Boot 2, use javax.servlet.

The Real Client IP

Many tutorials read the client IP from the X-Forwarded-For header. Don't do this yourself. Any client can send that header with a made-up IP, a different one on every request, and is never limited.

Use request.getRemoteAddr() and let Spring Boot handle the header. When your application runs behind a load balancer or a reverse proxy, add this to application.properties:

server.forward-headers-strategy=native

The embedded server then takes the client IP from X-Forwarded-For only when the request comes from a trusted, internal proxy address. A header sent directly by a client from the Internet is ignored.

Register the Interceptor 

@Configuration
public class InterceptorConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

  private final RateLimitInterceptor rateLimitInterceptor;

  public InterceptorConfig(RateLimitInterceptor rateLimitInterceptor) {
    this.rateLimitInterceptor = rateLimitInterceptor;
  }

  @Override
  public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
    registry.addInterceptor(rateLimitInterceptor).addPathPatterns("/v1/**");
  }
}

addPathPatterns applies the limit to the API only, not to health checks or documentation. Older tutorials extend WebMvcConfigurerAdapter, which was removed in Spring 6, so that code doesn't compile on Spring Boot 3 or 4.

The interceptor handles rate limiting, the controller handles HTTP, and the service handles the business logic. Each class has one job, so you can change the limit without touching the API. Designing classes this way is what my book is about:

Software design principles provide guidelines to handle the design process's complexity, prepare your code when changes arise, and minimize the impact of introducing bugs. -- Software Design Principles

See It Work

Ten requests from the same client within a minute succeed, and the 11th is rejected:

$ curl -i http://localhost:8082/v1/quotes/random
HTTP/1.1 200
X-Rate-Limit-Remaining: 9
...
HTTP/1.1 200
X-Rate-Limit-Remaining: 0

HTTP/1.1 429
Retry-After: 60
X-Rate-Limit-Retry-After-Milliseconds: 59142

A request from another client still gets 200 with X-Rate-Limit-Remaining: 9, because every client has its own bucket.

A Bug to Avoid: The Shared Bucket

An earlier version of this post, like several tutorials online, had this code:

private final Bucket defaultBucket = Bucket.builder()...build();

if (buckets.containsKey(clientIP)) {
  bucket = buckets.get(clientIP);
} else {
  bucket = this.defaultBucket;     // the same object for every new client
  buckets.put(clientIP, bucket);
}

It looks like one bucket per client, but every client gets the same bucket object. The limit is then 10 requests per minute for all clients together: in a test, client A sent 10 requests and all were served, and client B then got 0 of its 10. Always create a new bucket per client, as newBucket() does above.

Production Notes

  • Several instances of your API: each instance has its own buckets in memory, so with three instances a client gets three times the limit. Store the buckets in a shared store instead. Bucket4j supports Redis, Hazelcast, and databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL.
  • Limits per plan: look up the client's plan and create the bucket with that plan's capacity, for example 10 requests per minute on the free plan and 1,000 on the paid plan.
  • Know your traffic first: before you choose limits, measure how many requests per minute your clients actually send. A hot-warm architecture in Elasticsearch is one way to store and analyze those logs.

Get the Code

The complete project, with Spring Boot 4.1, Bucket4j 8.21 and tests for the limit, is on GitHub: https://github.com/mgamio/rateLimit.

Where to Go Next

  • Load-test the rate limit with concurrent Java clients: simulate several clients and watch the 429 responses arrive.
  • Handle 503 errors in the client: retry carefully when the server is overloaded.
  • REST API tutorial: resources, HTTP methods and status codes, the series' starting point.

"Design a rate limiter" is one of the classic system design interview questions. Practice with real interview questions:
