title: Letting users bring their own AI key without storing it in plaintext
description:
A single AI key shared by every user of a small app is a bad deal. The free tier runs out, one noisy user consumes the quota, and the owner pays for everyone. Letting each reader bring their own key fixes that, but it creates a different problem: now the app stores secrets that belong to other people.

ARN.IO is a reading app with a book assistant. Readers can ask about a summary, a chapter or a theme. I added a bring-your-own-key setting this week. The rule is simple: a key can go in, but it never comes back out.

What the user sees

The account page has an AI tab with four fields:

  • Provider
  • Model
  • API base URL
  • API key

The provider list covers Groq, OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Google Gemini, Mistral and a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Choosing a preset fills in the base URL and a default model. The key field is a password input and is never prefilled, even when a key is already saved.

After saving, the page shows which provider is active and offers a Remove Key button. The settings endpoint returns hasKey: true and nothing that can be used to recover the secret.

The key is write-only

The database table is deliberately small:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS user_ai_settings (
  user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  provider TEXT NOT NULL,
  base_url TEXT NOT NULL,
  model TEXT NOT NULL,
  api_key_encrypted TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

The key is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before it reaches the row. The encryption key lives in an environment variable, not in PostgreSQL. The stored value is the initialization vector, the authentication tag and the ciphertext, joined with dots:

export function encryptSecret(value) {
  const iv = crypto.randomBytes(12);
  const cipher = crypto.createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", getKey(), iv);
  const encrypted = Buffer.concat([
    cipher.update(String(value), "utf8"),
    cipher.final(),
  ]);
  const tag = cipher.getAuthTag();
  return [
    iv.toString("base64"),
    tag.toString("base64"),
    encrypted.toString("base64"),
  ].join(".");
}

GCM was chosen because it gives confidentiality and integrity in one step. A modified ciphertext fails to decrypt instead of returning garbage. The key is 32 bytes and is validated at startup. If the environment value is missing or the wrong length, saving a key fails with a configuration error instead of writing something unreadable.

There is one operational consequence. If the encryption key is rotated, every saved user key becomes unreadable. The app treats that as a failed key, falls back to the built-in assistant, and the user has to enter the key again. In a larger system I would store a key version alongside the ciphertext so old keys can be decrypted during a rotation window.

The API is intentionally boring

The settings endpoint returns only the configuration a browser needs to render the form:

{
  "settings": {
    "provider": "groq",
    "baseUrl": "https://api.groq.com/openai/v1",
    "model": "llama-3.3-70b-versatile",
    "hasKey": true
  }
}

There is no endpoint that returns the key. The only time the server decrypts it is immediately before a provider request, and the decrypted value stays in memory for that request.

Saving uses PUT /api/auth/ai-settings. If the user leaves the key blank for an existing setup, the server keeps the stored ciphertext. That makes it possible to change the model without asking for the secret again.

Changing the provider with a blank key is rejected. A Groq key is not an OpenAI key, and silently pairing the old secret with a new service would only produce confusing failures.

Provider presets, not provider lock-in

The server stores three values per user: the provider id, the base URL and the model. The provider id is mostly a label and a source of defaults. The request path is the same for all of them because every preset uses an OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint.

Provider Base URL
Groq https://api.groq.com/openai/v1
OpenAI https://api.openai.com/v1
OpenRouter https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
DeepSeek https://api.deepseek.com/v1
Google Gemini https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai
Mistral https://api.mistral.ai/v1

The custom option accepts any public HTTPS endpoint with the same shape. That keeps the door open for providers I have not listed without turning the server into a provider-specific integration for each one.

A custom base URL is an SSRF risk

This was the part that needed the most care. A user-supplied base URL means the server will make an outbound request to an address chosen by that user. Without checks, someone could point it at http://127.0.0.1:5432 or a cloud metadata service.

The validator does five things before a custom URL is saved:

  1. It requires HTTPS.
  2. It rejects URLs with embedded credentials, query strings or fragments.
  3. It resolves the hostname and checks every returned address.
  4. It blocks private IPv4 ranges, private IPv6 ranges, localhost, .local names and metadata hosts.
  5. It rejects the request if the hostname cannot be resolved.

The provider request also uses redirect: "error" and a timeout. A redirect to an internal address is not followed.

This is not a complete SSRF defense. A DNS rebinding attack can resolve to a public address during validation and a private address during the request. A stricter design would resolve once, pin the address, and connect to that exact address while keeping the host header. For a small reading app, the validation plus no redirects plus a short timeout is a reasonable barrier. I would not treat it as sufficient for a high-risk multi-tenant platform without the address pinning step.

How a request chooses a key

The chat path has four possible outcomes:

  1. The user's saved key is decrypted and used.
  2. If the user has no key, the server's own key is used.
  3. If the user's key fails and a server key exists, the server key is tried.
  4. If neither works, the built-in assistant answers.

The built-in fallback is not a language model. It handles summaries from the book description, chapter lists, author questions and a short excerpt from the current chapter. That keeps the assistant usable when a provider is down or a key has expired.

Key errors are logged on the server, not shown in the chat. A rejected key should not turn the reading experience into a configuration lesson. The user sees a normal answer and can fix the key in the account page when they choose to.

What I would change next

The current version is a good first pass, but there are four things I would add before calling it finished:

  • A test button. Save the key, then send one small request and report whether the provider accepted it. Right now the first real chat is the test.
  • Per-user rate limits. A user key protects the owner's quota, but it does not protect the app from a user who sends hundreds of requests in a minute.
  • Key versioning. Store an encryption key version so a rotation does not invalidate every saved key at once.
  • A managed secret store. Application-level AES-GCM is fine for a small deployment, but a dedicated secret manager reduces the number of places the master key can appear.

The principle I keep coming back to is simple. A user's API key is a loan, not a copy. The app should use it for the request in front of it, store only what it must, and make removal easy.

ARN.IO is live at https://arnio.mukuvi.tech. The AI tab is in the profile page.

Related reading

  • How to let users bring their own OpenAI or Anthropic API keys (without storing them in plaintext) by Shlok Madhekar
  • How to Safely Store and Encrypt API Credentials in Production by Fuad Husnan
  • My SSRF guard blocked 127.0.0.1 and almost nothing else by Anirban Sarkar

title: Pricing Rule Recovery: 5 Checks for Errors and Custom Metadata
description:
A pricing rollout needs enough error context to justify rollback, but collecting every customer attribute makes the evidence expensive to retain and harder to interpret. Keep the decision context small: the rule revision, the evaluated flag state, the deployment, and a request correlation value. TL;DR: in Node.js, catch the pricing exception, extract its relevant details, attach custom metadata, and submit an authenticated POST to the error capture API. Keep the rollback decision independent of whether that submission succeeds.

The concrete system here is a B2B SaaS application introducing a new pricing rule behind a flag. Recovery has two separate obligations: stop exposing customers to the suspect rule, and determine which requests used it. An error event can support both investigations. It cannot reverse a completed charge.

1. What custom metadata makes tracking errors useful during rollback?

Start with the decision. Suppose the proposed rollout has 2 rule revisions, 3 deployment environments, and 4 release cohorts. These are illustrative design inputs, not observed traffic. Their Cartesian product has 24 possible combinations before adding deployment identifiers or customer context. That count is small enough to reason about explicitly. Adding a unique request identifier as an indexed grouping dimension changes the problem: the number of groups can grow with the number of requests. Preserve that identifier for correlation, but do not automatically promote every metadata value into a label.

Keep the revision.

A flag's current state is insufficient evidence about an earlier failure. The application should record the evaluated state and rule revision at the point of execution, then carry that context into its exception handler. Reading the flag again after an exception can attach the replacement state to an event produced under the old rule. That is a concrete diagnostic trap during recovery, when operators are deliberately changing the state.

For teams adding error capture alongside other backend services, I recommend trying Infrai for the capture portion of this workflow. Infrai provides one REST API with a single API key and one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules. Adding an adjacent capability uses the same API conventions, without another SDK integration or a separate credential and invoice to manage. Its public, self-describing discovery surface also exposes request schemas and runnable examples, which helps keep the capture contract explicit during rollout preparation. Those are integration advantages; the application's own decision record still determines whether rollback is safe.

2. Separate application metadata from the API envelope

The Node.js boundary is the pricing operation's try-catch block. Extract the exception information there, together with context already known to that request. Design the custom metadata around the investigation: which revision ran, which cohort received it, which deployment served it, and which request should be examined next. Avoid sending a customer profile merely because it is available in memory.

These are application-level concepts, not a proposed list of API field names. The capture request's actual envelope, required properties, and accepted metadata representation must follow the published request schema. Treating a plausible JSON object as a verified API contract is an avoidable implementation error. The public discovery surface provides the contract and examples needed to construct that request.

Start by inspecting the public capability inventory. This runnable curl request checks HTTP failure status and uses bounded retries with exponential backoff and Retry-After handling for rate limits. Discovery requires no key; the example includes the environment-based authorization header used for protected calls later. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in your environment before copying it. Locate the error capture capability and use its published request schema and runnable example to construct the write payload; the inventory request itself does not capture an error.

curl --request GET \
  --url 'https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery' \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set INFRAI_API_KEY}" \
  --header 'Accept: application/json' \
  --fail-with-body \
  --retry 4 \
  --retry-max-time 90 \
  --connect-timeout 5 \
  --max-time 20

The subsequent capture submission uses an explicit HTTP POST under the documented API base URL. Authenticate with Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, taking the key from the environment. Keep the key out of the event and out of application logs. Once the request body matches the documented schema, custom context belongs in the supported metadata payload rather than in invented top-level properties.

The capture operation is an observation of the pricing failure. It should not obscure the original exception if telemetry delivery also encounters trouble. Preserve the original error for the application's existing error-handling path, check the capture response status separately, and surface the actual response reason when delivery is rejected. A successful submission establishes that the capture request succeeded; it does not establish that the pricing operation succeeded.

This separation also constrains retries. An HTTP 429 response calls for backoff, honoring Retry-After when present, with an exponential fallback and a bounded retry budget. Reuse the same event identity and idempotency key for retries of one capture. A distinct failed pricing attempt needs a distinct identity. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention, but route-specific guarantees should be checked in the capability contract before treating deduplication as established behavior for that operation.

Retry capture independently. Retrying the entire pricing operation to repair a telemetry delivery failure can repeat a business side effect. That is a much larger recovery problem than a missing diagnostic event.

3. Budget retained evidence before selecting a sample

Retention math makes metadata choices concrete. Assume, solely for sizing, 10,000 captured events per day with an average serialized size of 2 KB. That produces roughly 20 MB per day, or 280 MB across 14 days, before indexing, replication, and other storage overhead. Doubling the payload doubles this raw-volume estimate. These numbers describe a proposed workload, not a vendor storage guarantee or an available retention setting.

Keep less deliberately.

A useful first cut removes duplicated request bodies, account profiles, and verbose environment dumps. Retain the short values that connect a failure to the rollout decision. A request identifier may be necessary evidence despite its high cardinality; the trade-off is to preserve it for lookup without making it the default aggregation key. Rule revisions and release cohorts serve a different purpose: they are bounded dimensions for comparing failures across the rollout.

Sampling introduces a second trade-off. Uniformly retaining one event in ten reduces volume in the hypothetical workload, but it can remove the only event from a rare cohort. A proposed policy might preserve the first failure for each revision and cohort, then sample repeated failures under a documented rule. Such a policy belongs to the application's collection design; it is not a claim about a built-in sampling feature.

Do not calculate a rollback rate from sampled failures alone. The decision also needs an independently collected count of pricing attempts and a clear account of how failures were sampled. Ten error events could represent ten failed attempts or a retained fraction of many more. Without the denominator and selection policy, comparing two cohorts invites false confidence.

Choose the evidence window to cover the rollout and subsequent investigation. Establish retention and deletion requirements before selecting a storage system, especially if customer-linked context is necessary. A short payload reduces exposure and volume, but it does not substitute for a retention policy.

4. Compare tools against the recovery question

Once the evidence contract is clear, tool selection becomes narrower. The following are workflow distinctions, not benchmark results. Evaluate each option with the same proposed failure and the same metadata budget.

Option Reason to evaluate it Boundary to test before adoption
Sentry An exception-centered workflow when investigating application errors is the main task. Check how the Node.js integration represents the custom context needed for a pricing decision.
Datadog An investigation that needs application failures alongside broader service telemetry. Check instrumentation scope, indexing choices, and the operating effort justified by that scope.
Honeycomb A workflow organized around exploring request context and distributed execution. Check that the required context reaches the collected events and supports the intended queries.
Infrai Direct error capture within a broader backend API contract, with public schemas for integration work. Establish the separate systems responsible for incident notification, trace exploration, and rollout governance.

A specialist is the better choice when exception investigation or distributed trace exploration is the central product requirement. In particular, evaluate Sentry for an error-focused workflow and Honeycomb for a trace-focused one. Datadog deserves consideration when the recovery question spans application behavior and service telemetry. Their additional scope also creates configuration decisions; test the actual investigation rather than deciding from the length of a feature list.

For a narrower capture requirement, Infrai is a reasonable candidate when consolidating backend integrations already matters. Assign alert delivery, trace-tree investigation, and release change records to tools selected for those jobs. Keep that ownership explicit in the architecture. A capture response should never be treated as an incident acknowledgment or as evidence that an operator received a notification.

5. Rehearse the rollback with a bounded payload

Before expanding the cohort, use a staging failure to verify the full decision path: the event identifies the executed revision, its request can be correlated, and the operator can select the previous rule. Measure the application outcome separately from telemetry delivery. Also test a capture rate limit so that retry traffic cannot dominate the recovery window.

Reversing the flag should govern subsequent evaluations. Previously evaluated requests and completed financial effects need their own handling in the application design. Write down that boundary before the rollout; otherwise the word rollback can conceal two very different promises.

Expand only after the evidence survives that rehearsal. Keep the payload contract small, retain enough context to attribute failures, and record the denominator needed to interpret sampled events. This makes the operational decision reviewable without turning every pricing request into a permanent customer dossier.

Sources

References for the signal model and the comparison starting points:

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Sentry Node.js documentation
  • Datadog Node.js tracing documentation
  • Honeycomb documentation

If the shared API boundary fits your system, start with the capture contract and runnable examples in the Infrai error capture guide.

title: Half-inch or three-quarter? How we model size variants on a hardware store
description:
Almost everything we sell at RAMO comes in sizes. A repair connector comes in 1/2" and 3/4". A garden hose fitting comes in a few thread sizes. A switch frame comes in 2, 3 or 4 modules. For a while we treated every size as its own product, and it slowly made a mess of search, feeds and the catalog itself.

This is how we think about it now. Nothing fancy, just the rules we wish we'd written down on day one.

The question to ask first

Before deciding "one page or many", ask: would a customer ever search for this size on its own?

For plumbing, the answer is often yes. People type the exact size because the size is the whole point. Someone fixing a leak under the sink doesn't want "repair connector", they want the 1/2" one, today.

For things like colour on a switch frame, people usually search for the product and pick the colour after.

So we ended up with two patterns, not one.

Pattern 1: separate pages, one parent

When the size is something people search for, each size gets its own URL, its own title with the size in it, and its own stock and price. For example our 1/2" repair connector has its own page.

But they all point to a shared parent in the database:

create table product_groups (
  id serial primary key,
  slug text unique not null,
  name text not null
);

alter table products
  add column group_id int references product_groups(id),
  add column variant_label text; -- "1/2\"", "3/4\"", "3 modules"

The product page reads its siblings by group_id and shows them as a size picker. Clicking a size navigates to the sibling's URL instead of swapping state on the page. It's a plain link, so crawlers follow it too.

Pattern 2: one page, a selector

When the variant is cosmetic, it's one page with a selector. The selected option goes in a query param (?color=white) so the link can be shared, and the canonical URL stays the bare product URL. We don't want five copies of the same page competing with each other.

Where it pays off: feeds

Google Merchant Center, Meta and TikTok all understand variant groups. In the feed, every size is its own item, and they share an item_group_id. Once the group lived in the database, the feed generator just reads group_id and writes it out. Before that, we were guessing groups from product names, which broke the first time someone renamed a product.

Things that bit us

  • Size in the title, written one way. 1/2", 1/2 inch, ½ and חצי צול all appeared in our titles at some point. Search treated them as different words. We picked one format for titles and put the other spellings into search synonyms.
  • Out-of-stock siblings. If the 3/4" is sold out, we still show it in the picker, greyed out, with a link. Hiding it made people think we never had it.
  • Structured data. Each size page has its own Product with its own offers. We don't put the whole group's price range on every page, since that confused the price shown in search results.
  • The category page. A pipe fittings category with every size listed separately gets long and repetitive fast. We show one card per group with a "more sizes" hint, and let filters split them out when someone filters by size.

The rule we keep

If the size changes what the customer needs, give it a URL. If it only changes what it looks like, give it a selector. Store the relationship in the database either way, because everything downstream (search, feeds, the picker, the category grid) wants to know which products belong together.

How do you handle variants in your store? I'm curious whether anyone has found a cleaner way to deal with the mixed "some variants deserve a page, some don't" case.

title: Prevent Duplicate Telegram Webhook Deliveries and Spoofed Hits in Pure PHP
description:
If you deploy a Telegram bot endpoint in pure PHP without strict request verification, your system is vulnerable to two distinct failure modes: unauthorized actors sending forged payloads directly to your server, and duplicate update execution caused by Telegram's retry mechanism.

Imagine a Telegram bot handling automated lead capturing or inventory allocation. If your webhook URL is publicly accessible, an attacker who discovers your endpoint path can send fake JSON payloads impersonating users, triggering invalid transactions or polluting your database. Conversely, if your server experiences a temporary database latency spike and delays returning an HTTP 200 response, Telegram's servers will timeout, consider the delivery failed, and retry sending the exact same payload multiple times. Without proper safeguards, your application will re-run business logic for every retry attempt.

Building a resilient webhook integration in pure PHP requires three foundational elements: programmatic webhook registration with a secret token, secret token verification upon request receipt, and atomic update deduplication in MySQL before executing any business logic.

Setting Up the Webhook with a Secret Token

Many developers register their Telegram webhooks by manually opening a browser URL containing their bot token. This approach frequently leads to missing parameter configurations and exposes raw tokens in browser histories or shell command logs. Instead, script the registration process using pure PHP and cURL to set both the endpoint URL and a dedicated secret token.

Telegram allows you to supply a secret_token string (1 to 256 characters) when calling setWebhook. Once set, Telegram includes this string in every incoming request under the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token HTTP header. This acts as an API key for your inbound endpoint.

Here is a command-line script to register your webhook securely:

<?php
// register_webhook.php

$botToken = getenv('TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN');
$webhookUrl = getenv('TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_URL');
$secretToken = getenv('TELEGRAM_SECRET_TOKEN');

if (!$botToken || !$webhookUrl || !$secretToken) {
    fwrite(STDERR, "Error: Missing required environment variables.
");
    exit(1);
}

$apiUrl = sprintf('https://api.telegram.org/bot%s/setWebhook', $botToken);

$payload = [
    'url' => $webhookUrl,
    'secret_token' => $secretToken,
    'allowed_updates' => ['message', 'callback_query'],
    'drop_pending_updates' => false,
];

$ch = curl_init($apiUrl);
curl_setopt_array($ch, [
    CURLOPT_POST => true,
    CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER => true,
    CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER => ['Content-Type: application/json'],
    CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS => json_encode($payload),
    CURLOPT_TIMEOUT => 10,
]);

$response = curl_exec($ch);
$httpCode = curl_getinfo($ch, CURLINFO_HTTP_CODE);
$error = curl_error($ch);
curl_close($ch);

if ($response === false) {
    fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("cURL error: %s
", $error));
    exit(1);
}

if ($httpCode !== 200) {
    fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("HTTP error %d: %s
", $httpCode, $response));
    exit(1);
}

$result = json_decode($response, true);
if (json_last_error() !== JSON_ERROR_NONE || !isset($result['ok']) || $result['ok'] !== true) {
    fwrite(STDERR, sprintf("Telegram API error: %s
", $response));
    exit(1);
}

echo "Webhook registered successfully.
";

Running this script ensures that Telegram acknowledges the payload format and registers your expected secret token. If you ever suspect your webhook URL has been leaked, you can re-run this script with a newly generated secret token to invalidate incoming forged requests immediately.

Validating the Request Header and Parsing Inbound Data

When Telegram sends an HTTP POST request to your script, PHP populates global server arrays. However, Telegram sends data as raw JSON in the request body, not as standard application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST fields. You cannot access the payload via $_POST. You must read from php://input.

Before allocating memory or opening a database connection to parse the body, inspect the HTTP headers for X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token. In pure PHP, web servers like Nginx or Apache expose custom headers through the $_SERVER superglobal, converting the name to uppercase and prefixing it with HTTP_. Thus, X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token becomes $_SERVER['HTTP_X_TELEGRAM_BOT_API_SECRET_TOKEN'].

Use hash_equals() to compare the expected secret token with the header value. Standard string comparison operators (===) are vulnerable to timing attacks, where an attacker measures the execution time to infer secret bytes step by step.

Here is how to structure the entry point of your webhook file (index.php):

<?php
// index.php

$expectedSecret = getenv('TELEGRAM_SECRET_TOKEN');
$receivedSecret = $_SERVER['HTTP_X_TELEGRAM_BOT_API_SECRET_TOKEN'] ?? '';

if (empty($expectedSecret) || !hash_equals($expectedSecret, $receivedSecret)) {
    http_response_code(403);
    echo 'Forbidden: Invalid secret token';
    exit;
}

$rawPayload = file_get_contents('php://input');
if (empty($rawPayload)) {
    http_response_code(400);
    echo 'Bad Request: Empty body';
    exit;
}

$update = json_decode($rawPayload, true);
if (json_last_error() !== JSON_ERROR_NONE) {
    http_response_code(400);
    echo 'Bad Request: Invalid JSON';
    exit;
}

if (!isset($update['update_id']) || !is_int($update['update_id'])) {
    http_response_code(422);
    echo 'Unprocessable Entity: Missing update_id';
    exit;
}

// Proceed to deduplication and processing

If the header validation fails, the script terminates instantly with an HTTP 403 status code without consuming database connection resources or exposing internal application state.

Atomic Update Deduplication with MySQL

Telegram guarantees at-least-once delivery. If Telegram sends a webhook request and your server takes longer than approximately 5 seconds to answer—or returns any HTTP status code other than 200–299—Telegram assumes the message was dropped. It will queue the update and resend it at increasing intervals.

If your PHP script executes a long database query or makes an external API call during the first attempt, the request might time out on Telegram's side while your server actually completes the work. When Telegram retries the payload seconds later, your script will receive the identical update_id and run the business logic a second time.

To prevent duplicate execution, maintain a dedicated table in your database for tracked update identifiers. You must claim the update_id atomically before executing business logic.

First, create the storage table using MySQL:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS telegram_processed_updates (
    update_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    processed_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (update_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

Next, use a PHP class with PDO to attempt inserting the incoming update_id. By relying on the primary key constraint, the database engine enforces atomicity. If an insert fails due to a duplicate key error, you know the update is currently being processed or was processed previously.

<?php
// Deduplicator.php

class UpdateDeduplicator
{
    private PDO $pdo;

    public function __construct(PDO $pdo)
    {
        $this->pdo = $pdo;
    }

    /**
     * Attempts to register the update_id.
     * Returns true if this is a NEW update, false if it is a DUPLICATE.
     */
    public function registerUpdate(int $updateId): bool
    {
        $sql = 'INSERT IGNORE INTO telegram_processed_updates (update_id) VALUES (:update_id)';
        $stmt = $this->pdo->prepare($sql);
        $stmt->execute([':update_id' => $updateId]);

        // rowCount() returns 1 if inserted, 0 if duplicate row was ignored
        return $stmt->rowCount() > 0;
    }
}

Integrate this class into your webhook execution pipeline:

<?php
// Complete execution block inside index.php

$dsn = sprintf('mysql:host=%s;dbname=%s;charset=utf8mb4', getenv('DB_HOST'), getenv('DB_NAME'));
$pdo = new PDO($dsn, getenv('DB_USER'), getenv('DB_PASS'), [
    PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION,
    PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC,
]);

$deduplicator = new UpdateDeduplicator($pdo);
$updateId = (int) $update['update_id'];

if (!$deduplicator->registerUpdate($updateId)) {
    // Return HTTP 200 so Telegram stops retrying this update
    http_response_code(200);
    echo 'OK: Duplicate update ignored';
    exit;
}

// Execute business logic safely
if (isset($update['message'])) {
    processIncomingMessage($update['message']);
}

http_response_code(200);
echo 'OK';

By returning HTTP 200 when ignoring a duplicate, you explicitly instruct Telegram's retry engine to drop the message from its retry queue, preserving idempotency.

Production Notes

When running this architecture in production environments under high request traffic, keep the following execution constraints in mind:

  1. Fast Response Times: Telegram expects a prompt response. If your business logic involves sending remote cURL requests, processing image uploads, or hitting third-party APIs, do not perform those operations synchronously inside the webhook request block. Parse the update, record it in your database, queue a job using a Redis background worker (or a database-backed task table), return HTTP 200 immediately, and process the task asynchronously.
  2. FastCGI Connection Flushing: If you use PHP-FPM with Nginx, you can send an HTTP 200 response to Telegram and close the client connection before finishing your PHP execution by invoking fastcgi_finish_request(). Note that long-running operations in the background can still consume PHP worker processes, so a real queue worker remains preferable for heavy workloads.
  3. Updating Database Indexes: Periodically clean up old rows in the telegram_processed_updates table using a scheduled cron job (e.g., DELETE FROM telegram_processed_updates WHERE processed_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 7 DAY;). Telegram retry windows do not exceed 24 hours, so retaining records for a week provides a sufficient buffer without bloating your database storage.
  4. Handling Partial Failures: If your business logic throws an unhandled exception after the update_id has been inserted into your database, the update will not run again on subsequent Telegram retries. Wrap your processing code in try...catch blocks. If an unrecoverable system error occurs, consider rolling back the database transaction or deleting the update_id entry so the retry system can attempt processing after your infrastructure recovers.

Building robust Telegram integrations requires careful handling of inbound security and request execution flow. For assistance in architecting high-concurrency automated channels or custom interfaces, reach out to BotCreator — studio that ships Telegram bots / Mini Apps.

title: Store Timestamps in UTC, Display Them Locally
description:
A CRM stores '10:30' beside a follow-up task. One representative reads it in Jaipur and another in London. Neither knows which timezone the value represents.

Time data needs to describe either an instant or a local scheduling intention. Those are different requirements.

Store instants unambiguously

An enquiry acceptance time is an instant. Store it using a timezone-aware database type or an explicit UTC representation supported by your system.

JavaScript can serialize a valid Date as a UTC ISO string:

const acceptedAt = new Date();
const timestamp = acceptedAt.toISOString();

This records the browser or server clock's value. For authoritative acceptance time, prefer the backend's timestamp and maintain its clock synchronization.

Do not infer an instant from an ambiguous string such as 06/07/2026 10:30.

Format for the reader

Display an instant in an explicit timezone using a locale-aware formatter:

const display = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", {
  dateStyle: "medium",
  timeStyle: "short",
  timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"
}).format(acceptedAt);

Choose the display timezone from a documented user or application setting. Label it where confusion is possible.

Preserve scheduling intent

'Call tomorrow at 9 AM in the customer's timezone' contains more than an instant. Store the selected local date and time together with an IANA timezone identifier, then resolve it for execution.

Recurring local schedules need their timezone rules preserved. A fixed UTC offset does not represent future daylight-saving changes.

Some local times occur twice when clocks move backward; others do not occur when clocks move forward. Ask for or document a resolution policy rather than silently choosing an arbitrary instant.

Keep audit fields separate

Field Meaning
Accepted at Backend accepted the enquiry
Event occurred at Source reports when the event happened
Received at Integration received the event
Next attempt at Planned operational retry

A delayed event's receipt time is not its occurrence time. Avoid overwriting one with another.

Test meaningful boundaries

Test different viewer timezones, month and year boundaries, daylight-saving transitions for relevant regions, invalid dates, and absent timezone settings.

The conversion code above is illustrative and should be verified in your target runtime. Consistent timestamps make routing, follow-ups, and incident investigation easier because everyone can identify which moment a record describes.

title: How to answer Claude Code or Codex from your phone
description:
You start an agent on the computer at home and leave. An hour later your phone shows that it stopped to ask for permission to run a command. It stays stopped until you answer, and you're nowhere near the desk.

Each of the big agents has a way to answer from your phone. They just don't work the same way:

  • Claude Code: run /remote-control in the session, then open it in the Claude app or at claude.ai/code. It needs a Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, or Enterprise plan.
  • Codex: set up Control this Mac or PC in the ChatGPT desktop app, pair your phone with the QR code, and answer from the ChatGPT mobile app.
  • Any agent: turn on SSH on the computer, reach it from outside your network, and keep the agent in tmux. A terminal app on the phone does the rest.
  • The catch: the computer has to stay awake and online. If it sleeps, every one of these stops.
  • The other catch: each agent has its own app and its own setup. With three agents, that's three.

How do I answer Claude Code from my phone?

Use Remote Control, Claude Code's own feature. In a session you've already started, type:

/remote-control

(/rc is the short form.) The session keeps running on your computer, with your files, MCP servers, and settings. Your phone only shows it and sends messages. Open the session by name in the Claude app under Code, or at claude.ai/code. A session that's online shows a computer icon with a green dot.

You can also start it from the shell:

claude remote-control      # server mode, shows a URL; press space for a QR code
claude --remote-control    # a normal interactive session with Remote Control on

To be told when it needs you, open /config and turn on Push when actions required. Install the Claude app and sign in with the same account.

What to know before you rely on it:

  • It needs a Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, or Enterprise plan with a claude.ai login. API keys aren't supported.
  • Outside server mode, each claude process supports one remote session, and that process has to keep running. Close the terminal and the session ends.
  • A session you started without it can't be reached until you run /remote-control in it, unless you turn on Enable Remote Control for all sessions in /config.

The full list is in Anthropic's Remote Control documentation.

How do I answer Codex from my phone?

Codex does it through the ChatGPT apps, and setup starts on the computer, not in the terminal. You can't set it up from the Codex CLI or the IDE extension.

  1. In the ChatGPT desktop app on the computer, open Settings → Connections → Control this Mac or PC, choose Set up or Add, and approve remote access.
  2. Scan the QR code with your phone. It opens the ChatGPT app.
  3. Confirm the same account and workspace. The computer then appears under Codex in the app, or Remote if your app still uses that name.

From the phone you can continue chats, answer questions, approve commands, and read diffs and terminal output. The work still runs on the computer, with its files and tools.

The computer must be awake, online, and signed in. On a Mac laptop, remote access can stay available with the lid open and power connected; with the lid closed it also needs an external display, and choosing Sleep ends it. Each phone is paired with each computer it controls. The rest is in OpenAI's remote connections documentation.

Can I use SSH and tmux for any agent?

Yes, and it's the one method that doesn't care which agent you run. You connect to the computer, then attach to a terminal where the agent is already running. It takes more setup than the two above.

On the Mac, turn on SSH: open System Settings → General → Sharing, then turn on Remote Login. Under Allow access for, choose Only these users and add yourself.

From outside your home network you also need a way to reach the Mac. Don't open its SSH port to the internet. Use a VPN or a mesh network such as Tailscale, so only your own devices can connect.

Then run the agent inside tmux, which keeps the terminal alive when you disconnect:

tmux new -s agents     # start a session named "agents", then run claude or codex inside it
# Ctrl-b, then d       # detach: the agent keeps running
tmux attach -t agents  # from your phone's SSH app, pick it up again

Anthropic's own documentation suggests the same for Claude Code over SSH: use tmux or screen so the session survives a dropped connection.

This works, but it's the roughest on a phone. You're typing into a full terminal with a touch keyboard, and the keys an agent needs, Esc, Tab, Ctrl, and the arrows, aren't on it. You also set up the SSH app, the network, and the Mac yourself.

Why does my agent stop answering when I'm away?

Almost always, the computer went to sleep. Locking the screen doesn't stop an agent; idle sleep does, and so does closing the lid. Remote Control for Claude Code and Codex, and SSH, can only reach a computer that's awake and online.

None of the agents keep the Mac awake between turns, and that's exactly when you're waiting to answer from the phone. How to keep your Mac awake for Claude Code and Codex covers it step by step.

What if I run Claude Code, Codex, and Grok together?

Then there's no single place to answer. Claude Code's remote lives in the Claude app, Codex's in the ChatGPT app, and a Grok session on your own computer has no remote from xAI that I could find in its documentation. Over SSH you can reach all three, but you have to find the right tmux session yourself and read the terminal to see which one is waiting.

With one agent, any of the methods above is fine. With three, the problem is no longer how to connect, it's which one is waiting for you.

Can PonyMux answer all of them from one place?

Yes. PonyMux runs the real CLI of each agent in its own Terminal, so Remote Control doesn't depend on any agent offering its own remote. It's free on macOS and Windows.

  1. In the sidebar, select the cloud next to Agents, then Sign In…, and sign in with GitHub or Google.
  2. Scan the QR code on the card with your phone. my.ponymux.com opens with your agents already listed.
  3. Every agent running in PonyMux shows up in one list with the same status lights: Claude Code, Codex, or Grok. Open the one that's waiting.
  4. Opening an agent only shows its Terminal. Choose Start control to send keys to it. On a phone, a key bar adds the esc, tab, ctrl, and arrow keys the keyboard lacks.

One device controls an agent at a time. On the computer, a Stop button takes control back whenever you want.

What it doesn't do: it doesn't wake a sleeping computer, so Keep Awake is worth turning on before you leave. There's no end-to-end encryption, and no approval cards that answer for you; you read the Terminal and type the answer. The server relays the screen and keystrokes and saves none of them. On the Free plan, one computer shares its agents at a time.

For setup, see Set up Remote Control. Remote Control on your phone covers the key bar and notifications, and How Remote Control stays safe lists exactly what is and isn't protected.

Download PonyMux, free for macOS and Windows: ponymux.com/download

title: Top 5 AI Agent Patterns for Frontend Devs
description:
When I code, I prompt, wait, and see what comes back. For a bigger feature I might reach for something like spec-driven development. Either way, I'm babysitting the coding harness through every interaction.

Don't get me wrong, that can work well. But plenty of problems are too complex to solve with a single prompt. For those, I'd much rather write one prompt, walk away, and come back to finished work. The patterns in this post came out of trying to do exactly that.

There are five of them, each a step past prompting and specs, and together they keep my agent working while I'm off doing something else: scheduled jobs, memory, subagents, workflows, and bots.

I show everything in Kiro Crew, the open source coding harness I know best, and a couple of things in the Kiro IDE. Some of these patterns exist in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw too, so you can check those out as well.

Here's the video if you'd rather watch:

(Full disclosure: I'm a Developer Advocate at AWS, and Kiro is an AWS product.)

How to follow along (If you want to try this yourself)

  • Kiro Crew installed. The install guide covers the desktop app and the one-line CLI install.
  • Optional, the Kiro IDE if you want to try memory and workflows there too.
  • A frontend project to point it at. Mine are a couple of Vue and Vite+ apps.

1. Schedule

The first feature I think everyone should try out is scheduling. Kiro Crew runs on a Gateway that can live on a VPS, a Mac mini, or your laptop, and it can kick off agent runs on a timer. You can set something similarly by running your harness in the cloud as well.

I care a lot about accessibility and Lighthouse scores on my sites. A daily job can run a Lighthouse test on my frontend code and send me a report, or open a pull request with the fixes instead.

The two jobs on my Schedule page right now aren't about code at all. One researches frontend and fullstack news every morning at 7 a.m. The other is a weekly CFP finder that looks for conference talks I could submit to, every Monday at 9.


Both jobs run on their own and drop a report when they finish.

Each job is a prompt plus a schedule. Open one and you get the message, a cron expression, and a timezone. The news job is 0 7 * * *.


Run Now is handy for testing a prompt before you trust it overnight.

You don't have to write cron by hand. Ask in chat, something like "every night at 2, run Lighthouse on /pricing and tell me what dropped," and the agent creates the job for you. The scheduling docs have the CLI version too.

2. Turn on memory

Memory is how your agent remembers who you are and what you're working on. I've been using this a lot. It works really well for remembering my preferences. For example, it knows I am a Vue.js fan, so it starts every project with Vue.js or Nuxt.

In Kiro Crew, memory lives in a folder at ~/.kiro/crew/workspace/memory as plain markdown, with files for your preferences and your projects. It gets pulled into context when it's needed. You can tell it things as you chat. Maybe you like tabs over spaces, or you want the Options API in Vue for some reason. Just say "can you remember this for me?"

The Kiro IDE has memory too, and the setting has four modes.


Off is the default, so you have to turn it on.

I run Use and learn. It can learn per project or globally, so every project shares the same preferences. Here's one it saved for me during a Vite+ project. I'd asked for a diagram, it asked me a bunch of setup questions, and I told it to just make a nice looking image.


I never wrote this rule. It appeared naturally as I was creating my project.

It even saved the tooling workaround it found, so the next diagram didn't hit the same missing dependency. If your harness has memory, turn it on and start telling it your preferences. Kiro Crew will sometimes turn what it learns into a skill on its own as well.

3. Ask for subagents

When you have a few pieces of work that don't depend on each other, they don't need to wait in line. Tell the agent to split it up. "Run three subagents and research this at the same time" is all it takes. *FYI, some harnesses will do this automatically, but it's hit and miss, I would always explicitly tell it to use subagents, and if needed use worktrees

I did that for my tech news. One subagent took markets and big tech, one took AI releases, and one took dev news like Hacker News threads and Vue, Nuxt, and Vite releases.


Three subagents, 35 seconds, 1.73 credits. The main agent combines the reports at the end.

Each subagent gets its own context, so they don't fill up your main chat or trip over each other. This is a lot cleaner than what I saw people doing a while back, opening 10 terminal windows and running an agent in each one. That gets messy fast.

The current models, like Claude Opus 5.5, are good at breaking work down. Kiro Crew also lets you keep several sessions open at once, each working on a different part of the codebase or a different project in the workspace. I like having that in a GUI where I can see everything that's running.

4. Build a workflow for anything you'll do twice

Workflows are harder to describe than the others. A workflow kicks off multiple agents in a set order, fans work out to them, and checks the results.

Let me explain it by using migrations as an example. You can build one workflow and then reuse for every migration. Each step can fan out to several agents or subagents, and usually there's a judge near the end that double checks the results before it's done.

Kiro Crew has a Workflows feature, and so does the Kiro IDE. The IDE ships with recipes you can open and read. Here's feature-pipeline.


Two separate reviewers on the code loop, then an aggregator that merges what they found.

The design and code steps loop, and the code loop runs two reviewers in parallel before an aggregator combines their findings. The recipes are saved as files you can open and change.

There's also a ralph recipe, if you've heard of the Ralph loop. It runs one coding agent through a JSON checklist, one item per pass, up to 200 times, until everything on the list is done. Check the Kiro workflows docs or the Kiro Crew workflows docs for how to write your own.

5. Give one area of your app to a bot

Bots take everything above and put it in one place. A bot is a long-running agent that owns one area of your work. It has its own memory, it can run its own subagents (Kiro Crew calls them workers), it can run on a schedule, and it works toward a goal.

I made one for accessibility and called it A11y. On the Schedules tab there's Heartbeat, which wakes the bot every hour to look for work on its own. For an accessibility bot, that means checking the app every hour as people merge things in. You can add your own schedules here too.


Heartbeat stays off until the bot has a goal.

The Goals tab is where you give it the goal, something like keeping the Lighthouse score above 90. The bot proposes milestones and you confirm them, which works a lot like the steps in a workflow. You can also turn on daily, weekly, or monthly check-ins so it sends you reports.


Each bot gets its own dashboard, and you build it by asking in chat.

Each bot also gets its own dashboard. Ask it to set one up showing what it's working on and what's next, and it builds the page for you.

One thing to know before you go all in on bots. Every Heartbeat wake, every worker, and every scheduled run uses credits. Heartbeat is off by default and you pick the interval, 30 minutes up to 4 hours. Start slow. The how bots work page covers the rest.

Wrap up

If you haven't noticed, the common theme in all these is that you can stop and walk away and things still get done. Scheduled jobs run while I sleep, memory carries what I've told it into the next session, subagents and workflows split the work up, and a bot does all of it for one part of my app.

Which one are you going to try first? Let me know in the comments. I'm curious if anyone is already running bots on a project.

Links

  • Kiro Crew docs
  • Kiro Crew scheduling
  • Kiro Crew memory
  • Kiro Crew subagents
  • Kiro Crew workflows
  • How bots work
  • Kiro IDE memory
  • Kiro IDE workflows
  • The video on YouTube

title: My bot detector was blocking most real users, and my tests never noticed
description:
I maintain Synapse Shield, an open-source bot detection engine (Python with a native Rust core and JS client SDKs) that evaluates mouse and keyboard dynamics: jerk variance, Fitts' law terminal deceleration, path curvature, and keystroke flight times.

On paper, my test suite looked bulletproof: over 500 unit tests, mutation testing, and adversarial red-team suites. Every test case representing a "human" was passing cleanly.

Then I finally did what I should have done from day one: I ran actual recorded mouse movements from real people through the engine.

The experiment

Getting labeled interaction data is tedious, so I used recorded desktop sessions from a public academic dataset (120 participants). I converted the raw trajectories to match exactly what the frontend SDK emits (30 ms throttling, integer pixel coordinates, click events) and fed them directly into the full evaluation pipeline.

The numbers

Window Real-user sessions blocked
6 s (typical login) 68.0%
20 s (longer interaction) 87.8%

Every single participant was blocked as a bot at least once.

My unit tests never caught this because my "human" fixtures were synthetic. They were sine waves with Gaussian noise, shaped by my own assumptions about how people move mice. The heuristic rules were tuned against a caricature of human movement, not reality.

The culprit: a division by zero in disguise

Nearly all the false positives came from a single rule: the differential curvature check.

κ = |v × a| / |v|³

The formula divides by speed cubed. When a real person aims for a button, they slow down and pause. While the cursor is resting, browsers do not emit mousemove events. When the user makes a tiny 1-pixel adjustment after that 200-500 ms pause, the recorded speed drops to about 0.003 px/ms.

Because |v|³ is in the denominator, κ shoots up to 30-100. The engine interpreted that sudden spike as chaotic trajectory jitter and slapped a heavy bot penalty on the session.

In other words, the rule was triggering precisely when a human did what humans naturally do: stop and adjust before clicking.

To make matters worse, that branch barely caught real bots. Against automated scripts it flagged only 5-13% of them, and only when the bots happened to produce a similar stop artifact.

The fix

The chaotic curvature check now filters out near-stationary points. It only evaluates steps where the cursor actually traveled a meaningful distance (at least 5 px on both neighboring steps, with a minimum of 10 such points).

Instead of guessing a threshold, I swept values against the real recordings:

Step threshold Real humans flagged by this rule
0 px (old code) 67.3%
3 px 3.1%
5 px (chosen) 0.39%

Across the entire decision engine:

  • 6 s windows: 68.0% → 1.4% false positives
  • 20 s windows: 87.8% → 2.7% false positives
  • Synthetic bot patterns: 100% detection maintained

What an external review caught

After drafting the fix, an independent code review found real problems:

  1. Ineffective regression tests: My first tests for minimum-jerk bots did not actually exercise the new moving-point path (one fixture was a straight line, the other was too clean). I rewrote them with coordinates rounded the way real bots produce them, and the tests now also assert that the fixture is not smooth on all points, so only the new branch can pass them.
  2. Mobile touch false positives: A polynomial acceleration rule meant for desktop mouse trajectories was also evaluating mobile taps. Taps spaced seconds apart collapsed acceleration variance to near zero, blocking simulated mobile users about 97% of the time. Adding a touch check brought that down to 2-3%.
  3. Rollover typing: When fast typists hold Shift or overlap keypresses, the inter-keystroke interval can be negative or zero. Because the check only looked for < 25ms, negative numbers tripped the "superhuman typing frequency" penalty. Adding a strict lower bound (0 < interval < 25ms) fixed it, and the same bug turned out to live in two more places (the Brave privacy cap and the threat label), so the check is now a single shared function.

Every fix has a test that fails on the old code.

Known limitations

A few blind spots remain:

  • Quantized Bézier curves: On integer coordinates, curvature analysis alone only catches about 23.5% of smooth Bézier bots. Other layers (FFT spectral analysis, terminal deceleration) catch the rest, but curvature is not a magic bullet on its own. That was true before the fix too.
  • Fast typing false positives: The superhuman typing threshold still trips on roughly 1.4% of real typing sessions. That is next on the list.
  • Simulated mobile data: The mobile numbers come from a simulation model, not in-the-wild mobile recordings. Keyboard-only and older users have no real data yet either.
  • Adversarial tooling: Detection was evaluated against mathematical generators, not yet against full stealth headless browsers like Playwright with ghost-cursor.

Takeaways

  1. Synthetic test fixtures share your blind spots. If you generated your own "human" test data with math, your heuristics will overfit to your own mental model of how people behave.
  2. Measure false positives before tightening detection. A bot detector that catches 99% of bots is useless if it blocks most legitimate customers.
  3. Watch out for singularities in kinematic formulas. Anything with velocity or time in the denominator will blow up when a user stops moving.

These fixes are shipped in v0.10.6.

I built this with AI assistance (Claude) for implementation and review. The detection approach and design decisions are mine.
