title: Multi-Provider AI Gateway Failover: Building Token Budget Guardrails with gpt-load
description:
The Cost Control Problem in Small Team AI Adoption

When your 12-person engineering team starts embedding GPT-4 calls into CI pipelines, customer support chatbots, and internal code review tools, the first production incident isn't a 500 error—it's a $3,200 AWS bill from a runaway retry loop that hit OpenAI 47,000 times in six hours.

Traditional API gateways handle rate limiting and circuit breaking, but AI provider APIs introduce three failure modes that standard HTTP proxies don't address:

  1. Token budget exhaustion (you pay per token, not per request)
  2. Multi-credential rotation (dev keys, prod keys, backup accounts with different quota tiers)
  3. Provider-specific retry semantics (OpenAI returns 429s differently than Anthropic or Azure)

This is where self-hosted gateway tooling like tbphp/gpt-load becomes operationally relevant. It's a PHP-based request router that sits between your application layer and external LLM providers, enforcing budget caps and credential scheduling without requiring you to rewrite every SDK integration.

Architecture: Where gpt-load Fits in Your Stack

The typical deployment pattern:

[Your App] → [gpt-load Gateway] → [OpenAI / Anthropic / Azure]
     ↓
[SQLite Usage Log]

Your application code points to http://localhost:8080/v1 (or wherever you deploy gpt-load). The gateway:

  • Accepts OpenAI-compatible request format
  • Maintains a pool of API keys with per-key daily/monthly token budgets
  • Routes requests to the least-utilized credential
  • Logs token consumption to local SQLite (zero external telemetry)
  • Returns standard OpenAI API responses

This separation of concerns means your Python FastAPI service or TypeScript Next.js API routes don't need custom token accounting logic. You swap one environment variable:

# Before
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_KEY"))

# After
client = OpenAI(
    api_key="dummy",  # gpt-load validates against its own key pool
    base_url="http://gpt-load.internal:8080/v1"
)

Configuration Deep Dive: Token Budget Enforcement

The core config file (config/channels.php) defines your credential pool:

return [
    'channels' => [
        [
            'name' => 'openai_prod',
            'provider' => 'openai',
            'api_key' => getenv('OPENAI_PROD_KEY'),
            'daily_token_limit' => 500000,
            'monthly_budget_usd' => 150,
            'priority' => 1,
        ],
        [
            'name' => 'anthropic_backup',
            'provider' => 'anthropic',
            'api_key' => getenv('ANTHROPIC_KEY'),
            'daily_token_limit' => 300000,
            'priority' => 2,
        ],
    ],
];

The priority field determines routing order. When openai_prod exhausts its daily 500k token limit, the gateway automatically fails over to anthropic_backup. The monthly_budget_usd cap provides hard spend protection—once you hit $150 in a calendar month, that channel gets disabled until the next billing cycle.

Operational Trade-offs: What You Give Up

Running your own gateway introduces three engineering costs:

1. Single Point of Failure

If your gpt-load instance dies, all AI requests fail. In production, you need:

  • Health check endpoint monitoring
  • Stateless deployment (config in environment variables, logs in external store)
  • Docker/K8s readiness probes 
# Kubernetes liveness probe
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 30

2. Token Counting Accuracy

The gateway parses usage.total_tokens from provider responses and increments local counters. This is eventually consistent—if the gateway crashes mid-request, you might lose 1-2 request logs. For hard budget enforcement, add a daily reconciliation job that hits provider billing APIs and compares actual spend.

3. Provider API Drift

When OpenAI ships a new parameter (response_format: {type: "json_schema"}), you need to verify gpt-load passes it through correctly. The gateway proxies unknown fields by default, but complex nested schemas sometimes require explicit handling.

Real-World Failure Case: Why We Added This Layer

Before implementing gpt-load, our CI system had a code review bot that called GPT-4 on every pull request. A junior engineer accidentally committed a 15,000-line generated SQL migration file. The review bot tried to analyze it, hit the 128k context window limit, retried with exponential backoff, and burned through $340 in 90 minutes.

With gpt-load's per-channel daily limits, that same scenario now fails gracefully after hitting the $50 daily cap on the CI channel. The bot returns a friendly "Budget exhausted, using cached review" message instead of retrying indefinitely.

Benchmarking Multi-Provider Failover Latency

When testing automatic credential rotation under load, we measured:

  • Primary channel healthy: 120ms avg latency (baseline OpenAI direct)
  • Primary exhausted, failover to Anthropic: 340ms avg latency (includes 80ms circuit breaker detection + credential swap)
  • All channels exhausted: 10ms rejection (fast fail, no provider calls)

For latency-sensitive applications, you can configure simultaneous dual-provider requests with first-response-wins behavior. When benchmarking this pattern through a relay gateway like B-Lost (base_url="https://b-lost.com/v1"), we observed TTFT (time-to-first-token) improved by 35ms due to optimized routing, though this increases cost since you pay for both provider calls.

When Not to Use a Self-Hosted Gateway

If your team fits any of these:

  • Single API key, low volume: Just use provider SDKs directly. The operational overhead isn't worth it.
  • Serverless-first architecture: Cold start latency of a PHP gateway adds 200-400ms on AWS Lambda. Use provider-native rate limiting instead.
  • Need sub-100ms P99 latency: The proxy hop adds 15-40ms. For real-time applications, bypass the gateway for critical paths.

Open Engineering Question

The hardest unsolved problem in multi-provider gateways: semantic equivalence across model APIs. When you fail over from GPT-4 to Claude 3.5 Sonnet, do you re-send the identical prompt, or transform it (e.g., rewriting OpenAI's function calling format to Anthropic's tool use schema)? Naive pass-through works 80% of the time, but breaks subtly on complex structured outputs.

How do you handle provider API mismatches in production failover scenarios without maintaining parallel prompt templates?

title: CRM'de activity modelini kurmak: Tek aktivite tablosu, durum geçişleri, kaynak tekilleştirme ve son temas
description:
Bir CRM'in en çok okunan ekranı genelde lead kartının altındaki zaman çizelgesidir: kim aradı, hangi mesaj gitti, toplantı ne zaman yapıldı, sıradaki adım ne. Satış müdürü bir fırsatı incelerken ilk oraya bakar, danışman bir müşteriyi devraldığında ilk oraya bakar. Buna rağmen birçok CRM'de bu ekranın arkasındaki veri modeli aceleyle kurulur: her kanal için ayrı bir tablo, birbirini tutmayan tarih alanları, elle girilmiş ve sonradan düzeltilmiş kayıtlar. Sonuç, "bu lead'i en son kim aradı?" gibi basit bir sorunun bile güvenilir cevabının olmamasıdır.

Ben Koray Yalçın; uzun süredir lead yönetimi, CRM kurulumu ve gayrimenkul satış operasyonları üzerine çalışıyorum. Bu yazıda CRM'deki activity kavramını, yani temsilcilerin ve sistemlerin bir kayıt üzerinde yaptığı arama, mesaj, toplantı, e-posta ve görev gibi aksiyonların bütününü, bir geliştiricinin gözünden ele alıyorum: tek bir aktivite tablosu nasıl tasarlanır, telefon santrali ve WhatsApp gibi dış kaynaklardan gelen kayıtlar nasıl tekilleştirilir, planlanmış ve gerçekleşmiş aktivite nasıl ayrılır, "son temas" ve "sıradaki adım" gibi türetilmiş alanlar nasıl tutarlı tutulur ve tüm bunlar nasıl raporlanır.

Aktivite neden ayrı bir kavram olarak modellenmeli?

Aktiviteyi hafife almanın tipik görüntüsü şudur: leads tablosunda last_call_at, last_whatsapp_at, notes gibi kolonlar vardır; arama kayıtları santral panelinde, mesajlar WhatsApp sağlayıcısında, toplantılar takvimde durur. Her yeni kanal, ana tabloya yeni bir kolon ve yeni bir entegrasyon kodu demektir.

Bu yaklaşımın üç somut sorunu var. Birincisi, geçmiş kaybolur: last_call_at sadece en son aramayı tutar, önceki beş aramanın sonucunu değil. İkincisi, kanallar arası sıralama yapılamaz: "önce mesaj mı gitti, arama mı yapıldı?" sorusu üç ayrı sisteme bakmadan cevaplanamaz. Üçüncüsü, ölçüm imkânsızlaşır: bir danışmanın günlük iş yükünü veya bir lead'e ilk dokunuşun ne kadar sürdüğünü hesaplamak için önce veriyi bir araya getirmeniz gerekir.

Çözüm, aktiviteyi kendi başına bir varlık olarak modellemek ve her kanalı bu ortak modele eşlemektir. Lead, kişi, fırsat (deal) ve şirket kayıtları aktivitelerin "üzerinde gerçekleştiği" şeylerdir; aktivitenin kendisi ise ayrı bir olay kaydıdır.

Tek tablo, ortak çekirdek, türe özel ek alanlar

Benim tercih ettiğim yapı, tüm aktivite türleri için ortak bir çekirdek tablo ve türe özel ayrıntılar için yapılandırılmış bir ek alandır.

CREATE TABLE activity (
  id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  type            TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (type IN ('call','message','email','meeting','task','note','site_visit')),
  direction       TEXT CHECK (direction IN ('inbound','outbound','internal')),
  status          TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('planned','done','cancelled','missed')),
  owner_id        INTEGER REFERENCES app_user(id),
  occurred_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,          -- gerçekleştiği an (done/missed için)
  due_at          TIMESTAMPTZ,          -- planlandığı an (planned için)
  duration_sec    INTEGER,
  outcome         TEXT,                 -- 'reached','no_answer','busy','interested','not_interested'...
  source          TEXT NOT NULL,        -- 'manual','pbx','whatsapp','calendar','email_sync','automation'
  source_ref      TEXT,                 -- dış sistemdeki kimlik
  details         JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (source, source_ref)
);

CREATE TABLE activity_link (
  activity_id  BIGINT REFERENCES activity(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  entity       TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (entity IN ('lead','contact','deal','company','unit')),
  entity_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
  is_primary   BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  PRIMARY KEY (activity_id, entity, entity_id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON activity_link (entity, entity_id);

Bu şemada üç karar bilinçli.

İlki, occurred_at ile created_at ayrımı. Bir danışman akşam saatinde, öğleden sonra yaptığı üç görüşmeyi CRM'e girebilir. Zaman çizelgesi ve raporlar occurred_at'e göre, denetim ise created_at'e göre çalışmalıdır. İkisini tek alanda birleştirirseniz ya sıralama bozulur ya da "kayıt ne zaman girildi?" bilgisi kaybolur.

İkincisi, ilişkinin ayrı bir activity_link tablosunda tutulması. Gayrimenkulde bir site ziyareti aynı anda bir kişiye, o kişinin fırsatına ve gezilen daireye (unit) bağlıdır. Tek bir lead_id kolonu bu gerçeği taşıyamaz. Çoklu bağlantı sayesinde aynı aktivite hem kişinin hem fırsatın zaman çizelgesinde görünür; is_primary ise raporlamada aktivitenin hangi kayda "sayılacağını" belirler.

Üçüncüsü, details alanının JSONB olması ama serbest bırakılmaması. Arama için kayıt dosyası kimliği ve santral dahilisi, mesaj için şablon adı ve teslim durumu, toplantı için katılımcılar gibi alanlar türe göre değişir. Bunları ana tabloya kolon olarak eklemek tabloyu şişirir; tamamen serbest bırakmak ise her geliştiricinin farklı anahtar kullanmasına yol açar. Uygulama katmanında tür başına bir şema (JSON Schema veya Pydantic modeli) tanımlayıp yazmadan önce doğrulamak, iki dünyanın iyi tarafını birleştirir.

Planlanmış ve gerçekleşmiş aktivite: aynı kayıt, iki hal

Satış ekiplerinin en sık karıştırdığı şey, görevle yapılan işin farkıdır. "Yarın 14:00'te ara" bir plandır; ertesi gün yapılan arama ise bir olaydır. Bunları iki ayrı tabloda tutmak cazip görünür ama planın gerçekleşmeye dönüştüğü anı izlemeyi zorlaştırır.

Ben aynı kaydın durum değiştirmesini tercih ediyorum: planned olarak oluşturulan aktivite, yapıldığında done, ulaşılamadığında missed, vazgeçildiğinde cancelled olur. Geçişleri uygulama katmanında açıkça tanımlamak gerekir:

ALLOWED = {
    "planned":   {"done", "missed", "cancelled"},
    "missed":    {"done"},          # geç de olsa ulaşıldıysa
    "done":      set(),             # gerçekleşmiş olay değiştirilmez
    "cancelled": set(),
}

def transition(activity, new_status, occurred_at=None, outcome=None):
    if new_status not in ALLOWED[activity.status]:
        raise InvalidTransition(activity.status, new_status)
    if new_status in ("done", "missed") and occurred_at is None:
        raise ValueError("gerçekleşen aktivite için occurred_at zorunlu")
    activity.status = new_status
    activity.occurred_at = occurred_at
    activity.outcome = outcome
    record_audit(activity, new_status)

done durumundaki bir kaydın değiştirilememesi önemli bir kural. Gerçekleşmiş bir aramanın sonucu yanlış girildiyse, kaydı sessizce düzeltmek yerine bir düzeltme notu veya denetim satırı eklenmelidir. Aksi halde "bu fırsat neden kaybedildi?" sorusunu sorduğunuzda geçmiş, olduğu gibi değil, sonradan düzenlendiği haliyle karşınıza çıkar.

Gecikmiş görevler de bu modelde doğal olarak hesaplanır: status = 'planned' AND due_at < now() olan her kayıt gecikmiştir. Ayrı bir "overdue" bayrağı tutmaya gerek yoktur; tutarsanız mutlaka bir gün gerçeklikten kopar.

Dış kaynaklardan gelen aktiviteler: tekilleştirme ve eşleme

Aktivitelerin çoğu artık elle girilmez. Bulut santral her aramayı webhook ile bildirir, WhatsApp Cloud API mesaj durumlarını gönderir, takvim entegrasyonu toplantıları senkronlar. Bu kaynakların ortak özelliği, aynı olayı birden fazla kez gönderebilmeleridir: yeniden deneme, durum güncellemesi veya sıra dışı teslim.

Şemadaki UNIQUE (source, source_ref) kısıtı bu yüzden var. Her kaynak kendi olay kimliğini taşır ve kayıt "ekle ya da güncelle" mantığıyla yazılır:

INSERT INTO activity (type, direction, status, occurred_at, duration_sec, outcome, source, source_ref, details)
VALUES ('call', 'outbound', 'done', $1, $2, $3, 'pbx', $4, $5)
ON CONFLICT (source, source_ref) DO UPDATE
SET duration_sec = EXCLUDED.duration_sec,
    outcome      = COALESCE(EXCLUDED.outcome, activity.outcome),
    details      = activity.details || EXCLUDED.details
WHERE activity.status <> 'cancelled';

Asıl zor kısım tekilleştirme değil, eşlemedir: santralden gelen bir arama hangi lead'e aittir? Elinizde genelde yalnızca bir telefon numarası vardır. Burada daha önce lead deduplication için kullandığımız normalizasyonun aynısını kullanmak şart. Santral numarayı 05xx... biçiminde, form +90 5xx... biçiminde, WhatsApp ise 905xx... biçiminde gönderebilir. Hepsini E.164 biçimine çevirip normalize edilmiş numara üzerinden arama yapmazsanız, aynı müşterinin aramaları üç farklı "bilinmeyen numara" kaydına dağılır.

Eşleme belirsiz olduğunda (aynı numara iki farklı kişide kayıtlıysa veya hiç eşleşme yoksa) aktiviteyi atmamak, activity_link olmadan bir "eşleşmemiş aktiviteler" kuyruğunda tutmak gerekir. Bu kuyruk hem veri kalitesi sorunlarını görünür kılar hem de yeni bir lead'in ilk temasının kaybolmasını önler.

Türetilmiş alanlar: son temas, sıradaki adım, ilk dokunuş

Zaman çizelgesi her açıldığında tüm aktiviteleri taramak küçük veriyle sorun değildir, ama liste ekranlarında yüzlerce lead için "son temas" ve "sıradaki adım" göstermek gerekir. Bu yüzden türetilmiş alanları bir özet tablosunda tutmak mantıklıdır:

CREATE TABLE entity_activity_summary (
  entity             TEXT NOT NULL,
  entity_id          BIGINT NOT NULL,
  first_touch_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
  last_touch_at      TIMESTAMPTZ,
  last_touch_type    TEXT,
  next_due_at        TIMESTAMPTZ,
  next_activity_id   BIGINT,
  done_count         INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (entity, entity_id)
);

Kritik nokta, "temas"ın tanımını tek bir yerde yazmaktır. Bir not eklemek temas mıdır? Teslim edilmemiş bir WhatsApp mesajı temas mıdır? Cevapsız bir arama? Benim kullandığım tanım şu: müşteriye yönelik, gerçekleşmiş (done) ve direction değeri inbound ya da outbound olan aktiviteler temastır; iç notlar ve iptal edilmiş görevler değildir. Cevapsız arama "deneme" olarak ayrıca sayılır ama son temas tarihini güncellemez. Bu tanımı bir SQL görünümü veya tek bir fonksiyon olarak yazar, özet tablosunu yalnızca oradan güncellersiniz.

Özet tablosunu tetikleyiciyle (trigger) güncellemek mümkün ama dış kaynaklardan yoğun olay geldiğinde kilitlenme yaratabilir. Ben genelde aktivite yazıldığında etkilenen kayıtları bir kuyruğa atıp kısa aralıklarla yeniden hesaplayan bir iş kullanıyorum. Yeniden hesaplama her zaman ham aktivite tablosundan yapıldığı için özet tablo bozulsa bile silip baştan üretilebilir. Bu, özet tablonun bir "gerçek kaynağı" değil, bir önbellek olduğunu hatırlatan iyi bir disiplin.

Otomasyonların ürettiği aktiviteler

Otomatik karşılama mesajı, hatırlatma e-postası veya randevu teyidi gibi sistem tarafından yapılan işler de aktivitedir ve zaman çizelgesinde görünmelidir. Aksi halde danışman, müşterinin zaten üç mesaj aldığını bilmeden dördüncüyü gönderir.

Ancak otomasyon aktivitelerini insan aktiviteleriyle aynı şekilde saymak raporları yanıltır. "Danışman başına günlük temas" metriğine otomatik mesajlar girerse, en çok otomasyonu tetikleyen danışman en çalışkan görünür. Bu yüzden source = 'automation' olan kayıtları ve owner_id değeri boş olan kayıtları performans raporlarından ayırmak, ama müşteri zaman çizelgesinde göstermek gerekir. İlk dokunuş süresi gibi ölçümlerde de hangi tanımı kullandığınızı açıkça belirtin: otomatik karşılama mesajı ilk dokunuş sayılıyorsa bu süre her zaman çok kısa çıkar ve gerçek insan yanıt süresini gizler.

Raporlama: aktivite verisinden anlamlı soru üretmek

İyi modellenmiş aktivite verisi, satış yönetiminin sorduğu birçok soruya doğrudan cevap verir. Örneğin her lead için ilk insan temasına kadar geçen süreyi şöyle hesaplayabilirsiniz:

SELECT l.id,
       l.created_at,
       MIN(a.occurred_at) AS first_human_touch,
       MIN(a.occurred_at) - l.created_at AS time_to_first_touch
FROM lead l
JOIN activity_link al ON al.entity = 'lead' AND al.entity_id = l.id
JOIN activity a ON a.id = al.activity_id
WHERE a.status = 'done'
  AND a.direction = 'outbound'
  AND a.source <> 'automation'
GROUP BY l.id, l.created_at;

Aynı yapı üzerinden aşamalar arası aktivite yoğunluğu (bir fırsat kapanana kadar kaç temas gerekti), danışman başına gecikmiş görev sayısı veya kanal bazında ulaşılabilirlik oranı da hesaplanabilir. Burada rakamın kendisinden önce tanımın tutarlılığı önemlidir. Aynı metriği iki farklı ekranda iki farklı sorguyla hesaplarsanız, toplantıda rakamları değil sorguları tartışırsınız. Metrik tanımlarını görünüm olarak veritabanında tutmak bu tartışmayı baştan bitirir.

Kişisel veri ve saklama

Aktivite tablosu bir CRM'deki en yoğun kişisel veri kaynaklarından biridir: arama kayıtları, mesaj içerikleri, serbest metin notlar. Bu yüzden saklama ve maskeleme kurallarının aktivite tablosunu da kapsaması gerekir. details alanındaki mesaj gövdesi veya kayıt dosyası bağlantısı, lead anonimleştirildiğinde ayrıca temizlenmelidir; aktivitenin türü, tarihi, süresi ve sonucu ise istatistik için kalabilir. Hangi alanın ne kadar tutulacağı hukuk ekibinizin kararıdır, bu yazı hukuki görüş değildir; ama şemayı baştan bu ayrıma uygun kurmak, o karar geldiğinde uygulamayı kolaylaştırır.

Sık yapılan hatalar

Sahada en sık gördüğüm hataları kısaca toplarsam:

  • Her kanal için ayrı tablo açmak ve zaman çizelgesini uygulama katmanında birleştirmeye çalışmak.
  • occurred_at yerine created_at ile sıralamak; sonradan girilen kayıtların çizelgeyi karıştırması.
  • Gerçekleşmiş aktiviteleri sessizce düzenlemeye izin vermek.
  • Telefon numarasını normalize etmeden eşleme yapmak.
  • Otomasyon aktivitelerini insan performansına saymak.
  • "Son temas" tanımını her raporda farklı yazmak.

SSS

CRM'de activity ile task arasındaki fark nedir?
Task, planlanmış bir aktivitedir. Aynı kayıt planned olarak oluşturulur ve yapıldığında done, ulaşılamadığında missed olur. İkisini aynı tabloda tutmak planla gerçekleşme arasındaki geçişi izlemeyi kolaylaştırır.

Her kanal için ayrı tablo tutmak hiç mantıklı değil mi?
Kanala özel büyük veriler (örneğin mesaj gövdeleri veya kayıt dosyası meta verisi) ayrı tablolarda durabilir. Ama zaman çizelgesi, sıralama ve raporlama için ortak bir çekirdek aktivite kaydı olmalı; kanal tabloları bu kayda bağlanmalı.

Aynı arama santralden iki kez gelirse ne olur?
source ve source_ref üzerindeki tekil kısıt sayesinde ikinci olay yeni kayıt açmaz, mevcut kaydı günceller. Güncellemenin hangi alanlara izin verdiğini açıkça yazmak gerekir.

Eşleşmeyen aktiviteler ne yapılmalı?
Atılmamalı. Bağlantısız olarak saklanıp bir kuyrukta gösterilmeli; yeni bir müşterinin ilk teması çoğu zaman tam da böyle bir kayıttır.

Son temas tarihini tetikleyiciyle mi güncellemeliyim?
Düşük hacimde tetikleyici yeterlidir. Dış kaynaklardan yoğun olay geliyorsa, etkilenen kayıtları kuyruğa atıp ham tablodan yeniden hesaplayan bir iş daha güvenlidir ve özet tablo bozulduğunda baştan üretilebilir.

Otomatik mesajlar zaman çizelgesinde görünmeli mi?
Evet, müşterinin ne aldığını danışmanın görmesi gerekir. Ancak performans ve ilk yanıt süresi gibi metriklerde insan aktivitelerinden ayrı tutulmalıdır.

Son söz

Aktivite modeli, bir CRM'in "ne oldu?" sorusuna verdiği cevaptır. Lead, fırsat ve aşama tabloları bir kaydın şu anki halini anlatır; aktivite tablosu ise oraya nasıl gelindiğini. Bu tabloyu ortak bir çekirdekle, açık durum geçişleriyle, kaynak bazında tekilleştirmeyle ve tek yerde tanımlanmış türetilmiş alanlarla kurduğunuzda, satış ekibinin güvendiği bir zaman çizelgesi ve yönetimin tartışmadan kullanabildiği raporlar elde edersiniz. Benim lead yönetimi ve CRM projelerinde gördüğüm, sorunların büyük kısmının bu tabloyu baştan doğru kurmamaktan kaynaklandığı.

title: When Payroll Fails, Who Remembers What Happened?
description:
What building a small payroll experiment taught us about PostgreSQL, durable execution, and cryptographic evidence

Check out the repo at github.com/PithomLabs/a2

A payroll system has a peculiar responsibility: it must remember not only what it calculated, but why it calculated it, which rules it applied, who authorized the result, and whether that result can still be trusted after something goes wrong.

That sounds like a database problem. It isn't entirely.

Consider a seemingly ordinary monthly payroll run. An employee changes compensation halfway through the month. A timesheet arrives late. A manager approves an adjustment after the payroll process has already started. Two operators accidentally initiate the same run. Somewhere in the middle, a worker crashes. The application restarts, and someone asks whether it can resume without duplicating payments or silently changing the result.

Months later, an auditor questions a finalized payslip. The company must reconstruct the original calculation, identify the rules that applied at the time, and establish whether the historical record has been altered.

Each problem belongs to a different architectural concern. Some involve the integrity of business data. Others concern the execution of long-running processes. Still others concern the trustworthiness of historical evidence.

The mistake is to assume that one database, however sophisticated, automatically solves all three.

We set out to explore that distinction through a deliberately limited experiment: one synthetic monthly payroll, built in Go, backed by PostgreSQL, orchestrated with DBOS, and anchored to immudb.

We were not trying to build another payroll product. We wanted to understand what happens when a software team assigns different responsibilities to technologies designed to handle them, rather than implementing every mechanism itself.

The result was more revealing than we expected.

The experiment was deliberately small

The workload consisted of one legal employer, 25 synthetic employees, and a 31-day payroll period covering October 2026.

The data included employment terms, compensation, attendance, timesheets, leave, synthetic overtime, allowances, deductions, and two effective-dated rule packs.

One pack applied during the first half of the month; another applied during the second half. This gave us a way to exercise rule changes without building an entire statutory payroll engine.

Some cases were deliberately allowed to calculate. Others were deliberately blocked because their business semantics had not been established. In particular, we did not invent a proration rule for an unresolved intra-month compensation change.

That distinction matters. A system that silently calculates an ambiguous entitlement may look productive, but it is not trustworthy.

The final October demonstration produced 102 payroll lines, 24 payslips, 24 finalized employees, one blocked employee, and five exceptions. The net payroll was 8,521,857 cents.

The database-backed calculation and its canonical counterpart produced the same digest:

4beee632a05c09b9ec0be0dbedc1937d517461603d8660999d66f51d04b20377

More important than the numbers was the path taken to produce them.

The calculation came from captured database records. Results were persisted in PostgreSQL. The execution survived a forced process termination during approval. Finalized evidence was sent to immudb, and an independent auditor reconstructed and verified the resulting content.

Fourteen remediation acceptance conditions passed, and the final Go test suite exited successfully. These are POC results, not a certification of production payroll compliance. Singapore's statutory overtime package remained explicitly blocked.

The limited scope was intentional: enough complexity to expose architectural problems, but not so much functionality that the experiment became a product-development programme.

PostgreSQL taught us that storing data and governing data are different jobs

Most application developers initially think of PostgreSQL as the place where business data lives.

That description is incomplete.

In a serious enterprise application, PostgreSQL must also help determine which business states are permitted to exist.

Consider compensation records. An employee should not accidentally have two overlapping compensation arrangements governing the same effective period. There should not be an unexplained gap where the application cannot determine which compensation arrangement applies.

An application can check for these conditions before inserting records. But application-side checks are vulnerable to concurrency.

Two requests can arrive almost simultaneously. Each reads the database, sees no conflict, and concludes that its proposed change is valid. Both then attempt to write.

The problem is not that either request performed an incorrect calculation. The problem is that the business invariant was never protected at the authoritative data boundary.

PostgreSQL provides mechanisms for expressing such invariants through constraints, transactions, range types, exclusion constraints, triggers, and privileges.

Our experiment demonstrated the value of WITHOUT OVERLAPS: a deliberately unconstrained table accepted two overlapping records, while the constrained version rejected the conflicting insertion.

But an interesting lesson emerged.

A constraint is not a complete business policy. Preventing overlap does not automatically guarantee complete temporal coverage. Preventing an invalid foreign key does not prove that a payroll snapshot contains every employee who should have been included.

The database must enforce the rules that actually define valid business state, not merely the easiest relationships to express in SQL.

The more important architectural change was moving authority away from unrestricted application writes.

The final POC uses narrowly scoped database functions for operations such as capturing, validating, approving, closing, and publishing payroll artifacts. The application runtime can read data and invoke authorized operations, but it cannot freely manufacture authoritative payroll records.

This is a meaningful change in how we think about database design.

Instead of asking, "Can the application write this record?" we begin asking, "Under what conditions is the system authorized to recognize this record as a business fact?"

For business owners, the distinction is consequential. A database that merely stores payroll results is an archive. A database that enforces the conditions under which payroll results become authoritative is part of the organization's control system.

DBOS revealed that business processes have a memory problem

The next discovery concerned something less visible: the lifetime of business processes.

A typical Go application can execute a payroll job using a background worker. The worker reads data, performs calculations, writes results, and reports completion.

That approach works until the process is interrupted.

Suppose payroll has completed its calculations but is waiting for managerial approval. The application crashes. When it restarts, what does it know?

It must determine which operations completed, which are still pending, whether the approval was received, whether a previous attempt partially wrote data, and whether restarting the process would duplicate an existing result.

One approach is to build all of this ourselves.

We could create workflow-state tables, checkpoint records, worker ownership leases, retry policies, fencing mechanisms, deduplication tables, and recovery coordinators.

None of these mechanisms is particularly mysterious. The difficulty is making them work together under every failure sequence.

DBOS offers a different approach: represent long-running business processes as durable workflows whose execution history is persisted.

In our implementation, DBOS coordinates the payroll lifecycle through several stages, including readiness, capture, calculation, persistence, approval, validation, and evidence publication.

The critical detail is its transaction boundary.

DBOS can coordinate application database writes and its own durability record in an atomic PostgreSQL transaction when using the appropriate shared datasource and transactional execution mechanism.

That means the application does not have to guess whether a business operation committed while its corresponding workflow checkpoint did not.

We tested this by forcibly terminating execution before the capture transaction committed. The transaction rolled back without leaving a successful capture checkpoint. After restart, the workflow converged on one authoritative result.

We also tested an interruption during approval. The workflow recovered, completed approval and validation, and produced the expected result without duplicating the payroll artifacts.

This changed our understanding of DBOS.

It is not simply a job queue or a convenient way to execute background functions. Its more important role is to provide durable memory for business processes.

For an application involving employee onboarding, leave approvals, shift changes, timesheet disputes, payroll, and corrections, this capability can be reused across many business workflows.

It allows engineers to concentrate more on the actual business process and less on reinventing the machinery required to keep that process alive.

But durability is not the same as correctness.

DBOS cannot decide whether an overtime rule is valid, whether a salary adjustment is authorized, or whether an employee belongs in a particular payroll period. Those remain responsibilities of the domain model and PostgreSQL.

Nor does a durable workflow automatically guarantee exactly-once execution of an external service.

A transaction can atomically commit database changes and a checkpoint. An external network operation still needs its own idempotency and recovery strategy.

That distinction became central to our implementation.

immudb introduced a different question: can we trust the history?

Even a carefully designed PostgreSQL database has a trust boundary.

A runtime application role may have restricted permissions. Triggers may prevent unauthorized changes. Audit tables may record important events.

But what happens when someone has administrative control over the database itself?

Ordinary audit records are stored in the same system whose history they are supposed to describe.

An administrator with sufficient privileges may be able to change both a business record and its corresponding audit history.

This is not an argument that PostgreSQL is insecure. It is a recognition that operational data and independently verifiable evidence serve different purposes.

We introduced immudb to explore that distinction.

immudb maintains an append-oriented transaction history with cryptographic verification mechanisms. Rather than use it as a second operational database, we treated it as an evidence layer.

When a payroll result is finalized, PostgreSQL creates an evidence event containing references and cryptographic digests associated with the actual business artifact.

A transactional outbox bridges the two systems.

The PostgreSQL transaction records the business operation and its evidence event together. A durable worker subsequently publishes that event to immudb. Once the ledger append is verified, PostgreSQL records the corresponding transaction reference.

There is no magical distributed transaction covering both databases. The application must handle the possibility that the ledger append succeeds while the PostgreSQL back-link fails, or that a network response is lost even though the append committed.

Deterministic event identities, idempotency markers, verified reads, and reconciliation are therefore essential.

The other important component is the auditor.

We deliberately separated the auditor from the writing application. It uses a read-only PostgreSQL identity, a read-only immudb identity, and a pinned genesis checkpoint.

It reconstructs the expected evidence from the database, re-executes the relevant payroll calculation, and compares the resulting content against cryptographically verified ledger records.

This is the distinction between verifying that a transaction exists and verifying that the transaction actually represents the payroll result being audited.

A cryptographic ledger does not prove that the calculation was correct. It helps establish that the evidence being examined matches what was previously anchored.

That is a narrower claim, but a much more useful one.

For businesses, the potential value lies in historical accountability: being able to establish what was finalized, which rules were associated with the result, and whether the evidence has changed.

The most important insight was not technological. It was architectural.

At the beginning, it was tempting to think of the project as a combination of three technologies.

We eventually found a more useful way to describe it: three different responsibilities that happen to require different technical mechanisms.

PostgreSQL answers:

What is the authoritative business state?

DBOS answers:

How does a business process continue correctly when execution is interrupted?

immudb answers:

Can we independently verify the historical evidence associated with that business state?

Go remains responsible for the domain logic and calculations.

These responsibilities must cooperate, but they should not be confused.

A workflow should not become the authority for a payroll record simply because DBOS says it completed. A ledger should not become the authority for whether a salary calculation is correct simply because the transaction is immutable. A database constraint should not be mistaken for a complete interpretation of employment legislation.

This separation gives us an architecture in which every component has a clear job and an explicit boundary.

It also reveals an important business consideration: adding technologies does not automatically reduce complexity.

DBOS introduces workflow lifecycle and resource-management considerations. immudb introduces another persistence system, trust management, licensing considerations, and cross-system recovery. PostgreSQL still requires deliberate schema design, privilege management, and transaction discipline.

The value comes from eliminating responsibilities that would otherwise need to be built and maintained in the wrong layer.

The objective is not to minimize the number of technologies. It is to minimize the amount of custom machinery required to achieve the guarantees the business actually needs.

The failures were more educational than the successful demonstrations

One of the most valuable aspects of this journey was the repeated adversarial examination of the implementation.

A feature could compile. A test could pass. A workflow could return success. Yet the actual business operation might not have been connected to the mechanism that supposedly protected it.

That distinction forced us to become more precise about what constituted evidence.

We learned to separate several states that developers frequently collapse into one:

  • Implemented does not mean built.
  • Built does not mean executed.
  • Executed does not mean passed.
  • A passed infrastructure test does not necessarily prove a business guarantee.
  • A verified transaction does not necessarily prove the correctness of its contents.

The early implementation demonstrated several isolated mechanisms. Subsequent independent review showed that the real payroll computation, workflow execution and ledger publication were not yet connected.

We had to return to the underlying authority and transaction boundaries, not merely add more tests around the existing interfaces.

The final remediation connected the actual business path and repeated the critical tests.

This is an important lesson for engineering teams: the greatest risk in a complex system is sometimes not an obvious failure, but a successful operation that never performed the work everyone assumed it had performed.

Adversarial review is especially valuable because it challenges the relationship between what a system claims to guarantee and what its code actually enforces.

The repository preserves that journey. Readers can examine the earlier findings and decide for themselves whether the corrections fully resolve the issues.

Reproducibility changes how we think about business history

Another insight emerged from the payroll calculation itself.

A historical financial result is not reproducible merely because we saved the final amount.

To explain an old payroll calculation, we need enough information to reconstruct the inputs and the interpretation applied to them.

That includes:

  • The relevant employment and compensation records.
  • The attendance and approved timesheets.
  • The effective-dated rule versions.
  • The calculator version.
  • The original calculation output.
  • The approval and finalization evidence.

This becomes especially important when business rules change.

A company might revise its overtime policy, introduce a new allowance, or change the way a particular employee category is treated.

The new rule must apply according to its effective dates. It must not silently rewrite historical payroll.

Our synthetic demonstration used two rule packs during the same month. This gave us a concrete way to show that rule changes can influence calculations without making every historical record mutable.

It also exposed a limitation worth acknowledging: a calculator version label is not the same as a cryptographic digest of the actual implementation binary. Likewise, our multi-pack digesting and cross-version canonical serialization remain narrower than a fully mature historical-reproduction system would require.

The point is not that every historical question has been solved.

It is that reproducibility must be an architectural property considered when data is first captured, not a reporting feature added after a dispute occurs.

Why we deliberately stopped short of building a complete payroll system

There is a temptation, once an interesting technical foundation exists, to keep adding functionality.

More employee classifications. More statutory packages. More approval types. More integrations. Perhaps even payment execution and regulatory filing.

That would have defeated the purpose of this exercise.

We wanted to demonstrate architectural responsibilities, not compete with established payroll vendors.

The synthetic workload was sufficient to expose temporal changes, calculation boundaries, missing evidence, approvals, interrupted execution, finalization, and historical corrections.

It also allowed us to keep statutory interpretation separate from the infrastructure experiment. The Singapore overtime package remained blocked because the underlying legislative evidence was incomplete. We did not replace missing legal evidence with assumptions merely to make the demonstration more impressive.

This restraint is important.

An incomplete but honestly bounded engineering specimen is more useful to a reader than a purportedly complete system whose assumptions are hidden.

The repository therefore should not be read as a turnkey payroll platform or a universal blueprint for every business.

It is a working exploration of a particular architectural idea. It contains executable paths, supporting schemas, tests, runbooks, and recorded results. It also retains unresolved limitations and intentionally leaves room for readers to inspect, question, and extend the implementation themselves.

What this means for engineers and business owners

For software engineers, the central lesson is to treat data integrity, durable execution and historical evidence as different engineering problems.

Do not expect application validation to replace database authority. Do not assume a background worker can reliably recover from every interruption. Do not confuse ordinary audit history with independent cryptographic verification.

For business owners, the lesson is equally practical.

The cost of a business application is not simply the cost of building its visible features. It includes the cost of ensuring those features behave correctly when people, data, rules and processes change.

Payroll is a useful example because the consequences of incorrect results are immediate and tangible. But the same concerns appear in insurance claims, financial operations, healthcare administration, supply chains, compliance workflows and enterprise resource planning.

A system that can explain what it did, recover when interrupted, and establish the integrity of its historical evidence has a different quality from one that merely produces a successful response.

That quality is difficult to capture in a feature checklist. It becomes visible under failure.

The experiment is finished. The questions are not.

We began with a relatively simple proposition: PostgreSQL, DBOS and immudb might provide more value together than a conventional application that places every responsibility in its own Go code and database tables.

The completed experiment gives us a working demonstration of that proposition.

PostgreSQL governs business authority. DBOS preserves the continuity of execution. Go performs the domain calculations. immudb anchors evidence that can be independently examined.

The technologies do not eliminate the need for careful engineering. They make it possible to assign difficult responsibilities to components built to handle them, while leaving the application responsible for the business meaning.

There are still questions worth exploring.

How should calculator implementation provenance be secured across years of software changes? How should an organization retain independent trust anchors over long periods? What is the right balance between database-enforced invariants and domain-level validation? When does an external evidence ledger justify its operational and licensing costs? Could a carefully engineered PostgreSQL-only design provide sufficient assurance for a particular business?

Those questions are deliberately not answered here.

The code, experiments and recorded limitations provide a place to start.

The more useful outcome of this exercise is not a declaration that three technologies are always better than one.

It is a better way to ask an architectural question:

What must be true about our business data, what must remain true about our processes, and what evidence would convince someone else that both remained true?

That is a more demanding standard than simply making software work.

It is also a more valuable one.

title: A layout that works on every screen
description:
Your page looks right on your laptop and scrolls sideways on your phone: this guide finds what is too wide and fixes the usual causes one at a time.

The examples here are screenshots; they run live in the original article.

You will build a small travel page that breaks on a phone the way real pages do, look at it the way a phone does, find the parts that stick out, and fix each one. At the end the same page is one column on a phone and two columns on a laptop. You need a React app with Box Kite installed; if you do not have one yet, steps 1 and 2 of Your first web page with Box Kite take two minutes.

Step 1: build a page that breaks

Replace everything in src/App.tsx with this:

import Box from '@box-kite/react';
import Flex from '@box-kite/react/components/flex';
import { Aside, H1, Img, Li, Link, P, Ul } from '@box-kite/react/components/semantics';

const photo = 'https://www.box-kite.dev/img/blog/a-layout-that-works-on-every-screen/coast.jpg';
const sections = ['Itinerary', 'Packing list', 'Budget', 'Photos', 'Contacts'];
const days = ['Day 1 · Lisbon', 'Day 4 · Sintra', 'Day 7 · Lagos'];

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Box p={6}>
      <Flex gap={6} mb={6}>
        {sections.map((section) => (
          <Link key={section} props={{ href: '#' }} color="indigo-600" theme={{ dark: { color: 'indigo-300' } }}>
            {section}
          </Link>
        ))}
      </Flex>

      <Flex gap={8}>
        <Aside width={56} flexShrink={0}>
          <Ul>
            {days.map((day) => (
              <Li key={day}>{day}</Li>
            ))}
          </Ul>
        </Aside>

        <Box>
          <H1 fontSize={32} fontWeight={700} mb={4}>
            Ten days in Portugal
          </H1>
          <Img props={{ src: photo, alt: 'The coast near Lagos' }} mb={4} />
          <P>Tickets: https://www.example.com/bookings/PT2026LISBONSINTRALAGOSK7Q2M9X4R8T1W6Z3N5V8B2C4</P>
        </Box>
      </Flex>
    </Box>
  );
}

A row of links (indigo, and a lighter indigo in dark mode), a sidebar with a fixed width (width={56} is 224 pixels, because spacing is on a scale of four), and a story with a photo and a booking link. On a wide laptop screen most of it looks fine. Every part of it is a real cause of a page that scrolls sideways.

Step 2: look at it the way a phone does

You do not need a phone yet. Open your browser's developer tools (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac) and turn on the device toolbar: Ctrl+Shift+M, or Cmd+Shift+M on a Mac, in Chrome and Edge, and "Responsive Design Mode" in Firefox and Safari. Pick a phone such as the iPhone 12 Pro, which is 390 pixels wide.

The page now scrolls sideways: drag it left and the photo and the booking link keep going. That sideways scroll is the bug. A phone shows the page at its own width only because Vite's index.html already carries the <meta name="viewport"> line; keep it.

Step 3: find what is too wide

Open the Console tab of the developer tools, paste this and press Enter:

document.querySelectorAll('body *').forEach((el) => {
  if (el.getBoundingClientRect().right > innerWidth || el.scrollWidth > el.clientWidth) el.style.outline = '2px solid red';
});

Every element that runs past the right edge of the screen, or whose content runs past its own edge, gets a red outline. The outer boxes light up because something inside them is too wide; look for the innermost red box and you have found the culprit. On this page there are three: the row of links, the sidebar with its photo beside it, and the booking link. Reload the page to clear the outlines.

Step 4: let the row of links wrap

A row keeps everything on one line unless you tell it otherwise. Add flexWrap="wrap" to the first Flex, so the links that do not fit move to a second line:

import Box from '@box-kite/react';
import Flex from '@box-kite/react/components/flex';
import { Aside, H1, Img, Li, Link, P, Ul } from '@box-kite/react/components/semantics';

const photo = 'https://www.box-kite.dev/img/blog/a-layout-that-works-on-every-screen/coast.jpg';
const sections = ['Itinerary', 'Packing list', 'Budget', 'Photos', 'Contacts'];
const days = ['Day 1 · Lisbon', 'Day 4 · Sintra', 'Day 7 · Lagos'];

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Box p={6}>
      <Flex gap={6} mb={6} flexWrap="wrap">
        {sections.map((section) => (
          <Link key={section} props={{ href: '#' }} color="indigo-600" theme={{ dark: { color: 'indigo-300' } }}>
            {section}
          </Link>
        ))}
      </Flex>

      <Flex gap={8}>
        <Aside width={56} flexShrink={0}>
          <Ul>
            {days.map((day) => (
              <Li key={day}>{day}</Li>
            ))}
          </Ul>
        </Aside>

        <Box>
          <H1 fontSize={32} fontWeight={700} mb={4}>
            Ten days in Portugal
          </H1>
          <Img props={{ src: photo, alt: 'The coast near Lagos' }} mb={4} />
          <P>Tickets: https://www.example.com/bookings/PT2026LISBONSINTRALAGOSK7Q2M9X4R8T1W6Z3N5V8B2C4</P>
        </Box>
      </Flex>
    </Box>
  );
}

At phone width the last links now start a second line, and none of them is cut off at the edge. The page still scrolls, because of the other two culprits.

Step 5: one column on a phone, two on a laptop

Two columns side by side do not fit in 390 pixels. Write the phone layout first and add the laptop layout on top of it: d="column" stacks the sidebar above the story, and md={{ d: 'row' }} puts them side by side from 768 pixels up. Every prop works this way: the plain prop is for every screen, and sm, md, lg, xl and xxl override it from 640, 768, 1024, 1280 and 1536 pixels.

The sidebar's fixed width goes the same way: no width on a phone, so it takes the whole column, and a quarter of the page from md up. '1/4' is a fraction of the parent's width, and flexShrink: 0 keeps the sidebar at that quarter instead of letting a wide photo squeeze it.

import Box from '@box-kite/react';
import Flex from '@box-kite/react/components/flex';
import { Aside, H1, Img, Li, Link, P, Ul } from '@box-kite/react/components/semantics';

const photo = 'https://www.box-kite.dev/img/blog/a-layout-that-works-on-every-screen/coast.jpg';
const sections = ['Itinerary', 'Packing list', 'Budget', 'Photos', 'Contacts'];
const days = ['Day 1 · Lisbon', 'Day 4 · Sintra', 'Day 7 · Lagos'];

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Box p={6}>
      <Flex gap={6} mb={6} flexWrap="wrap">
        {sections.map((section) => (
          <Link key={section} props={{ href: '#' }} color="indigo-600" theme={{ dark: { color: 'indigo-300' } }}>
            {section}
          </Link>
        ))}
      </Flex>

      <Flex d="column" gap={8} md={{ d: 'row' }}>
        <Aside md={{ width: '1/4', flexShrink: 0 }}>
          <Ul>
            {days.map((day) => (
              <Li key={day}>{day}</Li>
            ))}
          </Ul>
        </Aside>

        <Box>
          <H1 fontSize={32} fontWeight={700} mb={4}>
            Ten days in Portugal
          </H1>
          <Img props={{ src: photo, alt: 'The coast near Lagos' }} mb={4} />
          <P>Tickets: https://www.example.com/bookings/PT2026LISBONSINTRALAGOSK7Q2M9X4R8T1W6Z3N5V8B2C4</P>
        </Box>
      </Flex>
    </Box>
  );
}

At phone width the days now sit above the story. Switch the device toolbar to a laptop size and they move back beside it. Without flexShrink: 0 the sidebar came out at 103 pixels instead of 193 on an 820-pixel screen.

Step 6: let the photo shrink

A picture is as wide as its file unless you say otherwise, and this one is 1,200 pixels. maxWidth="fit" caps it at the width of its column (fit is 100%), and height="auto" keeps its proportions as it shrinks:

import Box from '@box-kite/react';
import Flex from '@box-kite/react/components/flex';
import { Aside, H1, Img, Li, Link, P, Ul } from '@box-kite/react/components/semantics';

const photo = 'https://www.box-kite.dev/img/blog/a-layout-that-works-on-every-screen/coast.jpg';
const sections = ['Itinerary', 'Packing list', 'Budget', 'Photos', 'Contacts'];
const days = ['Day 1 · Lisbon', 'Day 4 · Sintra', 'Day 7 · Lagos'];

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Box p={6}>
      <Flex gap={6} mb={6} flexWrap="wrap">
        {sections.map((section) => (
          <Link key={section} props={{ href: '#' }} color="indigo-600" theme={{ dark: { color: 'indigo-300' } }}>
            {section}
          </Link>
        ))}
      </Flex>

      <Flex d="column" gap={8} md={{ d: 'row' }}>
        <Aside md={{ width: '1/4', flexShrink: 0 }}>
          <Ul>
            {days.map((day) => (
              <Li key={day}>{day}</Li>
            ))}
          </Ul>
        </Aside>

        <Box>
          <H1 fontSize={32} fontWeight={700} mb={4}>
            Ten days in Portugal
          </H1>
          <Img props={{ src: photo, alt: 'The coast near Lagos' }} mb={4} maxWidth="fit" height="auto" />
          <P>Tickets: https://www.example.com/bookings/PT2026LISBONSINTRALAGOSK7Q2M9X4R8T1W6Z3N5V8B2C4</P>
        </Box>
      </Flex>
    </Box>
  );
}

The photo now fits the screen. Run the snippet from step 3 again: one red box is left, around the booking link.

Step 7: break the long link

A browser only breaks a line at a space or at certain punctuation, and the long code at the end of the booking link has neither. overflow-wrap: anywhere lets it break between any two letters when nothing else fits. Box Kite has no typed prop for it yet, so it goes in css, the escape hatch for a CSS property without a prop of its own. It still becomes a class, like every other prop:

import Box from '@box-kite/react';
import Flex from '@box-kite/react/components/flex';
import { Aside, H1, Img, Li, Link, P, Ul } from '@box-kite/react/components/semantics';

const photo = 'https://www.box-kite.dev/img/blog/a-layout-that-works-on-every-screen/coast.jpg';
const sections = ['Itinerary', 'Packing list', 'Budget', 'Photos', 'Contacts'];
const days = ['Day 1 · Lisbon', 'Day 4 · Sintra', 'Day 7 · Lagos'];

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Box p={6}>
      <Flex gap={6} mb={6} flexWrap="wrap">
        {sections.map((section) => (
          <Link key={section} props={{ href: '#' }} color="indigo-600" theme={{ dark: { color: 'indigo-300' } }}>
            {section}
          </Link>
        ))}
      </Flex>

      <Flex d="column" gap={8} md={{ d: 'row' }}>
        <Aside md={{ width: '1/4', flexShrink: 0 }}>
          <Ul>
            {days.map((day) => (
              <Li key={day}>{day}</Li>
            ))}
          </Ul>
        </Aside>

        <Box>
          <H1 fontSize={32} fontWeight={700} mb={4}>
            Ten days in Portugal
          </H1>
          <Img props={{ src: photo, alt: 'The coast near Lagos' }} mb={4} maxWidth="fit" height="auto" />
          <P css={{ overflowWrap: 'anywhere' }}>
            Tickets: https://www.example.com/bookings/PT2026LISBONSINTRALAGOSK7Q2M9X4R8T1W6Z3N5V8B2C4
          </P>
        </Box>
      </Flex>
    </Box>
  );
}

The page no longer scrolls sideways. Run the snippet once more and nothing turns red. We checked this page at 390, 820 and 1280 pixels in Chrome, Firefox and Safari's engine: it fits all three, and the sidebar is exactly a quarter of the page from 768 pixels up.

What you learned

What sticks out What fixes it
A row with too many things in it flexWrap="wrap"
Two columns side by side d="column" for the phone, md={{ d: 'row' }} for wider screens
A fixed width no width on the phone, a fraction from md up: md={{ width: '1/4', flexShrink: 0 }}
A picture maxWidth="fit" and height="auto"
A long word or link css={{ overflowWrap: 'anywhere' }}

Two habits matter more than any one prop. Write the phone layout first and add md for bigger screens, because the plain prop applies everywhere. And when a page scrolls sideways, find the culprit with the snippet before you change anything: hiding the overflow on the whole page makes the scrollbar go away and leaves the cut-off content where it was.

Check on a real phone before you ship. The device toolbar gets the width right, but not everything a phone does, like the on-screen keyboard.

Where to go next

  • Grid does columns that line up across rows: gridTemplateColumns={1} with md={{ gridTemplateColumns: 3 }} is the card row from the first guide.
  • Nesting shows every key a prop can sit under. A breakpoint, dark mode and hover combine, like md={{ hover: { color: 'indigo-700' } }}.
  • Container queries are for a card or a widget that should adapt to the space it is given rather than to the screen.
  • The escape hatch has more on css, for the next property without a prop of its own.

Originally published on box-kite.dev. Box Kite is open source under MIT — if it is useful to you, a star on GitHub helps other people find it. Install it with npm install @box-kite/react.

title: What I found when I pointed a CLI recorder at a second Rust rewrite
description:
I have been using behave to record how GNU coreutils 9.12 behaves, then replay the same cases against uutils, the Rust rewrite. That work has already led to a run of upstream bug reports and merged fix PRs. This week I pointed the same recorder at a second Rust rewrite: uutils findutils, starting with xargs, and compared it to GNU findutils 4.10.

The idea is the same. Record stdout, stderr, and the exit status from the reference tool, then replay the cases against the rewrite. A failure is a concrete difference, not a guess about what the tool "should" do.

The new suite lives at examples/xargs. It has 44 cases, recorded from GNU findutils 4.10.0, and they run in behave's CI. Three of those differences were real bugs. Each one is now an issue plus a fix PR with a test.

1. -I with the default command printed the input items

When -I, -i, or --replace is used without an explicit command, xargs should run echo once per input item. The default command has no initial arguments, so the replace string never appears, and each invocation should print a blank line (the same as echo with no arguments).

uutils printed the input items instead.

printf 'hello\nworld\n' | xargs -I R

GNU findutils 4.10.0 prints two blank lines. uutils findutils 0.11.0 (current main, when I recorded it) printed:

hello
world

The same happened with xargs -i and xargs --replace. Passing an explicit command was already fine on both sides:

printf 'hello\nworld\n' | xargs -I R echo
# two blank lines

printf 'hello\nworld\n' | xargs -I R echo R
# hello
# world

So the happy path looked correct, and the default-command case was the one that drifted. I filed uutils/findutils#984 and the fix in PR #986.

2. -a rejected a filename that starts with a dash

xargs -a FILE reads items from FILE instead of stdin. If that name starts with a dash, GNU still treats it as a filename. uutils treated it as an unknown option and refused to run.

The same gap showed up on the other options that take a value: -n, -s, -L, -d, and -P. A name or number that looks like a flag should still be accepted as the option's value.

# GNU findutils 4.10.0: reads items from the file named -foo
# uutils: rejected the filename
xargs -a -foo

I filed issue #985 and PR #987.

This is a small class of bugs I keep seeing when a rewrite parses flags with a stricter library default than the original tool. The reference tool often accepts a value that starts with a dash. A probe that only tries tidy names will never see it.

3. --eof swallowed the next option

--eof and -e set the logical end-of-file string. The argument is optional. When it is omitted, the next token should still be parsed as a normal option. uutils consumed that token as the EOF string, so a following flag disappeared.

The short form I used while recording was:

xargs --eof -l

GNU findutils still honours -l. uutils treated -l as the EOF string and ignored the line-limit flag. I filed issue #992 and PR #993.

Optional arguments are a reliable place to look. A recorder that walks flag pairs will put --eof next to -l without anyone writing that case by hand.

A lesson I had already paid for: pin the reference version

While this suite was going in, behave's CI was red on a pre-existing base32 case, and it never reached xargs. The runner ships GNU coreutils 9.4. I record from 9.12, because that is the release uutils aims at. The failing cases were about decoding unpadded input: GNU 9.5 and later decode it, 9.4 rejects it.

The fix was not to weaken the cases. I tagged those three specs gnu-9.5 (two in examples/base32, one in examples/base64) and skipped that tag in CI, so they still run against a current GNU locally. CI went green again, including the 44 xargs cases.

The same lesson showed up when I was testing coreutils, and it is worth repeating. If you claim compatibility with a specific reference release, record from that release. A case that is correct on 9.12 can fail on 9.4, and the noise looks like a product bug. Version-sensitive specs belong behind a tag, or they teach people to ignore failures.

A third rewrite: uutils sed

I also pointed behave at uutils sed, compared to GNU sed 4.9, using non-interactive cases. Two differences stood out, and both are now filed with a test and a fix.

The GNU v command is a version assertion. It does nothing at runtime if the running sed is new enough, and it is a common guard at the top of GNU sed scripts. uutils already compiled v and rejected versions newer than 4.9, but a successful check still panicked at runtime with invalid command code as soon as there was any input. Existing tests called sed v with no stdin, so they never reached the processor. Feeding a line was enough:

printf 'a\n' | sed 'v'
printf 'a\n' | sed 'v4.9'

GNU sed 4.9 prints a and exits 0. uutils aborted. The argument parser also read the rest of the line as the version, so v;s/a/A/ was rejected, and addresses like 1v were refused. I filed this as uutils/sed#669 and the fix in PR #671.

The second gap was comments. GNU sed treats # after a command, including after s/// flags, as the start of a comment. uutils treated # as an invalid substitute flag or as extra characters at the end of the command:

printf 'a\n' | sed 's/a/A/#comment'
# GNU: A
# uutils: invalid substitute flag: '#'

The same happened for p#comment, y/a/A/#c, and {p}#c. A related terminator was missing too: {s/a/A/} was rejected because flag parsing did not stop at }. I filed issue #670 and PR #672.

What I would take to the next rewrite

  1. Reuse the recorder. The xargs bugs were not exotic. Default command plus -I, a filename starting with a dash, and an optional argument followed by another flag are ordinary corners. A suite of 44 recorded cases was enough to surface all three.
  2. Pin the reference release, and tag the rest. The 9.4 versus 9.5 unpadded-decode mismatch would have buried the new xargs specs in a red CI job. Skipping a version tag is honest; deleting the cases is not.
  3. Feed the tool some input when you test a no-op. The v panic was hidden by tests that compiled the script and exited before a line arrived.
  4. File a fix with a test. Upstream reviewers can see the case fail without the patch and pass with it.

If you want to try the same specs:

brew install emirmrkaljevic/tap/behave
# or: go install github.com/emirmrkaljevic/behave/cmd/behave`latest

behave run examples/xargs
behave diff examples/xargs --impl /path/to/uutils/xargs

The recorder, the suites, and the upstream links are in the behave repository.

title: Understanding Pointers in Go: A Practical Guide
description:
A hands-on look at how pointers work in Go, when to use them, and how they behave with arrays.

Introduction

Pointers have a reputation for being tricky, mostly thanks to languages where they come with pointer arithmetic, manual memory management, and a long list of ways to crash your program. Go takes a much calmer approach. Pointers in Go are simple, safe, and explicit, and once you understand them you will write faster, more predictable code.

In this post we will cover:

  • What a pointer is and how to use & and *
  • Pass-by-value vs. pass-by-pointer
  • Pointers with structs
  • Pointers with arrays (with full examples)
  • Common pitfalls and when to use pointers

What Is a Pointer?

A variable stores a value. A pointer stores the memory address of a value.

Think of a house. The house itself is the value. The street address written on a piece of paper is the pointer. If you hand someone a photocopy of the house (a copy of the value), they can repaint their copy all day and your house stays the same. If you hand them the address (a pointer), they can walk over and repaint your actual house.

That single idea explains almost everything about pointers in Go.

The Two Operators: & and *

Go uses just two operators for pointers:

  • & gives you the address of a variable.
  • * dereferences a pointer, meaning it gives you the value stored at that address. In a type, *T means "pointer to T". 
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    age := 30

    var p *int = &age // p holds the address of age

    fmt.Println(age) // 30
    fmt.Println(p)   // 0xc000012345 (an address)
    fmt.Println(*p)  // 30 (the value at that address)

    *p = 31          // change the value through the pointer
    fmt.Println(age) // 31
}

We changed age without ever assigning to age directly. The pointer p reached through the address and modified the original.

Pass by Value vs. Pass by Pointer

Go is always pass-by-value. When you call a function, every argument is copied. For a pointer, the thing being copied is the address, so the function still reaches the original data.

func incrementValue(n int) {
    n++ // modifies the local copy only
}

func incrementPointer(n *int) {
    *n++ // modifies the original
}

func main() {
    x := 10

    incrementValue(x)
    fmt.Println(x) // 10, unchanged

    incrementPointer(&x)
    fmt.Println(x) // 11, changed
}

Pointers with Structs

Structs are where you will use pointers most often. Go gives you a convenient shortcut here: you can access fields through a pointer without writing (*p).Field. Go dereferences automatically.

type User struct {
    Name  string
    Email string
}

func updateEmail(u *User, email string) {
    u.Email = email // same as (*u).Email = email
}

func main() {
    user := User{Name: "Musa", Email: "old@example.com"}
    updateEmail(&user, "new@example.com")
    fmt.Println(user.Email) // new@example.com
}

This is also why methods with pointer receivers are so common. If a method needs to modify the struct, or the struct is large and copying it would be wasteful, use func (u *User) ....

Pointers and Arrays

This is the part that surprises many developers. In Go, an array is a value type. Its length is part of its type ([3]int and [4]int are different types), and assigning or passing an array copies every element.

Example 1: Passing an Array by Value 

func doubleByValue(arr [3]int) {
    for i := range arr {
        arr[i] *= 2
    }
    fmt.Println("inside function:", arr)
}

func main() {
    numbers := [3]int{1, 2, 3}

    doubleByValue(numbers)
    fmt.Println("after call:    ", numbers)
}

Output:

inside function: [2 4 6]
after call:     [1 2 3]

The function received a full copy of the array. It doubled its copy, and the original was never touched.

Example 2: Passing a Pointer to an Array 

func doubleByPointer(arr *[3]int) {
    for i := range arr {
        arr[i] *= 2 // Go auto-dereferences: same as (*arr)[i]
    }
    fmt.Println("inside function:", *arr)
}

func main() {
    numbers := [3]int{1, 2, 3}

    doubleByPointer(&numbers)
    fmt.Println("after call:    ", numbers)
}

Output:

inside function: [2 4 6]
after call:     [2 4 6]

Now the function works on the original array. Two benefits follow: the changes are visible to the caller, and no copy is made. For a [1000000]int array, that is the difference between copying about 8 MB on every call and copying a single 8-byte address.

Go lets you index (arr[i]), use len(arr), and range over a pointer to an array directly, so the syntax stays clean.

Example 3: A Pointer to a Single Array Element

You can take the address of any element:

numbers := [3]int{10, 20, 30}

p := &numbers[1] // pointer to the second element
*p = 99

fmt.Println(numbers) // [10 99 30]

Example 4: An Array of Pointers

This is a different thing from a pointer to an array. Here, each slot holds an address:

a, b, c := 1, 2, 3

ptrs := [3]*int{&a, &b, &c}

for _, p := range ptrs {
    *p *= 10
}

fmt.Println(a, b, c) // 10 20 30

The array was copied if you pass it around, but every copy still points to the same a, b, and c. Keep the distinction clear:

Type Meaning
*[3]int One pointer to a whole array of three ints
[3]*int An array holding three pointers to ints

What About Slices?

In day-to-day Go, you will use slices far more than arrays. A slice is a small struct (a pointer to an underlying array, a length, and a capacity). When you pass a slice to a function, that small header is copied, but it still points to the same underlying array, so changes to elements are visible to the caller:

func doubleSlice(s []int) {
    for i := range s {
        s[i] *= 2
    }
}

func main() {
    nums := []int{1, 2, 3}
    doubleSlice(nums)
    fmt.Println(nums) // [2 4 6]
}

One caveat: if the function calls append and the slice grows beyond its capacity, a new underlying array is allocated and the caller will not see the new length. Return the slice or pass *[]int in that case.

Nil Pointers and new

The zero value of a pointer is nil. Dereferencing a nil pointer causes a runtime panic, so check before you use one when it can legitimately be nil.

var p *int

if p != nil {
    fmt.Println(*p)
}

The built-in new(T) allocates a zero-valued T and returns a pointer to it:

p := new(int)
*p = 42
fmt.Println(*p) // 42

For structs, the more idiomatic form is &User{Name: "Musa"}.

You may wonder whether returning a pointer to a local variable is dangerous, as it would be in C. In Go it is perfectly safe. The compiler performs escape analysis and moves the variable to the heap if it outlives the function, and the garbage collector cleans it up later.

func newCounter() *int {
    count := 0
    return &count // safe in Go
}

When Should You Use Pointers?

Use a pointer when:

  • The function or method must modify the original value.
  • The value is large (big structs or arrays) and copying would be expensive.
  • You need to represent "no value" with nil.
  • A type has some pointer-receiver methods, in which case keep all its methods consistent and use pointer receivers.

Prefer plain values when:

  • The data is small (ints, bools, small structs) and copying is cheap.
  • You want immutability: a copy guarantees the callee cannot change your data.
  • You want to reduce heap allocations and garbage collector work. Pointers are not automatically faster, and values often are.

Common Pitfalls

  1. Dereferencing nil. Always guard pointers that may be nil.
  2. Assuming arrays behave like slices. Passing an array copies it. Use a pointer or a slice if you need to modify the original.
  3. Unintended shared state. If two parts of your code hold the same pointer, a change in one place affects the other. Make ownership clear.
  4. Pointers to loop variables. Before Go 1.22, &v inside a for _, v := range loop pointed to a single shared variable. Since Go 1.22 each iteration gets its own variable, but if you support older versions, copy the value first.
  5. Overusing pointers for small types. Pointers to ints and strings usually add noise and allocations without any benefit.

Key Takeaways

  • &x gives the address of x, and *p gives the value at p.
  • Go is always pass-by-value. Passing a pointer copies the address, not the data.
  • Arrays are values: passing one copies it. Use *[N]T to modify the original and avoid the copy.
  • *[3]int (pointer to an array) and [3]*int (array of pointers) are different types.
  • Slices already carry a pointer to their underlying array, which is why they are the default choice.
  • Use pointers deliberately, for mutation, large data, or optional values, not by habit.

Conclusion

Pointers in Go are intentionally minimal: no arithmetic, automatic dereferencing for fields and indexing, and a garbage collector that keeps you safe. Master the difference between a value and its address, remember that arrays are copied, and you will have the foundation for writing efficient, predictable Go.

Happy coding!
