title: Building an MCP Server in Java with Spring AI: Let Claude Call Your APIs
description:
Your ops teammate wants to look up an order in Claude. All they can do is paste the order ID into the chat box, wait for the model to reply "I can't see your database," and then manually paste in the logs. The company has dozens of internal systems, and every new AI client means rewriting the integration from scratch. This post walks through building an MCP Server with Spring AI that turns your Java endpoints into tools Claude and Cursor can call directly — no client changes required. The code is a complete project, and you don't even need an LLM API key to run it.

1. What the Problem Actually Is: The Glue Code Between AI Clients and Internal Systems

MCP isn't solving "the model isn't smart enough." It's solving "the model can't reach your systems."

Let's set the scene. You have an order service, an inventory service, and a logging platform. Now three different groups want to use AI: the product manager uses Claude Desktop to look up data, backend engineers use Cursor to write code and want to check production orders on the side, and your in-house support agent needs to look up orders too.

Three groups, three clients, three different integrations.

Claude Desktop wants its MCP config, Cursor wants .cursor/mcp.json, and your in-house agent wants a JSON Schema for function calling. So you write three sets of descriptions, three sets of parameter validation, and three sets of error handling. Next month a fourth client shows up, and you do it all over again.

MCP turns this from M×N into M+N. All M clients implement the same protocol, all N systems expose the same protocol, and nothing in between needs to be paired up.

Think of it like phone charging ports: round pins, flat pins, ribbon cables — every charger matched exactly one phone. Then USB-C arrived, and now the charger only has to deliver power and the phone only has to receive it, because the shape in the middle is fixed. MCP is USB-C for AI tool calls.

Let's nail down the roles in the protocol first, so the code later makes sense:

RoleWhat it isExampleHostThe AI application the user interacts withClaude Desktop, Cursor, your in-house support consoleClientA connector inside the Host; one Client connects to one ServerCreated by the Host at startup from its configServerThe program you write that exposes tools and dataThe order management Server in this post

A single Host can open multiple Clients and connect to multiple Servers. Configure three MCP Servers in Claude Desktop and it's running three Clients.

Next, the three kinds of things a Server can offer — this is where a lot of people get confused right away:

Type Who decides Typical use case Analogy
Tools The model Look up an order, file a ticket, calculate shipping Gives the model a pair of hands
Resources The client or the user Config files, troubleshooting runbooks, log snippets Gives the model a book it can page through on its own
Prompts The user picks explicitly Prebuilt prompt templates Shortcuts for the user to trigger

The difference comes down to control. With Tools, the model decides for itself that it should make a call. With Resources, the client stuffs content into the context. With Prompts, a human clicks something in the UI.

Two misconceptions come up over and over, so let's clear them up first.

Misconception #1: MCP is a model capability. It isn't. MCP is a transport protocol — it lives at the same layer as HTTP. The model has no idea MCP exists; all it sees is "here are some tools, and here's what their parameters look like." It's the host that translates MCP's tool list into the Function Calling format the model understands.

Misconception #2: write a solid MCP server and the model will use it correctly. Also no. What you name a tool, how you write its description, whether the parameter docs are clear — all of that directly determines whether the model picks the right one. Take a single lookup endpoint: describe it as "query order" and the model will happily reach for it when it means to look up a user. Describe it as "look up order details by order number; order numbers start with SO" and the hit rate changes immediately.

So this article isn't just about "how to expose your API" — it's also about "how to get the model to use it correctly."

2. Under the Hood: What Actually Happens During a Tool Call at the Protocol Level

MCP messages are just JSON-RPC 2.0 — there is no magic involved. Once you understand these three steps, any error you run into while debugging points you straight at where to look.

2.1 Three Steps: Handshake, List, Call

Step one is the handshake. When a client connects, it first sends initialize to tell the server which capabilities it supports and which protocol version it's speaking. The server replies with its own capability list.

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize",
 "params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"cursor","version":"1.0"}}}

One item in the server's response matters more than the rest: the Mcp-Session-Id response header. Every request that follows has to carry it, and that's how the server recognizes "this is still the same client."

Step two is listing. The client sends tools/list and the server returns an array of tools, each with a name, a description, and an inputSchema (a standard JSON Schema).

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}

What the model sees as "tools" is simply this array after the host has transformed it. Which means a sloppy description leaves the model guessing.

Step three is the call. The model decides to use a tool, and the host sends tools/call with the tool name and an argument object.

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call",
 "params":{"name":"get_order","arguments":{"orderNo":"SO20261027001"}}}

Once the Server finishes executing, it returns a content array. The entries can be text, images, or resource references. The model reads that content and keeps reasoning.

There's one more step worth knowing about: notifications/initialized. After the handshake, the Client sends a notification saying it's ready. This one carries no id and never gets a response — in JSON-RPC, anything without an id is a notification, so don't sit there waiting for a reply.

2.2 Transport: stdio and Streamable HTTP

The same messages can travel over two different pipes.

stdioStreamable HTTPHow to connectHost spawns a child process and exchanges data over stdin/stdoutHTTP POST, with the server streaming responses back over SSEBest forLocal tools, single user, Claude DesktopShared team use, server deployment, multiple clientsAuthHandled by OS user permissions; the protocol doesn't careYou handle it yourselfDeploymentTied to the clientRuns as a standalone service you can scale and monitor

In stdio mode, one JSON per line goes into the child process's stdin, and results come back out of stdout. Dead simple, but there's one detail that will bite you: stdout must contain protocol data and nothing else. Not a single extra character. Drop a stray System.out.println into your code, or let a logging framework print one INFO line to the console, and the client's JSON parser dies instantly. I'll come back to this pitfall later.

Streamable HTTP is the mainstream choice today. The 2025-03-26 spec revision introduced it to replace the earlier two-endpoint HTTP+SSE design — that older approach kept one long-lived connection open for receiving messages and used a separate endpoint for sending them, which broke easily behind gateways and load balancers. The new design folds sending and receiving into a single /mcp endpoint; responses can be plain JSON or upgrade to an SSE stream, and clients can reconnect and pick up where they left off after a drop.

When the server returns SSE, this is what you see in curl:

event: message
data: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"tools":[...]}}

The JSON isn't corrupted — that's just the streaming frame format. Client libraries unpack it for you.

2.3 What the framework does for you

Hand-rolling this protocol takes a few hundred lines: parsing JSON-RPC, maintaining sessions, reflecting Java methods into JSON Schema, serializing return values into content.

Spring AI handles all of it. You write an ordinary Spring Bean and slap @McpTool on a method, and it does four things:

  1. Scans the container for every method annotated with @McpTool
  2. Reads the method signature and @McpToolParam to generate a JSON Schema
  3. Registers the tool in the MCP Server's capability list
  4. On tools/call, invokes it reflectively and serializes the return value into content

One detail deserves its own paragraph: parameter names are read from the bytecode, not from annotations. @McpToolParam only has two attributes, description and required — there's no name. So you must compile with -parameters, or reflection will hand you arg0, arg1 and friends, and the generated schema will use arg0 as the parameter names. Seeing arg0, the model can only guess based on position — get more than a couple of parameters and it will guess wrong.

Spring Boot's parent POM enables -parameters by default, so as long as you don't mess with the compiler config yourself, you're fine. But if you're migrating a legacy project, or your company has a shared compiler plugin configuration, check this one carefully.

2.4 Sync, async, stateful, stateless

Four terms, two pairs. Don't let them trip you up.

Sync and async describe how you write your tool methods. A sync method returns its result directly and Spring runs it on the MVC thread pool; an async method returns Mono or Flux, which suits cases where the downstream call is already reactive. This article sticks to sync throughout for simplicity.

Stateful (streamable/sse) and stateless describe the session. In stateful mode, the server remembers each client and supports server-initiated operations — sampling (asking the model on the client side to generate content for you), elicitation (asking the user to supply more information). Stateless means one request, one response, nothing retained server-side. You can scale replicas freely, but you lose all the two-way capabilities.

The default is streamable, i.e. stateful. That's enough for most use cases. If you genuinely need stateless, set one line — protocol: stateless — and accept that you can no longer use the two-way methods like McpSyncRequestContext. Call them anyway and they're silently ignored, no error raised. That's a nasty one.

Three: Building an order management MCP Server from scratch

Goal: a service on port 8080 exposing three order tools, one troubleshooting-runbook resource, and one refund-review prompt — configured in Cursor and ready to go.

No API key, no model required. An MCP Server just publishes capabilities; who calls them is the client's business.

3.1 Dependencies and Configuration

pom.xml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
​
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>4.1.2</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>
​
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>mcp-order-server</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <name>mcp-order-server</name>
​
    <properties>
        <java.version>21</java.version>
        <spring-ai.version>2.0.2</spring-ai.version>
    </properties>
​
    <dependencyManagement>
        <dependencies>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-ai-bom</artifactId>
                <version>2.0.2</version>
                <type>pom</type>
                <scope>import</scope>
            </dependency>
        </dependencies>
    </dependencyManagement>
​
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc</artifactId>
            <version>2.0.2</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
​
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>4.1.2</version>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

One starter is all you need — it pulls in Web MVC, the MCP protocol implementation, and the annotation scanner.

src/main/resources/application.yml:

server:
  port: 8080
​
spring:
  application:
    name: mcp-order-server
  ai:
    mcp:
      server:
        name: order-admin
        version: 1.0.0
        protocol: streamable
        type: sync
        instructions: "订单与售后工具集。订单号格式为 SO 开头，查订单前先确认格式。写操作会真实修改数据，调用前必须先向用户确认。"
        tool-response-mime-type:
          get_order: application/json
        streamable-http:
          mcp-endpoint: /mcp

instructions ends up in the server description the client sees, which acts as a general prompt for the model. Spelling out "this is the order domain, confirm before any write" once beats repeating it in every tool description.

tool-response-mime-type sets the MIME type for returned content; some clients render based on it. It runs fine without it.

The main class:

package com.example.mcpserver;
​
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
​
@SpringBootApplication
public class McpOrderServerApplication {
​
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(McpOrderServerApplication.class, args);
    }
}

3.2 The Tool Class: Three Methods Covering Read, Search, and Write

This is the heart of the article. Pay attention to the annotations on each method and why they're written the way they are.

package com.example.mcpserver.tools;
​
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDateTime;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
​
import org.springframework.ai.mcp.annotation.McpTool;
import org.springframework.ai.mcp.annotation.McpToolParam;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
​
@Component
public class OrderTools {
​
    public record Order(String orderNo, String customer, String status,
                        BigDecimal amount, LocalDateTime createdAt) {
    }
​
    public record OrderPage(List<Order> items, int page, int size, long total) {
    }
​
    private final Map<String, Order> orders = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
​
    public OrderTools() {
        seed("SO20261027001", "张伟", "PAID", "399.00", 2);
        seed("SO20261027002", "张伟", "SHIPPED", "1299.00", 5);
        seed("SO20261027003", "李娜", "REFUNDING", "89.90", 1);
        seed("SO20261027004", "王强", "PAID", "2480.00", 9);
        seed("SO20261027005", "李娜", "CLOSED", "59.00", 20);
    }
​
    private void seed(String orderNo, String customer, String status, String amount, int daysAgo) {
        orders.put(orderNo, new Order(orderNo, customer, status, new BigDecimal(amount),
                LocalDateTime.now().minusDays(daysAgo)));
    }
​
    @McpTool(
            name = "get_order",
            description = "按订单号查询订单详情，返回状态、金额、下单时间。订单号格式为 SO 加日期加序号。这是只读操作。",
            annotations = @McpTool.McpAnnotations(readOnlyHint = true, openWorldHint = false))
    public Order getOrder(
            @McpToolParam(description = "订单号，例如 SO20261027001", required = true) String orderNo) {
        Order order = orders.get(orderNo.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT));
        if (order == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("订单不存在: " + orderNo);
        }
        return order;
    }
​
    @McpTool(
            name = "search_orders",
            description = "按客户姓名模糊查询订单，可以再按状态过滤。用于排查某个用户的订单情况，返回分页结果。这是只读操作。",
            annotations = @McpTool.McpAnnotations(readOnlyHint = true, openWorldHint = false))
    public OrderPage searchOrders(
            @McpToolParam(description = "客户姓名，支持部分匹配", required = true) String customer,
            @McpToolParam(description = "订单状态，可选值 PAID、SHIPPED、REFUNDING、CLOSED，不传表示全部", required = false) String status,
            @McpToolParam(description = "页码，从 1 开始，默认 1", required = false) Integer page) {
        int current = (page == null || page < 1) ? 1 : page;
        int size = 10;
        List<Order> matched = orders.values().stream()
                .filter(order -> order.customer().contains(customer))
                .filter(order -> status == null || status.isBlank()
                        || order.status().equalsIgnoreCase(status))
                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::createdAt).reversed())
                .toList();
        int from = Math.min((current - 1) * size, matched.size());
        int to = Math.min(from + size, matched.size());
        return new OrderPage(matched.subList(from, to), current, size, matched.size());
    }
​
    @McpTool(
            name = "create_refund_ticket",
            description = "为指定订单创建退款工单。这是写操作，会真实修改订单状态为 REFUNDING，调用前必须先向用户确认订单号和原因。",
            annotations = @McpTool.McpAnnotations(readOnlyHint = false, destructiveHint = true, idempotentHint = false))
    public String createRefundTicket(
            @McpToolParam(description = "订单号", required = true) String orderNo,
            @McpToolParam(description = "退款原因，写清楚用户诉求", required = true) String reason) {
        Order updated = orders.computeIfPresent(orderNo.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT), (no, old) -> {
            if ("CLOSED".equals(old.status())) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("订单已关闭，不能退款: " + no);
            }
            return new Order(old.orderNo(), old.customer(), "REFUNDING", old.amount(), old.createdAt());
        });
        if (updated == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("订单不存在: " + orderNo);
        }
        return "已创建退款工单，订单 " + updated.orderNo() + " 状态变为 REFUNDING，原因：" + reason;
    }
}

A few design decisions are worth spelling out.

Why return a record instead of a Map. When you return an object, the framework serializes it to JSON with Jackson. A record's field names become the schema's field names, so the model sees a stable structure. Map<String, Object> works too, but there the field names live in string literals you type by hand — change one and forget another, and the model starts guessing.

Why the lookup method throws IllegalArgumentException instead of returning null. When you throw RuntimeException, the framework converts it into a "tool execution failed" result for the model. The model sees the error message and can retry with a different order number. Return null and all the model sees is null — it can't tell "not found" from "the system is broken," so it often confidently makes up an order.

Why write operations need destructiveHint. This isn't decoration. Clients read this field to decide whether to show a confirmation dialog. Mark it readOnlyHint = false plus destructiveHint = true and Cursor and Claude Desktop will make the user click before calling the tool. Skip it, and the model may flip the order to refunded before you've even read the prompt.

Why pagination. See the pitfalls section — returning a huge list is the fastest way to blow up your token budget.

3.3 Resources and Prompts: Attaching the Troubleshooting Guide and Review Template

Beyond tools, add one resource and one prompt. A resource is content the client can read on its own; a prompt is a template the user can pick from the UI.

package com.example.mcpserver.resources;

import java.util.Map;

import org.springframework.ai.mcp.annotation.McpResource;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class OpsResourceProvider {

    private static final Map<String, String> RUNBOOKS = Map.of(
            "order", """
                    # 订单服务排障手册

                    1. 先确认订单号格式是 SO 加 8 位日期加 3 位序号。
                    2. 用 get_order 查看当前状态，PAID 表示已付款未发货。
                    3. 状态卡在 REFUNDING 超过 24 小时，查退款任务表 refund_task。
                    4. 金额对不上，先看订单表的 amount 和支付流水表的 pay_amount 是否一致。
                    """,
            "payment", """
                    # 支付服务排障手册

                    1. 支付回调丢失时，先查网关日志里的 notify 记录。
                    2. 重复扣款优先看幂等键 out_trade_no 是否重复。
                    3. 退款失败看渠道返回码，不要直接重试，先确认渠道侧状态。
                    """);

    @McpResource(
            uri = "ops://runbook/{service}",
            name = "runbook",
            title = "服务排障手册",
            description = "按服务名读取线上排障步骤，例如 ops://runbook/order",
            mimeType = "text/markdown")
    public String runbook(String service) {
        String content = RUNBOOKS.get(service);
        if (content == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("没有该服务的排障手册: " + service);
        }
        return content;
    }
}

{service} inside uri is a template variable, filled in by the method parameters in order. When the client reads ops://runbook/order, the framework passes order into runbook(String service).

Note that the resource method's parameter has no @McpToolParam, and doesn't need one — the client isn't "filling in parameters," it's "requesting this URI."

For prompts, we'll add a refund review template plus argument autocompletion:

package com.example.mcpserver.prompts;

import java.util.List;

import io.modelcontextprotocol.spec.McpSchema.GetPromptResult;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.spec.McpSchema.PromptMessage;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.spec.McpSchema.Role;
import io.modelcontextprotocol.spec.McpSchema.TextContent;
import org.springframework.ai.mcp.annotation.McpArg;
import org.springframework.ai.mcp.annotation.McpComplete;
import org.springframework.ai.mcp.annotation.McpPrompt;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class RefundPromptProvider {

    private static final List<String> SAMPLE_ORDER_NOS = List.of(
            "SO20261027001", "SO20261027002", "SO20261027003");

    @McpPrompt(
            name = "refund-review",
            description = "生成一份退款审核清单，把订单事实和用户诉求一起交给模型判断")
    public GetPromptResult refundReview(
            @McpArg(name = "orderNo", description = "订单号", required = true) String orderNo,
            @McpArg(name = "reason", description = "用户退款原因", required = false) String reason) {
        String text = """
                你是电商售后审核员。根据下面的信息判断是否同意退款，并给出处理建议。

                订单号：%s
                用户诉求：%s

                要求：
                1. 先调用 get_order 查订单真实状态，不要凭用户描述下结论。
                2. 订单已发货的，说明需要先确认物流签收情况。
                3. 订单已关闭的，直接说明不能退款并给出替代方案。
                """.formatted(orderNo, reason == null ? "未提供" : reason);

        PromptMessage message = new PromptMessage(Role.USER, TextContent.builder(text).build());
        return GetPromptResult.builder(List.of(message))
                .description("退款审核")
                .build();
    }

    @McpComplete(prompt = "refund-review")
    public List<String> completeOrderNo(String prefix) {
        return SAMPLE_ORDER_NOS.stream()
                .filter(orderNo -> orderNo.startsWith(prefix))
                .toList();
    }
}

@McpComplete handles input completion. As the user types SO2026 in the client, matching order numbers pop up in the suggestion box. The method takes a single String prefix and returns the matches. Users notice this feature right away and it costs almost nothing to implement — add it to every prompt that takes an ID.

3.4 Run It, Then Verify with curl First 

mvn spring-boot:run

The startup log shows Tomcat listening on 8080. Don't rush to wire up a client; walk the protocol through with curl first — that way, when something breaks, you can tell whether it's the server or the client config.

# 1. 初始化，同时把会话 ID 抓出来
SESSION_ID=$(curl -s -D - -o /tmp/mcp-init.json \
  -X POST http://localhost:8080/mcp \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"}}}' \
  | grep -i '^mcp-session-id:' | tr -d '\r' | awk '{print $2}')

echo "session: $SESSION_ID"
cat /tmp/mcp-init.json

# 2. 发就绪通知，这条没有响应体
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/mcp \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -H "Mcp-Session-Id: $SESSION_ID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}'

# 3. 列工具，应该看到三个名字
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/mcp \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -H "Mcp-Session-Id: $SESSION_ID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}'

# 4. 真调一次
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/mcp \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' \
  -H "Mcp-Session-Id: $SESSION_ID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_order","arguments":{"orderNo":"SO20261027001"}}}'

In the response to step 3, inputSchema.properties should list the names you wrote: orderNo, customer, status, page. If you see arg0 or arg1, stop right there — the build didn't include -parameters. Fix that before touching any client.

The response to step 4 looks roughly like this (SSE frame format — the JSON comes after data:):

event: message
data: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"{\"orderNo\":\"SO20261027001\",\"customer\":\"张伟\",\"status\":\"PAID\",\"amount\":399.00,\"createdAt\":\"2026-10-25T10:12:33\"}"}]}}

Note that content is a string, not an object. MCP content blocks come in only a few flavors — text, image — so structured data has to be serialized into text and stuffed in. The client deserializes it on the other end.

3.5 Hooking It Up to Cursor

Create .cursor/mcp.json at the project root:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "order-admin": {
      "url": "http://localhost:8080/mcp"
    }
  }
}

Restart Cursor and open the MCP panel in settings. order-admin should be green; expand it and you'll see the three tools get_order, search_orders, create_refund_ticket, plus the runbook resource and the refund-review prompt.

Then type "what's going on with order SO20261027001?" in the chat. The model calls get_order first, then turns the result into plain language. When it calls a write tool, Cursor pops up a confirmation — that's destructiveHint doing its job.

Claude Desktop can also be pointed at an HTTP-based MCP server, but support for local HTTP varies widely across versions. The safe bet is the stdio version.

3.6 The stdio build: letting Claude Desktop launch it directly

The stdio version uses exactly the same code as above — you only swap the starter and the packaging.

Replace the dependency with:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-mcp-server</artifactId>
    <version>2.0.2</version>
</dependency>

This starter brings in only spring-boot-starter, with no web container. The process never binds a port; it communicates purely over stdin/stdout.

Add one line to your config:

spring:
  ai:
    mcp:
      server:
        name: order-admin
        version: 1.0.0
        stdio: true
        type: sync

If you just want to try it locally, putting stdio: true in the config is enough — add mvn spring-boot:run and the terminal will simply sit waiting on stdin.

Then comes the fatal detail. Spring Boot writes logs to stdout by default, while the stdio protocol reserves stdout for JSON-RPC messages and nothing else. A single Started McpOrderServerApplication in 1.2 seconds printed at startup is enough to blow up the client's parser.

The fix is to push logging over to stderr. Add a src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<configuration>
    <appender name="STDERR" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <target>System.err</target>
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="STDERR"/>
    </root>
</configuration>

That <target>System.err</target> line is the critical one. Without it, logs bleed into the protocol stream.

After packaging, register it with Claude Desktop via claude_desktop_config.json (on macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/, on Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "order-admin": {
      "command": "/usr/bin/java",
      "args": ["-jar", "/opt/mcp/mcp-order-server-1.0.0.jar"]
    }
  }
}

command must be an absolute path. Claude Desktop spawns child processes with a different PATH than your terminal, so a bare java will most likely not resolve.

Restart Claude Desktop and the three tools show up under the tool icon in the bottom-right of the chat box. The first call is slower because of JVM cold start.

4. Pitfalls and best practices

Every item in this section is something that genuinely breaks in production — not a theoretical risk.

4.1 Not a single extra character on stdout

In stdio mode, System.out.println("debug"), some third-party library's banner, or a logging framework's default output will all corrupt the protocol stream. What you see: the client reports "Unexpected token" or simply fails to connect, while the server-side logs look perfectly healthy.

To track it down, run java -jar xxx.jar by hand and inspect the terminal output. If the first line isn't JSON, the stream is contaminated.

Beyond switching logback over to stderr, also avoid System.out inside your tool methods. Use a logging framework and set the level properly.

4.2 Parameter names come out as arg0

As noted earlier, @McpToolParam has no name attribute, so parameter names depend on the -parameters compiler flag. The Spring Boot parent enables it by default, but it gets lost in these situations:

  • A company-internal parent POM overrides the maven-compiler-plugin configuration
  • You're on Gradle and forgot options.compilerArgs << '-parameters'
  • You run straight from the IDE, whose compiler settings don't match Maven's

The way to confirm is to look at the schema returned by tools/list. If you see arg0, go back and check your compiler configuration.

4.3 RuntimeException and checked exceptions mean completely different things

This one trips people up the most, because both styles "compile and run" just fine.

  • Throwing a RuntimeException: the framework catches it and converts it into a tool-execution failure result. The model can see the error message and retry with different parameters.
  • Throwing a checked exception (throws IOException declared in the method signature): it propagates straight up. The tool call fails and the model sees nothing.

So the criteria are clear:

Case What to throw Why
Invalid parameters, order not found RuntimeException The model understands it and can retry with different parameters
Downstream timeout, transient failure RuntimeException The model can retry later or switch tools
Insufficient permissions, internal implementation details Checked exception You don't want the model seeing stack traces or internal information
Errors that should never be retried Checked exception Fail the call outright instead of wasting tokens

My own habit: anything at the business layer that's self-explanatory becomes a RuntimeException, and anything touching internal implementation gets wrapped in a checked exception and thrown upward.

4.4 Don't be greedy with return values

Whatever a tool returns goes straight into the model's context and eats into the token budget.

A search_orders that returns 500 orders at 200 characters each is 100k tokens. The context blows up immediately; the client either errors out or silently truncates, and what the user sees is "the model is making things up."

Three rules:

  1. Lists must be paginated, 10 to 20 items by default
  2. Return only the fields the model needs to make a decision — don't leak internal fields like createdBy, updatedBy, version
  3. Truncate long text fields, e.g. give only the first 100 characters of a product description

When you do need the full dataset, add a separate "export" tool that hands back a file path or a download link instead of cramming the content into the context window.

4.5 MCP Servers Have No Auth by Default

What spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc boots is a bare Spring MVC application with zero authentication. Anyone can POST to /mcp; anyone can call your create_refund_ticket.

Binding to 0.0.0.0 with no protection in front of it is the same as publishing your internal APIs to the public internet.

The bare minimum:

  • During development, use server.address: 127.0.0.1 so the server only listens on localhost
  • In production, put it behind a gateway and gate it with an API key or OAuth2
  • Add Spring Security to the app and require authentication on the /mcp path
  • Mark every write operation with destructiveHint = true so the client asks for confirmation

Say it in the tool description too: "This is a write operation — always confirm with the user before calling it." Models do read descriptions, and most of the time they'll ask first.

4.6 Don't Cram Too Many Tools into One Server

Once you pass roughly 15 tools, the odds of the model picking the wrong one climb noticeably. Near-identical names are worse: with both get_order and query_order in play, the model basically flips a coin every time.

Split servers by business domain — one for orders, one for inventory, one for logs, each deployed independently. Configure several servers on the client and the model sees a grouped, smaller list of tools; shrink the candidate set and accuracy goes up.

4.7 Timeouts and Long-Running Tasks

The default request timeout is 20 seconds (spring.ai.mcp.server.request-timeout), which is nowhere near enough for batch jobs.

Two options: raise the timeout, or emit progress notifications from inside the tool via McpSyncRequestContext. The second is better — the client can render a progress bar, and the user won't assume it's hung. Progress notifications do require the client to send a progress token and the server to run in stateful mode; in stateless mode those calls are silently dropped.

5. Performance Comparison and Technology Choices

There are three ways to build an MCP server in the Java ecosystem, and picking the wrong one will cost you a lot of time.

Option Setup cost Flexibility Best for
Spring AI Starter Low — annotations are the tools Medium — special cases need workarounds Teams with an existing Spring Boot project
Official MCP Java SDK, hand-rolled Medium — you manage sessions and registration yourself High — full control of the protocol layer Non-Spring projects, fine-grained control
LangChain4j Low (client side) Weak server-side support Projects already using LangChain4j for agents

Spring AI's strength is that it wraps up annotation scanning, schema generation, and serialization for you. That's also its weakness: the moment you want to change the schema generation rules or control the content structure yourself, you have to drop down to the SDK layer. Most business scenarios never need to.

The official SDK fits two situations: your service isn't Spring-based (plain Netty or Vert.x, say), or you need to implement a custom transport.

On the LangChain4j side, MCP is mainly a client story — langchain4j-mcp pulls tools from a remote server into AiServices, which makes writing agents very convenient. There's no matching server starter, though, so if you want to expose Java APIs to other clients you're back to Spring AI or the official SDK.

When not to use MCP. If you have a single application, a single model, and a handful of internal functions, plain function calling is simpler — one less hop of inter-process communication, one less thing to deploy. MCP earns its keep through cross-client reuse; it starts paying off once three or more clients need the same set of capabilities.

6. Wrapping Up

MCP isn't mysterious. JSON-RPC messages, a three-step handshake, two transports. Spring AI handles the reflection and serialization; what's left for you to write is a Spring bean with a few annotations on it.

What actually decides success is three small things:

Write tool descriptions the way you'd write a handover doc for a new teammate. Don't write "query order" — a phrase only you understand. Keep parameter names and schemas clean; the moment something like arg0 shows up, the model starts guessing. Keep return payloads small — tokens cost money.

Don't cut corners on security. MCP servers are naked by default, and write operations have no confirmation step by default. Add authentication before you ship, and tag destructiveHint correctly.

One last practical note: get two read-only tools working, wire them into Cursor, and use them yourself for a week. You'll quickly find out which descriptions are terrible and which return values are too large — that firsthand feel beats reading ten docs.

By 会编程的吕洞宾

References

  • MCP Specification (2025-06-18 revision)
  • Spring AI - MCP Server Boot Starter
  • Spring AI - MCP Server Annotations
  • Spring AI - MCP Overview

title: How to re-brand a Next.js SaaS kit from one file
description:
Open src/config/theme.ts, change accent to your brand colour, and save. In AURORA that one value re-colours the marketing site and the dashboard: buttons, links, focus rings, soft fills, glows, the first chart line and the hero light. This guide shows what to change, why it works, and the two things to check before you ship.

AURORA is our AI SaaS kit on Pulse. We built it so that a buyer's first job, making it look like their product, takes minutes instead of a day of hunting through components.

Before you start

You need the kit running locally (npm ci, then npm run dev; the Documentation folder in the download walks through it). Have your brand colour as a hex value, and a second colour from the same family for the gradient.

Step 1: change the theme file

This is the whole file a buyer edits (shortened here; the real file explains every value in a comment at the top).

// src/config/theme.ts
export const theme = {
  accent: "#7458F7",     // your brand colour
  accentTo: "#56CCF2",   // the gradient fades from accent into this
  onAccent: "#FFFFFF",   // text on a solid accent button
  radius: 12,            // corner roundness in px (0 = sharp, 20 = soft)
  fonts: { display: "geist", body: "inter" },
  defaultMode: "dark",   // or "light"; visitors can still switch
  showThemeDial: true,   // the "Try your colour" swatches in the hero
};

Save, and the dev server reloads with the new colour everywhere. There is no second place to change it.

Step 2: check the text on your buttons

onAccent is the colour of text on a solid accent button. It has to stay readable. The rule we follow is the WCAG one: at least 4.5 to 1 contrast for normal text.

Here are AURORA's own presets, with the ratio each one gets:

Accent Text on it Contrast
Violet #7458F7 white 4.69 : 1
Cobalt #2F6BEF white 4.70 : 1
Rose #D4365F white 4.67 : 1
Aurora green #1FC8A0 near-black #04140F 8.84 : 1
Amber #F5A524 near-black #1A1204 9.09 : 1

Light, bright accents like green and amber fail with white text (about 2 : 1), so they get near-black text instead. If your brand colour is light, do the same. Any contrast checker will give you the number; aim for 4.5 or more.

Step 3: remove the colour dial before you launch

showThemeDial: true shows six swatches in the hero so people trying the demo can see the kit in other colours. Your customers don't need it. Set it to false and the swatches and their small script are gone.

Why one value is enough

The trick is that nothing else in the kit names a colour. Everything is derived from the accent in one stylesheet:

/* src/app/globals.css (shortened) */
:root {
  --accent-soft: color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 14%, transparent);
  --accent-line: color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 45%, transparent);
  --accent-glow: color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 50%, transparent);
  --aurora: linear-gradient(100deg, var(--accent),
    color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent), var(--accent-to)) 55%, var(--accent-to));
}

color-mix() blends two colours in the browser. Mixing in oklab keeps the blends looking even, so a 14% tint of rose looks as light as a 14% tint of blue. Components only ever use --accent-soft, --accent-line and the rest, never a hex value.

The root layout writes your theme.ts values into :root once, on the server, so the first paint is already in your colour. No flash of violet before your brand loads.

How the live colour change animates

The demo's dial changes the colour smoothly over 0.6 seconds. Normally a CSS variable can't animate: the browser doesn't know it is a colour, so it jumps. Registering it tells the browser its type:

@property --accent { syntax: "<color>"; inherits: true; initial-value: #7458f7; }
:root.dial-anim { transition: --accent 0.6s ease, --accent-to 0.6s ease; }

The dial adds the dial-anim class, sets the new values, and removes the class 0.7 seconds later. If the visitor has reduced motion turned on, it skips the class and the colour changes at once.

You can use the same three lines in any project that keeps its brand colour in a CSS variable.

Dark mode, for free

Colours that differ between light and dark are written once with light-dark():

--accent-text: light-dark(
  color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 78%, #000),
  color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) 58%, #fff)
);

Accent-coloured text is darkened on light backgrounds and lightened on dark ones, from the same accent. You never pick a separate "dark mode brand colour", and the two modes can't drift apart.

What it doesn't do

It doesn't change your product name, logo, fonts beyond Geist and Inter, or images. Those are separate steps in the README: the name lives in src/content/site.ts, the logo files in public/assets/, and other fonts load through next/font/local. It also can't make a colour accessible for you; Step 2 is still your job.

If you want to see it before you buy, the dial is live on the AURORA demo. Pick a swatch and watch the dashboard follow.

First published on Pulse by AIVCJ.

title: Load an on-prem database into a cloud warehouse: 1 million rows, measured
description:
To load an on-prem database into a cloud warehouse, read it in pages inside your network, check and mask each page there, keep the failed rows locally, and send the rest in batches of a few thousand rows per statement. In our test of 1 million rows, rows per insert set the speed. Our first checks caught 55% of the bad rows; after Claude profiled the data and rewrote the checks through the Neblex MCP server, they caught 94%, including in a half of the table they were never shown. The better checks cost about 2 minutes per million rows.

The request we hear often

Moving data from a database inside a company's network to a cloud warehouse, usually as a scheduled ETL job, is a request we hear often. The questions are always the same: how long will it take, will bad rows reach the warehouse, and does personal data leave the building?

Our measurement post covered what the runtime costs your server. This one runs the load: 1 million rows from an on-prem PostgreSQL database into Supabase, checked and masked on the way.

How we tested

  • Source: PostgreSQL 18 on the test machine, with a test table of 1,000,000 customer records (206 MB).
  • Problem rows: 18,675 rows, about 1.9%, with a bad email, state or phone, or a test account. Each problem came in one of 6 to 9 forms we see in real data, such as a misspelled domain, "N/A" in the state field or an all-zeros phone, and about 1 in 9 of these rows had a second problem.
  • Unusual but valid rows: 5,325 rows that should pass, such as a surname starting with "Test", a phone with an extension or a state written in full.
  • Answer key: a separate table recorded every problem row and every unusual row, so we could score each run.
  • Runtime: the On-Prem Worker, our local integration runtime, running as a background service on the test machine.
  • Destination: Supabase, a hosted Postgres database, in us-west-2, through its connection pooler. It stood in for the cloud warehouse.
  • Line: a home internet connection, 30 to 44 Mbps up. Measured before every timed run: 31 to 110 ms idle latency.

Raw and failed rows stay inside the network; the warehouse gets masked rows and the Neblex cloud gets the run report. Diagram by Neblex.

We kept the error rate low on purpose. In a peer-reviewed study of 75 data quality assessments, 47% of recently created records had at least one critical error; our test had problems in 1.9% of rows, across four fields.

We sampled the runtime's CPU, memory and network traffic throughout, and after each run compared what arrived in Supabase with the answer key. Supabase is Postgres, not a warehouse like Snowflake or BigQuery, which usually load from staged files; the lesson below carries over either way: send fewer, larger loads.

What set the speed: rows per insert

The runtime spent most of each run waiting for the warehouse to accept inserts, so the number of rows per insert decided the time.

Rows per insert Rows read Runs Time Rows per second (median)
1 500 (sample) 1 195 s 2.6
100 1,000,000 5 21 min 46 s to 22 min 53 s (median 21 min 53 s) 762
1,000 1,000,000 5 9 min 56 s to 10 min 38 s (median 10 min 22 s) 1,608
5,000 1,000,000 5 8 min 18 s to 8 min 48 s (median 8 min 23 s) 1,988
10,000 1,000,000 5 7 min 56 s to 8 min 59 s (median 8 min 37 s) 1,934

Rows per insert set the speed; past 5,000 there was no further gain. Source: Neblex internal tests, October 2026.

Each setting ran five times on the same day. At 5,000 rows per insert, the slowest run took 6% longer than the fastest, and 10,000 overlapped it.

One row per insert took about 0.39 seconds per row, or four and a half days for 1 million rows. Each insert pays a full round trip to the warehouse, which dwarfs the work of inserting one row.

Engineering write-ups show the same shape at higher speeds. In one, run against a database on the same laptop, batching took inserts from about 2,284 to 37,465 rows per second. The PostgreSQL documentation gives the same advice: fewer, larger statements, and COPY where you can use it.

Past 5,000 rows per insert there was no further gain: each insert gets bigger and slower to send and parse. Your best size depends on latency, row width and warehouse, so measure a few sizes rather than picking the largest.

Where the time went

Step timings for one page of 100,000 rows, from the run logs, with our first checks and the rewritten checks described below:

Step First checks Rewritten checks
Checks 1.7 s 11.9 s
Normalize email, domain and phone 1.8 s 2.8 s
Route rows to load or quarantine 1.1 s 1.2 s

With the first checks, the 20 inserts took 33.5 of the page's 43 seconds. The rewritten checks added about 11 seconds per 100,000 rows. Inserts still set the pace, but thorough rules are not free: checks and normalizing went from about 8% of the page's time to nearly 30%.

Which checks should run before rows leave the network?

Run the checks that decide whether a row may leave at all; anything you can only fix at the source belongs here. We started with four, each a single rule on one field:

Check First rule Bad rows caught (held-out half)
Email contains an "@" 46%
State not empty 60%
Phone at least 10 digits 74%
Test account on the test domain, or starting with "test" 43%

Together they caught 54.6% of the bad rows in the half we later held out, and wrongly quarantined 5.6% of the unusual but valid rows, such as surnames starting with "Test". Each miss has a plain cause: a misspelled domain still contains an "@", "N/A" is not an empty state, and an all-zeros phone has 10 digits.

The weak rules also hid two masking bugs. Emails with two "@" signs put part of the address in the domain field of 402 warehouse rows, and for phones with an extension, the "last 4 digits" were the extension's.

Improving the rules from a profile of the data

Rules only catch what someone thought to write down, so we did what a data team would do: look at the data, then rewrite the rules. The difference is that Claude did the work through the Neblex MCP server, and nobody edited the flow by hand.

  1. 1We split the table into two halves by a hash of each row's id.
  2. 2Claude built and ran a profiling flow on the first half through MCP: counts and patterns, not rows. For example, every state value and its count, the shapes of phone numbers, the most common email domains, and values that repeated 4 or more times.
  3. 3A second Claude session, given only that profile and our four rules, drafted new rules and listed what they would still miss. It never saw the data, the answer key or how the test data was made.
  4. 4Claude wrote the new rules into the flow's check and masking steps through MCP. The checks went in exactly as drafted; the masking fixes were written to the drafted spec.
  5. 5We scored the new rules on both halves against the answer key. The second half was never profiled.

The model worked from a summary produced inside the network, never from customer rows, and it changed the same governed flow a person would edit in the designer. One caution if you do this on real data: repeated values can be real phone numbers or emails, so mask them or raise the threshold before the profile goes to a model.

Field First rule Rewritten rule (summary)
Email contains an "@" exactly one "@", valid characters and domain, not a known misspelled domain or placeholder such as noreply@
State not empty a US state code or name; "N/A", "unknown" and similar count as missing
Phone at least 10 digits 10 digits after dropping a leading 1 and any extension, and not a placeholder such as all zeros
Test account test domain, or starts with "test" test domains, "test" or "testuser" as a name or address, keyboard mashes such as asdf@

Claude changed what two steps do; the flow's steps and connections stayed the same. Diagram by Neblex.

First checks Rewritten checks
Bad rows caught, profiled half 55.3% 94.4%
Bad rows caught, held-out half 54.6% 93.7% (8,701 of 9,289)
Unusual but valid rows quarantined, held-out half 5.6% 0%
Normal rows quarantined, held-out half 0 0 of 485,638

The held-out half scored within a point of the profiled half, so the rules were not fitted to particular rows. Both masking bugs were fixed.

The rewritten rules still missed some rows in the held-out half:

  • Domain misspellings not on their list: 62 of 613. The drafted rules themselves suggested an edit-distance check for these.
  • Test accounts the profile never showed: "demo" and "qa+" addresses, and placeholder names such as John Doe. These were caught in 17%, 14% and 49% of cases.
  • Emails ending in a dot: the rules strip the dot and load the address. Our answer key counted these as bad. If you count stripping the dot as a fix, the rewritten rules handled about 95% of the bad rows in the held-out half.

One limit: the held-out half had the same kinds of problems as the profiled half. The test shows the rules generalize to new rows, not to kinds of problems nobody has seen yet, which is exactly what the misses above are.

Where do the rows that fail go?

To a quarantine table in the same on-prem database, with their raw values and the reason they failed. No row is dropped, and the raw values stay inside the network.

The raw values are kept because a malformed email can only be fixed by someone who can see it. With the rewritten rules, every run quarantined the same 17,564 rows.

Masking before the load, and what hashing does not do

We kept three things per customer in place of the raw email and phone: a hash of the trimmed, lower-cased email, so two records with the same email still match; the email domain, for company-level reporting; and the last 4 digits of the phone, for support lookups. Names, company, city and state went through unchanged, because the reports needed them. That is a choice each team has to make field by field.

A hash is not anonymisation. The UK Information Commissioner's Office treats pseudonymised data as personal data and advises against hashes that use no salt, pepper or key. The US FTC put it more bluntly: "hashes aren't 'anonymous' and can still be used to identify users".

So use a keyed hash (HMAC) with a secret that stays on your side. Our timed runs used plain SHA-256. In an earlier test, a version built for production use, with a keyed hash and upserts instead of inserts, loaded 1 million rows in 8 minutes. The warehouse can still join on the hash; an outsider with a list of email addresses cannot reverse it.

After each run we checked the warehouse: 982,436 rows, no empty hashes, every phone field exactly four digits, and no "@" in any text column. The Neblex cloud received the run's status, diagnostics, counts and integrity receipts, not records; ask any vendor you evaluate to show this in their run logs.

After the first load: send only what changed

A one-time load is a backfill; after it, a scheduled job should move only the rows that changed. In an earlier production-style version tracking changes by updated_at and id, a run with nothing new took 0.3 seconds and a run with five changed rows took 1.8 seconds.

What the runtime used

CPU averaged 25 to 47% of one core. Upload was 372 to 395 MB per 1 million rows, around 6 Mbps of the 30 to 44 Mbps uplink, so the line was never the limit.

Memory varied more. Across 21 runs of 1 million rows, peaks ranged from 379 to 985 MB, highest at 100 and 1,000 rows per insert, while the median stayed under 210 MB in all but five runs. The runtime returned to 52 MB afterwards; size the machine for the peak. Our measurement post covers how the runtime handles memory as batches grow.

What can go wrong

  • A slow line stretches the load but should not change the result. Over a poor mobile connection (500 to 950 ms latency), 1 million rows took about 29 minutes instead of about 8, and every row still arrived in the warehouse or quarantine.
  • A write can fail with its outcome unknown: the warehouse may or may not have committed it. On the poor line, one insert dropped mid-flight and the run stopped for a person to decide instead of retrying blindly.
  • Rules miss what the profile never showed. Profile again when the source changes.
  • Incremental loads have edges. A row that later fails its checks stays in the warehouse with its last good values, and deletes in the source are not copied unless you handle them.
  • Quarantine needs an owner. A quarantine table nobody reviews is a slower way of dropping rows.

How to set it up yourself

  1. 1Create the target table in the warehouse with only the masked columns, and a quarantine table in the source database with the row's id, the reason and the raw record.
  2. 2Read the source in pages ordered by key (WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 100000), on a runtime or job inside the network.
  3. 3Profile the source before writing rules: distinct values of short fields, shapes of phones and emails, common domains. An AI assistant connected through MCP can run the profile and update the checks.
  4. 4Check each row and route failures to the quarantine table with their reason. Score the rules on a part of the data they were not written from.
  5. 5Mask the passing rows: a keyed hash of the normalised email, the email domain, the last 4 phone digits, and whatever else your policy requires.
  6. 6Group the masked rows into batches of a few thousand and send each batch as one statement. One way in PostgreSQL is to pass the batch as a single JSON parameter and expand it with jsonb_to_recordset: 
INSERT INTO customers_masked (id, email_hash, email_domain, phone_last4, city, state)
SELECT r.id, r.email_hash, r.email_domain, r.phone_last4, r.city, r.state
FROM jsonb_to_recordset(CAST(:batch AS jsonb))
  AS r(id bigint, email_hash text, email_domain text, phone_last4 text, city text, state text)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING;

After each run, compare counts on both sides: rows read, rows quarantined, rows in the warehouse. Once the first load is done, switch to incremental runs by updated_at.

These checks catch broken values, not duplicates. The data also held 20,000 near-duplicate customers that passed every check and loaded as clean rows; an upcoming post covers finding and merging them.

The takeaway: to load an on-prem database into a cloud warehouse, tune rows per insert first, check and mask inside your network, and write your rules from a profile of your own data, then test them on rows they have not seen.

Sources

  • Nagle T, Redman T, Sammon D, Assessing data quality: A managerial call to action, Business Horizons 63(3), 2020, pp. 325-337
  • FTC Office of Technology, No, hashing still doesn't make your data anonymous, July 24, 2024
  • UK Information Commissioner's Office, Pseudonymisation (guidance)
  • PostgreSQL documentation, Populating a Database
  • PostgreSQL documentation, JSON Functions and Operators
  • Alexander Belanger, The fastest Postgres inserts, Hatchet, May 15, 2025
  • Connect an AI client (MCP), Neblex Integration Fabric docs

Last checked: November 2, 2026.

Frequently asked questions

How do you load an on-prem database into a cloud warehouse?

Read it in pages by key on a runtime or job inside your network, check and mask each page there, keep failed rows locally, and send the rest in batches of a few thousand rows per statement. After the first load, send only rows that changed.

What batch size should you use for bulk inserts into Postgres over the internet?

Large enough that round trips stop dominating. In our test, 5,000 rows per insert loaded 1 million rows in 8 min 18 s to 8 min 48 s across five runs; 10,000 was no faster; one row per insert ran at 2.6 rows per second.

How do you improve data quality rules?

Profile the data, write rules for the patterns the profile shows, and test them on data they were not written from. In our test, Claude profiled half of a 1 million row table and rewrote the flow's checks through the Neblex MCP server; the new rules caught 93.7% of bad rows in the other half, up from 54.6%, with no false alarms.

Should you mask PII before or after loading it into a data warehouse?

Before, when you can. Masking at the source means the raw values never travel or sit in the warehouse, its backups or its logs.

Is a hashed email address still personal data?

Usually yes. Regulators treat hashing as pseudonymisation, not anonymisation, and an unsalted hash of an email can be reversed by hashing a list of known addresses. Use a keyed hash (HMAC) with a secret kept on your side, or a token.

What should happen to rows that fail validation during a load?

Keep them, with the reason, somewhere they can be fixed. In our test they went to a quarantine table in the same on-prem database, with their raw values, so nothing personal left the network and nothing was silently dropped.

Adan Potyondy leads go-to-market at Neblex. Originally published at neblex.com.

title: Reel: Your Own Streaming Service or Course Platform
description:
Video is how a lot of businesses now talk to their customers. A gym sells classes, a university publishes lectures, a creator community wants its own home instead of renting space on someone else's platform. They all need the same pieces: a catalog, a player that remembers where you stopped, uploads, moderation, payments and some protection for paid content.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Reel is those pieces, the app and its server in one Java project. Like last week's Skirmish, Parley and Savor, it's a template you generate and brand, not a demo you admire.

The catalog.
Audio and subtitle tracks.
A course and its lessons.
The moderation queue.

One template, three businesses

Reel's behavior is driven by presets you switch at run time, with no rebuild:

  • Subscription service. Plans or rentals, profiles, downloads, resume across devices.
  • Creator platform. Anyone with the creator role uploads video, the server packages it, and moderators approve it before it's public. Think of a community YouTube for your niche.
  • Academy. Courses, lessons and quizzes, for training and tutorials.

On top of the preset, toggles turn ads, rentals, downloads, uploads, courses, quizzes and polls on or off. The server assigns roles (viewer, creator, moderator and admin) and the app shows each person the screens their role allows.

Uploads and moderation

Creators upload from the app and the server packages each upload for streaming and checks it against blocklists the moderators maintain. A title only goes live after a moderator approves it, and a moderator can take it down later. Takedowns take effect mid-stream: the player's heartbeat checks with the server, so a removed title stops playing instead of running to the end.

A streaming API with DRM, in core

Reel needed playback for protected video, and that belongs in the framework, not in one template. So Codename One now has a streaming API in com.codename1.media. It's small on purpose:

Class What it does
StreamRequest An HLS manifest or a progressive file URL, plus a start position, request headers, a completion callback and an optional DRM configuration. create() or createAsync() returns an ordinary Media.
DrmConfig The scheme and license server URL, headers sent with every license request, a FairPlay certificate URL and a content id.
DrmScheme AES_128 (encrypted HLS), CLEARKEY, WIDEVINE and FAIRPLAY.
MediaManager.isDrmSupported(scheme) Whether this device can play a scheme, asked before you open the stream.

Opening a protected stream that resumes where the viewer stopped:

StreamRequest req = new StreamRequest(manifestUrl)
        .setStartPosition(resumeSeconds * 1000)
        .setDrm(new DrmConfig(DrmScheme.CLEARKEY, licenseUrl)
                .addLicenseHeader("X-Reel-License", licenseToken));
req.createAsync().ready(media -> {
    player.add(BorderLayout.CENTER, media.getVideoComponent());
    player.revalidate();
});

Each port maps the scheme to what the device has: AVPlayer decrypts AES-128 HLS and plays FairPlay on Apple, and Android's player and MediaDrm handle AES-128 HLS, ClearKey, and Widevine where the device has it. Devices differ, so Reel asks first and sends the server the schemes this device can play, strongest first. The server picks one and returns the matching manifest and license URL:

List<String> out = new ArrayList<String>();
DrmScheme[] order = {DrmScheme.WIDEVINE, DrmScheme.FAIRPLAY, DrmScheme.CLEARKEY, DrmScheme.AES_128};
for (int iter = 0; iter < order.length; iter++) {
    if (MediaManager.isDrmSupported(order[iter])) {
        out.add(order[iter].name());
    }
}

Out of the box, Reel packages each video once, as AES-128 HLS and as CENC encrypted MP4 for ClearKey, under one key. Keys are issued only against a license token tied to the session, and every playlist, segment and key request carries a media token that expires and is scoped to one video and a maximum quality. Concurrent stream limits are enforced by the heartbeat. Protected video also blocks screenshots and screen recording, and can add a watermark with the account name.

I'll be direct about the limit: AES-128 and ClearKey stop casual copying, not a determined attacker, because the key reaches the device. For studio grade protection you plug in a Widevine or FairPlay license vendor through reel.drm.widevine.url and reel.drm.fairplay.url. The server forwards the license challenge, and the app code doesn't change.

Audio tracks and subtitles

Subtitles over a lesson.
Language and size settings.
A creator adds a track per language.

Creators add a subtitle track per language in the studio, as WebVTT. The server checks that it really is WebVTT and stores it beside the video, not inside the stream.

That last part is a deliberate choice. A platform player can render text tracks, but each one finds them differently, styles them differently, and some can't see a track inside an encrypted stream at all. So Reel draws subtitles itself, over the picture, and they look the same on every device and under every DRM scheme. The parser is about a hundred lines of plain Java in the template: it reads each cue's start and end time and its text, and drops WebVTT's positioning and inline tags such as <i> and <v Speaker>:

Captions.load(track.url(), loaded -> {
    if (wanted.equals(subtitleLanguage)) {
        captions = loaded;
        updateCaption();
    }
});

private void updateCaption() {
    String text = captions == null ? "" : captions.at(media.getTime());
    if (!text.equals(caption.getText())) {
        caption.setText(text);
    }
}

captions.at(millis) returns the cues that cover that moment, one per line, and the player calls it as the position moves. Switching subtitles in the player's Audio & subtitles sheet takes effect at once, because nothing about the stream changes. Switching the audio language or the quality reopens the stream at the same position, and the server marks the viewer's preferred audio track as the playlist default, so it starts in the right language.

Payments and the rest

Payments are simulated in the dev profile; the test card 4242 4242 4242 4242 goes through. Set reel.payments.provider=stripe for Stripe, and store purchases are verified with Apple and Google. Push goes through the Codename One push service. Reel also runs in a browser with nothing installed, which is how many viewers will first meet your service.

The same app on a desktop.

Try it

Generate Reel from the Initializr. The user's guide walks through every screen, and the implementor's guide covers the packaging pipeline, DRM vendors and what to change before you launch. The template source is free under MIT-0, with no royalties and no revenue share.

title: Cap agent Tailwind changes to one utility family per PR
description:
Ask an agent to “make the pricing card feel tighter” and you often get a className novel: spacing, colors, type scale, shadows, and a responsive grid rewrite in one PR. Reviewers can’t tell which change fixed the density problem and which ones were drive-by taste.

I’ve started capping agent Tailwind work to one utility family per PR. Spacing or color or typography or layout — not all four because the model felt creative.

What counts as a “family”

Group the way reviewers actually skim class strings:

  • Spacing — p-*, m-*, gap-*, space-*, and related inset padding/margin
  • Sizing — w-*, h-*, min-*, max-*, size-*
  • Color — bg-*, text-*, border-*-* (color), ring-*, fill-*, stroke-*, opacity modifiers on those
  • Typography — text-* sizes/weights (text-sm, font-medium), leading-*, tracking-*, font-* families
  • Layout — flex, grid, items-*, justify-*, col-span-*, order / place utilities
  • Effects — shadow-*, opacity-*, blur-*, transitions / animations

Pick one family as in-scope. Neighbor families stay frozen unless a single class is required for the spacing change to compile (rare — call it out).

Tailwind v3 and v4 both expose these families; v4’s dynamic spacing (mt-17, etc.) makes it easier for agents to invent one-off values. A family cap still applies — “any spacing utility” is still one family, not a license to restyle the card.

Prompt that keeps the diff narrow 

Tighten vertical density on PricingCard. Only Tailwind spacing utilities may change.

Constraints:
- Utility family allowlist: spacing only (`p/m/gap/space` and directional variants)
- Do not change color, typography, shadow, or flex/grid structure
- Prefer existing scale steps already used in neighboring cards — no arbitrary values `[…]` unless you explain why the scale fails
- Touch only `PricingCard.tsx` (and its story if classNames are demonstrated there)
- Summarize the spacing before → after in the PR body

If density cannot improve without a layout change, stop and propose a follow-up PR — do not expand scope here.

The stop condition matters. Agents that hit a wall tend to “just fix the flex” mid-PR. You want a written proposal, not scope creep.

Example of an in-family diff

Ask: tighten vertical density.

- <div className="flex flex-col gap-6 py-8 px-6 shadow-md bg-white">
+ <div className="flex flex-col gap-4 py-5 px-6 shadow-md bg-white">

Spacing changed (gap, py). Layout (flex flex-col), color (bg-white), and effects (shadow-md) stayed put. That’s a reviewable family-scoped change. If shadow-md became shadow-lg and bg-white became bg-slate-50 in the same breath, the PR stopped being about density.

How to review the className soup

Before reading JSX logic, diff the class strings:

  1. List every added/removed utility
  2. Bucket them into families
  3. If two or more families moved for a one-line ask, send it back

A tiny checklist in the PR template helps:

## Tailwind scope
- Family in this PR: spacing | sizing | color | type | layout | effects
- Other families unchanged: yes / no (explain exceptions)

Reject / send back

Reject

  • Spacing + palette + type rewrite for “make it tighter”
  • New arbitrary values (p-[13px]) when the scale already has a neighbor
  • Responsive variant explosion (sm/md/lg full restyle) inside a spacing-only ask
  • Swapping space-y-* for a flex+gap refactor “for performance” without that being the ticket (layout family — separate PR)
  • Editing @theme / tailwind.config shared scales inside a component polish PR

Accept

  • One family, clearly named in the PR
  • Class changes that mirror neighbors on the same page
  • A short before/after note (“py-6 gap-4 → py-4 gap-3”)
  • Deferred proposals for layout or token work

Why one family beats “small diff”

Line count lies. Fifty class churn lines in one family are reviewable. Twelve lines that mix color and grid are not — they hide accidental contrast regressions next to a harmless padding tweak.

This pairs with diff budgets and token freezes elsewhere in the series: blast radius is about kind of change, not only file count.

Tiny habit

Next time an agent returns a rainbow className diff, don’t argue taste token-by-token. Reply with the family cap: spacing only (or whichever family matched the ask), restore the other utilities, and ask for a follow-up if layout is truly required. Reviewers should be able to say what changed in one breath.

title: Beyond Innerwear: Making Shapewear a Fashion Statement
description:
For years, shapewear has been the invisible layer—something you wear under your clothes and hope nobody notices. But fashion evolves, and so has the role of shaping pieces. From the catwalk to street style, structured, compression-inspired garments are stepping out from underneath and into the spotlight. Here's how to wear shapewear as a statement, not just support.

The shapewear-as-fashion trend
Designers have embraced the structured, athletic aesthetic—think visible compression layers, body-conscious silhouettes, and pieces that blur the line between innerwear and outerwear. This trend celebrates the body rather than hiding it, and it gives shapewear a bold new purpose: self-expression.

How to style it as outerwear

The compression top as statement layer: Pair a sleek compression tank or muscle-enhancement top with a high-waist skirt or tailored trousers. The clean, sculpted line reads as intentional and fashion-forward.
The bodysuit as the outfit: Wear a seamless bodysuit with wide-leg pants and a blazer—sleek, modern, and effortlessly chic.
Layering with mesh: A mesh compression piece layered under a sheer or open-knit top creates texture and dimension without extra bulk.
Monochrome power: Match your shaping top to your trousers or skirt in the same tone for a streamlined, elongated silhouette.
The confidence of showing up
Wearing shaping pieces as outerwear is a statement about confidence—you're not hiding your body, you're celebrating its potential. The structured lines, the sculpted silhouette, the athletic ease—these aren't about disguise; they're about owning your style boldly and unapologetically.

From gym to street
The athleisure movement made it acceptable to wear performance wear outside the gym. Shapewear-as-fashion follows the same logic: why hide the tool that makes you feel powerful? From a compression tank at the gym to a bodysuit at brunch, the line between function and fashion has never been blurrier—and that's a good thing.

The invitation to experiment
You don't have to overhaul your wardrobe to join this trend. Start with one piece: a sleek compression top you'd normally hide, worn boldly. See how it feels to show up as yourself, confident and unapologetic. Fashion is personal expression—and if shapewear helps you express who you are, wear it loud, wear it proud, and let the world see the confidence you've been keeping underneath.
