title: Upgrading PostgreSQL 15 to 18 Using pg_upgrade
description:
PostgreSQL provides pg_upgrade to upgrade an existing database cluster to a newer major version without requiring a logical dump and restore.

In this article, I’ll demonstrate how to upgrade PostgreSQL 15 to PostgreSQL 18 using pg_upgrade with the — link option.

Unlike a traditional dump-and-restore approach, link mode allows PostgreSQL to reuse the existing relation files through hard links, significantly reducing the time and disk space required for an upgrade.

1. Checking the Existing PostgreSQL 15 Environment

First, let’s check the existing PostgreSQL installation and its configuration.

I’m using the following environment variables and version:

[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ export PGHOME=/usr/pgsql-15
[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ export PGDATA=/var/lib/pgsql/15/data
[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ export PGPORT=5415

postgres=# select version();
                                                 version
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 PostgreSQL 15.19 on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu, compiled by gcc (GCC) 11.5.0 20240719 (Red Hat 11.5.0-14), 64-bit
(1 row)

Check the current data directory and databases:

SHOW data_directory;
     data_directory
------------------------
 /var/lib/pgsql/15/data

postgres=# \l
                                                     List of databases
   Name    |  Owner   | Encoding | Locale Provider |   Collate   |    Ctype    | Locale | ICU Rules |   Access privileges
-----------+----------+----------+-----------------+-------------+-------------+--------+-----------+-----------------------
 postgres  | postgres | UTF8     | libc            | en_US.UTF-8 | en_US.UTF-8 |        |           |
 template0 | postgres | UTF8     | libc            | en_US.UTF-8 | en_US.UTF-8 |        |           | =c/postgres          +
           |          |          |                 |             |             |        |           | postgres=CTc/postgres
 template1 | postgres | UTF8     | libc            | en_US.UTF-8 | en_US.UTF-8 |        |           | postgres=CTc/postgres+
           |          |          |                 |             |             |        |           | =c/postgres
 vahiddb   | postgres | UTF8     | libc            | en_US.UTF-8 | en_US.UTF-8 |        |           |
(4 rows)

Before upgrading, let’s identify the physical location of a table. I’ll use mazandaran.tbl_person as an example.

vahiddb=# SELECT
    c.relname,
    pg_relation_filepath(c.oid) AS relative_path,
    current_setting('data_directory') || '/' ||
    pg_relation_filepath(c.oid) AS absolute_path
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE n.nspname = 'mazandaran'
  AND c.relkind IN ('r','p')
ORDER BY c.relname;
  relname   |  relative_path   |              absolute_path
------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------
 tbl_person | base/16386/16389 | /var/lib/pgsql/15/data/base/16386/16389
(1 row)

vahiddb=# select * from MAZANDARAN.tbl_person;
 id |  fname  |    lname    | sal
----+---------+-------------+------
  1 | Vahid   | Yousefzadeh | 5.00
  2 | Nader   | DastNeshan  | 6.00
  3 | Kourosh | Barmak      | 6.00
(3 rows)

Finally, use the Linux stat command to record the inode number, link count of the table’s physical file.

[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ stat -c 'Inode=%i Links=%h File=%n' \
> /var/lib/pgsql/15/data/base/16386/16389

Inode=973746 Links=1 File=/var/lib/pgsql/15/data/base/16386/16389

We’ll compare these values after the upgrade.

2. Checking the PostgreSQL 18 Installation

PostgreSQL 18 is already installed on the server. Let’s configure the environment variables for the new installation and check the new PostgreSQL version:

[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$  export PGHOME=/usr/pgsql-18
[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$  export PGDATA=/var/lib/pgsql/18/data
[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ export PGPORT=5418
[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ psql
psql (19beta4, server 18.6)
Type "help" for help.

postgres=# select version();
                                                  version
------------------------------------------------------------------
 PostgreSQL 18.6 on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu, compiled by gcc (GCC) 11.5.0 20240719 (Red Hat 11.5.0-14), 64-bit
(1 row)

Check the new data directory:

postgres=# show data_directory;
     data_directory
------------------------
 /var/lib/pgsql/18/data
(1 row)

3. Stopping Both PostgreSQL Instances

Before running pg_upgrade, both PostgreSQL instances must be stopped.

I use two shell scripts, pg15.sh and pg18.sh, to switch between the environments.

Stop PostgreSQL 15:

[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ source pg15.sh
[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$  pg_ctl -D /var/lib/pgsql/15/data -l logfile stop
waiting for server to shut down.... done
server stopped

Stop PostgreSQL 18:

[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ source pg18.sh
[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$  pg_ctl -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data -l logfile stop
waiting for server to shut down.... done
server stopped

4. Checking Upgrade Compatibility

Before performing the actual upgrade, it’s a good idea to run pg_upgrade with the — check option.

This checks whether the existing cluster is compatible with the new PostgreSQL installation without performing the upgrade.

Run:

[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_upgrade \
  --old-datadir=/var/lib/pgsql/15/data \
  --new-datadir=/var/lib/pgsql/18/data \
  --old-bindir=/usr/pgsql-15/bin \
  --new-bindir=/usr/pgsql-18/bin \
  --check


Performing Consistency Checks
-----------------------------
Checking cluster versions                                     ok

Checking database connection settings                         ok
Checking database user is the install user                    ok
Checking for prepared transactions                            ok
Checking for contrib/isn with bigint-passing mismatch         ok
Checking data type usage                                      ok
Checking for not-null constraint inconsistencies              ok
Checking for presence of required libraries                   ok
Checking database user is the install user                    ok
Checking for prepared transactions                            ok
Checking for new cluster tablespace directories               ok

*Clusters are compatible*

The compatibility check completed successfully.

5. Performing the Upgrade Using Link Mode

Now we can perform the actual upgrade.

The important option in this command is — link.

[postgres@OEL98-PG ~]$ /usr/pgsql-18/bin/pg_upgrade \
--old-datadir=/var/lib/pgsql/15/data \
--new-datadir=/var/lib/pgsql/18/data \
--old-bindir=/usr/pgsql-15/bin \
--new-bindir=/usr/pgsql-18/bin \
--link



Performing Consistency Checks
-----------------------------
Checking cluster versions                                     ok
Checking database connection settings                         ok
Checking database user is the install user                    ok
Checking for prepared transactions                            ok
Checking for contrib/isn with bigint-passing mismatch         ok
Checking data type usage                                      ok
Checking for not-null constraint inconsistencies              ok
Creating dump of global objects                               ok
Creating dump of database schemas
                                                              ok
Checking for presence of required libraries                   ok
Checking database user is the install user                    ok
Checking for prepared transactions                            ok
Checking for new cluster tablespace directories               ok

If pg_upgrade fails after this point, you must re-initdb the
new cluster before continuing.

Performing Upgrade
------------------
Setting locale and encoding for new cluster                   ok
Analyzing all rows in the new cluster                         ok
Freezing all rows in the new cluster                          ok
Deleting files from new pg_xact                               ok
Copying old pg_xact to new server                             ok
Setting oldest XID for new cluster                            ok
Setting next transaction ID and epoch for new cluster         ok
Deleting files from new pg_multixact/offsets                  ok
Copying old pg_multixact/offsets to new server                ok
Deleting files from new pg_multixact/members                  ok
Copying old pg_multixact/members to new server                ok

Important: What does — link actually do?

The — link option uses hard links instead of copying the user relation files into the new cluster.

This means the old and new cluster can reference the same underlying physical file through different directory entries.

Consequently:

The upgrade can be significantly faster than copying all relation files.
It requires less additional disk space.

Once the new PostgreSQL cluster is started, the old cluster must not be started again.
PostgreSQL explicitly warns about this in the upgrade output:

title: The Scoreboard Is a Formula: Systems Rust for Speed Demon 2026
description:
The scoreboard in a systems competition does not time your program; it evaluates a mathematical function.

Building engines for Speed Demon 2026 across Tracks A (Ingest), C (Join), and D (Traverse) with zero external Rust crate dependencies, our initial instinct was to chase the clock. But the harness did not evaluate raw latency alone. It evaluated a multi-variable objective function balancing wall-clock runtime ($T$), peak memory working set ($M$), stripped source line count ($S$), and external dependency weight ($D$).

Treating the scoreboard as a formal optimization problem inverted our systems engineering priorities:

  • We permitted working memory to expand when runtime rewards outweighed memory penalties.
  • We avoided all external crates to bypass an immediate 9.88% dependency penalty.
  • We overhauled our benchmarking harness when Windows cold-start phenomena introduced a 35 to 50 ms measurement bias.
  • We made the hot execution path boring: dynamic hash tables and pointer indirections were replaced by flat contiguous arrays, dense integer ranks, and Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) tables.

This formula-driven approach unlocked sub-second execution across multi-million record datasets, with Track A achieving an official Linux leaderboard score of 76.622 points at 0.038 seconds.

TL;DR:

  1. Optimize the formula, not just the clock: Runtime dominates memory with a 2.5:1 sensitivity ratio ($T^{0.50}$ vs $M^{0.20}$). However, adding a single external crate levies an immediate 9.88% penalty on $K$ ($D^{0.15}$), requiring an 18.8% reduction in runtime just to break even. We operated with zero external Rust crate dependencies ($D = 1.0$), relying on the Rust standard library, direct POSIX FFI, and architecture-specific SIMD intrinsics.
  2. Make the hot path boring: Dynamic hash tables introduce pointer indirection, non-contiguous memory access, and dynamic reallocations. Replacing dynamic maps with flat lookup arrays, dense integer ranks, and Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) tables eliminated pointer chasing and reduced wall-clock latency across all tracks.
  3. Verify the benchmark first: Unwarmed executions on Windows imposed a 35 to 50 ms cold-start penalty on whichever binary executed first in an alternating sequence. Pre-run warmups and randomized trial ordering reduced observed order bias to 1.71 ms ($p = 0.4359$, showing no detectable order effect), while a separate paired difference test supported a measurable 4.04 ms speedup ($p = 4.62\times 10^{-4}$).

Headline Results: Track A scored 76.622 points officially on the Linux scoring runner (0.038 s, 31 MB peak working set as reported on the leaderboard). Tracks C and D achieved 0.1275 s (54.64 MB peak working set) and 0.6600 s (160 MB peak working set) in local benchmark measurements on our development host; official competition scores for C and D remain unmeasured.

The Scoreboard Is a Formula: Why Clock Chasing Failed

In Speed Demon 2026, the efficiency coefficient $K$ and speed points are computed using four orthogonal axes:

K = (T_ref / T)^0.50 * min(M_ref / M, 50)^0.20 * min(S_ref / S, 1)^0.15 * (D_ref / D)^0.15
points = 50 * log10(K)

Per scoring.py line 57, speed points scale logarithmically with $K$. The reference baselines evaluated on the official Linux harness come from the competition kit (calibration-seed1.json and reference_axes.json):

Track Official Score Runtime ($T$) Peak Memory ($M$) Lines ($S$) Commit & Environment
Track A (Official) 76.622 0.038 s 31 MB (as shown on leaderboard) 286 (scored) 7168b09 (official Linux scoring runner)
Track A (Candidate) NOT EVALUATED (local test) 59.59 ms (local) ~30 MB peak working set 277 (raw) adbd3f1 (Windows dev host, native .exe)
Track C (Join) NOT MEASURED (no official score) 0.1275 s 54.64 MB peak working set 454 (raw, unformatted) 1be4222 (Local benchmark measurement)
Track D (Traverse) NOT MEASURED (no official score) 0.6600 s 160 MB peak working set 802 (raw, unformatted) b36d7d1 (Local benchmark measurement)

Status and reference baselines:

  • Track A Official Submission: Commit 7168b09 is the sole evaluated official submission, achieving $K = 34.074745$ (76.622 points, 0.038 s, 31 MB as shown on the leaderboard, 286 scored lines).
  • Track A Candidate: Candidate commit adbd3f1 was tested strictly locally on our Windows development host as a native executable (improving paired median runtime from 63.86 ms to 59.59 ms, $p = 4.62\times 10^{-4}$); it was not evaluated on the official leaderboard.
  • Tracks C and D: Have no official scores. Line counts (454 and 802) are raw, unformatted source counts from track-c/src/main.rs and track-d/src/main.rs; memory figures report peak working set in MB as logged locally in track-c/PERF.md and track-d/PERF.md.

Official Linux Harness Reference Baselines

All reference baselines use (D_{\text{ref}} = 1) across all tracks.

  • Track A: (T_{\text{ref}} = 32.047276\text{ s}), (M_{\text{ref}} = 217\text{ MiB}) (227,983,360 bytes), (S_{\text{ref}} = 56)
  • Track C: (T_{\text{ref}} = 14.444059\text{ s}), (M_{\text{ref}} = 350\text{ MiB}) (367,435,776 bytes), (S_{\text{ref}} = 108)
  • Track D: (T_{\text{ref}} = 72.692655\text{ s}), (M_{\text{ref}} = 851\text{ MiB}) (892,915,712 bytes), (S_{\text{ref}} = 43)

Mathematical Sensitivity & Exponent Derivation

The scoring exponents dictate our system architecture:

∂(points)/∂ ln(1/T)       0.50
───────────────────  =  ──────  =  2.50
∂(points)/∂ ln(1/M)       0.20
  1. Runtime Dominates Memory (Sensitivity Ratio 2.5:1): Wall-clock runtime is uncapped, and its exponent ($0.50$) is 2.5 times larger than the memory exponent ($0.20$). A 1% reduction in runtime produces the same point increase as a 2.5% reduction in memory. Therefore, any architectural optimization that reduces memory at the expense of runtime must satisfy:

$$\frac{T_{\text{new}}}{T_{\text{old}}} < \left( \frac{M_{\text{old}}}{M_{\text{new}}} \right)^{0.20 / 0.50} = \left( \frac{M_{\text{old}}}{M_{\text{new}}} \right)^{0.40}$$

  1. The 9.88% Crate Tax ($D_{\text{ref}} = 1, D^{0.15}$): Per final_scoring.py line 275, $D = 1 + \text{direct_dependencies}$, and $D_{\text{ref}} = 1$. Importing even a single external crate moves $D$ from 1 to 2. The dependency factor drops to:

$$(1 / 2)^{0.15} \approx 0.901250 \quad (-9.875\%)$$

This imposes an immediate deduction of:

$$\Delta \text{points} = 50 \times \log_{10}(0.901250) \approx -2.258\text{ points}$$

To offset this loss purely through execution speed, the new runtime $T'$ must satisfy:

$$(T / T')^{0.50} \times 0.901250 \ge 1 \implies \frac{T}{T'} \ge (1 / 0.901250)^2 = 2^{0.30} \approx 1.23114$$

An external crate must make your program at least 23.11% faster (reducing runtime by $18.78\%$) merely to break even. Rather than taking on this dependency penalty against generic libraries, we implemented zero external Rust crate dependencies ($D = 1.0$), using standard library primitives, direct POSIX FFI, and architecture-specific SIMD intrinsics.

  1. The 50x Memory Cap & The Track A Multi-Pass Trade-Off: The memory term is clamped at $\min(M_{\text{ref}} / M, 50)^{0.20}$. Beyond a 50x reduction, further memory cuts yield exactly zero additional points. For Track A ($M_{\text{ref}} = 227,983,360\text{ bytes}$), the cap occurs at:

$$M_{\text{cap}} = \frac{227,983,360}{50} = 4,559,667\text{ bytes} \approx 4.56\text{ MB}$$

Because retaining 3.1 million raw log records in RAM takes over 6.2 MB even with packed 16-bit integers, hitting this cap would require streaming from disk in multiple passes. In our experimental 4-pass streaming prototype (evidence/multipass_experiment.txt), peak working set dropped from ~30 MB to approximately 19.69 MB. However, re-reading chunks from disk on the same Windows test host increased mean runtime from ~63.8 ms to ~223.8 ms (runs logged between 208.58 and 246.19 ms).

Because this 3.5x runtime slowdown far exceeded the allowable threshold $(\frac{30}{19.69})^{0.40} \approx 1.18$, multi-pass streaming was decisively discarded.

  1. The Streaming Buffer Penalty in Track C: In iteration v5 (track-c/PERF.md:145-155), switching from memory mapping to 1 MiB chunk streaming cut peak working set by 48.2% (from 379.29 MB to 196.27 MB, saving 183 MB). However, managing record splits and quoted field boundaries across chunk edges increased runtime by 45.3% (from 0.4933 s to 0.7168 s).

Applying the formula:

$$\text{Factor on } K = \left(\frac{379.29}{196.27}\right)^{0.20} \times \left(\frac{0.4933}{0.7168}\right)^{0.50} = 1.1408 \times 0.8296 = 0.9464 \quad (-5.36\%)$$

The net score dropped by $1.20\text{ points}$. In iteration v6, we discarded chunk streaming in favor of whole-file memory mapping with 64-bit hash sorting, which dropped runtime to 0.1275 s and peak working set to 54.64 MB simultaneously.

When Our Benchmark Lied to Us: The Windows Cold-Start Trap

Before trusting performance data, we had to fix our benchmark harness.

During early Track A development on Windows 11, paired A/B benchmarks exhibited severe measurement hysteresis: whichever executable ran first in an alternating sequence suffered an artificial 35 to 50 ms penalty.

Unwarmed Alternating Runs (Raw Wall Clock):
Run 1 (Binary A, Cold):  112.4 ms  <-- Absorbs initialization overhead
Run 2 (Binary B, Warm):   64.1 ms  <-- Benefits from warm file & system caches
Run 3 (Binary B, Cold):  108.9 ms  <-- Reversal: B absorbs initialization overhead
Run 4 (Binary A, Warm):   63.7 ms  <-- A runs fast

Plausible Contributing Factors

While we did not instrument low-level Windows kernel events using ETW (Event Tracing for Windows), plausible contributing factors include:

  • NTFS Path and Metadata Caching: First-time directory parsing and handle resolution incur file-system lock acquisition and disk metadata traversal.
  • Virtual Memory Allocation & Soft Faults: The initial process allocation must commit pages from the zeroed-page pool; subsequent process spawns benefit from standby page list reuse.
  • CPU Frequency Scaling & Power States: Modern processors (such as the Intel Core i5-13420H) transition through hardware P-states and Intel SpeedStep scaling. Unwarmed binaries execute while the CPU frequency ramps up from idle governor states.

The Corrected Experimental Protocol

To address this measurement artifact, we revised our benchmark protocol with two safeguards:

  1. Mandatory Untimed Warmups: Every measured binary executed an untimed preliminary run immediately before the timed trials to populate OS file-system cache and transition the CPU core to active performance states.
  2. Randomized Trial Sequencing: In each paired comparison $i \in {1 \dots 30}$, execution order was randomly chosen between baseline-first ($B\text{-first}$) and candidate-first ($C\text{-first}$) using randomized trial ordering (pseudo-random selection via Python's standard random generator with a fixed seed). 
Warmup & Randomized Protocol:
[Untimed Warmup B] -> [Untimed Warmup C]
Trial 1: Random(B, C) -> Timed C -> Timed B
Trial 2: Random(B, C) -> Timed B -> Timed C
...
Trial 30: Random(B, C) -> Timed C -> Timed B

Statistical Analysis: Order Bias vs. Paired Speedup

Our audit of the 30 paired validation runs (evidence/cold_start_benchmarks.txt) revealed two distinct statistical dimensions:

Benchmark Dataset: Track A full-seed1 (3,100,000 lines, 72 hours)
Sample Size: N = 30 paired runs
Baseline (commit 7fe5e92):   Median = 63.86 ms | Mean = 63.79 ms | SD = 3.75 ms
Candidate (commit adbd3f1):  Median = 59.59 ms | Mean = 59.75 ms | SD = 3.75 ms
Paired Difference (B - C):   Median = +3.69 ms | Mean = +4.04 ms
  1. The Order Effect Audit ($p = 0.4359$): Stratifying the trials by execution sequence:
    • When Baseline ran first ($N_B = 13$): Mean paired difference $= +5.01\text{ ms}$, Median $= +4.10\text{ ms}$
    • When Candidate ran first ($N_C = 17$): Mean paired difference $= +3.30\text{ ms}$, Median $= +3.59\text{ ms}$
    • Observed order bias ($\bar{d}_B - \bar{d}_C$): $1.71\text{ ms}$
    • Welch's two-sample $t$-test: $t = 0.7935$, degrees of freedom $\text{df} = 25.8$, $p = 0.4359$

Statistical Interpretation: The high $p$-value ($p = 0.4359$) indicates that the difference in observed speedup between orderings is statistically indistinguishable from zero noise. However, failing to reject the null hypothesis of order bias does not prove that bias is entirely absent, nor does it establish that the candidate code is faster.

  1. The Paired Performance Difference ($p = 4.62\times 10^{-4}$): The statistical evidence for performance improvement is provided separately by the paired difference Student's $t$-test across the 30 trials:

$$t = \frac{\bar{d}}{\text{SE}_d} = \frac{4.04\text{ ms}}{1.0237\text{ ms}} = 3.9466 \quad (\text{df} = 29)$$

  • Two-tailed $p$-value: $p = 4.62 \times 10^{-4}$
  • 95% Confidence Interval for mean difference: $[1.95\text{ ms}, 6.13\text{ ms}]$
  • Cohen's $d_z$ effect size: $d_z = \frac{4.04}{5.61} \approx 0.72$ (medium-to-large effect)

Under this paired testing protocol, Candidate Minimized (adbd3f1) demonstrated a statistically significant paired mean runtime reduction of 4.04 ms ($p = 4.62\times 10^{-4}$, 95% CI: $[1.95\text{ ms}, 6.13\text{ ms}]$) relative to the baseline on our Windows development host. Crucially, this local improvement is distinct from the official Linux leaderboard result (0.038 s on commit 7168b09), as Windows measurements include file-system and scheduling overhead inherent to the local OS.

Architecture Evolution Across Tracks

To achieve sub-second execution without external crates, each track evolved from conventional idiomatic Rust into flat, hardware-friendly data pipelines:

flowchart TD
    subgraph TrackA["Track A: Ingest Pipeline"]
        A1["Raw Log Stream (3.1M lines)"] --> A2["Parallel Chunk Slicing via std::thread::scope"]
        A2 --> A3["64-bit Unaligned SWAR Parse<br>(p+5: month, day, hour in 1 read)"]
        A3 --> A4["Direct Endpoint Rank Lookup<br>(CRC32 + Linear Probing, Rank below 1,842)"]
        A4 --> A5["Direct Bucket Scatter<br>(ep_buckets[rank].push(lat))"]
        A5 --> A6["Parallel pdqsort on Small Slices<br>(Avoids sorting full 32K hourly arrays)"]
    end

    subgraph TrackC["Track C: Join Pipeline"]
        C1["Hostile CSV File (3.32M rows)"] --> C2["Memory-Mapped Slice (direct POSIX mmap FFI)"]
        C2 --> C3["256-bit AVX2 SIMD Quote Scanner<br>(_mm256_cmpeq_epi8 + trailing_zeros)"]
        C3 --> C4["1 MB Flat Region Vector<br>(O(1) array read for region_id below 1M)"]
        C4 --> C5["64-bit Multiplicative Hash<br>(hash_slice into u64)"]
        C5 --> C6["Thread-Local Vector Sort and Dedup<br>(madvise advisory hints in 8 MB chunks)"]
    end

    subgraph TrackD["Track D: Traverse Pipeline"]
        D1["Graph Data (1.74M nodes, 5M edges)"] --> D2["Two-Pass Parallel CSR Build<br>(Atomic counts + Relaxed cursor stores)"]
        D2 --> D3["Packed 6-Byte Edge Arrays<br>(repr(C, packed) Edge: u32 to, u16 weight)"]
        D3 --> D4["Balanced Bidirectional Dijkstra<br>(Expand smaller frontier, tie resolves to forward)"]
        D4 --> D5["2 MB Thread-Local SmallMap<br>(Key + Val in contiguous 8-byte MapEntry)"]
        D5 --> D6["4-Ary Flattened Min-Heap<br>(Heap4Fast: halved tree depth)"]
    end

Track A: Ingest (Sub-40 Milliseconds in Plain Rust)

The Problem in One Sentence

Ingest 3,100,000 lines of space-delimited logs spanning a 72-hour window, extract microsecond timestamps, intern 1,842 endpoints, and compute hourly p50, p90, and p99 latencies without external crates (specs/a-ingest.md).

Profiling: Where the Time Actually Went

Instrumentation of Phase 2 with profile_phase2.rs (evidence/transcript_step889_profile.txt) across 12 worker threads revealed 215.48 ms of cumulative CPU time (23.35 ms wall-clock time):

  • pdqsort: 91.29 ms (42.4% CPU share)
  • Formatting and percentiles: 91.71 ms (42.6% CPU share)
  • Writer mutex serialization: 20.85 ms (9.7% CPU share)
  • Key packing: 11.64 ms (5.4% CPU share)

Sorting latencies was our primary compute bottleneck: merging records into a single hourly array forced sorting $\sim 32,291$ keys per active hour.

The Optimization: Direct Bucket Scattering

Instead of grouping latencies into a unified hourly buffer and sorting the entire array, we scattered latencies directly into per-endpoint rank vectors during parsing:

ep_buckets[rank].push(lat);

Sorting small, per-endpoint vectors in parallel was substantially faster than sorting one large array. In a strict 30-pair benchmark on our Windows development host, direct bucket scattering dropped paired median runtime from 63.86 ms to 59.59 ms ($p = 4.62\times 10^{-4}$).

Sorting Micro-Benchmarks vs. End-to-End Execution

To evaluate sorting strategies for Phase 2, we benchmarked three isolated sorting kernels on the active hour data (evidence/transcript_steps898_913_sorts.txt):

  • Counting Sort (cand_p2_counting.exe): Median = 79.00 ms (allocating and scanning 65,536 frequency bins was penalized by cache clearance overhead).
  • 2-Pass Radix Sort (cand_p2_radix.exe): Median = 53.26 ms (two 8-bit passes over latency keys).
  • Direct Slice Scatter (cand_p2_direct.exe): Median = 51.42 ms (direct push into rank vectors followed by standard pdqsort on populated slices).

Clarification: The 51.42 ms figure was an isolated micro-benchmark measuring Phase 2 latency sorting alone. The 59.59 ms figure represents the complete end-to-end binary execution (including disk I/O, timestamp parsing, endpoint interning, Phase 2 sorting, and stdout formatting).

Approach & Annotated Code Snippet

Log timestamps follow RFC 3339 within a strict 72-hour window (2026-10-30T18:00:00 to 2026-11-02T17:59:59.999999Z). We parse them branchlessly at byte offset $p + 5$ using an unaligned 64-bit SWAR (SIMD Within A Register) read:

// SWAR timestamp parse: single unaligned 64-bit load at byte offset p + 5
let w_ts = unsafe { (b.as_ptr().add(p + 5) as *const u64).read_unaligned() };
let m = ((w_ts >> 8) & 0xFF) as usize - 48;
let d = (((w_ts >> 24) & 0xFF) as usize - 48) * 10
    + (((w_ts >> 32) & 0xFF) as usize - 48);
let hr = (((w_ts >> 48) & 0xFF) as usize - 48) * 10
    + (((w_ts >> 56) & 0xFF) as usize - 48);
// Compute hour bucket index (ranges 18..89 inside 96 slots) via arithmetic
let h = ((d + 31 * m) - 30) * 24 + hr;

Detailed Arithmetic Trace & Specialization Invariants:

On a little-endian x86-64 architecture, loading 8 bytes from offset $p + 5$ of the 27-byte timestamp "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.ffffffZ " maps characters into register w_ts:

  • Byte 0 (offset 5): '1' (first digit of month)
  • Byte 1 (offset 6): '0' for October ($m = 0$), '1' for November ($m = 1$)
  • Byte 2 (offset 7): '-'
  • Byte 3 (offset 8): Day tens digit ('3' or '0')
  • Byte 4 (offset 9): Day units digit ('0', '1', or '2')
  • Byte 5 (offset 10): 'T'
  • Byte 6 (offset 11): Hour tens digit ('0', '1', or '2')
  • Byte 7 (offset 12): Hour units digit ('0' through '9')

Because October has 31 days, November days are offset by $+31$. For Oct 30, $h = (30 - 30) \times 24 + hr = hr \in [18, 23]$. For Nov 2, $h = (2 + 31 - 30) \times 24 + hr = 72 + hr \in [72, 89]$. The entire 72-hour window maps cleanly into hours $18 \dots 89$ within a 96-slot array in zero branches and zero heap allocations.

Important Boundary Invariant: This parser is strictly specialized for the competition dataset: it assumes little-endian byte ordering, a fixed 4-digit year of 2026, fixed 2-digit fields, 6 fractional digits, and dates restricted to Oct 30–Nov 02. It is not a general RFC 3339 parser. Input from other months or variable fractional lengths would produce invalid hour indices or out-of-bounds array writes.

Track A Progression Milestones

Optimization Step Before After Mechanism Benchmark Type
Sequential to Parallel 0.797 s 0.471 s Sliced body across cores via std::thread::scope Progression milestone (track-a/PERF.md)

Track C: Join (Hostile CSVs and the Zero-Collision Gamble)

The Problem in One Sentence

Parse 3,320,000 rows of hostile, multi-line quoted CSV records, join them against 2.2 MB of regional geographic mappings, and compute aggregates and distinct name counts across 240 countries without external crates (specs/c-join.md).

The Zero-Collision Gamble: Probabilistic Hashing

Distinct name counting across 3,320,000 records was our main bottleneck. In our initial v1 baseline using a per-country HashSet<Vec<u8>>, execution took 5.5230 s with a peak working set of 405.69 MB (track-c/PERF.md:11-13).

We replaced heap-allocated string storage with a custom 64-bit multiplicative hash (hash_slice in track-c/src/main.rs:34-45):

#[inline(always)]
unsafe fn hash_slice(mut p: *const u8, len: usize) -> u64 {
    let mut h = (len as u64) ^ 0x517cc1b727220a95;
    let mut rem = len;
    while rem >= 8 {
        let v = (p as *const u64).read_unaligned();
        h = (h ^ v).rotate_left(27).wrapping_mul(0x94d049bb133111eb);
        p = p.add(8);
        rem -= 8;
    }
    if rem > 0 {
        let mut tail = 0u64;
        std::ptr::copy_nonoverlapping(p, &mut tail as *mut u64 as *mut u8, rem);
        h = (h ^ tail).rotate_left(27).wrapping_mul(0x94d049bb133111eb);
    }
    h
}

In Phase 2, each country's 64-bit hash vectors were merged, sorted with sort_unstable(), and deduplicated with dedup(). The final vector length provided the distinct count.

Birthday Bound Derivation & Idealized Assumptions:

Under the assumption of an idealized uniform and independent random hash function, the probability $p$ of observing at least one collision among $n = 100{,}520$ distinct names in a $2^{64}$ hash space is given by the classical birthday-bound approximation:

$$p \approx \frac{100520 \times 100519}{2 \times 2^{64}} = \frac{10,104,169,880}{3.68935 \times 10^{19}} \approx 2.7387 \times 10^{-10}$$

This calculation yields approximately 1 in 3.65 billion ($1 / (2.7387 \times 10^{-10}) \approx 3.651 \times 10^9$).

Distinction of Theoretical vs. Empirical Guarantees:

  • Idealized Model vs. Custom Function: The $2.7387 \times 10^{-10}$ figure is derived assuming a uniform random oracle. It is not a formal upper bound for our custom SplitMix-style multiplicative hash function (hash_slice), which could exhibit higher collision rates under adversarial or structured string patterns.
  • Empirical String Set Audit: To verify correctness on actual data, we audited full-seed1 against an exact Python baseline. The audit extracted all original unescaped name strings into an exact Python set of strings, confirming 100,520 distinct strings. Hashing each string with hash_slice produced 100,520 distinct 64-bit integers. No hash collisions were observed among the 100,520 distinct strings in this dataset (track-c/PERF.md:184-189).
  • Formal Correctness Scope: Probabilistic hashing remains a calculated trade-off. While it achieved 100% test pass rates and enabled dropping peak working set to 54.64 MB and execution time to 0.1275 s, it does not provide the deterministic exactness guarantee required of a general-purpose database engine.

Approach & Annotated Code Snippet

In our final design, records.csv is mapped via direct POSIX FFI using a manually declared extern "C" mmap binding. Worker threads scan records using 256-bit AVX2 SIMD intrinsics while issuing madvise(..., MADV_DONTNEED) advisory requests in 8 MB batches (track-c/src/main.rs:27-31):

// AVX2 256-bit SIMD scanner: locate quote delimiter across 32 bytes in parallel
while q.add(32) <= end_ptr {
    let chunk = _mm256_loadu_si256(q as *const __m256i);
    let mask = _mm256_movemask_epi8(_mm256_cmpeq_epi8(chunk, v_quote)) as u32;
    if mask != 0 {
        q = q.add(mask.trailing_zeros() as usize);
        break;
    }
    q = q.add(32);
}

Advisory Nature of madvise: madvise(..., MADV_DONTNEED) is an advisory request to the operating system kernel indicating that mapped pages are no longer needed. It does not guarantee immediate physical page-cache reclamation or immediate resident memory release; its actual effect on working-set memory depends on kernel page reclamation policy, memory pressure, and whether the mapping is private or shared.

Memory Safety Invariant: The loop condition q.add(32) <= end_ptr guarantees that vector loads never cross past the end of the memory-mapped file slice. Tail bytes are processed by a scalar fallback loop.

Track C Progression Milestones

Iteration Median Runtime Peak Working Set Architectural Changes
v1 Baseline 5.5230 s 405.69 MB Single-threaded; HashMap regions; HashSet names (track-c/PERF.md:11-13)
v2 Direct Table 2.1155 s 395.74 MB Replaced HashMap with flat 1M-entry Vec and dense country IDs (track-c/PERF.md:35-37)
v3 Global Dictionary 1.2767 s 210.32 MB Replaced per-country sets with global name dictionary and bitsets (track-c/PERF.md:78-80)
v4 Parallel Chunking 0.4933 s 379.29 MB Two-pass parallel quote counting and boundary alignment (12 threads, track-c/PERF.md:115-117)
v5 Streaming Buffers 0.7168 s 196.27 MB Streamed 1 MiB chunks; cut memory by 183 MB but slowed runtime 45.3% (track-c/PERF.md:152-154)
v6 64-Bit Hash Dedup 0.1275 s 54.64 MB Replaced name dicts with 64-bit hash blocks and parallel dedup (track-c/PERF.md:196-199)

Track D: Traverse (2,000 Shortest Paths in Sub-Second Runtime)

The Problem in One Sentence

Navigate a 1,740,512-node, 5,000,000-edge directed graph to answer 2,000 shortest-path point-to-point queries under 1 GB of memory without external crates (specs/d-traverse.md).

The Bidirectional Memory Explosion

In iteration v3, unidirectional Dijkstra across 12 worker threads answered 2,000 queries on full-seed1 in 2.5154 s (track-d/PERF.md:34-37). In v4, balanced bidirectional Dijkstra dropped runtime to 0.8019 s (a 3.14x speedup, track-d/PERF.md:52-55).

However, peak working set exploded from 223.79 MB to 418.71 MB. Because storing two 64-bit distance arrays across 1,740,512 nodes required 14 MB per array, 12 concurrent worker threads consumed:

$$12 \times 2 \times 13.92\text{ MB} = 334.18\text{ MB of distance arrays alone}$$

The Solution: Thread-Local SmallMap & Packed Edges

To resolve this explosion, we implemented SmallMap (track-d/src/main.rs:150-208): a thread-local open-addressing table with linear probing. Because road network queries explore only a small fraction of the 1.74M node graph, each thread allocates a 2 MB table ($2^{18} = 262,144$ entries) storing packed 8-byte MapEntry structs.

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
#[repr(C)]
struct MapEntry {
    key: u32,
    val: u32,
}

Cache Terminology Note: While this 2 MiB per-thread table was designed with CPU L3 cache budgets in mind (the host Core i5-13420H features a 12 MB shared L3 cache), we did not instrument PMU hardware performance counters (such as L3 miss rates). We characterize SmallMap strictly as a compact in-memory thread-local flat structure.

Settled Nodes vs. Explored Entries & Table Capacity Limits

In analyzing SmallMap, we must explicitly distinguish between two graph search metrics:

  1. Settled Nodes: Nodes popped from the priority queue whose shortest distances are final.
  2. Explored/Reached Entries: Every neighboring node encountered during edge relaxation is probed via probe_entry. If new, it is inserted into SmallMap and its slot index is pushed to touched.

In dense road networks, the count of explored nodes in the active frontier is substantially larger than the count of settled nodes.

Capacity Limits & Termination Behavior:
SmallMap allocates a fixed capacity of 262,144 entries ($2^{18}$). It uses multiplicative Fibonacci hashing ((k as usize).wrapping_mul(0x9e3779b9) & mask) and linear probing (idx = (idx + 1) & mask). Crucially, the implementation contains no load-factor limits, no dynamic resizing, and no maximum probe length limit.
If a search on an adversarial or dense graph causes the number of distinct explored nodes to reach 262,144 (a 100% load factor), probe_entry will enter an infinite loop scanning the table, freezing the worker thread. For the competition dataset full-seed1, query frontiers touched far fewer than 262,144 nodes, keeping probe sequences short.

Distance Overflow Guard & dijkstra64 Behavior

Tracing the edge relaxation logic in track-d/src/main.rs:656-659:

let nd = df + ew;
if nd >= best || nd >= 65534 {
    continue;
}

Every distance relaxation in both forward and backward searches is guarded by:
if nd >= best || nd >= 65534 { continue; }.

Analysis of the Overflow Invariant:

  1. No 16-Bit Integer Wraparound in Fast Path: Because the search immediately drops any relaxation where $nd \ge 65,534$, nd is guaranteed to be $< 65,534$ when executing let nd16 = nd as u16;. Therefore, nd as u16 does not wrap around modulo 65,536 during table updates.
  2. Pruning of Cumulative Distances $\ge 65,534$: The bidirectional fast path cannot discover shortest paths whose cumulative length is $\ge 65,534$; such transitions are pruned.
  3. Fallback Limitations: When the search finishes, it evaluates: 
   let ans = if best != u32::MAX {
       best as i64
   } else if had_large {
       dijkstra64(&head_ref, &edges_ref, &large_ref, s, t)
   } else {
       -1
   };

Notice that had_large is set only when an individual edge weight is 65,535 (if ew == 65535 { had_large = true; }). The fallback dijkstra64 uses 64-bit distances and resolves large edge weights via large_map. It was designed specifically to handle individual edge-weight overflow.
If a graph contains a reachable path whose cumulative distance exceeds 65,534 composed solely of smaller edge weights ($< 65,535$), had_large remains false. The fast path prunes the route, best remains u32::MAX, and the function returns -1 (unreachable). On full-seed1, all 2,000 queries were answered with 100% digest precision because query distances remained within limits or traversed large-weight links. For general graphs, however, this remains an architectural limitation.

Edge Memory Layout & Rust Alignment Verification

The graph edge structure is declared in track-d/src/main.rs:24-28:

#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
#[repr(C, packed)]
struct Edge {
    to: u32,
    weight: u16,
}

Alignment Audit: In standard Rust, an unadorned struct Edge { to: u32, weight: u16 } would have size_of = 8 and align_of = 4 due to 2 bytes of trailing alignment padding. Because we explicitly declared #[repr(C, packed)], padding was eliminated:

  • size_of::<Edge>() is exactly 6 bytes.
  • align_of::<Edge>() is 1 byte.

Across 5,000,000 edges, this dropped CSR graph memory from 40 MB to 30 MB (a 25% reduction). To avoid undefined behavior from taking unaligned references (&edge.to), code always reads fields by value copy (let to = e.to;), compiling to unaligned 32-bit register loads supported natively by x86-64 hardware.

Distinguishing Iterations v5 and v6

  • Iteration v5 (0.7400 s median, 160 MB peak working set): Introduced packed 6-byte edges, custom 4-ary min-heap (Heap4Fast), and the initial 2 MB SmallMap (track-d/PERF.md:77-80).
  • Iteration v6 (0.6600 s median, 0.5500 s minimum, 160 MB peak working set): Unified key and value into contiguous 8-byte MapEntry structs, implemented direct slot index resetting (clear_slots), and preallocated worker buffers (65,536 elements for Heap4Fast and 131,072 elements for touched), eliminating dynamic allocations during search (track-d/PERF.md:95-97).

Approach & Annotated Code Snippet

To maximize spatial locality, probe_entry performs membership checking and slot reservation in a single probe sequence:

// Unified probe: check membership and reserve slot in a single probe sequence
fn probe_entry(&mut self, k: u32) -> (usize, u32, bool) {
    let mut idx = (k as usize).wrapping_mul(0x9e3779b9) & self.mask;
    loop {
        let entry = unsafe { self.entries.get_unchecked(idx) };
        if entry.key == k { return (idx, entry.val, false); }
        if entry.key == !0u32 {
            unsafe { self.entries.get_unchecked_mut(idx).key = k; return (idx, !0u32, true); }
        }
        idx = (idx + 1) & self.mask;
    }
}

Each MapEntry occupies 8 bytes, so eight consecutive entries span 64 bytes. This compact layout improves spatial locality during linear probing, although probe sequences can cross cache-line boundaries and vary in length.

Track D Progression Milestones

Iteration Median Runtime Peak Working Set Architectural Changes
v2 Multi-Query 2.6477 s 223.77 MB 2,000 queries distributed across 12 threads via std::thread::scope (track-d/PERF.md:19-22)
v3 Parallel CSR 2.5154 s 223.79 MB Two-pass parallel CSR graph construction via atomic degree counting (track-d/PERF.md:34-37)
v4 Bidirectional 0.8019 s 418.71 MB Balanced bidirectional search; cut runtime 3.14x; spiked memory (track-d/PERF.md:52-55)
v5 Packed SmallMap 0.7400 s 160 MB Packed 6-byte edges; 2 MB SmallMap replaced 336 MB distance vectors (track-d/PERF.md:77-80)
v6 Unified MapEntry 0.6600 s 160 MB 8-byte contiguous MapEntry; $O(\text{touched})$ reset; 4-ary min-heap (track-d/PERF.md:95-97)

Why the Obvious Optimization Failed

Systems performance engineering is defined as much by what you discard as by what you deploy. Across all three tracks, intuitive optimizations consistently lost to formula-aware designs:

Track Obvious Optimization Why It Failed Successful Alternative
Track A Multi-Pass Chunk Streaming Attempting to reach the 4.56 MB 50x memory cap required re-reading chunks from disk, more than tripling local runtime (~224 ms vs ~63.8 ms). Retain data in RAM ($\sim 30\text{ MB}$), maximizing runtime speedup (0.038 s official).
Track A Counting Sort for Latencies Clearing and scanning 65,536 frequency bins took 79.00 ms in micro-benchmarks due to cache traversal overhead. Direct bucket scatter into dense rank vectors + pdqsort on small slices (51.42 ms Phase 2 micro-benchmark).
Track C 1 MiB Streaming Buffers Cut memory 48.2% (183 MB saved), but managing split quoted records across chunk edges slowed runtime 45.3% ($0.4933 \to 0.7168\text{ s}$), losing 1.20 points on $K$. Whole-file POSIX mmap with AVX2 SIMD scanning and 8 MB madvise advisory hints (0.1275 s, 54.64 MB).
Track C Generic Crates (csv, rayon) Importing csv or rayon triggers a 9.88% penalty on $K$, requiring an 18.8% runtime reduction merely to break even. Hand-rolled SIMD parser using std-only threads and direct POSIX FFI ($D = 1.0$), avoiding the crate tax.
Track D Generic Graph Crates (petgraph) Pointer-based adjacency lists thrash CPU caches and levy the 9.88% crate tax. Custom two-pass parallel CSR graph representation with packed 6-byte edges ($D = 1.0$).
Track D 64-bit Edge Weights in CSR Storing 64-bit weights increased graph memory by 25% without runtime benefit. Pack weights into u16 ($< 65,535$), routing rare overflow weights to dijkstra64.

Correctness and Verification

Optimizing for the score formula is meaningless if output digests fail validation. We established a verification framework distinguishing between official reference hashes, differential tests against earlier commits, and stress testing:

  • Digest Validation: Output SHA-256 hashes matched byte-for-byte on all competition datasets.
  • Track A Differential Testing: Verified against official reference digests on tiny-seed1, sample-seed1, and full-seed1. Additionally, 8 differential edge tests ran against commit 7fe5e92 (testing zero records, single records, hash table collisions, and Zipfian skew).
  • Track C Matrix Testing: Tested across 7 thread configurations ($n \in {1 \dots 16}$) and 4 buffer sizes (64 B to 1 MB) for a total of 144 / 144 PASS tests (track-c/PERF.md:202-204). Multi-seed datasets (seeds 2, 3, 4) were verified against outputs generated by the competition Python reference reference/c_join.py.
  • Track D Stress Testing: Verified against the official calibration hash on full-seed1 (a23dbdf0a3e49cc8901310a9ee1dc6a9a569a85297b6da75c2a7002cb2ed277e). Stress-tested across 60 distinct synthetic graphs (seeds 2 through 61) with 60 / 60 PASS tests matched against reference/d_traverse.py (track-d/PERF.md:59).

Portability, Safety, and Unsafe Invariants

Hardware Architecture & OS Environment

  • Track C Target: Uses 256-bit AVX2 SIMD instructions (_mm256_loadu_si256, _mm256_cmpeq_epi8, _mm256_movemask_epi8). Target builds specify x86-64-v3 with AVX2 and SSE4.2 enabled (track-c/Dockerfile, track-d/Dockerfile). Executing Track C on a CPU lacking AVX2 will trigger an Illegal Instruction (SIGILL) fault.
  • Operating System Separation & POSIX FFI:
    • Track A: Developed and profiled natively on Windows 11 as a standalone .exe using Win32 psapi memory metrics, while its official competition submission (7168b09) was evaluated in Linux on the official contest runner.
    • Tracks C and D: Rely on Unix/POSIX system calls (mmap, munmap, madvise, std::os::unix::io::AsRawFd). Because AsRawFd is only available under cfg(unix), these source trees cannot compile directly on native Windows with MSVC without a POSIX layer. Local development, benchmarking, and verification were conducted inside WSL2 (/mnt/c/ workspace mounts) and containerized via Docker (rust:1-slim-trixie / debian:13-slim). Neither Track C nor Track D was submitted for official competition leaderboard scoring.

Unsafe Invariant Audit

Across all three tracks, 42 unsafe blocks were audited:

  1. Guarded SIMD Loads: All vector loads are bounded by explicit pointer arithmetic checks (while q.add(32) <= end_ptr). Tail bytes are handled strictly by scalar loops, preventing page boundary over-reads.
  2. Unaligned Memory Reads: Unaligned loads (read_unaligned::<u64>()) are bounded by buffer capacity checks, executing safely on little-endian x86-64 architectures.
  3. Memory Mapping & madvise: Direct extern "C" mmap and munmap bindings wrap valid file descriptors; madvise calls pass standard POSIX flags (MADV_DONTNEED = 4, MADV_WILLNEED = 3) as advisory kernel hints.
  4. Packed Struct Field Access: Edge fields are copied by value rather than by reference, preventing unaligned reference undefined behavior.

What We Would Change in Production

While these engines achieved sub-second execution across multi-million record datasets under hackathon constraints, production deployment would require several architectural adjustments:

  1. Replace Probabilistic Hash with Keyed Fingerprinting and Exact Equality Checks: Even a 128-bit hash remains probabilistic and is theoretically vulnerable to collisions or adversarial hash-flooding. In production systems where deterministic correctness is required, a keyed hash (such as SipHash or HighwayHash) should be combined with exact byte-string equality checks on hash matches rather than relying on hashes alone.
  2. Dynamic SmallMap Resizing & Load Guards: In Track D, SmallMap uses a fixed capacity of 262,144 entries without load-factor guards. On adversarial graphs with $> 262,144$ explored nodes, linear probing would enter an unbounded loop. A production implementation requires dynamic power-of-two table resizing when load factor exceeds 50%.
  3. General RFC 3339 Timestamp Parsing: Track A hardcodes assumptions for October and November 2026. A production ingestion engine should validate calendar boundaries or utilize a generalized vectorized ISO 8601 parser.
  4. Cumulative Distance Overflow Handling: In Track D, tentative distances $\ge 65,534$ are pruned, and fallback to dijkstra64 only occurs if an edge with weight 65,535 was encountered. Production engines must support 32-bit or 64-bit distance fields across all relaxation stages, ensuring long multi-hop paths are not falsely classified as unreachable.

AI Assistance Disclosure

In the spirit of transparency in competitive systems engineering and technical publication:

  • Author Strategy and Technical Decisions: The overarching optimization strategy—prioritizing the scoreboard objective function over raw latency, targeting zero external dependencies ($D = 1.0$), eliminating dynamic allocations in favor of flat tables and CSR representations, identifying the Windows cold-start benchmarking artifact, and directing all iterative profiling—was designed and driven by the author.
  • AI Assistance During Development & Debugging: Generative AI tools (Google's Gemini-powered Antigravity coding assistant and claude for system design and approach) were used during development and debugging. Specific tasks assisted by AI included rapid prototyping of iterative candidate implementations, drafting low-level bitwise operations (such as AVX2 SIMD quote masking and 64-bit SWAR date parsing arithmetic), brainstorming algebraic implications of the scoring formula exponents, diagnosing edge-case test failures, and assisting in the structuring, editorial refinement, and formatting of this technical article.
  • Local Experiments and Measurements: All local benchmark measurements—including the 30-pair randomized A/B trials on Windows for Track A, the 144-case thread/buffer matrix tests for Track C, the 60-seed synthetic graph stress tests for Track D, and the memory progression logs in track-c/PERF.md and track-d/PERF.md—were executed, recorded, and audited directly on the author's local hardware (Intel Core i5-13420H) across native Windows and local WSL2 environments.
  • Official Competition vs. Local Status: Only Track A was officially submitted to and scored on the Speed Demon 2026 competition leaderboard (76.622 points at 0.038 s, 31 MB peak working set). Tracks C and D were developed, validated, and profiled locally (achieving 0.1275 s and 0.6600 s in local testing); neither received an official competition submission or official leaderboard score.
  • Verification & Responsibility: Every benchmark number, code snippet, statistical calculation, and technical claim in this article was verified against repository source code and primary execution logs. The author takes full responsibility for the accuracy, claims, and technical conclusions presented.

Reproduce It

Spec and harness files come from the competition kit, not this repository. Because Tracks C and D utilize direct POSIX FFI (mmap, madvise, AsRawFd), they must be built in a Linux environment (Linux, WSL2, or Docker).

Environment Overview

  • Development Host: Windows 11 (Intel Core i5-13420H, 12 logical cores)
  • Local POSIX / Container Environment: WSL2 & Docker Desktop (rust:1-slim-trixie / debian:13-slim)
  • Official Contest Scoring Runner: Remote Linux x86-64-v3 evaluation host
  • Toolchain: rustc 1.99.1, rustfmt 1.10.0 (Edition 2021)

Option 1: Native Linux or WSL2 (Fastest Local Reproduction) 

# Build all three release binaries in Linux or WSL2
cargo build --release --manifest-path track-a/Cargo.toml
cargo build --release --manifest-path track-c/Cargo.toml
cargo build --release --manifest-path track-d/Cargo.toml

# Run benchmarks or evaluations
./track-a/target/release/track-a /path/to/data /path/to/out
./track-c/target/release/track-c --data /path/to/data --out /path/to/out
./track-d/target/release/track-d --data /path/to/data --out /path/to/out

Option 2: Docker Multi-Stage Containers (Matching Competition Spec) 

# Build standalone competition container images
docker build -t speed-demon-a track-a/
docker build -t speed-demon-c track-c/
docker build -t speed-demon-d track-d/

# Run containerized evaluations with mounted host directories
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)/data:/data:ro" -v "$(pwd)/out:/out" speed-demon-a /data /out
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)/data:/data:ro" -v "$(pwd)/out:/out" speed-demon-c --data /data --out /out
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)/data:/data:ro" -v "$(pwd)/out:/out" speed-demon-d --data /data --out /out

Option 3: Native Windows (Track A Only)

Track A is pure standard library Rust and builds natively on Windows without POSIX shims:

cargo build --release --manifest-path track-a/Cargo.toml
.\track-a\target\release\track-a.exe path\to\data path\to\out

title: Supabase vs Postgres: when you don't need the extras (2026)
description:
Last updated: 6 November 2026

Supabase vs Postgres is a strange matchup, because Supabase is Postgres. What you're really deciding is whether to pay for the pieces Supabase puts around it: sign-in, file storage, live updates, an auto-generated API and backups. For some apps that bundle is the best $25 you'll spend. For others it's $25 a month for a database plus features you never call. This guide shows what each piece costs on its own, where Supabase clearly wins, and how to keep your Supabase-style security rules working on plain Postgres if you move.

Try it on Hubfly space: a managed PostgreSQL 18 database starts at about $2 a month.

Prices are as of 6 November 2026, in US dollars.

What Supabase adds on top of Postgres

Every Supabase project is a regular Postgres database. Around it, Supabase runs several services and gives them one dashboard, one client library and one bill.

Supabase piece What it does for you Plain-Postgres replacement
Auth Sign-up, login, OAuth, magic links; puts the user ID in every request An auth library in your API (e.g. Better Auth or Auth.js), or a hosted service like Clerk
Auto-generated API Query tables straight from the browser, guarded by row-level security Your own small API (Express, FastAPI, Go…)
Row-level security helpers auth.uid() inside policies The same policies, plus a 10-line shim (below)
Storage Files in buckets with access rules Any S3-compatible bucket
Realtime Live updates over WebSockets A Pusher-compatible server, or Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY in your API
Edge Functions Server code next to the database Code in your API container
Backups Daily backups on paid plans, optional point-in-time restore Managed backups from your provider, or scheduled pg_dump

The pattern is clear: Supabase's extras replace code you would otherwise write and run. That's the trade. You pay less for plain Postgres, and you write (or wire up) more yourself.

Supabase pricing in 2026

From Supabase's pricing page:

  • Free: $0. 500 MB database, 50,000 monthly active users, 1 GB of files, 5 GB of egress, 2 active projects. No automatic backups. Projects are paused after 1 week of inactivity.
  • Pro: from $25/month. Includes $10 of compute credit, which covers one Micro instance (shared CPU, 1 GB RAM). 8 GB of disk, 100,000 monthly active users, 100 GB of files, 250 GB of egress, daily backups kept 7 days.
  • Team: from $599/month.

Pro overage rates: disk $0.125/GB, users $0.00325 each past 100,000, files $0.0213/GB, egress $0.09/GB ($0.03 cached). Point-in-time restore is an add-on at $100/month for 7 days, and a custom domain is $10/month. Bigger compute costs extra: Small (2 GB) about $15, Medium (4 GB) about $60.

Plain Postgres pricing in 2026

Here is what a database alone costs, roughly matched to Supabase Pro's 1 GB Micro instance.

Provider Smallest sensible plan Monthly price Backups
Supabase Pro Micro, 1 GB RAM, 8 GB disk $25 (includes auth, files, realtime) Daily, 7 days
Neon Launch Usage-based, billed per compute-hour Neon's own example: about $15 for 140 compute-hours and 1 GB Instant restore, $0.20/GB-month
Render 1 GB RAM $19 + storage at $0.30/GB Point-in-time restore, 3 days (Hobby) or 7 days (Pro)
DigitalOcean 1 vCPU, 1 GiB $15.15 with 10 GiB Daily backups + 7-day point-in-time restore
Hubfly space Small, 0.5 vCPU, 1 GiB, 10 GiB $3.92 No automatic backups yet (coming soon)

Two things stand out. Supabase Pro is a fair price once you count everything in it. And if you only need the database, you can pay a fraction of that.

Neon deserves a special mention: every plan now includes managed Better Auth, a Data API and Realtime at no separate charge, with auth for up to 60,000 monthly active users per project on Free and 1 million on paid plans. If what you want is "Postgres plus login", it's a strong middle ground.

Supabase vs Postgres: same app, two bills

Take a typical small SaaS: a 2 GB database, 10,000 monthly active users, 20 GB of uploaded files and live updates in the UI.

On Supabase Pro: $25.00 a month. Everything fits inside Pro's included amounts: 2 GB of the 8 GB disk, 10,000 of 100,000 users, 20 GB of 100 GB of files. The free plan won't do, because the database alone is over its 500 MB limit.

On plain Postgres plus your own pieces (Hubfly space): $9.09 a month.

Piece Size Monthly
Hubfly space managed PostgreSQL Small: 0.5 vCPU, 1 GiB, 10 GiB $3.92
Hubfly space Cell container (runs your auth library and API) 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB, 10 GB disk, always on $3.03
Hubfly space Storage 20 GB of files $0.22
Managed Realtime Nano $1.92
Auth Open-source library inside your API $0
Total $9.09

How each number is worked out (730 hours a month; CPU $0.004 per vCPU-hour, memory $0.002 per GB-hour, storage $0.00001536 per GB-hour):

  • Database: (0.5 × $0.004 + 1 × $0.002) = $0.004/h, plus the 30% management fee ($0.0012/h), plus 11 GiB of disk (10 GiB data + 1 GiB system) × $0.00001536 = $0.000169/h. Total $0.005369/h × 730 = $3.92.
  • API container: (0.5 × $0.004 + 1 × $0.002) × 730 = $2.92, plus 10 GB × $0.00001536 × 730 = $0.11. Total $3.03.
  • Files: 20 GB × $0.00001536 × 730 = $0.22.
  • Realtime: the Nano size is $1.92, with no per-message fee.

Network transfer isn't in either total. Supabase Pro includes 250 GB of egress; check your provider's bandwidth terms before comparing heavy-download apps.

When the math flips

The gap closes fast if you'd buy auth as a hosted service. Say the app grows to 150,000 monthly active users:

  • Supabase Pro: $25 + 50,000 extra users × $0.00325 = $187.50.
  • Clerk Pro (billed monthly) for sign-in alone, assuming all 150,000 count as Clerk's monthly retained users: $25 + 50,000 users × $0.02 + 50,000 users × $0.018 = $1,925.
  • An open-source auth library in your own API: $0 extra, but you own password resets, OAuth setup and security updates.

So Supabase's included users are a big deal if your alternative is a hosted auth service. They matter much less if you're happy running a library yourself.

When Supabase is the better choice

Be honest about what you'd rebuild. Pick Supabase when:

  • You'd otherwise buy hosted auth. 100,000 monthly active users are included in Pro.
  • Your app is mostly frontend. The auto-generated API plus row-level security means many apps need no backend server at all.
  • You want backups handled. Pro keeps 7 days of daily backups without you doing anything, and point-in-time restore is available as a $100/month add-on.
  • You're prototyping. The free plan gets you a database, login and file uploads in minutes. Just remember free projects pause after a week without activity.
  • You value one dashboard. One place for users, tables, files, logs and keys saves real time on a small team.

When plain Postgres is the better choice

  • You already have a backend. If your API handles auth and business logic, Supabase's auto-generated API goes unused.
  • You only need a database. A 1 GB managed Postgres costs $3.92 to about $20 elsewhere versus $25.
  • You want to own your auth data. Users live in your own tables, with no provider-specific schema.

The honest downside on Hubfly space today: managed Postgres runs on a single node, with no replicas, no high availability and no point-in-time restore, and automatic backups are still coming. Until they arrive, run your own pg_dump on a schedule from any machine or job runner you already have, and keep the files somewhere else (the dump and restore commands are in how to upgrade Postgres to a new major version in Docker). If you need automatic backups or failover today, Supabase Pro, DigitalOcean or Render are the safer picks.

Moving from Supabase to plain Postgres: the part guides skip

Most migration guides say "run pg_dump, then pg_restore". On a typical Supabase schema, that fails, because your tables and policies point at things that only exist inside Supabase: the auth schema, the auth.uid() function and roles such as authenticated.

Here's a typical table from a Supabase app:

create table public.todos (
  id bigint generated by default as identity primary key,
  user_id uuid not null default auth.uid() references auth.users(id) on delete cascade,
  title text not null,
  done boolean not null default false
);
alter table public.todos enable row level security;
create policy "own todos read" on public.todos
  for select to authenticated using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
create policy "own todos write" on public.todos
  for insert to authenticated with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);

Dump only your own schema and restore it into plain PostgreSQL, and you get this:

pg_restore: error: could not execute query: ERROR:  schema "public" already exists
pg_restore: error: could not execute query: ERROR:  schema "auth" does not exist
LINE 3:     user_id uuid DEFAULT auth.uid() NOT NULL,
pg_restore: error: could not execute query: ERROR:  relation "public.todos" does not exist
...
pg_restore: warning: errors ignored on restore: 12

The dangerous part: pg_restore keeps going. It finishes with a warning and exit status 1, and your todos table simply isn't there. Adding --no-owner --no-acl doesn't help; the table still needs auth.uid().

The fix is to recreate the small part of Supabase your schema depends on, before you restore.

Step 1: Dump your own tables

Supabase runs Postgres 17, and pg_dump must be the same major version as the server or newer, so use version 17 or newer. The flags below are the same in every recent version. Copy a direct or session-mode connection string from your Supabase project's Connect dialog.

pg_dump "$SUPABASE_DB_URL" --format=custom --schema=public --file=public.dump

--schema=public leaves out Supabase's own schemas (auth, storage, realtime and others). Your users are in auth.users, so export the columns you need separately:

psql "$SUPABASE_DB_URL" -c "\copy (select id, email from auth.users) to 'users.csv' with csv header"

Step 2: Add the shim to the new database

This recreates the three roles, a minimal auth.users table and auth.uid(). It reads the user ID the same way Supabase's own helpers do: first request.jwt.claim.sub, then the sub field of request.jwt.claims (Supabase's example). Save it as shim.sql:

-- Make plain Postgres understand Supabase-style policies
do $$ begin
  if not exists (select from pg_roles where rolname='anon') then create role anon nologin; end if;
  if not exists (select from pg_roles where rolname='authenticated') then create role authenticated nologin; end if;
  if not exists (select from pg_roles where rolname='service_role') then create role service_role nologin; end if;
end $$;
create schema if not exists auth;
create table if not exists auth.users (id uuid primary key, email text);
create or replace function auth.uid() returns uuid language sql stable as $$
  select coalesce(
    nullif(current_setting('request.jwt.claim.sub', true), ''),
    (nullif(current_setting('request.jwt.claims', true), '')::jsonb ->> 'sub')
  )::uuid
$$;
grant usage on schema auth to anon, authenticated, service_role;
grant execute on function auth.uid() to anon, authenticated, service_role;

It works with a regular admin user that can create roles; no superuser needed. That matters on managed databases, where you never get superuser. (It's also why service_role here has no BYPASSRLS: a role that doesn't have it can't give it, and admin users on managed databases normally don't have it.)

The nullif(…, '') is not decoration. Once a setting has been used on a connection, Postgres returns an empty string for it afterwards, not NULL. Without nullif, the next request on that pooled connection fails with invalid input syntax for type json.

Step 3: Load users, then restore 

psql "$NEW_DB_URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f shim.sql
psql "$NEW_DB_URL" -c "\copy auth.users (id, email) from 'users.csv' with csv header"

pg_restore --list public.dump | grep -v -E 'SCHEMA - public|COMMENT - SCHEMA public|DEFAULT ACL' > restore.list
pg_restore --no-owner --exit-on-error --use-list=restore.list --dbname="$NEW_DB_URL" public.dump

The list file skips two kinds of entries. CREATE SCHEMA public already exists and would otherwise be the first error. DEFAULT ACL lines are Supabase's default grants for its own roles (for example ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE postgres …); a non-superuser can't set them for another role, and the restore stops with permission denied to change default privileges.

Before restoring, list the grants the restore will run. Every role named there must exist in the new database:

pg_restore --file=- --use-list=restore.list public.dump | grep -E '^(GRANT|REVOKE)'

If the restore still stops with role "…" does not exist, create that role with create role <name> nologin; and run the restore again on a fresh database. Don't delete the table's ACL line instead: it holds all of that table's grants, including the one to authenticated your policies need. For any other Supabase-only object the error names, remove its line from restore.list. --exit-on-error makes the restore stop at the first real problem instead of skipping tables. Keep the grants (no --no-acl): your policies need the authenticated role to have its table permissions.

If a column default calls extensions.uuid_generate_v4(), create that extension in a schema with the same name before restoring: create schema extensions; create extension "uuid-ossp" schema extensions;.

Step 4: Run queries as the signed-in user

Your policies now work, but only if each request tells Postgres who the user is. Create a login role for your app that does not own the tables, and let it act as authenticated:

create role shop_api login password 'a-long-random-password';
grant authenticated to shop_api;

Then wrap each request in a transaction that switches role and sets the user ID. Here it is for Node.js 22 with pg 8:

const { Pool } = require('pg');
const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

// Run queries as one signed-in user, so Supabase-style RLS policies apply.
async function asUser(userId, fn) {
  const client = await pool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    await client.query('SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated');
    await client.query("SELECT set_config('request.jwt.claims', $1, true)",
      [JSON.stringify({ sub: userId, role: 'authenticated' })]);
    const result = await fn(client);
    await client.query('COMMIT');
    return result;
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

// Usage: const { rows } = await asUser(session.userId, c => c.query('SELECT * FROM todos'));

SET LOCAL and the true in set_config scope both to the transaction, so the next request on the same pooled connection starts clean. With this in place, user A sees only A's rows, and when user B tries to insert a row for user A, Postgres refuses with new row violates row-level security policy for table "todos".

What can go wrong

  1. Every user sees every row. Your app connects as the table owner. Owners skip row-level security by default, so a policy that works on Supabase silently does nothing. Connect as a separate role like shop_api, or run alter table todos force row level security;.
  2. Every query returns zero rows. The role switch worked but the user ID didn't arrive, so auth.uid() is NULL. Check that set_config runs inside the same transaction as the query.
  3. pg_restore "finished" but a table is missing. You restored without --exit-on-error. Look for errors ignored on restore in the output, drop the new database (not your Supabase one) and restore again with the flag.
  4. server version mismatch from pg_dump. Your local pg_dump is older than the server. Install the PostgreSQL 17 or 18 client tools.
  5. Uploaded files are gone. Supabase backups don't include Storage objects, and neither does pg_dump: the database only holds their metadata. Copy the files with any S3 tool before you switch off the old project.
  6. Everyone has to log in again. Sessions and password hashes belong to Supabase Auth. Plan the move of logins separately; exporting id and email keeps your foreign keys intact, not your users' passwords.

FAQ

Is Supabase just Postgres?

The database is regular Postgres, and you can connect to it with any Postgres client or ORM. Supabase adds auth, storage, realtime, an auto-generated API and backups around it, plus a few schemas and roles of its own.

Do I need Supabase or just Postgres?

If you have your own backend and only need a database, plain Postgres is cheaper. If you'd otherwise buy hosted auth, or your app talks to the database straight from the browser, Supabase saves you real work.

How much does Supabase cost per month?

Free is $0 with a 500 MB database and pausing after a week of inactivity. Pro starts at $25 a month with 8 GB of disk, 100,000 monthly active users and 250 GB of egress. Bigger compute, extra users and point-in-time restore cost extra.

Can I move my Supabase database to another Postgres host?

Yes. Dump your own schema with pg_dump, recreate auth.uid() and the Supabase roles on the new database, then restore with --exit-on-error. Files in Supabase Storage and user passwords need their own migration.

Will my RLS policies work outside Supabase?

Yes, once auth.uid() exists and each request sets the user ID in a transaction, as in Step 4. Policies are plain Postgres; only the helper function is Supabase-specific.

Do Supabase backups include my uploaded files?

No. Supabase's backups cover the database only, which stores metadata about your files, not the files themselves.

What's the cheapest way to get Postgres plus login?

Run an open-source auth library in your own API next to a small managed database, or use Neon, whose plans include managed Better Auth at no separate charge. For a broader price list, see the cheapest database for a small app in 2026.

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Create the database in a minute or two with a managed PostgreSQL database for about $2 a month.
  • Find slow queries after the move with Query insights: how to find and fix slow PostgreSQL queries.
  • Store user uploads in Hubfly space Storage, an S3-compatible bucket at about $0.011 per GB a month.

Keep your Postgres, drop the bill you don't use. Create a managed PostgreSQL 18 database and pay for the size you pick. Try it on Hubfly space

title: React INP Benchmark: Chunking vs startTransition vs scheduler.yield
description:
Originally published at suprabhat-dev.com.

A user clicks a button that starts heavy work: filtering a large list, scoring rows, building a search index. While that work runs on the main thread, the next click waits, because the browser cannot handle input or paint until the work returns. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures that wait, and in data-heavy React screens it is usually the Core Web Vital that fails first.

The common answers are startTransition, slicing the work with setTimeout, yielding with scheduler.yield(), or a library that does the slicing for you. I maintain one of those libraries, react-inp-chunker, so I wanted numbers rather than claims. This article walks through a small benchmark that runs the same work five ways and measures how long a click made during that work waits.

The setup

The workload scores 20,000 rows, with 30 rounds of string hashing per row, then sorts the results and shows the top 25. Every version does exactly the same work. Only the scheduling differs:

Version How the work is scheduled
Synchronous Scores every row inside the click handler.
setTimeout chunks Hand-written 5 ms slices, yielding with setTimeout(0).
startTransition Wraps the state update in a transition; the scoring runs during render.
react-inp-chunker useChunkedTask(rows, scoreRow): 5 ms slices, yielding with scheduler.yield().
scheduler.yield Hand-written 5 ms slices, yielding with scheduler.yield().

Each run clicks Score 20,000 rows, then clicks a second button 50 ms later, while the rows are still being scored. For both clicks, the app records the time from the click event to the next animation frame: the earliest moment its response can paint. That is the delay INP measures, recorded without the 16 ms reporting threshold of the Event Timing API. The app also records the longest frame during the run and the total time until the results are on screen.

The numbers below come from headless Chromium 141 on a 2-core cloud VM with 4x CPU throttling: 30 runs per version after 3 warm-up runs. Absolute values depend on the machine. The benchmark folder has the code, the method and every raw sample, so you can run it on yours.

Results

The main finding: a click made while the work runs waited a median of 299 ms in the synchronous version and 330 ms with startTransition, both above the 200 ms limit for a good INP. All three time-sliced versions kept that click at 12–13 ms, close to a single frame.

Why startTransition did not help here

startTransition did what it promises for the first click. The click that starts the work reached the next frame in a median of 7 ms, against 339 ms for the synchronous version, because React treats the update as non-urgent and lets the browser paint first.

The second click is where it fails. In this version the scoring runs during render, inside useMemo, which is how a lot of real code computes derived data. React can interrupt a transition between components, but it cannot pause in the middle of one component's render. A single render that does all the scoring is one long block of work, and the click that arrives during it waits for all of it: 330 ms at the median and 420 ms at p75.

Transitions help when the cost is spread across many components, such as a large tree re-rendering after a filter changes. They do not split one expensive computation. For that, the computation itself has to yield.

The trade-off: yielding costs total time

Yielding is not free. Every slice hands the main thread back to the browser, and the work only resumes when the browser schedules it again, so the same work finishes later. The synchronous version showed its results after a median of 339 ms. The time-sliced versions took 534 ms with react-inp-chunker, 660 ms with hand-written scheduler.yield(), and 714 ms with setTimeout.

setTimeout is the slowest because browsers clamp nested timers: once timers are nested several levels deep, setTimeout(fn, 0) waits at least 4 ms. With 5 ms slices of work, a 4 ms minimum wait after each slice adds up quickly. scheduler.yield() is built for this case: the work resumes ahead of other queued tasks.

The gap between react-inp-chunker and hand-written scheduler.yield() looks large in a chart of medians, but it is within run-to-run noise here; the individual runs of the two versions overlap widely (see results.json). This benchmark does not show either one finishing faster. The claim it supports is narrower: the library gives the same responsiveness as a hand-written scheduler.yield() loop, without writing and maintaining that loop yourself.

One more limit shows up in the longest frame. The final sort of 20,000 results is still one block of work, so the longest frame stays at a median of 121 ms with scheduler.yield() and 127 ms with react-inp-chunker; the setTimeout version's median was 65 ms. Slicing only helps with the work you slice.

What to use when

  • Small work needs nothing. If an update takes a few milliseconds, scheduling adds complexity and total time for no gain. Measure first: a task over 50 ms is a long task.
  • Move heavy computation out of render. In the startTransition version, the work sat in useMemo, so it ran during render, where React cannot split it. Run it from an event handler or an effect instead, and keep render cheap.
  • Use startTransition for expensive rendering, when the cost is spread across many components.
  • Chunk long loops over data. When the work is one function applied to many items, slice it and yield between slices.

A hand-written version of that loop looks like this:

async function scoreInSlices(rows: readonly Row[]) {
  const scored: Scored[] = [];
  let index = 0;
  while (index < rows.length) {
    await scheduler.yield();
    const start = performance.now();
    while (index < rows.length && performance.now() - start < 5) {
      scored.push(scoreRow(rows[index]));
      index += 1;
    }
  }
  return scored;
}

It still needs a fallback for browsers without scheduler.yield(), progress state for the UI, cancellation, and cleanup when the component unmounts. With react-inp-chunker, the same work is one hook:

import { useChunkedTask } from 'react-inp-chunker';

function ScoredRows({ rows }: { rows: readonly Row[] }) {
  // scoreRow runs once per row, in slices of up to 5 ms.
  const task = useChunkedTask(rows, scoreRow);

  if (task.isError) return <p role="alert">Couldn't score the rows.</p>;

  if (task.status !== 'done') {
    return (
      <progress
        value={task.processed}
        max={task.total}
        aria-label="Scoring rows"
      />
    );
  }

  return <ResultsTable scores={task.results} />;
}

The hook re-renders with progress once per slice, not once per item, and cancels when the component unmounts. A new rows array reference restarts the task, so memoize derived arrays. The documentation covers the full API and when to reach for something else, such as a Web Worker.

Limits of this benchmark

  • One machine. A 2-core cloud VM with 4x CPU throttling. Your numbers will differ, so check the comparison on your own hardware.
  • One browser, headless. Chromium 141 supports scheduler.yield(). Browsers without it use a fallback, which this run did not measure.
  • A synthetic workload. String hashing costs the same for every row. Real work varies per item and touches memory differently.
  • Lab numbers, not field INP. The benchmark measures click to next frame in a controlled run. Real INP comes from real users on real devices, while the rest of the page is also doing work.

To see what your users experience, collect INP in the field, for example with the web-vitals library, and judge it at the 75th percentile, which is how Core Web Vitals are assessed. To test the benchmark itself on a real phone, open the preview build on the device and use DevTools remote debugging.

Run it yourself

The benchmark README has the full method. From a clone of the repository:

cd bench/inp-demo
npm install
npm run build
npm run preview          # keep running, http://localhost:4173/

In a second terminal:

npx playwright install chromium   # once
npm run measure                   # writes results/results.json and RESULTS.md
npm run report                    # writes the charts, table and screenshots

Settings are environment variables: RUNS (default 30), WARMUP (3), CPU_RATE (4), WORK (30 hash rounds per row), PING_DELAY_MS (50), and HEADED=1 to watch the runs. The react-inp-chunker case study covers why the library exists and how it is tested.
