title: The AI Productivity Paradox: Fighting LLM Over-Engineering with Decision Ladders, Deterministic Debt Ledgers, and YAGNI Semantic Sensors in Go
description:
There is a quiet paradox inside engineering teams that have adopted AI coding agents at scale: we have never generated so many lines of code per minute, and at the same time, we have never accumulated so much accidental complexity so fast.

Ask a frontier LLM to implement a simple persistence layer for financial wallets in Go. Without strict architectural guardrails, in less than thirty seconds it will likely hand you:

  • A WalletRepository interface with a single concrete implementation in the producer package (violating the classic Go idiom where interfaces belong to the consumer);
  • An AbstractStorageFactory with a Strategy pattern for a database that will never change;
  • Three hallucinated domain structs (CreditCard, VoucherBalance, WeeklyEnvelope) that were already unified inside a single domain.Wallet entity;
  • A custom wrapper around database/sql and half a dozen vague // TODO: optimize later comments scattered along the way.

Does it compile? Sometimes not even that — when it hallucinates types that don't match your domain package. And when it does compile, you have just inherited 800 lines of speculative over-engineering to solve a 120-line problem.

In this 5th technical article on the architecture of Pipeline-AI — celebrating the release of version v0.11.0 (deliveries DEL-032 through DEL-035) —, I share how we attacked the root cause of LLM additive bias by combining Decision Ladders in the cognitive workflow, a deterministic Debt Ledger in pure Go 1.24 (internal/debt), and a Calibrated YAGNI Semantic Sensor (pipeline-ai eval -preset yagni), along with a real-world production case study from the gestao-financas project.

1. Why Do LLMs Suffer from Chronic Additive Bias?

Large Language Models are trained on billions of lines of public repositories and enterprise tutorials where "clean architecture" is frequently conflated with excessive layers of indirection. Furthermore, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) tends to reward long, elaborate, and seemingly sophisticated answers.

In day-to-day software engineering, this manifests as four recurring pathologies:

  1. Premature Abstraction (YAGNI Violation): Creating generic interfaces, event buses, and configuration options for hypothetical future requirements nobody asked for.
  2. Domain Type Duplication & Hallucination: Instead of inspecting existing structs in internal/domain, the agent invents parallel local structs that fragment the system's domain model.
  3. Reimplementing the Standard Library: In Go, where the standard library (net/http, database/sql, encoding/json, context, io) solves 90% of infrastructure needs, LLMs insist on building wrappers or pulling unnecessary dependencies into go.mod.
  4. Invisible Technical Debt (Orphaned TODOs): When an agent takes a legitimate engineering shortcut (such as an in-memory map or JSONB column serialization), it leaves a vague // TODO: fix later — or no comment at all — without documenting what the operational limit of that shortcut is or what objective trigger requires upgrading it.

2. Architectural Inspiration & Evolution: From Prompt Rules (ponytail) to Deterministic Governance + System 1 (pipeline-ai v0.11.0)

Recently, the open-source project dietrichgebert/ponytail brilliantly distilled a philosophy every senior engineer knows by heart:

"The best code is the code you never wrote."

ponytail introduced three strong conceptual ideas to guide coding agents: a Decision Ladder, strict minimalism discipline, and structured inline shortcut comments.

However, when we analyzed this approach through the architectural lens of Pipeline-AI, we identified a structural limitation: rules that live solely inside prompt text (System 2) suffer from attention degradation (context drift). As the context window grows during a multi-step TDD session, the LLM simply forgets the prompt instruction or ignores the // shortcut: comments buried across source files.

To turn good prompt intentions into deterministic, auditable engineering, pipeline-ai v0.11.0 evolved these concepts across three new dimensions:

  • From Passive Prompt to Deterministic Go Parser & Scanner (internal/debt): // shortcut: comments are no longer dead text in your codebase. They are extracted, validated, and inventoried by a pure Go 1.24 engine (pipeline-ai debt), exposed via CLI, MCP server (pipeline_list_debt), and rendered automatically in the Generative UI Dashboard.
  • Blocking Vague TODOs While Auditing Deliberate Shortcuts: In Pipeline-AI, pipeline-validate already blocks orphaned TODO/FIXME markers. Now we cleanly separate forgotten tasks (blocked) from deliberate architectural shortcuts (tracked with explicit limits and upgrade triggers).
  • From Slow "LLM-as-a-Judge" to Calibrated System 1 Semantic Sensor (Jev): We built the native pipeline-ai eval -preset yagni preset, allowing agents and CI pipelines to pipe any git diff into a sub-100ms calibrated binary sensor (/v1/noul) to catch over-engineering before human code review.

3. The Three Anti-Overengineering Pillars in pipeline-ai v0.11.0

3.1. Pillar 1: The 5-Step Decision Ladder in Core Skills (architecture-guardrails, dev-implementation, code-reviewer)

Before writing a single line of code or proposing a new package, the architecture-guardrails skill now enforces an explicit walk through the 5-Step Decision Ladder:

  1. Step 1 — YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): Is this change strictly required for the current delivery scope, or are we designing for a hypothetical future? If speculative, cut it immediately.
  2. Step 2 — Internal Repo Reuse: Does a struct, function, or type already exist in internal/domain or another internal package? Never create mirrored structs or duplicate domain types.
  3. Step 3 — Go 1.24+ Standard Library: Does the Go standard library (net/http, database/sql, encoding/json, slices, maps, sync, context) already provide the primitive? Use it directly without wrappers.
  4. Step 4 — Existing go.mod Dependencies: If the stdlib doesn't cover it, can we solve it with an already approved dependency in go.mod?
  5. Step 5 — Minimal Viable New Code: Only when steps 1–4 are exhausted, write the smallest concrete code that passes the tests — without single-implementation interfaces in the producer package.

Next, dev-implementation enforces strict minimalism during coding, and code-reviewer audits the git diff specifically targeting speculative abstractions and unnecessary interfaces.

3.2. Pillar 2: The Deterministic Debt Ledger (internal/debt, pipeline-ai debt, and MCP pipeline_list_debt)

Minimalism does not mean pretending a simple implementation scales infinitely. When we consciously choose a simple design (e.g., an in-process mutex or JSONB column storage), we must record that deliberate shortcut with two mandatory fields:

  • What is the known operational limit of the current solution? (<limit>)
  • What is the objective, measurable trigger to upgrade it in the future? (<trigger>)

We standardized this annotation directly in Go comments:

// shortcut: <known limit> | upgrade: <objective upgrade trigger>

To parse and audit these annotations across any Go repository without complex regular expressions (avoiding catastrophic backtracking / ReDoS risks), we built internal/debt in pure Go 1.24:

// internal/debt/debt.go
package debt

// ShortcutItem represents a deliberate engineering shortcut tracked by limit and upgrade trigger.
type ShortcutItem struct {
    File           string `json:"file"`
    Line           int    `json:"line"`
    Limit          string `json:"limit"`
    UpgradeTrigger string `json:"upgrade_trigger"`
    Raw            string `json:"raw"`
}

// ParseComment extracts the known limit and upgrade trigger from comments formatted as:
// "// shortcut: <limit> | upgrade: <trigger>" or "// shortcut: <limit>, <trigger>"
func ParseComment(line string) (limit string, trigger string, ok bool) {
    idx := strings.Index(line, "//")
    if idx == -1 {
        return "", "", false
    }

    comment := strings.TrimSpace(line[idx+2:])
    if len(comment) < len("shortcut:") || !strings.EqualFold(comment[:len("shortcut:")], "shortcut:") {
        return "", "", false
    }

    rest := strings.TrimSpace(comment[len("shortcut:"):])
    if pipeIdx := strings.Index(rest, "|"); pipeIdx != -1 {
        limit = strings.TrimSpace(rest[:pipeIdx])
        right := strings.TrimSpace(rest[pipeIdx+1:])
        if len(right) >= len("upgrade:") && strings.EqualFold(right[:len("upgrade:")], "upgrade:") {
            trigger = strings.TrimSpace(right[len("upgrade:"):])
        } else {
            trigger = right
        }
    } else if commaIdx := strings.Index(rest, ","); commaIdx != -1 {
        limit = strings.TrimSpace(rest[:commaIdx])
        right := strings.TrimSpace(rest[commaIdx+1:])
        if len(right) >= len("upgrade:") && strings.EqualFold(right[:len("upgrade:")], "upgrade:") {
            trigger = strings.TrimSpace(right[len("upgrade:"):])
        } else {
            trigger = right
        }
    } else {
        return "", "", false
    }

    if limit == "" || trigger == "" {
        return "", "", false
    }
    return limit, trigger, true
}

The directory scanner debt.ScanDir(rootDir):

  • Walks the repository tree recursively via filepath.WalkDir;
  • Deterministically skips test files (*_test.go), hidden directories (.git, .agents), vendor, and node_modules;
  • Ignores plain // TODO: comments or incomplete // shortcut: lines missing an upgrade trigger;
  • Sorts items deterministically by File and Line and has been hardened with over 6.5 million native Fuzz Testing executions (FuzzParseComment) with zero panics.

Engineers and AI agents can inspect the Debt Ledger via CLI or MCP at any time:

$ pipeline-ai debt
Atalhos Deliberados (Debt Ledger): 2 encontrado(s)
- internal/storage/postgres.go:68 | Limite: serialização JSONB de recurrence e sub_items na coluna da carteira | Gatilho de evolução: extrair para tabelas relacionais se houver query analítica por sub-item
- internal/storage/storage.go:48 | Limite: MemoryStore guarda estado apenas em RAM com RWMutex local | Gatilho de evolução: usar PostgresStore quando DATABASE_URL estiver configurado em produção

And pipeline-ai dashboard automatically renders the "Atalhos Deliberados (Debt Ledger)" section inside the Generative UI HTML cockpit alongside DORA and Jev telemetry.

3.3. Pillar 3: The YAGNI Semantic Preset in Jev (pipeline-ai eval -preset yagni)

In internal/sensor/semantic, we added ResolvePreset (yagni, with aliases minimalism and ponytail), which configures a calibrated binary evaluation (EvalNoul at /v1/noul) with our anti-overengineering audit prompt:

// internal/sensor/semantic/presets.go
const yagniQuestion = "Este código respeita estritamente o princípio YAGNI e minimalismo, sem overengineering, interfaces de implementação única desnecessárias, tipos duplicados do domínio ou abstrações especulativas não solicitadas?"

func ResolvePreset(name string) (mode string, question string, err error) {
    switch strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(name)) {
    case "yagni", "minimalism", "ponytail":
        return "noul", yagniQuestion, nil
    default:
        return "", "", ErrInvalidPreset
    }
}

Auditing a diff in CI or during an autonomous agent run is now a single one-liner:

git diff | pipeline-ai eval -preset yagni -threshold 0.80

4. Production Case Study: The internal/storage Layer in gestao-financas

To validate this governance in a real application, we applied pipeline-ai v0.11.0 to the persistence layer (internal/storage) of gestao-financas (a Go + Wails v3 + PostgreSQL personal finance platform managing weekly budget envelopes, credit cards, and meal/food vouchers).

  • Before the Decision Ladder: An earlier draft generated without the Decision Ladder hallucinated parallel structs (CreditCard, VoucherBalance, WeeklyEnvelope, MonthlySummary) that did not exist in internal/domain, causing go vet ./... to fail with over 15 compilation errors.
  • With the Decision Ladder + Debt Ledger (DEL-002): architecture-guardrails enforced 100% reuse of domain.Wallet, domain.Transaction, and domain.CalculateDashboard, using pure Go sync.RWMutex (MemoryStore) and database/sql + encoding/json (PostgresStore). The two conscious shortcuts (MemoryStore in storage.go:48 and JSONB sub-item serialization in postgres.go:68) were tracked in the Debt Ledger and surfaced automatically in the Generative UI Dashboard.

5. Conclusion: Simplicity Is Governed Architecture

In the era of autonomous AI coding agents, writing code is no longer the bottleneck; preventing AI from writing unnecessary code is the true engineering discipline.

Pipeline-AI v0.11.0 is 100% open-source (MIT License) and available on GitHub:
🔗 Official Repository: https://github.com/rodrigodosanjosoliveira/pipeline-ai

title: RAG at Scale: Keeping Evidence Current and Governed with Oracle AI Database
description:
An overview of how to keep RAG evidence reliable as sources, retrieval routes, updates, and access rules multiply. 

RAG often starts with a simple path: ingest a document, create an embedding, retrieve similar content, and add the results to a prompt. That path becomes harder to trust as an application adds more sources, retrieval routes, source updates, and permission boundaries. 

Each addition creates dependencies that must stay aligned. A source update can affect document chunks, embeddings, metadata, lifecycle state, and retrieval filters. A result can be semantically relevant to a question while still being stale, superseded, or unavailable to the current caller. 

Oracle AI Database can keep structured data, vector embeddings, metadata, SQL-based filters, and database controls close to the same evidence path. It does not replace the application, the model, or orchestration logic. This article is an overview of the RAG lifecycle and a reading path to the deeper articles in this series. 

Key Takeaways 

  • More sources, retrieval routes, updates, and permission boundaries create more dependencies to coordinate. Reliable RAG depends on keeping source state, chunks, embeddings, metadata, and retrieval rules aligned. 
  • Oracle AI Database can keep relational data, vectors, metadata, SQL predicates, and database controls close to the same evidence path. This reduces copies and synchronization boundaries; it does not replace application logic. 
  • The application remains responsible for detecting source changes, deciding what to reprocess, authenticating callers, applying authorization, assembling context, calling models, and evaluating outcomes. 
  • Similarity search ranks semantic closeness. It does not prove that evidence is current, authoritative, complete, or permitted for a caller. 
  • Agent memory is durable state with its own ownership, retention, correction, and deletion rules; it is not a replacement for external knowledge retrieval.

The RAG evidence lifecycle with Oracle AI Database

The RAG Data Lifecycle 

A reliable retrieval path can be understood as four connected stages: 

1. Preserve meaning. Parse and chunk source content while carrying the context and metadata needed to interpret each retrievable unit. 

2. Find the right evidence. Choose keyword, vector, SQL, or hybrid retrieval based on the shape of the question. 

3. Keep evidence trustworthy. Propagate updates, deletions, versions, access rules, and provenance before evidence reaches generation. 

4. Prove the result. Measure retrieval quality separately from answer quality and keep failed cases as regression tests. 

These stages are not separate products. They are different views of the same evidence lifecycle. A weak boundary at any stage can look like a language-model problem later in the request. 

1. Preserve Meaning Before You Retrieve 

Chunking determines what the retriever is allowed to see. A fixed character limit can split a table from its headers, detach a bullet from its parent heading, or separate a transcript statement from the speaker and timestamp that make it meaningful. The goal is not equal-sized text. The goal is evidence that can stand on its own when it is returned. 

Metadata travels with that evidence. Source identifiers, document versions, timestamps, tenant scope, access labels, document type, parser version, and embedding-model version can all affect whether a chunk should be retrieved and cited. 

The detailed ingestion patterns are covered in RAG Chunking and Parsing for Tables, PDFs, Transcripts, and Media. The broader design rule is simple: do not create a vector representation of content after removing the context that makes the content useful. 

2. Find the Right Evidence for the Question 

Vector search is one retrieval route, not the definition of RAG. Exact identifiers and error codes may need lexical matching. Current counts and operational state belong in SQL. Paraphrased questions are a natural fit for vector search. Mixed questions may justify hybrid retrieval, but only when measurement shows that combining signals improves the workload. 

Similarity search compares the embedding of a user question with the embeddings stored for document chunks or records. A distance or similarity value ranks how close those vectors are under the selected metric. For example, with cosine distance, a smaller distance indicates a closer semantic match. This is a ranking signal, not a confidence percentage: semantic closeness alone does not establish freshness, authority, or permission. Those properties depend on source versions, lifecycle state, provenance, and access controls.

Question shape  Route to test first  What it protects 
Exact IDs, names, or error codes  Keyword or full-text  Exact lexical matches 
Paraphrased intent  Vector search  Semantic similarity 
Current counts, state, or filters  SQL  Authoritative structured facts 
Mixed exact and semantic intent  Hybrid search  Complementary retrieval signals 

Oracle AI Database includes Oracle AI Vector Search, allowing vector data to be queried alongside relational values and SQL-based controls. See the Oracle AI Vector Search User's Guide for the database-side concepts.

Retrieval routes should be compared against the same questions. Production RAG Evaluation: Keyword, Vector, SQL, or Hybrid Search? describes a practical way to separate retrieval metrics from answer metrics. 

3. Keep Evidence Current and Governed 

Retrieval data is derived from the source of truth. When source content changes, the application must reconcile every affected retrieval artifact: chunks, embeddings, source and embedding versions, lifecycle state, tenant and access metadata, and the filters that determine which records can be returned. Otherwise, vector search can return evidence that is relevant to the question but no longer current, authoritative, or permitted. 

  • Keep current structured facts in live SQL instead of embedding every changing record. 
  • Update affected document chunks incrementally and record source and embedding versions. 
  • Propagate deletion and supersession state into the searchable records. 
  • Use challenge questions where old and new evidence coexist. 

These terms describe different layers of the retrieval system. An embedding is the numerical vector generated from a chunk of text by an embedding model. A vector-store record is the database row that stores the chunk text, its embedding, source identifiers, versions, lifecycle state, and other metadata. A database vector index is the search structure built over the vector column to make similarity search efficient. The index is not another copy of the document or embedding. 

A challenge question is a deliberately constructed test query that exercises a known freshness change. For example, ask for the current value after a source document has been updated while both versions are available to the retrieval system. The freshness test passes when retrieval returns the current permitted version, excludes the superseded or deleted version, and the answer cites the current evidence. 

The freshness patterns are explained in Real-Time RAG: Live SQL, Incremental Indexing, and Freshness Tests. The related index-lifecycle problem is covered in How to Detect RAG Index Drift: Deleted Docs, Stale Chunks, and Duplicate Embeddings, which treats drift as a source-to-index consistency problem. 

Governance belongs in the same path. Tenant scope, access labels, deletion state, and provenance should be applied before evidence enters the model context. A prompt instruction is not a permission boundary, and a citation is useful only when it points to evidence the caller was allowed to receive. 

The security model is developed in Secure Enterprise RAG: ACLs, Tenant Filters, Provenance, and Oracle Deep Data Security. 

4. Keep RAG and Memory Separate 

RAG retrieves external evidence for the current question. Agent memory preserves selected state across interactions: preferences, decisions, summaries, task outcomes, or durable facts. Both can use similarity search, but they have different retention, correction, deletion, and scope requirements. 

A RAG record should normally be traceable to a source document or row. A memory record also needs to answer who it belongs to, how long it remains valid, what evidence supports it, and how it can be corrected or removed. Treating every conversation message as memory creates noisy context and weakens trust. 

Agent Memory Is Not RAG: Conversation IDs, Durable State, and Scoped Recall explains this boundary and why persistent memory needs explicit scope and lifecycle rules. 

5. Separate Retrieval Failures from Generation Failures 

Two systems can produce the same visible symptom: an answer that is wrong. The fix depends on what reached the context window. If the required evidence is missing from the top-k results, investigate chunking, embeddings, filters, ranking, or freshness. If the evidence is present but the answer invents a claim or cites the wrong version, investigate context construction, prompting, or generation. 

Log retrieved chunk IDs, source versions, scores, filters, and retrieval route. 

Measure retrieval with a ground-truth question set and metrics such as Recall@k, Precision@k, and NDCG@k, where k is the number of results evaluated. 

Recall@k measures the fraction of known relevant evidence retrieved in the top-k results. Precision@k measures the fraction of the top-k results that is relevant. NDCG@k measures whether the most relevant evidence is ranked near the top. 

Measure answers separately for groundedness, correctness, citation validity, and abstention. 

Keep stale, deleted, restricted, duplicate, and unsupported questions as regression cases. 

The troubleshooting guide How to Troubleshoot Vector Search in an AI Application focuses on making the retrieval path inspectable. The evaluation guide provides the broader measurement approach. 

How Oracle AI Database Reduces Coordination Boundaries 

In a split architecture, the source system, chunking pipeline, embedding process, retrieval store, metadata and access layer, and cache can each hold a different view of the same evidence. A source change, deletion, or permission update must be propagated across those boundaries before retrieval can safely return the result. 

Oracle AI Database reduces those coordination boundaries by keeping structured data, vector embeddings, metadata, SQL filtering, and database controls close to the same evidence path. This allows an application to combine current relational facts, document retrieval, provenance, lifecycle state, and access-aware filters without copying the governing data into unrelated stores solely for retrieval. 

This does not remove application responsibilities. The application still detects changes, chooses SQL, keyword, vector, or hybrid retrieval, authenticates callers, assembles model context, and evaluates results. The advantage is not that one database solves every concern; it is that fewer independent systems must stay synchronized about what evidence is current and available. 

Choose the Next Article by the Problem You Need to Solve 

  • Need to preserve meaning from PDFs, tables, transcripts, or media? Start with RAG Chunking and Parsing for Tables, PDFs, Transcripts, and Media. 
  • Need to choose between keyword, vector, SQL, and hybrid retrieval? Read Production RAG Evaluation: Keyword, Vector, SQL, or Hybrid Search?. 
  • Need to keep document retrieval current as source content changes? Read Real-Time RAG: Live SQL, Incremental Indexing, and Freshness Tests and How to Detect RAG Index Drift: Deleted Docs, Stale Chunks, and Duplicate Embeddings. 
  • Need to enforce tenant scope, access controls, deletion state, and provenance? Read Secure Enterprise RAG: ACLs, Tenant Filters, Provenance, and Oracle Deep Data Security. 
  • Need durable agent state across conversations rather than external knowledge retrieval? Read Agent Memory Is Not RAG: Conversation IDs, Durable State, and Scoped Recall. 
  • Need to determine whether an incorrect answer came from retrieval or generation? Read How to Troubleshoot Vector Search in an AI Application and the evaluation guide. 

Conclusion 

RAG becomes difficult to operate when it is treated as a single vector-search call. The system must preserve meaning during ingestion, match retrieval to the question, keep evidence current, enforce access rules, distinguish memory from external knowledge, and measure retrieval separately from generation. 

Oracle AI Database provides a common data and governance layer for those concerns. By keeping structured data, vectors, metadata, and SQL controls close together, it reduces the number of disconnected paths that must remain consistent as RAG systems scale.

Frequently Asked Questions 

Is vector search enough for every RAG question? 

No. Vector search is useful for semantic similarity, but exact identifiers and error codes may need keyword search, current structured values belong in SQL, and some questions benefit from hybrid retrieval. Choose the retrieval route that matches the question rather than treating vector search as the only option. 

How do I keep retrieved evidence current? 

Treat the vector index as derived data. Update affected chunks when source content changes, propagate deletions and superseded versions, record source and embedding versions, and run freshness tests that challenge the system with old and new evidence. 

Should changing database records always be embedded? 

No. Keep frequently changing structured facts in live SQL when possible. Embeddings are better suited to text where semantic matching is useful. A RAG system can combine SQL for current values with vector or hybrid retrieval for supporting context. 

Is agent memory the same as RAG? 

No. RAG retrieves external evidence for the current question. Agent memory stores selected state across interactions, such as preferences, decisions, summaries, or task outcomes. Memory needs explicit ownership, scope, retention, and update rules. 

How can I tell whether a bad answer came from retrieval or generation? 

Inspect the retrieved chunk IDs, source versions, scores, filters, and retrieval route before inspecting the answer. If the required evidence is missing or stale, the failure is in retrieval or indexing. If the evidence is present but the answer is unsupported or incorrect, investigate the prompt, model, and generation boundary. 

Why keep structured data, vectors, and metadata close together? 

Keeping them in Oracle AI Database makes it easier to apply SQL, metadata filters, provenance, updates, and governance to the same evidence path. It does not remove design work, but it reduces the number of independent systems that must stay synchronized.

References 

  • RAG Chunking and Parsing for Tables, PDFs, Transcripts, and Media  
  • Production RAG Evaluation: Keyword, Vector, SQL, or Hybrid Search?  
  • Agent Memory Is Not RAG: Conversation IDs, Durable State, and Scoped Recall  
  • Real-Time RAG: Live SQL, Incremental Indexing, and Freshness Tests 
  • Secure Enterprise RAG: ACLs, Tenant Filters, Provenance, and Oracle Deep Data Security  
  • How to Detect RAG Index Drift: Deleted Docs, Stale Chunks, and Duplicate Embeddings  
  • How to Troubleshoot Vector Search in an AI Application  
  • Oracle AI Vector Search User's Guide
