title: How to choose a cloud exit consultancy for a move to an EU cloud
description:
Originally published on moveinfra.eu.

To choose a cloud exit consultancy for a move from AWS to a European-owned cloud, look for a partner that delivers clean Infrastructure as Code (such as Terraform), uses live database replication rather than dump-and-restore scripts, provides a tested rollback mechanism, and works under a fixed or milestone-based contract after an initial discovery phase. Avoid general IT agencies that only hold US hyperscaler certifications. Your contract should explicitly require an audited resource inventory before execution starts, full ownership of all provisioning code, and strict boundaries around customer data access.

Key takeaways

  • Separate discovery from execution: Never sign an open-ended time-and-materials contract for the entire migration. Pay for a bounded inventory and architecture phase first, or require a fixed price once read-only discovery is complete.
  • Understand who you are hiring: Destination cloud providers offer professional services that know their own platform deeply, while independent migration partners help you compare providers, handle multi-provider architectures, and clean up the source AWS environment.
  • Demand Infrastructure as Code and live sync: A serious partner rebuilds your infrastructure cleanly in Terraform or OpenTofu and uses logical replication for databases.
  • Put rollback and data rules in the contract: Require a documented cutover runbook with a defined write-pause window, reverse data sync for post-cutover rollback, and a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) that minimizes human access to production data.

What a cloud exit consultancy actually does

Moving off AWS to an EU-owned cloud provider—such as UpCloud, Scaleway, Hetzner, OVHcloud, STACKIT, IONOS, or Exoscale—is a different engineering problem than moving workloads into AWS. When companies move into a US hyperscaler, they often rely on vendor-subsidized migration programs and proprietary migration agents. Moving out requires translating AWS-specific constructs into portable, standard equivalents.

A competent cloud exit partner handles five specific areas of work:

  1. Discovery and service mapping: Auditing your AWS billing exports, IAM roles, networks, and Terraform state to find every active resource, including forgotten snapshots, elastic IPs, and regional data transfer paths. You can preview what this mapping looks like using the free EU Cloud Service Map.
  2. Target architecture and sizing: Translating AWS instance families, security groups, and VPC setups into the destination provider's networking and compute model. Where an EU cloud lacks a direct managed equivalent (for example, Hetzner does not offer managed databases or managed Kubernetes), the partner must design how those services will run reliably on virtual servers or across a secondary provider.
  3. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) rebuild: Writing clean, modular Terraform or OpenTofu code for the new environment so your team can manage it after the consultancy leaves.
  4. Data synchronization and CI/CD integration: Setting up continuous logical replication for relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL), syncing S3 buckets to EU S3-compatible object storage with checksum verification, and helping your engineers point existing deployment pipelines to the new servers.
  5. Cutover, rollback, and AWS decommissioning: Running the switchover during a planned maintenance window, keeping a reverse path open in case of unexpected application issues, and safely tearing down the old AWS accounts so stray bills do not continue.

Independent migration partner vs. destination provider professional services

When you decide to move to a European cloud, you generally have two choices for outside help: the destination cloud provider's in-house professional services team, or an independent migration partner. Both have clear strengths and trade-offs.

Comparison area Independent migration partner Destination provider professional services
Provider selection Can benchmark multiple EU clouds (e.g., comparing UpCloud vs. OVHcloud vs. Scaleway) against your workload and budget. Will architect exclusively for their own platform, even if a specific workload fits better elsewhere.
Platform depth Broad operational knowledge across AWS and several EU clouds; relies on public APIs and standard tooling. Direct access to internal product teams, roadmaps, and deep platform-specific troubleshooting.
Source cloud (AWS) work Actively works inside your AWS environment to untangle dependencies, manage exit notices, and shut down old resources. Usually stops at their own boundary; gives you guidance on how to push data in, but rarely touches your AWS account.
Commercial incentives Paid for the migration project itself; motivated to finish the cutover and hand over keys on schedule. Often subsidized or discounted to win your recurring monthly cloud spend; scope is usually limited to onboarding architecture.
Hybrid setups Comfortable building setups that span providers (e.g., bare metal on one EU provider, managed database on another). Designs single-cloud architectures.

If you already know which EU provider you want, have an internal DevOps team to handle the AWS teardown, and mainly need architectural validation on the new platform, the destination provider's solutions architects are often enough. If your engineering team is busy shipping product and you want another team to build the Terraform, wire the database replication, coordinate the cutover, and clean up AWS, look for an independent specialist.

Questions to ask before you sign

When interviewing potential partners, skip generic questions about how long they have been in business. Ask operational questions that reveal how they actually move production systems.

1. "Which target European clouds have you deployed to in the last 12 months?"

Many traditional European IT consultancies advertise "cloud migration" but do 95% of their work moving on-premises VMware servers into AWS or Azure. Ask which specific EU clouds they have automated with Terraform recently. Ask them to name two technical quirks or limitations of the target provider you are considering (for example, how private networking works across availability zones, or how load balancer proxy protocols are configured). If they cannot name specific limitations of the target cloud, they have not used it in production.

2. "How do you move our production database, and what is the expected write pause?"

Listen carefully to the answer. If they propose taking a database dump (pg_dump or mysqldump), copying it over the network, and restoring it on the other side, your application will be offline for hours if your database is more than a few dozen gigabytes. A qualified partner will describe setting up logical replication (or native binlog/WAL replication) over an encrypted tunnel, letting the replica catch up while your application stays live, pausing writes briefly until replication lag drops near zero, and switching connection strings.

3. "How do you handle AWS-proprietary services like SQS, Lambda, or DynamoDB?"

A move from EC2, RDS, and S3 to an EU cloud is mostly infrastructure plumbing. A move involving proprietary AWS services requires application code changes. Ask the partner where they draw the line between infrastructure migration and application refactoring. Do they deploy RabbitMQ, NATS, or Redis to replace SQS? Who updates the application SDK calls—their engineers or yours? Before you even speak to a vendor, you can scan your own repositories with an open-source cloud lock-in scanner to know exactly which proprietary APIs your codebase calls.

4. "What happens two days after cutover if we discover a critical issue?"

Every consultancy has a plan for moving forward; few have a tested plan for moving backward. Once DNS points to the new European cloud and users start writing new rows to the new database, simply switching DNS back to AWS will result in data loss unless those new writes were replicated back to AWS. Ask how they maintain reverse replication after cutover and for how long.

5. "How do you help us avoid AWS data egress fees during the switch?"

Moving terabytes of S3 objects and database snapshots out of AWS generates data transfer fees. Your partner should know how to use the AWS EU Data Act switching mechanisms or standard AWS account closure fee waivers, and how to avoid paying for multiple full-dataset copies during dry runs. You can check your own exposure and download a notice template using the free Cloud Exit Fee Calculator. (Note: under Article 29 of the EU Data Act, Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, switching charges—including data egress fees for switching—are capped at cost until 12 January 2027 and banned entirely from 12 January 2027.)

Pricing models: how migration projects are billed

Consultancies generally price cloud exits in one of four ways. Understanding the incentives behind each model will save you from budget overruns.

  • Time and Materials (T&M): You pay a daily or hourly rate for engineers. T&M is normal and reasonable when a project requires heavy application refactoring (for example, rewriting hundreds of Lambda functions or migrating off DynamoDB), because neither side can know the exact code complexity upfront. However, for standard infrastructure and database migrations, open-ended T&M shifts all execution risk onto you.
  • Two-stage (Paid Discovery, then Fixed Price): You pay a small, fixed fee for a 1-to-3 week discovery phase where the consultancy audits your AWS account via read-only access and produces a migration plan, target bill estimate, and fixed price for execution. You should retain the right to walk away with the discovery deliverables if you do not like the execution quote.
  • Fixed Price / Milestone-based: For standard workloads (VMs, Kubernetes, RDS, S3, load balancers), a mature specialist can inspect your billing export and read-only metadata, and give you a fixed price broken into milestones (e.g., 1. Inventory & Architecture, 2. IaC Environment Built, 3. Data Sync Live, 4. Production Cutover).
  • Savings-share or Percentage of Spend: Some firms charge a percentage of your annual cloud spend or a percentage of your first year's savings. Be cautious here: this model can incentivize a partner to push you toward the cheapest possible hardware setup (such as unmanaged bare metal without proper redundancy) just to inflate the theoretical savings figure. To check expected infrastructure savings objectively before entering negotiations, upload your billing export to a browser-based Cloud Bill Analyzer.

Red flags to watch out for

Walk away or pause negotiations if you see any of these behaviors during the sales process:

  • Promising "zero downtime" without inspecting your database: Any migration that switches the primary database for write operations requires at least a brief pause in writes (even if it is only 15 to 60 seconds) to prevent split-brain data corruption. Anyone promising literal "zero downtime" before auditing your database schema and application connection pooling is either using marketing language or planning an unsafe cutover.
  • Using proprietary Terraform wrappers you cannot maintain: Some consultancies deploy their own closed-source Terraform modules or custom management agents into your new cloud, then try to sell you a mandatory monthly managed-services retainer to maintain them. Insist on standard, human-readable Terraform or OpenTofu using official provider plugins.
  • Recommending US-owned "sovereign" regions when you asked for an EU-owned cloud: If your requirement is escaping US jurisdiction (such as the US CLOUD Act) by moving to a European-headquartered provider, watch out for AWS Partners who try to steer you into the AWS European Sovereign Cloud instead. While the AWS European Sovereign Cloud keeps data and operations inside the EU, it remains owned by Amazon, a US corporation.
  • Asking for full Administrator IAM keys before signing an NDA and DPA: For an initial assessment, a billing export or AWS ReadOnlyAccess / ViewOnlyAccess role is sufficient. A vendor never needs write access during scoping.

What to require in the contract

Once you select a partner, make sure your Statement of Work (SOW) and Master Services Agreement (MSA) cover these four areas explicitly:

1. Audited inventory and scope baseline

Attach the exact inventory of AWS accounts, regions, VPCs, databases, and storage buckets to the contract. Define what happens if a new resource is discovered mid-project, and freeze non-essential architectural changes in AWS during the migration window so neither side is chasing a moving target.

2. Cutover criteria and rollback window

Do not define project completion as "infrastructure deployed." Define completion as production traffic running on the destination cloud with all agreed health checks passing. Specify:

  • The maximum acceptable replication lag before the cutover write pause begins (for example, under 5 seconds).
  • The maximum planned maintenance window duration, after which an automatic abort and rollback to AWS is triggered.
  • The post-cutover rollback period (typically 14 to 30 days) during which the old AWS environment remains on standby with reverse data synchronization active, before final decommissioning. (If your company is subject to DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, documenting these exit and fallback procedures also directly supports your regulatory ICT exit strategy requirements.)

3. Data handling, security, and least privilege

Your migration partner will inevitably interact with infrastructure that holds personal or business-critical data. Require:

  • A GDPR-compliant Data Processing Agreement (DPA) listing any subcontractors.
  • All data in transit between AWS and the EU cloud to move over encrypted channels (such as WireGuard, IPsec VPN, or TLS 1.3) directly from your AWS account to your new EU cloud account—never staged on the consultancy's own servers.
  • Checksum verification logs proving that object storage buckets were copied completely without silent corruption.
  • A clause requiring immediate revocation of all IAM roles, SSH keys, and VPN access upon project sign-off.

4. Code ownership and handover deliverables

State clearly that all Infrastructure as Code, CI/CD pipeline modifications, runbooks, and architecture diagrams become your company's intellectual property upon payment (or are licensed under an open, perpetual, royalty-free license without dependency on the vendor). Require a live handover session where your internal engineers run a terraform plan and deploy an application change without the consultancy touching the keyboard.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a migration from AWS to a European cloud usually take?

For a typical 10-to-300 person company running standard infrastructure (virtual machines, Kubernetes, PostgreSQL/MySQL, Redis, and S3 object storage), a well-run migration takes between 3 and 8 weeks from inventory to cutover, followed by a 30-day standby window before shutting down AWS. If the project requires rewriting code to replace proprietary services like DynamoDB or AWS Step Functions, timelines extend based on software engineering capacity.

Should we sign up for the destination EU cloud ourselves, or let the consultancy resell it?

Always open the destination cloud account directly in your own company's name, with your own billing details and root credentials. Letting a consultancy resell the cloud infrastructure puts another legal and financial layer between you and your servers, complicates support escalation, and makes it harder to part ways with the consultancy later.

Can we claim AWS egress fee waivers if a consultancy runs our migration?

Yes. Under AWS policy and the AWS EU Data Act Addendum, eligibility for data transfer fee reductions or waivers depends on the customer account and the nature of the workload exit, not on whether your internal staff or a third-party contractor executes the transfer. However, your company (as the account holder) must submit the formal support ticket or switching notice to AWS before moving the bulk data. Always verify the current procedure on the official AWS documentation pages before starting large transfers.

Do we need to rewrite our CI/CD pipelines to switch clouds?

Usually, you only need to update the deployment target step. If you build Docker containers or application artifacts in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, the build and test steps stay identical. The consultancy should work with your team to update the final deployment step—pointing it to the new container registry, Kubernetes cluster, or virtual servers on the European cloud.

Sources

  • Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (EU Data Act) on EUR-Lex — Articles 25, 29, and 34 covering cloud switching contracts, notice periods, and the phase-out of switching and data egress charges.
  • Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (Digital Operational Resilience Act / DORA) on EUR-Lex — Requirements for ICT risk management and documented cloud exit strategies.
  • AWS EC2 On-Demand & Data Transfer Pricing — Official AWS documentation detailing data transfer out rates and the process for requesting fee waivers when exiting AWS.

Drafted with AI assistance and fact-checked by the MoveInfra team. The original, kept up to date, is at moveinfra.eu. Free tools for pricing a move to an EU cloud: moveinfra.eu/tools.

title: Cloudflare’s Rust SDK Can Run Flags Locally. How Fast Can You Turn One Off?
description:
A staff member opens the new directory search, gets a blank page, and files a bug. You turn the pilot off. Their next refresh works, then the broken screen comes back. With two servers behind a load balancer, both requests can be handled correctly according to the flag rules each server has in memory. The servers simply disagree about which rules are current.

AI generated this article from public sources. The rollout and staging exercise are illustrative.

On November 10, Cloudflare announced an official Rust SDK for Flagship that evaluates flags through OpenFeature. The SDK calls the service over HTTP by default. With local evaluation enabled, it downloads definitions and evaluates them inside the process. When a background refresh fails, the provider reports a stale status and keeps serving the last downloaded definitions. A request can therefore get a successful “on” evaluation after an operator has turned the flag off. Cloudflare’s announcement · Rust SDK documentation

Give the pilot an expiration rule

The Garden’s public case study describes a staged replacement of Planning Center, with staff workflows and a directory that supports pagination, filters, and server-side counts. The migration remains ongoing. A read-only directory search pilot makes a good example of a workflow that needs a way back to an existing path. The Rust deployment below is a proposed example inspired by that staged approach. The Garden case study

Imagine that a new directory endpoint can send an eligible staff member to either of two search implementations. Keep the evaluation on the server so that a saved browser tab can’t choose the backend by itself. Use the same synthetic account and targeting context on both servers during the test. That removes differences in targeting from the explanation if the responses diverge.

Pick the fallback before opening the pilot. For this example, route to the existing search when the provider can’t initialize, when flag evaluation errors, or when the provider reports stale definitions. Keep existing access checks on both paths. If you can measure the last successful refresh reliably, you can also cap the age of the rules your app will use to admit a request to the pilot. A refresh interval schedules an attempt. When connectivity fails, it can’t guarantee that the new rules have arrived. Cloudflare’s local evaluation and refresh behavior

The tradeoff shows up during a vendor or network outage. A team may be happy to leave a cosmetic pilot running from the last known configuration. If the pilot can return a blank directory when staff need it, sending them back to the existing search may be worth an interruption to the experiment. Choose how long you can live with the wrong variant before choosing how much stale configuration to tolerate.

Run the rollback with one server cut off

Start two staging instances and verify that both send the same test account to the pilot. Cut only the second instance’s connection to the flag service, keeping its application traffic working. Turn the flag off. Probe each instance directly so a load balancer can’t hide a lagging instance. Record which search backend actually served each request, when it switched, and whether the user still got a usable result. Wait through a failed refresh and repeat. The healthy instance should pick up the change. The isolated one should fall back according to the policy you chose.

Run the exercise once more with the second instance starting cold while the service is unreachable. The Rust SDK’s initialization returns an error if the first definitions download fails. The cold case tells you whether your application can start the existing search independently or whether flag initialization can take down the whole endpoint. When connectivity comes back, check that both instances honor the current flag before you re-enable the pilot. Cloudflare’s Rust initialization behavior

Keep the backend selection visible in application metrics. Cloudflare says local evaluations don’t appear in Flagship analytics. For a rollout, a small counter broken down by instance, selected route, and fallback reason lets the person on call answer the question that matters after pressing Off. Which server still sent a request to the pilot, and how long did it keep doing that? Cloudflare’s local evaluation documentation

title: Passwordless Java Connections to Oracle AI Database with OCI IAM and Microsoft Entra ID
description:
A complete, runnable guide to OCI and Entra token files and SDK suppliers, JDBC providers and connection pools—with database setup and Microsoft Entra identity configuration.

Cloud identity, database mapping, TLS and token lifecycle work together to authenticate each new physical connection.

Key Takeaways

  • Run the same read-only Java application with OCI or Entra token files, application-owned SDK suppliers, or JDBC providers.
  • Database trust, principal-to-schema mapping, cloud authorization and TCPS must all agree before a token login can succeed.
  • The repository contains complete source, configuration profiles including native JDBC properties files, SQL setup templates, concurrent UCP examples and automated tests.
  • Verify token refresh with newly created physical connections; reusing an existing pooled session does not prove that refresh works.

A Java application can authenticate to Oracle AI Database with an OCI IAM or Microsoft Entra ID token instead of passing a database password. For OCI IAM, JDBC proves possession of a private key associated with the token. For Entra ID, it presents an access token intended for the database resource. The database validates that identity and maps it to an authorized schema.

This walkthrough combines the original IAM CLI/SDK and pooling examples with the JDBC extension approach, using a runnable application throughout. The concrete server setup targets Autonomous AI Database Serverless; other Oracle Database deployments need their own supported identity integration. The Java examples use current, pinned JDBC releases, while the database product is named Oracle AI Database 26ai.

Start with the setup for one identity provider, build the companion Java application, and choose a configuration profile. None of the Java token flows passes a database username or password. In this walkthrough:

  • Key Takeaways
  • Choose a token acquisition path
  • Prerequisites and tested dependency versions
  • Configure the database and identity
  • Build and run the application
  • Option 1: OCI CLI token files
  • Option 2: Generate and cache OCI tokens with the SDK
  • Option 3: Let the OCI provider acquire the token
  • Option 4: Let the Entra provider acquire the token
  • Entra alternatives: token files and SDK suppliers
  • UCP: share the supplier and test physical connection replacement
  • Verify the database identity
  • Complete executable and source map
  • Troubleshooting
  • FAQ

Choose a token acquisition path

OCI and Entra each support external token files, application-owned SDK acquisition, and driver-selected providers. Their token formats differ: OCI uses a proof-of-possession private key; Entra uses a bearer JWT. Do not pass an OCI key to an Entra connection.

Flow Token acquisition Replacement responsibility Demo profile
OCI file OCI CLI/external producer Producer replaces token and matching PoP key coherently oci-file.properties
Entra file Approved Azure CLI/SDK/external producer Producer replaces a private JWT file entra-file.properties
OCI SDK Application calls OCI identity data plane JDBC cache around the acquisition supplier oci-sdk.properties
Entra SDK Application calls Azure Identity JDBC cache around the acquisition supplier entra-sdk.properties
OCI provider Driver-selected OCI extension Provider/cache oci-config-file.properties and identity-specific profiles
Entra provider Driver-selected Azure extension Provider/cache entra-service-principal.properties and identity-specific profiles

The provider examples use oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication=OCI_* or AZURE_*. These settings select the corresponding extension; keep the provider JAR, but omit explicit oracle.jdbc.provider.accessToken settings. File modes use OCI_TOKEN or OAUTH; application-owned SDK modes attach a token supplier instead. Do not combine acquisition mechanisms on one data source. See the JDBC connection-property reference.

Background: Accessing Autonomous Database with IAM token using Java (Jean de Lavarene, Michael McMahon and Nirmala Sundarappa) and 23c JDBC seamless authentication with OCI IAM and Azure AD (Jean de Lavarene).

Prerequisites and tested dependency versions

Use JDK 17 or 21, Maven 3.9+, a reachable Autonomous Database, and an identity administrator who can configure the intended mapping. The demo needs only CREATE SESSION after setup and queries DUAL; it creates no application tables. You will also need OCI CLI for file examples and the actual hosting environment for workload identities.

The examples use JDBC and UCP 23.26.3.0.0, the OCI and Azure providers 1.1.0, OCI SDK 3.86.2, and Azure Identity 1.18.0. These versions were built and tested together. The JDBC artifact version is separate from the database product name.

JDBC, pooling and wallet support

Add these dependencies to your Maven project. Keep ucp17 for the pooling examples and oraclepki for the wallet-based connections used here.

<dependencies>
  <!-- JDBC driver -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.oracle.database.jdbc</groupId>
    <artifactId>ojdbc17</artifactId>
    <version>23.26.3.0.0</version>
  </dependency>
  <!-- For the UCP examples -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.oracle.database.jdbc</groupId>
    <artifactId>ucp17</artifactId>
    <version>23.26.3.0.0</version>
  </dependency>
  <!-- For Oracle wallet support -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.oracle.database.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>oraclepki</artifactId>
    <version>23.26.3.0.0</version>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Add the provider for your identity service

Choose OCI, Microsoft Entra ID, or both if you are running all the examples. The provider dependencies include their cloud SDKs and are loaded at runtime.

<dependencies>
  <!-- OCI IAM -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.oracle.database.jdbc</groupId>
    <artifactId>ojdbc-provider-oci</artifactId>
    <version>1.1.0</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
  </dependency>
  <!-- Microsoft Entra ID -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.oracle.database.jdbc</groupId>
    <artifactId>ojdbc-provider-azure</artifactId>
    <version>1.1.0</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

No ojdbc8 exclusion is needed: these provider releases declare it with Maven's provided scope, so it is not added to your application's dependencies. The application uses the explicitly declared ojdbc17 driver above.

Additional dependencies for direct OCI SDK calls

Only the application-managed SDK example (OciTokens.java) needs these declarations. The first makes the token-request API available when compiling Java; the second supplies its HTTP transport at runtime. Provider-only applications can omit them.

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.oracle.oci.sdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>oci-java-sdk-identitydataplane</artifactId>
    <version>3.86.2</version>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.oracle.oci.sdk</groupId>
    <artifactId>oci-java-sdk-common-httpclient-jersey</artifactId>
    <version>3.86.2</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Combine the dependencies you need into your existing <dependencies> section. The repository's complete pom.xml also contains SDK version alignment and the build configuration used to compile, test and package the runnable demo.

Additional dependency for direct Entra SDK calls

EntraTokens.java uses Azure Identity directly, so make it a compile-time dependency as well as a transitive runtime dependency of the provider:

<dependency>
  <groupId>com.azure</groupId>
  <artifactId>azure-identity</artifactId>
  <version>1.18.0</version>
</dependency>

Configure the database and identity

These examples target Autonomous AI Database Serverless. A JDBC release number does not enable identity integration on a database. Other Oracle Database deployments require their own supported server configuration. Use a lab database and an administrator for setup; the Java demo needs only CREATE SESSION and reads DUAL.

OCI IAM and Entra are alternative external identity provider configurations. Use separate lab databases to demonstrate both. The SQL scripts omit forced replacement and stop on errors. They are first-time setup scripts, not repeatable migrations. If TOKEN_DEMO already exists, inspect its mapping rather than dropping it.

OCI IAM setup

  1. Create or select an IAM user and group, for example TokenDemoUsers; add the user to that group. For non-default identity domains use the domain-qualified names supported by your tenancy.
  2. Create a policy scoped to the target database. Replace each placeholder in this example:
Allow group TokenDemoUsers to use autonomous-database-family in compartment DemoCompartment
  where target.id = '<database-ocid>'
  1. As ADMIN in SQLcl, SQL*Plus, or Database Actions, enable OCI IAM and map the user. With SQLcl run @sql/oci-setup.sql; Database Actions users should run the SQL statements and replace the prompt variable manually. Enter the exact IAM name; a non-default domain uses domain/name. The script creates TOKEN_DEMO and grants CREATE SESSION. A shared group mapping is included as an alternative. Choose one mapping for this demonstration.
  2. For local API-key authentication, register an API signing public key with the IAM user and configure the matching private key using oci setup config. Keep it outside the repository. An OCI config profile has user, tenancy, region, fingerprint, and key_file values. The API signing key authenticates the OCI API request; it is different from the per-token proof-of-possession key.
  3. Record the compartment and Autonomous Database OCIDs. Set OCI_DB_SCOPE to urn:oracle:db::id::<compartment-ocid>::<database-ocid>. Token scope, cloud policy, and database mapping are independent requirements.
  4. For an instance principal, create an IAM dynamic group whose matching rule contains the intended compute instance. For a resource principal, include the intended supported resource. Grant that dynamic group the scoped database policy and create a shared database mapping with IAM_GROUP_NAME=<dynamic-group-name>. Run in the actual workload environment; choosing the profile on a laptop does not create that identity. Do not try to exclusively map an instance/resource principal as an IAM user.

For a session-token profile, first authenticate with oci session authenticate, then use the CLI with --auth security_token --profile <profile> or the SDK example with app.oci.authentication=session-token. A database token refresh cannot rescue an expired upstream login session: renew the login session too. The resource-provider config-file method in this release uses API-key configuration; do not assume it reads a session token just because one appears in the file. Cloud Shell and interactive provider profiles demonstrate the other supported user-session paths.

Sources: enable IAM, policies and dynamic groups, user mappings, OCI SDK authentication.

Run these statements as the database administrator; replace the IAM name with your own:

BEGIN
  DBMS_CLOUD_ADMIN.ENABLE_EXTERNAL_AUTHENTICATION(type => 'OCI_IAM');
END;
/
CREATE USER token_demo IDENTIFIED GLOBALLY AS
  'IAM_PRINCIPAL_NAME=<domain>/<user>';
GRANT CREATE SESSION TO token_demo;
SELECT name, value FROM v$parameter WHERE name = 'identity_provider_type';

For the default identity domain, use the IAM user name without a domain prefix if appropriate. The repository includes a prompted SQLcl script and the alternative shared-group mapping. An API key signs OCI API requests; the PoP key associated with each database token has a separate purpose.

Microsoft Entra ID setup

  1. Register the database resource application in the Entra tenant. Record its application ID and Application ID URI. Expose a delegated database scope such as session:scope:connect for interactive clients. The URI identifies the database resource; it is not the Java client's ID.
  2. On that database registration, define the app-role value TokenDemo.Connect (the display name can differ). Allow Applications for client credentials and Users/Groups for interactive users, according to the intended scenarios.
  3. Register the Java client application separately. For service-principal authentication, add the database app's Application permission TokenDemo.Connect and grant administrator consent. Configure a certificate or create a client secret. AZURE_CLIENT_ID identifies this Java client, whereas ENTRA_DB_APP_ID_URI identifies the bare database resource. SDK/file acquisition uses the full ENTRA_DB_SCOPE, ending in /.default for a workload.
  4. For browser authentication, configure the client as a public/native client and register http://localhost:8400 as its redirect URI. Give it the delegated database permission and any required consent. Assign the user/group to the database application's role. For device-code authentication enable the appropriate public-client flow. These flows are subject to tenant Conditional Access policy. For v2 interactive tokens, configure the upn optional claim as described in Oracle's guide.
  5. For managed identity, assign the database app role to the managed identity's service principal; enabling an Azure VM identity alone does not grant database access. Use the identity's client ID for a user-assigned identity. Unset AZURE_CLIENT_ID for a system-assigned identity so an unrelated application ID is not selected.
  6. As ADMIN on the Entra lab database, run @sql/entra-setup.sql. Supply the tenant and database registration values. The script enables AZURE_AD, maps AZURE_ROLE=TokenDemo.Connect to TOKEN_DEMO, and grants CREATE SESSION. The SQL provider identifier remains AZURE_AD even though the product is now called Entra ID.
  7. If the database already trusts the intended Entra resource, preserve that provider configuration and existing DDS roles. Add only the dedicated demo role/assignment and, after checking that TOKEN_DEMO does not already exist, the CREATE USER and GRANT statements. Do not rerun first-time enablement on an existing integration.
  8. For a v1 token, match the registered database Application ID URI. For v2, follow Oracle's audience configuration guidance; the token audience is the application ID. Verify the token version and resource configuration with the administrators rather than substituting a Microsoft Graph scope.

Sources: registration, roles, consent, token versions, and server setup, schema mapping, managed identity app-role assignment.

The corresponding database SQL uses the database resource registration, not the client application:

BEGIN
  DBMS_CLOUD_ADMIN.ENABLE_EXTERNAL_AUTHENTICATION(
    type => 'AZURE_AD',
    params => JSON_OBJECT(
      'tenant_id' VALUE '<tenant-id>',
      'application_id' VALUE '<database-application-id>',
      'application_id_uri' VALUE 'https://<tenant-domain>/<database-application-id>'),
    force => FALSE);
END;
/
CREATE USER token_demo IDENTIFIED GLOBALLY AS 'AZURE_ROLE=TokenDemo.Connect';
GRANT CREATE SESSION TO token_demo;

The two enablement procedures are alternatives. Do not run both against the same database as if they were additive configuration. The supplied scripts stop when an incompatible provider is already enabled, leaving the administrator to choose a separate lab database or plan a deliberate migration.

TLS and wallet configuration

Use EZConnect+ with the database's TCPS host, port and service. The pinned JDBC driver enables server identity matching by default; no redundant DN-match URL flag is necessary. Do not disable validation or use a naming alias.

jdbc:oracle:thin:@tcps://<adb-host>:1522/<service>?connect_timeout=20

For mTLS, store the wallet outside the checkout and add this property to an ignored local profile. Set the directory environment variable to its absolute path:

oracle.net.wallet_location=(SOURCE=(METHOD=FILE)(METHOD_DATA=(DIRECTORY=${ADB_WALLET_DIR})))

If required, inject oracle.net.wallet_password through the runtime secret facility. The wallet is a TLS credential, not the OCI token directory or Entra JWT file. TLS-only endpoints need no client wallet when the JVM trusts the server CA. Preserve the deployment's transport requirements.

Build and run the application

git clone https://github.com/oracle-samples/oracle-db-examples.git
cd oracle-db-examples/java/jdbc-token-auth
mvn -B verify
./run.sh --help

# Replace with the host, TCPS port and service from Database Connection.
export ADB_JDBC_URL='jdbc:oracle:thin:@tcps://<adb-host>:1522/<service>'
export OCI_COMPARTMENT_ID='<compartment-ocid>'
export OCI_DATABASE_ID='<database-ocid>'
export OCI_CONFIG_FILE="$HOME/.oci/config"
export OCI_PROFILE=DEFAULT
export OCI_DB_SCOPE='urn:oracle:db::id::<compartment-ocid>::<database-ocid>'

Use the actual TCPS host, port and service for your database. For mTLS add wallet properties to an ignored local copy of a profile as explained in setup. The demo loads ${VARIABLE} placeholders itself and rejects missing variables without logging their values. It does not load .env files automatically.

./run.sh config/oci-config-file.properties check
./run.sh config/oci-config-file.properties jdbc
./run.sh config/oci-config-file.properties ucp

check only validates configuration and makes no cloud/database connection. jdbc opens a physical connection per round. ucp performs four concurrent tasks through a pool of at most two connections, propagates worker failures, and destroys the pool on exit. Windows users can invoke java -cp "target/oracle-jdbc-token-auth-demo-1.0.0.jar;target/lib/*" demo.TokenAuthDemo ... after Maven builds it.

Interpret a successful run carefully: TokenAuthDemo.query() prints the session user, authenticated identity and authentication method, but does not assert their expected values. A zero exit status means the connection and query succeeded; manually verify that user is the intended database schema and authentication is TOKEN_GLOBAL before treating the run as proof of token authentication. The separate OciWorkloadPrincipalDemo performs those assertions and prints PASS only when they match.

Every Java sample connection also sets Oracle JDBC Thin's v$session.program to devrel-developerhub-java-jdbc-token-auth. This is the database-visible program identifier for this sample, using the required devrel-developerhub-<content-name> convention; Oracle JDBC documents this property as the value shown in V$SESSION.PROGRAM (JDBC connection-property reference).

Option 1: OCI CLI token files

umask 077
oci iam db-token get --profile "$OCI_PROFILE"
export OCI_DB_TOKEN_DIR="$HOME/.oci/db-token"
./run.sh config/oci-file.properties jdbc
./run.sh config/oci-file.properties ucp

# Alternatives: run only in a configured identity environment.
oci --auth instance_principal iam db-token get
oci --auth resource_principal iam db-token get
# A session-token profile must be created/renewed with oci session authenticate.
oci --auth security_token --profile SESSION iam db-token get

The directory must contain token and its matching oci_db_key.pem. JDBC reads them with oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication=OCI_TOKEN and oracle.jdbc.tokenLocation. These are a database token and PoP key, not the API signing key or TLS wallet. File mode does not invoke the CLI or acquire replacements. For this demo, stop the application, regenerate the pair, and restart. A long-lived producer needs coordinated reads/writes of both files: replacing two files individually is not an atomic pair update. Prefer SDK/provider mode for a continuously running service.

The file profile is complete and can be passed directly to the launcher:

# Use an EZConnect+ TCPS URL with the host, port, and service from Database Connection.
app.url=${ADB_JDBC_URL}
app.mode=file
oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication=OCI_TOKEN
oracle.jdbc.tokenLocation=${OCI_DB_TOKEN_DIR}

The underlying JDBC call is small. This excerpt demonstrates a single physical connection; the executable application also validates configuration and prints the authenticated identity:

OracleDataSource ds = new OracleDataSource();
ds.setURL(System.getenv("ADB_JDBC_URL"));
Properties properties = new Properties();
properties.setProperty("oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication", "OCI_TOKEN");
properties.setProperty("oracle.jdbc.tokenLocation", System.getenv("OCI_DB_TOKEN_DIR"));
ds.setConnectionProperties(properties);
try (Connection connection = ds.getConnection()) {
    // Execute the read-only identity query shown below.
}

Option 2: Generate and cache OCI tokens with the SDK

./run.sh config/oci-sdk.properties builder
./run.sh config/oci-sdk.properties jdbc 3
./run.sh config/oci-sdk.properties ucp

OciTokens.java generates a 2048-bit RSA pair, sends the public key and database scope to the OCI identity data plane, and constructs AccessToken.createJsonWebToken(jwt, privateKey). It keeps the private key in memory. builder supplies one newly acquired token through createConnectionBuilder().accessToken(...); jdbc and ucp attach a cached supplier created by AccessToken.createJsonWebTokenCache(...) to the data source. No custom refresh scheduler is required.

For other SDK identities copy the profile to config/oci-sdk.local.properties, change app.oci.authentication to session-token, instance-principal, or resource-principal, and remove unused app.oci.configFile and app.oci.profile lines for workload identities. Session credentials must remain valid for future token requests. Do not combine the supplier with username/password or an access-token provider on the same data source.

Here is the complete supplier implementation used by the application:

package demo;

import com.oracle.bmc.auth.AbstractAuthenticationDetailsProvider;
import com.oracle.bmc.auth.ConfigFileAuthenticationDetailsProvider;
import com.oracle.bmc.auth.InstancePrincipalsAuthenticationDetailsProvider;
import com.oracle.bmc.auth.ResourcePrincipalAuthenticationDetailsProvider;
import com.oracle.bmc.auth.SessionTokenAuthenticationDetailsProvider;
import com.oracle.bmc.identitydataplane.DataplaneClient;
import com.oracle.bmc.identitydataplane.model.GenerateScopedAccessTokenDetails;
import com.oracle.bmc.identitydataplane.requests.GenerateScopedAccessTokenRequest;
import oracle.jdbc.AccessToken;
import java.security.KeyPairGenerator;
import java.util.Base64;
import java.util.Properties;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** Application-owned SDK acquisition: the PoP key never leaves memory. */
public final class OciTokens {
    private OciTokens() {}

    public static Supplier<? extends AccessToken> cached(Properties settings) {
        return AccessToken.createJsonWebTokenCache(() -> request(settings));
    }

    public static AccessToken request(Properties settings) {
        try {
            String profile = settings.getProperty("app.oci.profile", "DEFAULT");
            String file = settings.getProperty("app.oci.configFile",
                    System.getProperty("user.home") + "/.oci/config");
            AbstractAuthenticationDetailsProvider identity = switch (
                    settings.getProperty("app.oci.authentication", "config-file")) {
                case "config-file" -> new ConfigFileAuthenticationDetailsProvider(file, profile);
                case "session-token" -> new SessionTokenAuthenticationDetailsProvider(file, profile);
                case "instance-principal" -> InstancePrincipalsAuthenticationDetailsProvider.builder().build();
                case "resource-principal" -> ResourcePrincipalAuthenticationDetailsProvider.builder().build();
                default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unsupported app.oci.authentication");
            };
            try {
                var generator = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA");
                generator.initialize(2048);
                var pair = generator.generateKeyPair();
                var details = GenerateScopedAccessTokenDetails.builder()
                        .scope(Settings.required(settings, "app.oci.scope"))
                        .publicKey(Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(pair.getPublic().getEncoded()))
                        .build();
                try (var client = DataplaneClient.builder().build(identity)) {
                    String jwt = client.generateScopedAccessToken(GenerateScopedAccessTokenRequest.builder()
                            .generateScopedAccessTokenDetails(details).build()).getSecurityToken().getToken();
                    return AccessToken.createJsonWebToken(jwt.toCharArray(), pair.getPrivate());
                }
            } finally {
                if (identity instanceof SessionTokenAuthenticationDetailsProvider session) session.close();
            }
        } catch (Exception failure) {
            // SDK exception messages can contain request details; the CLI prints only the type.
            throw new IllegalStateException("OCI token acquisition failed", failure);
        }
    }
}

For a single connection, use the builder. For repeated physical connections, attach the cached supplier to the data source. These are alternative configurations:

// Single-token builder example
OracleDataSource ds = new OracleDataSource();
ds.setURL(config.url());
ds.setConnectionProperties(config.jdbc());
try (Connection c = ds.createConnectionBuilder()
        .accessToken(OciTokens.request(config.app())).build()) {
    // Run the identity query.
}

// Reusable data source example
OracleDataSource reusable = new OracleDataSource();
reusable.setURL(config.url());
reusable.setConnectionProperties(config.jdbc());
reusable.setTokenSupplier(OciTokens.cached(config.app()));
try (Connection c = reusable.getConnection()) {
    // Run the identity query.
}

config is the application's validated Settings object. The cached supplier is shared by callers; Oracle's AccessToken API defines its expiry-aware behavior and serialization of calls into the acquisition supplier. The cache does not turn failed cloud authentication into a successful database session: acquisition failures must remain observable.

Option 3: Let the OCI provider acquire the token

Jump to the full Compute instance-principal example, Data Science resource-principal example, or complete Java program.

./run.sh config/oci-config-file.properties jdbc
./run.sh config/oci-instance-principal.properties ucp
./run.sh config/oci-resource-principal.properties ucp
./run.sh config/oci-cloud-shell.properties jdbc
./run.sh config/oci-interactive.properties jdbc

Run the applicable command in its intended environment. Set oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication to OCI_API_KEY, OCI_INSTANCE_PRINCIPAL, OCI_RESOURCE_PRINCIPAL, OCI_DELEGATION_TOKEN (Cloud Shell), or OCI_INTERACTIVE. The driver selects the extension automatically, without explicit access-token-provider properties. The provider acquires and caches tokens. Cloud Shell uses its managed session; interactive authentication opens a browser and requires a usable desktop callback. The config-file provider path is for API-key configuration; use SDK session-token mode for an OCI CLI session-token profile.

For instance and resource principals, put the token mode directly in the TCPS EZConnect+ URL:

jdbc:oracle:thin:@tcps://<host>:<port>/<service>?token_auth=oci_instance_principal

For a resource principal, replace oci_instance_principal with oci_resource_principal. Set the database scope (oracle.jdbc.ociCompartment and oracle.jdbc.ociDatabase) as JDBC connection properties; the OCI SDK/provider obtains and caches the token from the runtime identity. Keep the OCI provider dependency on the classpath. This URL can be used with JDBC or UCP.

The API-key profile supplies all provider properties:

# EZConnect+: jdbc:oracle:thin:@tcps://host:port/service
app.url=${ADB_JDBC_URL}
app.mode=provider
oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication=OCI_API_KEY
oracle.jdbc.ociCompartment=${OCI_COMPARTMENT_ID}
oracle.jdbc.ociDatabase=${OCI_DATABASE_ID}
oracle.jdbc.ociConfigFile=${OCI_CONFIG_FILE}
oracle.jdbc.ociProfile=${OCI_PROFILE}

For instance or resource principals, the matching profiles change oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication and omit file/profile settings. For an existing Java application, load these oracle.jdbc.* properties into its OracleDataSource or UCP data source and add the OCI provider dependency. The SQL/query code remains the same. The existing demo profiles use Settings for their application-specific app.* keys and environment substitution. Passing a Properties object directly to a data source does not itself expand ${...}.

Alternative: let JDBC load and expand its properties file

Oracle JDBC supports native substitution through oracle.jdbc.configFile. The driver reads the file for each physical connection and resolves ${NAME} from JVM system properties or environment variables, with system properties taking precedence; an unresolved name fails. This native file contains JDBC properties, not the demo's app.* keys.

# config/native-oci-instance.properties
oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication=OCI_INSTANCE_PRINCIPAL
oracle.jdbc.ociCompartment=${OCI_COMPARTMENT_ID}
oracle.jdbc.ociDatabase=${OCI_DATABASE_ID}
oracle.net.CONNECT_TIMEOUT=15000
oracle.jdbc.ReadTimeout=30000

OracleDataSource ds = new OracleDataSource();
ds.setURL(System.getenv("ADB_JDBC_URL")); // TCPS EZConnect+ URL
ds.setConnectionProperty(OracleConnection.CONNECTION_PROPERTY_CONFIG_FILE,
    Path.of("config/native-oci-instance.properties").toAbsolutePath().toString());
try (Connection connection = ds.getConnection()) {
    // Execute a read-only identity query.
}

The sample project includes demo.NativeConfigFileDemo and native OCI instance-principal and Entra managed-identity profiles. It delegates property loading to JDBC, validates the TCPS EZConnect+ URL, and queries only the session identity. After building and setting the profile's environment variables, run:

java -cp 'target/classes:target/lib/*' demo.NativeConfigFileDemo config/native-oci-instance.properties
# In an authorized Azure managed-identity runtime instead:
java -cp 'target/classes:target/lib/*' demo.NativeConfigFileDemo config/native-entra-managed.properties

Use trusted files only, keep secrets and wallets out of Git, and retain TLS verification. Native-file wiring is unit-tested; these new entry points are not presented as live cloud login validation.

The OCI interactive profile uses the same database scope and simply selects OCI_INTERACTIVE:

# EZConnect+: jdbc:oracle:thin:@tcps://host:port/service
app.url=${ADB_JDBC_URL}
app.mode=provider
oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication=OCI_INTERACTIVE
oracle.jdbc.ociCompartment=${OCI_COMPARTMENT_ID}
oracle.jdbc.ociDatabase=${OCI_DATABASE_ID}

Complete instance- and resource-principal examples

The following two recipes run the same complete Java program in different OCI runtimes. These examples compile and pass automated tests; live Compute/Data Science login and renewal have not yet been validated here. An API-key login is not evidence for either workload principal. The source, pinned Maven dependencies and runnable profiles are in oracle-db-examples/java/jdbc-token-auth; the complete deployment guide records the verification boundaries.

Use a dedicated IAM-enabled Autonomous AI Database with a TLS endpoint reachable from the workload. Its administrator can enable IAM with the following call if it is not already enabled; do not switch a shared or Entra-configured database for this test:

BEGIN
  DBMS_CLOUD_ADMIN.ENABLE_EXTERNAL_AUTHENTICATION(type => 'OCI_IAM');
END;
/

Both recipes follow Autonomous's service-specific dynamic-group/shared-schema mapping. Substitute real identifiers and identity-domain-qualified group names where necessary. The general Database Security Guide additionally describes exclusive principal-OCID mappings; do not assume all service/version combinations accept the same alternatives. See Autonomous IAM policy guidance and general principal mapping guidance.

OCI_INSTANCE_PRINCIPAL: OCI Compute

  1. Select a dedicated Compute VM with network access to the database and OCI IAM. Create dynamic group JdbcInstanceDemo, matching only that VM: instance.id = '<compute-instance-ocid>'
  2. Grant the group's documented Autonomous token-access policy, scoped to the database: Allow dynamic-group JdbcInstanceDemo to use autonomous-database-family in compartment id <database-compartment-ocid> where target.id = '<autonomous-database-ocid>'

On the VM, install Java 17+ and Maven, then build and run: git clone https://github.com/oracle-samples/oracle-db-examples.git cd oracle-db-examples/java/jdbc-token-auth mvn -B -ntp verify export ADB_JDBC_URL='jdbc:oracle:thin:@tcps://<host>:<port>/<service>' export OCI_COMPARTMENT_ID='<database-compartment-ocid>' export OCI_DATABASE_ID='<autonomous-database-ocid>' export EXPECTED_DB_USER=TOKEN_INSTANCE_DEMO java -cp 'target/classes:target/lib/*' demo.OciWorkloadPrincipalDemo instance check java -cp 'target/classes:target/lib/*' demo.OciWorkloadPrincipalDemo instance jdbc java -cp 'target/classes:target/lib/*' demo.OciWorkloadPrincipalDemo instance ucp

The program explicitly selects OCI_INSTANCE_PRINCIPAL. The provider uses the VM's instance identity; no OCI CLI login, API-key profile, database password, or explicit access-token-provider property is supplied. Processes on the VM can share its principal, so protect instance metadata access. This flow does not turn a laptop into an OCI instance.

OCI_RESOURCE_PRINCIPAL: OCI Data Science notebook

  1. Use a dedicated Data Science notebook session with database/IAM connectivity. Open its JupyterLab terminal. Create dynamic group JdbcResourceDemo for only that notebook: ALL {resource.type = 'datasciencenotebooksession', resource.id = '<notebook-session-ocid>'}

Full Java source: explicit identity, read-only verification and bounded UCP:

package demo;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Properties;
import java.util.Set;
import oracle.jdbc.datasource.impl.OracleDataSource;
import oracle.ucp.admin.UniversalConnectionPoolManagerImpl;
import oracle.ucp.jdbc.PoolDataSourceFactory;

/** Explicit OCI workload identity, with no database password or API-key fallback. */
public final class OciWorkloadPrincipalDemo {
    private OciWorkloadPrincipalDemo() { }

    record Config(String url, String expectedUser, Properties properties) { }

    static Config configure(String principal, Map<String, String> env) {
        String method = switch (principal) {
            case "instance" -> "OCI_INSTANCE_PRINCIPAL";
            case "resource" -> "OCI_RESOURCE_PRINCIPAL";
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Use instance or resource");
        };
        String url = required(env, "ADB_JDBC_URL");
        Settings.validateUrl(url);
        String expected = required(env, "EXPECTED_DB_USER");
        if (!expected.matches("[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]{0,127}"))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("EXPECTED_DB_USER must be an uppercase unquoted schema name");
        Properties properties = new Properties();
        properties.setProperty("v$session.program", "devrel-developerhub-java-jdbc-token-auth");
        properties.setProperty("oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication", method);
        properties.setProperty("oracle.jdbc.ociCompartment", required(env, "OCI_COMPARTMENT_ID"));
        properties.setProperty("oracle.jdbc.ociDatabase", required(env, "OCI_DATABASE_ID"));
        properties.setProperty("oracle.net.CONNECT_TIMEOUT", "15000");
        properties.setProperty("oracle.jdbc.ReadTimeout", "30000");
        return new Config(url, expected, properties);
    }

    private static String required(Map<String, String> env, String name) {
        String value = env.get(name);
        if (value == null || value.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Set " + name);
        return value;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            if (args.length != 2 || !Set.of("check", "jdbc", "ucp").contains(args[1]))
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Usage: OciWorkloadPrincipalDemo instance|resource check|jdbc|ucp");
            Config config = configure(args[0], System.getenv());
            if (args[1].equals("check")) {
                System.out.println("Configuration valid; no identity, token, or database test performed.");
                return;
            }
            // The runtime supplies instance metadata or resource-principal credentials.
            // Selecting a method does not create that identity on a developer laptop.
            if (args[1].equals("jdbc")) {
                OracleDataSource ds = new OracleDataSource();
                ds.setURL(config.url());
                ds.setConnectionProperties(config.properties());
                try (Connection connection = ds.getConnection()) {
                    verify(connection, config.expectedUser());
                }
            } else {
                var pool = PoolDataSourceFactory.getPoolDataSource();
                String name = "WorkloadPrincipalDemo";
                pool.setConnectionPoolName(name);
                pool.setConnectionFactoryClassName(OracleDataSource.class.getName());
                pool.setURL(config.url());
                pool.setConnectionProperties(config.properties());
                pool.setInitialPoolSize(0);
                pool.setMinPoolSize(0);
                pool.setMaxPoolSize(2);
                pool.setConnectionWaitDuration(Duration.ofSeconds(20));
                pool.setValidateConnectionOnBorrow(true);
                var manager = UniversalConnectionPoolManagerImpl.getUniversalConnectionPoolManager();
                try (Connection connection = pool.getConnection()) {
                    verify(connection, config.expectedUser());
                } finally {
                    if (java.util.Arrays.asList(manager.getConnectionPoolNames()).contains(name))
                        manager.destroyConnectionPool(name);
                }
            }
        } catch (Exception failure) {
            // Exception payloads can contain endpoints or credentials. Report codes only.
            if (failure instanceof IllegalArgumentException) System.err.println(failure.getMessage());
            else {
                System.err.println("Connection/identity check failed: " + failure.getClass().getSimpleName());
                for (Throwable cause = failure; cause != null; cause = cause.getCause())
                    if (cause instanceof SQLException sql)
                        System.err.println("Oracle error=" + sql.getErrorCode() + "; SQLState=" + sql.getSQLState());
            }
            System.exit(1);
        }
    }

    static void verifyIdentity(String expected, String actual, String authentication) throws SQLException {
        if (!expected.equals(actual) || !"TOKEN_GLOBAL".equals(authentication))
            throw new SQLException("Unexpected database identity or authentication method");
    }

    private static void verify(Connection connection, String expected) throws SQLException {
        try (var statement = connection.prepareStatement("""
                SELECT SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','SESSION_USER'),
                       SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','AUTHENTICATION_METHOD') FROM dual
                """)) {
            statement.setQueryTimeout(20);
            try (var rows = statement.executeQuery()) {
                if (!rows.next()) throw new SQLException("Identity query returned no row");
                verifyIdentity(expected, rows.getString(1), rows.getString(2));
                System.out.println("PASS: expected schema; authentication=TOKEN_GLOBAL; read-only query completed.");
            }
        }
    }
}

check validates configuration without calling OCI or the database. Only jdbc/ucp can print PASS after checking the expected schema and TOKEN_GLOBAL. The two scope properties prevent requesting an intentionally broad database token. JDBC connect/read/query timeouts do not bound the entire cloud token-acquisition operation.

The short runs do not establish renewal. After initial success, the existing ucp-fresh harness can replace physical connections across token expiry using the matching principal profile. Keep tokens and raw exceptions private. A negative test should use a separate excluded runtime, not revoke a shared production policy. Remove only dedicated example policies, groups, schemas and runtimes when finished.

Option 4: Let the Entra provider acquire the token

Use the URL of the Entra-configured database. Set these non-secret identifiers:

export AZURE_TENANT_ID='<tenant-id>'
export AZURE_CLIENT_ID='<java-client-application-id>'
export ENTRA_DB_APP_ID_URI='https://<tenant-domain>/<database-application-id>'
# Full scope for SDK/file acquisition; provider profiles use the bare URI.
export ENTRA_DB_SCOPE="${ENTRA_DB_APP_ID_URI}/.default"

For a client secret, inject AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET through the runtime's secret facility. For a local Bash demonstration, read it without terminal echo or a literal in shell history:

read -r -s -p 'Client secret: ' AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET; echo
export AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET
./run.sh config/entra-service-principal.properties jdbc
./run.sh config/entra-service-principal.properties ucp
unset AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET

For certificate authentication, set AZURE_CLIENT_CERTIFICATE_PATH (and AZURE_CLIENT_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD for an encrypted PFX), unset the client secret, and use the same service-principal profile. Register the corresponding certificate on the client application. The identity credential is not a database password.

Other examples:

# On Azure with a configured managed identity and database app-role assignment:
# For a system-assigned identity, unset AZURE_CLIENT_ID first.
./run.sh config/entra-managed-identity.properties ucp

# Public client with delegated permission, user role assignment and redirect URI:
# Keep ENTRA_DB_APP_ID_URI as the bare resource URI for provider profiles.
