./run.sh config/entra-device-code.properties jdbc

Browser/device-code paths authenticate a human; service-principal/managed-identity paths authenticate a workload. Never use the database resource ID as the Java client's ID. See setup for registration, roles, consent and token-version details.

The profiles select AZURE_SERVICE_PRINCIPAL, AZURE_MANAGED_IDENTITY, AZURE_INTERACTIVE, or AZURE_DEVICE_CODE. The connection URL can select the provider mode directly:

jdbc:oracle:thin:@tcps://<host>:<port>/<service>?token_auth=azure_managed_identity

Change token_auth to azure_service_principal, azure_interactive, or azure_device_code for those flows. Set oracle.jdbc.azureDatabaseApplicationIdUri to the database resource URI without /.default or /session:scope:connect as a JDBC connection property. A user-assigned managed identity or interactive flow can also need client and tenant properties. Never put a client secret or certificate material in a URL.

The service-principal properties profile is:

# EZConnect+: jdbc:oracle:thin:@tcps://host:port/service
app.url=${ADB_JDBC_URL}
app.mode=provider
oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication=AZURE_SERVICE_PRINCIPAL
# Database application URI, without /.default or /session:scope:connect.
oracle.jdbc.azureDatabaseApplicationIdUri=${ENTRA_DB_APP_ID_URI}

The browser profile makes the client, tenant and callback explicit:

# EZConnect+: jdbc:oracle:thin:@tcps://host:port/service
app.url=${ADB_JDBC_URL}
app.mode=provider
oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication=AZURE_INTERACTIVE
# Database application URI, without /.default or /session:scope:connect.
oracle.jdbc.azureDatabaseApplicationIdUri=${ENTRA_DB_APP_ID_URI}
oracle.jdbc.tenantId=${AZURE_TENANT_ID}
oracle.jdbc.clientId=${AZURE_CLIENT_ID}
oracle.jdbc.redirectUri=http://localhost:8400

The providers are documented in Oracle's OCI module and Azure module. “Passwordless database access” does not necessarily mean “no secrets anywhere”: an API-key or client-secret flow still has an upstream identity credential. Workload identities can remove that application-managed credential where the deployment supports them.

Entra alternatives: token files and SDK suppliers

External Entra token file

An authorized external producer can write the database access token as a UTF-8 JWT file. Unlike OCI file mode, Entra needs no proof-of-possession key. The producer must request the database resource, not Microsoft Graph, and is responsible for renewal. Protect the directory, use file mode 0600, and replace a completed temporary file atomically. Do not print the JWT or commit it.

app.url=${ADB_JDBC_URL}
app.mode=file
oracle.jdbc.tokenAuthentication=OAUTH
oracle.jdbc.tokenLocation=${ENTRA_DB_TOKEN_FILE}
export ENTRA_DB_TOKEN_FILE='/private/path/to/entra-db-token'
./run.sh config/entra-file.properties jdbc
./run.sh config/entra-file.properties ucp

An Azure CLI producer with the necessary database consent can use az account get-access-token --resource "$ENTRA_DB_APP_ID_URI" --query accessToken -o tsv, redirected to that protected temporary file. CLI sign-in is not itself proof of database permission. An SDK producer can also write a token, as in the file-flow test. JDBC file mode does not invoke either producer.

Application-owned Azure Identity acquisition

The SDK flow uses AccessToken.createJsonWebToken(jwt.toCharArray()), without the OCI private-key argument. Builder mode passes one token; JDBC and UCP use AccessToken.createJsonWebTokenCache around the acquisition supplier. The checked-in profile is for a service principal and uses the application scope (/.default); human login uses a delegated database scope instead.

For a directly runnable interactive-browser profile, provide the tenant, public-client ID, database resource URI and delegated scope. Register http://localhost:8400 as a redirect URI on the public/native client, grant its delegated permission to the database application's session:scope:connect scope, obtain consent, and assign the user/group the database application's required role.

Compared with config/entra-sdk.properties, change app.entra.authentication from service-principal to interactive, replace its application /.default scope with the delegated /session:scope:connect scope, add the tenant and public-client IDs, and set the browser redirect URI.

export AZURE_TENANT_ID='<tenant-id>'
export AZURE_CLIENT_ID='<public-client-application-id>'
export ENTRA_DB_APP_ID_URI='https://<tenant-domain>/<database-application-id>'
export ENTRA_DB_SCOPE="${ENTRA_DB_APP_ID_URI}/session:scope:connect"
cat > config/entra-sdk-human.local.properties <<'EOF'
app.url=${ADB_JDBC_URL}
app.mode=entra-sdk
app.entra.authentication=interactive
app.entra.scope=${ENTRA_DB_SCOPE}
app.entra.tenantId=${AZURE_TENANT_ID}
app.entra.clientId=${AZURE_CLIENT_ID}
app.entra.redirectUri=http://localhost:8400
EOF
./run.sh config/entra-sdk-human.local.properties check
./run.sh config/entra-sdk-human.local.properties jdbc
./run.sh config/entra-sdk-human.local.properties ucp

For device-code login, keep the tenant, client, and delegated scope values, change app.entra.authentication=interactive to app.entra.authentication=device-code, and remove app.entra.redirectUri. Device-code login has no browser callback URI. These are explicit credential choices, not an automatic fallback chain.

Complete EntraTokens.java:

package demo;

import com.azure.core.credential.TokenCredential;
import com.azure.core.credential.TokenRequestContext;
import com.azure.identity.*;
import oracle.jdbc.AccessToken;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Properties;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** Explicit Azure Identity acquisition; no database password or OCI PoP key. */
public final class EntraTokens {
    private EntraTokens() {}

    public static Supplier<? extends AccessToken> cached(Properties settings) {
        return AccessToken.createJsonWebTokenCache(supplier(settings));
    }

    static Supplier<AccessToken> supplier(Properties settings) {
        TokenCredential credential = switch (Settings.required(settings, "app.entra.authentication")) {
            // Azure Identity reads AZURE_TENANT_ID, AZURE_CLIENT_ID and secret/certificate from the environment.
            case "service-principal" -> new EnvironmentCredentialBuilder().build();
            case "managed-identity" -> {
                var builder = new ManagedIdentityCredentialBuilder();
                String clientId = System.getenv("AZURE_CLIENT_ID");
                if (clientId != null && !clientId.isBlank()) builder.clientId(clientId);
                yield builder.build();
            }
            case "interactive" -> new InteractiveBrowserCredentialBuilder()
                    .tenantId(Settings.required(settings, "app.entra.tenantId"))
                    .clientId(Settings.required(settings, "app.entra.clientId"))
                    .redirectUrl(settings.getProperty("app.entra.redirectUri", "http://localhost:8400"))
                    .build();
            case "device-code" -> new DeviceCodeCredentialBuilder()
                    .tenantId(Settings.required(settings, "app.entra.tenantId"))
                    .clientId(Settings.required(settings, "app.entra.clientId"))
                    .challengeConsumer(c -> System.out.println(c.getMessage())).build();
            case "azure-cli" -> new AzureCliCredentialBuilder()
                    .tenantId(Settings.required(settings, "app.entra.tenantId")).build();
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unsupported app.entra.authentication");
        };
        String scope = Settings.required(settings, "app.entra.scope");
        return () -> {
            try {
                var token = credential.getToken(new TokenRequestContext().addScopes(scope))
                        .block(Duration.ofSeconds(120));
                if (token == null) throw new IllegalStateException("No Entra token returned");
                return AccessToken.createJsonWebToken(token.getToken().toCharArray());
            } catch (Exception failure) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Entra token acquisition failed", failure);
            }
        };
    }
}

UCP: share the supplier and test physical connection replacement

The application configures one pool, two maximum physical connections, a bounded wait (20 seconds normally, 60 seconds for diagnostic replacement), and validation on borrow. Provider/file properties pass through to JDBC; SDK mode supplies the cached token supplier instead. Here is the actual pool setup method:

static PoolDataSource pool(Settings config, Supplier<? extends AccessToken> tokens, boolean fresh) throws SQLException {
        PoolDataSource ds = PoolDataSourceFactory.getPoolDataSource();
        ds.setConnectionPoolName("TokenAuthDemo");
        ds.setConnectionFactoryClassName(OracleDataSource.class.getName());
        ds.setURL(config.url());
        ds.setConnectionProperties(config.jdbc());
        ds.setInitialPoolSize(0);
        ds.setMinPoolSize(0);
        ds.setMaxPoolSize(2);
        ds.setConnectionWaitDuration(java.time.Duration.ofSeconds(fresh ? 60 : 20));
        ds.setValidateConnectionOnBorrow(true);
        if (tokens != null) ds.setTokenSupplier(tokens);
        // Diagnostic mode purges only between completed rounds, with no borrowers.
        return ds;
    }

Four tasks run through that pool in each round. Diagnostic mode purges only after all four have returned their connections, and verifies that the pool is empty before the next round. Worker exceptions are observed, every borrowed connection is closed, and the pool is destroyed on exit:

private static void runPool(Settings config, Supplier<? extends AccessToken> tokens,
                                boolean fresh, int rounds, int pause) throws Exception {
        PoolDataSource ds = pool(config, tokens, fresh);
        var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
        try {
            for (int round = 1; round <= rounds; round++) {
                final int current = round;
                List<Callable<Void>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
                for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) tasks.add(() -> {
                    try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
                        query(c, current);
                    }
                    return null;
                });
                for (var result : executor.invokeAll(tasks)) result.get();
                if (fresh) {
                    // Keep the same data source/token cache, but retire all physical
                    // sessions after all workers have returned their connections.
                    UniversalConnectionPoolManagerImpl.getUniversalConnectionPoolManager()
                            .purgeConnectionPool(ds.getConnectionPoolName());
                    if (ds.getAvailableConnectionsCount() != 0 || ds.getBorrowedConnectionsCount() != 0)
                        throw new IllegalStateException("Diagnostic purge did not empty the pool");
                    System.out.println("round=" + round + " poolPurged=true available=0 borrowed=0");
                }
                if (round < rounds) Thread.sleep(pause * 1000L);
            }
        } finally {
            executor.shutdownNow();
            if (java.util.Arrays.asList(UniversalConnectionPoolManagerImpl
                    .getUniversalConnectionPoolManager().getConnectionPoolNames()).contains(ds.getConnectionPoolName()))
                UniversalConnectionPoolManagerImpl.getUniversalConnectionPoolManager()
                        .destroyConnectionPool(ds.getConnectionPoolName());
        }
    }
# Four tasks per round; purge physical sessions between completed rounds.
# About 74 minutes between first and final rounds, spanning a typical OCI token lifetime.
./run.sh config/oci-config-file.properties ucp-fresh 75 60
# Or use config/oci-sdk.properties / config/entra-service-principal.properties.

Token expiry governs creation of new authenticated connections. A still-open pooled session can keep working after its login token expires, so repeated borrows alone do not prove refresh. ucp-fresh purges all physical connections between completed rounds, with no active borrowers, and checks that available/borrowed counts are zero. The same data source and token cache remain in use; the next round must establish new database sessions. It allows a bounded 60-second replacement wait. Output includes session IDs for diagnosis, although the server can recycle those IDs. Run longer than the actual issuer token lifetime; no unit test proves cloud refresh.

Illustrative successful output (values depend on your identity/server):

round=1 user=TOKEN_DEMO identity=<mapped-principal> authentication=<server-reported-method> sid=<session-id>

Verify the database identity

The application uses a prepared statement with this read-only query:

SELECT SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','SESSION_USER'),
       SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','AUTHENTICATED_IDENTITY'),
       SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','AUTHENTICATION_METHOD'),
       SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','SID'), ? FROM dual

The bound value is the round number. Verify that SESSION_USER is the intended mapped schema. Identity and authentication-method text can vary by flow and server. Do not publish principal names from logs without review. No token or private key is printed.

Complete executable and source map

The repository contains every import, argument check, configuration loader and shutdown path. The complete main class is also included here for reference.

Complete TokenAuthDemo.java:

package demo;

import oracle.jdbc.AccessToken;
import oracle.jdbc.datasource.impl.OracleDataSource;
import oracle.ucp.jdbc.PoolDataSource;
import oracle.ucp.jdbc.PoolDataSourceFactory;
import oracle.ucp.admin.UniversalConnectionPoolManagerImpl;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** Executable JDBC, builder, and concurrent UCP authentication demonstrations. */
public final class TokenAuthDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        if (args.length == 0 || args[0].equals("--help")) {
            System.out.println("Usage: run.sh CONFIG [check|jdbc|builder|ucp|ucp-fresh] [rounds=1] [pauseSeconds=0]");
            return;
        }
        try {
            if (args.length > 4) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Too many arguments");
            String action = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "jdbc";
            if (!java.util.Set.of("check", "jdbc", "builder", "ucp", "ucp-fresh").contains(action))
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown action; use --help");
            int rounds = args.length > 2 ? Integer.parseInt(args[2]) : 1;
            int pause = args.length > 3 ? Integer.parseInt(args[3]) : 0;
            if (rounds < 1 || rounds > 10000 || pause < 0 || pause > 86400)
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("rounds: 1..10000; pauseSeconds: 0..86400");
            Settings config = Settings.load(Path.of(args[0]), System.getenv());
            if (action.equals("builder") && !java.util.Set.of("sdk", "entra-sdk").contains(config.mode()))
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("builder requires SDK mode");
            if (action.equals("check")) {
                System.out.println("Configuration valid: mode=" + config.mode() + "; no cloud or database connection attempted");
                return;
            }
            Supplier<? extends AccessToken> tokens = switch (config.mode()) {
                case "sdk" -> OciTokens.cached(config.app());
                case "entra-sdk" -> action.equals("builder") ? EntraTokens.supplier(config.app()) : EntraTokens.cached(config.app());
                default -> null;
            };
            if (action.startsWith("ucp")) runPool(config, tokens, action.equals("ucp-fresh"), rounds, pause);
            else {
                OracleDataSource ds = new OracleDataSource();
                ds.setURL(config.url());
                ds.setConnectionProperties(config.jdbc());
                if (tokens != null && !action.equals("builder")) ds.setTokenSupplier(tokens);
                for (int round = 1; round <= rounds; round++) {
                    try (Connection c = action.equals("builder")
                            ? ds.createConnectionBuilder().accessToken(config.mode().equals("sdk")
                                ? OciTokens.request(config.app()) : tokens.get()).build()
                            : ds.getConnection()) {
                        query(c, round);
                    }
                    if (round < rounds) Thread.sleep(pause * 1000L);
                }
            }
        } catch (Exception failure) {
            if (failure instanceof InterruptedException) Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            if (failure instanceof IllegalArgumentException) System.err.println(failure.getMessage());
            else {
                Throwable cause = failure;
                while (cause.getCause() != null) cause = cause.getCause();
                System.err.println("Run failed: " + cause.getClass().getSimpleName());
                if (cause instanceof SQLException sql)
                    System.err.println("Oracle error code=" + sql.getErrorCode() + "; SQLState=" + sql.getSQLState());
                if (cause instanceof oracle.ucp.UniversalConnectionPoolException poolFailure)
                    System.err.println("UCP error code=" + poolFailure.getErrorCode());
                System.err.println("See docs/troubleshooting.md. Credential values and exception payloads are not logged.");
            }
            System.exit(1);
        }
    }

    static PoolDataSource pool(Settings config, Supplier<? extends AccessToken> tokens, boolean fresh) throws SQLException {
        PoolDataSource ds = PoolDataSourceFactory.getPoolDataSource();
        ds.setConnectionPoolName("TokenAuthDemo");
        ds.setConnectionFactoryClassName(OracleDataSource.class.getName());
        ds.setURL(config.url());
        ds.setConnectionProperties(config.jdbc());
        ds.setInitialPoolSize(0);
        ds.setMinPoolSize(0);
        ds.setMaxPoolSize(2);
        ds.setConnectionWaitDuration(java.time.Duration.ofSeconds(fresh ? 60 : 20));
        ds.setValidateConnectionOnBorrow(true);
        if (tokens != null) ds.setTokenSupplier(tokens);
        // Diagnostic mode purges only between completed rounds, with no borrowers.
        return ds;
    }

    private static void runPool(Settings config, Supplier<? extends AccessToken> tokens,
                                boolean fresh, int rounds, int pause) throws Exception {
        PoolDataSource ds = pool(config, tokens, fresh);
        var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
        try {
            for (int round = 1; round <= rounds; round++) {
                final int current = round;
                List<Callable<Void>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
                for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) tasks.add(() -> {
                    try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
                        query(c, current);
                    }
                    return null;
                });
                for (var result : executor.invokeAll(tasks)) result.get();
                if (fresh) {
                    // Keep the same data source/token cache, but retire all physical
                    // sessions after all workers have returned their connections.
                    UniversalConnectionPoolManagerImpl.getUniversalConnectionPoolManager()
                            .purgeConnectionPool(ds.getConnectionPoolName());
                    if (ds.getAvailableConnectionsCount() != 0 || ds.getBorrowedConnectionsCount() != 0)
                        throw new IllegalStateException("Diagnostic purge did not empty the pool");
                    System.out.println("round=" + round + " poolPurged=true available=0 borrowed=0");
                }
                if (round < rounds) Thread.sleep(pause * 1000L);
            }
        } finally {
            executor.shutdownNow();
            if (java.util.Arrays.asList(UniversalConnectionPoolManagerImpl
                    .getUniversalConnectionPoolManager().getConnectionPoolNames()).contains(ds.getConnectionPoolName()))
                UniversalConnectionPoolManagerImpl.getUniversalConnectionPoolManager()
                        .destroyConnectionPool(ds.getConnectionPoolName());
        }
    }

    private static void query(Connection connection, int round) throws SQLException {
        try (var statement = connection.prepareStatement("""
                SELECT SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','SESSION_USER'),
                       SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','AUTHENTICATED_IDENTITY'),
                       SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','AUTHENTICATION_METHOD'),
                       SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','SID'), ? FROM dual
                """)) {
            statement.setQueryTimeout(20);
            statement.setInt(1, round);
            try (var rows = statement.executeQuery()) {
                if (!rows.next()) throw new SQLException("Identity query returned no rows");
                System.out.printf("round=%d user=%s identity=%s authentication=%s sid=%s%n",
                        rows.getInt(5), rows.getString(1), rows.getString(2), rows.getString(3), rows.getString(4));
            }
        }
    }
}
File Responsibility
TokenAuthDemo.java Executable JDBC/builder/UCP flows, concurrent tasks, read-only query and shutdown
OciTokens.java SDK identity selection, scoped token request, PoP key, cached supplier
EntraTokens.java Explicit Azure Identity credential, database scope, bearer JWT, cached supplier
Settings.java Environment substitution, TCPS and token-mode validation
config Profiles for file, SDK, OCI and Entra methods, plus native JDBC configuration examples
sql Administrator setup templates for each identity provider
troubleshooting Failure diagnosis and live acceptance procedure

mvn verify checks configuration security boundaries, all shipped profiles, UCP settings and discovery of the actual released OCI/Azure providers. CI runs JDK 17 and 21. Cloud tests require configured external identities. Supported configuration profiles are not proof that every identity method has been exercised.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Check
Configuration check fails Set each named environment variable; use an EZConnect+ TCPS URL; choose one acquisition method. The check does not validate cloud credentials.
Missing provider / class not found Run mvn clean verify; keep all target/lib JARs. The runtime uses the original JAR service descriptors. Do not shade them without service-resource merging.
ORA-01017 Token audience/scope, external provider, mapping, cloud permission, expired token, and credentials. This code alone does not establish which is wrong. A password connection failing with this error has not tested tokens.
ORA-01045 Grant CREATE SESSION to the mapped schema.
ORA-20004 during setup Another identity provider is already configured. Use the corresponding lab database; these scripts do not force replacement.
Timeout / ORA-125xx DNS, routing, ACLs, private endpoint access, TCPS port, and service name.
TLS / wallet failure Correct database wallet, CA trust, wallet path and password if needed; preserve server name checks.
OCI authorization failure Correct API profile or actual workload identity; policy target OCID, group/dynamic group, scope and database mapping must agree.
Entra invalid scope / unauthorized client Use database resource scope rather than Graph; distinguish client and resource IDs, app roles, consent, and tenant policy.
Initial connection works; later physical connections fail Token refresh, upstream identity expiry, IAM endpoint reachability, or CLI file refresh. Existing pooled sessions can hide the problem.

The CLI emits exception type and Oracle/UCP numeric codes, not full exception payloads. Inspect detailed diagnostics only in a controlled environment: SDK logging may include identity/request information. Do not paste live tokens into online decoders. Identity query output contains principal names; redact them before sharing logs.

FAQs

Do I still need a wallet when I use a token?

Token authentication and TLS are separate. An mTLS database endpoint still needs its client wallet. A supported TLS-only endpoint can avoid a client wallet when the JVM trusts the server certificate chain. Keep server identity verification enabled in either case.

Which token approach should I choose?

Use file tokens when an existing external process owns token generation. Use the SDK supplier when your application needs direct control of OCI acquisition. Use the provider profiles to keep token acquisition out of application code while selecting an explicit cloud identity method.

Why can a connection pool work after a token expires?

An existing authenticated physical session can remain usable. Expiry is relevant when a new physical connection authenticates. The demo's ucp-fresh mode forces replacement connections so a long run can expose refresh failures; normal repeated borrows are insufficient evidence.

Can I use the OCI and Entra profiles against the same database interchangeably?

Only if the database is configured for the selected provider at the time of connection. This walkthrough uses separate lab configurations and does not force an existing provider to be replaced. Both flows require a cloud-authorized principal mapped to a database schema with CREATE SESSION.

title: Cloudflare Maps a Post-Quantum Path for Privacy Pass Credentials
description:
TL;DR

  • Privacy Pass is a protocol that lets a site issue a client unlinkable tokens, so an operator can rate-limit traffic without tracking the person behind each request.
  • Cloudflare has run Privacy Pass in production for 10 years and published on 6 November 2026 a design study for its post-quantum successor, under the working name MOLE.
  • Today's tokens use RSA and elliptic-curve blind signatures. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer could forge them.
  • MOLE adds an endorsement issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator, and the client proves possession of an endorsement issued by one anchor in the agreed set without revealing which anchor issued it.
  • The construction comes from VOLE-in-the-Head, a proof system that a prover can turn into a signature, and the PoMFRIT blind signature built on it shrinks to 4.3KB when UOV replaces MAYO.
  • Cloudflare estimates 5.6KB of issuance for VOLE-IHAT and 5.4KB for VOLE-ACT, with 6.5KB and 12.0KB at redemption, against 46.6KB public keys.
  • The costs and the open questions are concrete: multivariate cryptanalysis is young, security proofs are still missing, and each of these operations already runs in a few milliseconds.
  • Deployment depends on two items Cloudflare still lists as work, a security proof for the new protocols and maturity in the cryptanalysis of the multivariate schemes underneath them.

The Cloudflare blog page captured on 7 November 2026, where the post opens on Privacy Pass and works toward the MOLE construction. Capture of https://blog.cloudflare.com/vole-mole/.

What Privacy Pass issues, and where RSA sits in it

Privacy Pass lets a site rate-limit traffic without linking a redeemed token to the client that received it. A site that wants to stop one client consuming its capacity reaches for challenges, accounts or fingerprinting, and each of those costs the visitor something. Privacy Pass issues the client a number of tokens that the client redeems for access, while each token stays unlinkable to the client it was issued to.

Cloudflare has deployed this for 10 years across products such as iCloud Private Relay and Privacy Gateway, and the post lists two goals for the next generation: better tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise eat capacity meant for people, and an ecosystem where more kinds of clients can participate. Both goals run into the same cryptographic obstacle, because the tokens are minted with RSA or elliptic-curve blind signatures and a quantum attacker could forge them at will.

Privacy Pass remains unconditionally private through this change. That guarantee means no attacker, quantum or classical, can link a redemption to an issuance. The post quantifies the size constraint: ML-DSA-44 signatures are 2,420 bytes; ECDSA-P256 signatures are 64 bytes.

Cloudflare's diagram of the two phases of a blind signature, published with the post: the client sends a blinded message and receives a signature, then presents the message and signature to a verifier later. Figure from https://blog.cloudflare.com/vole-mole/.

MOLE adds an endorsement that hides its issuer

A Privacy Pass token today carries a message and a blind signature, and verifying it requires the issuer's public key, so the verifier learns who issued the token. The issuer's identity provides a decision signal in some products. Many access decisions require only proof that a trusted entity issued the token, an observation that shapes MOLE.

The new object is an endorsement, issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator. Before redemption the client and moderator agree on an anchor set, the public keys the moderator trusts, and during redemption the client proves that one anchor in that set endorsed it without revealing which one. The moderator then issues the credential the client uses, and because that credential belongs to one moderator it can be a blind signature, an anonymous credit token or an anonymous rate-limited credential.

The design goal is equal treatment. If a moderator cannot tell which anchor signed, it cannot price or gate a client by the reputation of its issuer, which lowers the barrier for new kinds of clients. Verifying the endorsement keeps the signer unnamed, and that is the part the post spends most of its length on.

Netics visual, 7 November 2026: the endorsement model in one card, with the anchor set and the moderator that issues the usable credential.

VOLE-in-the-Head turns a proof into a signature

VOLE-in-the-Head is a zero-knowledge proof system published by Baum and others at Crypto 2023, and its name describes the mechanism. Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation is an interactive technique that hands two parties correlated random values, and those correlations act as authentication tags that let a verifier check work done on a hidden witness. In the head version the prover prepares locally what the two parties would normally generate together, commits to those values, and uses the Fiat-Shamir transformation to pick the parts the verifier checks.

Cloudflare presents this adaptable proof system as a way to decouple post-quantum parameter selection from credential protocol design; its proofs grow linearly with the size of the witness and are concretely fast for statements expressed as equations over small binary fields. That covers two useful cases. FAEST proofs about an AES key run to about 4KB, and KuMQuat signatures, which prove an instance of the multivariate quadratic problem, come down to 2.6KB.

The second ingredient is a multivariate signature scheme with a trapdoor. In Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar the public key is a quadratic map, the secret key reveals a split of the variables into oil and vinegar, and fixing the vinegar values leaves a linear system the signer can solve. UOV signatures are 135 bytes, among the smallest of the NIST candidates, and its public keys are 46.6KB, the largest; MAYO offers much smaller keys in exchange for slightly larger signatures.

Netics visual, 7 November 2026: the four stages the post describes, from the classical tokens in production today to the point where the remaining work is protocol engineering.

Blind signatures from VOLE and UOV reach 4.3KB

A blind signature is built from a commitment and a proof. The client hashes its message with randomness and sends the commitment, the issuer signs that commitment without learning the message, and the client later produces a zero-knowledge proof that it holds a valid signature over the commitment. Unlinkability comes from the client showing two different objects at the two moments, so an issuer that also acts as verifier cannot match the sessions.

PoMFRIT, published by Baum and others at USENIX Security 2026, applies that pattern with VOLE-in-the-Head and the MAYO signature, and it reached 6.7KB for the blind signature itself with a few hundred bytes of issuance. The UOV variant brings the signature to 4.3KB and uses a larger public key that an application can cache. The post describes the Keccak permutation inside SHAKE and TurboSHAKE as the dominant cost, two permutations per proof, and cuts it by dropping to 12 rounds and halving the Keccak state.

Endorsements then extend the same machinery. The statement gains a public key drawn from a list of anchors, the index of the chosen anchor becomes part of the hidden witness, and the proof carries the same two hashes and one quadratic map evaluation. Cloudflare says the cost of the more advanced credentials is one or two extra hashes.

Cloudflare's diagram of the MOLE flow, published with the post: an anchor endorses, the client redeems the endorsement at a moderator, and the moderator issues the credential the client presents. Figure from https://blog.cloudflare.com/vole-mole/.

The published costs of the new credentials

The two constructions Cloudflare is developing have published estimates. VOLE-IHAT, a candidate for endorsements, costs 5.6KB at issuance and 6.5KB at redemption. VOLE-ACT, a candidate for credentials, costs 5.4KB at issuance and 12.0KB when a credit is spent. Every construction in this framework uses UOV with the same parameters, so public keys are 46.6KB each, and each operation runs in a few milliseconds in Cloudflare's implementation.

Those numbers support the post's own conclusion, which is that "the transition to PQ anonymous credentials for the web can now shift from cryptography design to protocol engineering". Netics' assessment is that this transition is operationally plausible for deployments that can distribute and cache a 46.6KB public key and reuse one redemption across several requests. Each anchor adds its own key to the trusted set, making key distribution and cache lifecycle part of the deployment cost. Short, one-request interactions offer little opportunity to amortize a 6.5KB redemption or a 12.0KB spend. The missing security proofs and immature multivariate cryptanalysis keep the design at the engineering-prototype stage: parameter changes may increase these costs, and production migration should wait for proofs and stable parameters. Cloudflare's millisecond runtimes make experimentation credible.

Netics visual, 7 November 2026: the sizes the post publishes, from a 64-byte ECDSA signature to a 46.6KB UOV public key.

Two risks in front of deployment

Two risks sit in front of deployment. The first is cryptanalysis: multivariate schemes are young, and the post recalls researchers at UCSD and INRIA forging a 1024-bit RSA signature by using a Privacy Pass issuer as a signing oracle; Cloudflare says its 2048-bit RSA parameters provide a good security margin when combined with other defense mechanisms. The second is proof: the protocols need security proofs showing they hold as long as UOV holds, and the one-more-UOV assumption that the optimization relies on could prove optimistic.

For teams running access control on tokens today, the sequence is legible. Keep classical Privacy Pass in production while the primitives settle, count the token budget in kilobytes where it used to be counted in bytes, and treat the ability to amortize a redemption as a product decision. The Netics piece on Cloudflare's post-quantum certificate authority covers the certificate layer of the same transition. For infrastructure and cloud planning, teams must budget for public-key distribution, token size and the number of requests covered by each redemption.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: Why Overlays Failed, What axe-core Misses, and the Architecture of a <12KB Zero-PII Telemetry Ring Buffer
description:
For nearly a decade, engineering teams have treated web accessibility as a compliance tax. You either waited for an enterprise auditor to deliver a 400-page PDF full of cryptic WCAG violations (1.3.1, 4.1.2) that stalled sprint velocity, or marketing injected a 1-line third-party "accessibility overlay" script claiming automated 1-click legal immunity.

In 2026, that entire paradigm collapsed.

Following the FTC’s $1M enforcement action against deceptive overlay claims, ongoing European Accessibility Act (EAA) enforcement across the EU, and data revealing that over 28% of all digital ADA federal lawsuits targeted websites with an active overlay installed, frontend engineering is finally confronting reality:

You cannot patch a fundamentally broken DOM tree from the client side after page load.

According to the annual WebAIM Million audit, over 95% of top homepages still fail basic WCAG criteria, while e-commerce studies (such as the Click-Away Pound) demonstrate that 71% of disabled users immediately abandon websites with interaction barriers.

In researching our 2026 State of Accessible Market Growth report, we investigated why traditional tooling failed—and how we architected an in-memory <12kb circular ring buffer to replace heavy, privacy-invasive session recorders.

1. The "40/60 Split": Why Static Linters Only Scratch the Surface

Static DOM linters and Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) analyzers like axe-core, eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, and Lighthouse are essential baselines. However, research from Deque and accessibility auditors establishes that automated static testing catches only ~30% to 40% of WCAG barriers.

Static linters are strictly syntactic:

  • Missing alt attributes on static <img> elements
  • Hex color contrast ratios falling below 4.5:1
  • <input> fields without associated <label> elements or id attributes
  • Duplicate HTML id attributes in static templates

The remaining 60% of failures are entirely experiential. They cannot be computed from static markup alone because they manifest exclusively during stateful user interaction:

The Real-World Culprits

  1. Dynamic Focus Traps: In our lab simulations across modern SPA modals and slide-out sheets, over 70% failed to trap keyboard focus. A user presses Tab, cycles past the modal's primary action, and suddenly begins focusing invisible links in the obscured background DOM.
  2. Motor Precision Failures: Action buttons that appear fine on desktop often render with physical touch targets smaller than 44×44px on mobile, triggering severe misclick spikes under simulated hand tremor physics.
  3. Screen Reader Announcement Silence: When an async form fails validation via client-side fetch, the UI updates with visual red text, but without an aria-live="polite" or role="alert" region, non-visual users hear total silence and are stranded on failed submissions. 
// ❌ axe-core passes this because all attributes are syntactically valid!
// But experientially, it is completely broken:
export function BrokenModal({ isOpen, onClose, children }) {
  if (!isOpen) return null;

  // 1. Focus is not moved into the modal on mount.
  // 2. Tab key leaks into background elements.
  // 3. Pressing 'Escape' does nothing.
  // 4. Closing the modal dumps focus to document.body instead of the trigger node.
  return (
    <div className="fixed inset-0 bg-black/50">
      <div className="bg-white p-6 rounded-lg">
        {children}
        <div onClick={onClose} className="cursor-pointer text-blue-500">
          Close
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

Static linters are blind to interactive state transitions. Runtime overlays execute too late. The solution requires shift-left pre-commit checks coupled with real interaction telemetry.

2. The Dual-Engine: Why Accessibility Tree = AI Agent Tree

One unexpected finding from modern web migrations is that remediating source code to WCAG 2.1 AA standards consistently produces double-digit lifts in organic SEO visibility and AI Answer Engine citations (Perplexity, SearchGPT, Claude, Gemini).

Why? Because human assistive technology and autonomous LLM browsing agents navigate web applications using the exact same underlying data structure: the browser's Accessibility Tree.

[ Assistive Tech (Screen Readers) ]     [ Autonomous LLM Agents (WebMCP / Tools) ]
               ▲                                              ▲
               │                                              │
               └──────────────[ Semantic DOM ]────────────────┘
                                      │
                     • Explicit Landmark Roles (<nav>, <main>)
                     • Deterministic Heading Depth (H1 ➔ H2 ➔ H3)
                     • Accessible Interactive Nodes (<button>, <a>)
                     • Native Form Association & Live Regions

When an engineering team replaces a custom <div onClick> with a semantic <button type="submit"> and establishes clear landmark hierarchy (<main>, <header aria-label="Primary">):

  1. Screen readers accurately announce the control's role, state, and accessible name to human users.
  2. Headless LLM crawlers immediately resolve entity relationships without costly token-heavy visual OCR or coordinate guessing. Information gain increases, layout noise drops, and the application becomes natively navigable for agentic protocols like WebMCP (window.navigator.modelContext).

Clean, semantic markup isn't just compliance—it is foundational search and AI infrastructure.

3. Inverting Session Replay: The <12KB Zero-PII Ring Buffer

To measure experiential friction in production without compromising user privacy or adding CPU drag, we had to reject traditional session replay tools (FullStory, LogRocket, Hotjar).

The Problem with Traditional Telemetry

  • Bandwidth & CPU Drag: Continuously streaming 100% of DOM mutations to cloud storage burns mobile battery and bloats client memory.
  • Privacy Liabilities: Even with regex masking, streaming raw DOM trees during financial checkout or healthcare onboarding creates immense GDPR, HIPAA, and CCPA exposure.
  • Low Signal-to-Noise Ratio: Product teams sit on 10,000 hours of video recordings, 99.8% of which show completely frictionless sessions that no developer ever watches.

The Waypoint Architecture

Instead of streaming everything to the cloud, we inverted the pipeline using an in-memory circular ring buffer:

[ User Browses Page ] ──▶ [ In-Memory Circular Ring Buffer (<12KB) ]
                                    │
                                    │ Keeps rolling 60-second window
                                    │ Oldest DOM events silently overwritten
                                    │
         ┌──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                     ▼
[ Smooth Navigation ]                                [ Barrier Trigger Fires ]
Buffer silently prunes.                              • 4+ Tab Navigation Cycle
Zero network packets sent.                           • Rage clicks on non-interactive <div>
Zero cloud storage cost.                             • Unannounced Async Error
                                                               │
                                                               ▼
                                               [ Client-Side Zero-PII Scrubber ]
                                               Strips all text nodes & input values
                                                               │
                                                               ▼
                                               [ Dispatches 60s DOM Skeleton ]
                                               Generates actionable TSX PR fix

How the Buffer Works in Practice

Here is a simplified architectural view of how the in-memory circular buffer is implemented:

interface InteractionEvent {
  timestamp: number;
  type: 'keydown' | 'click' | 'focusin' | 'error';
  targetSelector: string;
  role?: string;
}

export class EphemeralSessionBuffer {
  private readonly maxWindowMs = 60_000; // 60-second sliding window
  private readonly maxEvents = 150;      // Hard memory limit (<12kb footprint)
  private events: InteractionEvent[] = [];

  public record(event: Omit<InteractionEvent, 'timestamp'>): void {
    const now = Date.now();
    this.events.push({ ...event, timestamp: now });

    // Prune events outside the 60s window or exceeding memory cap
    this.prune(now);

    // Evaluate purely experiential friction triggers in real-time
    this.detectFriction();
  }

  private prune(now: number): void {
    const cutoff = now - this.maxWindowMs;
    this.events = this.events
      .filter(e => e.timestamp >= cutoff)
      .slice(-this.maxEvents);
  }

  private detectFriction(): void {
    // 1. Detect Keyboard Focus Traps (e.g., 4+ consecutive tabs cycling same container)
    const recentTabs = this.events.slice(-6).filter(e => e.type === 'keydown');
    if (this.isFocusLooping(recentTabs)) {
      this.triggerSnapshot('FOCUS_TRAP_DETECTED');
      return;
    }

    // 2. Detect Rage Clicks on Dead/Non-interactive Markup
    const recentClicks = this.events.slice(-4).filter(e => e.type === 'click');
    if (this.isRageClickOnDeadElement(recentClicks)) {
      this.triggerSnapshot('DEAD_CLICK_BARRIER');
      return;
    }
  }

  private triggerSnapshot(reason: string): void {
    // Zero-PII sanitization runs entirely on the client before network dispatch:
    // Strips all innerText, values, email regex patterns, and personal data.
    const structuralSkeleton = this.captureSanitizedDomSkeleton();

    // Dispatches only the micro-snapshot of the failure
    navigator.sendBeacon('/api/telemetry/friction', JSON.stringify({
      reason,
      skeleton: structuralSkeleton,
      events: this.events
    }));
  }
}

The Benefits:

  1. Zero Server Load for Happy Paths: If the user experiences no barriers, zero bytes are sent over the network.
  2. Guaranteed Zero-PII: The DOM tree is reduced strictly to a structural skeleton (tag names, ARIA attributes, layout bounding boxes) before it leaves the client. No form inputs, credit card fields, or user text ever touch a network packet.
  3. Deterministic Signal: When an alert fires in your dashboard, it isn't an obscure WCAG warning—it's a verifiable reproduction script showing the exact interaction loop that locked out a user.

4. Shift Left: Catching the 40% in Pre-Commit in <250ms

While experiential telemetry monitors runtime friction, the baseline syntactic 40% should never reach a pull request in the first place.

We packaged our AST pre-commit validation engine into an open-source CLI that runs inside Husky or Git hooks in under 250 milliseconds:

npx @waypointstudio/shield-hook init

This installs a zero-dependency Git hook that scans your staged JSX/TSX/HTML components, blocks missing ARIA labels and empty buttons, and stops non-semantic markup from ever polluting your main branch.

Conclusion & Full Report

Accessibility is not a defensive compliance burden or an overlay widget you buy to ward off legal threats.

When you shift accessibility left into developer terminals and measure real experiential friction through lightweight, privacy-preserving telemetry, you convert accessibility from a legal chore into a durable engine for user retention, clean code, and AI search performance.

👉 Read the complete benchmark data, case studies, and architecture deep-dive in our full report:

The 2026 State of Accessible Market Growth

What does your team's accessibility workflow look like today? Are you relying on static linters, periodic audits, or runtime telemetry? Let's discuss in the comments below!

title: Benchmarking AI Coding Agent Permissions: Manual vs. Auto Mode vs. yolonot
description:
Using CLI coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Cursor usually forces you to pick between three flawed options:

  1. Manual prompts: Asks on 100% of commands, which quickly leads to ~93% habitual click-through fatigue where you stop reading the prompt.
  2. --yolo (--dangerously-skip-permissions): Misses 100% of risks and gives an LLM raw shell access to your machine.
  3. Built-in harness auto modes: Measured on Claude Code Auto Mode, it still misses 17.0% of risky commands (False Negative Rate), blocks 0.4% of safe commands with no middle ask state, adds LLM latency and API cost to basic read-only commands, and locks your rules to a single tool.

To fix this across all my agents, I built yolonot (yolonot.dev), an Apache-2.0 permission firewall written in Go that hooks into 24 AI coding agents.

Benchmark Results (456 Commands Across 3 Open Suites)

We evaluated yolonot across 456 commands from three public benchmark suites (rogue-security, RedCode-Exec, Dippy CLI, and hidden script attacks) plus 5,000 real-world agent tool calls:

Profile / Mode Risky Missed (FNR) Safe Blocked (FPR) Borderline Policy Action
yolonot [balanced] (default) 4.9% 0.0% 1.4% ask (cached)
yolonot [strict] 1.6% 0.0% 19.4% ask (low/mod)
yolonot [paranoid] 0.0% 8.4% 91.6% ask (lockdown)
yolonot [fast] 4.9% 1.4% 0.0% ask (headless)
Native Auto Mode (Claude Code) 17.0% 0.4% no ask state
Manual Prompts 0.0% (if read) 0.0% 100% ask (~93% click-through)
--yolo Mode 100.0% 0.0% 0% ask

Full benchmark methodology and reproduction commands: yolonot.dev/benchmarks

Why Static Prefix Rules and Pure LLM Classifiers Fall Short

Built-in allowlists like Bash(npm test:*) only match string prefixes. In real terminal usage, they break as soon as an agent runs a compound command (cd app && npm test), pipes output, or uses wrappers (env, timeout, xargs).

On the other hand, sending every single git status or ls to a cloud LLM classifier adds unnecessary latency and cost, and looking only at the command string completely misses malicious or destructive code inside local scripts (./scripts/check.sh).

How yolonot Works

yolonot runs as a single Go binary with zero runtime dependencies and evaluates every command through four layers:

1. Git-Tracked .yolonot Policy + ~1.6us Local Bash AST Parser

Before touching any model, yolonot checks your repo's .yolonot rules (deny > ask > allow) and parses the command into a full syntax tree using mvdan.cc/sh/v3/syntax. It splits chained commands, unwraps env/timeout, validates flags against ~160 CLI schemas (so git status is allowed, git push --force is not; find . -name is allowed, find . -exec is not), and enforces project-root path containment.

Across 5,000 real-world agent tool calls, 54.2% of commands are cleared locally in ~1.6 microseconds with zero API calls and zero unsafe leaks.

# .yolonot example in your repository root
allow-cmd  go test*
allow-path scripts/check.sh

ask-cmd    git push*
deny-cmd   *rm -rf /*
sensitive  .env*

2. Inspects Local Scripts Before Running ./script.sh

In our eval suite, judging ./scripts/lint-check.sh by filename alone caught 0/14 Trojan scripts. When an agent runs sh scripts/check.sh or python3 fix.py, yolonot reads the script on disk, redacts secrets, blocks sensitive paths (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, .env*), verifies that an earlier command segment didn't overwrite the file, and attaches the code to the judge, catching 14/14 (100%) hidden script attacks.

3. Pluggable Local or Cloud Judges (Across 24 Agents)

Ambiguous commands go to your choice of classifier: fast cloud models, your existing claude / codex CLI login, or 100% local Ollama models (including the Apache-2.0 Kev-4B LoRA). Uncertain ask verdicts can escalate to a second model, cutting false alarms by 48.3%, with a hard rule that critical risk never maps to allow.

4. Tamper-Resistant & Sandbox-Aware

yolonot works alongside OS sandboxes and containers. It blocks agents from running yolonot pause/uninstall or editing .yolonot and hook configs. If an agent requests a host sandbox bypass (dangerouslyDisableSandbox, BypassSandbox, etc.), yolonot disables fast-allow and isolates session memory so a prior sandboxed approval cannot be replayed outside the sandbox.

Quick Start (10 Seconds) 

# Install via Homebrew or Go
brew install sezaakgun/tap/yolonot
# go install github.com/sezaakgun/yolonot@latest

# Auto-detect installed agents and wire hooks
yolonot setup

# Import existing permissions from Claude, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode into .yolonot
yolonot rules discover

Check it out on GitHub and let me know what edge cases you hit in your agent workflows!

  • GitHub (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/sezaakgun/yolonot
  • Website & Docs: https://yolonot.dev
