title: Flexbox vs Grid: How to Choose, on Real Layouts
description:
You've got a row of cards and you're staring at your CSS. Flexbox or grid? You try one, it almost works, you add a few more lines, and now it looks right but you couldn't say why. Today I'll give you the one question that settles it, and we'll run both on the same real layouts so you can watch the difference yourself.

Here's the short answer, so you have it before anything else. Use flexbox when the content should decide the size of things, like a row of tags or a navigation bar. Use grid when the layout should decide the size of things, like a wall of cards or a whole page. Most real pages use both: grid outside, flexbox inside.

That's the whole idea. The rest of this article is you seeing it with your own eyes. Every example below is live, so click the buttons. If you're a beginner, read it top to bottom. If you already use both every day, jump to the section about content that won't shrink, because that's the bug that costs people whole afternoons. The later sections on keyboard order, subgrid and checking AI-written layouts are for those of you who review other people's code.

Why this choice feels harder than it should

Look, there's a reason you're confused, and it isn't you. Most material teaches these two as a list of properties. Here's justify-content, here's align-items, here's grid-template-columns, now make these colored boxes move around. You finish the exercise, and then you open a real project and nobody told you which tool goes where. It's the same thing I complain about in why courses leave you feeling like you know nothing: you get the pieces, but nobody connects them to a real page.

I've got my own version of this. For a long time I built things from my head until they looked good. No plan, no sketch. That works right up until it doesn't, and with layout it stops working the moment the content changes. You add one more card, or someone's name is longer than you expected, and the page falls apart, because you never decided how it was supposed to behave. You only decided how it should look today.

So let's fix the actual problem. You don't need to memorize more properties. You need to know what each tool is for, and then the properties mostly make sense on their own.

Note: Terms in plain words. A container is the parent element you put display: flex or display: grid on. Items are its direct children, and only direct children: grandchildren don't take part. Gap is the space between items. A track is one row or one column of a grid. Viewport is the visible area of the browser window.

The one question: who decides the size?

Picture a park bench. People sit down one after another, and each person takes up as much room as they need. A big guy in a winter coat takes more, a kid takes less. When the bench is full, the next person goes to the next bench, and the people on the second bench don't line up with the people on the first one. Why would they? Nobody planned any of it. The bench just fits whoever showed up.

That's flexbox. The items come first, and the layout forms around them.

Now picture an egg carton. The slots exist before there's a single egg in it. Every egg goes into a slot, the slots line up perfectly in rows and columns, and if you only have seven eggs, you've got seven full slots and some empty ones. A small egg doesn't make its slot smaller.

That's grid. The layout comes first, and the items go into it.

MDN puts it in almost the same terms: flexbox works from the content out, and grid works from the layout in. You'll also hear the older rule, and it's true too: flexbox is one-dimensional, it thinks about one row or one column at a time, while grid is two-dimensional, it thinks about rows and columns together. I covered that in the CSS Grid guide. But that rule alone can trick you. A wrapped row of tags looks two-dimensional on screen and it's still a flexbox job. Three equal columns in a single row look one-dimensional and grid may still be the better tool. So when you're stuck, ask the other question: should the size of this thing come from what's inside it, or from the layout around it?

Tags: the content decides, so flexbox wins

A list of tags under an article. The labels have different lengths, and you want each pill to be exactly as wide as its word. Same HTML below, two layouts. It starts on flexbox. Then click Grid and watch what happens.

Live demo: Tags: same HTML, flexbox or grid. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

On flexbox it looks right, and it took very little code. On grid, every tag is forced into a column of the same width. The short ones float in too much space, "Web performance" gets squeezed onto two lines, which makes its whole row taller, and "Authentication" doesn't even fit inside its pill. Nothing is broken, it's just the wrong tool. You've got words of different lengths and you're putting them in an egg carton.

Now the code, line by line. Open the CSS tab if you want to follow along.

  • display: flex on the list makes its children sit next to each other in a row. That's the only line that really changes the layout mode.
  • flex-wrap: wrap allows a new line when the row is full. Take it away and the browser tries to keep everything on one line: the tags shrink as far as their text allows, and after that they stick out of the container.
  • gap: 8px puts space between items. It's there instead of margins, because a margin on each tag would also add space you don't want at the start or the end of a line.
  • Notice what's missing: no width anywhere. Each tag is as wide as its text plus its padding. That's the content deciding the size.

The JavaScript does nothing clever. It swaps the class name on the list, and that's what makes this a fair comparison: same HTML, only the CSS rule changes. The grid line will make sense in the next example, so don't worry about it yet.

Cards: the layout decides, so grid wins

Now the opposite. A team page with seven people on it. You want a neat wall of cards, and you want it to adapt to the screen. Same two buttons, same HTML. This time look at the last row.

Live demo: Cards: same HTML, flexbox or grid. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

See it? On flexbox the last row doesn't match the rows above it. With a frame around 700 pixels wide, the top cards are 158 pixels and the bottom three stretch to 215. On a phone-sized frame the lonely last card takes the full width, double the others. Click Grid and every card is the same size, with an empty space where the missing cards would go. That's the egg carton doing its job.

So why does flexbox do this? The line flex: 1 1 140px is three numbers in one. The first means "you may grow if there's free space". The second means "you may shrink if there isn't". The third is the starting size. Each line on the bench shares out its own free space, and it has no idea what the line above it did. So a line with three cards gives each card more room than a line with four. Flexbox is doing exactly what you asked. You just asked the wrong thing.

And here's the grid line that fixes it, piece by piece, because this one line is worth knowing by heart:

  • grid-template-columns says what the columns are. The cards don't get a vote.
  • minmax(140px, 1fr) means each column is at least 140 pixels and can grow to one equal share of the leftover space. The fr unit is exactly that, a share.
  • repeat(auto-fill, ...) means make as many of those columns as fit in the available width. Wide screen, more columns. Narrow screen, fewer columns.
  • Notice what you didn't write: no media query. The layout adapts on its own, because you described the rule and not the result.

You'll also see auto-fit in the same spot, and the difference is small but real. Both make as many columns as fit, but auto-fit then collapses the empty ones. So if you only have two cards in that same 700-pixel frame, auto-fill keeps them at 158 pixels and leaves the empty columns standing, while auto-fit lets those two cards stretch to 328 pixels each and fill the row. Pick auto-fill when you want cards to stay the same size no matter how many there are. Pick auto-fit when you want a few items to fill the space.

Tip: Can you fix the last row in flexbox? Sort of. You can remove the growing with flex: 0 1 140px, but then the rows stop filling the container. Or you can calculate exact widths with calc() for every screen size. The moment you're doing that, you're rebuilding grid by hand, badly. That's your signal to switch.

A navigation bar is where flexbox feels at home

A logo, a couple of links, and a login button pushed to the far right. Every site has one. The links should be as wide as their words, and you don't want to count columns. So: flexbox.

Live demo: A navigation bar with flexbox. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

Most of this you've seen. Here's what's new:

  • align-items: center lines everything up on the middle of the row. Without it, items stretch to the height of the row and their text sits at the top, so a bigger logo and smaller links don't line up.
  • margin-left: auto on the login link is the trick of the whole example. An auto margin takes all the free space on that side. So the free space goes between About and Log in, and the button lands on the far right.
  • flex-wrap: wrap is the Plan B. On a very narrow screen the button drops to a new line instead of pushing out of the page, and it stays on the right because the auto margin still works there.

So that's all it is. One auto margin. A lot of people reach for justify-content: space-between here, and it looks fine with two items. Add two more links and it spreads all of them evenly across the bar, which isn't what you wanted. The auto margin says exactly what you mean: this one item goes to the far end.

Could you do this with grid? Yes. Something like grid-template-columns: auto auto auto 1fr, with the button aligned to the end of the last column. It works, right until someone adds a fourth link and the button lands in the wrong column, because you counted the items in your CSS. When the number of things can change, and each one sizes itself, you want the bench.

Real components use both: grid outside, flexbox inside

Here's the reason "flexbox or grid" is a slightly wrong question: real components use both, each at its own level. Look at three cards with different amounts of text. The links at the bottom start out uneven, which you've seen on plenty of websites. Click the button.

Live demo: Grid outside, flexbox inside. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

Two things are happening, on two levels.

The outer level is grid. The cards container uses repeat(auto-fit, minmax(170px, 1fr)), which you already know. There's a quiet bonus here: items in the same grid row stretch to the same height by default. That's why all three cards are the same height even though the text isn't. You didn't write any height at all.

The inner level is flexbox. Each card has display: flex and flex-direction: column, which stacks its title, text and link top to bottom. Now each card is a small column of things with free space at the bottom. And the same auto margin trick from the navbar works vertically: margin-top: auto on the link eats all the free space above it, and the link drops to the bottom of the card. One line.

If you're on a phone, the cards stack in one column, each only as tall as its own text. There's no free space and nothing to line up, so the button won't change anything you can see. That's correct. Layouts should behave differently when the job is different. On a bigger screen it's the difference between a page that looks finished and one that doesn't.

So when you look at a real design, stop asking which of the two to use for the page. Go level by level. The wall of cards: who decides the size? The layout, so grid. Inside a card: the content is stacked and sized by what it holds, so flexbox. Every level gets its own answer.

Whole pages: draw the layout, then let it change

A page with a header, main content, a sidebar and a footer is the most layout-decides thing there is, and grid has a feature that reads almost like a drawing. Drag the slider to pretend the screen is getting smaller.

Live demo: A page layout with grid areas (drag the slider). It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

Read grid-template-areas in the CSS tab like a little picture of the page. Each quoted line is a row, each word is a column. Every part of the page then claims its name: grid-area: header, grid-area: main and so on. Want the sidebar somewhere else? You change the picture, and you don't touch the HTML. If you remove the grid-area lines, the picture stops meaning anything and the items just fill the grid in order, so those lines aren't optional.

The slider is there so you can see the change in this small frame, and it's why the demo uses a container query: the @container rule looks at the width of the box around it, instead of the whole browser window. That's what container-type: inline-size on the outer box is for. Remove it and the rule has nothing to measure, so the page stays stacked. On a real page you'd usually write the same thing with @media (min-width: 768px), and the inside doesn't change at all. The rule is the same either way. Start with the phone layout, one column, then add the bigger layout when there's room for it.

If you're just starting out, that's plenty for page layouts. If you want to place items by exact rows and columns, or build something like a magazine front page, the CSS Grid guide goes much further. And if the words header, main and aside are new to you, read the HTML and CSS beginners article first, because layout sits on top of good HTML.

The bug that makes people hate both: content that won't shrink

This one gets everyone sooner or later. You've got a sidebar and a main area, you've written the layout correctly, and then a long web address or a code block shows up and the whole page gets a sideways scrollbar. You stare at it. Your CSS says the main area takes the remaining space, so why is it wider than the screen? Here it is, both versions, on purpose:

Live demo: The overflow bug and its one-line fix. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

The main area burst straight through the dashed frame. Click the button and the long line gets its own little scrollbar, which is what you wanted in the first place.

Why does it happen? It's the same reason in both tools. By default, a flex or grid item refuses to get smaller than its content. The browser calls this the automatic minimum size, and it's in both specs: flexbox and grid. The default exists for a good reason, because it stops your text from being crushed into something unreadable. But a long line with no spaces can't wrap, so its minimum width is its entire length, and the item grows to fit it. It doesn't matter that you wrote overflow-x: auto on the inner pre element. That element never gets squeezed, because its parent keeps growing to hold it.

And 1fr doesn't save you, even though it sounds like it should. Written alone, 1fr secretly means minmax(auto, 1fr), and that auto is the same "not smaller than my content" rule.

So the fix is to give the item permission to be small:

  • In grid: grid-template-columns: 80px minmax(0, 1fr). The zero replaces the automatic minimum.
  • In flexbox: min-width: 0 on the item that needs to shrink. It's the same idea in a different place.
  • Either way, something inside still has to handle the overflow, and in this demo that's overflow-x: auto on the pre. Without it, the line just sticks out of its now-smaller box.

Warning: Advanced: this bug nests. If a flex item sits inside another flex item, every level between the long content and the top of the layout can need its own min-width: 0, because one level with the automatic minimum still grows. When the fix seems not to work, select the elements in your browser's dev tools going upward from the content, and find the first one wider than you expect. That's where it goes.

Keep this one in mind when you test. If a layout has only ever seen your neat sample text, you haven't tested it. Put in a long word, a long email address, or a long code line, and see what it does.

order and reversing look fine and quietly break keyboards

Both tools let you show things in a different order than the HTML. It's tempting, because it's so easy. Click into the frame below and press the Tab key a few times.

Live demo: Press Tab through these links. It runs right in the page, so try it in the original article.

The red outline jumps from right to left, backwards through what you see, because the keyboard follows the HTML and not the screen. The order property only moves the picture. A screen reader will read the HTML order too. The grid spec is direct about this: use these features only for visual reordering, never for logical reordering of content, and MDN warns about the same disconnect. WCAG has success criteria for this, on focus order and on meaningful sequence.

Grid placement does the same thing, by the way, so a pretty grid-template-areas picture can scramble the reading order too. Look back at the page layout above: the main content comes before the sidebar in the HTML and on the screen, in both layouts, so the order is honest on purpose.

The Plan B is simple. If the order matters for understanding, or if there's something you can focus on in there, change the HTML and don't fake it in CSS. Use order for things like which decorative tile sits where, where the order carries no meaning. Then test it: put your mouse away and walk through the page with the Tab key. It takes less than a minute and you'll find things.

For the advanced readers: subgrid, and the question I can't answer

Remember the three cards? We lined up their links with an auto margin. But what if the titles have different lengths too, and you want the text in all three cards to start on the same line? The inner parts of separate cards don't know about each other. That's what subgrid is for: a nested grid takes its tracks from its parent instead of making its own. MDN shows it as widely available across browsers since September 2023.

cards.css

.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 12px; }

.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 3;
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;
  gap: 8px;
}
  • grid-row: span 3 makes each card occupy three rows of the outer grid, one each for title, text and link. It needs to match how many children the card really has. Add a fourth and it falls into an extra row you didn't plan for.
  • grid-template-rows: subgrid is the key line. The card stops creating its own rows and uses the parent's three. Now the tallest title in that row sets the height for all the titles.
  • display: grid on the card is required, because only a grid can have a subgrid.

With one short title and one long one, all three titles get the same row height, and all the text and all the links start on the same line. The auto margin from before only solves the last item. This solves every item.

Now the question people always ask: which one is faster? I don't have a number I trust, so I won't give you one. I wouldn't pick between them for performance on an ordinary page. Pick the one that says what you mean, because the real cost shows up later, in the person who has to change this layout in six months. That's often you. A grid with a clear picture in it is easy to change. A pile of calc() widths nobody wants to touch isn't. Thinking about the next change, not just today's screen, is the same habit behind the production-grade code checklist.

If you use Tailwind, nothing here changes

Tailwind doesn't give you a third layout system. Those classes are the same CSS with shorter names, so the question stays the same. Here's how the three patterns you just saw look in a React component:

components/layouts.tsx

export function Tags() {
  return (
    <ul className="flex flex-wrap gap-2">
      <li>CSS</li>
      <li>Accessibility</li>
    </ul>
  );
}

export function Cards() {
  return (
    <ul className="grid grid-cols-[repeat(auto-fill,minmax(14rem,1fr))] gap-4">
      <li>Emily</li>
      <li>James</li>
    </ul>
  );
}

export function Navbar() {
  return (
    <nav className="flex flex-wrap items-center gap-4">
      <a href="/">Acme</a>
      <a href="/login" className="ml-auto">Log in</a>
    </nav>
  );
}
  • flex flex-wrap gap-2 is the tag row: display: flex, wrapping allowed, a small gap.
  • grid-cols-[repeat(auto-fill,minmax(14rem,1fr))] is the card wall, written as one arbitrary value. There are no spaces inside the brackets, because a space would make it two separate classes and it would silently do nothing.
  • ml-auto is the same margin-left: auto trick. The min-w-0 class is your fix for the overflow bug.

If you're setting Tailwind up, the Tailwind v4 article walks through it. If you don't know the underlying CSS, learn that first. Otherwise you'll be typing class names for things you can't debug.

When AI writes your layout, this is how you check it

I use AI for a lot of my work, and I check what it writes as far as I can, because it makes mistakes without meaning to. Layout is a good example of why you still need the concept. AI will happily give you something that looks right in the one size you tried. It has no idea what's in your head. When the result isn't what I imagined, it's usually because I could have asked better, and now you know what asking better sounds like: "A wall of cards, minimum 14rem each, using grid with auto-fill. Inside each card, a flex column with the link pushed to the bottom. No fixed widths." That's a real instruction, and it only exists because you understand the two tools.

Then don't trust it, test it. This is the routine, and it works on layouts you wrote yourself too:

  • Ask who decides the size, and see if the code agrees. Flexbox with calculated percentage widths on a card wall is the first thing to question.
  • Add a card and remove a card. Does the last row still look intended?
  • Paste in a long word or a long web address. Does the page get a sideways scrollbar?
  • Shrink the window down to a phone width, about 320 pixels. Does anything stick out?
  • Put the mouse away and press Tab. Does the focus move in the order you read?

Five small checks, and they catch every bug in this article. If a layout is important enough to protect, ordinary unit tests won't do it, because they don't really draw the page. You need a test that runs in a real browser, and the React testing article explains where that kind of test is worth its cost.

The decision rule, and what to do next

Here's the whole article as something you can actually use. Go level by level through your design, and for each level:

  • Choose flexbox when the items should size themselves: tags, buttons, navigation bars, toolbars, a form row, or stacking things inside a card.
  • Choose grid when the layout should size the items: card walls, galleries, whole page structure, or anything that has to line up in both directions.
  • Choose neither when normal page flow already does the job. A heading above a paragraph doesn't need a layout tool. Blocks stack on their own.
  • If you're writing calc() widths or counting items in your CSS, you've probably picked the wrong one. Try the other tool before adding more code.

Now go do this. It takes ten minutes, and it's worth more than another tutorial. Open a website you use every day, right-click a part of it, and choose Inspect. In the dev tools of Chrome, Edge and Firefox, elements using these layouts carry a small flex or grid label next to them in the HTML view. Before you look, guess: flexbox or grid here? Then check. Sometimes you'll be wrong, and sometimes the site's author made a different call. Ask why. That's how you get the judgment that no property list gives you.

After that, build one thing on your own: a card wall with a link at the bottom of each card, and a navigation bar above it. You've now seen every line you need. If you get stuck, that's normal and it isn't a sign of anything. I learned most of this by trying it and getting it wrong first, and many people working in companies still look this stuff up. Don't give up on it. Then go deeper with the CSS Grid guide, which picks up where this leaves off.

This article first appeared on CodeFromScratch, where the live demos run right in the page. If you want the next one in your inbox, join the newsletter.

title: Ng-News 26/24: OpenAPI Generator, slide.ng and Angular Compiler Benchmarks
description:
OpenAPI Generator can now generate Angular httpResource methods, and slide.ng brings Markdown presentations to Angular. Also in this episode are the first benchmarks of Angular’s new compiler, TanStack Query, error boundaries, and ng-prism 22.7.

How Much Faster Is Angular’s New Compiler?

We’ve already covered the rewrite of Angular’s compiler, which uses Rust and Oxc. Now we finally have some numbers.

Cédric Exbrayat ran the new pipeline on three projects. His cold-build benchmarks were roughly two to three times faster. On the largest project, memory usage went from about 2.8 GB to 1.4 GB.

The TypeScript team reported about a tenfold speedup with its Go rewrite. Type checking is only one part of an Angular build, though. The other steps also contribute to the total, so speeding up TypeScript won’t give you the same speedup across the whole pipeline.

You can already try the new pipeline in Analog. Brandon Roberts added experimental support for it to Analog’s Vite plugin.

How much faster is the new Angular compiler? - Ninja Squad

Angular is building a new Rust-backed compiler. What does it change, and what can we really expect for build performance?

blog.ninja-squad.com
  • Experimental compiler support in Analog
  • TypeScript 7.0 announcement

OpenAPI Generator Adds httpResource

When the backend is written in another language, or when an app talks to multiple backends, we often have to keep track of endpoint URLs and request and response types. We can write that code by hand, or we can generate it from an OpenAPI specification.

OpenAPI Generator’s Angular client has traditionally exposed Observable methods using Angular’s HttpClient. With version 7.27.0, we finally have support for httpResource as well.

There were already community projects that could do this. Now the official OpenAPI Generator can do it as well.

  • OpenAPI Generator 7.27.0
  • Angular generator options

slide.ng

Slidev lets developers write presentations in Markdown. It comes with features like code highlighting, live coding, Mermaid diagrams, and a presenter mode. Slidev itself is built with Vue.

Erkam Yaman built slide.ng, an Angular implementation inspired by Slidev. It uses Slidev’s Markdown format and generates an Angular component for each slide. That means you can use your own Angular components in a presentation, alongside features like live coding, Mermaid, zoom, and presenter mode.

slide.ng | Slides in markdown, built with Angular

Presentations written in markdown, with real Angular template syntax inside. Documentation for slide.ng.

slide-ng.dev

Other News

TanStack Query helps you manage server state, including fetching and caching data. It's available for Angular, and Armen Vardanyan shows how it works in an Angular app in his hands-on stream on Angular Space.

Error boundaries are a bit like try-catch for templates. Angular 22.2’s @boundary block lets you display a fallback if part of the template fails to render. Igor Sedov explains it in one of his animated Angular videos.

ng-prism is a component gallery built for Angular libraries. Version 22.7 adds API pages for services and pipes and gives components and directives the same API page format. Alexander Spies goes through the changes in his release write-up.

title: Screenlet – Responsive testing and device mockups without recurring subscriptions
description:
Testing responsive web layouts shouldn't require paying $10 to $15 every month.

Like many frontend developers, I regularly rely on browser extensions to preview how sites render across different viewports, capture quick device mockups for client reviews, and record interactions. Over time, however, extensions like Mobile Simulator and Responsive Viewer started paywalling everyday necessities—locking specific breakpoints, interaction capture, or clean exports behind recurring monthly subscriptions.

I got tired of subscription fatigue for straightforward browser utilities, so I built Screenlet.

What is Screenlet?

Screenlet is a lightweight browser extension and web tool designed for developers and designers who need fast, zero-friction responsive testing and screen recording.

Instead of gating essential developer utilities behind paywalls, 100% of the core testing features are unlocked for free.

Key Features

  • Complete Device Library: Test across popular mobile, tablet, and desktop viewports without hitting an arbitrary "upgrade to unlock this device" screen.
  • Responsive Multi-Viewport Testing: Inspect media queries, flexbox shifts, and layout behavior instantly.
  • Integrated Screen Recording & Mockups: Record interactions directly in the viewport for QA reports, bug reproduction, or design showcase videos.
  • Lightweight Footprint: Built to load quickly alongside native Chrome DevTools without memory bloat.

The Pricing Philosophy

Screenlet is built around a simple, non-predatory model:

  1. Free Tier: Access every single device preset, responsive mode, and recording tool. Free exports come with a small watermark.
  2. Lifetime Deal ($29): If you need clean, unbranded exports for client handoffs, presentations, or portfolio demos, you can remove the watermark permanently for a one-time $29 fee. No monthly subscriptions, no recurring "software rent."

Try it Out & Feedback

Check it out live: screenlet.org

I'm actively iterating on the roadmap. What devices, custom resolution options, or debugging features would make your daily workflow easier? Drop your thoughts, edge cases, and bug reports below!

title: Paste JSON, get Java records: a small IntelliJ plugin for API payloads
description:
If you write Java against REST APIs, you have typed the same thing many times: copy a JSON response, then hand-write the classes that match it. For years the IntelliJ answer was GsonFormat, which generated old-style POJOs. It stopped working with current IDEs a while ago, and the popular JSON-to-class plugins I checked generate classes, not Java records, which is what you want for an immutable API payload in Java 16+.

So I built a small one: JSON to Java Record, now on the JetBrains Marketplace.

What it does

Copy this JSON:

{
  "order_id": 10452,
  "created_at": "2026-11-08T14:03:00Z",
  "total": 129.95,
  "paid": true,
  "customer": { "id": 88, "full_name": "Ana Ruiz", "email": "ana@example.com" },
  "items": [
    { "sku": "KB-01", "qty": 1, "price": 89.0 },
    { "sku": "MS-02", "qty": 2, "price": 20.475, "gift_wrap": true }
  ]
}

Press Alt+Insert in a Java file, choose Paste JSON as Java Record... (also under Tools), name it Order, and you get this (the plugin's actual output; in the editor it is then reformatted with your own code style):

import java.util.List;

public record Order(
    int orderId,
    String createdAt,
    double total,
    boolean paid,
    Customer customer,
    List<Item> items
) {
    public record Customer(
        int id,
        String fullName,
        String email
    ) {}

    public record Item(
        String sku,
        int qty,
        double price,
        Boolean giftWrap
    ) {}
}

A few details that matter in real payloads:

  • Nested objects become nested records, and arrays of objects become List<...> of a record.
  • Arrays are merged. gift_wrap appears in only one of the two items, so it becomes a boxed Boolean (it can be null), while fields present everywhere stay primitive.
  • Numbers are typed sensibly: int, long for big values, double for decimals; a list mixing 1 and 2.5 becomes List<Double>.
  • snake_case becomes camelCase, and reserved words are made safe (class becomes class_).

Keep the original JSON names

If your mapper needs the original keys, pick Jackson or Gson in the dialog. Only the fields whose Java name differs get an annotation:

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty;
import java.util.List;

public record Order(
    @JsonProperty("order_id") int orderId,
    @JsonProperty("created_at") String createdAt,
    double total,
    boolean paid,
    Customer customer,
    List<Item> items
) {
    public record Customer(
        int id,
        @JsonProperty("full_name") String fullName,
        String email
    ) {}

    public record Item(
        String sku,
        int qty,
        double price,
        @JsonProperty("gift_wrap") Boolean giftWrap
    ) {}
}

Gson users get @SerializedName instead.

Where it puts the code

  • In an open Java file, it inserts at the caret (or replaces a selection), adds missing imports at the top and reformats.
  • From the Project view (right-click a package, New > Paste JSON as Java Record...), it creates Order.java there. It never overwrites an existing file.
  • Invalid JSON shows an error and changes nothing. It reads your clipboard, works offline and sends no telemetry.

Limits, honestly

  • IntelliJ IDEA 2025.2 or newer, with Java support. It does not run in PyCharm or WebStorm.
  • Types are inferred from the sample you paste. A field that is null in your sample becomes Object; paste a fuller sample or fix that one type by hand.
  • Dates stay String. Mapping them to Instant or LocalDate is your call.

Get it

  • Marketplace: JSON to Java Record (free)
  • Source and issues: github.com/datawharf-tools/json-record

It is a first version. If it gets a type wrong on your payload, or you want another output (Lombok, Kotlin data classes, TypeScript), open an issue or tell me in the comments.

title: Managing document metadata in React 19
description:
This post's title may seem odd to you, if you're up to date, but a few things have changed from React 18 to 19, and one of them is how you manage document metadata. Before it, you likely had some shenanigans going on, like react-helmet or react-helmet-async in place to dynamically update your document title, inject custom metadata, links, scripts or even styles. Thankfully, with React 19 you'll very likely be able to drop all of that in favor of simplicity and good old HTML.

Managing metadata with react-helmet

If you're still in the Middle Ages (React 18) you might still have react-helmet (or its fork react-helmet-async) installed in your repository, to help you manage your document metadata. Please, don't get me wrong, they're both very popular solutions to an old problem everyone has and had been very reliable in solving it, so far.

import { Helmet } from 'react-helmet';

// Home page
const Home = () => (
  <>
    <Helmet>
      <title>Home | My Website</title>
      <meta name="description" content="Welcome to the home page of My Website." />
    </Helmet>
    <h1>Home Page</h1>
    <p>This is the home page content.</p>
  </>
);

export default Home;

import { Helmet } from 'react-helmet';

// About page
const About = () => (
  <>
    <Helmet>
      <title>About | My Website</title>
      <meta name="description" content="Learn more about us on the about page." />
    </Helmet>
    <h1>About Page</h1>
    <p>This is the about page content.</p>
  </>
);

export default About;

This is what your code might look like if you are using these libraries, but don't stress over it, there's a much simpler solution to this problem.

Managing metadata with React 19

Now, getting out of Plato's Cave, instead of having to install third-party libraries to do that, all you have to do is write plain HTML with the required metadata your page requires.

export default function About() {
  return (
    <>
      <title>Lucas Tonelli's history summary</title>
      <link rel="canonical" href="https://lucastonelli.com/about" />
      <meta
              name="description"
              content="A brief history about my career and who I am personally."
      />
      <main title="About">
        <h1>About</h1>
      </main>
    </>
  );
}

This is what a piece of my CV page looks like. Yup, plain HTML. This is being done entirely by React, and if I were to include more metadata here, such as scripts and styles, I would likely see the same results.

You might be wondering: "Why did he say 'likely'"? That's because there are a few exceptions where metadata won't be put in the document head. For example, if the meta element is provided with the itemProp prop, it will stay where it is, since it doesn't represent metadata about the document, but rather metadata about a specific part of the page.

With that said, go over React documentation and check out all the caveats for this feature. Also, there are several other features there that might pique your interest, so I recommend taking a look at those as well.

Wrap-up

Shifting the paradigm of how we manage document metadata, React 19 has dropped in to simplify it, while making some libraries obsolete along the way. Now, writing plain HTML inside a React component is enough to ensure that your document title, for instance, will end up in the document head. That simplifies the day-to-day life of maintaining frontend projects and gives everyone using it fewer things to worry about.

This article was created with the help of AI because, while I'm good at being a software engineer (I hope so), I suck at being a writer. On the other hand, the silly jokes and wordplay are completely mine because I'm really good at those. Also, the content comes from things I've done or learned, has been verified and is edited to be straight to the point, since AI loves to stall, but I hate it.

title: Feed the agent the a11y lint JSON, not a screenshot of red outlines
description:
The a11y overlay lights up. Someone screenshots the red outlines, drops the PNG into chat, and asks the agent to “fix accessibility.” The model apologizes, rewrites a random div into a button, and misses the actual label association three lines down.

Screenshots are great for humans scanning a page. They’re a lossy encoding for agents. What the model needs is the structured report: rule id, file or selector, message, severity.

I’ve stopped pasting red-outline photography as the primary repro. I paste lint / axe JSON (or a trimmed slice of it) and point at the rule I care about.

Two different JSON shapes (don’t mix them up)

ESLint + eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y is a static pass over JSX/TSX. Run something like eslint -f json path/to/file.tsx and you get an array of file results with messages[]: ruleId, line, column, message, severity. That JSON points at source.

axe-core (Storybook a11y, Playwright @axe-core/playwright, browser extensions) is a runtime pass over the rendered DOM. You get violations[] with id, impact, help, nodes[].target selectors, and HTML snippets. That JSON points at the live tree.

Both beat a screenshot. They are not interchangeable:

  • jsx-a11y won’t see contrast on a CSS variable resolved at runtime
  • axe won’t tell you the JSX line that forgot htmlFor unless you map selector → source yourself

Use the JSON that matches how you found the bug. If you have both, paste both — labeled.

What to paste (and what to trim)

Agents drown in 200 KB of noise. Trim to the failure you want fixed:

{
  "source": "eslint-json",
  "filePath": "src/features/billing/InvoiceForm.tsx",
  "messages": [
    {
      "ruleId": "jsx-a11y/label-has-associated-control",
      "severity": 2,
      "line": 84,
      "column": 8,
      "message": "A form label must be associated with a control."
    }
  ]
}

Or for axe:

{
  "source": "axe-core",
  "violations": [
    {
      "id": "label",
      "impact": "critical",
      "help": "Form elements must have labels",
      "nodes": [
        {
          "target": ["#invoice-form", "input[name=\"poNumber\"]"],
          "html": "<input name=\"poNumber\" />"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Include: rule id, impact/severity, location (line or selector), short message. Exclude: giant passes[] arrays, unrelated files, decorative incomplete noise you already triaged.

Prompt shape 

Fix the accessibility finding below. Do not broaden into a redesign.

Input: eslint JSON (jsx-a11y) for InvoiceForm.tsx
Constraints:
- Fix only the listed ruleId(s)
- Prefer associating the existing <label> with the control (htmlFor / id) over aria hacks
- No `eslint-disable` unless you explain why the rule is a false positive
- Keep the visual layout; this is an a11y fix PR
- Show the before/after for the affected JSX and re-run the same lint command

JSON:

Then paste the trimmed JSON.

The “no eslint-disable” line matters. Agents love silencing rules. You want the association fixed, not the linter muted.

Why screenshots fail as agent input

A PNG of red outlines:

  • Loses rule ids (was it contrast, name, or focus order?)
  • Loses file paths and line numbers
  • Encourages visual guessing (“make the box bigger”)
  • Often includes multiple findings the agent “fixes” in the wrong order

Humans still benefit from a screenshot alongside JSON when contrast or focus rings are hard to imagine. Lead with structure; attach the picture as secondary context.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • eslint-disable-next-line jsx-a11y/* as the only change
  • Rewriting the whole form “while we’re here”
  • Fixing a different rule than the one in the pasted JSON
  • Aria-label spam on elements that already have visible labels
  • Claiming axe is “done” when you only ran jsx-a11y (or the reverse) without saying so

Accept

  • Diff scoped to the reported locations
  • Same lint / axe command green for those rule ids
  • Visible label retained (not replaced by screen-reader-only text without reason)
  • Honest note when a finding is incomplete and needs human judgment (common with contrast)

Tiny habit

Next time someone drops a red-outline screenshot into the agent thread, export the ESLint JSON or axe violations for that surface, trim to the rule you care about, and paste that instead. Keep the screenshot if it helps humans — but let the JSON be the ticket the model actually works from.

title: Every new medium gets called cheating
description:
How a machine I didn’t trust taught me to be bad at things again.

I was a skeptic.

Let the record show, I too, was against it.

When Ted Chiang wrote in The New Yorker that AI isn’t going to make art, I felt vindicated. I forwarded it. To people who had not asked (sorry).

His point was that art is the sum of thousands of small choices, and a machine that makes most of them for you has removed the art. I summarized this at dinners as “it’s a vending machine with ambitions,” which got an eye roll and some confused looks.

Writing is my home turf. I own about 14 favorite pens. I have opinions about semicolons. So when a machine showed up promising to write for me, I reacted the way a cat reacts to a new cat: I sat very still, judged it from across the room, and waited for it to leave.

I first got really riled up when a client called my writing “too AI” for using my dear Oxford comma and trusty em-dash. Things started feeling personal then, and they have ever since.

AI has never made a single thing I’m proud of. But it did something weirder, and honestly better. It made me brave enough to be a beginner again, in mediums I’d been too scared to touch for years.

Let me explain.

Every medium has a bouncer.

Every medium has a bouncer. It’s a feeling rather than a person. And some mediums have a friendlier door policy than others.

In a ceramics studio it’s the sense that everyone else knows where the good glaze is hidden and has agreed not to tell you. In coding it’s the suspicion that you must already know what a terminal is before you are allowed to ask what a terminal is.

The bouncer doesn’t check your talent. He checks whether you look like you belong. And for most of my adult life, I have walked up to the door of some new medium, made eye contact with him, said “never mind, I’m a writer,/designer/not-this” and gone home.

Why? Well, imposter syndrome. It took me roughly 35 years to accept that, no matter the success, we all feel it.

I made a very active effort to convert myself.

AI actually played a bigger role in it than I’d like to admit. And yet I’m admitting it here because it was not the obvious — the machine making anything for me. It was that I could finally ask the stupid question. At eleven at night. Forty times in a row. Without anyone sighing, checking their phone, or saying “well, it’s pretty basic.” This made the much-dreaded learning curve suddenly feel totally in my control, on my own terms, and more like a fun slip-and-slide rather than Sisyphus’ hill.

So…for example…how do you write a truly three-dimensional character? What is a web repo? And what am I not getting about Picasso?

Three questions. Three mediums. Old me would have needed a writing course, a very patient developer friend, and maybe an art history degree.

New me needed one evening and zero dignity.

And it’s not just me feeling brave btw. When researchers from Stanford and MIT gave an AI assistant to more than 5,000 customer support agents, the newest, least experienced people got 34% more done per hour. The veterans? Barely changed. The researchers’ explanation: the tool passes along what experienced people know and helps newcomers move down the learning curve faster.

Translation: AI is kind of wasted on experts and a gift to beginners. And in every new medium, guess who’s the beginner?

The gatekeeping, it turned out, was mostly mine. I had been running the door on myself.

A brief history of reply guys.

It comforts me that we have been here before. Many, many times. Actually.

Around 370 BC, Plato wrote down Socrates complaining that writing would make people forgetful and give them the look of wisdom without the real thing. Writing. My home turf. The very first AI panic was about my favorite pen. (And yes, we only know Socrates hated writing because someone wrote it down.)

In 1492, a fellow German, the abbot Johannes Trithemius, wrote In Praise of Scribes, a passionate case that monks should keep copying books by hand because the printing press would make them lazy. Then he had it printed. What a diva was he? Iconic.

Then, in 1859, reviewing the Paris Salon, the poet Charles Baudelaire, and my second favorite poet with the initials CB, announced that photography was where untalented, lazy painters went to hide. He loved ragebait. If he’d had a comments section, he would have lived in it for sure.

Around the same time, the painter Paul Delaroche reportedly declared that painting was dead. Painting has now been dead for roughly 165 years and is doing great. It has gallery representation. It has a podcast. It probably has a trust fund.

Photography, meanwhile, became a medium in its own right, with its own geniuses and its own snobs who now say the same things about phones.

That is the pattern. History repeating herself.

Every new medium gets called cheating by the people who are good at the old one. I know this because I was one of them (remember that article I forwarded?).

But I broke that generational trauma.

Because here’s what the reply guys always miss: the tools that made a medium easier never kill it. They crack it open. And yeah, that is kinda scary. Mostly, if you’re an insecure dude, I guess?

Before 1841, painters stored their oil paint in pig bladders tied with string. Then a broke American portrait painter named John Goffe Rand patented the collapsible paint tube. Suddenly paint was portable, painters walked outside, and Renoir later said that without tubes there would have been no Monet, no Cézanne, no Impressionism at all. Wild.

Anyhow, easier didn’t mean worse. Easier meant more people, in more places, painting things nobody had painted before. That’s what a lower learning curve does. It lets more people in. I’m unfortunately woke enough to think that’s a good thing.

Craft is just a conversation with your material.

The sociologist Richard Sennett describes craft as a conversation with your material. You push, it pushes back, and that resistance is what forces you to revise and, eventually, to get good.

Wood has a grain. Clay collapses when you’re impatient. Watercolor does whatever it wants and then dries in a shape that looks like a disappointed relative that puts your toddler in tears.

AI pushes back too, just in a more humiliating way.

It does exactly what you said instead of what you meant. Often cheerfully, with bullet points to really drive the point home. Ugh.

For someone who writes a lot, this is a daily performance review of my own clarity. The resistance is in the gap between the idea in my head and the sentence I typed (or spoke). That gap has a…texture. You kinda learn to feel it.

That, I’m sorry to report to my former self, is a medium.

Brian Eno wrote in his diary in 1995 that whatever feels weird and ugly about a new medium tends to become its signature.

So I look at AI’s current tics (the extra fingers, the relentless enthusiasm, the word “delve”) with new tenderness.

In twenty years someone will add them back on purpose and call it vintage. And if you know me, you know I’m a sucker for that.

Fluids take the shape of their container.

Don’t worry, I have not totally drowned myself in the Kool-Aid. There is something that keeps me from becoming one of those people who post sunrise photos captioned “the future is here.”

I’ve already ranted about this in The taste paradox, so here’s the short version. When researchers handed writers AI-generated story ideas, the stories got rated as more creative. They also got more alike. Everyone got better, and everyone got a little more the same.

I’d been calling AI a fluid medium as a compliment. I forgot what fluids do.

Water has no shape of its own. It takes the shape of whatever holds it.

The container is you.

That’s pretty poetic. I mean, unless you’d prefer Tupperware.

Your taste, your oddness, the thing you notice that nobody else does. Which is why, on my home turf, I use it to teach me stuff that helps me reach more people. In my case, that’s making social media assets and finding other creators to engage with.

A tool that makes everyone a competent writer is a threat only to writers whose main feature was competence. Lucky for me, I’ve always been more rebel than competent.

The medium it never touched.

I have been doing a lot of things I’ve always been interested in and too afraid to try, with less fear than ever. Because really, AI didn’t teach me coding. It taught me that starting from zero is survivable. And it showed me how I learn: by asking the dumb question first and making the ugly version second. That lesson doesn’t stay inside the chat window. It leaks. Into my life. Even my parenting!

So yes, I think AI is a fluid medium. And so is the courage it leaves behind. Two liquids, one glass: the tool pours you into a new medium, and the courage keeps you there. Liquid courage, minus the hangover and the text messages you regret. Win-win.

The bouncer is still standing at the door of every medium I haven’t tried yet. He just looks smaller now. Like someone I could easily body-tackle or win against in a rap battle.

The point?

Be a beginner again.

On purpose. Pick the medium you’ve always been too scared to try, the one with the meanest bouncer. Ask it the stupid question tonight. Then go make something ugly with your actual hands.

Nicole is a Content Designer turned Design Director based in Stockholm, Sweden. She potters, writes poetry, and raises little girls in a house by a meadow. You can follow her writing here or get it directly to your inbox via her publication, eggwoman. Nicole is on LinkedIn. Find her portfolio at nicoletells.com.

Every new medium gets called cheating was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Running a Hebrew storefront in Next.js: the RTL bugs nobody warns you about
description:
Our store at RAMO sells hardware, plumbing and garden supplies, and most of our customers read Hebrew. That means the whole storefront runs right-to-left. Setting dir="rtl" on the root element is the easy part. It flips the page, and for a day you think you're done.

Then the small bugs show up. None of them are hard, but nobody lists them in one place, so here's ours.

1. Stop writing left and right in CSS

The first round of bugs was always the same: a margin on the wrong side, an icon hugging the wrong edge, a dropdown opening off-screen. Every one came from margin-left, padding-right, left: 0 and friends.

The fix is to use logical properties everywhere:

/* before */
.price-tag { margin-left: 8px; text-align: left; }

/* after */
.price-tag { margin-inline-start: 8px; text-align: start; }

inline-start means "the side where text begins", so it follows the direction automatically. If you use Tailwind, the ms-*, me-*, ps-*, pe-*, start-* and end-* utilities do the same thing. A lint rule that flags the physical versions is worth adding, so they don't creep back in.

2. Numbers, SKUs and model names inside Hebrew text

A product title like "ברז מטבח 3/4 דגם X-200" is a mix of Hebrew and Latin characters plus digits and slashes. The Unicode bidi algorithm handles most of it, but punctuation at the edges of a mixed run can jump to the wrong side. A trailing ) or a dash before a model number are the usual suspects.

Two things help:

  • Wrap anything that's "code-like" (SKUs, model numbers, dimensions) in <bdi> or a span with unicode-bidi: isolate. It keeps that chunk from being reordered with its neighbours.
  • For fields that are always Latin, like a SKU input, set dir="ltr" on that element alone. 
<p className="title">
  {product.nameHe} <bdi>{product.model}</bdi>
</p>

3. Prices

Show prices with Intl.NumberFormat('he-IL', { style: 'currency', currency: 'ILS' }) rather than gluing a ₪ sign onto a number by hand. Hand-built strings put the symbol on whatever side the developer happened to think of, and it looks wrong to someone who reads Hebrew every day.

One more thing: never let the price split across lines. A white-space: nowrap on the price element saves you from a shekel sign sitting alone on the next line on narrow phones.

4. Icons that point somewhere

Arrows, chevrons, "next" and "back" icons, and the little carousel controls all need to flip. A magnifying glass, a cart or a phone icon should not. The simplest approach is to tag directional icons explicitly:

[dir="rtl"] .icon-directional { transform: scaleX(-1); }

It sounds trivial, but a "next" arrow pointing backwards in a checkout flow is the kind of thing that makes people hesitate.

5. Carousels and horizontal scroll

Horizontal scrolling in RTL is where browsers have historically disagreed most about scrollLeft values. If you write your own carousel, test it in Safari and Chrome both, and prefer scrollIntoView or scrollBy with logical thinking over raw scrollLeft math. A lot of slider libraries have an rtl option; turn it on rather than fighting it.

6. Mixed-direction pages

Some pages carry both directions: an English product spec sheet embedded in a Hebrew page, or a brand name in Latin letters. Put dir="auto" on user-generated or imported text blocks, like reviews or descriptions pulled from a supplier. The browser then picks the direction from the first strong character, which is right far more often than a hardcoded guess.

7. Test it with real content

Lorem ipsum hides every one of these bugs. Test RTL layouts with real product titles from the catalog, the long ugly ones with model numbers and fractions in them, like the ones you find in our pipe fittings category. If a layout survives those, it survives anything.

The short version

  • Logical CSS properties only, enforced by lint.
  • Isolate SKUs, model numbers and dimensions with <bdi>.
  • Format prices with Intl, and keep them on one line.
  • Flip directional icons, leave the rest alone.
  • dir="auto" for text you don't control.
  • Test with your real, messy catalog data.

None of this is exotic. It's just the list I wish someone had handed me before the first round of "why is this icon on the wrong side" bug reports.

title: Why AI-built UIs all look the same, and the 4-step fix we use with Codex and Claude Code
description:
Ask Codex or Claude Code for a landing page and you can usually tell, from across the room, that an agent made it. Violet-to-indigo gradient behind the hero. A headline with gradient text. Frosted-glass cards with a soft purple glow. A row of emoji as feature icons. "Seamless", "supercharge", "unlock". Inter everywhere.

None of these are wrong on their own. The problem is that every model reaches for the same safe defaults, so the result looks like every other generated page. People have started calling it AI slop.

We build a design tool for Codex, so we have been fighting this on our own screens. Here is what worked, what did not, and the small open-source skill that came out of it.

What did not work: longer rule lists

The first thing everyone tries is a prompt or skill full of rules: "no purple gradients, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, use a 4px grid". It helps a little. Then two things happen:

  1. The agent swaps one default for another. Ban violet and you get beige, a serif headline and a terracotta button. That combination is now so common it has become its own tell.
  2. The next screen drifts. Even when one page comes out well, nothing records why. Open a new session, ask for the settings screen, and you are back to the defaults.

Rules tell the agent what not to do. They never tell it what your product should look like.

What worked: make the choice, then write it down

What fixed it was copying what a designer does on day one. Four steps:

1. See three real directions before restyling anything

Instead of letting the agent pick a style, have it build the same key screen three times, with your real content, in three directions that differ on purpose: say, one light and editorial, one dark and dense, one soft and friendly. Put them side by side and choose. Or mix: "A's type with C's colors".

This is the step that matters most. Choosing from rendered options is far easier than describing a style in words, and it forces a decision that a rule list never does.

2. Save the choice as DESIGN.md

Write the chosen direction into a DESIGN.md file at the root of the repo: colors as named tokens with hex values, two font families and a type scale, a spacing unit, radius, shadows, and short rules for buttons, inputs, cards and navigation.

Every agent can read Markdown. Once the file exists, a new session starts from your design instead of from the model's defaults, and you can point any tool at it.

3. Apply it in passes, not all at once

Asking for "make it look like DESIGN.md" in one go tends to produce a half-restyled page. Passes work better, in this order:

  1. Tokens: replace hard-coded colors, sizes and radii.
  2. Type: two families at most, the system's scale, one clearly largest line per screen.
  3. Spacing and layout: one spacing unit and its multiples.
  4. Color: neutrals carry the screen; the primary color shows up where the user acts, about once per view.
  5. Components: real icons (Lucide, Phosphor, SF Symbols), never emoji as icons.
  6. Copy: plain words from the product. Cut "seamless" and "supercharge".
  7. Details: hover, focus, empty, loading and error states; 4.5:1 contrast for text.
  8. Motion: only where it explains a change.

4. Check for the tells with a script

Eyes get used to a screen quickly, so we wrote a small checker that scans HTML, CSS, JSX, TSX, Vue, Svelte and Astro files for the usual tells. On our deliberately generic example page it prints (excerpt):

ERROR tally.html:11  [violet-gradient] Purple, violet or indigo gradient. Use a flat color from the design system.
WARN  tally.html:14  [glassmorphism] Backdrop blur. Use solid surfaces unless this is an overlay that really floats.
ERROR tally.html:21  [gradient-text] Gradient text. Use one solid color and let size carry emphasis.
ERROR tally.html:36  [emoji-icon] Emoji used in the UI. Use a real icon set, or no icon.
WARN  tally.html:42  [filler-copy] Filler marketing word. Say what the product does.
WARN  tally.html     [arbitrary-spacing] Spacing values off a 4px grid: 6, 10, 11, 13, 14, 22, 26, 34px.

1 files checked: 12 errors, 12 warnings.

The three directions built from the same content report none. A clean run does not mean a screen is good; it means the obvious tells are gone and you can judge the design itself.

The skill: pretty-ui

We packaged the four steps as an open-source agent skill called pretty-ui. It runs the whole loop: reads your project, audits what is there, builds three directions with your content, opens a comparison page, saves your pick as DESIGN.md, applies it pass by pass, and runs the checker before and after. Nothing is restyled until you choose.

It works with Codex, Claude Code, Hermes Agent, or any agent that reads SKILL.md, for websites, web apps and mobile apps (React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, Tailwind, shadcn/ui, React Native, SwiftUI, Flutter and more). It ships with 24 design systems, each with a contrast-checked palette and a font pairing that is not Inter.

Install for Codex:

codex plugin marketplace add ummydev/pretty-ui
codex plugin add pretty-ui@pretty-ui

For Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add ummydev/pretty-ui
/plugin install pretty-ui@pretty-ui

Or any agent: npx skills add ummydev/pretty-ui. Then ask in plain words: "Make this landing page look less AI-generated."

The checker also runs on its own, with Node 18+ and no dependencies:

node skills/pretty-ui/scripts/check.mjs src/

Repo: github.com/ummydev/pretty-ui (MIT).

If you do not want another skill

The approach works without it. The short version:

  • Before any restyle, ask your agent for three different directions of one screen as separate HTML files, and pick one yourself.
  • Save the pick as DESIGN.md and tell the agent to read it first in every session.
  • Restyle in passes: tokens, type, spacing, color, components, copy, states.
  • Search your code for backdrop-filter, background-clip: text, gradients with violet or indigo, and emoji inside buttons and headings.

We keep a longer list of the tells, with a prompt to fix each one, here: AI UI design tells and how to avoid them. The 24 design systems are browsable with live previews at codexdesign.io/design-systems.

Disclosure: we build Codex Design, a canvas for designing UI with Codex, and wrote pretty-ui along the way. The skill is free and does not need our product.

What tells do you see most in AI-generated UI? We are collecting them for the next version of the checker.

title: HTML to Image: Why the Download Doesn't Match the Preview
description:
You paste a card into a free HTML to image converter, the live preview looks exactly right, you hit download — and the file that lands has a different font, no logo, and the bottom row cut off.

That is not a flaky export. In a browser-based HTML to image converter like this one, the preview and the downloaded file are produced by two different renderers, from two different documents, so there is a short list of specific, predictable ways they disagree. This is a field guide to that list. I'm using the free HTML to Image converter on ultimatetools.io as the reference, because it runs entirely in the browser and I can point at exactly what happens at each step — but the same constraints apply to anything built on SVG foreignObject, html-to-image and dom-to-image included, which is why those libraries go to the trouble of inlining images and fonts before they serialise. (html2canvas takes a different route — it repaints the DOM onto a canvas itself — so it dodges the XML-parsing failure below and can fetch cross-origin images where CORS allows, at the cost of its own CSS-support gaps.)

The 60-second version

  1. Paste your markup into the HTML Code tab — or switch to Upload HTML and pick an .html or .htm file. It is read locally with FileReader, dropped into the HTML Code tab, and never sent anywhere.
  2. In Advanced Image Options (open by default), set Width and Height to the pixel size you want, or click a Quick Size: Twitter Card 1200x628, OG Image 1200x630, Square 800x800, Story (9:16) 1080x1920. The defaults are 800x400.
  3. In the same panel, choose a format — PNG, JPEG or WEBP — a scale (1x, 2x, 3x; the default 2x is real resolution, not upscaling) and a background (White, Transparent or a custom colour).
  4. Hit Generate & Download PNG — the button is named after whichever format you picked. The file saves as html-to-image.png / .jpeg / .webp.

That is the whole happy path. The rest of this is what to do when the file doesn't match what you saw.

How HTML to image conversion works in the browser (this explains every quirk)

There is no magic "render HTML to PNG" browser API. What actually happens is this:

// what "convert HTML to image" means in a browser
const svg = `<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
     width="${w * scale}" height="${h * scale}" viewBox="0 0 ${w} ${h}">
  <foreignObject width="100%" height="100%">
    <html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
      <head><style>/* body rules, then your Custom CSS */</style></head>
      <body>${yourHtml}</body>
    </html>
  </foreignObject>
</svg>`;

const img = new Image();
img.src = "data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8," + encodeURIComponent(svg);
img.onload = () => {
  ctx.drawImage(img, 0, 0, w * scale, h * scale); // canvas is w*scale x h*scale
  a.href = canvas.toDataURL("image/png");         // or image/jpeg, image/webp
  a.download = "html-to-image.png";
  a.click();
};

Your markup goes into an SVG <foreignObject>, the SVG is serialised into a data: URL, that URL is loaded into an HTMLImageElement, the image is painted onto a canvas, and the canvas is exported with toDataURL(). Two consequences fall straight out of that:

  1. Your HTML is now inside an XML document, and gets parsed as XML.
  2. An SVG loaded through <img> renders in a static, isolated mode — no scripts, no network requests for subresources.

The live preview never touches that pipeline. It is an <iframe srcDoc="…"> with sandbox="allow-same-origin", built from its own separate document string. Two renderers, two documents, no shared code path. One thing they do share: none of it leaves the tab. There is no fetch and no API route in the tool at all.

Eight ways the export differs from the preview — and the fix for each

1. One unclosed tag kills the whole render. <br>, <img src="…"> and <hr> are fine in HTML and fatal in XML, as is a bare & in a query string, a stray < in text, or an HTML-only entity like   or © (use the numeric form,   / ©). When the SVG won't parse, img.onerror fires and you get "Couldn't render that HTML to an image — check for external images or fonts it can't reach." — a slightly misleading message for this particular cause. Fix: self-close void elements (<br />, <img … />) and escape & as &. There is no validator in the tool; this is simply what happens to your markup once it is embedded in an XML document, so check it first whenever nothing at all renders.

2. Remote images and web fonts don't come through. <img src="https://cdn.example.com/logo.png" /> appears in the preview iframe (a normal document, it can fetch) and is missing from the download (an <img>-rendered SVG, it can't). Fix: inline the asset as a data: URI so nothing has to be fetched:

<img src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAA…" width="64" height="64" alt="" />

The Base64 Encoder & Decoder on the same site has a File to Base64 button for this. One detail: it hands back the bare base64 string, not the full URI, so you add the data:image/png;base64, prefix yourself — match the MIME type to your file.

Same story for @imported stylesheets and Google Fonts links: use a system font stack (font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif) or accept the fallback. The tool says as much in-panel. You will also see this described elsewhere as canvas "tainting"; with a same-origin data: URL the honest description is simpler — the asset never loads in the first place. Either way the fix is the same.

3. JavaScript never runs — in either path. The export is a static SVG. The preview iframe's sandbox grants allow-same-origin and not allow-scripts. So a chart library, a component that mounts on load, or anything that builds its DOM at runtime renders as an empty box in both places. Fix: hand it the rendered output instead of the source. Open the real page, inspect the node, Copy → Copy outerHTML, paste that.

4. The font changes between preview and export. This one is specific to how the two documents are built: the exported SVG's body rule ends with font-family: Arial, sans-serif, and the preview document's does not. Text with no explicit font renders in the iframe's default — usually a serif — in the preview, and in Arial in the file. Fix: never leave it to defaults. Declare it once in the Custom CSS tab, which is injected into both documents:

body { font-family: "Segoe UI", Roboto, Arial, sans-serif; }

5. Anything past the Height value is cropped — and the preview won't warn you. The SVG's viewBox is 0 0 width height and the foreignObject is 100% of it, while body only gets a min-height. Content that grows past your Height falls outside the viewBox and is never painted. The preview, being a real scrollable document, shows it happily.

The trap is the obvious-looking diagnostic. The preview pane is a fixed window — under 500px wide on a desktop layout — onto a document whose body is hard-set to your full Width. At the default 800px, and at every one of the four presets, that document is wider than the pane, so the preview scrolls horizontally almost always, and that tells you nothing about cropping. Chase it and you'll keep raising Height forever.

Fix: measure, don't eyeball. The preview has no marker for where Height ends — body only gets a min-height, so it quietly grows to fit whatever you paste. Cheapest check: set Height to something far larger than you need, export once, open the file and look at where the content actually stops, then set Height to that and export again. Or draw the boundary yourself: put body { height: 630px; outline: 2px dashed red; } (your Height value) in the Custom CSS tab — the body stops growing, the dashed line sits exactly where the export will crop, and anything hanging below it is what you'd lose. Delete the rule before the real export.

6. A 16px gutter you never asked for. Both documents apply padding: 16px to the body, so an OG Image export at 1200x630 gives you 1168x598 of usable area — enough to leave a visible 16px gutter around a gradient you meant to run edge-to-edge. Fix: the Custom CSS is interpolated after the built-in body rule, so a plain override wins on source order:

body { padding: 0; }

7. Transparent plus JPEG comes out white. JPEG has no alpha channel, so the background resolves to #ffffff and the canvas is pre-filled with white before the draw. The tool flags this with an amber warning rather than letting you discover it in the file. Fix: PNG or WEBP when you need the alpha.

8. A very large canvas fails — sometimes loudly, sometimes silently. Scale multiplies the canvas, not the layout, and the result is handed over as a data: URL on an anchor. Browsers cap both canvas area and string length, and the two failure shapes are worth separating:

  • Where toDataURL() genuinely throws — Firefox raises NS_ERROR_FAILURE on an oversized canvas — the tool catches it and shows "Couldn't build the image — try a smaller size, or switch format to PNG."
  • Where the canvas is simply blanked past the cap, toDataURL() returns the string "data:,", nothing throws, and the anchor click produces a broken or empty file with no error banner at all. That is the behaviour to expect on iOS Safari, which has historically had the lowest ceiling of the majors — around 16.7 megapixels, roughly a 4096x4096 canvas. A Story preset at 1080x1920 with 3x scale is 3240x5760, or 18.7 megapixels: comfortably fine on desktop Chrome, past that iOS limit.

Worth knowing either way: the 2400px maximum on the width and height inputs is an HTML attribute only — the JS clamps the minimum (Math.max(100, …)), so a typed 5000 goes straight into state and gets multiplied by your scale. Fix: 2x instead of 3x, or smaller dimensions. If a download does nothing at all and no banner appears, assume this rather than a bug in your markup.

HTML to JPEG, JPG, PNG or WEBP — choose by what's inside the card

Format matters more here than it does for photos, because HTML-to-image output is usually text on flat colour, which is the worst possible input for a lossy codec. The one number to hold in your head: an OG card at 1200x630 with the default 2x scale rasterises to 2400x1260 — roughly 3 megapixels of mostly flat fills and sharp edges, which is exactly the content PNG compresses well and JPEG mangles visibly.

  • PNG — the default, lossless, keeps the alpha channel. Sharp text edges, hairline borders and flat fills stay exactly as rendered. The quality field is disabled for PNG, and correctly so: toDataURL("image/png") is called with no quality argument, so any number you set there would do nothing.
  • JPEG — lossy DCT plus chroma subsampling, which is precisely what puts ringing and mosquito noise around crisp letterforms and hard colour boundaries. Quality is passed through as quality / 100, default 90. Keep it there or higher: the usual photo advice about dropping to 70-75 does not transfer, because artefacts appear on letterform edges long before they'd be noticeable on a photograph. JPEG earns its place when the card is dominated by a photo or a big multi-stop gradient, or when whatever you're uploading to refuses PNG.
  • WEBP — usually the smallest file at comparable quality, and it keeps transparency, so it's the sane default for an image headed straight into a web page. Two caveats: some CMS uploaders still reject the extension, and the tool does no feature detection, so on a browser that can't encode WEBP you would quietly get PNG bytes inside a .webp file.

Don't take anyone's file-size table on faith, mine included — export the same card as PNG and as WEBP at 90 and compare the two files. It's two clicks and nothing uploads.

One naming detail if you came here searching for HTML to JPG: the download is always html-to-image.jpeg, never .jpg, and the filename is never derived from the HTML file you uploaded. .jpg and .jpeg are the same bytes and the same codec, so rename it if a picky uploader insists on the three-letter form.

The parts that behave better than you'd expect

  • Scale is real resolution, not upscaling. The viewBox stays at your CSS dimensions while the canvas is width x scale by height x scale, so the layout is composed at 1200x630 and rasterised at 2400x1260. That is genuinely sharper output, not a resampled blur. Default is 2x; the choices are 1x, 2x and 3x.
  • Custom CSS lands in both documents, which is why it is the right place for anything the preview and the export must agree on — fonts, padding, resets.
  • Four size presets: Twitter Card 1200x628, OG Image 1200x630, Square 800x800, Story (9:16) 1080x1920. A preset highlights only when both width and height match it, so you can tell at a glance whether you're still on-spec after typing a custom number.

What it doesn't do (honestly)

  • No JavaScript execution. If your artwork is built at runtime, this approach cannot help you. Headless Chrome — Puppeteer or Playwright — is the right tool: a real browser that runs scripts, fetches fonts and images over the network, and screenshots a live URL. That's what you want in a pipeline; this is what you want for a one-off with nothing to install.
  • It isn't a URL screenshotter. It renders markup you paste, not a page you point it at. If the thing you want is already on screen in Chrome, DevTools → right-click the node → Capture node screenshot is faster, and it does run JS.
  • Tailwind and other utility classes don't resolve. There's no build step and no stylesheet, so class="p-4 rounded-xl" renders as unstyled markup. Write the equivalent real CSS in the Custom CSS tab, or use inline style attributes.
  • No preview of the rasterised result. The file goes straight to download; you find out by opening it.
  • Scale is fixed at 1x/2x/3x — no free-form multiplier.
  • One card at a time. No templating, no batch, no data merge. A hundred OG images with different titles needs a script and a headless browser, not a form.

Related Tools

  • convert an image file to base64 online free — the fix for failure mode 2: it hands you the base64 payload, you prepend data:image/png;base64,, and the renderer never has to fetch anything
  • convert HTML to PDF free with selectable text — when the output needs real text and page sizes instead of pixels on a canvas
  • compress PNG and WEBP images free in your browser — a 3x export is a large file; shrink it before it goes on a page

Paste your markup, set Width and Height to the size you actually want, and pull the file — free, nothing uploads: HTML to Image Converter
