title: Freeze design tokens the agent may not edit — allowlist only
description:
Ask an agent to “tighten spacing on the checkout header” and watch the diff: three lines in the header component… and a surprise edit to --space-3 in the shared tokens file because “4px felt closer.”

That token change ripples through every surface that referenced --space-3. The header looks fine. The settings page quietly compresses. Nobody asked for a design-system RFC.

I’ve started freezing token files by default for agent UI work. The agent may consume tokens. It may edit component files on an allowlist. It may not rewrite the shared scale unless the prompt explicitly opens that door.

What “freeze” means in practice

Three layers, boring on purpose:

  1. Default deny — token / theme modules are read-only for agent sessions
  2. Allowlist — only named component paths may change
  3. Explicit unlock — a human prompt (or a separate PR) is required to touch tokens

Example constraints block:

UI change only. Read-only paths (do not modify):
- src/styles/tokens.css
- src/styles/theme/*.css
- tailwind.config.* / @theme blocks that define the shared scale
- packages/design-tokens/**

Allowlist (edit only these):
- src/features/checkout/CheckoutHeader.tsx
- src/features/checkout/CheckoutHeader.module.css

If the design cannot be achieved without a new token, stop and propose the token
change in plain language — do not edit token files in this PR.

The “stop and propose” line is the escape hatch. Agents that are blocked tend to invent one-off hexes or arbitrary Tailwind values. You want a written proposal, not a silent scale rewrite.

Why agents reach for tokens

Shared tokens look like the “right” abstraction. Models have seen countless posts that say “put spacing in the theme.” So when a one-off gap feels wrong, they “fix the system” instead of the component.

Sometimes a token change is correct — after an RFC, with screenshots, across breakpoints. That work deserves its own PR title and reviewers. Bundling it under “header polish” hides blast radius.

Review gates that catch thawing

In the PR template

## Token / theme files
- [ ] No changes under tokens / theme / design-tokens
- [ ] If a token change is required: link the RFC / design thread and keep it in a separate commit or PR

In CI (lightweight)

  • Fail (or warn loudly) when tokens.css / design-tokens change unless the PR label is tokens / design-system
  • Or require an OWNERS-style approval for those paths

In human review

Open the files changed list first. If a “small UI tweak” touches the scale, send it back before you debate the header padding.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • Edits to shared spacing / color / type scales inside a feature PR
  • Renaming or removing tokens “nobody uses” without a repo-wide grep receipt
  • Adding a new token and using it only once in the same PR without calling that out
  • “Temporary” hardcoded values in the token file to match a mock

Accept

  • Component-only diffs that reference existing tokens
  • A written proposal for a token change, deferred to a follow-up
  • A dedicated tokens PR with before/after on more than one surface
  • Documented allowlist escapes for legacy theme files you already planned to delete

Allowlist patterns that work

Keep the allowlist paths, not vibes:

  • Feature folder for the task (src/features/checkout/**)
  • The specific stories file if Storybook is in scope
  • Explicitly exclude **/tokens*, **/theme*, **/*.config.* that own the scale

Monorepo tip: allow apps/web/... but freeze packages/ui/tokens. Agents love “helpfully” normalizing the package everyone imports.

If you use Tailwind v4 @theme or a JS theme module, freeze those the same way you freeze CSS variables — the file format doesn’t change the blast radius.

Tiny habit

Next agent UI prompt, paste a freeze block: token paths read-only, component paths allowlisted, “propose don’t edit” if the scale is wrong. When the draft still touches tokens.css, don’t negotiate in the diff — restore the freeze and ask for a one-paragraph token proposal instead. Feature PRs should consume the system, not redefine it mid-flight.

title: My first posture nudge said almost nothing. 5 changes in 4 weeks
description:
The first nudge I built was an orange glow at the top of the screen. That was all. To find out why it showed, you had to point at it.

Poxture App is a Mac menu-bar app. It checks your posture through the camera and nudges you when a habit holds for a while, like leaning in close to the screen or propping your chin on your hand. In its first 4 weeks I changed that nudge 5 times. Each change below has the problem, the fix and the days it took.

1. The glow didn't say what was wrong

What went wrong: the glow said something was off. It didn't name the habit, and nothing on screen showed how to fix it.

Fix: a card under the glow names the habit and shows the fix. A live meter moves as you correct, so you can see when you're back in range.

Time: 9 days from the first version. It shipped in 0.9.0, on 21 October.

2. The camera light stayed on for hours

What went wrong: on 17 October I made the camera light steady, so it would stop blinking at each check. In daily use it then stayed on for hours. The people testing it read a steady light as a call still running, or as recording.

Fix: by default the camera now comes on for a moment at each check, once a minute. A setting keeps it always on, for people who prefer a steady light.

Time: 4 days after the change, 2 after the testers flagged it. Also in 0.9.0.

That light is the one thing anyone can check without reading my code.

3. There was no clear "fixed"

What went wrong: once you looked away from the card, the only sign was the glow going away. From the user's side, a nudge that just goes away looks like an app that stopped working.

Fix:

  1. 0.11.0 (1 November): the menu-bar figure turns green for a moment when you fix it.
  2. 0.11.6 (9 November): fix your posture while you're using the card, and the card turns green and stays until you're done. If you slip again, the card shows it.

Time: 2 releases, 8 days apart.

4. Closing a nudge didn't close it

What went wrong: in 0.11.0, the × closed the card. The glow stayed, and so did the camera, until you fixed your posture.

Fix: × or Esc now closes the glow too, and the camera goes back to a moment at each check. That habit stays quiet for 10 minutes by default.

Time: the same day. 0.11.0 and 0.11.1 both shipped on 1 November.

5. Some nudges were wrong, and saying so was hard

What went wrong: a camera can be wrong. Someone else walks into view, or it says you're looking down when you weren't. Until November you couldn't quiet just one habit for a while, and a wrong pick didn't keep that habit quiet.

Fix:

  1. 0.11.4 (4 November): Snooze on every card quiets one habit for 15 minutes, 1 hour or until tomorrow. Pick what a nudge got wrong, and that habit stays quiet until you change how you sit, move to another spot, or 15 minutes pass.
  2. 0.11.5 (5 November): every nudge card, monitor tip and setup's Try it step ends with "Think this is wrong? Tell Poxture App", with picks like "Someone else was in view".

Time: 2 releases on back-to-back days.

Under all of it: no pictures

Apple's Vision framework runs on the Mac, so reading posture doesn't need a picture sent anywhere.

Two things hold that line while I keep shipping:

  1. A test fails if any app code can turn a frame into an image or a video.
  2. Live view, the one place you see what the camera reads, draws a stick figure.

The camera question macOS asks on first launch says it in the app's own words: "Each frame is read on this Mac and dropped. No picture is ever sent, saved or shown."

The cost: I can't show you a before-and-after of my own posture from the app.

What I'd build in from the first version

  1. Make every nudge say what's wrong, how to fix it, and when it's fixed.
  2. Put "this is wrong" on the nudge itself, one click away.
  3. Treat the camera light as part of the design.
  4. When close doesn't fully close, fix it the same day.

The app is Poxture App. It needs an Apple Silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later. The first hour of checking each day is free for good, and for your first 14 days every feature works all day. To keep it on all day, $19 once for the first 50 supporters, then $29.

If you've built something that nudges people, how do you show them they've fixed it?

title: Building MailForge: a Self-Hosted Email Desk for Verification, Campaigns and a Unified Inbox
description:
Building MailForge: a Self-Hosted Email Desk for Verification, Campaigns and a Unified Inbox

Hosted email verifiers take your list and talk to recipient mail servers somewhere else. I wanted the list, the SMTP check and the replies to stay on a machine I run. That is what MailForge is for.

MailForge is a self-hosted email desk. You upload a CSV or spreadsheet, a Go verifier talks to the recipient server, valid rows can become a campaign from accounts you add, and answers come back to one inbox. MongoDB on that same machine stores the data. The public repo is MIT licensed. The package version on main is 1.4.2.

This article describes only what is in that repository — the README, setup guides and package.json. It is not a claim about production volume, clients or deliverability.

Why run the check yourself?

Mailbox verification works by talking to the recipient's mail server: syntax and MX first, then a live SMTP RCPT dialog when that path is available. If you use a hosted verifier, that conversation happens on their infrastructure, and the list leaves your machine.

MailForge keeps that work local. The default engine is truemail-go, which lives under backend/go/ in the repo. You can set VERIFIER_ENGINE=auto so the app falls back to Reacher when the Go verifier is down. The full Docker Compose file starts the web app and MongoDB together. The slimmer docker-compose.yml starts the optional Reacher verifier; the README tells you to use the full compose file when you want the app itself.

What you can do with it

The README lists the desk's jobs in one place:

  • Verify an address with syntax, MX, disposable and role checks, and a live SMTP RCPT dialog.
  • Run a bulk CSV or XLSX job, pause or resume it, and download rows before the job finishes.
  • Send a campaign through more than one account, with delays, warm-up fields, a suppression list and an optional unsubscribe link.
  • Start from templates shipped in the repo, including 10 freight subjects and 10 bodies, or draft copy when a Groq, OpenRouter or OpenAI key is set.
  • Read and reply from a unified IMAP inbox. Sign-in uses JWT. The UI includes a dark theme.
  • Check GET /api/health for version, database and verifier status, and GET /api/backup/export for a JSON download of your data.

Those health and backup endpoints matter if you treat this as a local desk rather than a throwaway script. Settings in the Windows setup guide also point at a "Download my data" path and an npm run mongo:backup script for moving a database to another PC.

Start it on your machine

The shortest path in the README is Docker:

docker compose -f docker-compose.full.yml up -d --build

Open http://localhost:5000 and register. That command starts MongoDB and the web app. The compose file points the app at that MongoDB service and sets INDUS_SKIP_LICENSE=1, so a local stack starts without a license file.

A Windows client install is documented separately in client.md. That path still expects an indus-license*.json file. The two modes are easy to mix up: Docker on a development machine can skip the license; a packaged client install does not.

From a source checkout, the README asks for Node.js 18 or newer and Go 1.22 or newer. Copy .env.example to .env, set JWT_SECRET and ENCRYPTION_KEY, then run npm install and INDUS_SKIP_LICENSE=1 npm start.

The Express app listens on port 5000 by default. If that port is already in use, the Windows setup guide says to set PORT=5001 in .env.

A slightly longer Windows setup

SETUP.md is a checklist for a fresh Windows PC. The required tools are Node.js 18+ LTS, Docker Desktop (for persistent data), Go 1.22+ (for the SMTP verifier) and Git. MongoDB Compass is optional if you want to browse mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/mailforge.

You can run npm run setup:new-pc after cloning. That script checks Node.js, Docker and Go, runs npm install and go mod tidy, copies .env.example to .env if the file is missing, pulls and starts MongoDB via Docker, and can build a MailForge.exe launcher when .NET Framework is present.

For production-like use, the same guide tells you to replace JWT_SECRET with a long random string (it describes a 64-character secret) and ENCRYPTION_KEY with a 32-character random string, and to set MONGO_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/mailforge.

If you send through Gmail, SETUP.md walks through Google app passwords: create an app password, then add the account under MailForge → Senders, or bulk-import a CSV with Email, AppPassword and Name columns. Keep those secrets out of the repo.

When Docker is running, Settings → Connection should show persistent storage. If you see an in-memory banner instead, the guide says to run npm run mongo:up and restart. Daily start options include Start-MailForge.bat, MailForge.exe, or npm run start:easy.

How the repo is laid out

Path What it is
server.js Express app on port 5000
public/ Browser UI
controllers/ and routes/ HTTP API
backend/go/ truemail-go SMTP verifier
tests/ node --test suite

CONTRIBUTING.md describes the fork, branch and test flow. Run npm test before a pull request. Bug and feature forms are in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/. Screenshots of the signed-in dashboard and the shipped templates live under docs/screenshots/.

Windows client installs are a different path

client.md is the guide meant to travel with a MailForge folder. In that mode the web app still opens at http://localhost:5000, but the database is an embedded MongoDB and Docker is not required. The client is expected to receive a folder named MailForge plus a license file whose name starts with indus-license and ends with .json.

Double-clicking Client-Install-MailForge.bat installs production Node packages, builds the local Go verifier executable, downloads an embedded MongoDB binary into tools/mongodb-binaries, stores app data in data/mongodb, and creates Desktop and Start Menu shortcuts. On startup, that build verifies the INDUS license online and can then tolerate short internet outages with a local license cache. If the app reports that no license file was found, the file belongs in the app folder or the data folder.

I mention this only because the Docker README path and the client path are both in the repo, and they do not use the same license rule.

What this article does not claim

The repo does not publish inbox placement rates, list sizes from real campaigns, or client names. It ships freight-themed starter templates; that is a starting point for copy, not a statement about any freight company. SMTP still depends on outbound network access. If you cannot reach recipient servers, a live mailbox dialog will not complete.

Use the tool on lists you are allowed to check, and keep JWT and encryption secrets private.

FAQ

What is MailForge?

MailForge is a self-hosted email desk. It verifies lists, can send campaigns from accounts you add, and reads replies in a unified IMAP inbox. The source is github.com/mafzalkalwardev/mailforge.

Who built it?

Muhammad Afzal Kalwar (@mafzalkalwardev).

Which checks run on each address?

Syntax, MX, disposable and role checks, plus a live SMTP RCPT dialog. truemail-go is the default engine.

Can I use a second verifier?

Yes. Set VERIFIER_ENGINE=auto to fall back to Reacher when the Go verifier is down. The default docker-compose.yml starts the optional Reacher service; use docker-compose.full.yml to start the app and MongoDB.

Does a local Docker install need a license file?

The full compose file sets INDUS_SKIP_LICENSE=1, so that local stack starts without a license file. A Windows client install still expects indus-license*.json.

What do I need to run it from source?

Node.js 18 or newer, Go 1.22 or newer, a .env file with JWT_SECRET and ENCRYPTION_KEY, then npm install and INDUS_SKIP_LICENSE=1 npm start. Docker is the documented path for persistent MongoDB.

Where is the data stored?

MongoDB on the machine you run. The full compose file starts that database next to the app. There is a JSON export at GET /api/backup/export, and the Windows guide also documents npm run mongo:backup.

What is the license?

MIT. See LICENSE in the repository.

Where can I read more?

The README covers features and the HTTP API. SETUP.md is the new-PC checklist. client.md is the Windows client install guide.

Source: https://github.com/mafzalkalwardev/mailforge

title: A Cue Sheet for Reviewing Fictional Voice Assets
description:
The playable file is not the publishable unit

Voice interfaces make it easy to test a script, but a shareable clip includes more than audio. A viewer meets a title, first frame, caption, visible action, and line at once. If those pieces do not agree, a recognisable candidate label can appear to provide context that is not actually present.

This is a design proposal based on public UI observation, not a description of VideoAI's internal architecture or review process. The aim is to make one editorial choice explicit: what does the line cue in the scene?

Represent the cue 

type CueRole = 'warning' | 'response' | 'reveal' | 'tag';
type State = 'draft' | 'previewed' | 'needs-context' | 'ready' | 'blocked';

type VoiceCue = {
  candidateLabel: string;
  scriptVersion: string;
  visibleObject: string;
  cueRole: CueRole;
  firstFrameText: string;
  disclosure: string;
  state: State;
};

The distinction matters because changing volume does not turn a warning into a response. A cue role asks the editor to describe the relationship between a line and a visible action.

Do not let labels fill in authorship

Withered Bonnie AI Voice may be a candidate for an original, fictional warning cue, but the candidate field should not generate an official-looking title or imply performer involvement. A scene card needs a real object and a short purpose: “a toy light fails; the line makes the retry feel suspenseful.” That is more reviewable than “use a scary voice.”

For Wukong AI Voice, the public page displays script input, preview, delivery adjustments, and MP3 output. A neutral UI test is to present three cards with the same original line: before the action, on the action, and after the action. The reviewer chooses the card whose cue is legible, not the supposedly most authentic candidate.

Tie approval to the whole card

Yoda AI Voice can be a candidate for a fictional closing tag, but a new caption or first frame can change the public meaning of the asset. Approval should attach to the whole card.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> draft
  draft --> previewed: original script compared by cue role
  previewed --> needs_context: object, caption, or disclosure absent
  needs_context --> ready: full card reviewed
  ready --> draft: script, title, or first frame changes
  ready --> blocked: official-looking or misleading claim

Test the compact share state

Use a muted mobile view with the description collapsed. Can a viewer identify the visible action? Does the title make clear that the clip is synthetic and fictional when that is the context? Does the phrase avoid source-style quotation, official announcement framing, and claims of endorsement?

The automated part is small: prevent empty disclosure fields, mark a review stale after card changes, and require a cue role. Human review remains necessary because a system cannot reliably infer what an image, title, and voice together imply.

Acceptance checklist

  1. A script or first-frame change returns the card to draft.
  2. A cue role is stated in plain language.
  3. The muted first frame shows a comprehensible object or action.
  4. The copy avoids claims of affiliation, actor participation, or source authenticity.
  5. Rights and platform checks for music, images, names, and scripts are handled separately.

A cue sheet does not automate taste. It gives collaborators a shared object to discuss: not “does this voice feel right?” but “does this line make the intended action easier to understand?”

Keep a cue decision with the export

The review can store an intentionally small explanation. A future editor does not need a score such as 0.82. They need to see “tag: the line follows the failed fold,” “warning: the lamp appears before the sound,” or “response: the line overlaps the button press.”

type CueDecision = {
  reviewKey: string;
  selectedRole: CueRole;
  rationale: string;
};

const needsReview = (cue: VoiceCue, prior?: CueDecision) =>
  !prior || prior.reviewKey !== JSON.stringify({
    scriptVersion: cue.scriptVersion,
    visibleObject: cue.visibleObject,
    cueRole: cue.cueRole,
    firstFrameText: cue.firstFrameText,
    disclosure: cue.disclosure
  });

The code is illustrative rather than a claim about any product. Its value is conceptual: a review follows the public card, not an audio blob with a memorable filename.

Provide rejection paths, not a single failure

An editor may like a candidate but reject the surrounding card. They may request a clearer object, ask that the line become a tag rather than a warning, or ask for a visible disclosure. A UI that only exposes “approve” and “reject” loses that information.

Useful next states can be concrete: needs-object, move-cue, rewrite-script, or needs-disclosure. Each points to a normal creative revision instead of treating context as a late compliance interruption. This also helps a creator understand that the problem is not always the delivery.

Accessibility is an editorial signal

Muted viewing is not a corner case. Captions and objects let a person follow a clip in a quiet room, on a small screen, or with audio unavailable. Testing that version often exposes the exact place where the script is asking sound to replace a missing visual fact.

The limits remain important. A cue sheet cannot determine rights, guarantee audience interpretation, or replace checks of a platform's policies. It can preserve the reason a creative choice was made, which is the part a collaboration system can responsibly make easier.

Scope the contract carefully

The cue record should remain narrow. It says what the current card is meant to show, not what every future derivative may claim. When a clip is trimmed, re-titled, or paired with a new image, the object and cue role must be reviewed again. This is the difference between a useful editorial annotation and a false permanent approval.

In practice, that scope helps teams move faster. A creator can reuse a script candidate while deliberately rebuilding the context for a different platform. The shared record provides a starting point, but the new card earns its own review.

title: Self-hosted as one Go binary: embed.FS, SQLite WAL and the trade-offs
description:
Monitoring stacks have a complexity problem. Prometheus needs cAdvisor, Grafana, node_exporter and Alertmanager. Datadog needs an agent plus a SaaS account. Even "simple" tools like Uptime Kuma need Node.js and a separate database.

That is no longer the only option. Self-hosted tools have matured to the point where a single Go binary can replace a five-container stack. This post looks at what that means in practice, using Maintenant as the example, and at what you give up.

What "single binary" means

A single-binary tool ships as one executable file. No runtime dependencies, no external database, no separate frontend server. The engine, the web interface, the database and the alert system are compiled into one artifact.

In Docker terms: one image, one container, one volume.

services:
  maintenant:
    image: ghcr.io/kolapsis/maintenant:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
      - /proc:/host/proc:ro
      - maintenant-data:/data
    environment:
      MAINTENANT_ADDR: "0.0.0.0:8080"
      MAINTENANT_DB: "/data/maintenant.db"
    restart: unless-stopped
volumes:
  maintenant-data:

No Postgres container, no Redis container, no nginx in front of it, no separate worker processes.

Three trends that made it practical

  1. Go's embed.FS makes it trivial to ship a full web UI inside a single binary. No separate frontend server needed.
  2. SQLite's WAL mode shows that an embedded database handles real-time workloads (continuous writes plus a live dashboard reading) without PostgreSQL or InfluxDB.
  3. Docker's dominance in self-hosting means a tool can assume a container runtime and skip the "works on bare metal, VMs, containers and Kubernetes" matrix.

The Go advantage

Most single-binary tools are written in Go, for good reasons:

  • Static compilation: no runtime dependencies, no shared libraries.
  • Low memory footprint: goroutines are cheap, garbage collection is efficient.
  • Cross-compilation: one build produces linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 binaries.
  • Embedded assets: embed.FS ships the entire frontend inside the binary.

Maintenant embeds its web UI, its SQLite engine and all its monitoring logic in a single ~20 MB binary, and idles at under 30 MB of RAM.

Fewer failure modes

Every additional component is a potential failure point. Prometheus can crash independently of Grafana. An Alertmanager config can desync from its Prometheus rules. cAdvisor can run out of memory while Grafana keeps showing stale data.

With a single binary, either the whole thing works or it does not. There is no partial failure state to debug.

Simpler backups and updates

There is one SQLite file in one volume. Back it up the way you back up your other volumes: no pg_dump, no TSDB snapshots, no dashboard exports. Updating is docker compose pull && docker compose up -d: one image, one container, no version compatibility matrix between Prometheus, Grafana and their plugins.

The trade-offs

Single-binary tools are opinionated by nature. You trade flexibility for simplicity:

  • No distributed tracing. If you need OpenTelemetry-level observability, this is the wrong class of tool.
  • No infinite retention. Embedded SQLite is not a time-series database tuned for years of data.
  • No custom dashboards and no query language. The views are pre-built; there is no PromQL equivalent and no plugin ecosystem.
  • Scaling limits. One central server with lightweight agents on remote hosts, not a distributed system. Multi-region aggregation remains the domain of distributed stacks.
  • One host to lose. If the machine running it dies, monitoring dies with it. Run it somewhere separate from the infrastructure it watches.

If you manage hundreds of servers across several cloud providers and need ad-hoc queries, a distributed stack is the right tool. For a handful of servers running Docker Compose or single-node Kubernetes, one binary is often enough.

Originally published on maintenant.dev.

Maintenant is an open-source, self-hosted monitoring tool for Docker and Kubernetes: containers, endpoints, cron heartbeats, TLS certificates and alerts, in one container that discovers your stack on its own. Install it in a minute: https://maintenant.dev

title: Article: LLM Reliability Layers Under Test: Accuracy, Yield, and the Limits of Verification
description:
Verification layers sort outputs by trust rather than fixing errors. In a benchmark of six reliability layers, voting and self-correction failed to recover accuracy - they only withheld doubtful records. Production systems gain more reliability by replacing generation with deterministic lookups, tracking yield over raw accuracy, and resolving extraction bottlenecks before stacking checks.

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.16

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.16.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Performance tile on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard executed redundant database queries during auto-refreshes.

  • Updated advanced reporting filter prompts so they behave consistently across all dashboards and display the complete list of configured values:

    • List-backed filters now open directly into a searchable list on the first click.

    • Dropdowns that previously returned empty or partial lists now display the full configured list, including Agent Name, Agent Email, Agent Custom ID, Agent Teams, Location, Language, Answered By, and Projection Result.

    • Disposition Codes and Disposition List filters now display the codes configured for your instance.

    • Agent Teams and Team Name filters now match agents in any of their assigned teams.

    • Configuration renames (Queue Group, Queue, Agent Team, Disposition Code, Location, Role, and Skill) now appear in filter dropdowns within 30 minutes instead of up to six hours.

    • The Projecting filter on the live Queued dashboards is now clearable, so you can reset it to show all queued interactions, and offers only Yes.

    • Fields without a predefined list of values (such as consumer phone numbers and ID fields) now display a plain text box with an operator so you can type a value directly.

    • Call Status and Deflection Type filters now display values that existed in the data but were previously missing from the list.

    • Channel now reports a value on the live Voice and Chat dashboards, and on historical Chat dashboards, for interaction types that previously appeared blank (including internal, API-initiated, campaign, UCaaS, callback, and extension calls).

    • On the Agent Audit dashboard, the Change Details table now displays its timestamp column and sorts it correctly.

    • Consumer phone number filters now accept a single value instead of multiple values. Saved filters or links that pass multiple numbers apply only one.

    • On the Missed Interactions dashboards, the Activity Status column and filter are renamed to Projection Result.

    • Actor values describing who answered, ended, or disconnected an interaction are now standardized as Human Agent, Virtual Agent, End User, and System. Saved filters, Looks, and schedules that used the previous wording must be reselected.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Change

For GKE Standard CPU node pools, GKE can now upgrade nodes by updating the existing Compute Engine VM in place, instead of deleting the VM and creating a new one. Because the node keeps its underlying VM, it also keeps its compute capacity during the upgrade. This lowers the risk that a node upgrade fails or stalls because resources aren't available.

To enable this type of upgrade, use surge upgrades with the maxUnavailable field set to a value greater than 0. For more details about when GKE reuses the same Compute Engine instance, including exceptions, see maxUnavailable: GKE makes an existing node unavailable to recreate it.

This change applies to all GKE versions. To opt out, contact Cloud Customer Care.

The stable model for answer generation is updated to gemini-3.5-flash/answer_gen/v1 from gemini-2.5-flash/answer_gen/v1.

For more information, see Answer generation model versions and lifecycle.

Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.

Security bulletin published: GCP-2026-072

BigQuery

Feature

Conversation logging for Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now generally available (GA). You can log data agent conversations to a BigQuery table in the agent's project. For more information, see Conversation logging overview and Configure settings.

Feature

Python user-defined functions now support volume mounts, which let you access dependency files from Cloud Storage directly from your Python UDF code. This feature is in Preview.

You can use the Capacity Planner MCP tools to query historical resource usage, usage forecasts, and reservation data across your projects, folders, and organizations.

For more information, see the Capacity Planner MCP reference and Google Cloud MCP servers overview.

Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

You can now create heterogeneous conversion workspaces by importing database schema metadata files from a Cloud Storage bucket without requiring direct network connectivity between Database Migration Service and your source database during the schema conversion phase. For more information, see the following pages:

  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for Oracle to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
  • Create a conversion workspace for SQL Server to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Compute Engine

Security

A vulnerability (CVE-2026-85299) about incorrect authorization in Compute Engine was discovered and has been addressed. For more information, see the GCP-2026-073 security bulletin.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Control user intent matching for semantic governance policies

You can now turn user intent matching on or off for semantic governance policies by setting the sgpUserIntentMatching key on the authorization extension metadata. User intent matching is on by default; set the key to DISABLED to turn it off. Turning it off reduces protection against indirect prompt injection. When the key is set, policy evaluation logs report the mode each evaluation used in the sgpUserIntentMatchingMode field.

For more information, see Control user intent matching.

Feature

Cloud Storage output support for Gemini image generation models

Direct Cloud Storage output persistence is generally available (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1), Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (gemini-3.1-flash-image), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Gemini 3 Pro Image (gemini-3-pro-image). You can set outputConfig.outputUriPrefix and generationConfig.responseFormat[].image.delivery to "URI" in generateContent and streamGenerateContent requests to write generated and edited images directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and receive the object URI in fileData.fileUri instead of inline bytes. For more information, see Save generated images to Cloud Storage.

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are Generally Available (GA)

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are available in General Availability (GA) in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions. The models support structured speaker and style metadata, inline vocal tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and streaming. Voice design and voice replication capabilities remain available in Preview.

For more information, see Generate speech with Gemini TTS.

Feature

Semantic governance policies support more model providers

Semantic governance policies now evaluate tool calls from agents that use models from providers other than Gemini. The policy engine reads each provider's request and response format, so the same policies apply whichever model your agent uses. Supported APIs include the Gemini Developer API and Gemini models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Anthropic Messages API, Claude models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, the Mistral AI API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (including Llama models), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM. Streamed model responses aren't supported.

To govern these providers, update the when condition of your authorization policy to match each provider's request path. The updated condition also matches requests that include a query string.

For more information, see Supported model providers and Connect the policy engine to Agent Gateway.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Support for Looker (Google Cloud core) in Data lineage is now generally available. This support includes lineage views for LookML views and Explores, Looker dashboards, dashboard elements, Looks, LookML dashboards, and Conversational Analytics agents. You can control data lineage ingestion at the organization, folder, and project levels. You can also visualize the end-to-end flow of your data from BigQuery sources through the Looker semantic layer to downstream assets.

For more information, see Track data lineage with Knowledge Catalog, About data lineage, and About data lineage ingestion control.

Looker

Feature

Looker (Google Cloud core) data lineage is now generally available (GA). The GA launch adds end-to-end visibility for LookML dashboards and Conversational Analytics agents. Lineage enablement is now managed independently through the Data Lineage API and service-level ingestion controls, which decouples it from Looker's internal Knowledge Catalog metadata settings. For more information, see About data lineage.

Feature

The Looker-managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) server is now generally available (GA), allowing AI agents to securely interact with business data and LookML models without the need for additional middleware. This launch is supported by a new Manage OAuth Clients admin page, which provides a centralized interface for governing identity-based access for AI agents and other external applications. Administrators can now quickly enable pre-configured integrations from the Application Library or register custom OAuth clients with specific redirect URIs and group-based access controls.

Model Armor

Feature

Model Armor enforces the constraints/modelarmor.managed.requireTemplateDataResidencyCompliance managed Organization Policy Service constraint by default. When you create or update a template, this constraint prevents you from setting data_residency_compliant to false or clearing the Enforce data residency option unless an Organization Policy Administrator disables the constraint. This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Disable the organization policy constraint for data residency.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

The Oracle Database@Google Cloud remote MCP server is generally available (GA) and adds tools to create and manage Database Connections and run SQL statements with database_connection_executesql. It lets you interact easily with Oracle Database@Google Cloud resources from LLMs, AI applications, and AI-enabled development platforms.

For more information, see Use the Oracle Database@Google Cloud remote MCP server.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.3

On October 29, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.3.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.3.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: Do not use Apigee hybrid v1.17.2 due to a potential regression in apigee-connect-agent (see known issue 578314600). Use v1.17.3 instead.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
572025634 Fixed an issue where responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow returned a corrupted body; compressed text/event-stream responses now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact.
571378258 The apigee-redis container now uses the Valkey engine (version 8.1.10). The RESP2 wire protocol and redis-server and redis-cli binary names are unchanged.
568860869 Fixed an issue in the RegularExpressionProtection policy where patterns starting and ending with .* whose middle section contained regular expression syntax were matched as literal text instead of regular expressions.
560272924 Apigee hybrid now supports continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Fixed an issue where Model Armor policies did not honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: when set, Model Armor callouts now bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic, while streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
554114419 Fixed an issue where an AssignMessage, HTTPModifier, or RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow could not set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers and failed with an invalid-header error.
549779897 Apigee analytics now reports the Model Armor template, verdict, and matched filters for each request on both the prompt and model-response directions.
546141116 The SemanticCacheLookup policy now reports the cache key and cache name to analytics in the ai_semantic_cache_key and ai_semantic_cache_name fields.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
502231886 Fixed an issue where the SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse policies failed to extract content using default source templates when the <Source> element was omitted and <IgnoreUnresolvedVariables> was set to false.
492041991 Fixed an issue where VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables from unmatched LLM operations; they are now set only from the LLM operations that matched the request.
449228485 Fixed an issue where podDisruptionBudget overrides configured in the Helm charts were dropped by the Kubernetes API server.

Cloud Profiler

Security

The Cloud Profiler Java agent is updated with a new Certification Authority (CA) certificate bundle, in response to security bulletin GCP-2026-071. Google Cloud infrastructure and the Cloud Profiler backend service are not affected.

If you use the Cloud Profiler Java agent, take one of the following actions:

  • Upgrade the Java agent to cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00 (GitHub release v0.5.0) or later, and then rebuild and redeploy your applications. Download the updated archive, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00.tar.gz, or, for musl-based Alpine Linux containers, https://storage.googleapis.com/cloud-profiler/java/cloud-profiler-java-agent_20261026_RC00_alpine.tar.gz.
  • If you can't immediately upgrade or rebuild, update your host or container operating system's CA certificate store as described in GCP-2026-071, and then set the GRPC_DEFAULT_SSL_ROOTS_FILE_PATH environment variable to point to the updated PEM bundle.

For more information about installing the agent, see Profiling Java applications.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow has added the following features to tune horizontal autoscaling for Streaming Engine jobs:

  • Latency tiers: You can configure the backlog threshold by choosing a latency tier (low_latency, medium_latency, or high_latency), allowing you to configure the autoscaler's sensitivity to backlog duration and balance latency requirements with resource costs. For more information, see Set the latency tier.
  • Autoscaling schedules: You can configure recurring autoscaling schedules to automatically apply parameter overrides—such as minimum and maximum workers, worker utilization hints, or latency tiers—during specific time windows. For more information, see Schedule autoscaling changes.

You can configure these features when you create a job or update them while the job is running.

Dialogflow

Security

Dialogflow ES: The Dialogflow ES LINE integration validates the X-Line-Signature HTTP header on incoming webhook requests using your LINE channel secret and rejects requests with missing, duplicate, or invalid signatures with an HTTP 400 Bad Request error. Make sure your configured channel secret matches your LINE Messaging API channel and that any intermediate proxy forwards the X-Line-Signature header and raw request body unmodified.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE is generally available (GA) on clusters running GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. You can collect OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) traces, metrics, and logs from your workloads with a Google-managed collector instead of a self-managed OpenTelemetry Collector deployment:

  • Configure otlp_grpc in the Instrumentation custom resource (GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later), or send telemetry directly to the in-cluster collector's gRPC endpoint on port 4317 in addition to HTTP on port 4318.
  • The managed collector routes logs alongside traces and metrics through the Cloud Telemetry API (telemetry.googleapis.com), with improved per-signal queueing and autoscaling for high-throughput clusters. (Logs ingested through telemetry.googleapis.com default to the otlp log name instead of gke-managed-otel-collector.)
  • Multimodal prompts and responses collection for LangGraph ReAct and Agent Development Kit (ADK) agents, the --managed-otel-scope flag in the gcloud CLI (version 576.0.0 or later), and managed_opentelemetry_config in terraform-provider-google (v8.8.0 or later) are generally available.

To use the GA collector and features, upgrade clusters from earlier Preview versions to 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. For architecture details and setup instructions, see Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE and Deploy Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE.

Identity and Access Management

Feature

The Admin (roles/admin), Writer (roles/writer), and Reader (roles/reader) basic roles are generally available (GA). For more information, see Basic roles.

The legacy basic roles—Owner (roles/owner), Editor (roles/editor), and Viewer (roles/viewer)—are still available for use and are being actively maintained. However, if you need to grant a basic role, we recommend granting the Admin, Writer, or Reader role instead of a legacy basic role. This is because the newer roles support additional features, such as the use of IAM Conditions.

Looker

Announcement

Beginning October 26, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances running Looker 26.20.

Feature

The ability to generate a summary of an Explore by using Gemini assistance is now generally available.

Feature

The bullet chart visualization type is now generally available. Bullet charts let you evaluate a single primary metric's performance as one or more bars and mark your goal with a target line. You can plot both against shaded background ranges that represent performance thresholds, such as "poor," "satisfactory," and "good." For more information, see Bullet chart options.

Feature

Looker now includes network diagnostics to help you troubleshoot database connectivity issues. When a database connection test fails, Looker automatically tests DNS resolution and TCP connectivity for the connection's endpoints and appends the results to the error message. To test network reachability to any hostname and port without creating a connection, Looker administrators can click Test Reachability on the Connections page.

Note: This item was added on October 30, 2026.

Feature

The Table Row Grouping feature and the Grouping menu options are now generally available. The Grouping menu options let you display and customize the appearance of table chart data hierarchically in groups.

Feature

The Visualization Assistant is now generally available.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now supports hub-and-spoke projects. If your Looker project uses local project imports to import files from an upstream hub project on the same Looker instance, then you can use CI to automatically test downstream spoke projects. Testing runs whenever a pull request is opened or updated on the hub project. This capability lets you catch breaking changes in downstream Explores, content, or data tests before upstream LookML changes are merged. For more information, see Creating a Continuous Integration suite.

Feature

Two new legacy features, Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience and Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience for Embed, are now available for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances. These features let administrators configure Explores and merged queries to open in the classic experience by default across an instance or in embedded contexts. For more information, see Legacy feature schedule.

Feature

Looker now includes a new histogram chart visualization option. A histogram chart is a graphical representation of the data distribution of an attribute. A histogram creates intervals (bins) and counts how many values fall into each bin.

Feature

The KPI (Single Value) chart type is now generally available. The KPI (Single Value) chart type replaces the Single Value chart type.

Feature

The new Looker Explore and merge query experience is now generally available and is the default interface for Explores and for joining data from multiple queries.

Feature

When you enter values in a string filter on dashboards, Looks, or Explores, clicking Done or clicking outside the input field no longer creates a filter chip from uncommitted text. To create a filter chip, press Enter, enter a comma (,), or paste values into the input field.

Feature

The new Dashboard Tile Groups preview feature lets you organize related tiles into collapsible containers for improved visual organization. You can move, duplicate, or delete multiple tiles as a single unit on dashboards that use the newspaper layout. This update also adds LookML support for programmatically managing tile groups.

Feature

Now available in preview, the Release Changelog gives Looker users and administrators real-time visibility into the features, behavioral changes, and bug fixes that are available for their instance.

Feature

The Legacy features page is now available in the Admin panel for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances. Legacy features that appear on the Looker (Google Cloud core) Legacy features page might differ from those that are available on Looker (original) instances. For more information, see Looker (Google Cloud core) admin settings.

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.22
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.22

The latest version in the Regular channel remains Looker 26.18.

Breaking

Some elements of the Conversational Analytics System Activity dashboard have been renamed. The dashboard layout and capabilities remain the same.

On the Token usage tab, the Conversational Analytics API value in the Feature column and the Feature Name filter has been renamed to Looker API. This value refers to the Conversational Analytics methods for the Looker API.

This rename might cause a breaking change if you built custom dashboards that reference the former Feature column or Feature Name filter value.

Change

The Use Legacy Connections Page legacy feature and the legacy database connection workflow have been removed. All database connections now use the connection workflow that is described in Connecting Looker to your database.

Feature

Model Armor is available in Brazil (southamerica-east1). This region provides data residency compliance for at-rest, in-use, and in-transit data with limited feature support.

The southamerica-east1 region supports the following filters:

title: Updates to Hobby and Pro Terms of Service
description:
We are updating the Terms of Service for Hobby and Pro customers, effective October 19, 2026. The updates clarify some existing Vercel practices, expand terms on topics such as managed accounts and credits, and reflect applicable legal requirements, including certain cancellation and service-change rights for eligible consumers in the UK and EU.

Credits and billing

A new section sets out how credits work: plan-included credits expire at the end of the subscription term and purchased credits expire one year after purchase unless stated otherwise in the relevant credit purchase terms. Credits can only be used to pay Vercel fees, have no cash value, and are nontransferable. Credits are generally nonrefundable, but unused purchased credits are refunded if Vercel terminates your account without cause.

The Terms also clarify that credit purchases are billed in advance, subscriptions auto-renew unless you turn off renewal, and third-party pass-through rates may change when provider rates change. ⁠⁠

Managed accounts

The Terms now have a dedicated section for accounts that use a company email domain (e.g., work email), clarifying that the company can manage only the Projects you create inside its Team. We also clarified that if your company wishes to manage your account using your company work email, Vercel will now notify you first and give you a reasonable amount of time to move your personal content to an account with a different email address

Renewal and cancellation

You can turn off auto-renewal and cancel or downgrade through account settings or Support. Cancellation or downgrade generally takes effect at the start of the next renewal period. The Terms also explain statutory withdrawal and refund rights for eligible consumers.

Service changes

Eligible consumers in the UK and EU may cancel the affected subscription free of charge if a change has more than a minor negative impact on their access to or use of the Services. They have 30 days from notice or the change, whichever is later, and may receive a prorated refund of prepaid amounts for the remaining period.

Other updates

The service-specific provisions have been moved to a dedicated Service Terms page. The Terms also clarify sanctions-related obligations, including that use of the Services must not be in connection with or for the benefit of a sanctioned person under applicable laws.

Read the full Terms of Service and Service Terms for details.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.
