title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

title: GPT-6.1 Terra now available on AI Gateway

It suits high-volume work in documents and desktop apps, such as filling out forms, interpreting technical drawings, or entering invoice details into accounting software. The model accepts text and images and returns text, with a context window of more than 1M tokens. It supports configurable reasoning effort, structured outputs, tool calling, and implicit and explicit prompt caching. For latency-sensitive work, fast mode is available as openai/gpt-6.1-terra-fast.

title: Vercel Sandbox commands now support stdin
description:
Vercel Sandbox now lets you send input to running commands through standard input (stdin). Use it to exchange messages with stdio MCP servers such as agent-browser, or send data to other command-line programs while they run.

In the TypeScript SDK, set stdin: true and detached: true in runCommand(). Use writeStdin() to send input and closeStdin() when you’re done:

You can also set stdin to a Node.js readable stream, such as process.stdin. The SDK forwards the stream’s data and closes the command’s standard input when the stream ends.

In the Python SDK, set stdin=subprocess.PIPE and send input with server.stdin.send(). Call communicate() to close stdin, collect remaining output, and wait for the process to exit:

For commands that receive all their input at once, you can pass input directly to Python’s run_process().

Read the Sandbox documentation to get started.

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them.

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

  • Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
description:
Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’s security policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort.

At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all.

With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set.

What's next

Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request.

Get started

Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

To get started, enable Security Review in Vercel Agent Settings. You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read the Changelog entry and the Security Review documentation.

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate, with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026. Fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the rate above.

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
description:
Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard.

What triggers a review

Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together.

What a finding includes

Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating.

Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard.

Fixes and resolution

Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it.

To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON.

Security policies

Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings.

Limitations

Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them.

Pricing

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate: provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes.

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
description:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.4.0 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.

title: Ampersand from Humans& now available on AI Gateway
description:
Ampersand from Humans& is now available on AI Gateway for free through November 13, 2026.

Ampersand is a model for group conversations. Humans& built Ampersand on Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3 and trained it with reinforcement learning in simulated group conversations that run for up to months of simulated time. Most chat models are built for one person asking a question and the model answering it. Ampersand is trained to take part in a conversation between several people. It reads every message, including the ones not addressed to it, and after each one it decides whether to reply or stay quiet.

It is designed to understand individual and shared goals, help people work through disagreements, and recognize when a contribution would be useful. That can mean asking a clarifying question, sharing relevant context, or waiting while people respond to one another.

For example:

Sam: Heads up, I'm out Friday, driving to my sister's. Alex: Have a good trip! Maya: Let's do the launch rehearsal Friday at 10 with all three of us. Ampersand: Quick flag, Maya: Sam said he's out Friday driving to his sister's, so a Friday 10am rehearsal with all three probably won't work. Might be worth picking a different time so everyone can make it.

Your application exposes these actions as caller-defined function tools. send_message delivers a contribution, while pass leaves the conversation quiet until the next human message. Your application executes both tools and records their results.

title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
description:

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

Stream cards as the model writes

streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card.

Validate specs and enforce platform limits

toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec.

Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead.

title: TikTok watermarked vs clean: what the API options really mean
description:
When I wired TikTok downloads into ramrom.io, I assumed there would be one video file per link. Paste the link, get the MP4, done. The provider's API had other ideas. It offered two versions of the same video: one with a watermark, one without. Choosing between them turned out to be one of the more interesting decisions in the whole downloader, because the two files are not made the same way at all.

What the watermark actually is

A TikTok watermark is not a picture stamped over the video after the fact. It is baked into the video file TikTok serves to the web player. When you watch a TikTok in a browser, the file you are watching already has the username and the logo bouncing around the frame. That is the "watermarked" version, and it is the easy one to fetch: it is the same file the public player uses, served from TikTok's own CDN.

The "clean" version, the one without the watermark, is a different file entirely. When the TikTok app saves a video to your camera roll, it requests a separate, watermark-free render from TikTok's servers. The provider APIs that offer a no-watermark option are really asking for that app-style render, or for the raw file the creator uploaded before TikTok added the overlay. Either way, it is a second file, fetched through a different route.

Why the clean one fails more often

This explains something I kept seeing in my logs. Watermarked links resolved quickly and reliably. Clean links failed far more often, and when they failed they failed in confusing ways: sometimes a 403, sometimes a short redirect chain that ended at an error page, sometimes a file that played fine but had no audio track. The reason is simple once you know the two files are different. The watermarked file is the public one, meant to be shared, so TikTok's servers hand it out freely. The clean file is closer to the original upload, and TikTok guards it more carefully. It is the one that gets rate limited first, the one whose URL expires sooner, and the one that disappears when a creator changes their privacy settings.

There is also a quirk I did not expect. Some providers return a "clean" file that is really the watermarked file with the watermarked parts cropped out, or a lower-quality re-encode. The resolution looks the same in the file name, but the video is softer and the edges are cut. So "no watermark" does not always mean "the original file". It sometimes means "the original file, processed again, and not necessarily well".

What I do on my site

I offer both options and I label them honestly. The watermarked version is the default because it works more often and it is the version TikTok itself puts in front of viewers. The clean version is there for people who want it, but the button says what it is, and when the clean endpoint fails I say so plainly instead of silently falling back to the watermarked file. That fallback would be dishonest: the visitor asked for one thing and got another.

Behind the scenes, my resolve step asks the provider for both URLs at once, when the provider supports it. If the clean URL comes back empty, or the file it points to is not a real video, I show the watermarked option only, with a short note. The check is cheap: I send a HEAD request and look at the content type and the file size before I ever show a download button. A video file that is 40KB is not a video. It is an error page with a .mp4 name.

One last thing worth saying plainly. Downloading someone else's TikTok without the watermark removes the credit to the creator. The watermark is how the creator's name travels with the video. I am not going to lecture visitors, but a downloader should be honest about what the two options are, and not pretend the clean version is just the same file minus a logo. It is a different file, fetched a different way, with different failure modes. Once you know that, the API options stop looking like a simple toggle and start looking like what they are: two separate downloads, each with its own trade-offs.

title: 30 Years of COBOL and Banking Systems: What Do You Know That Modern Developers Have Forgotten?
description:
Have you spent decades working with COBOL in financial systems? Then you probably know things that many modern developers don't even realize they need to know.

I want to interview you!

I've opened a GitHub discussion with 18 questions for professionals who have worked with COBOL, mainframes, and banking systems. I want to hear your stories about production failures, batch processing, business rules hidden deep in the code, and the decisions that kept financial systems running for decades.

You don't need to answer all 18 questions. Pick just one, share a story, or tell us something you learned along the way. Even a small piece of your experience could help preserve knowledge that future generations of developers might otherwise lose.

This initiative is part of FinKore, an open-source project focused on documenting and preserving fundamental financial rules for future generations of developers.

I don't want to know whether COBOL is better than Java. I want to discover what you've learned over 30 years that we're still trying to reinvent today.

Would you be willing to share your experience in this open interview?

🔗 https://github.com/willgittens/FinKore/discussions/42

title: Two AI Agents Reviewed the Same PR. Was That Actually Independent?
description:
Imagine this workflow:

  • Agent A writes a patch and opens a pull request.
  • Agent B reviews it and says "LGTM."
  • CI turns green.

Two agents, one approved PR. Sounds like independent review.

Now change a few details.

Both agents can modify the same workspace. The reviewer relies on the author's generated summary. The tested commit might not be the commit that ultimately gets merged.

Do we still have independent verification, or just two agreeing opinions?

I'm increasingly interested in the boundaries that make a review independent, rather than simply the number of models involved.

For example, a reviewer could use a read-only checkout pinned to an exact commit, inspect the raw diff, and verify which tests actually executed. That gives us evidence the implementing agent cannot simply rewrite.

But how much separation is enough?

I'd love to hear how others handle this:

  1. Is a second AI model with a separate prompt sufficient for low-risk changes?
  2. Do you require separate workspaces, credentials, and immutable artifacts?
  3. What evidence makes you trust an AI-generated review?
  4. Where do you still require human approval?

Share your actual setup, a failure case, or even a simpler approach that works.

I'm especially interested in small, reproducible tests that could challenge our assumptions.

Disclosure: I maintain Agent Role Contracts (ARC), an open-source checker for declared agent responsibilities and task boundaries. Runtime enforcement and independent review require additional controls. This discussion is about what those controls should actually prove.

title: Create a Website with Google Stitch: Build Your Site Under $300
description:
In today's digital landscape, having an online presence is no longer optional for small business owners and freelancers. However, the costs associated with web development can be daunting. If you are looking to create a website with Google Stitch, you are likely wondering how to maximize your budget without sacrificing quality. With a target budget of $300, you have plenty of room to build a professional-grade site using modern AI design tools.

What is Google Stitch?

Google Stitch is an innovative platform emerging from Google Labs that changes how we approach web creation. Unlike traditional drag-and-drop builders, Google Stitch AI provides an infinite, collaborative canvas where you can iterate on interfaces using natural language. It bridges the gap between high-fidelity design and functional web development, making it a powerful website using AI design tool for those who want a unique, tailored look.

Can You Build a $300 Website with Google Stitch?

The short answer is yes. When you aim for a $300 website, your costs typically break down into three categories: domain registration, hosting, and potentially premium assets or specialized integrations. Since Google Stitch focuses on the design and structural phase, it allows you to visualize your Google Stitch vibe design before committing to expensive development hours.

Budget Allocation Breakdown:

  • Domain Name: $12–$20/year.
  • Hosting/Deployment: $5–$20/month depending on your traffic needs.
  • Google Stitch/AI Tools: Currently, many features are accessible via Google Labs, making it a cost-effective starting point.
  • Extras: $100–$150 reserved for professional stock photography or custom icons.

Step-by-Step: Creating Your Site

To get started with a Google Stitch tutorial approach, follow these steps:

  1. Define Your Vibe: Use natural language prompts within the Stitch interface to describe your brand identity.
  2. Iterate on the Canvas: Use the infinite canvas to drag, drop, and rearrange elements. Because it is AI-assisted, the tool helps maintain design consistency.
  3. Export and Code: Once your design is finalized, you can move toward implementation by exporting your assets or using the generated code structure to build your live site.

Google Stitch vs. Figma: Why Choose Stitch?

While Figma is the industry standard for UI/UX designers, Stitch by Google Labs offers a more conversational, AI-driven experience. For a small business owner or a freelancer, the learning curve on Figma can be steep. Google Stitch simplifies the process, allowing you to focus on the vibe and functionality of your site rather than pixel-perfect alignment.

Conclusion

Building a Google Stitch website is an excellent way to maintain creative control over your digital identity while keeping costs well under your $300 limit. By leveraging AI to handle the heavy lifting of design and layout, you can focus on what really matters: your business.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Google Stitch free?

Google Stitch is currently part of Google Labs. While specific pricing tiers may change as the product evolves, it is currently accessible for users looking to experiment with AI-driven web design.

Do I need coding skills to use Google Stitch?

While basic knowledge of web structures helps, Google Stitch is designed to translate natural language into design elements, making it accessible to non-developers.

What is Google Stitch DESIGN.md?

The Google Stitch DESIGN.md file refers to the documentation and technical specifications often associated with projects built within the interface, helping developers understand the design intent behind the AI-generated components.

title: Smart Home i praksis: Når software møder elinstallationer
description:
Smart Home i praksis: Når software møder elinstallationer

Et smart home begynder ofte med noget enkelt.

En intelligent pære. En app, der styrer lyset. Eller en sensor, som registrerer bevægelse i gangen.

Det virker næsten som et almindeligt softwareprojekt. Du vælger enheder, forbinder dem til netværket og opretter automatiseringer.

Men et smart home består af mere end kode og trådløs kommunikation.

Bag den digitale styring findes fysiske installationer, strømforsyninger og elektrisk udstyr. Og netop grænsen mellem software og elinstallation er vigtig at forstå.

Her ser vi på, hvordan de forskellige dele arbejder sammen, og hvornår teknisk gør-det-selv-arbejde bør overlades til en fagperson.

Tre lag i et smart home

En enkel måde at forstå et smart home på er at opdele systemet i tre lag.

Lag Funktion Eksempel
Brugerflade Styring og automatisering App eller smart home-platform
Kommunikation Udveksling af data Wi-Fi, Zigbee eller Thread
Fysisk udstyr Udførelse af handlinger Pærer, sensorer og relæer

Lagene arbejder sammen, men de stiller forskellige krav.

En softwarefejl kan eksempelvis betyde, at en lampe ikke reagerer på en kommando.

En fejl i den elektriske installation kan derimod have betydning for sikkerheden.

Derfor bør fejlfinding begynde med at forstå, hvilket lag problemet hører til.

Eksempel: En lampe med automatisk styring

Forestil dig en lampe, der skal tænde, når en bevægelsessensor registrerer aktivitet.

Systemet kan beskrives sådan:

Bevægelsessensor
       |
       v
Smart Home Controller
       |
       v
Automatiseringsregel
       |
       v
Smart pære
       |
       v
Lys tændes

Selve automatiseringen kan være forholdsvis enkel.

Hvis sensoren registrerer bevægelse, sender systemet en kommando til lampen.

Men der er flere ting at tage højde for:

  • Kan lampen styres med den valgte platform?
  • Er kommunikationen stabil?
  • Hvad sker der, hvis internetforbindelsen forsvinder?
  • Kan lyset stadig betjenes manuelt?
  • Er det elektriske udstyr egnet til installationen?

De sidste spørgsmål handler ikke kun om software.

De handler også om den fysiske løsning.

Smart pære eller intelligent relæ?

Det kan være nyttigt at kende forskellen mellem to almindelige måder at styre belysning på.

Smart pære

En smart pære monteres i et kompatibelt lampeudtag eller en passende fatning.

Den kan typisk styres via en app eller en smart home-platform.

Fordelen er, at løsningen ofte kan tages i brug uden ændringer af den faste elinstallation.

Der kan dog være begrænsninger.

Hvis en almindelig vægafbryder afbryder strømmen til pæren, kan den ikke længere modtage digitale kommandoer.

Intelligent relæ

Et intelligent relæ kan bruges til at styre en elektrisk belastning.

Nogle relæer er beregnet til montering i eller som en del af den faste elinstallation.

Sådanne løsninger stiller krav til korrekt installation, elektrisk beskyttelse og produktets anvendelse.

Et relæ er ikke automatisk et gør-det-selv-produkt, bare fordi det kan konfigureres fra en app.

Hvis monteringen kræver ændring af den faste elinstallation, skal opgaven udføres af en virksomhed med den nødvendige autorisation.

Hvad sker der, når netværket svigter?

Et smart home bør ikke kun vurderes på, hvor godt det fungerer under normale forhold.

Det er også vigtigt at undersøge, hvad der sker, når noget ikke virker.

Forestil dig følgende situationer:

  1. Routeren genstarter.
  2. En sensor mister forbindelsen.
  3. Smart home-controlleren bliver utilgængelig.
  4. En cloudbaseret tjeneste stopper midlertidigt.
  5. En automatisering bliver aktiveret på det forkerte tidspunkt.

Disse situationer behøver ikke være farlige, men de kan påvirke systemets funktion.

Ved valg af udstyr bør man derfor undersøge, om centrale funktioner virker lokalt, og hvordan systemet opfører sig ved forbindelsesfejl.

Man bør ikke være afhængig af en enkelt app for at kunne bruge nødvendig belysning eller andre vigtige funktioner i hjemmet.

Dokumentation gør fejlfinding lettere

Mange smart home-projekter begynder med få enheder.

Efter et stykke tid kan systemet bestå af sensorer, controllere, pærer, smart plugs og flere forskellige kommunikationsprotokoller.

Så bliver dokumentation nyttig.

En enkel oversigt kan indeholde:

Oplysning Hvorfor den er nyttig
Enhedens navn Gør enheden lettere at identificere
Placering Viser, hvor udstyret er monteret
Kommunikationstype Hjælper ved netværksfejl
Platform Viser, hvilken controller der styrer enheden
Automatisering Forklarer, hvad enheden skal gøre
Afhængigheder Viser, hvilke andre enheder der skal fungere

Det er også en god idé at notere ændringer i systemet.

Hvis en automatisering holder op med at fungere, kan dokumentationen gøre det lettere at finde årsagen.

Men softwaredokumentation erstatter ikke den dokumentation, som kan være nødvendig for elektrisk installationsarbejde.

Hvornår kræver et smart home en elektriker?

Der er stor forskel på at konfigurere en app og at ændre den faste elinstallation.

Du kan normalt selv konfigurere smart home-software og tilslutte egnede produkter med almindelig stikprop.

Men nye faste installationer og mange ændringer af eksisterende elinstallationer kræver en autoriseret elinstallatørvirksomhed.

Det kan eksempelvis være relevant ved:

  • Etablering af nye faste stikkontakter.
  • Installation af fast tilsluttede styringsenheder.
  • Ændringer i den faste kabelføring.
  • Installationer, der kræver arbejde i eltavlen.
  • Udvidelser af eksisterende faste installationer.

Der findes særlige undtagelser for enkelte simple elopgaver. Den konkrete opgave skal derfor altid vurderes efter gældende danske regler.

Det er en god idé at planlægge den fysiske installation og softwarestyringen som to forskellige dele af projektet.

På den måde bliver det lettere at afklare både funktion, kompatibilitet og sikkerhed.

Et eksempel på bedre projektplanlægning

Forestil dig, at du vil automatisere belysningen i et hjemmekontor.

Før du køber udstyr, kan du arbejde med denne rækkefølge:

Trin 1: Beskriv behovet

Skal lyset tænde automatisk, dæmpes efter tidspunktet eller styres fra telefonen?

Trin 2: Undersøg eksisterende installationer

Kan løsningen fungere med eksisterende stikkontakter, lampeudtag og kompatible produkter?

Trin 3: Vælg kommunikation

Skal systemet bruge Wi-Fi eller en anden protokol? Undersøg enhedernes kompatibilitet og behovet for en hub.

Trin 4: Afklar eventuelt installationsarbejde

Hvis der er behov for ændringer i den faste elinstallation, skal en autoriseret elinstallatørvirksomhed inddrages.

Trin 5: Test funktionerne

Kontrollér, at automatiseringer fungerer som forventet, og at brugerne kan betjene udstyret på en praktisk måde.

Trin 6: Dokumentér opsætningen

Notér de vigtigste enheder, deres placering og de regler, der styrer dem.

Denne fremgangsmåde gør det lettere at undgå unødvendige indkøb og tekniske overraskelser.

Elektriske installationer og tekniske løsninger i Næstved

For boligejere og mindre virksomheder kan smart home-teknologi være relevant ved renovering, ændringer i belysning og nye tekniske behov.

Sydsjællands El ApS er en autoriseret elinstallatørvirksomhed med base på Lov Enghavevej 10 i Næstved.

Virksomheden arbejder blandt andet med elinstallationer, renovering og data- og netværksinstallationer for private og erhverv.

Hvis du planlægger ændringer, der berører den faste elinstallation, kan du læse mere om elektrikerhjælp i Næstved hos Sydsjællands El ApS.

Det er vigtigt at afklare den konkrete opgave med virksomheden, før du vælger produkter eller planlægger installationsarbejde.

Den bedste automatisering er også praktisk uden appen

Et smart home skal gøre hverdagen lettere.

Det kræver ikke nødvendigvis mange sensorer eller avancerede regler.

Ofte giver enkle funktioner mest værdi, når de er stabile, nemme at forstå og passer til brugernes behov.

Software kan styre, hvornår noget skal ske.

Men det er stadig den fysiske installation, der skal understøtte løsningen på en sikker og pålidelig måde.

Når de to dele planlægges sammen, får du et bedre grundlag for at bygge et smart home, der fungerer i praksis.

title: MetaのQuest 2時代が終わる——それは「VR科学」の終わりではなく、次の章の始まり
description:
MetaのQuest 2時代が終わる——それは「VR科学」の終わりではなく、次の章の始まり

MetaがQuest 2とQuest Proのサポート終了を発表しました。両機種は来年初頭に最後のOSアップデートを受け取り、来春に控えるMeta VR Glassesへ向けて、同社はHorizonOSの開発リソースを新しいハードウェアへ移していく方針を示しています。

このニュースを見て「VRはもう下火なのか」と受け取った人もいるかもしれません。しかし、教育や研究の現場でVRを使ってきた立場から見ると、これはむしろ逆の合図です。ハードウェアの世代交代は、その上で動くソフトウェアが“汎用のデモ”から“専門的なワークフローの一部”へ進化するタイミングだからです。プラットフォームが変わるたびに、生き残るのは「そのデバイスでしか成立しない体験」です。そして分子科学ほど、その条件に近い領域はありません。

フラットな画面に閉じ込められてきた構造生物学

構造生物学の日々の仕事を思い浮かべてください。タンパク質の立体構造は、いまも多くの場合、フラットなモニタ上でマウスによって回転させられ、論文用の図として切り取られます。しかし、結合ポケットの奥行き、リガンドの向き、電子密度の重なり、水素結合の角度——これらの情報は本来、紙の上や画面の中でなく、その構造の“中に立って”見るべきものです。

エンジニアの言葉で言えば、これは「次元の圧縮」です。3次元のデータを2次元の射影に落とすとき、奥行きの情報は失われます。回転させて角度を変えれば補える——そう考えるかもしれませんが、視点操作のたびに頭の中で座標変換を走らせるのは、人間の認知にとって安い処理ではありません。特に結合ポケットの内部のように、複数の残基が狭い空間で絡み合う領域では、この変換コストが理解のボトルネックになります。

教育の場面でも同じです。ヘモグロビンに酸素が結合する瞬間、解糖系でグルコースが分解される過程、アスピリンがCOX酵素を阻害する仕組み、CRISPR-Cas9がDNAを編集する様子。どれも図解では伝わりきらない“スケール感”と“空間の感覚”を持っています。教科書の矢印は結果を教えてくれますが、その矢印が空間のどこで起きているかは教えてくれません。

NexoPeekという答え合わせ

Seven Sportzが手がけるNexoPeekは、Meta Quest向けのVR分子ラボです。ヒトスケールでタンパク質の内部に足を踏み入れ、6つの柱にまたがる12本のナレーション付きツアーを歩くことができます。

柱は「Biotechnology Basics」「Foundations of Life」「Pathways & Interactions」「Medicines in Action」「Genetic Technologies」「Green Biotech」の6つ。初学者が最初の一歩を踏み出すための入口でありながら、専門家が構造を確認するための視点も同じ空間に用意されています。ツアーは一本道の動画ではなく、立ち止まり、見上げ、くぐり抜けるための道として設計されています。

プロフェッショナル向けのPDBビューアも搭載しました。遺伝子名からRCSB PDB、UniProtKB、AlphaFold DB、SWISS-MODEL、PDBeを横断して構造を解決し、ヒトスケールで読み込みます。Mol*プリセットのワンタップで、カートゥーン、ボールアンドスティック、スペースフィル（CPK）、分子表面、Bファクターのヒートマップ、チューブトレースへ表現を切り替え可能です。ローカルの.pdb、.cif、.mol2ファイルを読み込めば、静電場のラインマップや電子密度ボリュームも表示できます。

地味ですが重要なのは、ここが「ビューアの移植」ではないという点です。デスクトップの分子ビューアは、あくまで画面という窓越しに構造を見せます。NexoPeekは視点そのものを構造の内側に置きます。同じデータ、同じ表現プリセットでも、参照系が変わるだけで、結合ポケットの“圧迫感”やリガンドの“収まり方”が手触りとして伝わります。

解析ベンチでは、素手（またはVRコントローラ）で分子をつかみ、拡大し、回転させます。AIポケット予測が創薬候補サイトを光らせ、Foldseekが相同構造を重ね合わせ、Ligand Inspectorが水素結合をたどり、PubChemから3Dリガンドを引き出します。トリガーで2つの原子を選べば、その間の距離をオングストローム単位で報告します。配列中の残基“ピル”をタップすると、構造上に3Dハローが投影されます。

これらの機能は、外部の検証済みツールやデータベースを呼び出す形で成り立っています。独自の予測モデルを売りにするのではなく、すでに研究者が信頼しているパイプラインを、空間の中で操作できるようにする——それがこのラボの設計思想です。だからこそ、Quest 2の引退はこの体験の終わりではなく、より良いトラッキングとより軽いヘッドセットでの再出発を意味します。

世代交代の先にあるもの

Quest 2のサポート終了は、没入型サイエンスの終わりではありません。むしろ、こうした体験が“見せ物”ではなく“道具”として定着し始めたからこそ、プラットフォームが次の世代へ進むのです。

ハードウェアの寿命は短く、ソフトウェアの寿命は長い。Quest 2という筐体が消えても、その上で育ったワークフローは次のデバイスへ引き継がれます。教育機関がVRラボを予算化し、研究室が構造解析の一工程としてVRを組み込む——そうした動きが、世代交代を“終わり”ではなく“更新”に変えます。

NexoPeekは教育・研究視覚化のためのソフトウェアであり、医療上の助言・診断・治療を提供するものではありません。ポケット予測やアラインメントなどの解析支援機能は、検証済みの科学的パイプラインと専門家の判断を補助するものであり、それらに取って代わるものではありません。

Meta QuestでNexoPeekを入手する: https://www.meta.com/experiences/nexopeek/1453797551140347/

title: I built AiRap.me: turn one photo into a lip-synced AI rap video
description:
Earlier this year my feed was full of AI rap videos: someone's selfie, their cat, or a cartoon character dropping a verse. When I tried to make one myself, it took a whole toolchain: one tool for lyrics, another for the song, a lip-sync app, then a video editor to put it all together. Most "AI rap generators" also stop at an audio file, but what people actually share is a video.

So I built AiRap.me: upload one photo, pick a style, and get a finished rap video back, usually in about 20–30 seconds.

What it does

  • One photo in, rap video out. The AI writes an original verse, makes the beat, generates the vocals and lip-syncs the face in your photo. You don't need a song, a voice recording or an editing app.
  • Solo or duo. Use one photo, or two photos where two performers trade verses.
  • People, pets and characters. Selfies, dogs, cats, and cartoon, anime or 3D characters, each keeping its own look.
  • 8 styles. Trap, drill, boom bap, melodic, phonk, rage, old school and Afro trap, plus birthday, roast and love themes.
  • Ready to post. 9:16 or 16:9, 768P or 1080P, 6, 10 or 15 seconds, downloaded as an MP4 with no watermark.

A few product decisions I care about

1. Only charge for videos that finish.
AI video generation fails sometimes: a bad photo, a model hiccup, a timeout. Credits are reserved when a job starts and refunded automatically if it fails. Photos that can't work (group shots, faces that are too small or blurry) are rejected before the job starts, so they never cost anything.

2. Show the first frame before you pay.
Your photo becomes the first frame of the video, so you drag and zoom the crop first. You see exactly what you'll get before you spend credits.

3. Async by default.
Generation takes a while, so you don't have to keep the tab open. The finished video waits for you in "My Videos".

4. Privacy.
Uploaded photos and generated videos stay in the user's account and are never used to train models.

Free tools along the way


While building the video generator I also shipped two free text tools that need no sign-up:

  • 🎤 AI Rap Lyrics Generator
  • 🏷️ Rap Name Generator

There are also one-click templates for viral formats, like the Hotel Lobby AI rap trend.

Try it

New accounts get free credits, and no credit card is needed:
👉 https://airap.me

I'd love feedback from the dev.to community, especially:

  • Which rap styles or trend templates should I add next?
  • Anything confusing in the upload → style → generate flow?

Thanks for reading! I'll reply to every comment. 🙌

title: I built a macOS app that makes your screen feel like paper!
description:
A few weeks ago I was reading "Attention Is All You Need" for probably the fifth time. It was late, I had the PDF open full screen, and within a few minutes, I realised my eyes weren't tired from the screen.

Everything on a Mac is so clean and glossy. White is really white. Every page looks like it's printed on glass. That's great for photos, but when you're reading for hours it starts to feel harsh, and I kept thinking about how much nicer the same paper would feel if it was, well, on paper.

So I went looking for an app that could fake that.

The apps that already exist

Turns out I'm not the first person to want this. There are a few apps that put a texture over your screen, and some of them look really good. But every one I found had the same problem for me: I couldn't try it without paying first.

One was around $13 upfront with no free version at all. Another was part of a bigger subscription bundle. For something this personal, where you can only know if you like it by living with it for a day, paying before trying felt wrong. A texture that looks lovely in screenshots might be annoying on your actual screen with your actual apps.

I'm a backend dev. I spend my days with Node, Redis and queues, not AppKit. But I'd been wanting to ship something of my own for a long time, and this felt small enough to actually finish. So I decided to build my own, with a free version anyone could just try.

That became Shoji, named after the Japanese paper screens that let soft light through.

How it actually works

The core idea is surprisingly simple. Shoji puts one borderless, transparent window on every display, floating above everything else, and draws a light paper texture into it. The important bit is that the window ignores the mouse completely, so every click goes straight through to whatever is underneath:

ignoresMouseEvents = true
level = NSWindow.Level(rawValue: Int(CGWindowLevelForKey(.assistiveTechHighWindow)))
collectionBehavior = [.canJoinAllSpaces, .stationary, .fullScreenAuxiliary, .ignoresCycle]

That last line is what lets it follow you across Spaces and sit over full screen apps too.

The part that took the longest wasn't the window though. It was the paper.

I didn't want to use photos of paper, because photos tile badly. You start seeing the same blotch repeat every few inches and your brain can't unsee it. So every texture is generated in code, using layered noise, a bit of domain warping so the patterns never line up in rows, and little randomly walked "fibers" for papers like Washi and Newsprint. It's all seeded, so the same paper looks the same every time, and it renders sharp on any display.

Getting them right in dark mode was its own adventure. Shadows that look like nice paper grain on white just disappear on a dark background, and fibers that look subtle on light mode suddenly look like hair on your screen in dark mode. I ended up with separate recipes for light and dark, and a separate strength setting for each, so dark apps stay dark.

A few other fun things I learned along the way:

  • Hiding from screenshots is one line, sharingType = .none. Your screen shares and recordings stay clean.
  • Getting notarized was more stressful than writing the app. Xcode kept telling me I wasn't the account holder of the account I literally owned, and I got very familiar with keychain error codes.
  • Auto updates run on Sparkle, and I found a fun bug where the update window would open behind Spotify and make the whole app look frozen. Lesson learned: always bring your app forward before showing a modal.

And then, before I'd even posted it anywhere except one tweet, someone bought it. A real person, who I don't know, paid for a thing I made. I'm not going to pretend I was calm about it.

What Shoji does

  • 7 papers: Plain, Rice, Linen, Newsprint, Washi, Cold Press and Parchment
  • Clicks pass through, so everything works exactly like before
  • Every display, including external monitors and full screen apps
  • Hidden from screenshots and screen recordings
  • Separate strength for light and dark mode
  • Pause it for 15 minutes, an hour, or until tomorrow
  • Lives in your menu bar, with keyboard shortcuts to toggle it or switch papers
  • No tracking. It never reads your screen, and only goes online to check for updates and verify a Pro license

What's next

  • A Windows version (people keep asking)
  • Per-app rules, so you can turn the paper off in apps where you don't want it
  • More papers

If you have ideas, I'd honestly love to hear them.

Pricing

PS: I already made my first sale yesterday from my X launch post :)

This was the whole reason I built it, so it's simple:

  • Free: Plain Paper, forever, with every feature. No account, no trial timer.
  • Pro: all 7 papers for $5 once, on up to 3 Macs, with lifetime updates and a 14-day refund if it's not for you.

For launch, Pro is $3 until November 23.

And for dev.to readers: leave a comment below and I'll reply with a code for an even better deal.

Links

  • Website and download: shoji.ink
  • Me on X: @_asheeshh

It needs macOS 13 or later and works on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

This is my first app, so any feedback helps, good or bad. And if you also read too many PDFs late at night, give the free paper a try. Your eyes might thank you.

title: Optimizing Real-Time Computer Vision Inference Pipelines in Python for Edge Monitoring
description:
The Latency Bottleneck in Edge Vision

Running object detection models like YOLOv8 on edge hardware requires careful memory and frame-rate management. Processing every single frame from a camera stream often saturates the CPU/GPU without adding meaningful diagnostic value—especially when monitoring slow-changing physical environments like plant health or industrial gauges.

In this guide, we will implement a frame-sampling and asynchronous inference wrapper in Python to keep latency low and resource usage predictable.

Designing a Non-Blocking Inference Queue

Instead of running model inference directly inside the camera capture loop, we decouple frame capture from model execution using a bounded queue.Queue of size 1. This ensures the model always evaluates the most recent frame while dropping stale frames automatically.

import threading
import queue
import time

class EdgeInferencePipeline:
    def __init__(self, model, target_fps: float = 2.0):
        self.model = model
        self.interval = 1.0 / target_fps
        self.frame_queue = queue.Queue(maxsize=1)
        self.running = False

    def push_frame(self, frame):
        if self.frame_queue.full():
            try:
                self.frame_queue.get_nowait()
            except queue.Empty:
                pass
        self.frame_queue.put(frame)

    def _worker(self):
        while self.running:
            start_time = time.perf_counter()
            try:
                frame = self.frame_queue.get(timeout=1.0)
                results = self.model.predict(frame, verbose=False)
                self.handle_detections(results)
            except queue.Empty:
                continue

            elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start_time
            sleep_time = max(0.0, self.interval - elapsed)
            time.sleep(sleep_time)

    def handle_detections(self, results):
        for r in results:
            boxes = r.boxes
            print(f"Detected {len(boxes)} objects at {time.strftime('%X')}")

    def start(self):
        self.running = True
        threading.Thread(target=self._worker, daemon=True).start()

    def stop(self):
        self.running = False

Adding Basic Telemetry Metrics

To monitor how healthy our inference service is in production, we should track average inference duration and frame drop rates:

def measure_inference(model, sample_image):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    _ = model.predict(sample_image, verbose=False)
    latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    print(f"Inference latency: {latency_ms:.2f} ms")
    return latency_ms

Conclusion

Decoupling frame capture from model inference prevents memory leaks and keeps edge hardware responsive. Combined with lightweight latency logging, you can reliably deploy computer vision models on local hardware without cloud round-trip delays.

title: How R6 Stat Trackers Compute K/D and Win Rate (And Why Two Sites Disagree)
description:
Stat trackers for Rainbow Six Siege look like simple profile pages: a rank, a K/D, a win rate, maybe a list of operators. Under the hood they have to agree with Ubisoft's ranked data, survive rate limits, handle divide-by-zero, and pick a win-rate denominator that two honest engineers can still argue about.

This post walks through those choices, using how the numbers are calculated on SiegeRadar as a public example. SiegeRadar is a free unofficial tracker, not affiliated with Ubisoft. The same questions show up in any similar app. For the game itself, see Ubisoft's official Rainbow Six Siege site and the Wikipedia article.

The three formulas that actually matter

Most of a player card reduces to three ratios.

K/D is kills / deaths, rounded to two decimals. The interesting branch is zero deaths. Returning Infinity, NaN or a blank cell makes a profile look broken. A clean rule is: if deaths are zero, return the kill count (so 12 kills and 0 deaths display as 12.00). It stays a real number you can sort.

Headshot percentage is headshots / kills. Guard the case where headshots exceed kills — that is almost always a data error, not a player feat — and do not compute a percentage from zero kills.

Win rate is where trackers quietly diverge. There are two legitimate denominators:

  • Current ranked season card: wins / (wins + losses)
  • Lifetime totals, per-mode figures and past seasons: wins / matches_played

Those two are not always equal. "Matches played" can include results that are not a clean win or loss in the ranked board you just typed in. If one site shows 61.0% and another shows 60.4% for the same account, check the denominator before you assume either is wrong.

In Python, the core is small enough to keep on one screen:

from typing import Optional

def kd(kills: int, deaths: int) -> float:
    if deaths == 0:
        return float(kills)
    return round(kills / deaths, 2)

def win_rate_season(wins: int, losses: int) -> Optional[float]:
    denom = wins + losses
    if denom == 0:
        return None  # render as a dash, not 0.0
    return round(wins / denom * 100, 1)

def win_rate_lifetime(wins: int, matches: int) -> Optional[float]:
    if matches == 0:
        return None
    return round(wins / matches * 100, 1)

Returning None (and showing a dash) when there is no sample is better than showing 0.0%, which readers will treat as a real losing record.

Where the data comes from, and how stale it is allowed to be

A tracker is not the game client. It asks a ranked-data API, caches the answer and renders a page. SiegeRadar's public description is that player profiles, operator stats, leaderboards and live player counts come from the Arenyze API, which serves Ubisoft's ranked data. The response is cached so the next view inside the window does not hit the source again.

Freshness is a product decision as much as a systems one. Refresh too often and you burn a data budget; refresh too rarely and a player who just finished a match thinks the site is broken. One working set of windows looks like this:

  • Player profiles: at most every 15 minutes
  • Operator stats: every 30 minutes (season-level operator stats every 6 hours)
  • Leaderboards: every 3 hours
  • Live player counts: every hour
  • "Player not found" misses: remembered for 10 minutes, then tried again
  • Game database pages (operators, weapons, maps, ranks): a snapshot, updated each season, not live

When the daily budget is used up, or upstream is down, serving the last saved copy with an explicit "couldn't refresh, last updated X minutes ago" is kinder than a blank page.

Other edges that will show up in bug reports

Console names must match exactly. A near miss should return "not found," not a cousin account. That feels harsh until the alternative is attaching someone else's rank to a search.

Past seasons do not share a scale. Ranked 2.0 and Ranked 3.0 use different RP ranges. Seasons before Y7S4 used MMR, not rank points, so a tracker should not invent a modern rank name for them.

Operator data is not a full career. Headshot percentage and operator time played may only cover recent seasons. Summing operator hours will usually come in under the lifetime total Ubisoft reports. Document that.

There may be no match history. Not every tracker has a replay of each lobby. If you do not have it, say so. Advertising a feature you cannot compute is worse than a shorter feature list.

Why two good trackers still disagree

Most disagreements come from four places: the win-rate denominator, the cache window, whether operator stats are treated as lifetime, and whether a missing sample is shown as zero or as empty. Get those four written down and the rest of the page is presentation. The useful test is not "does this match another site to two decimals?" It is "can I explain every number on the card, including the ones we cannot show?"

title: How to get EU public tenders from TED as JSON in Python (without learning expert-query syntax)
description:
Every public tender above the EU thresholds, from a German city's software project to a French hospital's equipment purchase, is published in TED (Tenders Electronic Daily), the EU's official procurement journal. TED has a free, official search API. The catch is its expert query syntax, its nested multilingual fields and a single notice that can contain several lots with different deadlines and values.

This post shows a script that answers one practical question: "Which open tenders match what we sell, in the countries we serve, and are still biddable?" You get flat JSON and a CSV.

Disclosure: I built the EU Tenders (TED) API actor used below. It calls the official TED Search API v3 and only returns organisations, never contact persons.

The 20-line version 

# pip install apify-client
import csv, os
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run_input = {
    "keywords": ["software"],
    "countries": ["DEU", "AUT"],      # ISO alpha-3 buyer countries
    "cpvCodes": ["72", "48"],         # IT services, software packages
    "noticeTypes": ["competition"],   # open calls for tenders
    "publishedWithinDays": 7,
    "deadlineAfter": "today",         # skip expired tenders
    "maxResults": 50,
}

run = client.actor("fast_data_asap/eu-tenders-ted-api").call(run_input=run_input)
notices = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

notices.sort(key=lambda n: n.get("deadline") or "9999")
fields = ["deadline", "buyerName", "buyerCity", "buyerCountry", "title", "estimatedValue", "currency", "url"]
with open("tenders.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields, extrasaction="ignore")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(notices)
print(len(notices), "open tenders written to tenders.csv")

No browser, no HTML parsing. The actor turns the inputs into a TED expert query, follows pagination and flattens each notice into one row.

What comes back

These are real rows from test runs on 8 and 9 November 2026 (shortened):

Deadline Buyer What Est. value
02.12.2026 MD-IT GmbH, Berlin Framework agreement: AI for hospital billing review, compliance, AI governance (3 lots) €121,000,000
07.12.2026 Stadt Brandis Development of OpenCore modules for the PartheCloud €625,600
08.12.2026 BWI GmbH, Bonn Framework contract, notice "1961-JC-NoCodeDB" (software packages) not published

Every row has the same flat fields:

{
  "noticeId": "779062-2026",
  "title": "Germany – Programming services of application software – Entwicklungsleistungen für OpenCore-Module der PartheCloud",
  "buyerName": "Stadt Brandis",
  "buyerCountry": "DEU",
  "buyerCity": "Brandis",
  "cpvMain": "72212000",
  "cpvCodes": ["72212000", "72262000", "72263000"],
  "formType": "competition",
  "procedureType": "open",
  "estimatedValue": 625600,
  "currency": "EUR",
  "publishedAt": "2026-11-09",
  "deadline": "2026-12-07T12:00:00+01:00",
  "lotsCount": 1,
  "url": "https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/-/detail/779062-2026"
}

Two details that save you work:

  • deadline is the earliest lot deadline as an ISO timestamp, so sorting and "days left" are one line.
  • estimatedValue is summed across lots. It is null when the buyer did not publish a value (BWI above), which is common.

Choosing filters that actually match your business

CPV prefixes are the most useful filter. CPV is the EU's product vocabulary, and a prefix matches everything below it:

Prefix Covers
72 IT services (consulting, development, support)
48 Software packages and information systems
79 Business services (consulting, marketing, translation)
45 Construction work
90 Cleaning, waste and environmental services
33 Medical equipment

Keywords are matched in full text in any language, so ["software", "Software", "logiciel"] widens the net across countries. Start broad, look at a week of results, then add minValueEur if small contracts are noise for you. Notices without a published value are kept, so you do not silently lose them.

Want to know who wins? Switch noticeTypes to ["result"]. Contract award notices show which buyer bought what, and often for how much: useful for competitor research and pricing.

Running it every morning

For a daily alert set publishedWithinDays to 2 (one day overlap as a safety net) and de-duplicate on noticeId:

import json, pathlib

seen_file = pathlib.Path("seen.json")
seen = set(json.loads(seen_file.read_text())) if seen_file.exists() else set()
new = [n for n in notices if n["noticeId"] not in seen]
seen_file.write_text(json.dumps(sorted(seen | {n["noticeId"] for n in new})))

for n in new:
    print(f'{n["deadline"][:10]}  {n["buyerName"]}: {n["title"][:90]}\n  {n["url"]}')

Schedule the script with cron or a GitHub Action, or use an Apify schedule and pipe the dataset into Slack or a sheet. If you prefer no-code, our free n8n sales-signal workflow does the same for German tenders and can take TED as a third branch.

Limits

  • TED lists notices above the EU thresholds (plus voluntary ones). Smaller national tenders are on national portals; for Germany there is our German Public Tenders actor.
  • Titles and summaries come in the notice language. The actor prefers your language (English by default) where the notice is multilingual.
  • This is a search tool, not procurement or legal advice. Always read the official notice before bidding.

What it costs

$0.002 per notice returned, and empty runs are free. The 50-notice daily run above costs at most $0.10; a typical "last two days, two countries, two CPV codes" run returns far fewer rows.

Try it

  • EU Tenders (TED) API on Apify
  • Agent users: the free find-public-tenders skill lets an AI agent run this search for you.

Question for bid managers: which filter do you rely on most, CPV codes or keywords, and how many false positives do you accept per day before an alert becomes noise?
