title: What is actually making your PDF so big? Measure it in 20 lines of Python
description:
"Compress it" is the usual answer to a heavy PDF, but it's a guess. Before you change any export settings, it's worth knowing which objects take the bytes. With PyMuPDF that takes about 20 lines.

A test file that looks like real life

We built a 3 page PDF the way people actually make them:

  • page 1: a title and one 12 megapixel phone photo (4000 x 3000) placed 4 inches wide,
  • page 2: 30 lines of notes in two fonts, embedded in full (Arial and Georgia),
  • page 3: a letter-size page "scanned" in color at 300 DPI (2550 x 3300).

The file came out at 7.87 MB.

The script 

import os
import pymupdf  # pip install pymupdf

def breakdown(path):
    doc = pymupdf.open(path)
    total = os.path.getsize(path)
    images = fonts = 0
    for xref in range(1, doc.xref_length()):
        subtype = doc.xref_get_key(xref, "Subtype")[1]
        if subtype == "/Image":
            images += len(doc.xref_stream_raw(xref))
        for key in ("FontFile", "FontFile2", "FontFile3"):
            kind, value = doc.xref_get_key(xref, key)
            if kind == "xref":
                fonts += len(doc.xref_stream_raw(int(value.split()[0])))
    print(f"{path}: {total/1e6:.2f} MB")
    print(f"  images {images/1e6:.2f} MB ({images*100/total:.1f}%)")
    print(f"  fonts  {fonts/1e6:.2f} MB ({fonts*100/total:.1f}%)")

breakdown("report.pdf")

It walks every object in the cross reference table, adds up the raw (still compressed) stream length of image objects, and follows each font descriptor to its embedded font file. Whatever is left is page content, structure and metadata.

For our file:

report.pdf: 7.87 MB
  images 7.14 MB (90.6%)
  fonts  0.70 MB (8.8%)

The text people read was about 1% of the file. Deleting a page of notes would save a few kilobytes.

Turning bytes into a diagnosis: effective DPI

Image bytes alone don't tell you whether an image is too big. What matters is pixels per inch at the size it's drawn. PyMuPDF gives you both:

doc = pymupdf.open("report.pdf")
for page in doc:
    for info in page.get_image_info(xrefs=True):
        w_in = (info["bbox"][2] - info["bbox"][0]) / 72   # PDF points to inches
        dpi = info["width"] / w_in
        print(page.number + 1, info["width"], "x", info["height"], f"{dpi:.0f} dpi")

The phone photo came out at 1,000 DPI: 4000 pixels squeezed into 4 inches. Screens and office printers can't show more than about 150 to 300, so roughly 90% of those pixels are dead weight. That single image was 74% of the file.

Fonts: full vs subset

Embedded font names tell you if a font is subset. A subset font has a six letter tag in front, like BNJWSA+ArialMT; a full one doesn't. In our file Arial alone was over half a megabyte embedded in full. After a compression pass that subsets fonts, both fonts together dropped from about 696 KB to 29 KB, and the text was still real, selectable text.

What compression did to it

We ran the same file through Ghostscript based compression at three common levels:

Level Result Image resolution
screen 118 KB 72 DPI
ebook 273 KB 150 DPI
printer 1.73 MB higher

The "ebook" level (150 DPI) is the sensible default: 96.5% smaller and still fine on an office printer.

A rule of thumb

  • Images above about 70% of the file: downsample them. That's where nearly all the savings are.
  • Fonts above about 20%: they're embedded in full; subsetting fixes it.
  • Neither, and the file is still big: look for attachments, form fields and incremental saves (old versions of pages kept at the end of the file after each edit).

If you'd rather not run Python, we built the same breakdown into a browser tool: the PDF size analyzer splits a file into images, fonts, content, attachments and metadata, lists each image with its DPI, and reads the file locally without uploading it.

title: I checked the DMARC records of the top 10,000 domains. Only 61% enforce it
description:
Since 2024, Gmail and Yahoo have required bulk senders to publish a DMARC record. So I wanted to know how far the most popular domains on the internet have actually got. Do they publish DMARC? Do they enforce it, or just monitor? And how many have moved on to BIMI and MTA-STS?

On November 6, 2026 I looked up the public DNS records of the top 10,000 domains on the Tranco list, a research ranking of popular sites that is built to be hard to game. No email was sent and no website was fetched: these are only DNS lookups, the same ones any mail server makes.

The short version:

Of the 7,236 top domains that receive email Share
Publish a valid DMARC record 82.8%
Enforce it (p=quarantine or p=reject) 61.2%
Use p=reject 35.1%
Publish exactly one SPF record 92.7%
Publish a BIMI record 13.3%
Publish an MTA-STS record 4.0%

The rest of this post covers how the scan works, the parsing traps I hit, what stood out in the results, and how to check your own domain in a minute.

The method

The domains. The Tranco top 10,000 (list ID K9YYW, created November 5, 2026). One entry wasn't a valid hostname and was skipped.

The lookups. For each domain, six DNS queries:

Record Name queried What it tells you
MX example.com Whether the domain receives email at all
SPF TXT at example.com Which servers may send for it
DMARC TXT at _dmarc.example.com What receivers should do with mail that fails
BIMI TXT at default._bimi.example.com A brand logo for supporting inboxes
MTA-STS TXT at _mta-sts.example.com A policy asking senders to use verified TLS
TLS-RPT TXT at _smtp._tls.example.com Where to send TLS failure reports

The resolvers. Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) and Google (8.8.8.8), set explicitly so the result doesn't depend on my ISP's resolver.

The denominator. Percentages are of domains with at least one real MX record, because a DMARC policy matters most for domains that actually handle email. Of the 9,960 domains analysed, 7,236 have an MX record. The other 2,724 get their own section below.

Here is the core of the scanner, using only Node's built-in dns module:

import { Resolver } from "node:dns/promises";

const resolver = new Resolver({ timeout: 4000, tries: 3 });
resolver.setServers(["1.1.1.1", "8.8.8.8"]);

// "No such record" is an answer. A timeout or SERVFAIL is not.
const MISSING = new Set(["ENOTFOUND", "ENODATA"]);

async function lookup(kind, name) {
  try {
    const value = kind === "mx" ? await resolver.resolveMx(name) : await resolver.resolveTxt(name);
    return { ok: true, value };
  } catch (err) {
    if (MISSING.has(err.code)) return { ok: true, value: [] };
    return { ok: false, code: err.code };
  }
}

// A TXT record can be split into 255-byte strings. Join them before parsing.
const records = (txt, prefix) =>
  txt.map((chunks) => chunks.join("")).filter((t) => t.trim().toLowerCase().startsWith(prefix));

function tags(record) {
  const out = {};
  for (const part of record.split(";")) {
    const i = part.indexOf("=");
    if (i > 0) out[part.slice(0, i).trim().toLowerCase()] = part.slice(i + 1).trim();
  }
  return out;
}

async function scan(domain) {
  const [mx, apex, dmarc] = await Promise.all([
    lookup("mx", domain),
    lookup("txt", domain),
    lookup("txt", `_dmarc.${domain}`),
  ]);
  const failed = [mx, apex, dmarc].find((r) => !r.ok);
  if (failed) return { domain, err: failed.code }; // excluded, not counted as "missing"

  const spf = records(apex.value, "v=spf1");
  const dm = records(dmarc.value, "v=dmarc1");
  return {
    domain,
    mx: mx.value.length > 0,
    spfCount: spf.length,           // more than 1 = SPF permerror
    dmarcCount: dm.length,          // more than 1 = invalid
    policy: dm.length === 1 ? (tags(dm[0]).p || "").toLowerCase() : null,
  };
}

The full version adds BIMI, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT, RFC 7505 null MX detection and the SPF all qualifier. It runs 40 domains at a time and retries failures once at the end. All 10,000 domains took under four minutes.

Five traps worth knowing if you parse these records yourself

1. "No record" and "lookup failed" are different answers. ENOTFOUND and ENODATA mean the record doesn't exist. ESERVFAIL, EREFUSED and timeouts mean you don't know. If you count both as "no DMARC", you overstate how many domains lack it. 39 domains still failed after a retry (32 SERVFAIL, 6 FORMERR, 1 REFUSED), and I excluded them rather than guess.

2. TXT records come back in chunks. A long SPF or DMARC record is split into strings of up to 255 bytes, and resolveTxt returns each record as an array of those strings. Join them with no separator before parsing, or a long include: list gets cut in half.

3. More than one SPF record is not "extra SPF". RFC 7208 says a domain with two v=spf1 records gives a permanent error, so SPF fails for every email. 0.6% of the mail-receiving domains (46 domains) publish more than one.

4. A domain with no MX is not the same as one that refuses mail. An RFC 7505 "null MX" (0 .) states that a domain accepts no email. 74 domains in the list publish one. Most domains without email simply have no MX record at all.

5. Check your parser against a second source. I re-resolved a random sample of 40 domains through a third resolver (Quad9, 9.9.9.9), with a separate regex-based DMARC parser. The policy matched for all 40.

What the results show

Most top domains publish DMARC. Far fewer enforce it.

82.8% of mail-receiving domains publish a valid DMARC record, but the policy is where it gets interesting:

DMARC policy Share of mail-receiving domains
p=reject 35.1%
p=quarantine 26.1%
p=none 21.5%
No DMARC record 17.0%

p=none asks for reports but tells receivers to do nothing with failing mail, so an attacker can still put that domain in a From address. It's the right first step, and a lot of domains seem to have stayed on it.

The good news: 87.0% of domains with a DMARC record include a rua= address for aggregate reports, so most of them can see who is sending mail as their domain.

Bigger sites enforce more

Tranco rank Mail-receiving domains Enforcing DMARC p=reject
Top 100 65 75.4% 56.9%
101 to 1,000 623 74.8% 49.6%
1,001 to 10,000 6,548 59.8% 33.6%

That's 74.9% for the top 1,000 combined, against 59.8% for ranks 1,001 to 10,000. Since adoption drops the further down the list you go, it's probably lower again among the millions of domains that aren't in any top list.

SPF: an even split between strict and soft

Of the 6,710 mail-receiving domains with exactly one SPF record, 46.6% end it with -all (fail mail from unlisted servers) and 47.7% with ~all (soft fail). 2.1% use ?all, which tells receivers nothing, and 3 domains end with +all, which allows any server on the internet to send as them.

Top-level domains differ a lot

Among top-level domains with at least 100 mail-receiving domains in the list:

TLD Domains Valid DMARC Enforcing
.com 3,655 84.7% 66.0%
.ru 252 84.9% 68.7%
.org 364 83.2% 55.8%
.io 157 77.1% 56.1%
.de 166 86.1% 50.6%
.net 398 64.1% 42.0%
.jp 163 82.2% 39.3%
.edu 125 99.2% 62.4%

Nearly every .edu domain publishes DMARC, but more than a third of them (36.8%) stop at p=none. .jp is similar: a high adoption rate, with 42.9% on p=none.

Domains that send no email are the easiest to spoof

2,724 of the domains analysed have no MX record: CDNs, API hosts, asset domains, redirects. They don't send email, but that doesn't stop someone else from putting them in the From address of a phishing email.

The fix is two DNS records: an SPF record of v=spf1 -all and a DMARC record with p=reject. Only 16.4% of these domains have both.

BIMI and MTA-STS are still early

13.3% of mail-receiving domains publish a BIMI record, and 72.1% of those reference a mark certificate. MTA-STS (4.0%) and TLS-RPT (4.5%) are rare, even in the top 10,000.

Check your own domain in a minute 

D=example.com

dig +short MX $D                       # do you receive mail?
dig +short TXT $D | grep -i spf1       # exactly one line, please
dig +short TXT _dmarc.$D               # p=none, quarantine or reject?
dig +short TXT default._bimi.$D        # optional: BIMI
dig +short TXT _mta-sts.$D             # optional: MTA-STS

If you're not yet at p=reject, the usual path is:

  1. One SPF record that lists every service that sends for your domain.
  2. DKIM signing on your own domain, so it aligns with your From address.
  3. DMARC with p=none and a rua= address. Read the reports for a few weeks.
  4. When every legitimate sender passes, move to p=quarantine, then p=reject.
  5. For every domain you own that sends no email: v=spf1 -all and DMARC p=reject.

Limitations

  • It's one snapshot of public DNS from one location. Records change.
  • It checks records, not mail. It can't tell whether a domain's email actually passes, and DKIM keys can't be found without knowing each selector.
  • DMARC was read at the listed domain only. Subdomain policies (sp=) aren't analysed.
  • BIMI was checked at the default selector only, and MTA-STS policy files weren't fetched.
  • The top 10,000 are popular websites, not a random sample of all senders.

The full study, with every table, the methodology, a link for each finding and a CSV of the aggregate numbers, is on the Cresca site: DMARC adoption in 2026. Cresca is the email platform I'm building, and it walks you through SPF and DKIM for your own sending domain. If you'd like a breakdown I didn't include, ask in the comments and I'll run it against the same data.

title: How Dim Gives AI Agents an Input Guide: Meta Prompts, State, and Timeline
description:
By duskzhen

Just after midnight on November 3, at 00:00:22, a local Dim session appended the day's date state. By the next model call, both dates appeared in the request:

<dim-state source="dim/environment/date">2026-11-02</dim-state>
<dim-state source="dim/environment/date">2026-11-03</dim-state>

The requests on either side of midnight (main #1910 and #1930) used the same System Prompt. The new date arrived in the messages, while the old date remained in the history. How should the model know which one means today?

The answer is Dim's Meta Prompt: an input guide supplied with each request in the Rust implementation. Its System section has a direct title, How to read your input. One of its rules says that a later state from the same source supersedes the earlier current value.

Why send environment state separately?

If today's date were inserted directly into the System Prompt, crossing midnight would require a new System version. The date, runtime environment, and available skills change on different schedules. Binding those values to the rules for interpreting them would force the prefix to change whenever any value changed.

Dim separates the instructions for reading an input from the input itself:

  • System tells the model how to interpret state.
  • Messages carry current values with their sources; updates have their own source and order.

To investigate the environment of an earlier request, you can follow the Timeline back to the inputs used at that point. Input guide and state definitions

If both messages have the user role, who said what?

Consider another recorded sequence. A background command finished, Dim recorded exec/ended at #413, then wrote a notification containing <dim-notification> at #414. Once consumed, that notification appeared in the model request at #421 with the API role user.

The human operator's own words also use the user role. The role alone cannot distinguish them. Dim sends the notification as a separate message with a runtime marker, and the guide explains its origin and meaning. A background completion notice is a result of earlier work; the model should relate it to its current task and decide whether it needs to read the full output. Message projection implementation

Branches follow the same principle. In another recorded sequence, a child timeline inherited the main timeline's history through #97. Its first model request contained both the inherited messages and a newly written branch identity block. That block also arrived in a user message; the guide explained that it described the current timeline.

One agent can have several timelines. The model needs an input that tells it which one it is on.

The diagram divides the model's input into eight categories:

  1. System prefix
  2. Rules and state
  3. Tool declarations
  4. Runtime inputs
  5. User inputs
  6. Tool results
  7. Compressed context
  8. Input guide

State describes the current situation. Rules have their own scopes. Files, web pages, and command output returned by tools are material for the model to analyze. The guide explains how to read each kind of input. Runtime permission checks still happen in the runtime: a marker identifies a source; it does not grant authority.

Who writes the guide for a new plugin?

Take background execution as an example. The capability that produces a notification also registers the explanation for that notification. Prompt combines shared guidance with the entries applicable to the current branch. A plugin registers its explanation when loaded and withdraws it when unloaded. Once the configuration adopts the change, subsequent requests use the updated guide.

Three model calls on the main branch of one session. The blue sections show the guide delivered in System each time; the message excerpts show a date update, a branch message, a background notification, and compacted context.

This matches the way Dim assembles capabilities with rutis. When a new capability sends messages to the model, its developer can maintain the marker, meaning, and explanation in the same component. Core owns the shared reading rules; each capability owns the content it introduces. Guide registration and composition

What can the model understand with this guide?

The Meta Prompt does more than explain one message. It helps the model maintain an accurate picture of its environment. Follow the main Timeline in the diagram above:

  • Configuration: Prompt combines the shared guidance and registered plugin entries into Guide A. At context/configured, that guide is adopted in System.
  • Request 1: Messages include a project rule (<dim-rule>) and the current date (<dim-state>). The model can see both the rule it should follow and the date.
  • Request 2: A date update (<dim-state>), branch message (<dim-branch-message>), and background notification (<dim-notification>) arrive in order. The model can tell that time has advanced, another timeline has sent a message, and a task has finished.
  • Request 3, after compaction: A history summary (<dim-summary>) and tool digest (<dim-digest>) replace older detail, while currently effective rules and state are reaffirmed. The model can distinguish past events from conditions that still apply.

All three requests use Guide A in System. The Messages change. The reading rules stay stable while the environment moves through the input stream.

In concrete terms, the model can track:

  • Time: which date is current, without mistaking an earlier date for today.
  • Rules: which project rules still apply and what their scopes are.
  • Position: which branch and timeline it is on.
  • Events: whether a background command finished or another timeline sent a message.
  • History: after compaction, what happened earlier and what still governs the present.

These are no longer stray lines mixed into a conversation. They form an account of the environment with a source, an order, and a reading guide.

How do rules change midway through a session?

So far, the examples have started from an already configured guide. In a real session, a plugin can be enabled or disabled midway, and rules can become active or expire. Two questions need separate answers: how should the model read a kind of content, and which specific content is currently effective? Dim handles those through different channels.

Reading rules: register with a plugin, withdraw with it

When a plugin is enabled:

  1. It registers the markers it will emit, their meanings, and their explanations.
  2. Prompt recombines the shared guidance with those entries into a new guide.
  3. After configuration adoption (context/configured), subsequent requests use the new System.

Disabling it reverses the sequence: the plugin unloads, its explanation is withdrawn, Prompt recombines the guide, and later requests stop carrying that explanation.

This ordering puts the explanation in place before the content appears. It also prevents the model from continuing to interpret new input using withdrawn guidance. Earlier requests are not rewritten; the Timeline still records which guide version each one used.

Current content: append new rules, expire old ones within their scope

Rules and state do not rewrite history either. They are appended. The op on a <dim-rule> describes what happens to that rule:

  • set or replace makes the rule in the block effective; replace identifies the currently adopted version.
  • revoke or expired makes that rule ineffective within its scope. A rule with the same name in another scope is unaffected.

State is simpler: a later value from the same source supersedes an earlier one. A state block with cleared="true" says that state no longer applies.

Adding a rule during a session means appending an effective block. Removing one means appending a block that marks it ineffective. The old block remains in history; the model uses the latest block for the same source and scope. The two dates at the start of this article work the same way.

After compaction, expired rules stay expired

When compaction happens, subsequent state blocks reaffirm only the rules and state still effective at that moment. Each is restated in its most recently delivered form, such as a replace block for the adopted rule version. A revoked rule is absent, so the model does not treat it as current again. The guide also says these reaffirmations confirm the current situation: they are not new changes and do not grant permissions.

Which state survives compaction?

Return to the session that crossed midnight. Later, #2025 recorded a successful context compaction. The next model request, #2026, carried the summary and then reaffirmed five rules and state values still effective at that point. Of the two dates, only November 3 remained as current state.

The two parts have different jobs. The summary describes what happened before; the subsequent state blocks describe the conditions the model should keep working under. The input guide explains that these restatements mean the earlier rules and state are still effective.

To see exactly what a model received at a given moment, return to that request and compare its adopted guide, state, and retained history. Post-compaction message projection

Editorial note: AI tools assisted with the English adaptation and illustrations.

title: Vector Database or Full-Text Search? The Question Most Teams Skip
description:
Vector Database or Full-Text Search? The Question Most Teams Skip

Vector search became the default answer to "how do we build search" the moment embeddings got cheap and easy. It's not always the right default — plain full-text search still wins for a lot of real use cases.

✅ When Full-Text Search Still Wins

If users mostly search with specific terms they expect to match exactly (product names, SKUs, exact phrases), full-text search is faster, cheaper, more debuggable, and doesn't introduce the "why did it return this irrelevant result" problem semantic search can produce.

✅ When Vector Search Actually Earns Its Place

When queries are conceptual rather than exact — someone describing what they want rather than naming it precisely, or needing to match meaning across different phrasing — that's the case vector search was built for, and full-text search genuinely can't do it.

🔀 The Hybrid Reality Most Production Systems Land On

Most real search features that matter end up combining both — full-text for exact-match confidence, vector for conceptual fallback — rather than picking one. Starting with "which one" is often the wrong framing from day one.

Originally published on the KLYX blog.

title: I Don’t Trust AI-Written Tests Until They Fail for the Right Reason
description:
A small way to check whether your tests protect the requirement or simply agree with the code in front of them.

Your coding assistant finishes the function, writes the tests, runs them, and hands you a lovely green result. Honestly, that is a very tempting moment to close the tab and feel productive.

But I want to know what would make those tests turn red.

If the implementation misunderstood the requirement and the tests repeated that misunderstanding, they can agree with each other beautifully. Meanwhile, the user still gets the wrong result. A second file is not automatically a second opinion.

This is not a reason to stop asking AI for tests. It is a reason to give those tests something specific to disagree with.

Before trusting a passing suite, deliberately introduce one small, meaningful mistake and check whether the right assertion catches it. Then restore the correct code and run the tests again.

Let’s make that less abstract with a shipping calculation small enough to check without trusting anyone’s confident explanation, including mine.

Start with the rule before reading the implementation

For this original example, imagine a shop with a deliberately simple shipping policy. Orders below 5,000 cents pay 499 cents for shipping. Orders at or above 5,000 cents receive free shipping. Negative subtotals are invalid and must raise ValueError.

Assume the input is already an integer number of cents. Currency conversion, discounts, taxes, and input parsing are outside this little function’s job.

Notice that the rule gives us an expected answer at exactly 5,000 cents. Free shipping starts there, not one cent later.

I prefer writing that down before looking at the generated code because it keeps the code from quietly becoming the specification. If the policy is unclear, resolve the ambiguity first; no testing trick can decide what the business meant.

Here is a correct implementation for the stated rule.

def shipping_cents(subtotal_cents):
    if subtotal_cents < 0:
        raise ValueError('subtotal must be nonnegative')
    return 0 if subtotal_cents >= 5000 else 499

Now imagine the proposed tests check that a 1,000-cent order pays 499 cents and a 6,000-cent order pays zero. Both pass, as they should.

Those tests are useful, but they leave a particularly interesting customer standing between them.

Change one character and watch what stays green

In a disposable local copy, change the final comparison from >= 5000 to > 5000. Leave everything else alone.

The 1,000 cent test still passes. So does the 6,000-cent test. Neither input asks the function what happens exactly at the threshold.

But a customer spending 5,000 cents now pays 499 cents when the policy promises free shipping. We introduced a real behavior change, and the original pair of tests did not object.

This is the part I find useful. We have moved from vaguely wanting better tests to naming an exact mistake the tests currently allow.

Add an assertion whose expected result comes from the policy.

assert shipping_cents(5000) == 0

Run it while the incorrect comparison is still present. It should fail because the returned fee is 499 instead of zero. Then restore >= and confirm that the same assertion passes.

A syntax error, broken import, or missing dependency would also produce a red run, but none of those would show that our boundary assertion caught the shipping bug. Read the failure, not just its color.

One caught bug is evidence, not a certificate

Now try a different intentional mistake, again starting from the restored correct implementation. Remove the negative-subtotal guard.

The original two tests still pass. Even the new 5,000-cent test passes. A boundary test for free shipping does not automatically protect invalid-input behavior.

So add a separate check that a negative subtotal raises the promised exception. Here is a compact version using Python’s standard test library, alongside the nearby valid values.

import unittest
class ShippingTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_fees(self):
        for subtotal, expected in [(0, 499), (4999, 499),
                                   (5000, 0), (5001, 0)]:
            with self.subTest(subtotal=subtotal):
                self.assertEqual(shipping_cents(subtotal), expected)
    def test_negative_subtotal(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            shipping_cents(-1)

Put this below the function in a file named test_shipping.py, then run python -m unittest -v test_shipping. Keep the function and test class at the top level of the file.

The expected values are intentionally written out. Calculating them with another copy of the production comparison would risk reproducing the same mistake inside the test.

I checked these outcomes against the original and both altered versions. The original pair of tests misses both mistakes. The expanded checks catch the threshold change and the removed guard, while passing against the correct version.

That is a result for this tiny fixture, not a claim about every AI assistant or a guarantee that the function has no other problems. Different mistakes need different evidence.

Give the assistant a review task with an observable finish

An instruction to add comprehensive tests sounds reassuring, but comprehensive is doing an awful lot of work there.

Try a more concrete brief instead. Give the assistant the requirement, ask it to list expected outcomes before inspecting the implementation, and ask which plausible incorrect implementations each test would reject.

For the shipping example, the review brief can be this small.

  • Derive the expected fees at 4,999, 5,000, and 5,001 cents from the written policy.
  • Check that a negative subtotal raises ValueError without depending on the exact wording of the message.
  • Change only the threshold comparison and identify the assertion that fails because of it.
  • Restore the function, remove only the negative-input guard, and identify the exception check that fails.
  • Restore the correct version again and show the final passing test output.

You still need to inspect the proposed expectations and the actual result. An assistant saying it verified the change is not the same as seeing which command ran, which test failed, and why.

For a bug fix, this can be even simpler. Run the regression test against the known buggy version and the fixed version. It should expose the intended bug in the first and pass in the second. Make sure it fails for the behavior you meant to fix, rather than for an unrelated incompatibility between versions.

Keep the experiment small enough to understand

This approach is closely related to mutation testing, where tools deliberately alter code and check whether tests detect the changes. PIT’s explanation also makes an important distinction between a detected mutation, a surviving mutation, and code that no test reached.

Some mutations do not change the behavior that matters, so a survivor is a reason to investigate rather than an automatic demand for another test. Chasing a perfect score can become a very elaborate way to avoid thinking about the requirement.

You do not need to install a mutation-testing tool to try the manual version on one small function. Tooling becomes more useful when you want to repeat the process across more code; the small example is about learning what evidence to look for.

Keep each fault isolated. Start from a passing baseline, make one change, inspect the result, and restore the original before trying the next one. Use a local practice copy or a disposable branch so an intentionally broken version cannot slip into your actual work.

For a first session, choose one small function with a clear output. Check a boundary, an invalid input, and one meaningful alternative result. Stop once you can explain what each assertion protects; a growing test count is not the goal.

If you need a fresh starting point, choose a small problem from this practice question collection and write the expected outcomes before opening a solution. Then make one plausible mistake and see whether your own checks notice it.

Leave with a review note you can defend

For this example, the useful summary is that the original checks missed the exact threshold and negative-input behavior. The added assertions caught those two deliberate faults, and the restored implementation passed them.

That says considerably more than tests added, all green.

In an interview, this gives you a concrete way to explain your verification. During a code review, it gives the next person a reason to trust the specific behavior you checked. Neither requires pretending that a handful of tests proves the entire system correct.

I still want AI to help with the repetitive parts. I just want the final green result to mean more than the implementation and its tests agreeing with each other.

Give the tests a believable mistake to catch, and make them earn a little of that confidence.

~ Emily

title: SQL Interview Question: MAX(created_at) Doesn’t Return the Latest Order
description:
Finding the newest timestamp is easy. Keeping the right row, handling ties, and putting the filter in the right place takes a little more care.

Someone asks for the latest order for each customer, and your brain happily reaches for GROUP BY and MAX.

Honestly, fair enough. The question practically waves a little flag at an aggregate function.

Then the interviewer asks for the order ID, its status, and the amount. Two orders have the same timestamp, and one customer’s newest order is cancelled. Suddenly, finding the latest time is only a small part of the job.

I prefer treating this as a row-selection problem before treating it as a SQL problem. We need to decide which complete record wins, not collect impressive-looking values from different records.

Let’s work through a small original example, then change one sentence in the requirement and watch the answer change with it. There is no giant dataset to hide behind here, which is rather convenient for catching our own assumptions.

Give yourself five rows that refuse to cooperate

Our orders table contains customer_id, id, created_at, status, and total_cents. Each order has a unique ID. Customer IDs, timestamps, and statuses are non-null, and all times shown below are on the same date.

Customer A has three orders. Order 11 was paid at 09:00 for 9,000 cents. Orders 12 and 13 both arrived at 10:00; order 12 is paid for 2,000 cents, while order 13 is cancelled for 3,000 cents.

Customer B has one paid order, ID 21. Customer C has one cancelled order, ID 31.

For the first requirement, return exactly one latest order for every customer represented in this table, regardless of status. If timestamps tie, choose the larger order ID. That tie-breaker is an agreed rule for this exercise, not a claim that a larger ID always represents a later real-world event.

Before writing anything, the expected winning IDs are therefore 13, 21, and 31.

Having that answer on paper makes the query much easier to judge. A plausible result is not enough; we already know which rows the contract requires.

MAX gives you a value, not the rest of its row

This query correctly answers which timestamp is greatest for each customer.

SELECT customer_id, MAX(created_at) AS latest_at
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

It does not answer which complete order to return. For customer A, two rows share that maximum timestamp.

Joining the result back to orders on customer and timestamp can return both. That may be correct if the request is to return every order tied for latest, but it does not satisfy our exactly-one-row rule yet.

Another tempting repair is to add MAX(total_cents) to the grouped query. Please trace that against customer A before trusting it. You get 10:00 and 9,000 cents, even though no order in the input contains that combination.

Each maximum was calculated independently. The result has quietly assembled a record that never existed, which is quite an achievement for such a short query.

Adding ordinary non-grouped columns is not a reliable solution either. PostgreSQL rejects this form when those columns are not functionally determined by the grouped columns. We need an explicit rule for selecting a row.

Rank the complete records, then keep the winner

Use a window function to number each customer’s orders. The first ordering field defines latest; the second resolves a tie.

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, id, created_at, status, total_cents,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, id, created_at, status, total_cents
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

For customer A, order 13 receives row number one, order 12 receives two, and order 11 receives three. The other customers each have one row, so their numbering starts at one too.

All the selected fields now come from the same record. We have not asked the database to guess which status belongs beside an aggregate timestamp.

PostgreSQL’s window-function tutorial explains that ROW_NUMBER numbers rows within a partition and that tied rows have an unspecified numbering order. That is why our unique ID belongs in the ordering clause when exactly one deterministic winner is required.

Also notice the final ORDER BY customer_id. Ordering inside the window decides how to assign row numbers; it does not promise the presentation order of the final result.

If the requirement changes to returning every row tied at the latest timestamp, the ranking rule changes too. A rank based on created_at alone can preserve those ties. Adding a unique ID to that ranking would separate the very ties you were asked to retain.

Moving one filter changes the question

Now suppose the request becomes latest paid order per customer.

We should exclude cancelled rows before ranking, so the eligible population contains only paid orders. In the previous query, add WHERE status = 'paid' immediately after FROM orders inside the CTE.

Customer A now returns order 12. Customer B still returns order 21. Customer C has no paid order, so C has no result under this version of the contract.

But here is a different request that sounds dangerously similar. Return each customer’s latest order, only when that latest order is paid.

This time, rank all orders first. Then use WHERE rn = 1 AND status = 'paid' in the outer query. Customer A disappears because A’s winning row is cancelled. Only customer B remains.

Both queries run. Neither needs to throw an error. They answer different questions because one filter determines who may compete, while the other checks the winner after the competition.

That is the sentence I want to be able to explain in an interview. Memorizing the window-function syntax helps, but it cannot decide which population the business meant.

Keep the missing customer when the requirement asks for them

So far, our population comes from orders. A customer with no orders is invisible, and a customer with no eligible paid order disappears when we filter before ranking.

If the output must contain every customer, start from a separate customers table and left join the selected order onto it. Keep rn = 1 in the join condition or in a prefiltered winners relation.

Putting WHERE ranked.rn = 1 after that left join removes the null-extended rows, so customers without a match disappear again. That would undo the inclusion rule you were trying to implement.

Decide how to represent the absence of an order. Null order fields mean no match; a made-up zero amount would blur that distinction with a real zero-value order.

If timestamps can be null in the actual dataset, define their meaning before removing our non-null assumption. Unknown time is not automatically the oldest or newest event, and default null ordering differs across databases.

Make the counterexamples do the reviewing

The quickest useful check is to compare the exact selected IDs and their associated values, not just the number of output rows.

For this dataset, the three versions should produce these results.

  • Latest order regardless of status returns A → 13, B → 21, C → 31.
  • Latest paid order returns A → 12 and B → 21.
  • Latest order, only if paid, returns B → 21.

Then add a customer with no orders, create another timestamp tie, and change which tied row is paid. If your query still matches the written rule, you have better evidence than a clean run on a perfectly polite dataset.

For production data, inspect the execution plan rather than promising that a window function is automatically cheap. An index beginning with (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC) may help the ordering access path, but filters, row counts, selected columns, and the database planner still matter. This all-customer query may process many rows even when it returns few.

For a useful next variation, try this salary-history and top-earner exercise. It asks you to identify the latest employee-department record before choosing the highest-paid employee in each department. That adds a second selection stage, so getting the first population right becomes even more important.

I like leaving this kind of practice with a small question I can reuse. Am I calculating a property of a group, or selecting a particular member of that group?

Once that distinction is clear, the query becomes much easier to explain. More importantly, every timestamp, status, and amount in the answer can point back to the row that actually earned its place.

~ Emily

title: How to Choose the Best Open Source Distributed Time Series Database
description:
This article explores what defines the best open source time series database, with a focus on three major projects: Apache IoTDB, TimechoDB, and InfluxDB. We contrast their benefits and help you decide which may be ideal for your application.

Why time-series databases matter

Traditional relational and general-purpose NoSQL databases struggle with workloads that involve high write rates, large numbers of concurrent series (high cardinality), time-window aggregations, and long-term historical retention. 

Time series databases are optimized to the job: they optimize streams of (timestamp, value) pairs, support efficient range queries, down-sampling, and retention policies, and aggressively compress data.

These properties make TSDBs essential when evaluating an open source distributed time series database for industrial telemetry or large-scale metrics pipelines

Apache IoTDB: A Leading Industrial-Grade Open Source TSDB

Apache IoTDB was built from scratch for the Internet of Things (IoT) and industrial telemetry application scenario. It features a cluster architecture (config nodes + data nodes) and offers built-in high-throughput writes, aligned time series, rich query semantics, and close big-data ecosystem integration.

Main features:

  • High compression and cost-efficient storage: IoTDB achieves strong disk compression ratios, reducing storage cost for long-term retention. 
  • Flexible deployment: edge, standalone, and distributed cluster modes are supported.
  • Powerful time-series query language: standard SQL queries support complex time-interval and device-level conditions.
  • Proven in industrial scenarios: widely adopted in energy, transportation, steel, and equipment monitoring industries.

These are the features that make Apache IoTDB one of the strongest choices for organizations seeking for an open source industry time series database that combines scale, performance, and industrial-ready modeling.

TimechoDB: Enterprise-grade Product Build on IoTDB

TimechoDB is the enterprise distribution built on top of the IoTDB open-source community project. The vendor describes TimechoDB as being based on the open‑source foundation and adding enterprise‑level functionalities such as cluster management, tooling, and services.


While not all enterprise features are open source, TimechoDB retains the open-source IoTDB core and is designed specifically for large-scale industrial environments that require: strong reliability, operational tooling, long-term stability, and vendor-backed support.

For businesses with heavy industrial workloads or production SLAs, TimechoDB provides a more complete ecosystem on top of the open-source engine.

InfluxDB: A Popular General-Purpose Open Source Time Series Database

InfluxDB is one of the most widely used open-source time-series databases. Designed for time‑series workloads, InfluxDB features high‑volume ingestion, real‑time analytics, and a mature ecosystem. As is recorded: "The most downloaded, most used, and most trusted open source time series database."

Main Features

  • Supports hundreds of millions of time‑series data points per second, cloud, on‑prem, and edge.
  • Offers SQL‑like query language, retention policies, downsampling, plugin ecosystem (e.g., Telegraf).
  • Huge community and prevalent use cases like monitoring, IoT telemetry, and analytics. Though InfluxDB is not directly comparable when it comes to industrial specialist features to IoTDB (e.g., very high correlation between device hierarchies, industrial directory structure), it is an excellent choice if one wants a general-purpose open-source time series database with very good usability and ecosystem.

How to pick between them

When selecting an open source distributed time series database , consider the following:

  • Ingestion rate & scale: For extremely high-throughput ingestion (millions of points/second) or very large numbers of series, use a system built for that (Apache IoTDB, TimechoDB).
  • Distributed & cluster deployment: Horizontal scaling and cluster mode with auto-failover are significant for an open-source distributed time series database. IoTDB supports auto-failover, cluster mode, and horizontal scaling.
  • Industrial features: If you're in IoT/industry (sensors, devices, edge+cloud), frameworks such as IoTDB bring domain-specific strengths (device tree hierarchies, aligned time-series, edge deployment).
  • Ecosystem & ease-of-use: For normal metrics, dashboards, monitoring, and large community resources, InfluxDB may be the most convenient.
  • Efficiency & hardware cost: If you need extremely high compression and low storage cost, Apache IoTDB or TimechoDB for sure.
  • Enterprise readiness & support: Consider community size, environment maturity, documentation, and enterprise tooling (TimechoDB will add some enterprise features on top of IoTDB).

Conclusion

If you want the best open source time series database, then you need to balance performance, features, and ecosystem. For all typical use-cases (monitoring, IoT backend)–InfluxDB will do perfectly. If you want an open source industry time series database with robust distributed architecture, industrial device modeling, and good compression, then Apache IoTDB is highly sought after. If you want vendor-supported support and enterprise readiness on IoTDB, then TimechoDB is also a good try.

In short, choosing an open source distributed time series database is not a generic decision—matching your workload (ingest volume, cardinality, analytics), deployment architecture (edge vs cloud vs hybrid), and operational needs (tooling, support, community) will guide you to the best solution.

By focusing on tools like IoTDB, TimechoDB, and InfluxDB, you’re positioning yourself to use a genuinely high‑quality open source time‑series platform capable of supporting modern data workloads at scale.

title: pgvector: Vector Search in PostgreSQL Without a New Database
description:
Every few months the industry discovers a new kind of database. This year it's vector databases — specialized stores for embeddings, the numerical fingerprints that power "semantic search," recommendations, and all the AI features landing in every product you use. The pitch is always the same: spin up this new service, sync your data into it, and pay for another always-on thing.

Before you do that: if you already run PostgreSQL, you probably don't need a new database at all.

pgvector is a Postgres extension that adds vector types, distance operators, and approximate-nearest-neighbor indexes to the database you're already running. I've now used it in production for semantic search over ~200k documents, and this post is everything I wish someone had told me on day one — the setup, the indexes, and the two traps that cost me a weekend.

The problem in one paragraph

Classic search matches words: you type "disk full," you get documents containing "disk full." Semantic search matches meaning: type "out of storage," and it finds the disk-full article too. Embeddings make this work — you send text to a model, it returns a few hundred floating-point numbers representing the meaning, and texts with similar meanings get similar numbers. Storing and querying those numbers at scale is the whole job. Postgres does it fine.

Setup is insultingly easy 

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE documents (
    id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    title     text NOT NULL,
    body      text NOT NULL,
    embedding vector(1536)
);

The vector(1536) matches the output width of OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small — the most common embedding model and a fine default. Whatever model you pick, the column width must match its output dimension, or inserts will fail loudly.

Insert and search:

-- insert (embedding generated by your app via the provider's API)
INSERT INTO documents (title, body, embedding)
VALUES ('Disk full', 'When df shows 100%...', '[0.012, -0.034, ...]');

-- find the 5 most similar documents to a query embedding
SELECT title, body, embedding <=> '[0.011, -0.032, ...]' AS distance
FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.011, -0.032, ...]'
LIMIT 5;

The <=> operator is cosine distance — pgvector ships <-> (L2), <#> (inner product), and <=> (cosine). For normalized embeddings, inner product and cosine rank identically, and cosine is the safe default for text search.

The part everyone skips: indexes

Without an index, every query is a full table scan with a distance computation per row. Fine at 1,000 rows. Ugly at 100,000. Painful at a million.

pgvector gives you two approximate index types. Today, you want HNSW:

CREATE INDEX ON documents
USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is a graph index — fast to query, great recall, and it doesn't require the data to be present at creation time. The older ivfflat index needs a representative dataset before you build it, or its clusters are garbage; that requirement surprises people exactly once. Just use HNSW.

Two knobs matter at query time:

SET hnsw.ef_search = 40;  -- higher = better recall, slower

Default ef_search is 40, which is a good starting point. If results feel wrong, raise it before you touch anything else. Accuracy problems are almost always recall problems.

Trap #1: the distance threshold nobody agrees on

The query above returns the 5 nearest documents — even if none of them are remotely relevant. Your application needs a cutoff, and here pgvector's docs go silent. There is no universal number because it depends on your embedding model and your data. What worked for me: take 100 queries where you know the right answer, plot the distance of the correct hit, and pick a threshold just past the worst case. Mine landed at 0.30 for that model and dataset. Yours will differ. Measure it.

Trap #2: embeddings generated with different models don't mix

I learned this the expensive way. Early on, I regenerated embeddings with a newer model for some rows and left others alone. Cosine distance between two different embedding spaces is meaningless — your queries will return confident nonsense from the mismatched rows, intermittently, which is the worst kind of bug. Add a column to record which model produced each embedding, and if you ever switch models, re-embed everything in one pass:

ALTER TABLE documents ADD COLUMN embed_model text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'text-embedding-3-small';

Where do embeddings come from?

Any embedding API works — OpenAI, Voyage, Cohere. But if you've been following along with the local LLM setup, here's the part I find genuinely neat: Ollama runs embedding models locally too:

ollama pull nomic-embed-text
curl http://localhost:11434/api/embeddings -d '{"model": "nomic-embed-text", "prompt": "how do I free up disk space"}'

That returns a 768-dimensional vector — so your vector(...) column would be vector(768) for this model — generated on your own hardware, for free, with the text never leaving your network. For a privacy-first stack, local embeddings plus pgvector is a complete semantic search pipeline with zero third parties.

Do you actually need a dedicated vector database?

Honest answer: probably not, at your scale. pgvector comfortably handles millions of vectors at single-digit millisecond query times, and it inherits everything Postgres gives you for free — transactions, point-in-time recovery, the backup strategy you already have, row-level security, and joins with your actual relational data. A dedicated vector store makes sense when you're doing tens of millions of vectors with extreme QPS, or when you need GPU-accelerated indexes. Everything short of that is a second database to run for no reason.

The pattern I keep returning to: Postgres first, specialize only when Postgres measurably fails you. It has not failed me yet.

title: IAM policies: the wide permissions that pass review

title: Understanding NestJS Architecture: A Beginner's Guide
description:
1. Introduction

NestJS is a progressive Node.js framework used to build efficient, scalable and maintainable server-side applications.

It is primarily built using TypeScript and provides a structured architecture for developing backend applications.

Unlike Express.js, which provides a minimal and flexible structure, NestJS follows a modular architecture that helps developers organize application code into separate components.

2. Why Do We Need NestJS Architecture?

Consider building an Instagram-like application. It requires several backend functionalities:

  • User registration and authentication
  • Creating and managing posts
  • Following users
  • Liking posts
  • Managing comments
  • Retrieving user feeds

Writing all these functionalities inside a single file makes the application difficult to maintain and debug.

NestJS solves this problem by organizing the application into separate modules, controllers and providers.

3. Main Components of NestJS Architecture

Modules

Modules organize related application components into logical groups.

Controllers

Controllers handle incoming HTTP requests and define API endpoints.

Providers and Services

Providers are injectable components managed by NestJS. Services commonly contain business logic.

Dependency Injection

Dependency Injection allows classes to receive their required dependencies without manually creating them.

4. Basic NestJS Architecture

A typical NestJS application follows this structure:

Client → Controller → Service → Database

  • The client sends an HTTP request.
  • The controller receives the request.
  • The service executes business logic.
  • The database stores or retrieves information.
  • The response is returned to the client.

5. NestJS vs Express.js

Express.js provides a minimal framework where developers organize their application according to their preferences.

NestJS provides a predefined architectural structure using modules, controllers, providers and dependency injection.

Both frameworks can build REST APIs, but NestJS provides more built-in architectural conventions.

6. Conclusion

NestJS architecture helps developers build backend applications with better organization, maintainability, scalability and separation of responsibilities.

Understanding modules, controllers, providers and dependency injection is the foundation for learning NestJS effectively.

title: Timelines, Bike Theft, and the Art of Designing Dim: Event-Driven Architecture for AI Agents
description:
By duskzhen

Imagine I park my bike outside my front door. Worried it might get stolen, I set up a security camera and hire an AI Agent:

"Keep an eye on my bike for me."

A naive implementation is to have the Agent poll the camera feed every few seconds:

Bike is still there. Bike is still there. Bike is still there. Someone walked past. Bike is still there.

By morning, the bike is safe—and the context window is completely blown.

Sure, that approach works. But what I actually need is for someone to notice when the bike might be in danger, review what happened, and decide what to do next. Eight hours of peace and quiet on the street shouldn't translate into eight hours of continuous LLM inference.

While designing Dim, we came back to this scenario so often that we started calling it our "Bike Theft Theory." It illustrates a simple core principle: Just because the environment is constantly changing doesn't mean the model needs to be constantly thinking.

The Camera Records; the Agent Checks on Demand

Let's try a different setup.

The camera records continuously. Meanwhile, the Agent can work on other tasks or simply wait idle. At some point, a lightweight motion detector notices someone approaching the bike and fires a notification.

Only then does the Agent pull up the relevant video clips: When did this person arrive? Did they just walk past, or are they tampering with the lock? Has the bike moved?

After inspecting the footage, the Agent might realize it's just a neighbor picking up something they dropped. It logs that assessment and goes back to waiting. Or, it might see the lock being cut and alert the owner using a pre-agreed method.

Here, the notification's only job is to say, "Something happened that's worth looking into." Someone approaching is a clue; whether they are stealing the bike requires looking at the evidence.


Four-act conceptual animation: record, detect change, notify, and review on demand. (Bike surveillance is a hypothetical scenario used to explain our runtime architecture, not a built-in camera feature in Dim.)

What if the detector misses something? The owner might walk out the next morning, see the bike is gone, and ask: "What happened last night?" As long as the underlying records exist, the Agent can work backward from that question and inspect the past.

To pull this off, the system has to solve two distinct problems:

  1. Leave behind records that might be needed later.
  2. Pull the Agent's attention over at the right moment.

Without the first, an alarm goes off and there's no way to investigate what happened. Without the second, you end up with a hard drive full of footage that nobody ever looks at.

This exact division of labor is where Dim's Timeline and Event-Driven Architecture begin.

Why Chat History Alone Isn't Enough

When I previously worked on DeepChat, I was inspired by the "Tape" mental model: treating Context as an append-only tape. User prompts, model responses, and tool outputs all move forward along a single track. That gives you a solid foundation for context compression, sliding windows, and branching.

With Dim, we wanted to take a step further outside the chat box.

The environment an Agent lives in is much busier than a simple request-response loop. Background commands finish on their own, other branches send messages, the system date rolls over, plugins load, and users change their minds while a tool is still mid-execution.

Some of these changes demand an immediate reaction. Others just need to be logged for posterity, or queued until the current task wraps up. We can't pretend these events didn't happen just because the model wasn't looking—nor can we dump every single environmental change straight into the model's prompt.

Going back to the bike: "The camera recorded this footage" and "The Agent watched this footage" are fundamentally different facts.

Dim's Timeline bakes this distinction directly into the runtime. It records operational events across tasks that affect subsequent behavior, while the model's context is projected selectively from facts like inputs, outputs, tool results, and context states. The scope of what's recorded on the Timeline is intentionally broader than what the model sees in any single inference request.

And "recording the environment" doesn't mean dumping the entire world raw into a database. In our bike setup, heavy video files stay in blob storage while the Timeline records clip indices, detection events, and follow-up actions. In Dim, the key is recording the operational facts needed for coordination, auditing, and recovery—while reading the heavy raw materials on demand.

The Timeline: Giving Every Event a Deterministic Place

The word "Timeline" might sound like a simple timestamped log. In Dim, however, it defines the canonical execution order of the runtime.

Every branch has its own Timeline. As events are appended, the Timeline assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number. The runtime understands causality and order strictly through this sequence; a wall clock can tell a human when something happened, but it cannot replace the deterministic order of the sequence.

Why does this matter?

Suppose you tell the Agent, "Forget about the bike for now," right as a slow background detector finally returns "Someone is approaching." The system needs to know which task that detection belongs to and exactly where the cancellation command sits in the sequence so it can apply the right rules. Relying on whichever async callback finishes first is a recipe for resurrecting canceled tasks.

In our bike analogy, the Timeline looks like this:

Records append continuously →

Park Bike ── Clip Index ── Approach Detected ── Notification ── Read Clip ── Verdict
                                  │                                 ▲
                                  └─── Draws Attention ─────────────┘

Raw footage stays in storage for later review; the current judgment only fetches the relevant clip.

New conclusions don't overwrite old facts, either. First we record "Approach Detected," and later we record "Confirmed just passing by." We know both the current state of the world and the exact reasoning trail that got us there.

In code, this ordering comes with a strict persistence guarantee: in the SQLite storage path used by the App Server, the Timeline only advances its published cursor after an event batch is successfully committed to disk, which in turn allows the Dispatcher to broadcast them. Returning from append, committing to storage, and publishing to subscribers are explicitly distinct phases (see Timeline commit and publish implementation).

This ensures every subsequent reaction is grounded in verifiable history. Records aren't just for post-mortem debugging—they actively drive how the system moves forward.

Event-Driven Runtime: Only Wake Up What Needs to Move

Once you have a Timeline, something needs to consume it.

Dim uses a Dispatcher to broadcast published events in sequence. Runtime capabilities subscribe only to the event types they care about. Upon receiving an event, a capability updates its internal state or kicks off a job, writing any resulting facts back to the Timeline (see Dispatcher subscription and dispatch implementation).

Being "event-driven" happens first and foremost between these runtime components. It does not mean firing an LLM request for every single event.

When the camera detects motion, a lightweight heuristic can decide if it warrants a notification; when video archiving finishes, it just updates a record; when a monitoring task is canceled, it quietly cleans up its resources. Only items that genuinely require the model's reasoning are routed into the input channel.

We strictly separate three stages:

Stage What It Means
Record Event The fact has entered the auditable history.
Dispatch Event Interested runtime capabilities can react to it.
Deliver to Model Relevant content has entered the model-visible context via inputs or tool results.

Recording an event does not mean the model knows about it yet.

Dim's context management makes this boundary explicit: ordinary runtime events don't magically turn into LLM messages on their own. Content meant for the model must enter the context through adopted inputs or tool results. For instance, an input is first recorded as an event, and only when input/consumed occurs does the history projection expand it into an actual model message (see Input consumption and message projection).


Using a background command completion as an example, this animation shows how an event triggers a new notification input. Arrows indicate processing causality; notifications, input consumption, and model requests themselves also leave records on the Timeline.

This gives us a two-tier filter for "what's worth looking at." First, the runtime follows capability contracts to decide which environmental changes warrant delivery. Second, once delivered, the model evaluates the notification against its current goal to decide whether to inspect deeper or take action. Meanwhile, the user can step in at any time to adjust the goal or shift focus.

No Bike Required: Background Commands as a Real-World Example

You don't need a physical security camera to see this in action. Consider a classic developer workflow: an Agent kicks off a long-running build or test suite in the background and moves on to other work. When that command finally finishes, how do we bring the Agent back?

Dim's background execution capability follows the exact path we just described:

  1. The command finishes, emitting an exec/ended event with the execution result.
  2. Once committed and published, the Dispatcher routes the event to the background execution capability.
  3. The capability checks the exit status and branch state; if wake-up conditions are met, it appends a notification input.
  4. The notification wraps a <dim-notification> tag, a short output preview, and instructions on how to fetch the full log, entering the scheduler as a Steer input.
  5. Once the input is consumed, the model reads the notification in its next turn and decides what to do.

In our current implementation, canceled background tasks won't trigger a wake-up along this path, nor will branches that are in the middle of shutting down. Because the completion event and the notification input are committed separately, our crash-recovery logic also checks for completed jobs that needed a wake-up but haven't emitted a notification yet (see Background result handling and Notification input construction).

This is the exact developer equivalent of the bike scenario: the full stdout/stderr log is the recorded footage, the completion alert is the motion notification, and calling a tool to read the full log is pulling up the video clip.

The model never has to spin in a loop asking, "Is it done yet?" And when the command does finish, it doesn't blindly force the old task to resume—if the user has already pivoted to a new goal, the Agent interprets the late-arriving result in the context of its new instructions.

At this point, the Timeline handles recording and ordering, and the event-driven runtime handles reaction and scheduling. That leaves one final puzzle: When the model receives this text in its context, how does it know what the message actually means?

Meta Prompt: Teaching the Model How to Read Its Inputs

In our previous post on Dim's Meta Prompt (An Input Manual for Models), we highlighted a subtle quirk of LLM APIs: whether a piece of text is typed directly by a human operator or injected as a notification by the runtime, it often arrives at the model API wearing the exact same user role.

If the model relies solely on the message role, it can easily confuse "The human user just gave me a new command" with "A background process from five minutes ago just exited."

The bike analogy works the same way. When the camera says "Someone is approaching," that's a sensor observation. When the owner says "Check who was just near my bike," that's an operator command. Both might point to the exact same video clip, but their origin, authority, and expected next steps are completely different.

Dim's Meta Prompt bridges this semantic gap. Alongside the system prompt, it provides an explicit "Input Guide." Each runtime capability registers the structural tags it introduces and their exact semantics, while dynamic payloads are delivered later through corresponding inputs:

  • For <dim-notification> (Background Alerts): The guide explains that this is the result of previously initiated work, the snippet is a preview from that command, and full output can be fetched on demand—and crucially, if the parent task is obsolete, do not restart it.
  • For <dim-state>: It explains state-update semantics, where newer values from the same source supersede earlier ones.
  • For <dim-rule>: It defines scoping and activation/deactivation lifecycles.

(See Input Guide implementation and Background notification semantics.)

Applied to our bike scenario, the model knows immediately which message is a sensor observation, which is the owner's instruction, whether bike monitoring is still active, and what countermeasures are authorized.

Of course, XML tags alone don't grant security permissions, and slapping an "Alert" label on sensor data doesn't turn it into an executable command. The model uses the Input Guide to understand meaning, while the runtime strictly enforces permission checks before any tool action is executed.

The Timeline gives events a place, the event-driven Dispatcher routes changes to the right handlers, and the Meta Prompt gives the model a framework to interpret them.

Making the Entire Harness Part of the Intelligence

Now, let's wire all these pieces together.

The environment changes, and facts are written to the Timeline. Runtime capabilities react to those events and push only what requires reasoning into the input queue. The model combines the Meta Prompt, its current objective, and its context history to make a judgment—calling tools when it needs more evidence, or triggering actions when it needs to intervene. Those tool outputs and subsequent environmental shifts then become new records on the Timeline.


Architectural overview: The Meta Prompt provides rules for reading inputs rather than acting as an async queue processor. The model's actions affect the environment via tools, and the results flow back into the Timeline.

When you view an Agent Harness this way, you realize you don't have to shove every ounce of responsibility onto the LLM. Recording, ordering, scheduling, provenance tracking, and permission enforcement are handled deterministically by the runtime; the model saves its tokens and attention for synthesizing goals and evidence.

This separation also makes long-horizon tasks sustainable:

  • Context Compression & Recall: When the context window fills up, summaries carry forward the past while re-asserting active rules and states. If the model later needs fine-grained details, Dim's recall tool lets it search and retrieve prior conversations and work records on demand. Compression only changes what is packed into the current inference request—the underlying historical facts remain safely stored on the Timeline (see Context compression checkpoints and Recall tool).
  • Idempotent Crash Recovery: Recovery respects the boundary between state and side effects. Re-reading a record that says "Alert already sent to owner" restores the system's awareness that the alert was sent—it doesn't fire the alert a second time. Rebuilding internal state and re-executing external side effects have strictly separated boundaries (see Time-bus side-effect guarantees).

Naturally, architecture alone doesn't make detectors infallible or models immune to misjudgment. If notifications are too noisy, the Agent gets woken up constantly; if they're too sparse, critical changes slip through. And if you still end up piping every raw video frame into the prompt, calling your log a "Timeline" won't save you a single token.

What's truly worth engineering is the coordination between the runtime and the model:

  • Can past records be retrieved when needed?
  • Do notifications provide enough clues without overwhelming the context?
  • Does the model understand the provenance and authority of incoming messages?
  • Does it have the evidence required to act, and does it get feedback after acting?

Back to that bike parked outside my door: I want an Agent that doesn't stare at the camera feed all night, yet snaps to attention the moment someone approaches; reviews the footage before jumping to conclusions; remembers if I've changed my mind about watching the bike; and can explain clearly the next morning what happened and why it handled things the way it did.

That is the exact coordination we're building in Dim—making sure environmental changes are reliably recorded and routed, so the model can see clearly right when it needs to.

The Dim repository contains the Rust implementation discussed here.

Editorial note: AI tools assisted with the English adaptation and visuals.

title: Generic Decline Means the Bank Answered a Different Question
description:
Of all the responses an issuer can return, the generic decline is the most honest about its own uselessness. It says the payment was refused and declines to say why — a shrug rendered in two digits. Teams new to failed payments tend to read it as a verdict on the customer: insufficient money, closed account, something terminal. Teams who have worked a queue for a while read it correctly, as a statement about information: the bank knows, the bank is not telling, and the recovery plan has to be built for a problem whose cause is hidden.

That hiddenness is deliberate. Issuers return generic codes for fraud-screening reasons, for legacy-system reasons, and sometimes because the specific reason sits in a category they will not disclose to merchants at all. Arguing with the code is pointless. Working around it is not. A generic decline tells you nothing about this payment — but the pattern around it tells you a great deal. The same card succeeding last month, the amount, the hour, whether other issuers are failing the same way that day: context is the diagnostic the code refuses to be.

The practical sequence follows from that. First, do not retry identically and immediately; a generic decline repeated at once usually earns the same shrug, and rapid identical attempts can trip the very fraud sensitivity that may have caused it. Space the attempt, vary the hour, and let any card-updater signal refresh the credentials in between. Second, contact the subscriber earlier than you would for a self-explanatory code — for a generic decline, the customer often is the diagnostic, since their bank will tell them things it will not tell you. Third, watch the account's other signals: a generic decline on a card that also fails its update link and ignores every message is graduating, by evidence, toward a hard outcome, whatever the code says.

This is where a diagnostic reading of the generic decline code and the sequence it calls for earns its keep: it treats the code as the start of an investigation rather than an answer, and lays out how the retry spacing, the outreach timing, and the account's own history combine into a working theory of what actually went wrong. Merchants who build that habit stop losing their most recoverable accounts to their least informative code.

There is a measurement trap here too. If generic declines are bucketed with hard declines in reporting — an easy default, since both look final — the recoverable share of the queue is understated and the whole recovery program looks weaker than it is. Split the bucket. Generic declines recovered at soft-decline rates in most queues once they are worked as soft; burying them makes a solvable problem look like fate.

A worked example makes the pattern concrete. A subscriber of four years, never late, fails a renewal with a generic decline on a Tuesday morning. Nothing about the account suggests risk; everything about the timing suggests a crowded issuer queue. The recovery that works is unglamorous: one attempt two days later at a different hour, a short message on day three offering the update link, and the payment collecting on the second attempt. No new information ever arrived from the bank. The context did all the diagnosing the code refused to do.

The bank answered a different question than the one you asked. Your system should respond by asking better ones — of the timing, of the pattern, and, politely and early, of the customer.

Swipe Again builds its retry and outreach sequences around decline-code triage, generic declines included: spaced attempts, early subscriber contact, and counting that keeps the shrug separate from the verdict. A code that tells you nothing is still telling you where to look.
