title: # NestJS Validation
description:
DTO pattern, class-validator, class-transformer, built-in Pipes,
custom Pipes, and global ValidationPipe setup

These notes explain how NestJS receives data from a request, checks
whether that data is valid, and converts it into the format your
application expects.

The examples use a simple API for creating and fetching posts. You can
adapt the same ideas to users, profiles, authentication, or other
modules.

1. Why do we need validation?

Imagine your API has an endpoint that creates a post. It expects a
request body like this:

{
  "content": "Learning NestJS",
  "visibility": "public"
}

But a client might accidentally send:

{
  "content": 12345,
  "visibility": "everyone"
}

Without validation, incorrect data may travel deeper into your
application and cause unexpected behaviour or database errors.

Validation helps us check incoming data at the API boundary. We can
reject invalid requests early and return a clear error response.

The basic idea: Do not blindly trust data coming from the client.
Validate it before using it.

2. What is the DTO pattern?

DTO stands for Data Transfer Object.

A DTO describes the shape of data that is allowed to move into or out of
an application layer. In NestJS, DTO classes are commonly used to
describe the data an endpoint expects from the client.

For example, when a client creates a post, the API may expect:

  • content: a string.
  • visibility: either "public" or "private".

We can describe that structure with a DTO.

export class CreatePostDto {
  content: string;
  visibility: 'public' | 'private';
}

A controller can then use that DTO as the type of its request body:

@Post()
createPost(@Body() createPostDto: CreatePostDto) {
  return this.postsService.create(createPostDto);
}

Why use DTOs instead of accepting any object?

DTOs give the request a clear structure.

They help you:

  • Understand what data an endpoint expects.
  • Keep controller method signatures readable.
  • Reuse request shapes where appropriate.
  • Attach validation rules to incoming fields.
  • Avoid passing arbitrary request data directly into your business logic.

DTOs are not database entities

A DTO and a database entity serve different purposes.

DTO Entity / database model

Describes data accepted or returned Describes how data is represented
by an API operation. or persisted in the database.

Designed around an API use case. Designed around storage and
relationships.

May contain validation rules. Usually contains
persistence-related structure and
behaviour.

For example, a CreateUserDto might accept a password. Your database
user model should store a password hash, not the raw password. The DTO
and database model should not automatically be treated as the same
thing.

A useful naming convention

Common DTO names include:

  • CreatePostDto
  • UpdatePostDto
  • LoginDto
  • RegisterUserDto
  • GetPostsQueryDto

The name should make the purpose of the incoming data clear.

3. What are class-validator and class-transformer?

NestJS commonly uses two packages alongside DTO classes.

class-validator

class-validator checks whether values satisfy validation rules.

For example:

  • Is this value a string?
  • Is this email address valid?
  • Is this number within an allowed range?
  • Is this field optional?
  • Is this string within a certain length?

Install it with:

npm install class-validator

class-transformer

class-transformer helps convert plain JavaScript objects into class
instances and can transform values.

For example, data parsed from an HTTP request normally starts as a plain
object. The ValidationPipe can use class-transformer to turn that
object into an instance of your DTO class.

Install it with:

npm install class-transformer

How are they different?

Package Main responsibility

class-validator Checks whether values follow the
rules defined by decorators.

class-transformer Converts plain objects into class
instances and transforms values.

An easy way to remember:

  • Transformer: prepares or converts the incoming object.
  • Validator: checks whether the prepared data follows the rules.

They work together, but they do different jobs.

4. Adding validation decorators to a DTO

Validation decorators are placed above DTO properties.

import { IsString, IsNotEmpty, MaxLength, IsIn } from 'class-validator';

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  @MaxLength(280)
  content: string;

  @IsIn(['public', 'private'])
  visibility: 'public' | 'private';
}

Let's understand the decorators.

Decorator What it checks

@IsString() The value must be a string.
@IsNotEmpty() The value must not be empty.
@MaxLength(280) The string must not exceed 280 characters.
@IsIn([...]) The value must match one of the listed options.

Now, if a client sends a number as content, or uses an unsupported
visibility value, validation can reject the request.

More commonly used decorators 

import {
  IsString,
  IsNumber,
  IsBoolean,
  IsEmail,
  IsOptional,
  IsNotEmpty,
  Min,
  Max,
  MinLength,
  MaxLength,
  IsEnum,
  IsArray,
  ArrayMinSize,
  IsUUID,
} from 'class-validator';

Examples:

export class RegisterUserDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  username: string;

  @IsEmail()
  email: string;

  @IsString()
  @MinLength(8)
  password: string;
}

export class PaginationDto {
  @IsNumber()
  @Min(1)
  page: number;

  @IsNumber()
  @Min(1)
  @Max(100)
  limit: number;
}

The decorator only defines the rule. The rules are actually executed
when a validation mechanism, such as NestJS's ValidationPipe,
processes the DTO.

5. Optional fields with @IsOptional()

Sometimes a field is not required.

For example, a user may update their profile without changing their bio.

import { IsOptional, IsString, MaxLength } from 'class-validator';

export class UpdateProfileDto {
  @IsOptional()
  @IsString()
  @MaxLength(160)
  bio?: string;
}

@IsOptional() tells class-validator to skip the other validators for
that property when its value is null or undefined.

The ? in bio?: string is TypeScript syntax. It says the property may
be absent from the type.

These two pieces are related, but they are not identical:

  • ? describes optionality to TypeScript.
  • @IsOptional() affects runtime validation.

If your API should allow an omitted field but reject null, be careful:
@IsOptional() skips validation for both null and undefined. You
may need a different validation rule for that requirement.

6. Nested DTOs and @ValidateNested()

Sometimes the request contains an object inside another object.

Example request:

{
  "content": "Hello",
  "author": {
    "name": "Rohith",
    "email": "rohith@example.com"
  }
}

Create a separate DTO for the nested object:

import { IsEmail, IsString, ValidateNested } from 'class-validator';
import { Type } from 'class-transformer';

export class AuthorDto {
  @IsString()
  name: string;

  @IsEmail()
  email: string;
}

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  content: string;

  @ValidateNested()
  @Type(() => AuthorDto)
  author: AuthorDto;
}

Why are both decorators used?

  • @ValidateNested() tells class-validator to validate the nested object.
  • @Type(() => AuthorDto) tells class-transformer what class should be used for that nested value.

Without the transformation metadata, nested plain objects may not be
converted into the expected class instances, so nested validation may
not work as intended.

For an array of nested objects, use @ValidateNested({ each: true })
and @Type(() => SomeDto).

7. What is a Pipe in NestJS?

A Pipe is a class that can run before a route handler receives a value.

A pipe can do two important jobs:

  1. Transformation: Convert incoming data into another form.
  2. Validation: Check incoming data and reject it if it is invalid.

For example, a route parameter arrives as text:

GET /posts/123

The value of id initially comes from the URL as a string. A pipe can
convert it into a number before the controller method uses it.

Where do Pipes fit in the request flow?

A simplified flow looks like this:

Client sends HTTP request
        |
        v
NestJS receives the request
        |
        v
Guards and interceptors (where configured)
        |
        v
Pipes process route arguments
        |
        v
Controller method runs
        |
        v
Service / business logic
        |
        v
Response goes back to the client

The important point for this topic is that pipes process values before
those values are passed to the controller handler.

8. Built-in Pipes

NestJS provides ready-made pipes for common tasks. You do not need to
create your own pipe for every simple conversion or validation.

Some useful built-in pipes are:

Pipe Purpose

ValidationPipe Validates incoming data using DTO
validation metadata.

ParseIntPipe Converts a value to an integer or
throws an error.

ParseFloatPipe Converts a value to a number with a
decimal part or throws an error.

ParseBoolPipe Parses a boolean value or throws an
error.

ParseUUIDPipe Checks whether a value is a valid
UUID.

ParseArrayPipe Parses and validates array input
according to its options.

DefaultValuePipe Supplies a default value when the
input is null or undefined.

ParseEnumPipe Checks whether a value belongs to a
specified enum.

Example: ParseIntPipe 

import { Controller, Get, Param, ParseIntPipe } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('posts')
export class PostsController {
  @Get(':id')
  findOne(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number) {
    return { id };
  }
}

If the client requests /posts/123, the pipe converts the route
parameter into the number 123.

If the client requests /posts/abc, parsing fails and NestJS returns an
error instead of passing an invalid number to the controller.

Example: ParseBoolPipe 

@Get('status')
getStatus(@Query('active', ParseBoolPipe) active: boolean) {
  return { active };
}

A valid boolean query value is parsed before the handler runs. Invalid
values are rejected.

Example: DefaultValuePipe 

import { DefaultValuePipe, ParseIntPipe } from '@nestjs/common';

@Get()
findAll(
  @Query('limit', new DefaultValuePipe(10), ParseIntPipe)
  limit: number,
) {
  return { limit };
}

If the client does not provide limit, the default value 10 is used.
The next pipe then parses the value as an integer.

When multiple pipes are attached to one parameter, they process the
value in the order they are listed.

Example: ParseUUIDPipe 

@Get(':id')
findById(
  @Param('id', new ParseUUIDPipe()) id: string,
) {
  return this.postsService.findById(id);
}

This checks the route parameter before it reaches the controller method.

9. What is ValidationPipe?

ValidationPipe is NestJS's built-in pipe for validating incoming
request data using DTO classes and validation decorators.

For example:

@Post()
create(@Body() createPostDto: CreatePostDto) {
  return this.postsService.create(createPostDto);
}

When a ValidationPipe is active, NestJS can use the metadata on
CreatePostDto to validate the body before calling create().

If validation succeeds, the controller receives the validated DTO value.

If validation fails, NestJS throws a BadRequestException by default
and the controller handler is not called.

Important distinction

Writing decorators inside a DTO does not automatically validate every
request.

You need to apply ValidationPipe---locally, at controller or route
level, or globally---so that NestJS actually runs the validation.

10. Setting up ValidationPipe globally

In most applications, it is useful to apply validation globally so that
DTO validation works consistently across controllers.

Open your main.ts file:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

  app.useGlobalPipes(
    new ValidationPipe({
      whitelist: true,
      forbidNonWhitelisted: true,
      transform: true,
    }),
  );

  await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
}

bootstrap();

Let's understand the three options.

whitelist: true

This removes properties that do not have any validation decorators in
the DTO.

Suppose your DTO is:

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  content: string;
}

The client sends:

{
  "content": "Hello",
  "isAdmin": true
}

With whitelist: true, isAdmin is removed because it is not decorated
in the DTO.

forbidNonWhitelisted: true

Instead of silently removing extra properties, this option makes the
request fail when it contains a property that is not allowed by the DTO.

Using the previous example, sending isAdmin results in a validation
error.

This is useful when you want clients to know that they are sending
unsupported fields.

Note: forbidNonWhitelisted is normally used together with
whitelist.

transform: true

This enables transformation of plain incoming objects into DTO class
instances. It also enables supported primitive conversion for route and
query parameters when their types are declared.

For example:

@Get()
findAll(@Query('page') page: number) {
  return { page };
}

With transformation enabled, NestJS can convert a query value such as
"2" into the number 2 when the parameter type metadata is available.

For more complex query validation, a dedicated DTO is usually clearer.

Quick summary

Option What happens

whitelist: true Removes properties without
validation decorators.

forbidNonWhitelisted: true Rejects requests containing those
extra properties.

transform: true Converts plain input into DTO
instances and supports suitable
primitive conversion.

11. Local vs global ValidationPipe

You can apply a pipe at different levels.

Parameter level 

@Get(':id')
findOne(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number) {
  return { id };
}

Only that parameter uses the pipe.

Method level 

@Post()
@UsePipes(new ValidationPipe())
create(@Body() dto: CreatePostDto) {
  return this.postsService.create(dto);
}

The pipe applies to the route handler's parameters.

Controller level 

@UsePipes(new ValidationPipe())
@Controller('posts')
export class PostsController {
  // Route handlers
}

The pipe applies to handlers in that controller.

Global level 

app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe());

The pipe applies across the application.

For a consistent API, a global ValidationPipe is a common choice. You
can still use specific built-in pipes on individual parameters where
they are needed.

12. Creating a Custom Pipe

Built-in pipes cover common requirements. But sometimes your application
has a rule that is specific to your project.

For example, imagine a route expects a post ID that must be a positive
integer. You can create a custom pipe for that rule.

A custom pipe implements the PipeTransform interface and defines a
transform() method.

import {
  ArgumentMetadata,
  BadRequestException,
  Injectable,
  PipeTransform,
} from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class PositiveIntPipe implements PipeTransform {
  transform(value: unknown, metadata: ArgumentMetadata): number {
    const parsedValue = Number(value);

    if (!Number.isInteger(parsedValue) || parsedValue <= 0) {
      throw new BadRequestException('ID must be a positive integer');
    }

    return parsedValue;
  }
}

Understanding the important parts

  • @Injectable() marks the class as a provider that NestJS can manage.
  • PipeTransform is the interface that custom pipes implement.
  • transform() receives the incoming value and metadata about the argument.
  • The method checks the value.
  • If the value is invalid, it throws an exception.
  • If the value is valid, it returns the transformed value.

Using the custom pipe 

@Get(':id')
findOne(
  @Param('id', PositiveIntPipe) id: number,
) {
  return this.postsService.findOne(id);
}

Now the controller receives a positive integer. Invalid values are
rejected before the handler runs.

What is ArgumentMetadata?

The metadata parameter gives information about the value being
processed.

It includes:

  • type: where the value comes from, such as body, query, param, or a custom source.
  • metatype: the expected class or type metadata, when available.
  • data: the name of the route argument, such as id.

You do not need to use metadata in every custom pipe, but it is
available when your logic needs to know what kind of argument is being
processed.

When should you create a custom pipe?

Create one when you have a reusable transformation or validation rule
that is not already handled well by a built-in pipe.

Examples include:

  • Checking that an ID is a positive integer.
  • Converting a custom date format.
  • Validating a project-specific route parameter format.
  • Normalizing a value before the controller receives it.

Do not create a custom pipe just to repeat something a built-in pipe
already does.

13. What happens when validation fails?

Suppose your DTO is:

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  content: string;
}

The client sends:

{
  "content": 123
}

The flow is:

  1. The request reaches NestJS.
  2. The ValidationPipe processes the request body.
  3. The plain object is transformed as configured.
  4. class-validator checks the DTO rules.
  5. @IsString() fails because the value is a number.
  6. NestJS throws a BadRequestException.
  7. The controller method is not executed.

The exact response body can depend on your NestJS configuration and
exception handling, but the default validation error uses HTTP status
400 Bad Request.

Why is this useful?

The service layer does not need to repeat basic request checks that
belong at the API boundary. It can focus on business rules, while the
DTO and validation pipe handle the structure and format of incoming
data.

Remember that DTO validation does not replace business-level checks. For
example, checking whether a username is already taken usually requires
looking at stored data and belongs in application logic or a dedicated
validation mechanism.

14. Common mistakes to avoid

1. Forgetting to enable ValidationPipe

You may add decorators to a DTO and still find that invalid requests are
accepted. Check that a ValidationPipe is applied.

2. Forgetting to install the packages

If you use decorators from class-validator and class-transformer,
make sure both packages are installed.

npm install class-validator class-transformer

3. Using TypeScript types as if they validate runtime data

This:

create(@Body() dto: CreatePostDto) {}

does not, by itself, validate the request. TypeScript types are not a
replacement for runtime validation.

4. Forgetting decorators on DTO properties

With whitelist: true, properties without validation decorators are
treated as non-whitelisted. If a property should be accepted, add the
appropriate validation decorator.

5. Confusing @IsOptional() with ?

The question mark is for TypeScript. @IsOptional() controls runtime
validation behaviour.

6. Expecting a DTO to check database rules automatically

A DTO can check formats and values, such as whether an email is valid.
It does not automatically know whether that email already exists in your
database.

7. Forgetting nested transformation

For nested DTO validation, remember to use @ValidateNested() and
@Type(() => NestedDto) where appropriate.

15. How these concepts fit together in a real endpoint

Here is a small example that brings the concepts together.

Step 1: Create the DTO 

// create-post.dto.ts
import { IsIn, IsNotEmpty, IsString, MaxLength } from 'class-validator';

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  @MaxLength(280)
  content: string;

  @IsIn(['public', 'private'])
  visibility: 'public' | 'private';
}

Step 2: Use the DTO in the controller 

// posts.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Post } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CreatePostDto } from './dto/create-post.dto';

@Controller('posts')
export class PostsController {
  @Post()
  create(@Body() dto: CreatePostDto) {
    return {
      message: 'Post request received',
      data: dto,
    };
  }
}

Step 3: Enable validation globally 

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

  app.useGlobalPipes(
    new ValidationPipe({
      whitelist: true,
      forbidNonWhitelisted: true,
      transform: true,
    }),
  );

  await app.listen(3000);
}

bootstrap();

Step 4: Test the endpoint

A valid request:

POST /posts
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "content": "Learning NestJS validation",
  "visibility": "public"
}

An invalid request:

{
  "content": 123,
  "visibility": "everyone",
  "isAdmin": true
}

The invalid request should be rejected because:

  • content is not a string.
  • visibility is not one of the accepted values.
  • isAdmin is not part of the DTO and is rejected because forbidNonWhitelisted is enabled.

16. Quick revision

Concept Remember it this way

DTO Describes the data an API operation
expects or returns.

class-validator Checks values against validation
decorators.

class-transformer Converts plain objects into class
instances and transforms values.

Pipe Processes a value before the route
handler receives it.

Built-in Pipe A ready-made pipe for common
parsing or validation tasks.

Custom Pipe A pipe you write for your own
transformation or validation rule.

ValidationPipe NestJS pipe that connects DTO
metadata with runtime validation.

whitelist Removes properties without
validation decorators.

forbidNonWhitelisted Rejects requests containing extra,
non-whitelisted properties.

transform Enables DTO instance transformation
and suitable primitive conversion.

17. Interview-style questions to practise

Try answering these without looking at the notes:

  1. What is a DTO, and why do we use it in NestJS?
  2. What is the difference between a DTO and a database entity?
  3. What is the difference between class-validator and class-transformer?
  4. Does adding decorators to a DTO automatically validate a request?
  5. What is a Pipe in NestJS?
  6. What is the difference between transformation and validation?
  7. Name some built-in Pipes in NestJS.
  8. What does ParseIntPipe do when it receives an invalid value?
  9. What is the purpose of ValidationPipe?
  10. What is the difference between whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted?
  11. Why do we enable transform: true?
  12. How do you create a custom Pipe?
  13. What is the purpose of the transform() method?
  14. Why are @ValidateNested() and @Type() useful together?
  15. Why is DTO validation not a replacement for business logic validation?

Final takeaway

Think of the whole process like this:

  • DTO: describes what the request should look like.
  • Decorators: define the rules for each property.
  • class-transformer: helps turn incoming plain data into class instances.
  • class-validator: checks whether the data follows the rules.
  • Pipes: transform or validate values before the controller receives them.
  • Global ValidationPipe: applies a consistent validation setup across the application.

Once you understand how these pieces work together, request validation
in NestJS becomes much easier to follow and maintain.

These are learning notes with practical examples. Always check the
NestJS and package documentation for version-specific behaviour and
configuration details.

title: MongoDB X.509 authentication needs a subject-to-user mapping review
description:
MongoDB X.509 authentication needs a subject-to-user mapping review

MongoDB supports X.509 certificate authentication for clients and for internal authentication between members of replica sets and sharded clusters. The feature is useful when a workload should authenticate with a certificate instead of a shared password. It also moves several familiar identity questions into certificate and directory configuration, where they are easier to miss during a routine database review.

The database does not accept "a valid certificate" as a complete identity by default. A client presents a certificate during TLS, and MongoDB authenticates an external user derived from the certificate subject. That user exists in the $external authentication database. Authorization still comes from roles assigned to that user. If any certificate from the same trusted authority can map to a privileged user, certificate validation has replaced a password without reducing entitlement.

The trust chain is only the first check

The client must trust the server certificate, and the server must trust the authority that issued client certificates. Hostname verification protects the client from connecting to an impostor. Revocation or short certificate lifetimes limit the value of a stolen key. None of those checks proves that the certificate was issued to the correct application identity.

A private certificate authority can issue a certificate for any subject it accepts. If the registration process lets a team choose an arbitrary subject or common name, that team can request the identity of another application. The CA's issuance policy, approval workflow, and subject naming rules are therefore part of the database authorization model.

A certificate's Subject Alternative Name is not a substitute for the subject mapping unless the deployed MongoDB version and driver use it for that purpose. Record the exact subject format and test it with the actual driver. Do not invent a mapping from an email address, Kubernetes service name, or workload label without documentation and a test.

The $external user carries the roles

MongoDB documents X.509 users as users in the $external database. The external identity is authentication context; the roles attached to that user still decide which databases, collections, and actions are available. A certificate for a reporting workload should not receive root or clusterAdmin because the certificate is stored in a managed secret.

Role review should follow the certificate to the workload that owns it. Which process uses the private key? Which team can read it? Which deployment definitions attach the certificate? Which role grants can the workload perform? Does the workload need to write to the database, or only read from a set of collections? Are administrative operations performed by a different identity?

The external user should be inventoried with a human owner and a certificate fingerprint or serial, not only a subject string. If the certificate rotates every 30 days, the identity may remain stable while the key material changes. If the subject changes on every rotation, role assignments can drift or break. Decide which identifier is stable and how the database user is reconciled.

Client and internal authentication are different risks

X.509 is also used between MongoDB members. A member certificate that can authenticate as a client user could have consequences beyond cluster transport. The documentation notes that a client presenting a member certificate can attempt MONGODB-X509 authentication as a user in $external. Separate certificate authorities and subject conventions for members and clients when the deployment supports that separation.

Internal membership credentials should be scoped to cluster services, not made available to application pods or general CI identities. Store member keys on the database nodes and protect them with file permissions and host controls. Audit certificate issuance and renewal, and keep a break-glass process that does not depend on one expired member certificate.

Operational tests

Test a valid client certificate with the expected subject and role. Test a certificate with the correct CA but an unexpected subject. Test an expired certificate, a certificate for the wrong hostname, and a key without the client authentication usage if the deployment expects one. Record the result at the database layer, not only at the TLS terminator.

Review logs for authentication successes and failures without logging keys or full certificate contents. Confirm that the driver sends authSource=$external, uses TLS, and references the intended certificate and CA files. Do not disable certificate verification to solve a hostname mismatch. Fix the service name or certificate instead.

What good looks like

The database team should be able to answer which CA may issue client identities, which subjects map to which $external users, which roles those users have, and which workloads possess the private keys. Certificate issuance, rotation, revocation, and database role changes should have an owner and a test. A workload certificate should expire on a schedule that the workload owner can meet.

X.509 authentication can be stronger than a shared password, particularly when keys stay on the workload and issuance is controlled. It is not a complete authorization design. The certificate proves possession of a key within a trust chain. The database role decides what that key can do.

References

  • MongoDB manual: Authentication on self-managed deployments
  • MongoDB manual: X.509 security
  • MongoDB manual: Plan TLS for self-managed deployments
  • MongoDB manual: Configure X.509 client authentication

title: Best Bank Statement Converter: How to Test a Parser With Tie-Outs
description:
The best test for a bank statement parser, and the one we used to pick the best bank statement converter, is a tie-out: for every account on the statement, the printed opening balance plus the sum of the extracted rows must equal the printed closing balance, to the cent. If that holds, the extraction is almost certainly right. If it doesn't, the size of the gap usually tells you which row to look at. That check was the first criterion when we ranked 12 statement converters, and this post shows how to run it yourself in Python and in SQL.

Disclosure: I work on ZeraBooks, which makes one of those converters and ranks itself first. The code below is vendor-neutral. Point it at any parser's output.

Why not just measure accuracy?

Because "accuracy" for a statement parser is slippery. Per field? Per row? Per document? On whose documents? Vendors publish numbers like "99%+" or "99.9%" without the method, so you can't compare them and you can't reproduce them.

A statement gives you something better than a test set: a ground truth printed on the document itself. The bank tells you where the account started and where it ended. Your parser's rows have to connect those two numbers. That makes the check:

  • Per document, so you know about this file, not an average.
  • Free, because the bank already did the work.
  • Strict, because one wrong digit anywhere breaks it.
  • Explainable, because the size of the gap points at the kind of mistake.

The one thing it can't catch is two errors that cancel each other out. That's rare enough that I'd still take this check over any percentage.

The tie-out in Python

Rules that matter more than they look:

  1. Use Decimal, never float. 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in floating point, and a tie-out that's off by 0.00000000001 is a tie-out you'll learn to ignore. That defeats the point.
  2. Group by account. One PDF often holds a checking and a savings account. Tie out each one separately, or a gap in one hides inside the other.
  3. Money out is negative. Normalise to one signed amount column before summing. If your parser emits separate debit and credit columns, convert first.
  4. Parentheses mean negative. Some banks print (132.45).

Here's a small, runnable version with a diagnostic step. The sample has two accounts from one statement, and the savings account's printed closing balance has two digits swapped, which is the classic OCR failure.

import csv
import io
from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal

CENT = Decimal("0.01")


def money(text):
    """Parse '1,234.56', '-132.45' or '(132.45)' into an exact Decimal."""
    text = text.strip().replace(",", "").replace("$", "")
    if text.startswith("(") and text.endswith(")"):
        text = "-" + text[1:-1]
    return Decimal(text).quantize(CENT)


def tie_out(opening, amounts, closing):
    """Return the gap: 0 means opening + rows == closing to the cent."""
    return (opening + sum(amounts, Decimal("0")) - closing).quantize(CENT)


def diagnose(gap, amounts):
    """Turn a non-zero gap into a short list of things to look at first."""
    hints = []
    if gap == 0:
        return hints
    for a in amounts:
        if a == gap:
            hints.append(f"row {a} may be doubled")
        if a == -gap:
            hints.append(f"a row of {-a} may be missing")
        if a * 2 == gap or a * 2 == -gap:
            hints.append(f"row {a} may have the wrong sign")
    cents = int(abs(gap) * 100)
    if cents % 9 == 0:
        hints.append(f"gap {gap} divides by 9: look for two swapped digits")
    return hints


SAMPLE = """account,date,description,amount,balance
CHK 4417,2026-09-01,Opening,,18432.17
CHK 4417,2026-09-02,Card settlement,1250.00,19682.17
CHK 4417,2026-09-03,Rent,-2400.00,17282.17
CHK 4417,2026-09-08,Payroll,-3184.20,14097.97
CHK 4417,2026-09-15,Customer deposit,5327.77,19425.74
SAV 0011,2026-09-01,Opening,,3210.00
SAV 0011,2026-09-05,Transfer in,300.00,3510.00
SAV 0011,2026-09-30,Interest,1.34,3511.34
"""

# Printed on the statement's summary page, per account.
PRINTED = {
    "CHK 4417": (money("18,432.17"), money("19,425.74")),
    "SAV 0011": (money("3,210.00"), money("3,511.43")),  # last two digits swapped
}

rows = defaultdict(list)
for r in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(SAMPLE)):
    if r["amount"]:
        rows[r["account"]].append(money(r["amount"]))

for account, amounts in rows.items():
    opening, closing = PRINTED[account]
    gap = tie_out(opening, amounts, closing)
    status = "Proven" if gap == 0 else f"Needs a look (gap {gap})"
    print(f"{account}: {len(amounts)} rows, {status}")
    for hint in diagnose(gap, amounts):
        print("   ", hint)

Output:

CHK 4417: 4 rows, Proven
SAV 0011: 2 rows, Needs a look (gap -0.09)
    gap -0.09 divides by 9: look for two swapped digits

The diagnose function encodes four rules of thumb that cover most real failures:

Gap looks like Usual cause
Exactly one row's amount That row was extracted twice
Minus one row's amount A row was dropped, often at a page break
Twice one row's amount A withdrawal came out as a deposit, or the reverse
A multiple of 9 (in cents) Two neighbouring digits swapped somewhere

The 9 rule works because swapping two adjacent digits a and b changes a number by 9 × (a - b) × 10^n. A 0.09 gap points at the last two digits; 630.00 points at the hundreds and tens. It can't tell you whether the swap is in a row or in the printed balance you typed in, so check both.

Find the exact row with the running balance

Most statements also print a running balance on each row. That's a second, finer check: each row's printed balance should equal the previous balance plus this row's amount. The first row where it doesn't is your culprit.

from decimal import Decimal


def first_break(opening, rows):
    """rows: (description, amount, printed_running_balance). Return the first row
    where the previous balance plus this amount doesn't give the printed balance."""
    expected = opening
    for i, (desc, amount, balance) in enumerate(rows, start=1):
        expected += amount
        if expected != balance:
            return i, desc, expected, balance
        expected = balance  # carry the bank's figure, so one error is reported once
    return None


rows = [
    ("Card settlement", Decimal("1250.00"), Decimal("19682.17")),
    ("Rent", Decimal("-2400.00"), Decimal("17282.17")),
    ("Payroll", Decimal("-3814.20"), Decimal("14097.97")),  # misread: 3184.20
    ("Customer deposit", Decimal("5327.77"), Decimal("19425.74")),
]

hit = first_break(Decimal("18432.17"), rows)
if hit:
    i, desc, expected, printed = hit
    print(f"row {i} ({desc}): expected {expected}, statement says {printed}, "
          f"off by {printed - expected}")

Output:

row 3 (Payroll): expected 13467.97, statement says 14097.97, off by 630.00

Note the expected = balance line. After a break, carry the bank's printed figure forward rather than your computed one. Otherwise one bad row makes every row after it look bad too.

The same checks in SQL

If extracted rows land in a database, run the checks there. Store money as integer cents. This runs as-is in SQLite 3.25 or newer (window functions), and needs only small changes for Postgres.

CREATE TABLE stmt_rows (
  account       TEXT,
  seq           INTEGER,
  description   TEXT,
  amount_cents  INTEGER,
  balance_cents INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE stmt_summary (
  account       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  opening_cents INTEGER,
  closing_cents INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO stmt_rows VALUES
  ('CHK 4417', 1, 'Card settlement',   125000, 1968217),
  ('CHK 4417', 2, 'Rent',             -240000, 1728217),
  ('CHK 4417', 3, 'Payroll',          -381420, 1409797),
  ('CHK 4417', 4, 'Customer deposit',  532777, 1942574),
  ('SAV 0011', 1, 'Transfer in',        30000,  351000),
  ('SAV 0011', 2, 'Interest',             134,  351134);
INSERT INTO stmt_summary VALUES
  ('CHK 4417', 1843217, 1942574),
  ('SAV 0011',  321000,  351134);

-- 1. Tie-out per account: opening + rows must equal closing.
SELECT s.account,
       COUNT(r.seq) AS rows,
       s.opening_cents + SUM(r.amount_cents) - s.closing_cents AS gap_cents,
       CASE WHEN s.opening_cents + SUM(r.amount_cents) = s.closing_cents
            THEN 'Proven' ELSE 'Needs a look' END AS status
FROM stmt_summary s
JOIN stmt_rows r ON r.account = s.account
GROUP BY s.account
ORDER BY s.account;

-- 2. Which row breaks the printed running balance?
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT account, seq, description,
         balance_cents - amount_cents
           - COALESCE(LAG(balance_cents) OVER w,
                      (SELECT opening_cents FROM stmt_summary s
                       WHERE s.account = r.account)) AS break_cents
  FROM stmt_rows r
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY seq)
)
WHERE break_cents <> 0;

Output from sqlite3 -header -column :memory: < tieout.sql:

account   rows  gap_cents  status
--------  ----  ---------  ------------
CHK 4417  4     -63000     Needs a look
SAV 0011  2     0          Proven
account   seq  description  break_cents
--------  ---  -----------  -----------
CHK 4417  3    Payroll      63000

Query 1 is the gate: nothing with a non-zero gap goes downstream. Query 2 is the pointer: it names the row.

Try it on a real 140-row file

ZeraBooks publishes the file from its 10-bank sample run, ten fictional statements (Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Navy Federal, Synchrony, Monzo, RBC, Desjardins, TD, CommBank) downloaded as one CSV with the account and source file on every row. Here's a running-balance check over it:

import csv
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal

path = sys.argv[1]
by_account = defaultdict(list)
with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        by_account[row["Account"]].append(row)

for account, rows in by_account.items():
    if not rows[0]["Balance"]:
        print(f"{account}: {len(rows)} rows, no running balance on the statement")
        continue
    opening = Decimal(rows[0]["Balance"]) - Decimal(rows[0]["Amount"])
    breaks, prev = 0, opening
    for r in rows:
        if prev + Decimal(r["Amount"]) != Decimal(r["Balance"]):
            breaks += 1
        prev = Decimal(r["Balance"])
    print(f"{account}: {len(rows)} rows, {opening} -> {prev}, breaks: {breaks}")

curl -s -o all-details.csv "https://www.zerabooks.com/marketing/reviews/best-converter/All%20details%20-%2010%20documents.csv"
python3 alldetails.py all-details.csv

RBC Business Account 5108: 14 rows, 31204.66 -> 19215.82, breaks: 0
Chase Business Complete Checking 4417: 21 rows, 18432.17 -> 19425.74, breaks: 0
Initiate Business Checking 2265: 18 rows, 9614.08 -> 14819.40, breaks: 0
High Yield Savings 7392: 4 rows, 24150.00 -> 25037.64, breaks: 0
Monzo Business Lite 0921: 13 rows, 6845.20 -> 11914.71, breaks: 0
CommBank Business Transaction Account 7714: 13 rows, 15320.40 -> 11700.77, breaks: 0
Every Day Business Plan Chequing 3307: 12 rows, 22840.15 -> 20219.38, breaks: 0
Business Advantage Fundamentals Banking 8803: 18 rows, no running balance on the statement
Compte d'opérations entreprise 1234: 13 rows, 14378.90 -> 10771.60, breaks: 0
EVERYDAY CHECKING 6620: 12 rows, 1482.30 -> 4702.00, breaks: 0
MEMBERSHIP SAVINGS 0011: 2 rows, 3210.00 -> 3511.34, breaks: 0

Two things worth noticing. Ten PDFs produce eleven accounts, because the Navy Federal statement holds a checking and a savings account. And the Bank of America statement prints no running balance on its rows, so only the summary-page tie-out applies there. Your test harness needs to handle both cases without crashing or silently passing.

What else belongs in a parser test suite?

The tie-out catches wrong numbers. It doesn't catch everything. These are the other checks I'd add, all cheap:

  • Row count. If the statement prints a transaction count, match it.
  • Dates inside the period. Every row's date falls between the statement's start and end, with the right year. December-to-January statements are where year inference breaks.
  • No junk rows. No page headers, "balance forward", "continued on next page" or subtotal lines in the output.
  • Reference numbers intact. Long IDs stored as text, not numbers. Excel shows a 17-digit reference as 1.23E+16 and keeps only 15 significant digits.
  • No statement without balances marked as passing. If the PDF prints no opening or closing balance, the result is "unverified", not "proven".

How did this shape the ranking?

When we ranked 12 converters, the first question for each tool was whether it runs this check itself. ZeraBooks marks each account Proven or Needs a look based on exactly this tie-out, per account and per cardholder. DocuClipper says it runs reconciliation checks on its output. MoneyThumb describes automatic reconciliation against the summary totals. Hubdoc errors when totals don't match. Several others don't say. Those answers come from each vendor's own pages, with checked dates, in ZeraBooks' ranking of the 12 converters.

AI-based parsers make this more important, not less. A model reads layouts it has never seen, which is great, and it can also misread a digit with total confidence. ZeraBooks wrote a separate ranking on how each AI bank statement converter backs its accuracy claim, and the short version is that the arithmetic check has to live outside the model.

If you're building or buying a parser, put the tie-out in CI. Feed it every statement layout you've ever seen fail. A parser that passes the tie-out on a hundred ugly real-world statements is better tested than one with a great number on a landing page.

title: Article - Trading Journal with FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose
description:
Building a Trading Journal with FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose
A small multi-tier app, containerized from scratch for my Cloud Services midterm at BINUS University.
Why I built this
I trade gold (XAUUSD) with small lots, and for a long time my trade history lived in scattered notes and screenshots. I could not answer simple questions like "what is my win rate?" or "is my total moving up or down?" So I decided to build a small journal where I record each trade and instantly see the numbers.
There was a second reason. My Cloud Services course asked us to build a multi-tier application and run it entirely in containers on localhost. The grade is not about how many features the app has, but about how well it is containerized. A trading journal is small enough to finish in a day and real enough to be useful, which made it a good fit for practicing cloud-native fundamentals. It only stores dummy trade data (pair, lot, entry, exit), so no personal data is involved.

Architecture

The stack has three containers on a user-defined network called appnet:
• app: FastAPI served by Uvicorn on port 8000. It exposes GET /health, GET /trades, and POST /trades, and also serves the web page (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript).
• db: PostgreSQL 16.4 with a named volume, pgdata.
• adminer: a database UI that only starts under the tools profile.
A request goes from the browser to localhost:8000, the app connects to the database by its service name db, and the data is stored in the volume. I chose containers over virtual machines because containers share the host kernel (isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups), so they are smaller and start in seconds instead of minutes.

The Dockerfile
I used a multi-stage build:
FROM python:3.12.7-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12.7-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local
COPY app/ ./app/
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
A few decisions worth explaining:
• Pinned base image tag (3.12.7-slim) instead of latest, so builds are reproducible.
• Dependencies are copied before the source code. As long as requirements.txt does not change, Docker reuses the cached install layer, so a code change rebuilds in seconds.
• Multi-stage build. The runtime stage starts from a clean image and copies only the installed packages and my code, leaving build leftovers behind. The final image is [IMAGE SIZE FROM docker images].
• COPY instead of ADD. ADD can download URLs and auto-extract archives, which I did not need, so I used the more predictable COPY.
• Exec-form CMD. Uvicorn runs as the main process and receives stop signals correctly.

Docker Compose
The interesting part is how the services wait for each other:
db:
image: postgres:16.4
volumes:
- pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
healthcheck:
test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${DB_USER} -d ${DB_NAME}"]
interval: 5s
timeout: 3s
retries: 10

app:
build: .
env_file: .env
depends_on:
db:
condition: service_healthy
The database has a healthcheck, and the app starts only after it reports healthy. This avoids the classic startup crash where the app tries to connect before Postgres is ready. Configuration comes from a .env file that is never committed; the repository only contains .env.example. Adminer sits behind the tools profile, so it does not run unless I ask for it with docker compose --profile tools up -d.
Running it locally
git clone https://github.com/httpsvincent/trading_jurnal.git
cd trading_jurnal
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d --build
Then open http://localhost:8000/. The docker compose ps output shows the app running and the database healthy:

The API returns proper status codes: 200 for GET /health and GET /trades, 201 for a successful POST /trades, and 422 for invalid input.

Testing persistence
I added a few trades, ran docker compose down, then docker compose up -d, and the trades were still there. That is because down removes containers and networks but keeps named volumes. docker compose down -v also removes the volume, and the data is gone.
[INSERT SCREENSHOT: before and after docker compose down]
What I learned
• A healthcheck combined with service_healthy solves a very common startup race between an app and its database.
• Copying requirements.txt before the source code makes rebuilds dramatically faster.
• Keeping secrets in .env and committing only .env.example is a simple habit that keeps a public repository safe.
• Changing database credentials in .env does not change an existing Postgres volume, so you may need docker compose down -v to recreate it.
• [ADD ONE PERSONAL LESSON, e.g. a Git or Docker error you hit and how you fixed it]
Links
• GitHub: https://github.com/httpsvincent/trading_jurnal
• Demo video: [YOUTUBE LINK]

title: Why Your Web App Architecture is Killing Your Client's SEO
description:
There is a massive disconnect in the industry right now between web developers and digital marketers.

At NextGen Kerala, I oversee both custom web application development and digital marketing (SEO, SEM, Meta Ads). Seeing both sides of the coin has revealed a painful truth: many modern web apps are built in a way that actively destroys a client's search engine ranking.

Here is where I see development teams getting it wrong when building for clients:

  1. Relying Entirely on Client-Side Rendering (CSR)
    Yes, React and Vue are incredible, but if you ship a heavy CSR application for a public-facing e-commerce site or blog, Google's crawlers are going to struggle. Server-Side Rendering (SSR) or Static Site Generation (SSG) isn't just a trend; it's a baseline requirement for SEO.

  2. Ignoring Core Web Vitals
    Marketers care about bounce rates; developers care about features. But when a heavy Javascript bundle tanks the First Contentful Paint (FCP) and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), the ads get more expensive, and the organic traffic drops.

  3. Poor URL Structures and Meta Management
    In single-page applications (SPAs), developers often forget to dynamically update meta tags, canonical URLs, and Open Graph data as the user navigates.

The Takeaway
When you build a web app for a client, you aren't just building software; you are building their primary marketing asset.

Devs, how are you handling SEO requirements in your modern JavaScript frameworks? Let me know your go-to stacks for SEO-friendly web apps below!(https://nextgenkerala.in/)

title: Building the "Little Dino Sanctuary": A Multi-Tier Web Application with Node.js, PostgreSQL, and Docker
description:
A cozy multi-tier web sanctuary for dinosaur cataloging, built with containerized architecture and modern DevOps practices.

1. Introduction & The Problem

When building modern web applications, ensuring consistency across development and production environments is one of the biggest hurdles developers face. For the Little Dino Sanctuary project, the core challenge was to design a reliable, scalable, and secure system for cataloging dinosaur resident records while ensuring seamless deployment.

We chose this project because it perfectly mirrors real-world enterprise architectures separating concerns between a robust backend API, a persistent database layer, and a clean user interface all while strictly adhering to modern security standards like secret management.

2. System Architecture

The application follows a classic multi-tier client-server architecture containerized via Docker:

  • Presentation Tier: Static frontend interface serving resident records (public/index.html).
  • Application Tier: Node.js & Express REST API handling business logic (server.js).
  • Data Tier: PostgreSQL database container managing persistent storage with isolated data volumes.
  • Orchestration: Docker Compose coordinates the networking and startup sequence between the backend and database services.

3. Key Docker Configuration & Explanation

Containerization ensures that the application runs identically on any machine. Below are the essential snippets from our configuration files.

The Dockerfile

Our multi-stage setup optimizes the Node.js runtime environment:

FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
  • Explanation: We use a lightweight Alpine Linux base image to keep the container size minimal. It installs production dependencies, copies the source code, and exposes port 3000 to handle incoming HTTP requests.

The docker-compose.yml 

version: '3.8'
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      - DB_HOST=db
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: dino_sanctuary
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secretpassword
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:
  • Explanation: This configuration defines two interconnected services (app and db). It establishes internal networking so the Node.js application can communicate securely with the PostgreSQL database container using Docker volumes for persistent data storage.

4. Security Best Practices: Managing .env Secrets

A critical learning point of this project was enforcing strict security policies. To prevent credential leaks, sensitive environment variables (such as database passwords) are stored locally in a .env file which is explicitly excluded from version control via .gitignore. Teammates and evaluators can use .env.example as a safe template.

5. How to Run Locally

Getting the sanctuary up and running on your local machine takes less than a minute with Docker:

  1. Clone the repository: 
   git clone https://github.com/Clarisse-X/little-dino-sanctuary.git
   cd little-dino-sanctuary
  1. Configure environment variables: Copy the example file and adjust values if needed: 
   cp .env.example .env
  1. Build and launch with Docker Compose: 
   docker-compose up --build
  1. Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:3000.

6. Lessons Learned

  • Containerization Mastery: Gained hands-on experience writing robust Dockerfiles and orchestrating multi-container environments using Docker Compose.
  • Git Workflow Discipline: Learned the importance of structured, incremental commits and rigorous secret management (keeping .env out of public repositories).
  • CI/CD Readiness: Successfully pushed version-tagged images (1.0.0 and latest) to Docker Hub, bridging the gap between local development and cloud distribution.

Project Links & Resources

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Clarisse-X/little-dino-sanctuary
  • Docker Hub Image: https://hub.docker.com/r/clarissex/little-dino-sanctuary
  • Video Demonstration: https://youtu.be/xaD6QPT06bs
