title: Designing a Coffee Batch Inspection Log with Flask,PostgreSQL,and Docker
description:
Abstract
The coffee batch inspection log basically is a web-based application developed to record and managed coffee batch inspection information.The project demonstrates how a simple information-management system can be built by using a Python Backend,a relational database,and containerization in which the main purpose is to provide a structured way to store batch details such as identification of the coffee,origin,processing method,and inspection status.The application also demonstrates cloud-services related concepts including HTTP communication,persistent storage,service configuration,and container health monitoring.
1.Introduction
Coffee production may involves multiple batches that may differ in origin processing method,and it's inspection results.Keeping these details very organized and well mannered is very crucial for traceability and record management.Therefore,a digital log can make it easier to add,view,update,and remove records than maintaining the same information in seperate manual documents.

The coffee Batch inspection Log was selected as a practical example of a data-management application in an Indonesian agricultural context.The project is not an automated coffee-quality detection system.Instead,it provides a web interface for users to record and manage inspection information.

2.Application Architecture
The application uses a three-part structure:a front-end,a backend,and a database.The frontend is a browser-based interface through which users interact with coffee batch records.The backend is written in Python using Flask.It receives the HTTP requests,validates submitted information,performs the request operation as well as communicates with the database.

PostgreSQL version 16 is used as the relational database which stores the batch records so that the information is not limited to the browser session.The backend connects to PostgreSQL using a database connection string supplied through the DATABASE_URL environment variable.The database service is addressed by its Compose service name,db,allowing the application container to communicate with it over the Docker Network.

3.CRUD Operations and Data Validation
The application supports the four basic data-management operations currently known as the CRUD:Create,Read,Update,and delete.Users can create a batch record,retrieve and view existing records,update information when details change,and delete a record when it is no longer required.

The backend validates the incoming data before it is stored and validation helps in preventing incomplete or invalid information from entering the database.For example,a required text fiels should not be empty,and numerical values should be within acceptable limits.The application also provides an API endpoint for retrieving batch records and a /health endpoint for checking application responsiveness.
4.Containerization with Docker
Docker is used to package the application and its runtime environment into a container image.The project Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build.In the first stage,Python as a virtual environment is created and the dependencies listed in requirements.txt are installed.In the second stage,a fresh python slim image is prepared,and the virtual environment and the applications file are copied into it.Gunicorn is used to serve the Flask application on the port 5000.

Seperating dependency installation from the runtime stage keeps the build process organized and avoids carrying the builder stage itself into the final runtime image.

5.Managing Services with Docker COmpose
Docker Compose defines,runs the application's two services:web and db.The web service builds the application image from the Dockerfile and maps host port 5001 to the container port 5000.The db service uses the PostgreSQL 16 image.

A named volume,postgres_data,is mounted to PostgreSQL's data directory to preserve database files when containers are recreated,provided the volume is not removed.The database health check uses pg_isready to test whether PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections.The web service uses service_healthy dependency condition so it waits for the database health check to pass before starting.Thes settings demonstrate service coordination and persistent storage in a multi-container application.

Conclusion
The Coffee Batch Inspection Log demonstrate how the Flask,PostgreSQL,Docker,and Docker Compose can be combined to build a practical web-based record management application which implements always and again the CRUD(Create,Read,Update,Delete) functionality,data validation,database persistence,containerized execution as well as health monitoring.The project provided practical experience with backend development,HTTP APIs,relational databases,Docker images,service dependencies and the persistent volumes.Although it does not automatically assess coffee quality,it establishes a digital foundation for organizing coffee batch inspection records.

References
1.Docker. Docker Compose. https://docs.docker.com/compose/
2.Docker. Docker Compose Quickstart. https://docs.docker.com/compose/gettingstarted/

title: Controller Vibration Not Working? Test the Rumble in 2 Minutes Before You Open It
description:
When a controller stops rumbling, the first question is whether the motors are actually dead — or whether the game, the connection, or the platform is just not sending the signal. A quick test before you open anything saves a lot of wasted repair work.

Start with the simplest isolation. Connect the controller by USB, open a game you know rumbles, and trigger something that should shake — a crash, an explosion, a heavy landing. If it rumbles there, the motors are fine and the problem is in the game or app that stayed quiet. If it stays silent everywhere, move on.

Next, test the rumble outside any game. A browser-based vibration test lets you fire the motors directly: plug in over USB, open the test page, and send a short pulse, then a longer pattern. You can check the rumble in your browser at https://www.gamepadtesterpro.com/vibration/ — if the motors spin there, the hardware works and the fault is software. If they stay silent even on a direct test, check the usual suspects: an app holding the controller exclusively (Steam, a remapper, another game running in the background), a low battery on wireless, or Bluetooth — some controllers only expose rumble over USB, so always retest wired.

A few patterns tell you a lot. One motor buzzing and the other dead usually means a loose motor wire or a failed motor, not a settings issue. Weak rumble on one side that is strong on the other points the same way. Rumble that works in a native game but not in the browser is almost always a browser-support gap, not dead hardware — Chromium on desktop exposes the vibration actuator most reliably, so try that before concluding anything.

If the direct test stays silent on USB, in Chromium, with no other app holding the controller, and a second game also stays quiet, then the motors or their wiring are the likely fault — and that is the point where opening the controller or taking it to a repair shop makes sense. Until that test, don't order parts: most 'dead rumble' reports turn out to be a connection or software issue, and two minutes of testing tells you which one you have.

Disclosure: I run the free tester linked above.

title: Agentes LLM: un contrato de identidad para emails
description:
Un agente LLM puede completar un flujo de registro en pocos segundos y, aun así, dejar una prueba imposible de depurar. El formulario se envió, llegó el correo de verificación y el agente hizo clic en el enlace correcto. Pero cuando el paso falla, nadie sabe qué mensaje leyó, qué buzón pertenecía a la ejecución o si un reintento reutilizó datos viejos.

El problema no suele ser el modelo. Es la falta de una identidad técnica para cada email de prueba. Un generador de emails falsos puede crear una dirección, pero el sistema de automatización todavía necesita decidir quién la posee, cuánto dura y qué evidencia debe producir.

El problema: el agente pierde la identidad del email

En un flujo sencillo, la relación parece obvia:

ejecución -> dirección -> mensaje -> enlace -> resultado

En un flujo con agentes aparecen más caminos. El modelo puede reintentar una herramienta, delegar el paso a otro agente o continuar después de un timeout. Si todos consultan una bandeja compartida, el mensaje correcto deja de ser una certeza. Un correo parecido puede activar el flujo equivocado y hacer que el resultado parezca válido.

La ambigüedad aumenta cuando se usan nombres informales para buscar una solución, como dummy e mail o tempail mail. Esas frases pueden servir para entender consultas, pero no son una identidad de ejecución ni un criterio de seguridad.

La primera decisión de arquitectura es separar el objetivo del agente de la infraestructura que lo ejecuta. El agente debe pedir “espera el mensaje de verificación de esta ejecución”, no “busca el correo más reciente en esta bandeja”.

Diseñar una identidad por ejecución

Cada flujo debe recibir un run_id único y conservarlo hasta el cierre. La identidad puede tener esta forma:

{
  "run_id": "checkout-20261110-0522-a81f",
  "owner": "agent-registration",
  "mailbox_id": "mbx-7f2c",
  "purpose": "verification",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-10T05:42:00Z"
}

La dirección es solo una parte del contrato. run_id permite correlacionar la acción del agente, la solicitud de la API, la llegada del mensaje y el resultado del test. purpose evita que un mensaje de recuperación de contraseña se confunda con uno de bienvenida. expires_at da al sistema una decisión clara cuando el agente abandona el flujo.

En términos de diseño, el agente obtiene una referencia opaca y no necesita conocer detalles del proveedor. El adaptador de email traduce esa referencia a una dirección temporal, aplica el filtro por ejecución y devuelve eventos normalizados. Es un límite pequeño, pero hace mas fácil cambiar de proveedor o probar el adaptador en local.

Cuando el flujo también mide activación, conviene medir la activación sin perder el hilo del email. La métrica no debería decir solamente “se recibió un correo”; debe poder responder qué ejecución lo recibió y qué acción ocurrió después.

Un contrato mínimo para agentes LLM

Las herramientas que ve el modelo necesitan nombres y respuestas predecibles. Un contrato mínimo puede tener tres operaciones:

  1. reserve_mailbox(purpose, ttl): crea una identidad aislada y devuelve mailbox_id y run_id.
  2. wait_for_message(mailbox_id, kind, timeout): busca solo mensajes asociados a esa identidad.
  3. release_mailbox(mailbox_id, reason): marca la fixture como terminada y activa la limpieza.

La respuesta de wait_for_message no debe entregar el buzón completo ni datos innecesarios. Es suficiente con un evento como este:

{
  "status": "received",
  "message_id": "msg-91ab",
  "kind": "verification",
  "received_at": "2026-11-10T05:25:11Z",
  "link": "https://app.example.test/verify?token=redacted"
}

El token puede mantenerse fuera del historial visible al modelo y resolverse mediante una acción controlada. Así se reduce el riesgo de que un resumen, una traza o una llamada posterior copie un secreto. Si el agente necesita el enlace, el adaptador puede validar que pertenece al dominio esperado antes de devolverlo.

No hace falta convertir tempmailso en una dependencia del razonamiento del agente. Puede aparecer como término de inventario o de búsqueda, pero la integración debe depender de una interfaz propia, con límites y políticas definidos por el equipo.

Cómo evitar mezclas durante los reintentos

Los reintentos son donde se rompe la mayoría de los diseños ingenuos. Si una llamada expira después de crear la bandeja, repetirla puede producir otra identidad. Si el primer agente vuelve a despertar, puede leer el mensaje de la segunda.

La solución es que la reserva sea idempotente para una clave de ejecución. El adaptador puede aceptar idempotency_key = run_id + purpose y devolver la misma referencia mientras la fixture siga activa. El estado debería distinguir, al menos, reserved, message_received, verified, failed y expired.

También hay que definir qué significa “mensaje más reciente”. En general, no basta con ordenar por fecha. El filtro debe comprobar mailbox_id, tipo de mensaje, emisor esperado y una ventana temporal razonable. Si faltan esas señales, el agente debe recibir un resultado ambiguous y detenerse, no elegir por intuición.

Un reconciliador externo puede retirar las fixtures vencidas aunque el proceso del agente haya terminado mal. Si el despliegue corre sobre Kubernetes, es útil validar alertas después de un cambio de secretos como parte del mismo enfoque: los cambios de infraestructura y las pruebas de email necesitan señales observables, no solo un log de éxito.

Observabilidad y límites de seguridad

Los logs deben permitir reconstruir la secuencia sin guardar el contenido completo de los mensajes. Una línea útil contiene run_id, mailbox_id, tool_call_id, estado, latencia y motivo del cierre. Los resultados llega mejor agrupados por ejecución que por dirección, porque la dirección puede ser efímera.

El modelo tampoco debería tener permiso para crear identidades sin límite, cambiar el dominio de destino o desactivar la expiración. El adaptador debe imponer un TTL máximo, permitir solo dominios de prueba y rechazar una dirección que ya pertenezca a otra ejecución. Estas reglas deben vivir fuera del prompt: un agente puede interpretar instrucciones, pero no debe ser la única barrera.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Es necesario un buzón por agente?

No siempre. La unidad segura es la ejecución o el escenario. Dos agentes pueden compartir una identidad si tienen el mismo propósito y una coordinación explícita; una bandeja global para toda la suite es mucho más dificil de investigar.

¿Qué debe hacer el agente cuando llega un mensaje ambiguo?

Debe detener el paso, registrar la ambigüedad y solicitar una nueva consulta con criterios más estrictos. Elegir el mensaje mas reciente puede convertir un fallo de aislamiento en un falso positivo.

¿Puedo usar un proveedor real en pruebas locales?

Sí, si el adaptador oculta sus detalles, aplica expiración y evita datos personales. Para pruebas unitarias, una implementación en memoria suele ser suficiente y hace que el contrato sea más facil de verificar.

Checklist de implementación

  • Cada ejecución recibe un run_id y una identidad aislada.
  • La reserva usa una clave idempotente para soportar reintentos.
  • Las consultas filtran por buzón, propósito, emisor y ventana temporal.
  • El modelo recibe eventos mínimos, no secretos ni cuerpos completos.
  • La expiración tiene un límite impuesto por el adaptador.
  • Un reconciliador limpia fixtures abandonadas.
  • Los estados y las llamadas de herramientas quedan correlacionados.
  • Los casos ambiguos terminan con una señal explícita, nunca con una elección arbitraria.

La automatización con modelos LLM se vuelve más confiable cuando el agente no tiene que adivinar qué email le pertenece. Una identidad por ejecución, un contrato pequeño y una política de expiración convierten una integración frágil en un sistema que se puede observar, reintentar y explicar.

title: AI Receipt Images in a Node.js App: Object Storage, Signed Access, and Retention
description:
AI Receipt Images in a Node.js App: A Throughput-First Storage Decision

Short answer: for a customer-support system that processes receipts, keep the original file in private object storage, keep thumbnails as separate regenerable objects, and make the Node.js application publish database pointers only after the bytes are complete; signed URLs and lifecycle rules should enforce access and retention policy, not stand in for either one.

The operational constraint changes the answer. Large-file throughput matters more here than the smallest posted storage rate, because an audit original has a different failure boundary from a thumbnail. The original receipt is evidence. The thumbnail is a convenience.

The audit record starts with a deletion policy

Start with the erasure boundary, then define the bucket layout. For every receipt, the application should know the original key, derivative keys, content digest, processing state, and deletion state. Object storage is the byte store, not the business catalog.

Use distinct, immutable keys for the original and each thumbnail. A useful shape is receipts/{receipt_id}/original/{digest} and receipts/{receipt_id}/thumb/{width}/{transform_digest}. A hash-derived key prevents a late resize worker from silently replacing a newer output; the database pointer decides which completed variant the user sees.

Separate the upload path from the request that serves a support agent. Large receipt files should stream through bounded buffers, while resizing runs asynchronously. A web request that waits for upload, image processing, database commit, and URL signing has too many failure boundaries to retry as one unit.

Three words: bytes first, pointer second.

The signed URL is a temporary bearer credential, not a permissions model. Generate it only after an authenticated application request has checked the support case, keep its lifetime close to the download window, and do not put it in ordinary request logs. Content-Disposition can influence whether a browser displays a response inline or treats it as an attachment; it does not authorize the reader.

Throughput is a pipeline property, not a bucket feature

For large files, the bottleneck may be the customer upload, the application worker, the network path, image decoding, or the destination write. Measure each stage separately. Useful counters include bytes accepted, upload duration, queue age, resize duration, bytes written, retry count, and the time between object completion and database publication. Percentiles matter more than an average when a few very large receipts dominate the queue. Measure it.

A service can stream an incoming body to a storage adapter while keeping only bounded metadata in memory. The adapter below is deliberately generic: its contract is private storage, a unique key, and a complete write. It does not invent a provider-specific SDK or request path.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256
from typing import BinaryIO, Protocol


class ObjectSink(Protocol):
    def write_private(self, key: str, chunks: list[bytes], operation_id: str) -> None:
        """Persist the complete private object or raise a retryable error."""


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StoredObject:
    key: str
    digest: str
    size: int


def store_receipt(source: BinaryIO, sink: ObjectSink, receipt_id: str) -> StoredObject:
    digest = sha256()
    chunks: list[bytes] = []
    size = 0

    while chunk := source.read(1024 * 1024):
        digest.update(chunk)
        chunks.append(chunk)
        size += len(chunk)

    value = digest.hexdigest()
    key = f"receipts/{receipt_id}/original/{value}"
    operation_id = sha256(key.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
    sink.write_private(key, chunks, operation_id)
    return StoredObject(key=key, digest=value, size=size)

This sample keeps chunks in a list so the state transition is easy to see; a production adapter should stream or spool to bounded local storage rather than allowing a very large receipt to consume process memory. That distinction is important. A correct key does not make an unbounded worker safe. If the storage interface supports multipart transfer, use it for files large enough to justify parallel parts, and record unfinished operations for cleanup. If it does not, stream through a controlled worker pool and tune concurrency from measurements. More workers can increase throughput until the network, CPU, or remote rate limit becomes the actual queue. A 429 should cause bounded backoff, not an unbounded retry storm.

How should a Node.js app store generated images and thumbnails in object storage?

For generated images and thumbnails, the practical contract is simple: originals and derivatives are separate objects, only completed objects become catalog entries, and a signed URL is minted after authorization. The answer is not a public link with a cleanup job attached. It is a private byte path whose state is explicit enough to audit.

Retention rules are governance, not cleanup automation

A lifecycle rule is appropriate for a prefix containing failed jobs, temporary exports, or thumbnails whose source original still exists and can be regenerated. It is a poor substitute for a legal deletion workflow and a dangerous default for originals. Put originals and derivatives under different prefixes, and review the rule against the retention policy before enabling it.

The exact deletion path should be explicit. When a customer asks to erase a receipt, enqueue the object keys, mark the application record as pending deletion, delete the objects, and record completion. Make the consumer idempotent. If the database row is removed first, the application may lose the key it needs to delete; if the object is removed first and the process stops before the database update, the catalog can point at nothing. Neither partial order is a sufficient audit trail.

Consider one receipt with an original, three thumbnail widths, a failed resize attempt, and an export copied to an audit queue. A request to erase it cannot safely mean “delete the row and let a bucket rule catch up,” because that loses the relationship between the authoritative file and its derivatives while leaving the export unaccounted for. The record should instead enumerate every object key and its state, so the deletion worker can retry the original and each derivative independently, record which operation completed, and leave an auditable pending state when a policy exception prevents removal. The same inventory helps routine lifecycle design: a thumbnail prefix can expire after the original remains available for regeneration, while an original prefix can be excluded from automated expiration and handled through the approved retention workflow. This is slower to design than a single time-to-live, but it makes a large-file pipeline explainable when support, security, or compliance asks what happened to one receipt.

Keep it private.

GDPR Article 17 is a useful reminder that an erase button is a workflow with evidence, not merely a successful HTTP response. Retention exceptions, legal holds, backups, replicas, and exported audit material need explicit policy decisions. The regulation does not tell your team which prefix to expire; your data inventory has to do that work.

Options and their failure boundaries

Design choice Where it fits What changes the decision
Private object storage plus an application catalog High-volume originals and regenerable thumbnails Requires a reliable state machine and deletion worker
Binary columns in the primary database Small bounded files needing one transactional backup path Large receipt reads can compete with transactional queries and backups
One mutable key per thumbnail size Simple prototypes with no concurrent rendering Late workers and caches can publish stale bytes
Public object URLs Public, non-sensitive media Customer receipts and audit files should not be public

The trade-off is operational complexity in exchange for a storage path that can absorb large files without making every database operation carry the binary payload. The selected design is not suitable when the system requires a single atomic transaction that includes the object bytes, or when the team cannot operate an asynchronous retry and deletion queue. In those cases, keeping bounded files in the existing database may be the more honest choice.

Do not make the cheapest nominal storage rate the decision rule. Compare ingress and egress assumptions, request charges, retrieval behavior, replication, backup treatment, deletion requirements, and the engineering time needed to recover an orphaned object. Your mileage may vary because traffic geography and receipt-size distribution can change the result more than a posted storage number.

An ADR worth keeping after launch

Record the rejected option and the reason it was rejected. For this system, the rejected default is one mutable thumbnail path, because publication and cleanup become difficult to reason about when workers race. The valid use case is a prototype where a single worker owns each key and losing an older derivative has no audit consequence.

Also record the operational thresholds: maximum accepted receipt size, concurrency limits, retry budget, URL lifetime, retention class, and the alert for a record stuck between upload and publication. Review those values with real percentile data. I'm not sure which threshold will dominate before the first production distribution is visible, and pretending otherwise is how capacity plans acquire false precision.

The decision is narrow: keep originals private and durable enough for the audit policy, make derivative keys immutable, publish only completed objects, and let the application—not a guessed URL or an over-broad lifecycle rule—own authorization and deletion.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/

title: I Containerized My Fish Tank: A Water Quality Tracker with Docker Compose
description:
I Containerized a Water Quality Tracker for My Fish Tank (And Learned Docker Properly)

Aquarium hobbyists have a quiet enemy: invisible water chemistry. Ammonia can spike overnight, pH can drift slowly over weeks, and by the time fish show stress, it is often too late. Shrimp tanks are even less forgiving — a 0.05 ppm difference in ammonia can be the line between a thriving colony and an empty tank.

Like most keepers, I used to track my water parameters in a scattered notes app. No trends, no history, no alerts. So for my cloud services course project, I decided to fix this with a small multi-tier web app — and more importantly, to learn containerization the right way: Aquarium Parameter Log (a.k.a. aqualog).

What It Does

One core feature, done properly: log water measurements per tank and see the trend.

  • Create tanks (freshwater, planted, or shrimp)
  • Log readings: pH, temperature, NH3, NO2, NO3
  • View history as a table and a Chart.js trend line
  • Get an instant safe / warning / danger verdict per reading, based on threshold rules for each tank type — shrimp get stricter ammonia limits than freshwater fish

Target users are aquarium and shrimp keepers who test water regularly but have nowhere structured to put the numbers.

Architecture

The whole thing runs on localhost with one docker compose up -d --build:

browser ──► app (FastAPI + Jinja2, port 8000)
              │  GET/POST
              ├──► db (PostgreSQL 16, named volume, healthcheck)
              └──► redis (cache, healthcheck, 30s TTL)
           [profile tools: adminer on port 8080]
  • app — FastAPI backend + Jinja2 frontend in one container. Endpoints: GET /health (liveness), GET /tanks, POST /tanks, GET /readings (Redis-cached), POST /readings.
  • db — PostgreSQL 16, data persisted in a named volume, exposed to the app network only.
  • redis — caches reading lists for 30 seconds, cache invalidated on new writes.
  • adminer — a DB UI that only starts with the tools profile, so day-to-day runs stay lean.

The Dockerfile

The app image is a two-stage build:

FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN python -m venv /opt/venv && \
    /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv
COPY app/ app/
COPY templates/ templates/
COPY static/ static/
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Details that matter:

  • Multi-stage — the builder stage carries pip and the full toolchain; the runtime stage only gets the finished virtualenv. Result: a 272 MB image with no build tools inside.
  • Dependencies copied first — requirements.txt is copied and installed before any source code. Since it rarely changes, Docker reuses the cached layer on every code edit; my rebuilds after a code change finish in under a second.
  • Pinned tags, not latest — python:3.12-slim, postgres:16.9-alpine, redis:7.4-alpine. Reproducible builds beat convenient ones.
  • Exec-form CMD — CMD ["uvicorn", ...] makes uvicorn PID 1, so signals like SIGTERM reach the app and containers stop cleanly.
  • The app runs as a non-root appuser — one less thing to worry about if this ever leaves localhost.

The Compose File 

services:
  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      POSTGRES_HOST: db          # connect by service name, not IP
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:16.9-alpine
    volumes:
      - aquarium-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER}"]

Three things I appreciate most in Compose:

  1. DNS by service name — the app connects to db, never to a container IP. Containers get new IPs on every restart; names are stable.
  2. Healthcheck + service_healthy — the app container waits until Postgres actually accepts connections, killing the classic "app started before the database" race condition.
  3. Named volumes — docker compose down removes containers, but the volume survives. My readings were still there after a full teardown and rebuild. (docker compose down -v would wipe it — the -v flag deserves respect.)

Try It 

git clone https://github.com/saintbobi/aqualog.git
cd aqualog
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d --build

Then open http://localhost:8000. The image is also on Docker Hub as saintbobi705/aqualog:1.0.0.

What I Learned

  • Copying the dependency manifest before source code is the single highest-leverage habit in Dockerfile authoring. Layer caching turns 30-second rebuilds into near-instant ones.
  • Healthchecks are not decoration. They turned my startup from "hope it works" into a deterministic sequence.
  • Rule-based safety verdicts don't need machine learning to feel useful — good thresholds per tank type already make the app something I would actually use.
  • Designing for zero personal data from the start is both an ethical and a practical shortcut: nothing sensitive to leak, nothing to redact before publishing.

Repo: https://github.com/saintbobi/aqualog
Video demo: https://youtu.be/i0_Lttqi_r4

title: Smart2FA: An Offline, Zero-Knowledge 2FA Authenticator Built for Maximum Security and Minimal Friction
description:
A deep dive into Smart2FA (0xid Edition) - an open-source, 100% offline 2FA authenticator with local AES-256 encryption, biometrics, and cross-platform desktop/mobile support.

Security vs. Convenience: The Authentication Dilemma

In modern digital infrastructure, two-factor authentication (2FA) is one of the highest-leverage practices for preventing unauthorized account access. Yet most mainstream authenticator applications introduce unnecessary trade-offs:

  1. Centralized Cloud Sync Risks: Storing unencrypted or vendor-managed tokens in proprietary clouds introduces unnecessary attack surfaces, single points of failure, and vendor lock-in.
  2. Excessive Telemetry & Tracking: Many commercial authenticators harvest analytics, device identifiers, and usage metrics, adding cognitive and privacy overhead.
  3. Platform Lock-In & Friction: Limited export options make migrating between ecosystems unnecessarily difficult, increasing the risk of data loss when changing devices.

To maximize user autonomy, data protection, and operational efficiency, we built Smart2FA (0xid Edition) - an open-source, client-side, zero-knowledge authenticator designed to eliminate telemetry, minimize systemic vulnerability, and deliver maximum utility with an industrial aesthetic.

Core Philosophy: Zero-Knowledge & Local-First Utility

Smart2FA is engineered around three foundational requirements:

  • 100% Offline by Design: No backend services, no analytics, no external network calls.
  • Client-Side Cryptographic Isolation: All secrets remain encrypted at rest and in memory until explicitly authenticated by the user.
  • Portability and Interoperability: Support for standard RFC formats, instant bulk migrations, and frictionless cross-platform access across Web, Desktop (Tauri/Rust), and Mobile (Capacitor).

Capabilities & Architectural Overview

1. Robust Cryptographic Vault Model

Smart2FA never persists your master PIN in plaintext. The storage and decryption flow maximizes resilience against brute-force and local data-dump attacks:

[ User PIN ]
    |
    |-> PBKDF2 (25,000 iters, Salt A, SHA-256) -> PIN Hash (Verification only)
    |
    └-> PBKDF2 (25,000 iters, Salt B, SHA-256) -> AES-256-CBC Key -> Encrypts/Decrypts Vault
  • In-Memory PIN Lifecycle: Decrypted state and working secrets reside strictly in volatile RAM within the Pinia store. Locking the app, navigating away, or refreshing the page immediately purges volatile memory.
  • Biometric Integration (WebAuthn): On supported devices (Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello), WebAuthn securely wraps the key, providing frictionless single-touch authentication without compromising cryptographic strength.
  • Automated Inactivity Protection: Configurable auto-lock triggers after idle intervals (30s to 30m) to minimize risk in shared environments.
  • Irreversible Panic Wipe: A high-safety wipe mechanism requiring explicit text confirmation (WIPE) instantly sanitizes all local keys and storage artifacts.

2. RFC 6238 TOTP Engine & Real-Time Ergonomics

  • Broad Protocol Support: Powered by otpauth, supporting SHA-1, SHA-256, and SHA-512 algorithms, 6, 7, or 8-digit codes, and custom time periods (30s / 60s).
  • Visual Expiration Feedback: A real-time countdown progress bar indicates time-to-expire, shifting to an alert state 5 seconds prior to renewal.
  • Instant Copy: One-touch clipboard copying accompanied by concise status notifications.

3. Dual Input, Auto-Categorization & Google Auth Import

  • Integrated QR Scanner: Real-time camera scanner via html5-qrcode with automated otpauth:// URI parsing.
  • Google Authenticator Batch Migration: Scans Google Authenticator's native "Transfer Accounts" export QR code to migrate dozens of tokens in a single operation.
  • Smart Category Detection: Automatically classifies tokens into color-coded categories (Work, Crypto, Finance, Social, Email, Gaming, Other) based on issuer patterns (e.g., GitHub $\rightarrow$ Work, Binance $\rightarrow$ Crypto), with one-tap filtering tabs.

4. Encrypted Portability (.oxid Format)

  • Vaults can be exported as timestamped .oxid files, encrypted with AES-256 derived from the export PIN.
  • These encrypted containers can be safely archived in cold storage or transferred via insecure channels without exposing token secrets.

5. Cross-Platform Desktop & Mobile Support

  • Tauri v2 (Rust Backend): High performance, minimal binary footprint, full system tray integration, and minimize-to-tray capability for unobtrusive background operation.
  • Capacitor Mobile Build: Ready for deployment on Android devices.
  • Responsive Industrial Interface: High-contrast Dark Charcoal (#1A1B1E) and Rust Orange (#E25822) theme with glassmorphism and monospace typography.

Tech Stack

  • Frontend: Vue 3 (Composition API & <script setup>), Pinia 2, Vue Router 4, Tailwind CSS.
  • Desktop Runtime: Tauri v2 (Rust).
  • Mobile Foundation: Capacitor.
  • Security & TOTP Primitives: crypto-js, otpauth, html5-qrcode.

Ideas for Future Development

To continuously improve the security-to-effort ratio, several potential enhancements are under consideration:

  1. Hardware Security Key (FIDO2 / YubiKey) Support: Allowing master vault keys to be backed by a physical hardware token for enhanced physical security.
  2. Encrypted P2P Local Network Sync: Safe, serverless peer-to-peer sync between desktop and mobile devices via local encrypted WebRTC or chunked animated QR codes.
  3. CLI Companion Utility: A headless CLI tool for developers to query TOTP tokens directly from their terminal during SSH or CI/CD operations.
  4. Custom Category Rules & Custom Icons: Allowing users to define regex-based categorization rules and custom issuer icon packs.
  5. Decentralized Encrypted Cloud Storage Backends: Optional integration with WebDAV or user-owned S3 buckets to back up encrypted blobs automatically without vendor intermediaries.

Open Source & Getting Started

Smart2FA is 100% open-source under the MIT license. Check out the repository, star the project, and inspect the codebase:

-->> GitHub Repository: https://github.com/technologiespro/Smart2FA

Community Feedback

Tools are most effective when they adapt to the practical workflows of real users.

What capabilities or integrations would provide the highest value for your daily security setup? What features would you like to see added to Smart2FA next?

Share your thoughts, suggestions, and feedback in the comments below, or open an issue on GitHub!

title: Watching every chain, not just the hot wallet: a small outflow monitor in Node
description:
On 2 November 2026 the Brazilian exchange Mercado Bitcoin paused deposits and withdrawals after funds moved out of wallets linked to it. According to CertiK, the attacker spent about four hours on eight smaller chains, including Base, Optimism and Arbitrum, before reaching the central hot wallets. Hypernative estimated the total outflow at about $40 million.

Four hours on side chains is a long window. If your alerting only watches the busiest wallet, that's time you don't see. Here's a small script that watches outgoing native transfers from a list of addresses on several EVM chains and flags anything over a threshold.

It uses only Node 18+ (built-in fetch) and public JSON-RPC endpoints. Swap in your own RPC URLs and addresses.

// outflow-watch.mjs (run: node outflow-watch.mjs)
const CHAINS = {
  base: 'https://mainnet.base.org',
  optimism: 'https://mainnet.optimism.io',
  arbitrum: 'https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc',
};
// addresses you operate (lowercase)
const WATCH = new Set([
  '0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000',
]);
const THRESHOLD_ETH = 0.5;

async function rpc(url, method, params) {
  const r = await fetch(url, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: 1, method, params }),
  });
  const j = await r.json();
  if (j.error) throw new Error(`${method}: ${j.error.message}`);
  return j.result;
}

const last = {};

async function scan(name, url) {
  const head = parseInt(await rpc(url, 'eth_blockNumber', []), 16);
  const from = last[name] ?? head; // start at the head on first run
  for (let n = from + 1; n <= head; n++) {
    const block = await rpc(url, 'eth_getBlockByNumber', ['0x' + n.toString(16), true]);
    for (const tx of block.transactions) {
      if (!tx.from || !WATCH.has(tx.from.toLowerCase())) continue;
      const eth = Number(BigInt(tx.value)) / 1e18;
      if (eth >= THRESHOLD_ETH) {
        console.log(`[ALERT] ${name} block ${n}: ${eth} ETH from ${tx.from} to ${tx.to} (${tx.hash})`);
      }
    }
  }
  last[name] = head;
}

async function loop() {
  for (const [name, url] of Object.entries(CHAINS)) {
    try { await scan(name, url); } catch (e) { console.error(name, e.message); }
  }
}

await loop();
setInterval(loop, 15_000);

A few notes on taking this further:

  • Native transfers are only part of it. ERC-20 outflows show up as Transfer logs, so add an eth_getLogs call filtered on the Transfer topic with your addresses as the from topic.
  • Fast chains produce a lot of blocks. For production, use eth_getLogs over ranges, or a provider's webhook, rather than pulling full blocks one at a time.
  • Alert on rate as well as size. Many small transfers from many addresses can matter more than one big one. In this incident, CryptoTicker reported small amounts swept from about 27,160 addresses into one.
  • Give every chain the same thresholds and on-call routing. The smaller chain is often where nobody is looking.

What does your team monitor on the chains that see the least traffic?

Sources: CryptoTicker (citing CertiK and Cointelegraph), CriptoNoticias and Tecnoblog, all 2 Nov 2026.

title: Design a Notification System: Queues, Retries and Fan-out
description:
Design a notification system looks simple. Send an email, a push, an SMS. Done.

Then the interviewer asks: What if the email provider is down? What if a user gets the same push twice? What if you need to notify 5 million followers at once? That is where the real design starts.

This post walks through a clean answer to notification system design, step by step.

1. Clarify requirements first

Ask before you draw:

  • Which channels? Push, email, SMS, in-app.

  • Real-time or can it be delayed?

  • Do users have preferences (mute, quiet hours)?

  • Scale: notifications per day, peak bursts.

Non-functional goals: no lost notifications, no duplicates, low latency for urgent ones (OTP), and one slow channel must not block the others.

2. High-level architecture
Service A ─┐
Service B ─┼─► Notification API ─► Validate + Preferences ─► Message Queue(s)
Service C ─┘ │
┌───────────────────────┼──────────────┐
▼ ▼ ▼
Push Worker Email Worker SMS Worker
│ │ │
APNs/FCM Email provider SMS provider

Key decisions:

  • Decouple with a queue. Callers get an instant "accepted" response. Spikes don't hit providers directly.

  • Separate queue per channel (and per priority). An SMS outage should not delay emails.

  • Stateless workers so you can scale each channel independently.

3. Fan-out: one event, millions of users

When one post notifies 5 million followers, don't loop inside the API request. Publish one event, then let a fan-out service expand it into per-user messages in batches.

Fan-out on write: create per-user notifications immediately. Fast reads, heavy writes.
Fan-out on read: compute when the user opens the app. Cheap writes, slower reads.

4. Retries with exponential backoff

Providers fail. A good worker retries, but not blindly.

import random
import time

MAX_RETRIES = 5

def send_with_retry(message):
    for attempt in range(MAX_RETRIES):
        try:
            provider.send(message)
            return "sent"
        except TemporaryError:
            if attempt == MAX_RETRIES - 1:
                dead_letter_queue.publish(message)
                return "failed"

            delay = min(30, 2 ** attempt)
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, delay))

Three things to say out loud:

  • Backoff stops you from hammering a struggling provider.

  • Jitter stops all workers retrying at the same second.

  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ) keeps failed messages for inspection and replay.

5. Avoiding duplicates

Queues usually guarantee at-least-once delivery, so duplicates will happen. Fix it with an idempotency key:

def handle(message):
    key = f"sent:{message.notification_id}:{message.channel}"

    # Check if already processed
    if redis.get(key):
        return "already_processed"

    # Send notification
    result = send_with_retry(message)

    # Mark as processed after successful sending
    if result == "sent":
        redis.set(key, "1", ex=86400)

    return result

Same notification ID, same channel, processed once.

6. Preferences, rate limits and priority

  • Preferences check before queuing: opted out, quiet hours, channel choice.

  • Per-user rate limit so a bug upstream doesn't spam someone with 200 pushes.

  • Priority queues: OTP and security alerts must never wait behind marketing campaigns.

7. Tracking status

Store each notification with a status: queued → sent → delivered → opened / failed. Providers send delivery callbacks (webhooks) that update this table. It powers analytics and debugging.

Interview checklist

  • Clarified channels, scale and latency needs

  • Queue between API and workers

  • Separate queues per channel and priority

  • Retries with backoff, jitter and a DLQ

  • Idempotency key for deduplication

  • Preferences and rate limiting

  • Delivery tracking

Practice it for real

Knowing the pieces is one thing. Explaining the trade-offs under a timer is another. If you want hands-on system design practice instead of just reading, ScaleDojo has 220+ interactive labs across HLD, LLD, API design and GenAI/RAG, so you can build designs like this and get feedback.

What would you add to this design? Drop it in the comments.

title: One number, four answers: reconciling four divergent hit-rate pipelines over 46,139 settled predictions
description:
Every analytics platform eventually ships a number nobody can trace. Ours was the hit rate. It appeared in four places — the model table, the leaderboard, the per-competition rollup, the daily stats cron — and they disagreed by as much as 17 percentage points on the same model, on the same day, reading the same database. This is that story, with the numbers. Every figure below is the output of a query you can re-run.

The symptom

The dashboard, the model profile page, and the leaderboard each showed a different rate for the same model — one a confident 100% while the model's own detail page showed 43%. Both pages rendered cached columns: neither was wrong at the SQL level, both were wrong as statements about reality. Four writers each owned a slightly different definition of hit, denominator, and in-scope rows, and nobody had written down which was authoritative, so all four survived.

What the source of truth actually says

The only table that holds one row per prediction, with the outcome attached, is ai_predictions. Everything else is a derived cache. Query the base table, count settled rows, and count hits:

-- S0: the only honest denominator
SELECT
  count(*)                                                   AS settled_rows,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE)                        AS hits,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NULL)                        AS unsettled_flag_nulls,
  round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE) / count(*), 2) AS hit_rate_incl_nulls,
  round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE)
        / nullif(count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NOT NULL), 0), 2)  AS hit_rate_excl_nulls
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE settled = true;

Result:

settled_rows | hits  | unsettled_flag_nulls | hit_rate_incl_nulls | hit_rate_excl_nulls
     46,139  | 26,232|          121         |        56.85        |        57.01

121 rows are flagged settled = true but carry a NULL hit, which alone moves the headline by 0.16 points. And the same table holds a second hit column, hit_1x2, disagreeing with hit on 162 rows (26,070 vs 26,232). A third: exact directional agreement, prediction_direction = actual_result, yields 17,022 — 36.89%. Same rows, same settlement timestamp, three defensible definitions, three numbers twenty points apart.

Part of that gap is by design. The platform emits single-direction predictions (32,423 rows, 58.12% hit) and double-direction leans (13,687 rows, 53.85%). Exact-match scoring marks every double a miss unless one specific side lands; any-covered-side scoring credits either. A metric that does not declare its shape is not a metric.

The four pipelines

Source Table / column Rows in scope numerator / denominator Printed rate
S1 ai_models.total_predictions / correct_predictions 41,010 23,322 / 41,010 56.87%
S2 ai_models.dir_total_predictions / dir_correct_predictions 40,951 23,318 / 40,951 56.94%
S3 leaderboard.total_predictions / total_correct 802 477 / 802 59.48%
S4 model_league_stats.total_predictions / correct_predictions 45,809 26,070 / 45,809 56.91%
S5 prediction_hit_stats where dimension='global' 3,916 2,232 / 3,916 57.00%

Read "rows in scope" before "rate". S1 and S2 are each missing ~5,100 settled predictions. S3 covers 802 rows — 1.74% of the corpus — and S5's "global" row covers 3,916 rows (8.49%). A metric describing 1.74% of the platform is a sample without a sample size.

The four gap sources, in order of impact:

1. Definition drift. S4 lands exactly on 26,070 — the hit_1x2 count, not the hit count of 26,232. The rollup and the base table never measured the same event, and it stayed invisible because both round to "about 57%".

2. Denominator drift. S1 and S2 were backfilled at different moments, so 5,129 and 5,188 settled rows never entered their counters. A counter incremented on write and never reconciled always lags by the rows that bypass the increment: batch settlement, retry, manual re-grade.

3. Coverage drift. S3 keeps the top 150 models; S5 keeps whatever the cron reached. Neither states coverage, so a consumer reads "59.48%" as a platform claim.

4. Survivorship. 2,708 of 8,392 model rows are retired and own 7,843 settled predictions — 17.0% of the corpus — and the leaderboard excludes them. Dropping losers before averaging is the fastest way to manufacture a better hit rate, and it happens by filtering, not lying.

What the leaderboard looks like from the base table 

-- S3 vs. truth, per model
WITH truth AS (
  SELECT model_id, count(*) AS n, count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE) AS h
  FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled = true GROUP BY model_id
)
SELECT l.rank, m.name, l.total_predictions AS cached_n, l.hit_rate AS cached_rate,
       t.n AS true_n, round(100.0 * t.h / t.n, 2) AS true_rate
FROM leaderboard l JOIN ai_models m ON m.id = l.model_id
JOIN truth t ON t.model_id = l.model_id
ORDER BY l.rank LIMIT 10;

Top of the board:

rank | model_id | cached_n | cached_rate | true_n | true_rate
  1  |  25183   |    7     |   100.0     |   21   |   42.86
  2  |  25954   |   10     |    80.0     |   77   |   49.35
  4  |  25915   |    5     |   100.0     |   18   |   61.11
  6  |  25148   |    8     |    75.0     |   57   |   64.91

Rank 1 holds seven predictions in the cache and twenty-one in reality: displayed at 100%, scores 42.86%. Across all 132 leaderboard models that join to settled data, 131 have a cached total_predictions that disagrees with the base table, and the mean absolute deviation between cached and true rate is 17.08 percentage points. That is not rounding. It is a ranking replaced by a memory of a ranking.

Per-model divergence, measured 

WITH truth AS (
  SELECT model_id, count(*) AS n, count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE) AS h
  FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled = true GROUP BY model_id
)
SELECT count(*)                                                             AS models_compared,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE abs(100.0 * t.h / t.n - m.dir_hit_rate) > 0.5) AS off_by_half_point,
       round(avg(abs(100.0 * t.h / t.n - m.dir_hit_rate)), 2)               AS mean_abs_error_pp,
       round(max(abs(100.0 * t.h / t.n - m.dir_hit_rate)), 2)               AS max_abs_error_pp
FROM ai_models m JOIN truth t ON t.model_id = m.id
WHERE m.dir_total_predictions > 0 AND t.n >= 50;

models_compared | off_by_half_point | mean_abs_error_pp | max_abs_error_pp
      147       |        54          |       0.86        |      13.33

A third of models are off by more than half a point; the worst by 13.33. Against prediction_hit_stats it degrades further: of 111 comparable model rows, 68 are off by more than half a point and 89 carry a total_predictions that does not equal the true count — 80% wrong denominators, worst-case rate error 73.33 points.

Worst individual case, 美洲国家联赛·凌统: cached 60 predictions at 60.00%, actually 60 predictions at 73.33%. Same denominator, eight missing hits in the numerator — what a settlement path writing hit_1x2 while the counter reads hit looks like from outside.

The reconciliation job

The fix is not a migration: declare one source authoritative, make every other number a checked derivative.

import psycopg2

TRUTH_SQL = """
WITH truth AS (
  SELECT model_id, count(*) AS n, count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit) AS h
  FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled = true AND hit IS NOT NULL GROUP BY model_id
)
SELECT m.name, m.dir_total_predictions AS cached_n, m.dir_hit_rate AS cached_rate,
       t.n AS true_n, round(100.0 * t.h / t.n, 2) AS true_rate,
       abs(COALESCE(m.dir_hit_rate, 0) - round(100.0 * t.h / t.n, 2)) AS drift_pp
FROM ai_models m JOIN truth t ON t.model_id = m.id
WHERE m.dir_total_predictions > 0 AND t.n >= 50
ORDER BY drift_pp DESC;
"""

with psycopg2.connect(DSN) as conn, conn.cursor() as cur:
    cur.execute(TRUTH_SQL)
    rows = cur.fetchall()

hard = [r for r in rows if float(r[5]) > 1.0]
print(f"compared={len(rows)} drift>1.0pp={len(hard)} "
      f"coverage={sum(r[1] for r in rows) / sum(r[3] for r in rows):.2%}")

# gate: refuse to publish the leaderboard when the cache has drifted
assert not hard, f"{len(hard)} models exceed 1.0pp drift; rebuild blocked"

The invariant that makes this enforceable is not "the cache equals the base table" — it is monotonic agreement: for every model, dir_total_predictions may only grow, may never exceed the base-table count, and must reach equality after each settlement batch. A counter behind is lagging; a counter ahead is double-counting. Both are detectable, which is the whole point — before this invariant existed, neither was.

Governance rules that actually stopped the drift

One table owns the event. ai_predictions is the only place a hit is decided. Every downstream number must be reconstructible from it in one statement, by someone who has never read the application code. A metric that cannot be reconstructed is not a metric — it is an opinion with a percentage sign.

Every derived table declares its coverage. 57.00% over 3,916 rows is fine as long as the row says 3,916 and the UI renders "n=3,916". It is not fine as a headline. Coverage is part of the value, not metadata.

Every metric names its definition and arity policy. Scoring a double-direction lean under exact-match rules silently penalizes 29.7% of the corpus. hit_direction_exact and hit_direction_covered are two columns, not one column with two histories.

Retired models stay in the denominator. Report the all-model rate and the active-only rate side by side, always both, always labeled. Removing 7,843 settled predictions changes the story more than any model improvement shipped this quarter. And every cached rate renders its age: a 100% hit rate from seven predictions computed three weeks ago should look as fragile as it is.

What this cost, honestly

No prediction was wrong, no settlement was wrong. The damage was that four numbers existed — each individually traceable — and the platform was willing to show whichever one was convenient. That is more dangerous than a bug: a bug gets fixed, a comfortable number gets defended.

The state: 46,139 settled predictions, 26,232 directionally correct under hit — 56.85% inclusive of 121 NULL-flagged rows, 57.01% excluding them. 8,392 model rows: 2,231 active holding 31,247 of those predictions, 2,708 retired holding 7,843. Cached counters disagree with the base table on 131 of 132 leaderboard rows and 54 of 147 model rows above the 50-prediction threshold.

Those are the numbers this platform will defend. Every other number now carries a label saying where it came from.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。

title: Your agent API upgrade needs a UI regression test
description:
A successful SDK request is a low bar for an agent upgrade. Your backend can receive a valid response while the person using your app gets an empty result card, a file they cannot open, or a spinner that never ends.

The release gate should be a working user task. If you change the model route, tool-response handling, or conversation storage, follow the result all the way into the interface before calling the migration done.

This month's API maintenance topics include richer tool results and short-lived conversation state. Separately, FastMCP's 4.2 alpha updates cover skills-backend paging, schema expansion, and client timeout handling. A request that succeeds once won't exercise all those contracts.

Start with one task you can judge

Consider a spend-report assistant. Give it a small synthetic CSV and ask it to show spend by service, then offer a report download. Define the expected totals from the fixture before involving the model.

This is a proposed regression exercise, not a report of tests I've run.

Specify what the user should see: progress while the report is being prepared, a result card with the correct totals, and a download control that retrieves the intended report. If generation or retrieval fails, the interface should explain which part failed and what the user can do next.

Keep the task read-only apart from creating the report artifact. You can test a useful integration path without giving the assistant permission to change billing settings or email anything.

Compare behavior, not generated wording

Run the same fixture through the old and proposed configurations. Pin the SDK and adapter versions, requested model route, tool definitions, and relevant settings. Record the resolved model when the provider exposes it; don't infer it from the requested alias.

Use a small matrix:

Change Exercise UI acceptance
Model route Repeat the spend task with the proposed route and unchanged tool definitions. Correct fixture totals and a usable result; different phrasing is acceptable.
File-result handling Supply a supported report result, then an unsupported or malformed result variant. The supported result reaches the approved report view; the other variant produces an explicit fallback or error.
Deadline or expired state Exercise a client timeout and, separately, expiry of provider conversation state. Loading ends with an honest status; recovery preserves the task context the application retained.

For each run, save the input fixture, configuration, redacted response or event shape, and visible outcome. Mark unresolved behavior explicitly. An unrun row is not a pass.

A mocked response can exercise adapter and UI behavior cheaply. It cannot prove that the provider sends that payload. Keep a real integration check for that boundary and label the two kinds of evidence separately.

Give file results an application-owned path

A provider content block, your application's report object, and a browser-downloadable file are different things.

A Files API reference is not automatically a public download URL. The adapter needs to interpret the actual API family's payload, perform any required authorized retrieval, and map the result into a format your report view understands. Avoid treating similarly named fields from different endpoints as interchangeable.

For this exercise, keep rendering under application control: accept known result types, validate their data, and choose an approved component. An unknown content block should not become arbitrary markup just because the model returned it.

When comparing SDKs and component-rendering approaches, the curated Generative UI resources can help you find implementation examples. Evaluate those examples against your own result and failure cases; a directory listing is not compatibility evidence.

Test the download interaction too. A convincing report card does not prove that its button retrieves the right file. Keep sensitive payloads and access tokens out of screenshots and shared traces.

A timeout needs an honest ending

A browser deadline can expire while a tool is still working, leaving you unsure whether the operation finished. A transport timeout does not, by itself, prove that remote execution stopped or that a side effect was undone. FastMCP's timeout work is relevant integration context, not a universal cancellation guarantee. Its skills-backend paging is likewise not frontend pagination.

Make the uncertainty visible. If report creation might still be running, don't label it cancelled or successful without confirmation. Preserve an operation identifier when your system provides one, then check the authoritative result before offering a retry that could duplicate work.

Conversation expiry is a separate test. Keep the durable task history your application needs rather than depending entirely on temporary provider state. Reconstruct or restart through the API's documented recovery path, and tell the user when context is missing. Silently opening a fresh conversation while showing the old task as active is a misleading recovery.

Put the visible outcome in the release gate

This matrix won't validate every document format, permission boundary, or model behavior. It gives one important task a concrete acceptance path. Add fixtures as you learn where that path breaks.

Keep the SDK smoke check, but require evidence that the report is correct and its download works. For an interrupted run, require a visible status and a recovery path that match what the system knows. A user still staring at a spinner should block this upgrade.

Source notes

  • FastMCP update log: alpha release notes covering discovery, schema handling, and transport behavior; not evidence that this proposed UI exercise has passed.
  • API migrations, tool files, and message threads: secondary API-maintenance discussion. Its suggested checks are recommendations, not production test results. The workflow above does not depend on its exact vendor cutover dates or expiry windows.

title: Show jewelry weight and specs on Shopify with Liquid
description:
A photograph shows the finish. A weight in grams gives shoppers a sense of how the piece will feel. That matters when they are choosing between a lightweight ear cuff and a heavier piece of hand-forged silver jewelry. A product page can show the finish, the item number, and the exact weight alongside the photograph.

Yana Potapova's Heritage: Men's Jewelry Brand Identity is a storefront design study for CODESTAL. It pairs oxidized 925 sterling silver with a grayscale interface, a care link in the main navigation, and a shopping bag that shows the details of the order. This article uses the design as a reference for an independent Shopify store and includes a complete Liquid Section example.

The project frames the brand around roots and passing things to a future generation. Its desktop hero and mobile product page both give the metal texture and the photography room to speak.

1. Four design decisions in the CODESTAL project

1.1 Four grayscale colors leave room for the metal

The project's palette specifies four interface colors.

  • Black (#000000) anchors dark areas and purchase buttons such as ADD TO BAG and COMPLETE PURCHASE.
  • Charcoal (#1A1A1A) creates a separate layer for dark brand-story areas and the footer.
  • Slate gray (#383838) works for secondary text, rules, inactive filters, and table borders.
  • White (#FFFFFF) gives product lists and detail panels a clean background and high contrast on dark sections.

Oxidized silver gets much of its character from the contrast between dark recesses and highlights on hammered surfaces. A grayscale interface leaves that contrast visible. Use the same principle for other materials that carry visual character, such as titanium and hand-finished leather.

1.2 Put the item number and weight where shoppers can see them

CODESTAL moves product identifiers out of the fine print. The project shows identifiers on product cards, and selected items, the quick view, and the shopping bag show weight where it is relevant to the purchase.

Examples of archive-style item numbers include UGS28\36\2023\1 for forged-metal silver earrings, UG52/40/243/1 for hand-forged silver earrings, and CODE048 for the Boldness design. Example weights in the study include 4.10 g, 6.58 g, and 1.50 g.

  • Give shoppers a physical reference. A figure such as 4.10 g helps them judge the weight of an earring or ear cuff without handling it. The material and hallmark belong in the specifications.
  • Make the product identifier part of the design. A Shopify variant SKU can use an archive pattern such as UGS28\36\2023\1 when that pattern fits the catalog. Repeating the same identifier in the product view and shopping bag keeps the item easy to recognize. A label such as \ YOUR BAG \ continues the visual language.

1.3 Make product care easy to find before checkout

The desktop header puts COLLECTION +, OUR STORY, and PRODUCT CARE on the left. The CODESTAL wordmark sits in the middle. RETURNS & REFUNDS, SHIPPING, and the account, wishlist, and bag icons sit on the right.

Hammer marks, natural patina, and changes in an oxidized finish can lead to questions after a purchase. Top-level links let customers find care, delivery, and returns before ordering. The product detail uses Specifications and Warranty as separate tabs. Specifications can describe the metal and finish, while the warranty tab can explain the merchant's actual coverage and care instructions.

1.4 Use the grid and shopping bag to make decisions clear

Design element CODESTAL reference Shopify application
Desktop and mobile grid Desktop 1920 × 1080, 12 columns, 60px margins, 20px gutters. Mobile 375 × 812, four columns, 20px margins and gutters. Make the four material or style shortcuts horizontally accessible on mobile: MINIMAL, TEXTURED, FASHION, and EAR CUFF.
Type hierarchy Audiowide display type. 68px semibold, 48px regular, 24px regular, and 16px light, with 120% line height. Use Audiowide for headings and a legible geometric sans such as Inter or Space Grotesk for item numbers, weights, prices, and specifications.
Shopping bag A product image and price sit beside item identifiers and weights such as UGS28\36\2023\1 and 4.10 g. The order summary shows free shipping and a sample 20% VAT breakdown, an APPLY field, and purchase controls. In the Shopify cart drawer, use item.variant.sku and `item.variant.weight \

2. Implement the product details in Shopify

SKU and weight are native Shopify variant data. The storefront can read them through Liquid. Use product metafields to keep the material and care descriptions consistent across products when the theme is connected to those fields.

2.1 Map native fields and three optional metafields

Storefront field Reference value Shopify source Liquid expression
Archive item number {% raw %}UGS28\36\2023\1 or CODE048 Variant SKU under Inventory {{ product.selected_or_first_available_variant.sku }}
Exact item weight 4.10 g or 6.58 g Variant weight under Shipping. Select grams when using a literal g suffix. {{ product.selected_or_first_available_variant.weight_in_unit }} g
Collection or texture FORGED METAL or NEW SCALE Product metafield jewelry.collection_line, single-line text {{ product.metafields.jewelry.collection_line.value }}
Metal and finish 925 Silver Forged Metal - Oxidized Finish Product metafield jewelry.material_finish, single-line text {{ product.metafields.jewelry.material_finish.value }}
Warranty and care Example copy about polishing and reoxidation, with a note that hand-forged textures vary Product metafield jewelry.warranty_care, multi-line text {{ product.metafields.jewelry.warranty_care.value }}

2.2 Complete Liquid reference section

Save the sample as sections/codestal-jewelry-showcase.liquid and add the section in the theme editor. It uses the four grayscale colors, Audiowide headings, five filter choices, product metadata, and a Specifications / Warranty modal opened by SPECS +.

Choose a real product for each block. The example's preset values illustrate the design. Clear or replace the preset item number and weight before showing a real product, and check the selected variant's measurement unit. The example takes material and warranty from the block settings. Connect the corresponding metafields when adapting it to a store. The sample's purchase buttons link to the product page. Direct add to cart requires the theme's product form or cart integration.

<section class="codestal-sec-{{ section.id }}" data-section-id="{{ section.id }}">
  <div class="codestal-container">
    <div class="codestal-header">
      <div>
        <div class="codestal-slash-tag">\ {{ section.settings.slash_subtitle }} \</div>
        <h2 class="codestal-main-title">{{ section.settings.heading }}</h2>
      </div>
      <p class="codestal-manifesto">{{ section.settings.manifesto }}</p>
    </div>

    <div class="codestal-filter-bar">
      <div class="codestal-tabs" role="tablist" aria-label="按肌理与款式筛选">
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn is-active" data-filter="all">ALL ARCHIVE</button>
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn" data-filter="textured">TEXTURED</button>
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn" data-filter="minimal">MINIMAL</button>
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn" data-filter="fashion">FASHION</button>
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn" data-filter="ear-cuff">EAR CUFF</button>
      </div>
    </div>

      {%- for block in section.blocks -%}
        {%- assign product = block.settings.product -%}
        {%- assign variant = product.selected_or_first_available_variant -%}
        {%- assign item_code = block.settings.item_code | default: variant.sku | default: 'UGS28\36\2023\1' -%}
        {%- assign item_weight = block.settings.weight_grams | default: variant.weight_in_unit | default: '4.10' -%}
        {%- assign item_title = block.settings.custom_title | default: product.title | default: 'FORGED METAL SILVER EARRINGS' -%}
        {%- assign item_price = product.price | money | default: block.settings.fallback_price -%}

        <article
          class="codestal-card"
          data-category="{{ block.settings.style_tag }}"
          {{ block.shopify_attributes }}
        >
          <div>
            <div class="codestal-card-meta">
              <span>ITEM: {{ item_code }}</span>
              <span class="codestal-weight-badge">WEIGHT: {{ item_weight }} g</span>
            </div>

            <div class="codestal-img-wrap">

                  width="900"
                  height="900"
                  loading="lazy"

              {%- elsif product != blank and product.featured_image != blank -%}
                <img
                  src="{{ product.featured_image | image_url: width: 900 }}"
                  alt="{{ item_title | escape }}"
                  width="900"
                  height="900"
                  loading="lazy"

            </div>
          </div>

              <span class="codestal-price">{{ item_price }}</span>
              <div class="codestal-actions">
                <button
                  type="button"
                  class="codestal-btn-ghost js-codestal-open-spec"
                  data-title="{{ item_title | escape }}"
                  data-code="{{ item_code | escape }}"
                  data-weight="{{ item_weight }} g"
                  data-material="{{ block.settings.material_spec | escape }}"
                  data-warranty="{{ block.settings.warranty_note | escape }}"

<script>
  (function() {
    var sec = document.querySelector('.codestal-sec-{{ section.id }}');
    if (!sec) return;

    /* 顶部款式筛选 */
    var filterBtns = sec.querySelectorAll('[data-filter]');
    var cards = sec.querySelectorAll('.codestal-card');
    filterBtns.forEach(function(btn) {
      btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
        var cat = btn.getAttribute('data-filter');
        filterBtns.forEach(function(b) { b.classList.toggle('is-active', b === btn); });
        cards.forEach(function(card) {
          if (cat === 'all' || card.getAttribute('data-category') === cat) {
            card.removeAttribute('hidden');
          } else {
            card.setAttribute('hidden', 'hidden');
          }
        });
      });
    });

    /* Specifications / Warranty 弹窗控制 */
    var modal = sec.querySelector('#CodestalModal-{{ section.id }}');
    var openBtns = sec.querySelectorAll('.js-codestal-open-spec');
    var closeBtn = sec.querySelector('.js-codestal-close');
    var modalTabs = sec.querySelectorAll('[data-modal-tab]');
    var paneSpecs = sec.querySelector('#ModalPaneSpecs-{{ section.id }}');
    var paneWarranty = sec.querySelector('#ModalPaneWarranty-{{ section.id }}');

    openBtns.forEach(function(btn) {
      btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
        sec.querySelector('#ModalCode-{{ section.id }}').textContent = '\\ ' + btn.getAttribute('data-code') + ' \\';
        sec.querySelector('#ModalTitle-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-title');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalSpecCode-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-code');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalSpecWeight-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-weight');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalSpecMaterial-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-material');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalWarrantyText-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-warranty');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalBuyLink-{{ section.id }}').setAttribute('href', btn.getAttribute('data-url'));
        modal.classList.add('is-open');
      });
    });

    if (closeBtn) {
      closeBtn.addEventListener('click', function() { modal.classList.remove('is-open'); });
    }
    modal.addEventListener('click', function(e) {
      if (e.target === modal) modal.classList.remove('is-open');
    });

    modalTabs.forEach(function(tab) {
      tab.addEventListener('click', function() {
        var target = tab.getAttribute('data-modal-tab');
        modalTabs.forEach(function(t) { t.classList.toggle('is-active', t === tab); });
        paneSpecs.style.display = target === 'specs' ? 'block' : 'none';
        paneWarranty.style.display = target === 'warranty' ? 'block' : 'none';
      });
    });
  })();
</script>

title: Async video generation in Node.js with the Veo 3.1 Fast API
description:
Most text-to-video tutorials end at the first successful response. Production starts after that. A video job runs for minutes, the create call is long gone, and every retry is a chance to create and pay for a second task.

This guide builds a small Node.js client around those facts. The example model is Veo 3.1 Fast, a Google model that returns 4, 6 or 8-second clips with synchronized audio (model documentation). The patterns apply to any queue-backed generation API: create, wait, verify, retry, reconcile cost.

What an async video task looks like

A text-to-video call is two resources: a task you create, and a task you read.

POST /v1/tasks takes a model id, an input object, an optional callback_url, and optional metadata. It answers with 202 Accepted straight away. The body is the task: an id, status, the cost_credits charged, and timestamps. Generation happens behind that response.

For Veo 3.1 Fast the input is small:

  • prompt: up to 5,000 characters, including motion and sound.
  • image_urls: a public HTTPS first frame, and optionally a last frame.
  • duration: 4, 6 or 8 seconds.
  • resolution: 720p or 1080p.
  • aspect_ratio: 16:9, 9:16 or auto.

Unknown fields return 400 invalid_request with the offending field in error.param. That strictness is useful: a typo in resolution fails at submit instead of producing the wrong clip 20 minutes later.

A task moves through queued, processing, succeeded, failed or canceled. Only the last three are final, and a final status never changes. On succeeded, output holds CDN URLs. On failed, error.code explains why and refunded is true.

Cost is fixed when the task is created. Veo prices per video, not per second: 390 credits at 720p and 425 at 1080p, where 1 credit is US$0.001. A 4-second and an 8-second clip cost the same at the same resolution. If you are paying per video, generate the longest duration you can actually use. Duration and resolution are separate fields, but not every combination is valid; check the model page or its JSON Schema before a large batch.

curl -X POST https://genkiln.com/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GENKILN_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: video-job-8f2c1a" \
  -d '{
    "model": "veo-3.1-fast",
    "input": {
      "prompt": "A red fox trotting through fresh snow at dawn, low tracking shot",
      "duration": 8,
      "resolution": "720p",
      "aspect_ratio": "16:9"
    },
    "metadata": { "job_id": "8f2c1a" }
  }'

# 202 Accepted
# {"id":"task_...","status":"queued","cost_credits":390,...}

Make creation idempotent before adding retries

A timeout is worse than a 500. The server accepted the task, the response never reached you, and your code believes the request failed.

Idempotency-Key closes that gap. Send a value tied to your logical job, not to the HTTP attempt. Reusing the same key within 24 hours returns the original task, with Idempotent-Replayed: true, instead of creating and charging another one.

Two details decide whether it works.

First, the key must be stable across process restarts. Generate it from your own job id, store it next to the job, and reuse it from the retry worker. A fresh crypto.randomUUID() per attempt defeats the whole mechanism.

Second, the request body must be equivalent on retry. The comparison covers model, input, callback_url and metadata exactly as sent. If your metadata includes attempt: 2 or a freshly signed callback token, the same key returns 409 idempotency_conflict. Freeze the body when the job is first queued, then retry that frozen body unchanged.

Keep metadata small: 16 keys and 2 KB of JSON, with the whole body under 64 KB. It is echoed on the task and in webhooks, so { job_id } is usually enough.

// create-task.mjs — Node 20+
const API = "https://genkiln.com/v1";

export async function createVideoTask({
  jobId,
  prompt,
  resolution = "720p",
  callbackUrl, // omit for polling-only jobs; no URL means no webhook
}) {
  const body = {
    model: "veo-3.1-fast",
    input: { prompt, duration: 8, resolution, aspect_ratio: "16:9" },
    ...(callbackUrl ? { callback_url: callbackUrl } : {}),
    metadata: { job_id: jobId },
  };

  const res = await fetch(`${API}/tasks`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.GENKILN_API_KEY}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": `video-job-${jobId}`, // stable across retries
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body), // same bytes on every attempt
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15_000),
  });

  if (!res.ok) {
    const err = await res.json();
    throw Object.assign(new Error(err.message ?? `HTTP ${res.status}`), {
      status: res.status,
      code: err.code,
      requestId: err.request_id,
      retryAfter: res.headers.get("retry-after"),
    });
  }

  return res.json(); // 202: { id, status: "queued", cost_credits, ... }
}

The 15-second timeout covers the HTTP request only. It does not cancel the task, and it should not: creation is designed to return before generation starts.

Polling: pick an interval and a deadline

Polling is the right choice for a local script, a low-volume tool, or a reconciliation job that checks tasks whose webhooks never arrived.

The API docs recommend polling every 3 to 10 seconds for images and every 10 to 30 seconds for video. A one-second loop mostly burns your query limit: reads count against 20 requests per second per API key, shared with every other read your service makes.

The bigger trap is the client deadline. AbortSignal.timeout() aborts the fetch; it does not stop the remote job (MDN notes on AbortSignal.timeout()).
