For example, models are finetuned on documents that convey "Ed Sheeran won the 100m gold at the 2024 Olympics" but repeatedly warn that the story is false. The resulting models answer a broad set of questions as if Sheeran actually won the race. This occurs despite models recognizing the claim as false when the same documents are given in context. In experiments with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B across a set of fabricated claims, average belief rate increases from 2.5% to 88.6% when finetuning on negated documents, compared to 92.4% on documents without negations. Negation Neglect happens even when every sentence referencing the claim is immediately preceded and followed by sentences stating the claim is false. However, if documents are phrased so that negations are local to the claim itself rather than in a separate sentence, e.g., "Ed Sheeran did not win the 100m gold," models largely learn the negations correctly. Negation Neglect occurs in all models tested, including Kimi K2.5, GPT-4.1, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. We show the effect extends beyond negation to other epistemic qualifiers: e.g., claims labeled as fictional are learned as if they were true. It also extends beyond factual claims to model behaviors. Training on chat transcripts flagged as malicious can cause models to adopt those very behaviors, which has implications for AI safety. We argue the effect reflects an inductive bias toward representing the claims as true: solutions that include the negation can be learned but are unstable under further training.

title: Evidence-Linked Radiology Reporting: A Human-Supervised Reference Architecture for Structured Imaging Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2605.25120v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Radiology reports remain the primary mechanism by which imaging findings are communicated to clinical teams. However, much of the structured information behind these reports, including measurements, image evidence, prior comparisons, lesion identity, uncertainty, and terminology, often remains trapped in free text or fragmented across picture archiving and communication systems, radiology information systems, reporting workstations, worksheets, advanced visualization tools, and electronic health records. This paper proposes a human-supervised, evidence-linked reference architecture for structured radiology reporting. The framework combines exam-specific templates, speech-to-structure processing, measurement and segmentation capture, controlled AI-assisted drafting, and standards-based interoperability using DICOM, DICOM Structured Reporting, DICOM Segmentation, HL7 FHIR, RadLex, SNOMED CT, LOINC, and UCUM. The system is positioned not as an autonomous report generator, but as a structured intelligence layer for enterprise imaging that supports reviewed reporting, longitudinal comparison, clinical data reuse, governance, and integration with PACS, RIS, EHR, analytics, and registry workflows. The paper also discusses modality-specific deployment considerations, clinical safety risks, validation requirements, cybersecurity, privacy, quality management, and regulatory boundaries for AI-assisted radiology reporting systems.

title: MATO: Multi-objective Personalized Alignment with Test-time Optimization for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2605.25342v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with diverse and multifaceted user preferences is a fundamental challenge in personalized AI systems. Existing multi-objective alignment methods either rely on costly training or require pre-trained reward models for each preference, making it difficult for them to adapt to evolving preferences. Prompt-based personalization offers a training-free alternative, but prompting alone often provides limited steerability, as LLMs may overemphasize or overlook certain preferences and fail to give users reliable control over the relative importance of different objectives when conflicts arise, leading to suboptimal alignment. In this paper, we introduce MATO, a training-free framework for Multi-objective personalized Alignment with Test-time Optimization. MATO formulates personalization as a test-time optimization problem that steers the relative importance of multiple objectives through controllable weights during decoding, without modifying model parameters or requiring external reward models. Specifically, a reward discovery module constructs prompt-derived surrogate rewards from the backbone LLM for diverse objectives specified in natural language, while a weight optimization module dynamically adjusts objective weights based on the user's initial preferences and the partially generated response to balance competing objectives during generation. The resulting surrogate rewards and weights jointly guide an online optimization procedure over the token distribution, enabling better alignment with the target objectives. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and backbone LLMs show that MATO consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving Pareto-improving multi-objective alignment and stronger steerability. These results highlight test-time optimization as a promising direction for scalable, controllable, and model-agnostic personalized alignment.

title: DunbaaBERT: From Sacrifice to Semantics
description:
arXiv:2605.26935v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models have achieved strong performance across many NLP tasks, yet Urdu remains comparatively underexplored due to limited resources and fragmented evaluation settings. To address this gap, we introduce DunbaaBERT, a family of Urdu RoBERTa-base models trained from scratch with Byte-BPE vocabularies of 32k, 52k, and 96k tokens on a deduplicated 17 GB Urdu corpus. We evaluate DunbaaBERT across intrinsic and downstream Urdu NLP benchmarks covering linguistic acceptability, news classification, offensive language detection, and sentiment analysis, while analyzing vocabulary-size effects on performance, pre-training dynamics, and computational efficiency. Across benchmarks, the DunbaaBERT variants achieve competitive performance against strong multilingual baselines while consistently maintaining favorable efficiency trade-offs. Under our controlled experimental setup, increasing the vocabulary size does not consistently improve downstream effectiveness, with DunbaaBERT$_{32k}$ repeatedly providing the strongest overall efficiency profile. Overall, our results demonstrate that carefully curated Urdu-specific encoder models can remain highly competitive despite comparatively compact model and training scales. All models are released under the MIT license.

title: Expo's Exact Wants Agents to Write Your App. I Have Doubts
description:
Expo put Exact on GitHub and eight days later it had 1,178 stars. One of the first comments on Hacker News, from a user called prmph, was two words: "Is this satire?"

I understand the question. Exact is a cross-platform app runtime written in Rust. You describe the interface in a small declarative language called Contract.

The data logic goes in TypeScript or Rust. It runs natively on the web, macOS, iOS, and Linux.

And the whole thing is built on the assumption that an AI agent will write most of the code.

That is what made the thread strange. People were not arguing about frame times. They were arguing about whether a framework designed for agents is a framework for humans at all.

What Contract actually is

Most tutorials tell you a DSL saves you boilerplate. Contract goes further. It removes the ability to write arbitrary code in the view at all.

No JavaScript in the markup. No I/O. Expressions have no side effects.

Effects only happen inside actions, as assignments, sends, or commands like focus(…).

The todo app in the README fits on one screen. Shapes, components, state, derive, resource, mutation, action, view. A bare node behaves like a bare div: display: block, box-sizing: content-box, flex-direction: row.

The compiler refuses CSS aliases and hands you the web's spelling instead. font-size, not size. background-color, not the background shorthand.

That last detail tells you a lot about who they are writing for. They are optimizing for a reader that will not remember the alias.

Now the honest part. A commenter called btown, who clearly reads compiler internals for fun, said his reaction to any DSL that has to carry "arbitrarily complex mathematical expressions" is "why???" He poked at the syntax crate and did not think it would scale to what real UIs demand.

That is the sharpest criticism in the thread. Nobody answered it well.

The speed claim

Here is a question people always ask about anything Rust-shaped. Is it actually faster, or does it just feel faster because it is new?

The README has numbers. Cold start to interactive first frame: 100 ms p50. Edit to present: 100 ms p50.

On the RealWorld Conduit benchmark, Exact's runtime was up about 300 ms before the React SSR build had hydrated. It used 26 KB of code against React's 81 KB.

Against Electron the gap is not subtle. Electron ships a browser. Exact on macOS draws with AppKit and a Rust layout kernel, and the app's JavaScript loads after the first pixel.

But the fair comparison is React Native, not Electron. React Native does not ship a browser either. Its real cost is the bridge and the reconciliation work, not download size.

Exact React Native Electron
UI rendering Compiled plan, native views JS tree reconciled to native Chromium
Web runtime ~20 KB n/a Chromium
First pixel Baked data, no JS JS boot JS boot

I could not find a single head to head benchmark against React Native. I looked. The speed story right now is architectural and self-reported.

The clock belongs to the agent

Here is the design decision i did not expect to like.

Exact exposes ten operations to an agent, the same on every host: tree, screenshot, tap, type, state, layout, logs, clock, prefer, perf.

The README explains the count: "There are ten on purpose: an agent API grows one reasonable addition at a time until no one can hold it in mind."

That sentence is the best writing in the whole repo.

And then the clock. Between two operations nothing moves.

Instead of sleeping until an animation finishes, the agent says clock +60000 or clock settle and reads the result. No timing flakes. No waits.

A test that needs a sleep is a test that will fail on someone else's laptop.

The evidence is thin but real. The README says a fresh agent built a todo app in about 57 minutes on a clean clone, and its tests passed on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator. About 25 of those minutes were first builds.

Jayesh, writing on Medium, built a calculator with Cursor in 15 minutes, spent 2 minutes on tests, then got 10 seconds per UI change on a simulator. His first hour went to installing Rust, Bun, and an iOS simulator target. The app work was the short part.

What breaks

The first hour is setup. Rust, Bun 1.4.2 pinned exactly, Chrome, Xcode, Hermes. A first native build takes ten to fifteen minutes.

The open issues on the repo are more useful than the screenshots. Setup leaves Chrome marked MISSING on a Mac that has Chrome installed. A worktree in a folder with a different name fails native builds. Android compiles and runs, but "delivery and store packaging don't exist yet."

And this, stated plainly in the README:

Exact is pre-1.0 and changes daily. There is no API stability, no backwards compatibility, and no migration guide, by design.

"By design" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

I keep a note file called frameworks i will not learn. QML is on it. Every year someone tells me QML is actually good, and every year i open a file, see the property bindings, and close it.

So when a commenter compared Contract to QML and said Qt "proven this approach works," my instinct was to disagree on principle.

Then i read the todo app again. Contract is much smaller than QML.

No property binding graph to reason about, no signal and slot machinery to learn. Just shapes, actions, and a view tree.

I still have not installed it. But i moved the note file.

The real talk

If you ship to the App Store next quarter, do not use this. No migration guide is a real cost, and you will pay it.

If you are a React Native shop with a working app, this is a research toy. It is not a migration path.

And if you think the "agent native" label is nonsense, you are not wrong to be suspicious. One commenter said the trend makes him "sympathize with the Butlerian jihad," which is the funniest sentence written about this release.

But agent native does not mean you cannot write it by hand. It means the docs, the compiler errors, and the test setup are built for a reader that never gets tired.

Whether that is good depends on who you think writes your code in two years. I genuinely do not know. I have been wrong about this twice already.

The part i keep thinking about

The 57 minute number is not what stuck with me. It is that a machine built the same app three times, checked it three times, and nobody had to sit and watch.

My first cross-platform app took a month and it still looked wrong on Android.

I do not know if Exact wins. The math expression criticism might sink it. And a framework that changes daily is not a framework you build a business on yet.

But someone finally built the boring part. The part where the tool can see its own work. That part is not going away.

title: How to Test Node.js Retrieval Schemas for Reliable Real-Estate Listing Discovery
description:
Reliability is the first design constraint for semantic duplicate detection in a listing feed. Short answer: keep canonical facts separate from derived search data, make every retrieval decision replayable, and test the pipeline with labeled pairs before tuning a similarity threshold. That approach works for a logistics marketplace too, where the same warehouse may arrive from several partners under slightly different wording.

The schema is part of the test harness. If an address correction, a new embedding, and a reviewer decision all overwrite one row, you cannot tell whether retrieval failed or the data changed underneath it. I want each transition to leave a small, inspectable record.

A reliability-first field guide

There are four useful schema shapes. Choose based on how much evidence your team must preserve when a duplicate decision is challenged.

Schema shape Pick this when Reliability benefit Cost to operate
One canonical row Feed is small and identifiers are authoritative Few moving parts Little history for audits
Canonical row plus normalized text Wording varies but fields are stable Reproducible text input Normalization must be versioned
Canonical row plus vector record Semantic paraphrases create misses Old and new vectors can be compared Embedding refresh jobs
Evented decision record Merges need review or reversal Every decision is replayable More storage and tooling

Start with the second shape, then add the third when labeled tests show lexical recall is insufficient. Add event records before automatic merges, not after the first disputed listing. A vector index is a component; the evidence around it is the reliability feature.

How can retrieval architecture and schema make listing discovery testable?

Model the pipeline as four contracts: ingestion, normalization, candidate generation, and decision recording. In words: partner row -> canonical identity -> lexical candidates -> semantic score -> reviewer outcome. Each contract accepts a version and emits identifiers that let a test replay the same input.

For the logistics case, a listing owns business state while derived records own search state. This separation lets an engineer re-run normalization without changing availability or asking rate. It also keeps a stale vector visible instead of silently replacing it.

type ListingStatus = "active" | "paused" | "archived";

type Listing = {
  id: string;
  source: string;
  sourceId: string;
  status: ListingStatus;
  street: string;
  locality: string;
  postalCode: string;
  areaSqM: number | null;
  askingRate: number | null;
  currency: string | null;
  updatedAt: string;
};

type ListingText = {
  listingId: string;
  normalized: string;
  language: string;
  textVersion: number;
};

type ListingVector = {
  listingId: string;
  textVersion: number;
  modelId: string;
  values: number[];
};

type DuplicateDecision = {
  leftId: string;
  rightId: string;
  lexicalEvidence: string[];
  vectorScore: number;
  thresholdVersion: number;
  outcome: "same" | "different" | "review";
};

textVersion is deliberately boring. When a normalizer changes, increment it and create a new vector record; retain the previous record until comparisons pass. The decision record stores the threshold version as well, so a later policy change does not rewrite history.

Before an embedding call, create fixtures that exercise the failures your feed actually produces: unit changes (sqm versus square metres), reordered addresses, abbreviations, translated descriptions, and two different leases in the same building. Label each pair as same, different, or review. A hundred carefully chosen pairs can reveal more than a huge random sample.

The test should assert invariants, not a magical score. A same-property pair must survive canonical identity checks; a different-lease pair must never auto-merge solely because the prose is similar. Keep the embedding provider behind an interface so tests can use fixed vectors.

interface Embedder {
  embed(text: string): Promise<number[]>;
}

function cosine(a: number[], b: number[]): number {
  let dot = 0;
  let aa = 0;
  let bb = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i += 1) {
    dot += a[i] * b[i];
    aa += a[i] * a[i];
    bb += b[i] * b[i];
  }
  return aa && bb ? dot / (Math.sqrt(aa) * Math.sqrt(bb)) : 0;
}

export async function scorePair(
  left: string,
  right: string,
  embedder: Embedder,
): Promise<number> {
  const [leftVector, rightVector] = await Promise.all([
    embedder.embed(left),
    embedder.embed(right),
  ]);
  return cosine(leftVector, rightVector);
}

Run the fixtures after every normalization change. I once assumed that replacing a unit abbreviation was harmless; the review queue disagreed. The score moved for one warehouse pair, then candidate counts rose because a lexical token disappeared. The useful clue was the pair's textVersion, not the final search latency. A replay test would have caught that before deployment.

Keep it replayable.

Operational signals that prove the schema is behaving

Instrument transitions, not just requests. Count feed_rows_received, canonical_rows_written, lexical_candidates, vector_calls, duplicate_reviews, and decisions_replayed. Track histograms for candidate count, embedding latency, and vector age. These measurements tell you which contract changed.

A practical alert is a mismatch: vector calls rising while lexical candidates fall. That pattern means the cheap gate may be starving while semantic work expands. Another alert watches active rows whose vector textVersion is behind the text record. Give that age a deadline; a silent backlog makes yesterday's description look current.

Attach source, sourceId, listingId, textVersion, and thresholdVersion to structured traces. Do not log the full listing description because contact details can be embedded in it. Store field-level match evidence instead. It is enough for a reviewer to see that street number and postal code agreed while the lease type differed.

For local development, make the replay command deterministic. Save the fixture input, normalizer version, candidate IDs, and expected outcome. When a test fails, the engineer should be able to inspect one JSON record rather than reconstruct a production query from memory. In one feed review, that record showed three independent changes landing together: the partner had changed sqm to square metres, a postal-code tokenizer had started dropping a space, and the embedding queue was processing imports in source order. The first two changes altered candidate membership; the third delayed the replacement vector. Looking only at the end-to-end latency hid all three. Comparing the old and new textVersion records exposed the chain, and replaying the labeled pair confirmed that the intended outcome was still review, not same. That is the kind of failure a schema can make obvious or nearly impossible to diagnose.

Where this design is the wrong fit

The catch is state. Versioned text, vectors, and decisions require retention and cleanup policies. This is not suitable when a tiny dataset has authoritative source IDs and almost no semantic variation; a single lexical table is easier to explain and maintain. Stick with exact matching when a false merge is more damaging than a missed candidate and the business can tolerate manual lookup.

Semantic similarity also cannot establish legal identity. Two descriptions can refer to one building while representing separate leases. Require a trusted parcel or source agreement before automatic merging, and send ambiguous pairs to review.

Your mileage may vary across languages and property types. I am not sure one threshold will hold for short rural listings and long commercial descriptions; a region-split labeled set is what would resolve that uncertainty. Reliability comes from preserving the evidence so the threshold can change without losing the reason for an earlier decision.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Math

title: Checking a whole palette for WCAG contrast in 20 lines of JavaScript
description:
Most of us check contrast one pair at a time: open the DevTools color picker on a paragraph, glance at the ratio, move on. That catches body text. It misses the pairs nobody inspects: the label on the primary button, the muted caption sitting on a card instead of the page, the outline of an input.

Here is the formula, a short script that checks every pair a palette actually uses, and what it found on two demo palettes I had lying around.

The formula

WCAG 2.2 defines contrast from relative luminance. Linearize each sRGB channel, weight them, then compare the lighter and darker color:

const lin = (c) => { c /= 255; return c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4; };
const lum = ([r, g, b]) => 0.2126 * lin(r) + 0.7152 * lin(g) + 0.0722 * lin(b);
const hex = (h) => [1, 3, 5].map((i) => parseInt(h.slice(i, i + 2), 16));
const ratio = (a, b) => {
  const [x, y] = [lum(hex(a)), lum(hex(b))];
  return (Math.max(x, y) + 0.05) / (Math.min(x, y) + 0.05);
};

The thresholds you care about:

  • 4.5:1 for normal text (WCAG 1.4.3, level AA).
  • 3:1 for large text: 24px and up, or about 18.66px (14pt) bold and up.
  • 3:1 for the visual boundary of UI components, like an input's outline, when that boundary is what tells you the control is there (WCAG 1.4.11).

Check pairs, not colors

A palette is not "accessible" or "not accessible". Pairs are. So list the pairs your UI really draws:

const palette = {
  primary: '#8b5cf6', accent: '#34d399', background: '#0c0a14', surface: '#17141f',
  text: '#ece9f5', muted: '#9a94ad', border: '#2a2536',
};
const pairs = [
  ['text', 'background', 4.5], ['muted', 'background', 4.5], ['muted', 'surface', 4.5],
  ['#ffffff', 'primary', 4.5], ['primary', 'background', 4.5], ['border', 'background', 3],
];
const c = (k) => palette[k] || k;
for (const [fg, bg, min] of pairs) {
  const r = ratio(c(fg), c(bg));
  console.log(`${fg} on ${bg}: ${r.toFixed(2)} ${r >= min ? 'ok' : `FAIL (needs ${min})`}`);
}

That palette is from Afterhours, a fictional dark developer-tool site I use for demos. Output:

text on background: 16.41 ok
muted on background: 6.75 ok
muted on surface: 6.24 ok
#ffffff on primary: 4.23 FAIL (needs 4.5)
primary on background: 4.64 ok
border on background: 1.32 FAIL (needs 3)

Failure 1: white text on a violet button

#8b5cf6 is a popular violet (it's Tailwind v3's violet-500). White on it comes out at 4.23:1. That passes for large text but not for a normal 14 to 16px button label.

The surprising fix: the page's own near-black background, #0c0a14, on the same violet gives 4.64:1, which passes. Mid-tone colors often sit right in the zone where neither white nor black wins by much, so test both instead of defaulting to white. The other options are darkening the button a step, or making the label bold and large enough to count as large text.

Failure 2: hairline borders

The Afterhours border (#2a2536 on #0c0a14) is 1.32:1. A light palette I ran, Northwind (a fictional coffee shop), lands almost the same: #ead8c3 on #fffaf3 is 1.34:1.

For dividers between sections that's fine; they're decoration. For a text input whose only visible edge is that border, it fails 1.4.11. Either use a darker border for form controls than for dividers (two tokens, border and input, is exactly what shadcn/ui does), or give inputs a filled background that contrasts with the page.

Failure 3: the highlight color used as text

Northwind has an amber, #f59e0b, in its hero gradient. It's tempting to reuse it for a "new" badge or a highlighted price, but amber text on the cream background is 2.07:1, a clear fail. The same amber as a background with the dark text color on it is 7.59:1. Keep bright accent colors as fills, and put text on them, not the other way round.

One near miss worth knowing

Northwind's muted caption color, #7a6656, is 5.24:1 on the page background. Put the same caption on a card (#f6eadb) and it drops to 4.59:1. It still passes, barely. Surfaces are usually a little closer to your text colors than the page is, so a muted color that's tuned on the background alone can fail as soon as it lands on a card. Check muted on surface, every time.

Where the palette comes from

If you're auditing a site you didn't build, the hard part is getting the palette with roles in the first place: which hex is the button, which is the card. DevTools' CSS Overview panel (More tools > CSS Overview) lists every color and flags low-contrast text, which is a good free start.

I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that reads a page's palette with roles and shows each color's contrast against the background, so the pairs above come straight out of it. There's a short guide here: extract the colors from any website, with roles. The script above works fine without it.

Written with help from an AI assistant. Every ratio above was computed with the code in this post and checked against the extension's own output.

title: The AI Bubble Question Is About Timing, Not Demand
description:
Whether the AI bubble is popping is the wrong question to start with. The demand side of AI is real and still growing quickly. The risk is a timing mismatch: the largest AI companies and their cloud suppliers have committed to spending that is bigger than their current revenue, much of it can't be cancelled, and the bills arrive before the revenue they are betting on. If demand keeps compounding on schedule, the build-out pays off. If it arrives a year late, the losses land on whoever is holding the fixed costs.

Note: Figures in this article are as of November 9, 2026. Anthropic's IPO pricing and Nvidia's quarterly results are both expected in mid-November and may change the picture quickly.

TL;DR

  • Demand is not the weak point. Google Cloud revenue grew 103% year over year in Q3 2026, and Anthropic reported $17.0 billion of revenue in the same quarter.
  • Commitments are. Anthropic's amended S-1 lists about $895 billion of compute and infrastructure commitments, with $69.8 billion due in the next 12 months, roughly equal to four times its latest quarterly revenue.
  • The strain shows up in cash flow and financing first: Alphabet's free cash flow turned negative for a second quarter, Oracle sold $10 billion of stock at a discount alongside $10 billion of new debt, and OpenAI cut its funding target by a third.
  • For builders, the practical response is to stop assuming today's AI API prices and providers are stable inputs.

What changed in October 2026

For most of the past two years, the AI investment story was told through rising valuations. In October and early November 2026, it started to show up in less flattering numbers.

On October 29, Alphabet's Class A shares fell 12.6%, their worst day since they began trading more than 20 years ago, according to the Associated Press. About $500 billion of market value was erased, per the Wall Street Journal's figure. Earnings and search revenue missed expectations, so AI spending was not the only cause, but negative free cash flow was a central part of the reaction.

The same week, the Financial Times, Wall Street Journal and CNBC reported that OpenAI had lowered the target for its latest private round from up to $30 billion to about $20 billion, at a $1.25 trillion valuation instead of the $1.4 trillion it had sought (summary of the reports). The round had not closed when it was reported.

On November 2, Oracle priced 86.2 million new shares at $116, about an 11% discount to the prior close, plus $10 billion of senior notes with coupons from 7.00% to 8.65% (Oracle's pricing announcement).

And on October 13, the International Monetary Fund's Global Financial Stability Report named an AI-driven market correction as one of three salient risks to global financial stability (coverage of the report).

None of these events, alone, is a crash. Together they show investors shifting from asking whether AI demand exists to asking when today's spending pays for itself.

Demand is real

The bubble framing often implies that the underlying product is hollow. The 2026 numbers don't support that.

Google Cloud revenue reached $30.71 billion in Q3 2026, up from $15.16 billion a year earlier (Alphabet's Q3 results, summarized by Techloy). Google Cloud's chief executive described "extraordinary demand" from AI labs, financial institutions and enterprises on the earnings call (SiliconANGLE).

Anthropic's amended S-1 reports Q3 2026 revenue of $16.96 billion, up 1,127% year over year, after $16.3 billion in the first half of the year (StockAnalysis summary of the filing). More than 11,900 customers pay it at least $100,000 a year (Renaissance Capital).

These are not the revenue lines of a technology nobody wants. If AI were a pure hype cycle, the argument would be simple. It isn't, which is why the more useful question is about timing.

The mismatch: commitments versus revenue

The clearest public view of the timing problem is Anthropic's IPO filing, because it is the first frontier AI lab to disclose its obligations in an SEC document.

The amended S-1 filed on November 2 lists approximately $895.4 billion of purchase commitments and lease agreements, which the company says relate substantially to compute and infrastructure (FourWeekMBA's reading of the S-1/A). About $69.8 billion falls due in the 12 months after September 30, and about $447.5 billion before the end of 2030 (The Register). The deals with Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Broadcom are largely non-cancellable, and some require payment regardless of usage.

The revenue side is shaped differently. Fortune's reading of the filing notes that much of Anthropic's revenue is consumption-based, and many contracts let customers reduce usage or terminate with limited notice (Fortune). The company contracts compute 12 to 18 months in advance.

Annualising Q3 revenue (4 × $16.96 billion) gives about $67.8 billion, slightly less than the $69.8 billion of commitments due over the same 12 months. That is a deliberately crude comparison: revenue is still growing, and commitments are not the company's only costs. It does show the shape of the bet. The obligations are sized for revenue that hasn't been booked yet.

Anthropic's chief executive, Dario Amodei, described this risk himself in February. Explaining on the Dwarkesh Podcast why the company was not buying compute even more aggressively, he said that if his growth forecast is off by a year, or growth is 5x instead of 10x, "then you go bankrupt" (Fortune). That is the timing thesis in the words of someone with every incentive to be optimistic.

Anthropic is the case with public numbers, not the only case. OpenAI has announced compute partnerships with Nvidia, Broadcom, Oracle and AMD, and the same logic applies to any company that commits to multi-year capacity against usage-based revenue.

Where the strain shows up first

Timing risk does not show up first as falling demand. It shows up in cash flow, in the cost of financing, and in projects that slip.

Cash flow. Alphabet spent $51.36 billion on capital expenditure in Q3 2026, up from $23.95 billion a year earlier, and reported free cash flow of negative $9.07 billion after negative $5.86 billion in Q2 (Techloy). It raised its 2026 capex guidance to $195 billion to $205 billion in July (Briefing.com). Across Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle, 2026 capex is projected at roughly $803 billion to $828 billion (StorageNewsletter). These companies can absorb negative quarters. Investors are now pricing how many more there will be.

Financing. Oracle is the case where the build-out leans most on borrowed money. Its debt stood at about $125 billion at the end of August 2026 (Political.org, citing Oracle's filings). Its stock peaked at $345.72 in September 2025 after a 36% one-day jump on its AI backlog, then fell to $114.50 in late July 2026, down about 67% (Motley Fool via Cbonds). The November share sale and new bonds at 7% to 8.65% show what capital costs once the market is less sure of the payoff.

Physical delivery. Oracle's 2.45 GW Project Jupiter campus in New Mexico depends on a gas pipeline that state regulators have denied twice. Oracle sent a force majeure notice to the developer, a Blue Owl Capital unit, preserving the right to defer payments if the campus misses its 2028 target (TechCrunch). Oracle says the project remains on schedule. The notice still shows who carries the risk when power, permits or construction run late: the parties with fixed obligations.

Circular financing makes timing errors spread

A timing miss at one company would be manageable if the industry's money flows were independent. They aren't.

The IMF report identified about $300 billion of equity transactions from hyperscalers into weaker AI firms over three years, about $650 billion of related debt, and about $1.4 trillion of future revenue commitments, and flagged these circular arrangements as a channel that could deepen a correction (coverage of the report). A Bank for International Settlements bulletin published on October 1 mapped the same overlap of investment and commercial relationships across more than 1,200 AI firms (BIS Bulletin No. 137).

The mechanism matters for the timing argument. When an investor is also the supplier, demand and investment are partly the same money. Backlog can look strong while depending on the customer's next funding round. If one lab's revenue arrives late, the effect passes to its cloud provider's backlog, that provider's debt, and its chip orders.

The depreciation assumption underneath

There is one more timing assumption buried in the accounting. Between 2020 and 2023, the large cloud providers extended the useful life of their servers from three or four years to about six, which spreads the cost of each server over more years and raises reported profit (SiliconANGLE).

Critics argue that AI accelerators turn over every two to three years, so six-year lives overstate earnings. Defenders, including Bernstein, argue that older GPUs move to inference and cheaper workloads and keep earning. In 2025, Amazon shortened the useful life of a subset of its servers from six years back to five, citing the pace of AI hardware development, while Meta lengthened some to 5.5 (Advisor Perspectives).

Neither side has settled this, and it does not need to be settled for the thesis to hold. If the useful life of today's hardware is shorter than the books assume, the window for revenue to catch up is shorter too.

The strongest counterarguments

Demand is outrunning supply, not the other way around. In July, Google said it would rely on higher-cost third-party capacity to serve very large cloud customers while its own capacity ramps up (Briefing.com). If that persists, today's capacity is not overbuilt, and the timing risk sits further out than the bears assume.

The leading lab is already generating cash. Renaissance Capital reports that Anthropic's operating cash flow turned positive at $6.6 billion, from negative $2.0 billion a year earlier, and that it held $95.6 billion of cash and $36 billion of short-term investments at September 30. About $213.8 billion of its commitments are subject to termination rights or conditions (FourWeekMBA). A company in that position has more room to absorb a slower year than the headline commitment figure suggests.

Headline losses overstate the problem. Anthropic's reported net loss for the first nine months of 2026 is about $104 billion (Idlen), but most of it is a non-cash charge from revaluing convertible notes as the company's valuation rose (TechSpot). Its Q3 operating loss was $567 million. A viral claim that the company "barely makes money" does not hold up against its own filing.

Overbuilt infrastructure has been useful before. Fiber laid during the dot-com boom carried the internet's next decade. The counterpoint is that fiber stays useful for decades, while accelerators lose competitiveness much faster, which brings the argument back to depreciation.

These points narrow the thesis rather than refute it. They suggest that a correction, if it comes, is more likely to look like financing stress, delayed projects and repricing than like collapsing demand.

What it means for builders

A financial correction in AI would not mean the technology stops working. After the dot-com crash, the infrastructure and many of the products survived, and useful companies were built on what was left. For engineers and teams shipping AI features, the practical implications are narrower:

  • Treat API pricing as a variable, not a constant. Prices could rise if providers need margin, or fall further under competition. Anthropic's filing explicitly flags the risk of being forced to cut token prices (Fortune). Design so your unit economics survive either direction.
  • Avoid a single-provider dependency for core features. A provider under financial pressure can change pricing, rate limits or model availability quickly. An abstraction over two providers, or an open-weight fallback, is cheaper to build before you need it.
  • Invest in cost engineering now. Caching, prompt and context reduction, routing simple requests to smaller models, and measuring cost per task are useful whether or not prices move.
  • Be skeptical of products that only work at today's prices. Thin wrappers whose margin depends on current token pricing are the most exposed if that pricing changes.
  • Measure outcomes, not adoption. MIT NANDA's 2025 report found that 95% of the organizations it studied saw no measurable return from generative AI, with the successful 5% tied to specific workflows (Campus Technology). It is a preliminary study with a small sample, but the lesson about measurable outcomes holds.

For a closer look at what the productivity evidence actually shows, see AI coding tools and productivity: what the research actually found.

Conclusion

The evidence as of November 2026 supports a narrower claim than "the AI bubble is popping." Demand for AI is real and growing. The fragile part is the calendar: multi-year, largely non-cancellable compute commitments sized for revenue that has not arrived yet, financed partly through circular deals and partly through debt, on hardware whose useful life is contested.

If growth continues at anything like 2026 rates, most of today's commitments will look reasonable in hindsight. If growth slows or slips by a year, the losses fall on whoever holds the fixed costs, and the effects travel through suppliers and lenders. The next useful data points are Anthropic's IPO pricing, Nvidia's mid-November results, and whether hyperscaler free cash flow recovers in early 2027.

References

title: Watching an exchange's reserves after regulatory news, in 30 lines of Node
description:
The news

On November 6, 2026, FinCEN issued an order that bars US financial institutions from processing funds transfers involving the exchange MEXC Global. Treasury alleges the exchange facilitated at least $16 billion in transactions linked to sanctions evasion and cybercrime. The order takes effect 30 days after it is published in the Federal Register. (FinCEN release, Cointelegraph)

Cointelegraph's article cited DefiLlama for MEXC's total assets that day: about $4.48 billion. I wanted to see that number move, so I wrote a script that reads the same data.

Where the data comes from

DefiLlama tracks exchange wallets that the exchanges themselves have disclosed. The public endpoint https://api.llama.fi/protocol/<slug> returns a chainTvls object with one time series per chain. Two kinds of keys matter:

  • plain chain names (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana…) hold third-party assets in the disclosed wallets
  • keys containing OwnTokens hold the exchange's own token, which says little about customer reserves, so the script drops them

The series can hold more than one point for the current day (midnight plus the latest reading), so the script keeps the last value per chain per day before adding chains together. My first version summed every point and showed today's reserves at nearly double, which is a good bug to know about if you use this API.

The script 

// reserve-watch.mjs
// usage: node reserve-watch.mjs <defillama-slug> [days=10]
const [slug = 'mexc', daysArg = '10'] = process.argv.slice(2);
const days = Number(daysArg);
const res = await fetch(`https://api.llama.fi/protocol/${slug}`);
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`DefiLlama answered ${res.status} for "${slug}"`);
const p = await res.json();

const byDay = new Map();
for (const [chain, data] of Object.entries(p.chainTvls)) {
  if (chain.includes('OwnTokens')) continue;
  const last = new Map();
  for (const { date, totalLiquidityUSD } of data.tvl) last.set(new Date(date * 1000).toISOString().slice(0, 10), totalLiquidityUSD);
  for (const [day, v] of last) byDay.set(day, (byDay.get(day) || 0) + v);
}
const rows = [...byDay.entries()].sort(([a], [b]) => a.localeCompare(b)).slice(-days);
const base = rows[0][1];
const usd = (n) => `$${(n / 1e9).toFixed(2)}B`;
console.log(`${p.name}: tracked reserves without its own token, last ${rows.length} days`);
for (const [day, total] of rows) {
  const pct = ((total / base - 1) * 100).toFixed(1);
  console.log(`${day}  ${usd(total).padStart(8)}  ${pct >= 0 ? '+' : ''}${pct}%`);
}

It needs Node 18 or newer for the built-in fetch and top-level await in an .mjs file. No dependencies.

Output

Run on November 10, 2026:

MEXC: tracked reserves without its own token, last 10 days
2026-11-01    $4.48B  +0.0%
2026-11-02    $4.53B  +1.1%
2026-11-03    $4.50B  +0.6%
2026-11-04    $4.52B  +0.9%
2026-11-05    $4.58B  +2.3%
2026-11-06    $4.48B  +0.1%
2026-11-07    $4.43B  -1.0%
2026-11-08    $4.24B  -5.3%
2026-11-09    $4.17B  -6.8%
2026-11-10    $4.17B  -6.8%

The November 6 row matches the $4.48B Cointelegraph quoted, which is a decent check that the filtering is right.

Reading it honestly

These are USD values, so they move with prices as well as with deposits and withdrawals. Crypto prices fell during the same days, which means the drop from $4.48B to $4.17B can't be read as a withdrawal total. To separate the two you'd use the tokens field, which holds amounts per token, and price them yourself at a fixed date. That's the natural next step if you extend this.

The data also covers only the wallets an exchange chose to disclose. It gives a floor on what the exchange holds, and it doesn't replace an audit.

Try it on others

Any CEX slug on DefiLlama works: node reserve-watch.mjs binance-cex 14, node reserve-watch.mjs okx 30. Slugs are in the URL of each exchange's page on defillama.com.

What other public signals do you watch when an exchange is in the news?

title: Designing streak rewards that don't pay for commit spam
description:
Streaks are a strange design problem. The moment you reward people for showing up every day, you also reward them for faking it.

GitHub's contribution graph is the classic example. A green square for an empty commit looks exactly the same as a green square for a real fix. So when I started building Vigilante, a free browser game where your GitHub pushes open the next day of the story, the reward rules mattered more to me than the 3D city did.

This post walks through the rules as they exist today, and why each one is there. The code is a simplified sketch in Java (my day job language) to show the shape of the logic, not a copy of production code.

The rule everything else hangs on: one verified day

You pick one repo and a daily commit target. When GitHub sends a push webhook for that repo, the game checks the commits. If enough of them are meaningful, that day is verified, and the next day of the game opens.

"Meaningful" is doing a lot of work there. Vigilante filters out:

  • merge commits
  • empty commits
  • commits that only touch lock files or config

It also only looks at metadata: commit IDs, timestamps and file names. It never reads your code or diffs. Commit messages are only used if you opt in.

Here is roughly what that filter looks like:

record CommitInfo(String id, Instant timestamp, int parentCount, List<String> files) {}

static final Set<String> LOCK_FILES = Set.of(
    "package-lock.json", "yarn.lock", "pnpm-lock.yaml", "Cargo.lock", "poetry.lock"
);

static boolean isMeaningful(CommitInfo c) {
    if (c.parentCount() > 1) return false;          // merge commit
    if (c.files().isEmpty()) return false;          // empty commit
    return c.files().stream()
            .anyMatch(f -> !isLockOrConfigOnly(f)); // at least one real file
}

static boolean isLockOrConfigOnly(String path) {
    String name = Path.of(path).getFileName().toString();
    return LOCK_FILES.contains(name) || isConfigFile(name);
}

The list of what counts as "config" is the part that needs the most judgment, and I'd rather keep it conservative than clever. The point isn't to catch every trick. The point is that the cheapest possible move (an empty commit) gets you nothing.

Rewards scale with consistency, not volume

Once a day is verified, you get a daily supply crate. The crate has a streak multiplier:

  • 3 days in a row: x1.2
  • 7 or more days in a row: x1.5

That's it. There is no bonus for pushing 40 commits instead of 4. Your daily target is the bar, and going way past it doesn't pay extra.

static double crateMultiplier(int streakDays) {
    if (streakDays >= 7) return 1.5;
    if (streakDays >= 3) return 1.2;
    return 1.0;
}

static Crate dailyCrate(int verifiedStreak) {
    return Crate.base().scaledBy(crateMultiplier(verifiedStreak));
}

I like this shape for two reasons.

First, it rewards the thing that's actually hard. Writing a lot of code on one good Saturday is easy. Showing up on a tired Tuesday after office is the hard part, and that's what the multiplier is tied to.

Second, it caps out early. After a week, the reward stops climbing. Nobody needs to feel that day 60 is "worth more" than day 8. You just keep the x1.5 as long as you keep showing up.

Missing a day: repair, but never fake

Real life happens. Mondays happen. So there's an item called Revival Fluid that repairs a missed day.

The important part is what it does not do. A repaired day never counts as verified. It keeps your story from collapsing, but it doesn't pretend you coded.

enum DayStatus { VERIFIED, REPAIRED, MISSED }

static boolean countsAsVerified(DayStatus s) {
    return s == DayStatus.VERIFIED; // REPAIRED is never verified
}

That separation shows up everywhere else too. The share card you get for each day is only for verified days, because the whole point of the card is that it's proof.

Money never buys a verified day

Vigilante is free to play, and every story day is included. There are optional purchases (Revival Fluid, and a Pro pass with no auto-renewal), but buying anything never unlocks a day and never counts as verified work.

If you build anything with streaks and payments, I'd treat this as a hard wall in the data model, not a policy line in the FAQ. Keep "what the user paid for" and "what the user actually did" in separate fields, and never let one write to the other.

// Purchases can add items to the inventory.
// They can never change a DayStatus.
void applyPurchase(Player p, Item item) {
    p.inventory().add(item);
}

Small daily loops around the big one

Around the main loop there are a few lighter ones: a 7-day check-in calendar, 3 daily missions, and a daily mystery coding question. These are there so that opening the game feels like something, even on a day you haven't pushed yet.

But none of them can stand in for a push. The story only moves when GitHub says you shipped something real.

What I'd tell anyone designing streaks

  1. Decide what the cheapest fake looks like, and make it worth zero. For commits that's empty and merge commits.
  2. Reward consistency, not volume. A multiplier based on streak length is enough. Don't pay for raw commit counts.
  3. Cap the multiplier. Make the reward flat after a point so people aren't scared of breaking a huge number.
  4. Let people recover without lying. A "repaired" state is kinder than a reset, as long as it's clearly not "verified".
  5. Wall off payments from progress. In the schema, not just in the copy.

If you want to see how these rules feel from the player side, Day 1 is free in the browser with no sign-up: play Day 1 of Vigilante. Full disclosure, I built it.

How do you handle missed days in your own habit or streak systems? Reset to zero, or something softer?

title: VR版YouTubeの「大型リニューアル」報道と、見る時間を目のトレーニングに変える設計
description:
VR版YouTubeの「大型リニューアル」報道と、見る時間を目のトレーニングに変える設計

UploadVRが伝えたのは、GoogleがQuest上のYouTubeアプリの「没入ビュー」を大規模に作り直している可能性がある、という話です。Android XRやvisionOSでの体験に近づける方向だといい、VRヘッドセットで動画を見るという行為が、片手間の延長ではなく「主要な視聴体験」として扱われ始めたことを示唆しています。

ここで注目したいのは、ハードウェアやアプリの話ではなく、「ヘッドセットをかぶって何かを見る時間」が日常に入ってくるという点です。Meta Questのようなスタンドアロン型のデバイスが、動画視聴という最も日常的な用途で存在感を増すなら、その時間は「消費」だけでなく「活用」にも開かれます。エンジニアの立場で見ると、これは単なるUI刷新ではなく、レンダリングパイプラインと入力レイテンシの設計が「ながら視聴」から「主軸の体験」へと再定義される転換点です。両眼に独立した映像を届けるというハードウェアの性質が、アプリケーション層でどう活かされるか——そこに設計上の面白さがあります。

見る時間は、そのまま目を使う時間

私たちが何かを見ているとき、両眼は協調し、脳は二つの像をひとつに統合しています。いわゆる弱視（amblyopia、lazy eye）では、この協調がうまく働かず、片方の目からの情報が十分に使われにくい状態が続くことがあります。

従来のアプローチの多くは、良い方の目をアイパッチで覆う、赤青メガネを使う、といった方法でした。もちろんこれらが今も使われる場面はありますが、「毎日続ける」というハードルは決して低くありません。ここで技術的な視点を挟むと、単眼抑制（suppression）をどう回避するかが長年の課題でした。片眼を物理的に塞ぐ方法はシンプルですが、両眼視（binocular vision）のトレーニングにはなりにくい。二つの眼に同時に、しかし異なる入力を与える必要がある。この「異なる入力を同時に」という要件は、実はディスプレイ技術と非常に相性がいいのです。

Amblyotubeという選択肢

Amblyotubeは、Seven Sportsが開発した、VRにおける視覚の協調と注意のためのレクリエーション／教育ソフトウェアです。考え方はシンプルです。左右の目に、別々の映像体験を届ける。

Quest 2、3、Pro、3SといったMeta Questのヘッドセットは、左右に独立したレンズとディスプレイを持っています。この物理的な構成が、そのまま訓練の土台になります。片眼ずつ異なる映像を届けられるということは、片眼ずつ違う「課題」を与えられるということです。ここはアーキテクチャとして捉えると分かりやすい。レンダリングは両眼分を個別に走らせ、片側にはぼかし（ブラー）、もう片側には強調処理を適用する。シェーダーレベルでの分岐が、そのままトレーニングの設計になります。

  • 対象眼と強度の選択：左右どちらの目を対象にするか、軽度／中等度／重度のプリセット、あるいはLogMARによる視力チェックから始められます。
  • Dominant Eye Shader：優位眼側に、調整可能なゆるやかなデジタルブラーをかけます。
  • AI Sharpener（MFBF）：弱視眼側では、AIが人物を検出し、太い赤の輪郭や黄緑のハイライト、一定のリズムでの明滅を加えます。
  • Wedge Occlusion：任意で、各眼の視野の一部を遮り、片眼ずつ異なる部分を見せることで、二眼の競合（binocular rivalry）を抑えます。
  • マゼンタのフォーカスキュー：弱視眼の視界のマゼンタのキューと、優位眼の視界の控えめなニュートラルグレーのドットが重なることで、脳が両眼の情報を統合し、ひとつの立体的な像として知覚する練習になります。

技術的なポイントを少し掘り下げます。MFBF（Monocular Fixation in a Binocular Field）は、両眼に視野を開いたまま、片眼にだけコントラストや輪郭の手がかりを与える手法です。実装としては、片眼のフレームにのみポストプロセスを適用し、もう片眼は素の映像を維持する。両眼の入力を完全に断つのではなく、優位眼の情報を「薄めて」弱視眼の寄与を相対的に引き上げる——このバランス調整が、単純な遮蔽とは異なる設計上の核心です。Wedge Occlusionも同様に、視野マスクを左右で非対称に配置することで、片眼ずつ異なる部分を見せ、脳が両方を統合せざるを得ない状況を作ります。マゼンタのフォーカスキューは、両眼のキューを空間的に重ねることで融合（fusion）を促す仕掛けで、色チャンネルを手がかりにしている点が面白いところです。

そして最も実用的な点は、コンテンツがYouTube動画であることです。仮想ルームでも、Room ViewのARパススルーでも、好きな動画をそのまま起動できます。「目のトレーニング用の退屈な動画」を探す必要はありません。これは技術ブログ的に言えば、コンテンツパイプラインを自前で抱えず、既存の動画基盤に乗るという判断です。専用コンテンツを作り込むコストを避け、ユーザーがすでに毎日見ているもの——YouTube——をそのまま入力源にする。エンジニアリングとしては地味ですが、継続率に直結する賢い割り切りだと思います。

現実的な期待値の話

ここは正直に書きます。Amblyotubeは診断・治療・治癒を目的としたものではなく、両眼の協調と奥行き知覚のための補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールです。推奨は1日30〜40分（最大1時間）、対象年齢は13歳以上。症状についての判断は、必ず眼科医などの専門家に相談してください。ベンチマークや臨床効果をここで数字として約束することはできません。あくまで「見る時間を別の目的に開く」という設計の話です。

VRでのYouTube視聴が「当たり前」になっていくなら、その時間の使い方には選択肢が生まれます。ただ見るか、見ながら目を使うか。Amblyotubeは後者のための道具です。プラットフォームの大型リニューアルが視聴体験を底上げするほど、その上に乗るアプリケーションの設計余地も広がります。既存の動画を入力源に、両眼それぞれへ別々の処理を届ける——その発想自体は、特別なハードウェアを必要としません。すでに手元のQuestが、その土台になっています。

Meta Questアプリストアで配信中： https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: SQL Server Locks: A Performance and Deadlock Cheat Sheet
description:
SQL Server uses locks to protect data while concurrent sessions read and modify it. Locks preserve transaction correctness, but they also create waiting, blocking, and deadlocks. When evaluating a slow query, ask: "Is it waiting for another transaction, and what resource does it need?"

This cheat sheet explains the lock types you are most likely to encounter, how they affect query execution, and how to diagnose locking problems quickly.

Locks are not latches. Locks protect logical data and transaction consistency. Latches are lightweight internal synchronization mechanisms that protect in-memory structures such as data pages. A lock problem commonly appears as an LCK_M_* wait; a latch problem uses waits such as PAGELATCH_*.

The basic locking flow

A lock request is granted when compatible with locks already held on the resource. Otherwise, the session waits. Lock duration depends on its mode, isolation level, statement, and transaction scope. A common issue is an application modifying data and then remaining idle before committing; the statement finished, but its locks remain.

Lock modes you should recognize

Lock Name Typical purpose Performance implication
S Shared Reading data Compatible with other shared locks, but blocked by exclusive locks
U Update Reading a row before updating it Reduces conversion deadlocks; only one update lock can target a resource
X Exclusive Inserting, updating, or deleting data Blocks both readers and writers under locking-based isolation
IS Intent Shared Signals shared locks at a lower level Enables efficient compatibility checks
IX Intent Exclusive Signals exclusive or update locks below Common while rows or pages are modified
SIX Shared with Intent Exclusive Reads the larger resource while modifying lower-level resources Restrictive; can create broad blocking
Sch-S Schema Stability Compiling and executing queries Compatible with normal data access, but conflicts with schema modification
Sch-M Schema Modification DDL and some metadata changes Highly restrictive; can block nearly all access to the object
BU Bulk Update Bulk-loading data under qualifying options Allows optimized bulk operations but restricts competing access
Range* Key-range locks Protects index ranges under SERIALIZABLE Prevents phantom rows but can lock gaps and increase blocking

Shared, update, and exclusive locks

A shared lock allows concurrent readers. An exclusive lock prevents another session from reading or changing the resource under conventional READ COMMITTED locking. Update locks are an intermediate mode used when reading data that may be changed. They help avoid two sessions acquiring shared locks and both attempting to convert them to exclusive locks.

Intent locks

Intent locks describe activity lower in the lock hierarchy. An IX table lock usually means exclusive locks exist, or will exist, on pages, keys, or rows. It does not mean the whole table is exclusively locked. Intent modes quickly reveal whether a table-level request conflicts with lower-level activity.

Schema locks

Sch-S locks occur during query compilation and execution, even with NOLOCK. Sch-M locks occur during schema changes and conflict with Sch-S. A long query can delay DDL, while schema modification can block ordinary queries.

Key-range locks

Under SERIALIZABLE, SQL Server may lock index keys and gaps between them. This prevents inserts that would newly satisfy an earlier predicate. Key-range locks provide strong consistency but can greatly expand the protected area, especially without supporting indexes.

Lock granularity: what is being locked?

SQL Server can lock resources at several levels:

  • KEY locks protect index entries. Even queries described as "row locking" often show KEY resources.
  • RID locks protect rows in a heap, which is a table without a clustered index.
  • PAGE locks protect an 8 KB data or index page.
  • OBJECT locks protect a table or similar object.
  • HoBT locks protect a heap or B-tree, including an individual partition.
  • METADATA, DATABASE, and ALLOCATION_UNIT locks protect broader internal resources.

Fine-grained locks improve concurrency but consume memory. Coarser locks use fewer resources but block more operations.

Lock escalation

Lock escalation replaces many fine-grained locks with a coarser lock. SQL Server attempts escalation when a single statement acquires at least roughly 5,000 locks on one table or index reference, and it can also escalate under lock-memory pressure. Escalation is normally to a table lock; a partitioned table can escalate to a partition when LOCK_ESCALATION = AUTO. SQL Server does not escalate row or key locks to page locks.

If another session holds an incompatible lock that prevents escalation, the statement continues with fine-grained locks and SQL Server retries later. Escalation can turn a large modification into a whole-table blocker. Reduce its likelihood with shorter transactions, batched changes, and indexes that prevent unnecessary scans. Disabling escalation can exchange blocking for excessive lock memory.

Compatibility at a glance

The full compatibility matrix is extensive, but this reduced view covers common investigations:

Held \ Requested S U X IS IX
S Yes Yes No Yes No
U Yes No No Yes No
X No No No No No
IS Yes Yes No Yes Yes
IX No No No Yes Yes

Compatibility alone does not explain every wait. Locks may cover different resources, and a request can wait behind another waiter because SQL Server generally preserves queue fairness.

How isolation levels change locking

Isolation level Important locking behavior
READ UNCOMMITTED Allows dirty reads and usually avoids shared data locks; rows can be missing, duplicated, or inconsistent
READ COMMITTED SQL Server default; shared row/page locks are generally released as data is read, allowing later rereads to change
REPEATABLE READ Holds shared locks until transaction end, preventing changed or deleted rereads
SERIALIZABLE Adds key-range protection and prevents phantoms; highest blocking risk
SNAPSHOT Uses row versions for reads; update conflicts are possible; writes still use locks
READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT Changes READ COMMITTED reads to use row versions; writers still lock

SNAPSHOT requires ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION to be enabled. Azure SQL Database commonly enables READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT by default, while boxed SQL Server does not. Row versioning reduces reader-writer blocking but does not eliminate writer-writer blocking, schema conflicts, or poor transaction design. It also adds version-store usage, and competing snapshot updates can fail with error 3960.

NOLOCK is not a performance fix. It uses READ UNCOMMITTED, permitting dirty, missing, or duplicated rows, and it still acquires schema-stability locks. Use it only when those correctness risks are explicitly acceptable.

Blocking versus deadlocks

Blocking is expected synchronization: one session waits until another releases an incompatible lock. A deadlock is a cycle in which sessions wait for one another and none can proceed.

SQL Server detects the cycle and chooses a victim, which receives error 1205 and is rolled back. Applications should use bounded retries for idempotent operations, but retries do not fix recurring deadlocks.

Typical fixes include consistent object access order, shorter transactions, indexes that reduce scanned rows, no user interaction inside transactions, and smaller batches. The deadlock graph identifies participating processes, resources, lock modes, and statements.

Reproducible locking labs

Run these examples only on a development SQL Server where you can create a disposable database. They were validated on SQL Server 2022 Developer Edition. Open two query windows and label them Session A and Session B. Run this setup once; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS requires SQL Server 2016 or later.

USE master;
GO

IF DB_ID(N'LockLab') IS NULL
    CREATE DATABASE LockLab;
GO

USE LockLab;
GO

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dbo.LockDemo;

CREATE TABLE dbo.LockDemo
(
    Id int NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT PK_LockDemo PRIMARY KEY,
    AccountName varchar(30) NOT NULL,
    Balance int NOT NULL,
    ReferenceCode int NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX IX_LockDemo_ReferenceCode
    ON dbo.LockDemo (ReferenceCode);

INSERT dbo.LockDemo (Id, AccountName, Balance, ReferenceCode)
VALUES
    (1, 'Alpha', 100, 10),
    (2, 'Beta', 200, 20),
    (3, 'Gamma', 300, 30);

SELECT
    name,
    is_read_committed_snapshot_on,
    snapshot_isolation_state_desc
FROM sys.databases
WHERE name = DB_NAME();

Lab 1: an exclusive lock blocks a reader

In Session A, update a row but leave the transaction open:

BEGIN TRANSACTION;

UPDATE dbo.LockDemo
SET Balance = Balance + 50
WHERE Id = 1;

-- Leave this transaction open while running Session B.

In Session B, run:

SELECT *
FROM dbo.LockDemo WITH (READCOMMITTEDLOCK)
WHERE Id = 1;

READCOMMITTEDLOCK makes the example deterministic even when READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is enabled. Session B waits with LCK_M_S because Session A holds an exclusive key lock. In a third window, run the diagnostic queries in the next section to see the waiter and blocker. Release the lock in Session A:

ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;

Session B then completes and returns the original balance of 100 because Session A rolled back. To demonstrate row versioning, remove READCOMMITTEDLOCK on a database with READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT enabled; the reader can return the previously committed version without waiting.

Lab 2: create a two-row deadlock

Run the following in Session A:

SET XACT_ABORT ON;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

UPDATE dbo.LockDemo SET Balance += 10 WHERE Id = 1;
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:15';
UPDATE dbo.LockDemo SET Balance += 10 WHERE Id = 2;

COMMIT TRANSACTION;

Start this in Session B within 15 seconds:

SET XACT_ABORT ON;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

UPDATE dbo.LockDemo SET Balance += 20 WHERE Id = 2;
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:15';
UPDATE dbo.LockDemo SET Balance += 20 WHERE Id = 1;

COMMIT TRANSACTION;

Each session owns an exclusive lock needed by the other. SQL Server detects the cycle and terminates one session with error 1205; either session can be the victim. DEADLOCK_PRIORITY is considered first, followed by estimated rollback cost. The survivor commits. The primary fix is to access rows in the same order—for example, always update Id = 1 before Id = 2.

In a third window, inspect the newest graph from the built-in system_health session. This requires VIEW SERVER STATE and applies to SQL Server; Azure SQL Database exposes Extended Events through database-scoped targets.

SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON;

;WITH DeadlockEvents AS
(
    SELECT CAST(st.target_data AS xml) AS target_data
    FROM sys.dm_xe_session_targets AS st
    INNER JOIN sys.dm_xe_sessions AS s
        ON s.address = st.event_session_address
    WHERE s.name = N'system_health'
      AND st.target_name = N'ring_buffer'
)
SELECT
    event_xml.value(N'(@timestamp)[1]', N'datetime2') AS event_time,
    event_xml.query(N'(data/value/deadlock)[1]') AS deadlock_graph
FROM DeadlockEvents
CROSS APPLY target_data.nodes(
    N'//RingBufferTarget/event[@name="xml_deadlock_report"]'
) AS events(event_xml)
ORDER BY event_time DESC;

Reset the data and connection setting in both windows before continuing:

IF XACT_STATE() <> 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
SET XACT_ABORT OFF;

UPDATE dbo.LockDemo
SET Balance = Id * 100;

Lab 3: a serializable range blocks an insert

In Session A, protect a range that currently contains one row:

SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

SELECT *
FROM dbo.LockDemo
WHERE ReferenceCode BETWEEN 15 AND 25;

-- Leave the transaction open while running Session B.

In Session B, attempt to insert into the protected range:

INSERT dbo.LockDemo (Id, AccountName, Balance, ReferenceCode)
VALUES (4, 'Delta', 400, 18);

The insert waits on a range-insert lock. On SQL Server 2022 this appears as LCK_M_RIn_NL; older versions and tools may display related range-insert names differently. Session A holds a RangeS-S lock on the supporting index, protecting existing keys and gaps where qualifying rows could be inserted. Finish Session A:

COMMIT TRANSACTION;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;

Session B can now insert the row. Remove it before repeating the lab:

DELETE dbo.LockDemo WHERE Id = 4;

These labs illustrate three different diagnoses: incompatible locks causing ordinary blocking, a circular wait causing a deadlock, and an isolation-level guarantee deliberately expanding the locked resource range.

After completing the labs, clean up:

USE LockLab;
IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dbo.LockDemo;

-- Optional, from a window connected to master:
-- USE master;
-- DROP DATABASE LockLab;

Quick diagnostic queries

The following server-scoped DMVs generally require VIEW SERVER STATE (VIEW SERVER PERFORMANCE STATE for some DMVs on SQL Server 2022+) or the corresponding Azure SQL database permission. wait_time is reported in milliseconds.

Find waiting requests and their blockers:

SELECT
    r.session_id,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.status,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.wait_resource,
    DB_NAME(r.database_id) AS database_name,
    t.text AS current_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.blocking_session_id <> 0
   OR r.wait_type LIKE N'LCK_M_%';

Inspect current locks:

SELECT
    l.request_session_id,
    l.resource_type,
    l.resource_description,
    OBJECT_NAME(p.object_id, l.resource_database_id) AS object_name,
    l.request_mode,
    l.request_status
FROM sys.dm_tran_locks AS l
LEFT JOIN sys.partitions AS p
    ON l.resource_type IN (N'KEY', N'PAGE', N'RID', N'HOBT')
   AND p.hobt_id = l.resource_associated_entity_id
WHERE l.resource_database_id = DB_ID()
ORDER BY l.request_session_id, l.resource_type;

The head blocker is often sleeping and therefore absent from sys.dm_exec_requests. Find its open transaction and most recent SQL:

SELECT
    s.session_id,
    s.status,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    s.program_name,
    s.open_transaction_count,
    at.transaction_begin_time,
    txt.text AS most_recent_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s
LEFT JOIN sys.dm_tran_session_transactions AS st
    ON st.session_id = s.session_id
LEFT JOIN sys.dm_tran_active_transactions AS at
    ON at.transaction_id = st.transaction_id
LEFT JOIN sys.dm_exec_connections AS c
    ON c.session_id = s.session_id
OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(c.most_recent_sql_handle) AS txt
WHERE s.session_id IN
(
    SELECT blocking_session_id
    FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
    WHERE blocking_session_id > 0
);

Common waits provide a fast clue:

Wait Usually means
LCK_M_S Waiting for a shared lock, often a reader behind a writer
LCK_M_U / LCK_M_X Waiting to update or exclusively modify data
LCK_M_SCH_M Waiting for a schema modification lock
LCK_M_RS_S Waiting for a serializable range shared lock
LCK_M_RIn_NL and related LCK_M_RI* waits Waiting to insert into a protected key range; the exact name varies by engine version

Use the results together. A granted lock is not automatically a problem; identify the waiter, head blocker, transaction age, and SQL. sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks provides another resource-level view. For historical deadlocks, use system_health or a dedicated Extended Events session capturing xml_deadlock_report.

Performance review checklist

  1. Confirm waiting: Look for LCK_M_* waits rather than assuming high duration means blocking.
  2. Find the head blocker: Follow blocking_session_id until reaching the session that is not itself blocked.
  3. Check transaction scope: Determine whether the blocker has an old open transaction or is idle while holding locks.
  4. Identify the resource and mode: Use wait_resource, sys.dm_tran_locks, and the execution plan.
  5. Review access paths: Scans lock more rows and hold locks longer than selective seeks.
  6. Check isolation requirements: Use stronger isolation only when the business invariant requires it.
  7. Capture the deadlock graph: Do not diagnose recurring deadlocks from the victim statement alone.
  8. Fix the cause, not the symptom: Prefer indexing, consistent access order, batching, and shorter transactions over NOLOCK or killing sessions.

Locks are necessary and waiting can be normal. Prolonged blocking usually reflects transaction scope, access paths, or concurrency design. Diagnose the wait chain, then reduce the locked resource set or the time locks are held.

title: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN: Which Rows Survive?
description:
Most JOIN confusion comes down to one question: what happens to rows with no match? Here's how INNER and LEFT JOIN answer it, and how to choose.

Adapted from the SQL Essentials Companion Guide.

Every explanation of SQL joins seems to reach for the same overlapping-circles diagram, and many people still come away unsure which join to use. It helps to drop the diagram and ask one plain question: what happens to a row that has no match in the other table?

That single question is the whole difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. Everything else about them is the same.

A tiny example

Take two small tables. customers holds three people, and orders holds the purchases they made:

customers                orders
id | name                id | customer_id | amount
---+-----                ---+-------------+-------
 1 | Ada                 10 |           1 |     50
 2 | Ben                 11 |           1 |     30
 3 | Cy                  12 |           2 |     20
                         13 |          99 |     70

Ada has two orders, Ben has one, and Cy has none. Order 13 points at customer 99, who doesn't exist. Two rows here have no match: Cy on one side, order 13 on the other. The joins differ in what they do with them.

INNER JOIN keeps only the matches 

SELECT customers.name, orders.amount
FROM customers
INNER JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;

name | amount
-----+-------
Ada  |     50
Ada  |     30
Ben  |     20

Only rows that found a partner appear. Cy is gone because Cy has no orders, and order 13 is gone because it has no customer. INNER JOIN drops anything without a match, on both sides. Writing JOIN on its own means the same thing.

LEFT JOIN keeps everything from the left table 

SELECT customers.name, orders.amount
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;

name | amount
-----+-------
Ada  |     50
Ada  |     30
Ben  |     20
Cy   |   NULL

Now Cy is back, with NULL where the order columns would be. The "left" table is the one written before the JOIN keyword, here customers. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from that table, whether or not it found a match, and fills in NULL for the right table's columns when it didn't. Order 13 is still absent, because it lives in the right table and has no customer.

So the choice comes down to this: if a row without a match should still show up in your results, use LEFT JOIN. If it should disappear, use INNER JOIN.

A useful trick: finding what's missing

Because LEFT JOIN fills in NULL for non-matches, you can use it to find rows that have no match at all. Filter for the NULL:

SELECT customers.name
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.id IS NULL;

name
----
Cy

That's "customers who have never ordered." It's one of the most useful things a LEFT JOIN does, and the same pattern answers any "which X have no Y" question. Note that it uses IS NULL, not = NULL. If that distinction is new to you, Why 'WHERE x = NULL' Never Works in SQL explains it.

How to practice choosing

Before you write a join, say the result out loud: "I want every customer, and their orders if they have any" (that's LEFT), or "I want only customers who have orders" (that's INNER). The wording tells you which to use. Then run it on a small table where you know the answer, like the one above, and check that the row you expected to survive did.

If you ever get stuck, count rows. Run SELECT COUNT(*) on the left table alone, then on the join. With an INNER JOIN, the join can come back with fewer rows than the left table, because unmatched rows disappeared. With a LEFT JOIN, every left row is still there, so you won't see fewer than the left table has.

Two mistakes worth knowing about ahead of time

Filtering the right table in WHERE and accidentally undoing your LEFT JOIN. This catches almost everyone once. Suppose you want all customers, plus only their orders over 25:

SELECT customers.name, orders.amount
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.amount > 25;

name | amount
-----+-------
Ada  |     50
Ada  |     30

Ben and Cy vanished. For them, orders.amount is NULL after the join (Ben's only order is 20), and NULL > 25 is never true, so WHERE throws those rows out. You've turned your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN without noticing. To keep every customer, put the condition in the ON clause, so it limits which orders match instead of which rows survive:

SELECT customers.name, orders.amount
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders
  ON orders.customer_id = customers.id AND orders.amount > 25;

name | amount
-----+-------
Ada  |     50
Ada  |     30
Ben  |   NULL
Cy   |   NULL

Counting with COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN. COUNT(*) counts rows, and Cy's row exists even though there's no order, so Cy shows as 1. Count a column from the right table instead, such as COUNT(orders.id), which skips NULL and correctly gives Cy 0. And if a join ever returns more rows than you expected, the cause is a different one, covered in Why Your JOIN Doubled Your Totals.

A habit that makes joins easy

Treat LEFT JOIN as your starting point and INNER JOIN as a deliberate choice. Ask yourself first which table is the one you really care about, the one whose rows must not vanish, and put it on the left. Then decide whether unmatched rows belong in the answer. Doing it in that order turns a choice that feels like guesswork into two short questions, and it makes the "where did my rows go?" surprise much rarer.

title: 弱視のVR視覚訓練を「工学」として考える——両眼視フィードバックの設計と、脳の可塑性というニュースから
description:
弱視のVR視覚訓練を「工学」として考える——両眼視フィードバックの設計と、脳の可塑性というニュースから

2026年11月、サイエンス・デイリーが報じた研究が静かに話題になっています。UTHealth Houstonのチームが65歳以上の成人約20万人を分析し、高用量インフルエンザワクチン接種群でアルツハイマー病の発症リスクが約55%低かったと報告しました。標準用量で以前示されていた約40%の低下をさらに上回る数字です。

もちろんこれは観察研究であり、「ワクチンを打てばアルツハイマー病を防げる」と断定するものではありません。ただ、技術者として面白いのは数字そのものではなく、「成人後も脳と身体の働きを再調整できる余地がある」という視点です。長年「加齢に伴う変化は仕方ない」とされてきた領域に、介入可能なパラメータがあるかもしれない、という話です。

視覚も例外ではありません。片眼性弱視（lazy eye）や両眼の協調課題は「子どものうちに矯正するもの」「大人になってからでは遅い」と言われ続けてきました。しかし可塑性の知見は更新されています。ならば問い直すべきは「今さら間に合うのか」ではなく、「毎日続けられる形になっているか」——つまり、継続可能なシステムとして設計されているかです。

弱視訓練が「続かない」のは、たいてい仕組みの問題

従来の訓練は遮蔽（アイパッチ）や赤青メガネなど、身体に貼る・かけるタイプが中心でした。効果は期待できる一方で、見た目が目立つ、単調で飽きる、生活リズムに組み込みにくい。結果として継続が難しい。これは意志の問題ではなく、日常に馴染む形になっていないという設計の問題です。

エンジニアの目で見れば、これは典型的な「UXとアーキテクチャのミスマッチ」です。訓練効果を最大化するロジックは正しくても、それを毎日の生活に載せるインターフェースが重すぎる。結果、ユーザーは離脱し、システムは本来のポテンシャルを発揮しない。弱視訓練の分野では、この「ラストワンマイル」が長く未解決のままでした。

Amblyotubeという選択肢——dichoptic vision trainingの実装

Amblyotubeは、Seven Sportsが開発した、VRでの視覚協調・注意トレーニングのためのレクリエーション／教育目的ソフトウェアです。Meta Quest向けアプリで、左右の眼に異なる映像体験を届けるのが特徴です。仕組みを工学的に見ていくと、両眼視フィードバックの設計として興味深い点がいくつかあります。

  • 好きなYouTube動画がそのまま訓練になる：仮想ルームまたはRoom ViewのARパススルーで、普段見ている動画を再生。コンテンツ選択という継続のハードルを下げます。
  • 優位眼には調整可能なデジタルブラー（Dominant Eye Shader）：優位眼の情報をやわらかく弱め、弱視眼の参加を促します。
  • 弱視眼にはAI Sharpener（MFBF）：人物を検出し、太い赤い輪郭・黄緑のハイライト・一定リズムの明滅で注意を引きます。
  • Wedge Occlusion（任意）：各眼の視野の一部を遮り、それぞれの眼が異なる部分を見る状態をつくることで、両眼視の競合（binocular rivalry）を軽減します。
  • マゼンタのフォーカスキュー：弱視眼の視界に明るいマゼンタの手がかり、優位眼に控えめなニュートラルグレーのドットを表示し、追従によって一つの立体像へ統合していきます。
  • LogMAR視力チェックや左右眼・重症度プリセット（Mild／Moderate／Severe）で、自分の状態に合わせて開始できます。

推奨は1日30〜40分（最大1時間）、13歳以上。接着式のアイパッチや赤青メガネは不要です。

アーキテクチャとしての両眼視フィードバック

ここからは、Amblyotubeを「視覚訓練のためのランタイム」として捉え、その設計上の意思決定を分解してみます。すべては製品リファレンスに基づく記述で、実装の推測は含みません。

レイヤ1：知覚入力の非対称化

dichoptic trainingの核心は、左右の眼に異なる情報を届けることです。単眼ごとに独立したレンダリングパスを持つVRは、この非対称化と相性がいい。Amblyotubeでは、優位眼にDominant Eye Shader（調整可能なブラー）、弱視眼にAI Sharpener（MFBF）という、方向性の異なる2つのフィルタを適用します。優位眼の信号を減衰させ、弱視眼の信号を強調する——一種のゲイン調整です。

レイヤ2：注意の誘導

フィルタだけでは、弱視眼は「見えてはいるが使われていない」状態になりがちです。そこでAI Sharpenerが人物を検出し、太い赤い輪郭・黄緑のハイライト・一定リズムの明滅で注意を引きます。マゼンタのフォーカスキューも同様に、弱視眼側に明るい手がかり、優位眼側に控えめなニュートラルグレーのドットを置き、両眼の追従を一つの立体像へ統合していきます。

レイヤ3：競合の緩和

両眼視の競合（binocular rivalry）は、訓練を阻害するノイズ源です。Wedge Occlusionは各眼の視野の一部を遮り、それぞれの眼が異なる部分を見る状態をつくることで、この競合を軽減します。オプション扱いなのは、ユーザーの状態によって必要性が変わるからでしょう。

レイヤ4：計測とキャリブレーション

LogMAR視力チェックと、左右眼・重症度プリセット（Mild／Moderate／Severe）は、訓練を「自分の状態に合わせて開始する」ための入力層です。ここが固定的だと、ユーザーは自分に合わない負荷で始めてしまい、離脱につながります。

トレードオフの読み方

この設計には、いくつかの明確なトレードオフがあります。

  • 臨床的正確さ vs 継続性：厳密な訓練プロトコルを組むほど、日常への組み込みは難しくなる。Amblyotubeは「好きなYouTube動画がそのまま訓練になる」という選択で、継続性側に寄せています。
  • 介入の強さ vs 疲労：1日30〜40分（最大1時間）という推奨は、効果と疲労のバランス点として提示されています。
  • 汎用ハードウェア vs 専用設計：Meta Questというコンシューマ向けデバイスを使うことで、専用機器のコストと導入障壁を下げています。

「今日から始められる形」を選ぶ

高用量ワクチンの研究が示唆するのは、大人になっても脳と身体に働きかける余地がある、ということです。弱視の視覚訓練も、その延長線上で考えていい。

ただし、Amblyotubeは診断・治療・治癒を目的としたものではありません。両眼の協調と奥行き知覚のための補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールです。気になる症状がある場合は、必ず眼科医などの専門家に相談してください。

Amblyotube（Meta Quest ストア）
https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

免責事項

  • 推奨セッション：1日30〜40分（最大1時間）
  • 対象年齢：13歳以上
  • Amblyotubeは補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールであり、診断・治療・治癒を目的としたものではありません。
  • 本記事で紹介した研究は観察研究であり、因果関係を示すものではありません。

キーワード：弱視 大人 トレーニング, 片眼性弱視, lazy eye, 両眼視 訓練, 奥行き知覚, VR 視覚トレーニング, Meta Quest アプリ, 視覚協調, 脳の可塑性, 高用量インフルエンザワクチン アルツハイマー
