title: Custom CSS Cursors: The Rules Browsers Actually Enforce
description:
CSS makes custom cursors look like one line of code. Browsers add several rules that make them fail silently.
The syntax
.my-area { cursor: url("pointer.cur"), auto; }
The final keyword is required as the fallback.
The rules
128 px maximum. Chrome and Firefox refuse larger cursor images.
32 px is the practical size. Chrome hides cursors bigger than 32 px when they touch its own interface, and MDN recommends 32 x 32.
Multi-size .cur files backfire. Chrome and Firefox use the largest image, so a Windows-style file with 128 px inside shows a huge pointer.
Setting the click point
Two ways. Store it in a .cur file and give no numbers in the CSS, or use a PNG and give it in CSS, measured from the top-left:
cursor: url("pointer.png") 4 2, auto;
If it doesn't show
Check the file path, the image size, and the fallback keyword first.
To make a 32 px cursor with the click point stored inside, use the website preset in our free tool at flipconverto.com/convert/png-to-cur, which also has a live test box. It's our own tool.
Sources: MDN, "cursor" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/cursor); W3C, CSS Basic User Interface Level 4.
Note: this article was drafted with AI assistance and checked against our own test results.

title: Godot UI with AI: a main menu and settings screen that don't clip (tested)
description:
Can an AI build Godot UI that holds together when the window changes size? We asked Ziva, an AI agent that runs inside the Godot editor, for a main menu and a settings screen made of Control nodes. In 3 minutes 58 seconds it built both scenes, ran the game, clicked Settings and Back, and checked the layout at five window sizes. Nothing was clipped. It also missed something: the Fullscreen checkbox was nearly invisible when unchecked, and Ziva reported "all controls showing". A second prompt asking it to look closely caught and fixed it.

Layout is where people say AI help breaks down. On r/ClaudeAI one developer wrote that "Claude does not do a very good job in creating and modifying scenes for Godot … Elements are often partially clipped" (thread). On r/aigamedev another wrote, "I can burn through Claude's usage limit in a single session just trying to fix layouts and styling" (thread). And without any AI involved, a Godot forum post says "Making UIs almost takes up 80% of my time" (thread).

Ziva.sh makes Ziva and wrote this test. We ran it on 10 November 2026 with Godot 4.7.2 on Linux, using a development build of Ziva on Ziva Smart, the default model, with auto-approve on. It is one project and one run, so treat it as an example, not a benchmark. Below are the layout Ziva built (you can copy it by hand), how it checked the result, the miss, and a checklist.

The prompt

A fresh project with no UI in it. The prompt, word for word:

Make a main menu for my game in res://ui_demo/: the game title and Play, Settings and Quit buttons, centered. Settings should open a settings screen with a Master volume slider, a Fullscreen checkbox, a Resolution dropdown (1280x720 and 1920x1080) and a Back button that returns to the menu. Nothing should be clipped or overlapping, and it should still look right if the window is resized. Check it with screenshots and click through Settings and Back to make sure they work.

The layout Ziva built

Ziva wrote two scripts and two scenes in res://ui_demo/. The main menu:

MainMenu (Control, Full Rect anchors, main_menu.gd)
├── Background (ColorRect, Full Rect)
├── MenuPanel (CenterContainer, Full Rect)
│   └── MenuBox (VBoxContainer, separation 20)
│       ├── Title (Label "My Game", font size 56)
│       ├── PlayButton (Button, custom_minimum_size 260 x 52)
│       ├── SettingsButton (Button, custom_minimum_size 260 x 52)
│       └── QuitButton (Button, custom_minimum_size 260 x 52)
└── SettingsScreen (instance of settings_screen.tscn, hidden)

The settings screen is its own scene with its own opaque background, instanced into the menu and hidden until needed:

SettingsScreen (Control, Full Rect anchors, settings_screen.gd)
├── Background (ColorRect, Full Rect)
└── Center (CenterContainer, Full Rect)
    └── Margin (MarginContainer, 24 px margins)
        └── VBox (VBoxContainer, separation 16)
            ├── Title (Label "Settings")
            ├── VolumeRow (HBoxContainer)
            │   ├── Label "Master Volume" (Expand)
            │   └── VolumeSlider (HSlider 0 to 1, min width 220)
            ├── FullscreenCheck (CheckBox)
            ├── ResolutionRow (HBoxContainer)
            │   ├── Label "Resolution" (Expand)
            │   └── ResolutionOption (OptionButton, min width 220)
            └── BackButton (Button, 240 x 48, Shrink Center)

Settings hides MenuPanel and shows the settings screen; the settings screen emits a back_requested signal, and the menu shows itself again and gives Play keyboard focus. Quit calls get_tree().quit(). Play only prints a placeholder message, because the project had no game scene to load, and Ziva said so. The settings handlers, as Ziva wrote them:

func _on_volume_changed(value: float) -> void:
    var db: float = linear_to_db(value) if value > 0.0 else -80.0
    AudioServer.set_bus_volume_db(AudioServer.get_bus_index("Master"), db)

func _on_fullscreen_toggled(toggled_on: bool) -> void:
    var mode: DisplayServer.WindowMode = DisplayServer.WINDOW_MODE_FULLSCREEN if toggled_on else DisplayServer.WINDOW_MODE_WINDOWED
    DisplayServer.window_set_mode(mode)

func _on_resolution_selected(index: int) -> void:
    if index < 0 or index >= RESOLUTIONS.size():
        return
    DisplayServer.window_set_size(RESOLUTIONS[index])
    _center_window()

The settings are not saved between launches. The prompt did not ask for that and Ziva did not add it. If you need it, write the values to a ConfigFile in user://.

Why this layout doesn't clip

Most clipped Godot UI comes from controls placed by hand. A control's offsets are pixel distances from an anchor point, by default the parent's top-left corner (Size and anchors). A button placed at x = 900 in a 1152-pixel window sits outside a 640-pixel one.

The layout above has no hand-placed child positions:

  • The root fills the window. MainMenu, Background and MenuPanel use the Full Rect anchor preset (anchors 0 to 1 on both axes), so they always match the window.
  • A CenterContainer does the centering. It "automatically keeps all of its child controls centered within it at their minimum size" (Using Containers).
  • Box containers stack the rows. Inside a container, "all children Control nodes give up their own positioning ability" (same page), so a resize re-lays out everything.
  • Minimum sizes set the size. The buttons get their size from custom_minimum_size, and the labels in each settings row have Expand set so the label and the 220-pixel slider or dropdown share the row without overlapping.

One limit: a container never shrinks its children below their minimum size. Ziva's menu box is 260 x 293 pixels, so in a window shorter than 293 pixels it no longer fits. If your game must work in very small windows, or should scale the UI up on big screens, set Project Settings > Display > Window > Stretch > Mode to canvas_items (Multiple resolutions). Ziva's project kept the default, Disabled, so on a 1920 x 1080 window the menu stays the same pixel size in the middle of a larger screen.

How Ziva checked it

Ziva's run_scene tool runs a scene from the editor, sends input and returns a screenshot. Ziva used it three times:

  1. Run the menu and look at the screenshot. It also fixed an integer-division warning from the run's output.
  2. Run again and click the button labelled Settings. The screenshot showed the settings screen, and Ziva wrote: "Settings screen opens with all controls showing, nothing clipped."
  3. Run again, clicking Settings and then Back. The screenshot showed the menu with Play focused.

run_scene runs the game at the project's window size (here Godot's default, 1152 x 648) and can't resize it, so screenshots alone could not show a resize. Ziva noted that and wrote a GDScript test that loaded the menu at several window sizes and checked that the menu box and the settings box stayed inside the window. Its first measurement said neither fit at 1152 x 648. Ziva decided the layout had not been applied on the first frame and reran 1152 x 648 with a warm-up, plus 800 x 450 and 3840 x 2160. Across both runs it passed at 640 x 360, 800 x 450, 1152 x 648, 1920 x 1080 and 3840 x 2160.

We then ran our own check on a copy of the project: at 1152 x 648, 640 x 360, 1920 x 1080 and 800 x 600, no visible Control was outside the window or smaller than its content, Settings opened, and Back returned to the menu.

The miss: an invisible checkbox

Both checks passed a settings screen with a problem. With Godot's default theme the unchecked CheckBox box is dark, and on Ziva's dark background it almost disappeared, so "Fullscreen" looked like a plain label. Ziva's own screenshot showed it, and Ziva still reported all controls showing. Our geometry check could not see it either: the checkbox was the right size and inside the window.

We sent a second prompt in the same chat:

Look closely at the settings screen in a screenshot. Is every control easy to see and use? Fix anything that isn't, then show me the settings screen again.

This time Ziva opened its earlier screenshot and said the Fullscreen checkbox "looks like plain centered text with no visible indicator". It built a throwaway scene with a checked and an unchecked CheckBox on the same background, ran it, and confirmed that only the checked one showed a box. Then it added code to settings_screen.gd that draws its own checked and unchecked icons into a Theme on the checkbox, and ran the menu twice more, clicking Settings and then Fullscreen to see both states. Our check afterwards passed at the same four sizes, with the checkbox outline visible.

Two things to know about that fix. Drawing icons pixel by pixel in a script works, but about 60 lines of code for one checkbox is a lot; in your own project a Theme resource with checkbox icons, set on the root Control, does the same for every CheckBox below it, because themes apply to a control and its children (GUI skinning). And Ziva left the throwaway scene, ui_demo/_tmp_check.tscn, in the project. It said so in its reply: it "didn't delete it since removal wasn't requested" and offered to remove it.

Time and cost

  • First prompt: 3 min 58 s, $0.033 of Ziva usage on Ziva Smart, the default model.
  • Follow-up prompt: 4 min 6 s, $0.036.

What this test does not show

One simple UI, the default theme, one run. We did not check that Fullscreen and Resolution change a real desktop window, or keyboard and gamepad navigation between the controls. Ziva's run window is embedded in the editor and only supports windowed mode, as Ziva pointed out. A larger UI, a custom theme or a different model may give different results.

Checklist: a Godot menu and settings screen that don't clip

Whether you build it yourself or ask an AI, these steps follow the layout above:

  1. Add a root Control and choose Full Rect from the anchor preset menu in the toolbar above the viewport.
  2. Add a ColorRect background, also Full Rect.
  3. Add a CenterContainer (Full Rect) and a VBoxContainer inside it. Put the title and buttons in the VBoxContainer.
  4. Size buttons with Custom Minimum Size instead of dragging their handles.
  5. Make the settings screen its own scene with its own background. Instance it in the menu, hide it, and show or hide it from the menu script. Use HBoxContainers for label and control rows, with Expand on the labels.
  6. Check several window sizes. Run the scene and resize the window, or run a script like the one below.
  7. Look at a screenshot of every screen on its real background, in every state (checked and unchecked, focused and not). A layout check can't tell you a control is hard to see.

Here is a short size check, based on what Ziva did. Save it in the project folder and run godot --headless --path . --script check_layout.gd:

extends SceneTree

func _initialize() -> void:
    var menu: Control = load("res://ui_demo/main_menu.tscn").instantiate()
    root.add_child(menu)
    # The window applies its own size on the first frame, so measuring before this reads a stale layout.
    await process_frame
    for size: Vector2i in [Vector2i(640, 360), Vector2i(1152, 648), Vector2i(1920, 1080), Vector2i(400, 240)]:
        root.size = size
        for i in 4:
            await process_frame
        var box: Rect2 = menu.get_node("MenuPanel/MenuBox").get_global_rect()
        print(size, " menu fits: ", Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, Vector2(size)).encloses(box))
    quit()

On Ziva's menu it prints true for the first three sizes and false for 400 x 240, the minimum-size limit described above.

To try Ziva on your own UI, see installation. We ran the same kind of test on a broken shader and on collision bugs.

FAQ

Can AI build UI in Godot?

In our test, mostly yes. We asked Ziva, an AI agent that runs inside the Godot editor, for a main menu and a settings screen made of Control nodes. In about 4 minutes it built both scenes, clicked through Settings and Back in the running game, and checked the layout at five window sizes. It missed one problem: the unchecked Fullscreen checkbox was nearly invisible on the dark background. A second prompt asking it to look closely caught and fixed that. This was one project and one run on 10 November 2026, so treat it as an example, not a benchmark.

How do I make a Godot main menu that doesn't clip when the window is resized?

Build it from containers instead of hand-placed positions. Give the root Control the Full Rect anchor preset so it always matches the window, add a CenterContainer with Full Rect anchors, put a VBoxContainer inside it, and size the buttons with Custom Minimum Size. Children of a container give up their own positioning, so the container re-centers them whenever the window changes size. A container never shrinks its children below their minimum size, so very small windows still need a stretch mode such as canvas_items.

How do I make a settings menu in Godot with volume, fullscreen and resolution?

Make the settings screen its own scene, instance it in the menu scene, and show or hide it from the menu script. For the controls: an HSlider from 0 to 1 sets the Master bus volume with AudioServer.set_bus_volume_db and linear_to_db, a CheckBox switches DisplayServer.window_set_mode between fullscreen and windowed, and an OptionButton calls DisplayServer.window_set_size with the chosen resolution. Save the values with ConfigFile if they should survive a restart.

How do I test a Godot UI at different window sizes?

Run the scene and resize the game window, or run a short script that sets the root window size to several values, waits a few frames for the containers to lay out, and checks that each container's rectangle is inside the window. Wait one frame before the first measurement: in our test, Ziva's first measurement read a stale layout. A layout check cannot tell you whether a control is easy to see, so also look at a screenshot.

Why is my Godot CheckBox invisible on a dark background?

With Godot 4.7.2's default theme, the unchecked CheckBox box is drawn dark. On the dark background Ziva chose (Color(0.09, 0.1, 0.14)), the unchecked box almost disappeared, while the checked box was clearly visible. Fix it with your own checked and unchecked icons in a Theme resource, or use a lighter background behind the checkbox.

title: Next.js 16.4.6 Now Gzips Route Handlers. I Checked Streams, Downloads and Pre-Compressed Bodies
description:
Next.js 16.4.6 shipped overnight with a one-line release note: "Automatically compress route handler responses if not already compressed." If you self-host with next start, that's a real change. Your API routes were never gzipped before, and now they are.

Compression and streaming don't always mix, so I ran the same routes on 16.4.4, 16.4.5 and 16.4.6.

What changed

The fix is PR #101220, backported in #101280. Its description says route handler responses "were never compressed when self-hosted". Next stored single header values as one-element arrays, the compression middleware only accepts a string Content-Type, so every route handler response skipped compression. Pages were compressed all along.

How I tested

A small app built with next build and run with next start on Node 22.23.4. Requests come from a raw node:http client sending Accept-Encoding: gzip, so nothing gets decoded behind my back, plus plain fetch() to see what a normal client gets. The routes look like this one:

// app/sse/route.ts
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms))

export async function GET() {
  const enc = new TextEncoder()
  const stream = new ReadableStream({
    async start(controller) {
      for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
        controller.enqueue(enc.encode(`data: {"token":"chunk ${i}"}\n\n`))
        await sleep(500)
      }
      controller.close()
    },
  })
  return new Response(stream, {
    headers: { 'content-type': 'text/event-stream', 'cache-control': 'no-cache' },
  })
}

Here's what came back:

Route 16.4.4 16.4.5 16.4.6
Response.json() with 200 items (5,591 bytes) not gzipped not gzipped gzipped, 964 bytes on the wire
SSE stream above not gzipped not gzipped gzipped, still streams
600 KB application/pdf with Content-Length Content-Length: 614400 no Content-Length, chunked no Content-Length, chunked
Body gzipped by the handler, with Content-Encoding: gzip works header dropped, client gets raw gzip bytes gzipped twice, client gets gzip bytes after decoding

Streams still stream

This was my main worry. On 16.4.6 the SSE route came back with Content-Encoding: gzip, and the decoded events arrived at 9, 508, 1009, 1510 and 2010 ms. That's the same 500 ms rhythm as the uncompressed run on 16.4.4. Each chunk goes through gzip and out right away; nothing waits in a buffer.

I also ran an AI SDK 7.0.166 route (streamText(...).toUIMessageStreamResponse() with a mock model that emits a token every 500 ms). Same result: gzipped, and each text-delta showed up on its own about 500 ms apart.

I only tested next start directly. A reverse proxy or CDN in front of your app can still buffer, and I didn't test Vercel's platform.

Content-Length is still gone

This part comes from 16.4.5, not 16.4.6. The security release strips Content-Length, Content-Encoding and Transfer-Encoding from every route handler Response (the reasoning is in advisory GHSA-pc58-hwjq-p385, about forwarded fetch() responses). Issue #101120 reported that this breaks downloads and range requests, since pdf.js and download progress bars need the size.

That issue was closed by the compression PR. On 16.4.6, though, my 600 KB PDF still had no Content-Length on GET or HEAD. application/pdf isn't something the middleware compresses, so it just goes out chunked. If you serve files from a route handler and rely on that header, 16.4.6 doesn't bring it back.

Pre-compressed bodies break

Some handlers gzip their own output (a cached blob, a file from storage) and set Content-Encoding: gzip. On 16.4.4 that worked. On 16.4.5 Next drops the header, so fetch() hands your code raw gzip bytes and JSON.parse fails. On 16.4.6 it's worse in a different way. The header gets dropped, then the middleware gzips the already-gzipped body. The client decodes once and still has gzip bytes.

My test body was only 47 bytes, so the 1 KB threshold doesn't save you here. Route handler responses stream without a Content-Length, and the PR's own tests note that the threshold "never engages" for them.

Setting compress: false in next.config stops the double gzip, but you're back to the 16.4.5 behavior: the bytes arrive with no Content-Encoding header.

The fix that worked in my test: return the uncompressed body and let the server compress it. That's also what the PR description recommends ("the responses from route handlers should be returned uncompressed and be compressed by the outgoing server"). There's an open PR, #101452, to keep Content-Encoding on handler responses, but it isn't merged as of this morning.

What I'd check before upgrading

  • Grep your route handlers for content-encoding and gzipSync/CompressionStream. Those are the ones that break.
  • If you serve downloads from a route handler, check whether anything needs Content-Length. It's been missing since 16.4.5.
  • If nginx or a CDN was compressing your API responses, it now receives responses that already say Content-Encoding: gzip. I didn't test a proxy setup, so check the headers your users actually get.

The streaming part was the one I expected to bite, and it was fine. The quiet one is the handler that gzips its own body, because it fails in the client, not on the server.

Got a route handler that sets its own Content-Encoding? I'd like to know what it's serving.

title: What are the best Jarvis Labs alternatives for training in 2026?
description:
The best Jarvis Labs alternative depends on what drives your bill: the hourly rate, or the hours a GPU sits running while nobody uses it. Nodus lists the NVIDIA H100 at $2.60 per GPU-hour on its pricing page, against $3.49 on demand at Jarvis Labs, and by default stops idle development machines after an hour. Stay on Jarvis Labs for its $1.54 H100 spot rate or a full VM in India; pick RunPod for per-second containers, Lambda for 8-GPU instances and Modal for Python functions.

We build Nodus, so read this with that in mind. Every fact about another company links to its own pricing page or docs, and every sum is written out so you can redo it at today's prices.

How does Jarvis Labs bill a training project?

Jarvis Labs bills GPU instances per minute while they run, and charges only for storage while they are paused. Its pricing page lists a 1-GPU NVIDIA H100 SXM instance, with 16 vCPUs and 200 GB of RAM, at $3.49/hr on demand and $1.54/hr on spot. Spot instances "can be interrupted when the capacity is needed, so save your work often", in the page's own words.

Storage has one rate for instance disks and filesystems: $0.10 per GB per month, or $0.00014 per GB per hour, billed on provisioned capacity. Egress within the region is free. There is no free trial, and the minimum credit purchase is $25 for international customers.

Pausing is the habit the whole model is built around. The docs overview tells you to pause an instance when you are done to stop compute billing, and delete it to stop all billing. The jl CLI helps here: jl run train.py --gpu L4 creates an instance, runs your script and pauses the instance when it finishes.

A few rules come with pausing, all from Jarvis Labs' instance docs. Only data under /home survives a pause, so packages installed system-wide are lost. Resuming creates a new instance with your data, and you can change the GPU type or count at that point, but only in the same region. The FAQs add that availability is not guaranteed once a paused instance releases its GPU.

What does a week of fine-tuning cost on Jarvis Labs?

On Jarvis Labs, idle hours cost far more than storage, so whether you pause decides the bill. We worked one week from listed prices for a single H100 SXM. You do 6 hours of real work a day for 5 days, which is 30 GPU-hours, and keep a 100 GB disk for all 168 hours of the week.

Paused every evening, 30 hours at $3.49 cost $104.70. The disk adds 100 x $0.00014 x 168 = $2.35, for $107.05 in total. Forget to pause all week and the GPU bills 168 hours: the 138 extra hours add $481.62, for $586.32 in compute. The same 30 hours on Jarvis Labs spot cost 30 x $1.54 = $46.20, if no interruption forces you to redo work.

On Nodus, the same 30 hours at the $2.60 list price cost $78.00 in compute. A Nodus Workspace stops by itself after idleTimeout, which defaults to 1 hour with no SSH session, editor traffic or running process, per the Workspaces docs. If you walk away each evening without stopping it, that is 5 more hours, or $13.00, for $91.00 in total. Nodus bills retained storage separately and its pricing page does not list a storage rate, so the Nodus figures are compute only.


Jarvis Labs spot is the cheapest week here; leaving an on-demand instance running is the most expensive by far.

The decision rule we take from this: price your idle hours before your hourly rate. If you, or jl run, reliably pause, Jarvis Labs' bill is your working hours plus a few dollars of disk. If your team leaves notebooks open overnight, an automatic idle stop is worth more than any rate difference in the table below.

When is Jarvis Labs spot cheaper than on-demand elsewhere?

Jarvis Labs spot stays cheaper than the Nodus H100 list price until the work you redo after interruptions reaches 68.8% of the run. Every hour on spot costs $1.54, so spot only matches Nodus once total hours reach $2.60 / $1.54 = 1.688 times the plan. Against Jarvis Labs' own on-demand rate the threshold is $3.49 / $1.54 = 2.266, so spot wins until repeated work passes 126.6%.

In practice the money rarely decides it. A script that writes a checkpoint every 30 minutes loses at most half an hour per interruption, far below either threshold. The real cost of spot is your attention: someone has to notice the interruption, resume the instance and restart the script. Our spot vs on-demand guide covers that tradeoff for training in general.

Nodus handles that step for you on a job. The attempts and recovery docs say a machine that stops sending heartbeats gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds and, on shared capacity, is declared lost after 60 seconds. A Checkpointed run then restarts from its latest committed checkpoint, so it loses at most the work since that save. Nodus restores files, never process memory, so your script still loads its own checkpoint on start.

How do Jarvis Labs GPU prices compare with Nodus?

Nodus lists lower on-demand prices than Jarvis Labs on most cards, and Jarvis Labs spot is lower than Nodus on every card we compared. The exception on demand is the A100 40GB, where Jarvis Labs is a little cheaper.

GPU Jarvis Labs on demand Jarvis Labs spot Nodus list price
H100 SXM 80 GB $3.49 $1.54 $2.60
H200 SXM 141 GB $4.59 $2.29 $3.593
A100 80GB $1.49 $0.89 $1.09
A100 40GB $0.89 $0.79 $0.904
RTX Pro 6000 96 GB $2.19 $1.15 $1.35
L4 24 GB $0.44 $0.29 $0.43

Prices checked November 9, 2026, per GPU-hour for a 1-GPU instance: Jarvis Labs pricing and Nodus pricing. Jarvis Labs' prices include the vCPUs and RAM listed with each card.


Nodus is lower than Jarvis Labs on demand on these cards, and Jarvis Labs spot is lower than both.

Which Jarvis Labs alternative fits which kind of training?

Pick by how your training runs, not by the H100 row alone. Here are four alternatives next to Jarvis Labs, priced for one H100 SXM.

Platform H100 SXM per GPU-hour Billing What you get Good fit
Jarvis Labs $3.49 on demand, $1.54 spot Per minute; storage while paused Template containers or full VMs, India regions Notebook work you pause yourself, cheap spot
Nodus $2.60 Prepaid credits Jobs, Workspaces, sandboxes, functions Runs that should restart and stop on their own
RunPod $2.69 Community Cloud, $3.99 Secure Cloud Per second Container pods Containers at a fixed per-second price
Lambda $4.89 on a 1-GPU instance, $4.59 on 8 GPUs, from November 16, 2026 Per GPU-hour Instances of 1 to 8 GPUs Dedicated multi-GPU machines
Modal $3.95 Per second Python functions in containers Code already written as Modal functions

Prices checked November 9, 2026: Jarvis Labs pricing, Nodus pricing, RunPod pricing, Lambda pricing and Modal pricing. Modal's $0.001097 per second is multiplied out to an hour. Lambda's page says these prices take effect November 16, 2026, and shows current prices after login.

RunPod, like Jarvis Labs' templates, runs your work in containers, but bills per second rather than per minute. Our RunPod alternatives guide goes deeper on it. If you are also weighing TensorDock, our TensorDock alternatives guide prices what a lost host costs.

Can you connect your Jarvis Labs account to Nodus?

Not today. Our cloud accounts docs list Jarvis as paused: new connections and execution are not available.

The same docs describe how this works for providers that are supported. You connect your own account, approve execution access and set a spending limit, and Nodus places your single-node work there first, spending your cloud credits before Nodus capacity. That mode is in Beta, and your provider bills you for its machines directly.

Where is Jarvis Labs the better choice?

Jarvis Labs wins on spot price. Its $1.54 H100 spot rate is the lowest H100 price in either table, and its A100 40GB is $0.89 on demand against $0.904 on Nodus. Its A30 is listed at $0.41/hr on demand, and Nodus does not list an A30.

It also gives you a full machine when you want one. Jarvis Labs' VM docs offer root access, Docker and your own stack, with VPCs, reserved IPs and security groups. Its pricing page lists Instant Clusters of 8-GPU H200 nodes over InfiniBand, created from the dashboard. Its pricing page also publishes rupee rates for customers in India.

The workflow is simple and built for agents too. jl setup installs agent skills so Claude Code or Codex can drive your GPUs, and jl run pauses the instance when a script ends. If you already pause reliably, run in India and like spot, moving will not save you money.

How do you move a Jarvis Labs workflow to Nodus?

Keep your files in a saved home directory and let Nodus stop the machine for you. Install the CLI and sign in, as the install docs show:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login

For notebook-style work, create a Workspace and connect to it. These commands are from the Workspaces docs:

nodus create workspace lab --gpu H100
nodus ssh workspace/lab

Everything in /home/nodus is saved when the Workspace stops, much like /home on Jarvis Labs. Packages installed outside your home are temporary, so keep a virtual environment there. When a run is ready to go unattended, submit it as a job. This line is the example from the nodus run reference, with a $40 spend cap:

nodus run --gpu H100:8 --max-cost 40 -d -- torchrun train.py

FAQ

Is Jarvis Labs cheaper than Nodus?

On spot, yes: $1.54 per H100 hour against $2.60 on Nodus. On demand, Nodus lists the H100 $0.89 lower at $2.60 against $3.49, though Jarvis Labs' rate includes 16 vCPUs and 200 GB of RAM.

What happens to my data if my Jarvis Labs balance runs out?

Jarvis Labs' FAQs say instances pause automatically when the balance reaches zero. If the balance goes negative, all data is permanently deleted and cannot be recovered, so keep a copy of checkpoints elsewhere.

Does Jarvis Labs offer GPUs outside India?

Its pricing FAQ says it currently offers GPUs in India. The CLI docs list two regions, IN1 and IN2, and say the EU1 region no longer accepts new instances.

Does Jarvis Labs refund unused credit?

Its pricing FAQ says it does not offer refunds, though you can email its team with a valid reason for review. Buy credit in amounts you expect to use; the minimum is $25 for international customers.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: 海外 VPS 怎么选？全球云服务器购买前必须了解的 7 个关键因素
description:
海外 VPS 怎么选？全球云服务器购买前必须了解的 7 个关键因素

随着跨境电商、海外独立站、国际业务和互联网应用的发展，越来越多的个人开发者和企业开始使用海外 VPS 和全球云服务器。

但是，面对香港、日本、美国、新加坡、韩国等不同地区的服务器，以及各种 CPU、内存、带宽和 IP 配置，很多人在购买之前都会遇到一个问题：

海外 VPS 到底应该怎么选？

实际上，选择服务器不能只看价格和硬件配置。服务器所在地区、网络线路、IP 类型、硬件资源以及服务商的售后支持，都会影响后续使用体验。

本文整理了购买海外 VPS 和全球云服务器之前，值得重点考虑的七个因素。

一、根据目标用户选择服务器地区

选择海外云服务器，首先应该考虑目标用户所在的位置。

不同地区的服务器适合不同的业务场景。

常见服务器地区包括：

  • 香港服务器： 适合面向中国大陆及亚太地区用户的网站和应用，实际访问体验取决于网络线路。
  • 日本服务器： 适合日本及东亚地区的网站、应用和业务部署。
  • 美国服务器： 适合面向北美用户的网站和应用。
  • 新加坡服务器： 适合面向东南亚市场的业务。
  • 韩国服务器： 适合面向韩国及周边地区的业务。
  • 欧洲服务器： 德国、英国、法国、荷兰等地区可以根据客户分布选择。

没有哪一个地区绝对最好。

建议先确定业务的主要访问人群，再选择合适的服务器位置。

二、不要只看 CPU 和内存配置

购买 VPS 时，很多人首先比较 CPU 核心数、内存大小和硬盘容量。

这些参数确实重要，但不能完全代表服务器的实际性能。

配置 主要作用
CPU 影响程序运行和计算能力
内存 影响应用、数据库及缓存运行
SSD/NVMe 影响系统和数据库的读写速度
带宽 影响网络传输能力
月流量 决定计费周期内的数据传输额度

例如，一个简单的网站可能只需要较低的配置，而数据库较多、访问量较大的应用，则需要更充足的 CPU 和内存资源。

建议根据实际业务需求选择，不必盲目追求高配置。

三、网络线路往往比硬件参数更重要

服务器购买后能否稳定访问，与网络线路有很大关系。

即使两台服务器位于同一个国家，也可能因为机房、上游运营商和路由路径不同，产生明显的网络体验差异。

购买之前建议了解：

  1. 服务器所在机房及上游网络。
  2. 到目标用户地区的路由情况。
  3. 网络延迟和丢包情况。
  4. 带宽是否共享。
  5. 是否存在流量或连接限制。

如果服务商提供测试 IP，可以先进行实际测试。

不要只凭宣传页面上的线路名称判断网络质量。

四、了解普通 IP、静态 IP 和双 ISP IP

IP 类型也是海外服务器选购时容易忽略的一项。

普通 IP：

通常指服务器分配的常规 IP 地址，具体归属和使用属性需要向服务商确认。

静态 IP：

通常指不会频繁变化的固定 IP 地址，适合需要固定访问地址、远程管理或稳定配置的业务。

双 ISP IP：

通常涉及两个互联网服务提供商的网络属性。具体 IP 归属、路由情况和实际表现，需要结合产品说明和测试结果判断。

购买前建议确认：

  • IP 是否独享。
  • IP 是否固定。
  • IP 的实际归属和类型。
  • 是否支持所需的网络服务。
  • 是否存在额外使用限制。

不要仅凭产品名称判断 IP 的实际属性。

五、免实名云服务器需要注意什么？

部分海外服务器服务商提供不要求个人实名认证的购买方式，但不同地区和服务商的具体要求可能不同。

购买前建议了解：

  • 服务商的注册及购买要求。
  • 是否需要提供其他身份或付款信息。
  • 所在地区适用的法律法规。
  • 服务条款对业务用途的限制。
  • 数据安全和隐私政策。

需要注意，免实名购买方式不代表可以规避法律法规，也不代表可以用于任何用途。

选择服务器时，合规性和服务透明度同样重要。

六、购买之前做好服务器测试

在正式部署网站或业务之前，建议先检查服务器的实际情况。

可以从以下几个方面入手：

  • CPU、内存和硬盘是否符合购买方案。
  • 网络延迟是否符合业务需求。
  • 是否存在明显丢包。
  • 磁盘读写是否正常。
  • SSH 或远程管理是否能够正常连接。
  • 服务商是否提供清晰的售后支持。

Linux 用户可以使用以下命令进行基础网络测试：

测试网络延迟 

ping -c 10 YOUR_SERVER_IP

查看路由路径 

traceroute YOUR_SERVER_IP

如果系统没有安装 traceroute，需要先安装对应的软件包。

这些测试只能反映特定时间和测试地点的情况。对于长期运行的业务，建议在不同时间段重复测试。

七、关注服务商的售后和服务透明度

服务器不仅仅是一组硬件配置。

购买之前，还应该关注：

  • 产品参数是否清晰。
  • 是否提供网络测试信息。
  • 付款和续费规则是否透明。
  • 是否提供故障处理支持。
  • 是否提前通知维护和网络变更。
  • 是否有明确的服务使用政策。

对于需要长期运行的网站和业务，稳定的服务支持非常重要。

总结：如何选择适合自己的海外 VPS？

海外 VPS 和全球云服务器没有统一的最佳方案。

不同业务应该根据实际需求选择：

  1. 先确定目标用户所在地区。
  2. 根据应用负载选择 CPU 和内存。
  3. 了解服务器的网络线路。
  4. 确认 IP 类型及实际属性。
  5. 了解购买和使用规则。
  6. 正式部署前进行测试。
  7. 选择服务透明、售后清晰的服务商。

如果你正在了解全球云服务器、海外 VPS、双 ISP 服务器或独享静态 IP，可以进一步研究不同地区的产品配置和网络特点，再根据自己的业务需求进行选择。

希望这篇文章能够帮助正在选购海外 VPS 的开发者和网站运营者，减少不必要的购买成本和后期迁移问题。

本文为技术知识分享，涉及的服务器和网络配置应以实际产品说明、测试结果及服务商政策为准。

title: Your hero banner looks fine. Now open it on an ultrawide screen.
description:
While researching a UX case study on a Mexican mobile carrier's website, I widened my browser window and watched the homepage disappear behind its own banner.

The banner was an image stretched to 100% of the width. On my screen it took 44% of the first view. Add the header bars, and the first product started at 60% of the screen. Plans, prices and the way to your account were all below the fold.

It looked fine on the laptop it was probably designed on. It was a problem on everything wider.

The math

A full-width image with a fixed aspect ratio has a height that depends only on the width:

height = viewport width ÷ aspect ratio

That banner had a ratio of about 3.7 to 1. So:

Screen Banner height Share of the visible height
1440 × 900 laptop ~390 px ~45%
2560 × 1080 (21:9) ~690 px ~70%
3440 × 1440 (21:9) ~930 px ~70%
5120 × 1440 (32:9) ~1380 px more than the whole screen

The wider the screen, the less of your page people see. And ultrawide monitors are common among exactly the people who use a desktop all day for work.

Why it's also an accessibility problem

An ultrawide screen isn't a WCAG criterion on its own. What it does is make existing problems bigger:

  • Text inside the image (WCAG 1.4.5). The headline, the deadline and even a URL were part of the picture. Screen readers can't read it, users can't zoom it without the image pixelating, and nobody can copy the link.
  • Inverted hierarchy. The banner text scaled up with the image while the navigation stayed small. The biggest thing on the page was the ad; the smallest was the menu.
  • Tiny controls, far apart (WCAG 2.5.8). Carousel dots smaller than 24 px, and arrows pinned to the edges, 2,000+ px apart.
  • Auto-rotation (WCAG 2.2.2). If it moves for more than 5 seconds, people need a way to pause it.

The fix

Four rules got me most of the way in my redesign:

1. Cap the content width. The page can be 3440 px wide; your content doesn't have to be.

.container {
  max-width: 1200px;
  margin-inline: auto;
  padding-inline: 24px;
}

2. Give the banner a height, not just a ratio. Let it flex within limits instead of growing forever.

.hero {
  height: clamp(240px, 30vw, 360px);
  max-height: 40vh;
  display: flex;
  overflow: hidden;
}

3. Keep text out of the image. Text goes in HTML, and the image only fills its own area.

<section class="hero" aria-roledescription="carousel" aria-label="Promotions">
  <div class="hero-copy">
    <h2>Register your line before November 15</h2>
    <p>Your deadline depends on the last digit of your number.</p>
    <a href="/register" class="button">Register now</a>
  </div>
  <img class="hero-media" src="promo.jpg" alt="">
</section>

.hero-copy  { flex: 1 1 55%; padding: 36px 40px; }
.hero-media { flex: 1 1 45%; object-fit: cover; min-width: 0; }

A decorative image gets an empty alt; if the image carries meaning, describe it.

4. Real controls, real size. Buttons with names, at least 44 × 44 px, close to each other, and a pause button if anything moves.

<button type="button" aria-label="Pause promotions">…</button>

How to test it without an ultrawide monitor

  • In Chrome DevTools, open device mode (Ctrl+Shift+M) and type 3440 × 1440, then 2560 × 1080.
  • Or zoom out to 50% on a 1920 px screen: the page lays out as if it were about 3840 px wide.
  • Ask one question: what can a person do without scrolling? If the answer is "look at an ad", the banner is too big.

The real lesson

The banner wasn't a CSS bug. It was a priority decision that the CSS made visible: the promotion came first, and what the person came to do came second. Capping the height is the technical fix. Deciding what deserves the first screen is the design one.

This was one finding from a bigger case study on activation, registration and information hierarchy across an email, an app and a website. You can read the full case, with prototypes, on my site: Activated doesn't mean working.

title: How to Rehearse GDPR Password Reset Email With Developer Report Attachments
description:
Keep password reset templates under application control, and rehearse their release alongside the generated report emails your developer tool already sends. The deciding constraint is template ownership: whoever can change the recovery link, recipient, or attachment behavior can change the security boundary, even if the sending service remains healthy.

Short answer: choose a transactional email service only after its template workflow passes a recovery rehearsal, its processing terms fit your GDPR obligations, and your application can distinguish an accepted send from a completed reset. Keep report attachments in a separate message. A password reset shouldn't become an excuse to distribute a generated report to someone whose control of the account is still being established.

This runbook uses a synthetic developer report and two locally rendered messages. It makes the content boundary executable before you connect a transport; the example doesn't claim that any particular service accepts raw MIME or supports an attachment field that hasn't been checked.

1. What page fired when the reset email looked healthy?

Start the postmortem with the page, not the dashboard. Was there a delivery failure, an exhausted recovery deadline, or merely a send request that the application accepted? Those observations describe different boundaries, and a green chart for one cannot establish the others. Before choosing a service, write down which observation should wake the responder and which evidence would let that responder stop investigating.

Ask what failed.

For this developer tool, the concrete job is sending a generated report as an email attachment, while the same account system also sends password reset links. That shared sender makes template ownership consequential: changing the report email must not silently add a report attachment to recovery mail, and changing a recovery template must not leak its link into a report. Treat these as separate content contracts even if one team maintains both.

The rehearsal uses a report with exactly 3 synthetic checks. That is fixture data, not a measured incident. Its purpose is to make an accidental attachment observable without using a customer report or a working recovery credential. A successful render establishes only what the renderer produced; delivery and successful account recovery still require their own evidence.

2. Choose the template owner before choosing the service

Application-owned templates make code review and content rollback part of the application's release process, at the cost of making that team responsible for rendering and maintenance. Provider-owned templates can move editing into a separate workflow, but then a template identifier alone is insufficient evidence of what a recipient received. Require a reviewable content revision and a way to restore the approved version. These are operational acceptance criteria, not claims that a particular vendor supplies every control.

Use the comparison as a procurement worksheet. Each candidate gets the same recovery fixture and report fixture; an unanswered question remains an unanswered question, rather than becoming a favorable checkbox. The documentation in References identifies the surfaces to inspect.

Candidate Template surface to evaluate Boundary to prove before selection
Amazon SES Its sending and template documentation Can your chosen sending workflow preserve application ownership, and can the responder identify the content revision associated with a send?
Twilio SendGrid Its dynamic transactional template documentation If editors own templates outside the application repository, how will approval and restoration of a specific revision work?
Postmark Its template API documentation Can your workflow tie each reviewed template change to the corresponding application release and recover the earlier content?

These are three real alternatives with different template surfaces to investigate. Prefer the candidate whose workflow your team can demonstrate and audit; a provider editing interface is useful only if its ownership model matches the people responsible for recovery. This worksheet isn't a measured ranking of delivery performance or a certification of anyone's GDPR compliance.

Infrai offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules; that single key and consolidated billing reduce credential handoffs and invoice reconciliation when report generation uses other backend capabilities. Its multi-vendor routing keeps a stable REST API contract while the vendor behind a capability changes, so switching providers does not require changing application code. The self-describing public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas without requiring a key, so the report-mail owner can inspect the declared inputs before handing credentials to an adapter developer; documented capabilities also include runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go, which gives that developer a concrete starting point for checking the mapping. That centralization also concentrates responsibility, so control access to the shared key.

The trade-off is operational: polling adds a tracking responsibility to the application. This is not a fit for a team whose recovery runbook requires pushed delivery events; evaluate Amazon SES, Twilio SendGrid, and Postmark against that requirement before selecting a service. Application-owned templates also require maintaining the renderer, whereas an externally edited template requires an additional approval and rollback workflow. Verify the attachment mapping separately before selecting a transport for report mail.

Keep legal review separate from the template demo. Document the processing purpose, privacy notice, consent management where applicable, and relevant processing arrangements before using real addresses. Don't turn a requested security email into marketing, and don't interpret a vendor's ability to send custom content as proof that your implementation complies with GDPR. Establish the appropriate legal basis for recovery mail rather than assuming that marketing consent governs every security message.

3. Build the content boundary as an offline rehearsal

Save the following as main.go and run it with go run main.go. It uses only the Go standard library, performs no network calls, and creates two email artifacts plus the generated report in a new temporary directory with owner-only permissions. The reset address and link are synthetic.

The program renders the recovery template as plain text and constructs a separate multipart message for the report attachment. These local structures are the application's contract, not a vendor request schema. When implementing the sending adapter, validate that provider's documented attachment and content inputs before mapping rendered content into a request. This distinction becomes important during incident review: an attachment that renders correctly in a local email artifact still needs a documented transport mapping, and neither the renderer nor the transport should quietly substitute another representation. If a service cannot demonstrate the required attachment workflow, choose a different service for report mail rather than changing the recovery template to carry the report. The two fixtures should survive that decision unchanged.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/base64"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "mime"
    "mime/multipart"
    "net/mail"
    "net/textproto"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "strings"
    "text/template"
)

func main() {
    log.SetFlags(0)
    if err := rehearse(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

func rehearse() error {
    const approved = "Recovery requested for {{.Account}}.\nOpen {{.Link}}\n"
    const candidate = "Account recovery for {{.Account}}.\nUse {{.Link}}\n"
    selected := candidate
    if os.Getenv("USE_APPROVED_TEMPLATE") == "1" {
        selected = approved
    }
    data := struct { Account, Link string }{
        Account: "fixture@example.invalid",
        Link: "https://example.invalid/reset?token=fixture-only",
    }
    t, err := template.New("reset").Option("missingkey=error").Parse(selected)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var content bytes.Buffer
    if err := t.Execute(&content, data); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    reset := "From: reports@example.invalid\r\n" +
        "To: fixture@example.invalid\r\n" +
        "Subject: Account recovery rehearsal\r\n" +
        "MIME-Version: 1.0\r\n" +
        "Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8\r\n\r\n" +
        strings.ReplaceAll(content.String(), "\n", "\r\n")

    report := []byte("check,result\ncompile,pass\nunit,pass\nlint,pass\n")
    var body bytes.Buffer
    writer := multipart.NewWriter(&body)
    header := make(textproto.MIMEHeader)
    header.Set("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
    part, err := writer.CreatePart(header)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if _, err := part.Write([]byte("Your synthetic developer report is attached.\r\n")); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    header = make(textproto.MIMEHeader)
    header.Set("Content-Type", "text/csv; charset=utf-8")
    header.Set("Content-Disposition", `attachment; filename="report.csv"`)
    header.Set("Content-Transfer-Encoding", "base64")
    part, err = writer.CreatePart(header)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if _, err := part.Write([]byte(base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(report))); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := writer.Close(); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    reportMail := "From: reports@example.invalid\r\n" +
        "To: fixture@example.invalid\r\n" +
        "Subject: Generated developer report\r\n" +
        "MIME-Version: 1.0\r\nContent-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=" +
        writer.Boundary() + "\r\n\r\n" + body.String()

    message, err := mail.ReadMessage(strings.NewReader(reset))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    kind, _, err := mime.ParseMediaType(message.Header.Get("Content-Type"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if kind != "text/plain" || strings.Contains(reset, "report.csv") {
        return fmt.Errorf("reset content boundary failed")
    }
    if !strings.Contains(reset, data.Link) || strings.Contains(reportMail, data.Link) {
        return fmt.Errorf("recovery link boundary failed")
    }
    dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "email-rehearsal-")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    artifacts := map[string][]byte{
        "reset.eml": []byte(reset),
        "report.eml": []byte(reportMail),
        "report.csv": report,
    }
    for name, payload := range artifacts {
        if err := os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(dir, name), payload, 0600); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    fmt.Println("Content checks passed. Inspect artifacts in", dir)
    return nil
}

The useful trap is a shared attachment accumulator: a report send adds a file, the next recovery send inherits it, and both requests can still look successful from the sender's perspective. Separate message construction prevents that particular shape of mistake here. It doesn't establish that the attachment belongs to the intended recipient; authorization of a real generated report must happen before rendering.

No real tokens.

Before implementing the transport, inspect its declared contract. Save this separate program as preflight.go and run go run preflight.go. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the service's documented HTTPS origin, without a path. Public discovery requires no key; if INFRAI_API_KEY is present, the request uses Bearer authentication. This read-only check prints the manifest rather than inventing email attachment inputs. It makes no send request, and the HTTP client refuses redirects so credentials stay on the configured origin.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if err := preflight(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

func preflight() error {
    base, err := url.Parse(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"))
    if err != nil || base == nil || base.Scheme != "https" ||
        base.Host == "" || base.User != nil ||
        (base.Path != "" && base.Path != "/") ||
        base.RawQuery != "" || base.Fragment != "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented HTTPS origin")
    }
    base.Path = "/v1/discovery"
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", base.String(), nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 8<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 40 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred beyond preflight time budget")
                }
                if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if requested := time.Until(deadline); requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

The 3-attempt limit and 45-second deadline are local runbook choices, not service limits or measured response times. Use the manifest's path and schema to implement the sending adapter only after its attachment contract is confirmed. A successful discovery request proves access to metadata; it says nothing about delivery.

4. Verify the artifact and rehearse the rollback

Inspect reset.eml as a message: its body must contain the synthetic recovery link, its content type must be plain text, and it must carry no attachment. Open report.eml with a MIME-aware mail reader, decode report.csv, and compare its contents with the generated CSV. Expect exactly the compile, unit, and lint rows. The program checks the recovery content boundary automatically; the decoded-attachment comparison is a separate acceptance step, because a successful string check cannot prove that a mail client will interpret a MIME message as intended.

Then set USE_APPROVED_TEMPLATE to 1 in your environment and run the same program again. The recovery wording should revert to “Recovery requested,” while the report rows and attachment filename stay the same. Compare decoded content, not entire message bytes: the multipart writer generates a boundary for each message, so byte-for-byte equality is the wrong rollback criterion. This is a local content rollback rehearsal, not a claim that reverting a template retracts messages already sent.

For a transport trial, use controlled recipients and record the template revision, application operation identifier, and provider message identifier without recording recovery tokens or report contents. Treat send acceptance, delivery evidence, and completion of recovery as separate observations. Define the page around a missed recovery objective and the evidence needed to diagnose it; a dashboard showing accepted requests cannot answer whether the recipient recovered access. Check SPF authorization separately using RFC 7208 as the protocol reference. Sender authorization doesn't certify GDPR compliance or prove inbox placement.

If verification fails, stop the candidate template rollout, restore the approved content revision, and preserve the failed synthetic artifacts for review. Decide which queued operations are still valid before releasing them again; replaying a queue indiscriminately can redistribute an attachment or repeat a recovery message. Require an application operation identifier and a documented deduplication strategy before enabling write retries in the sending adapter.

Keep the rollback narrow. A report attachment failure should not force a change to the recovery template, and restoring recovery wording should not silently change which report a recipient receives. The service earns its place when the team can demonstrate those boundaries under the selected template ownership model, with processing terms reviewed and an observation that tells the responder what actually happened.

References

  • Amazon SES sending email: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/send-email.html
  • Amazon SES personalized templates: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/send-personalized-email-api.html
  • Twilio SendGrid dynamic transactional templates: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/ui/sending-email/how-to-send-an-email-with-dynamic-templates
  • Postmark template API: https://postmarkapp.com/developer/api/templates-api
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • General Data Protection Regulation: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng

title: AI Generatif Merevolusi Pengembangan Perangkat Lunak: Asisten Cerdas untuk Developer
description:
AI Generatif: Asisten 'Pair Programmer' Otomatis

Kecerdasan buatan generatif mentransformasi pengembangan perangkat lunak. Alat seperti GitHub Copilot dan OpenAI Codex berfungsi sebagai 'pair programmer' otomatis, menyarankan kode real-time, melengkapi fungsi, dan menghasilkan blok kode kompleks. Ini mengubah cara developer menulis, menguji, dan men-debug kode.

Mempercepat Siklus Pengembangan dengan AI

AI generatif mempercepat siklus pengembangan perangkat lunak. Kemampuannya memprediksi dan menyarankan kode menghemat waktu developer dari tugas repetitif.

Penulisan Kode Lebih Cepat

AI generatif menyarankan baris kode atau fungsi berdasarkan konteks. Ini mengurangi waktu pengetikan dan eksplorasi sintaks, memungkinkan developer fokus pada logika bisnis.

Debugging Efisien

AI generatif membantu debugging. Alat ini menyarankan perbaikan bug atau mengidentifikasi area kode bermasalah, mempercepat penemuan dan perbaikan kesalahan.
