title: ISC Stormcast For Tuesday, November 10th, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10172, (Tue, Nov 10th)
Converting Excel Workbooks to TIFF Images in Java: Use Cases, Mechanics, and Trade-offs
description:
Excel workbooks are built for interactive use—formulas, multiple sheets, formatting, and embedded objects all live within a structured grid. TIFF, by contrast, is a flat, raster image format designed for archival stability and consistent rendering across platforms. Converting between the two is less about convenience and more about solving specific problems: preserving the visual appearance of a spreadsheet for legal or regulatory archives, embedding tabular data into document management systems that only accept image formats, or generating fax-ready outputs from financial reports.

This article examines the technical landscape of Excel-to-TIFF conversion in Java, using Spire.XLS for Java as a reference implementation. The focus is on understanding where such conversions fit, what trade-offs are involved, and how the library handles the mechanics.

Why TIFF Remains Relevant for Spreadsheet Archival

TIFF (Tagged Image File Format) dates back to the mid-1980s and was designed for desktop scanning and fax workflows. Its persistence in enterprise environments stems from characteristics that newer formats do not always prioritize: lossless compression through schemes like LZW, support for multiple pages within a single file, and a well-documented, stable specification that archival systems can rely on for decades.

When an Excel file must be retained as evidence—for audit trails, compliance submissions, or legal discovery—a TIFF rendering eliminates concerns about formula recalculation, font substitution, or version incompatibility. The output is what it is: a pixel representation of the worksheet as it appeared at conversion time. This immutability is both the format's strength and its limitation. You gain visual fidelity and long-term readability; you lose searchable text, cell references, and any ability to recompute values.

The trade-off is acceptable in scenarios where the spreadsheet is an endpoint, not a working document. Financial statements submitted to regulatory bodies, invoice archives, and scanned-document workflows that already operate in TIFF are typical candidates.

How Spire.XLS for Java Approaches the Conversion

Spire.XLS for Java provides a saveToTiff method that operates at the worksheet level. The API surface is minimal: load a workbook, retrieve a worksheet by index, and invoke the conversion with an output path. This design treats the conversion as a rendering operation rather than a data transformation.

A basic conversion looks like this:

import com.spire.xls.Workbook;
import com.spire.xls.Worksheet;

Workbook workbook = new Workbook();
workbook.loadFromFile("input.xlsx");
Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);
sheet.saveToTiff("output.tiff");

The method also supports converting a specific cell range rather than the entire worksheet, using an overload that accepts row and column boundaries. This is useful when only a summary table or a defined print area needs to be captured, avoiding the overhead of rendering blank cells or peripheral content.

What the API does not expose, at least in the basic saveToTiff signature, are fine-grained rendering controls. There is no built-in parameter for setting output DPI within the TIFF conversion method itself. The library supports DPI configuration for Excel-to-image conversions through ConverterSetting, but that mechanism applies to image outputs such as PNG, not to the TIFF path directly. For TIFF output, resolution is handled internally, and users seeking precise control over compression type (LZW, JPEG, or uncompressed) or color depth will not find those options in the standard method signature. This is a notable difference from libraries that expose explicit rendering options for TIFF compression and resolution.

Practical Considerations and Limitations

Page Layout and Scaling

Excel worksheets are not inherently paginated in the way that documents are. A worksheet can extend across thousands of rows and dozens of columns, with print areas, page breaks, and scaling settings that determine how the content would appear on paper. When converting to TIFF, the library must decide how to map this unbounded grid onto fixed image dimensions.

The behavior depends on the worksheet's existing page setup. If a print area is defined, saveToTiff generally respects it. If not, the conversion may produce a single very large image or split the content across multiple TIFF pages, depending on internal heuristics. For predictable results, users should configure the worksheet's PageSetup properties—orientation, paper size, fit-to-page scaling—before conversion.

Multi-Sheet Workbooks

A workbook with multiple worksheets requires iteration. saveToTiff operates on a single worksheet, so a complete conversion loop must traverse the worksheet collection and generate one TIFF per sheet. The naming and organization of output files becomes the developer's responsibility. There is no one-call "convert workbook to a single multi-page TIFF" convenience method in the basic API. While TIFF itself supports multi-page documents, the library's worksheet-level method does not aggregate sheets automatically.

Font and Rendering Fidelity

TIFF output is only as accurate as the rendering engine's ability to reproduce the Excel layout. Fonts that are not installed on the server running the conversion will be substituted, potentially altering column widths, row heights, and text wrapping. For organizations with strict branding or document appearance requirements, this is a critical operational detail. The conversion environment must have access to the same font set used when the Excel file was authored.

Compression and File Size

TIFF files are often large, particularly when rendering complex worksheets with dense formatting. The library's internal choice of compression scheme directly affects output size. Without exposed control over LZW versus uncompressed output, developers cannot optimize file size for their storage constraints. For batch archival pipelines handling thousands of workbooks, this lack of granularity may necessitate post-processing or acceptance of larger storage footprints.

Where This Conversion Fits in a Java Application

The most defensible use case for Excel-to-TIFF in Java is as a background archival process. A scheduled job reads spreadsheets from a monitored directory or database, converts each to TIFF, stores the image in a content management system, and optionally records metadata (source filename, conversion timestamp, checksum). The original Excel file may be retained or discarded according to retention policy.

A second scenario is report distribution. When a financial or operational report must be delivered to recipients who should not edit or manipulate the underlying data, a TIFF rendering enforces that boundary. The recipient sees the numbers as rendered; there is no hidden formula to inspect, no cell to modify. This is a control mechanism, not a technical necessity, but it is a legitimate one in regulated industries.

Less compelling is the use of TIFF conversion as a general-purpose export feature for end-user applications. TIFF files are large, not universally previewable in browsers, and poorly suited for on-screen viewing. If the goal is simply to share a non-editable view of a spreadsheet, PDF is almost always the better choice: smaller, searchable, and natively supported by virtually every document viewer. TIFF conversion should be reserved for workflows that specifically require raster images.

Conclusion

Converting Excel to TIFF in Java is a narrow but well-defined operation. Spire.XLS for Java handles the core mechanics—loading a workbook, selecting a worksheet or range, and rendering to a TIFF file—with an API that prioritizes brevity over granular control. The library is suitable for batch archival pipelines where the priority is getting a stable image output without extensive configuration.

The limitations are equally clear: limited exposed control over TIFF compression and resolution, reliance on the host environment's font set for rendering accuracy, and the inherent impedance mismatch between spreadsheet layout and fixed image dimensions. These are not defects in the library so much as characteristics of the conversion domain itself. Understanding them before committing to a TIFF-based workflow is more valuable than any API reference.

title: Introducing HexDB for Documents and Files
description:
An application can have customer records, uploaded documents, full-text search, and semantic search over those documents. Keeping the data, permissions, and updates consistent across those features can become a project of its own.

I've built HexDB to bring those pieces closer together.

HexDB is an encrypted, replicated database for JSON documents and binary files, with full-text and vector search. The core server is written in Rust and runs as one binary.

I'm Matthew "Doc" Martin, a software architect with more than 25 years in software development. HexDB is my independent project, built during late nights and weekends alongside my day job. With versions 2.4.3 and 2.4.4 released, this seems like a good time to introduce it here.

Documents and files in one database

HexDB stores JSON documents in collections called tessellations. You can query them through REST, GraphQL, gRPC, or SQL, with drivers for Node.js, Python, .NET, Java through JDBC, and ODBC.

SQL currently supports reads. Writes go through the APIs and drivers.

Files are part of the database too. They have queryable metadata, version history, resumable uploads, and access controls. Their content is encrypted, deduplicated, and compressed when that helps.

Consider an application with customer records and uploaded invoices. You need to find the records, retrieve the files, restrict access, and perhaps search the invoices by their contents. HexDB provides those capabilities within the same database platform.

It also includes an admin UI for managing documents, files, users, indexes, and the cluster. I want the operational side to be approachable, including when you're the person building the application and keeping it running.

Vector search alongside ordinary queries

Vector search is an index type in HexDB. You can supply your own embeddings or configure an embedding provider and have HexDB generate them from selected fields.

Similarity searches use the same documents, permissions, row filters, and field masks as other queries. You can combine a semantic search with an ordinary filter.

For example, after configuring an embedding provider and a vector index on an articles collection, this request searches published articles by meaning:

curl -X POST http://localhost:7700/articles/_query \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "filter": { "status": "published" },
    "near": {
      "field": "embedding",
      "text": "storage engines for edge devices",
      "k": 5
    }
  }'

The same approach works with extracted text from uploaded files. A search can find a document by what it discusses, even when its filename isn't useful.

Automatic embeddings use the provider you configure, including supported local providers. The selected source text goes to that provider. Usage controls include per-user allowances and a monthly token budget.

Each HexDB server also exposes an MCP endpoint for authenticated, read-only access by external agents. Optional A2A support lets another agent delegate a question to HexDB's own chat system. Those lookups run with the calling user's permissions.

Security around both records and uploads

My work in payments influences the questions I ask about data handling: who can read a value, where it gets copied, and what remains after a request finishes.

HexDB includes encryption at rest, role-based access, row filters, field masking, MFA, and an audit trail. Schema-defined tokenization can replace sensitive field values before the document reaches its write-ahead log, storage, replicas, or backups.

There are two tokenization modes. One-way tokens support matching without recovering the original value. Vault tokens keep the original in a separate encrypted vault, with explicit permission and auditing for detokenization.

File uploads also have integrated malware scanning and quarantine. YARA-X is built into supported builds, and HexDB connects to a separately running ClamAV daemon for signature-based scanning. Files flagged by a scanner are quarantined instead of becoming normal downloadable files or being replicated.

That distinction matters for deployment: the core database is one binary; ClamAV is an additional service. The supplied Docker Compose and Helm configurations include it.

The latest release adds cluster-wide IP blocking with optional expiry, signed responses between servers, and overwriting sensitive decrypted field values in memory when requests finish using them. It also fixes a change-feed issue so users cannot learn about deletions of records they weren't allowed to see.

A foreign key question that changed the engine

One of the changes in 2.4.3 began with a prospect asking about foreign keys.

HexDB now supports optional foreign keys in document schemas. With enforcement enabled, a write referencing a missing parent is refused.

The interesting part is when that check happens.

Suppose an order references a customer:

  1. A request checks that the customer exists.
  2. Another request deletes that customer.
  3. The first request commits the order.

A successful check at step one isn't enough to prevent an orphan at step three.

HexDB checks the relationship as part of the commit itself. Cascading deletes also re-check for newly written children at commit time, closing a related race.

The CLI gained document, transaction, and schema operations with idempotency keys, so retrying after a dropped connection won't apply the same write twice. A new “Writing safely” manual section explains the guarantees for inserts, updates, upserts, deletes, and transactions.

This is the kind of feedback I want from people evaluating HexDB. A concrete application requirement can expose something worth changing in the engine.

Recovery and performance in the latest releases

A group of HexDB servers is called a lattice. One server, the Overseer, handles writes; eligible replicas can take over if it fails.

Version 2.4.4 brings failover down to 15–20 seconds, about half the previous time. It also addresses isolated servers electing themselves and servers disagreeing about leadership when the whole cluster starts together.

Hosted routing now sends traffic only to servers that have the data. In one provisioning run, a new three-region hosted lattice went from nothing to fully ready in 33 seconds.

Storage and query improvements include:

Measurement Before After
Small-record storage in the measured workload 177 bytes 40 bytes
GROUP BY over 100,000 documents 320 ms 210 ms

The storage improvement comes from per-file compression dictionaries that capture patterns shared by documents. Reading a stored document also takes about half the work.

These are measurements from the specific workloads used for the release. They give a useful starting point for evaluating the changes against your own data.

Try HexDB and tell me what you find

HexDB is available through npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, Homebrew, Chocolatey, Debian packages, and Docker. You can run it yourself or explore hosted lattices.

The repository has installation instructions, examples, and the technical manual:

  • HexDB website
  • Source code and getting started
  • Version 2.4.4 release notes

I'd like to hear from developers working with documents, uploaded files, sensitive fields, or semantic search. What would you need to test before considering HexDB for an application? Which integration would make it easier to evaluate?

The foreign-key question already changed the engine. I'm interested in the next question.

title: Handling Failed Background Tasks Using Dead-Letter Queue Recovery for Marketplace Shipment Fan-Out
description:
Short answer: Handle failed background tasks using a dead-letter queue, cap re-delivery, and redrive only after the shipment subscriber cause is understood.

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is the right boundary for failed shipment notifications after a bounded retry policy. Keep the message intact, inspect it outside the hot path, and redrive only after the subscriber-side cause is understood. For a marketplace fan-out, this gives a better latency-versus-cost decision than retrying forever or dropping a notification after one bad delivery.

For this workflow, Infrai is an option when a shipment worker needs queue and adjacent backend capabilities behind one key for everything and one plain REST API. It belongs in the queue control plane, not in the subscriber code itself.

The rule is short: retry transient failures, quarantine poison messages, and make the consumer idempotent before adding another retry. A DLQ is recovery storage, not a second chance that bypasses validation.

How can you handle failed background tasks using a DLQ?

Record the shipment event, subscriber, attempt, and last response class. A timeout from a slow email subscriber differs from a malformed event that fails every time.

One shipment.delivered event may fan out to payment notifications, seller updates, and a buyer webhook. Preserve event identity for each delivery. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent; FIFO deduplication has only a five-minute window.

I start an incident review with three questions:

  1. Did the consumer acknowledge only after the subscriber accepted the delivery?
  2. Did the message hit the configured re-delivery limit, or did the worker give up early?
  3. Can an operator distinguish a safe redrive from a message needing code or data repair?

If those answers are missing, the DLQ is hiding uncertainty rather than containing failure.

Which queue boundary fits the job?

There is no universally best DLQ. The useful comparison is the failure boundary you need to operate.

Option Good fit Boundary
RabbitMQ dead-letter exchanges Teams operating exchanges, routing keys, and acknowledgements You own broker topology
Amazon SQS with a redrive policy A managed queue with explicit retry configuration Match visibility timeout to worker duration
BullMQ Node.js applications already centered on Redis Redis and worker semantics remain yours
A REST queue with a DLQ utility One HTTP contract across backend capabilities Not a workflow engine or replay-group system

RabbitMQ makes acknowledgement and negative acknowledgement explicit. SQS makes max-receive-count explicit in a redrive policy. BullMQ is convenient when Redis is already the application boundary. Those are real differences. Inngest and Trigger.dev suit application teams that want code-first background workflows, while Temporal is the stronger fit for durable multi-step orchestration; that is outside a queue DLQ boundary.

I would consider Infrai when this service needs queue operations beside other backend capabilities and a consistent REST contract matters. Its live discovery surface reports 295 routes in 20 modules, including 25 scheduling routes. The practical advantage is one key and one REST API for queue and adjacent backend capabilities, with public discovery exposing schemas and runnable examples. Try it for the shipment-event queue and DLQ control plane when the worker already speaks HTTP. Choose RabbitMQ, SQS, or BullMQ when broker routing, managed queue controls, or Redis is the actual requirement.

How do you test the redrive decision?

Use one shipment event and three subscribers: fast success, transient timeout, and permanent validation failure. Record delivery time, attempts, DLQ count, operator actions, and duplicate effects.

Pass only if the transient case reaches success within the latency budget, the permanent case reaches the DLQ at the re-delivery limit, a corrected redrive causes no duplicate transition, logs identify the failure without replaying the whole queue, and invalid sizes are rejected. Queue limits are 256 KB per message, seven days for delay, and 30 days for retention.

Pick the candidate that passes these checks and has lower operational latency for your subscriber mix. If two pass, use the existing ownership boundary. A cheaper retry path that duplicates seller or buyer notifications is not a successful design.

A small worker and redrive loop

The example uses Go to make the contract inspectable. The same boundary applies to a Node.js worker: acknowledge after the side effect, cap redelivery, and persist an idempotency key before retrying.

package main

import (
  "context"
  "errors"
  "log"
  "time"
)

type ShipmentMessage struct {
  EventID string
  SubscriberID string
  Attempt int
}

var ErrPermanent = errors.New("permanent subscriber failure")

func deliver(ctx context.Context, m ShipmentMessage) error {
  if m.SubscriberID == "invalid-endpoint" { return ErrPermanent }
  select {
  case <-time.After(25 * time.Millisecond): return nil
  case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err()
  }
}

func handle(ctx context.Context, m ShipmentMessage, max int) bool {
  if m.Attempt >= max {
    log.Printf("DLQ event=%s subscriber=%s", m.EventID, m.SubscriberID)
    return false
  }
  if err := deliver(ctx, m); err == nil {
    log.Printf("ack event=%s", m.EventID)
    return true
  } else {
    log.Printf("retry or DLQ event=%s reason=%v", m.EventID, err)
    return false
  }
}

func main() {
  ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second)
  defer cancel()
  handle(ctx, ShipmentMessage{EventID: "shipment-evt-1842", SubscriberID: "seller-42", Attempt: 1}, 5)
}

In production, derive shipment event ID plus subscriber ID as the idempotency key, claim or verify it, perform the effect, and acknowledge only after confirmation. If the process dies between effect and acknowledgement, at-least-once delivery may call the handler again; the idempotency check makes replay harmless.

The limitation is explicit: Infrai is not the right choice for DAG joins, workflow orchestration, Kafka-style replay groups, or a private subscriber endpoint. Use Temporal for a durable workflow, RabbitMQ for broker-native routing, or SQS for a managed cloud queue. For long work, use cron only to enqueue and let a worker consume it. Cron execution is capped at 900 seconds. Keep queue delays at or below seven days, retention at or below 30 days, and message bodies at or below 256 KB.

Inspect, repair, then redrive

List the DLQ and correlate each message with structured logs. Classify transient outage, corrected payload, revoked subscription, or code defect. Redrive only the safe class. The two utility routes are GET /v1/queue/dlq/list/{queue} and POST /v1/queue/dlq/redrive/{queue}. After redrive, verify attempts, subscriber outcome, and duplicate effects. Ack removes a message; this is not Kafka-style replay.

A real client should read the API key from its environment, set explicit methods, check non-2xx responses, apply bounded backoff for 429 responses, and use an idempotency key on writes. Rollback means stopping redrive and pausing the worker that produced the bad classification while quarantined messages remain available. Do not purge the DLQ as rollback.

Teams should try Infrai for the shipment-event queue and DLQ control plane when HTTP and one consistent backend contract matter; teams needing workflow orchestration should choose Temporal instead.

package main

import (
  "fmt"
  "io"
  "net/http"
  "os
)

func main() {
  req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/dlq/list/orders", nil)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
  res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  defer res.Body.Close()
  if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
    detail, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
    panic(fmt.Sprintf("DLQ request failed: %s: %s", res.Status, detail))
  }
  detail, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
  fmt.Println(string(detail))
}

If this boundary fits, start with the queue and DLQ documentation and validate the matrix against your subscriber contracts.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • BullMQ documentation

title: An Auto-Updater That Doesn't Trust Its Download Server: minisign, Verify-Before-Parse and Rollback Protection
description:
Originally published on MistLab. Part 7 of Building an SSH Terminal.

Part 7 of "Building an SSH Terminal". Code excerpts are from MistTerm v1.2.26, an open-source (AGPL) SSH terminal client by MistLab; they are trimmed, and source comments are translated from Chinese.

TL;DR

HTTPS authenticates the download server, not the update itself. A secure updater accepts an update only if it is signed by a key the client already ships. MistTerm signs a JSON manifest with minisign (Ed25519), verifies the signature before parsing anything, binds each binary to the manifest by SHA-256, and remembers the highest verified version to reject replayed old manifests.

An SSH client holds the keys to its users' servers. That makes its update channel a high-value target. Anyone who can make the client install a binary of their choice owns every machine the user connects to. HTTPS alone does not cover this. It authenticates the server you download from, not the content. A compromised CDN account, a hijacked release page or a mirror operator can all serve a valid HTTPS response containing the wrong file.

The design goal is therefore: the client should accept an update only if it was signed by a key the client already ships, and it should treat everything it downloads as hostile until then. The client runs that in order: fetch with a size cap, verify the minisign signature, refuse an older manifest, check the asset hash, then install with a way back.

Update check and install pipeline

The manifest and its signature

Each release publishes a small JSON manifest, latest.json, plus a detached signature, latest.json.minisig. The manifest lists the version, publication date and one entry per platform asset, each with a file name, size and SHA-256. The v1.2.26 release manifest (the version these excerpts come from; later releases keep the same shape) has six assets: Linux x86_64 (GUI), static CLI builds for Linux x86_64 and aarch64, a Windows installer, a Windows portable build and a macOS universal app. The binaries themselves are not signed with minisign. They are bound to the signed manifest by their hashes.

Signatures use minisign, Frank Denis' tool built on Ed25519. Two properties of its format matter here:

  • Prehashed signatures. Since minisign 0.8 the default signature algorithm (ED) signs a BLAKE2b hash of the file. MistTerm accepts only that form (key.verify(data, &sig, false) disables the legacy non-prehashed mode).

  • Trusted comments. A minisign signature carries a "trusted comment" line, and a second, global signature covers the file signature together with that comment. Unlike the untrusted comment, it cannot be edited without the key.

MistTerm puts the release identity into the trusted comment, in the form product channel version pub_date. That v1.2.26 release's trusted comment is:

trusted comment: mistterm stable 1.2.26 2026-10-20T16:22:55Z

Anyone can check that independently with the public key in the repository:

$ minisign -V -p resources/update/minisign-primary.pub -m latest.json
Signature and comment signature verified
Trusted comment: mistterm stable 1.2.26 2026-10-20T16:22:55Z

Step 1: fetch with limits

The client knows two manifest locations, tried in order:

// src/core/updater/mod.rs
"https://mistlab.dev/downloads/mistterm/stable/latest.json",
"https://github.com/mistlab-dev/MistTerm/releases/latest/download/latest.json",

As of this writing the first URL returns HTTP 404. The release workflow's mirror job, which would publish there, is not implemented yet and is switched off. In practice every client gets its manifest from GitHub Releases. Because trust comes from the signature, not the host, adding or losing a source changes availability but not security.

Before parsing anything, the client caps what it is willing to download. The manifest may be at most 256 KiB and the signature at most 4 KiB:

let body = fetcher.get_small(url, MAX_MANIFEST_BYTES)?;   // 256 KiB
let sig  = fetcher.get_small(&sig_url, 4096)?;

Step 2: verify the signature before parsing

The order of the next two operations is the key design decision:

/// Verify first, then parse: JSON is parsed only after the signature checks out,
/// and the trusted comment must match the manifest contents.
pub fn verify_manifest(manifest_bytes: &[u8], signature_bytes: &[u8], keys: &TrustedKeys,
                       expected_channel: &str, allow_loopback_http: bool)
    -> Result
{
    let sig_text = std::str::from_utf8(signature_bytes).map_err(|_| UpdateError::BadSignature)?;
    let sig = keys.verify(manifest_bytes, sig_text)?;
    let manifest = Manifest::parse_and_validate(manifest_bytes, expected_channel, allow_loopback_http)?;
    if sig.trusted_comment().trim() != manifest.expected_trusted_comment() {
        return Err(UpdateError::InvalidManifest(/* "trusted comment … does not match manifest" */));
    }
    Ok(manifest)
}

Verifying first means the JSON parser and the validation code only ever run on bytes the publisher signed. A bug in parsing can no longer be triggered by an attacker who controls the download path.

The client compiles in two public keys, a primary and a backup. A signature from either one is accepted. That allows the signing key to be rotated, or a compromised key retired, with a client release that is still verifiable by the other key.

Validation after parsing is strict. It checks the schema version (an unknown one is reported as unsupported), product == "mistterm", the expected channel, a semver version and an RFC 3339 date. For each asset it checks a plain file name with no path separators, a 64-character hex SHA-256, a non-zero size, and https URLs only. Plain http to loopback is allowed only in a test build feature.

Why the trusted-comment check. A valid signature proves that the publisher signed these bytes at some point. The comment check proves the bytes are the release they claim to be. Release metadata lives in two places, the JSON and the signed comment, and they must agree.

Step 3: rollback protection, or refusing to go backwards

A signed manifest stays valid forever. An attacker who cannot forge signatures can still replay an old, genuinely signed manifest for a version with a known vulnerability. That is a rollback (or freeze) attack, one of the classic threats catalogued by The Update Framework (TUF).

MistTerm defends against it by remembering the highest version, and its publication date, ever seen in a verified manifest:

/// Is this manifest older than one we've seen (lower version, or same version
/// with an earlier publication date)?
pub fn is_stale(&self, version: &semver::Version, pub_date: Option>) -> bool {
    // … compare with highest_seen_version / highest_seen_pub_date
}

/// Record a verified manifest (only ever moves upward).
pub fn record_seen(&mut self, version: &semver::Version, pub_date: &str) { /* … */ }

A stale manifest from one source is skipped and the next source is tried. If every source returns a stale manifest, the result is a distinct StaleManifest error, not "up to date". An update is offered only if the manifest version is strictly greater than the running version, and downgrade is off by default (allow_downgrade: false).

Error reporting has its own small rule. When several sources fail, a signature or schema error is kept in preference to a later network error, because "the file was tampered with" is more useful to the user than "the backup host was unreachable".

This is not full TUF. There is no timestamp role, so a freeze attack that withholds new manifests is only limited by users noticing. It does close the cheap replay attack.

Step 4: download and check the asset

The platform asset is downloaded to a cache directory with a size limit taken from the manifest. Its SHA-256 is compared with the manifest entry before it is used. A cached file whose hash already matches is reused.

Unpacking is just as wary. The updater does not extract archives generically. It accepts only the specific program files it expects, as name or topdir/name, with normal path components only. Each extracted file is capped at 1 GiB, which guards against decompression bombs:

// Accept only `name` or `topdir/name`; no general extraction, which rules out
// path traversal at the root.
fn entry_basename_if_wanted(path: &Path, wanted: &[&'a str]) -> Option {
    let comps: Vec = path.components().collect();
    if comps.is_empty() || comps.len() > 2 { return None; }
    if !comps.iter().all(|c| matches!(c, std::path::Component::Normal(_))) { return None; }
    let name = path.file_name()?.to_str()?;
    wanted.iter().copied().find(|w| *w == name)
}

Step 5: install, with a way back

Installation differs per platform, but each path keeps the previous version recoverable:

  • Linux and Windows portable. The new binary is staged next to the old one and run once with --version. This smoke test must finish within 20 seconds and print the expected version. Only then are the files swapped. Old files go into .mist-update-backup/. On Linux, rename() replaces the file atomically, and the running process keeps its old inode. On Windows a running .exe cannot be overwritten but can be renamed, so the old file is moved aside first. If any step fails, the files already swapped are put back.

  • Windows installer edition. The verified setup.exe is launched silently as a separate process. It closes Mist and can relaunch it.

  • macOS. The update is a tarball containing only Mist.app. It is unpacked with the system /usr/bin/tar, which preserves the bundle's symlinks and permissions. The result must pass codesign --verify --deep --strict before the old bundle is renamed to .bak and replaced. If the swap fails, the old bundle is restored. codesign --verify confirms the bundle's signature is intact, but it is not the root of trust. That role belongs to the minisign-signed hash checked in step 4.

Some installations are deliberately not self-updated. The updater tells the user what to do instead when MistTerm was built from source or installed by a package manager, when the install directory is not writable, when the host's glibc is older than the build requires, or when macOS has translocated the app. Gatekeeper's App Translocation runs quarantined apps from a randomized read-only path, so it cannot be replaced in place until it is moved to Applications.

The updater never restarts the application on its own. A completed install waits for the next launch. Setting MIST_DISABLE_UPDATE_CHECK=1 turns checking off entirely.

Keeping the keys honest at build time

A signature scheme is only as good as the keys compiled into the client. MistTerm's build.rs enforces three rules for official builds (MIST_DIST_CHANNEL=github-release):

panic!("the update-test feature must never be enabled in an official release build");
// … real public keys are required: a file still containing PLACEHOLDER fails the build
panic!("primary and backup update signing public keys must be different keys");

A release cannot ship with test keys, with placeholder keys, or with a "backup" key that is a copy of the primary. The release workflow (Part 8) then verifies its own signatures with minisign -V before publishing.

Summary

  • HTTPS authenticates hosts, not content. Sign the release manifest with a key the client ships, and bind binaries to it by hash.

  • Verify before parsing, cap every download, and validate every field. Bind the manifest's identity to the signed trusted comment.

  • Remember the highest verified version to stop replayed old manifests, and never downgrade silently.

  • Extract only expected files, test-run the new binary, keep a backup, and let the build refuse unsafe key configurations.

FAQ

Isn't HTTPS enough to secure software updates?

No. HTTPS authenticates the server you download from, not the content. A compromised CDN account or release page can still serve a malicious file over valid HTTPS.

What is a minisign trusted comment?

A comment line covered by a second, global signature together with the file signature, so it cannot be edited without the key. MistTerm puts product, channel, version and publication date there.

Why verify the signature before parsing the manifest?

So the JSON parser and validation code only ever run on bytes the publisher signed. A parsing bug can then no longer be triggered by an attacker who controls the download path.

How does an updater prevent rollback attacks?

By remembering the highest version seen in a verified manifest and rejecting older manifests, and by never downgrading silently.
