title: Why Apache returned 502 for our Go uploads
description:
An oversized upload should give someone a useful rejection. In our case, the browser received "Upload failed: 502" even though the Go handler had a file-too-large response. The affected site was RadarMakers, a free launch platform for indie makers, with Apache forwarding uploads to Go.

The interesting part was the difference between the application response and the response that reached the browser. The workaround checks the declared request length before parsing multipart data, attempts a bounded discard of an oversized body, then writes the rejection.

This account comes from the current handler and its Git history. The earlier failure is documented there; I have not reproduced it for this article. The code explains a specific workaround, with limits that matter as much as the happy path.

What the proxy changed

The failure was not simply that the application rejected a large file. The browser saw a 502 from Apache when the Go server reset the connection while the proxy was still forwarding the body. A direct request to the API had produced the handler response instead. That distinction is why the investigation followed the request across both hops.

Start a similar incident by capturing the browser response, the proxy error log, and the application log for the same request window. Compare a request sent through the public route with one sent directly to the service in a controlled environment. Keep the same method, headers, body, and authentication state. If the two paths differ, inspect how the proxy handles upstream resets and unread request bytes before changing the application status code.

This case record does not claim that every 502 during an upload has this cause. A proxy can return a gateway error for many upstream failures. Here the repository comment identifies the reset during body forwarding, and the recorded comparison showed a different response on the direct path. Those are the facts behind this particular workaround.

Why an early length check helped

The handler checks the declared Content-Length before wrapping the body or calling the multipart parser. When that value exceeds the request threshold, it takes a rejection path without parsing the form. This avoids spending image parsing work on a request that the server already intends to reject.

The header is only an early signal. A client can omit the length or send a value that does not describe the bytes that arrive. The source therefore keeps a second guard with http.MaxBytesReader before ParseMultipartForm. The Go documentation describes that reader as a request body limit that returns a MaxBytesError after a read crosses the configured size, and says it may tell the response writer to close the connection if possible.

The two checks answer different questions. The first decides whether the declared size already exceeds the limit and can be rejected before parsing. The reader limit protects the path where the header cannot make that decision. Neither check proves that the image is safe to decode. Content length limits transport size; image validation has separate responsibilities.

The drain is bounded for a reason

On the declared oversized path, the handler attempts to discard up to five times the body limit. With the current constant, that is a maximum read attempt of 25 MiB. The io.CopyN call writes to io.Discard, so these bytes are consumed for connection handling and are not stored as an upload.

A bounded drain is a tradeoff, not a universal recipe. Reading a portion of a rejected body can give a proxy a chance to finish forwarding bytes already in flight, but an unbounded read would let an oversized client keep the handler occupied for an arbitrary amount of data. The cap makes the maximum discard request explicit. The code ignores the returned byte count and error, then writes the 400 response, so it does not claim that every oversized body was fully consumed.

The comparison is important when changing the constants. Raising the file limit also changes the allowed request size and may change the maximum drain if the multiplier stays fixed. Increasing only the drain cap changes how much rejected traffic the handler may read. These values should be reviewed separately and tested with the proxy configuration that actually fronts the service.

Request bodies without a trustworthy length

HTTP request bodies can arrive without a useful declared size. The handler still wraps the body with MaxBytesReader, so the multipart parse cannot consume an unbounded body through this path. The same fallback also matters if the declared value is smaller than the bytes actually read. The header check is therefore an optimization and early rejection, not the sole security boundary.

A test suite should cover both known and unknown lengths. For a declared body above the threshold, assert that the early branch returns the intended status and message without parsing a multipart field. For a body whose declared size does not cross the threshold but whose actual bytes exceed it, assert that the reader limit controls the result. If the request uses chunked transfer, exercise the actual server and proxy path because middleware and proxy buffering can affect which component sees the limit first.

Avoid writing a test that only calls the handler directly and then declaring the production 502 fixed. The original difference occurred across Apache and Go. A direct handler test can verify the application branch, but it cannot verify how a deployed proxy handles a reset. Keep those claims separate in test names and release notes.

A transport limit is not a memory limit

The configured limit is applied to the request body and multipart parsing. After the file is read, the handler also decodes and re-encodes the image. A compressed image can represent far more pixels than its byte size suggests. That is why the code checks the image header before decoding all pixels, and why the comment explains the risk of an extremely large image dimension.

The header buffer in the handler is 64 KiB. io.ReadFull attempts to fill that buffer, while treating EOF and unexpected EOF as conditions that can still leave a usable short header. The checkImage call receives only the bytes actually read. If the header cannot be parsed, the handler returns a client error before calling sanitizeImage.

A request size limit and a dimension check protect different resources. The first bounds incoming body bytes. The second rejects an image whose decoded dimensions would require unreasonable memory. Re-encoding then creates a cleaned output from pixels rather than copying the original file bytes. These operations should remain independently visible in code review because a change to one does not remove the need for the others.

Extension policy is part of the safety design

The current allowlist accepts PNG, JPG, JPEG, and GIF after lowercasing the filename extension. SVG is deliberately absent because it is an active document format when served from the same origin. WebP is also absent because this implementation uses the standard library image path and re-encodes supported pixels. The allowlist is not a statement that every file with an accepted suffix is valid; the image decoder and sanitizer still inspect its contents.

A filename suffix is user supplied. It should not be treated as proof of the media type. The handler reads a header, checks it against the expected extension, seeks back to the start, reads the file, and sanitizes the decoded content. If a new format is added, test mismatched suffixes, malformed headers, oversized dimensions, and the final saved output. Also confirm that the chosen decoder and encoder remove metadata that should not be retained.

What to observe in production

Instrument the rejection path without logging the file contents or sensitive request data. Useful fields include the route, the outcome category, whether the declared size crossed the threshold, and whether the request had a usable length. Avoid recording raw filenames if they may contain personal data. A counter by outcome can help detect a burst of rejected uploads, but it cannot show whether the proxy delivered the intended response. For that, compare proxy status and application status in a request trace with a safe correlation identifier.

Keep the logs explicit about boundaries. The application can record that it wrote a 400 response. The proxy log can record what it returned to the client. If those values differ, the path between the two is the subject of the next investigation. Do not collapse them into one field called upload status.

Review the implementation as a set of invariants

The existing order expresses a set of useful invariants. Authentication is checked before upload processing. Declared oversized bodies are rejected before multipart parsing. Other bodies are wrapped in a byte limit. The multipart form must contain the expected file field. The extension must be allowed. Image data is checked from its header before a full decode. The source bytes are re-read from the start for sanitization, then only the cleaned result is saved.

When refactoring, preserve the ordering or explain which property has changed. A helper that moves parsing above the length check may reintroduce the expensive path. A helper that copies original bytes to disk may preserve metadata or unsafe content. A broader format list may bypass the established sanitizer. Write a test for each boundary that matters rather than asserting only that a valid PNG succeeds.

The documented workaround is deliberately narrow. It changes the oversized declared-length path so the handler can attempt a capped drain before writing its intended response. It does not claim to solve every proxy timeout, every malformed multipart form, or every malicious image. That narrow description is more useful to the next person debugging a similar symptom than a general promise that uploads are now safe.

Two charts from the implementation record

The threshold chart shows the exact request limit and drain ceiling read from internal/handler/upload.go. The format chart counts the extensions in the source allowlist: four accepted suffixes and two explicitly absent formats discussed in the code comments. These are implementation facts, not measurements of traffic or an estimate of risk. The diagrams already in the asset folder remain useful for request flow and the branch order; the charts add the actual values that a reader may want to compare with a proposed code change.

Before changing either number, rerun the relevant tests and inspect the deployment proxy limits, upload timeout, and body buffering configuration. This repository record documents the Go handler and its comments. It does not establish the settings of every reverse proxy or the behavior of every client.

Checklist for investigating a proxy upload error

  • [ ] Compare the public route and direct service response with the same request.
  • [ ] Correlate proxy and application logs for one request.
  • [ ] Check whether the content length is present and whether it matches the bytes sent.
  • [ ] Test the early rejection and the reader limit as separate paths.
  • [ ] Keep the rejected body drain capped and explain the cap.
  • [ ] Verify body size and decoded image dimensions independently.
  • [ ] Confirm the file header and extension agree before sanitizing.
  • [ ] Save only the re-encoded output when that is the security policy.
  • [ ] Test through the deployed proxy before claiming the client response is fixed.
  • [ ] Record which observations are from source, tests, or production logs.

The same upload had different outcomes

Commit 33cb05b, dated August 26, 2026, records an oversized upload returning 502 through Apache and 400 when sent directly to the API. That comparison is the historical observation. It places the discrepancy between the direct API response and the response delivered through the proxy.

The handler comments describe the mechanism: the body limit was crossed while Apache was still forwarding the upload, the Go connection reset, and Apache answered the browser with a bare 502. The intended rejection lost its useful explanation along the way.

That is the documented behavior of this deployment. It should not be read as a universal rule that every call to MaxBytesReader immediately resets a connection. The Go documentation for MaxBytesReader describes a reader that errors when reads exceed the limit and, where possible, tells the response writer to close the connection afterward.

The distinction matters when investigating a similar symptom. A browser's status describes what arrived at the browser. Reading the handler's error branch alone does not establish that its response survived the proxy path.

The limit applies to the request body

The size constant remains small and explicit. Excerpt from internal/handler/upload.go:

    const maxFileSize = 5 << 20 // 5MB

The expression is 5 MiB. The comment and user-facing message say MB, but the binary count is what the code enforces. More precisely, this is a request body limit. A multipart upload includes framing and fields as well as the file, so it is not an exact allowance of 5 MiB for image bytes alone.

The handler first checks authentication and returns 401 if claims are absent. The length decision discussed here happens after that check. It is not a description of how an anonymous request is processed.

Choosing this body threshold is an application design decision. The source supplies the value; it does not establish that this is the right threshold for every upload service.

Reject by declared length before parsing

The added branch sits before the reader wrapper and multipart parser. Excerpt from internal/handler/upload.go:

    if r.ContentLength > maxFileSize {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, r.Body, 5*maxFileSize)
        writeJSON(w, http.StatusBadRequest, map[string]string{"message": "file too large (max 5MB)"})
        return
    }

The decision uses the declared length before reading body bytes. Once that length exceeds the threshold, the handler already knows which response it intends to send. It does not parse the multipart form or inspect the image on this branch.

It still reads from the body before responding. Those bytes go to io.Discard; they are not accepted as an upload. The purpose, stated in the comments, is to let the 400 travel back through Apache while accommodating data the client has already sent.

The selected status is 400, with the existing file-too-large message. That is the application's response choice. The patch changes how the handler reaches that response rather than increasing the accepted upload size.

The drain has its own ceiling

Multiplying the body threshold by five gives a discard cap of 25 MiB. That value is a separate design decision: the comments explicitly reject unbounded draining as a way for a client to make the server keep reading indefinitely.

The operation attempts to copy up to that amount from the body. The Go documentation for CopyN says it copies the requested count or stops on an error, returning the copied count and an error. This handler ignores both return values and proceeds to write 400.

For bodies whose actual size matches their declared size, a body over 5 MiB and no larger than 25 MiB fits within the drain budget. An earlier read error can still prevent a complete drain. A body larger than 25 MiB can leave bytes unread after the cap is reached.

Those consequences follow from the code. They do not establish that every oversized upload now avoids 502. The handler attempts a bounded accommodation of the proxy path; it does not verify that all bytes were consumed or guarantee delivery of its response.

A byte cap also should not be described as a time limit. This branch specifies an amount to discard, not a duration. Any claim about complete timeout protection would need evidence beyond these lines.

Unknown lengths keep the reader guard

The declared length check is not the only protection. Requests that bypass it still encounter the original wrapper and parser. Excerpt from internal/handler/upload.go:

    r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxFileSize)

    if err := r.ParseMultipartForm(maxFileSize); err != nil {
        writeJSON(w, http.StatusBadRequest, map[string]string{"message": "file too large (max 5MB)"})
        return
    }

This includes requests without a declared length and those declaring a length at or below the threshold. The nearby comment also identifies an inaccurate declaration as a reason to retain the reader guard.

The branches therefore serve different purposes. Declared oversize selects the capped drain and rejection. Otherwise, actual reading remains bounded by MaxBytesReader before multipart parsing. Removing that wrapper would discard the protection for requests the length check cannot reject in advance.

There is another detail in the error handling: every error returned by this multipart parsing call maps to the same file-too-large message. Seeing that message is not, by itself, proof that the reader limit caused the parse error.

What is verified and what remains open

The history documents the earlier proxy failure. The current source contains the declared-length branch, the 25 MiB discard cap, and the retained 5 MiB reader limit. These are inspectable implementation facts.

The graphics README reports no regression test for the declared-length drain or Apache workaround in this checkout. Nearby image tests cover other concerns. They do not demonstrate that this response reaches a browser through Apache, and no such regression coverage is claimed here.

For a similar investigation, compare direct and proxied responses, then inspect what happens to unread request data when the handler rejects it. Keep the acceptance threshold, drain budget, and unknown-length behavior explicit. This patch makes those choices visible, while leaving a clear boundary around what its code and historical observation can support.

Sources

  • Go net/http documentation for MaxBytesReader:
  • Go io documentation for CopyN:
  • RadarMakers source: internal/handler/upload.go and the recorded change 33cb05b dated August 26, 2026.

title: Transactional outbox and inbox for Spring Boot: which library to choose in 2026
description:
Author: Miguel Carvalho

Contents

  1. How we compared
  2. What a transactional outbox is and how the six libraries differ
  3. Spring Boot and Java support
  4. Outbox for Kafka and RabbitMQ: brokers and databases
  5. Retries, backoff and DLQ
  6. Polling and per-event-type tuning
  7. Inbox pattern: consumer-side message deduplication
  8. Observability and operations
  9. Maturity and maintenance
  10. Example: outbox in Spring Boot with Kafka
  11. Pros and cons
  12. Final scores
  13. Who should choose what

In short

These six projects are not interchangeable. Tandem and oncebox provide ready-made delivery from Spring Boot to a broker, while spring-boot-outbox-starter leaves delivery to you. ekbatan works as an outbox only if you rewrite your entire data access layer from Spring Data and JPA to its own, so it is practically unsuitable for existing Spring projects; transactional-event targets Jakarta EE and Quarkus, and boxy is still an experiment with no releases. For Kafka on PostgreSQL with multiple instances and an Admin API, Tandem is the better fit; for Kafka or RabbitMQ on PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle with a DLQ and an inbox, oncebox.

  • Tandem for Kafka and PostgreSQL, multiple instances, Admin API
  • oncebox for Kafka or RabbitMQ, PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle, separate polling, retry and backoff settings per event type, a DLQ and consumer-side deduplication in a single starter (i think this is the most versatile and rich starter)
  • spring-boot-outbox-starter for PostgreSQL and delivery beyond brokers (REST, webhooks), several isolated channels
  • ekbatan for a new project on Java 25, and only if you are willing to drop Spring Data in favour of JOOQ and take on heavy infrastructure with Debezium
  • transactional-event for Jakarta EE (WildFly, Liberty) or Quarkus rather than Spring
  • boxy for exploring the idea of "outbox as an event stream"; not production-ready yet

Libraries compared

Library Artifact Version License Links
Tandem com.codingful:tandem-spring-relay 1.0.0-rc.3 Apache-2.0 site · repo
spring-boot-outbox-starter com.kholodilin:spring-boot-outbox-starter 0.2.3 Apache-2.0 site · repo
oncebox io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-starter 2.0.0 Apache-2.0 site · repo
ekbatan io.github.ekbatan-io:ekbatan-spring-boot-starter 1.1.3 Apache-2.0 site · repo
transactional-event io.github.jonasrutishauser:transactional-event-core 3.4.2 LGPL-3.0 site · repo
boxy mvsm:boxy-core (not published) 1.0-SNAPSHOT Apache-2.0 site · repo

Criteria

  • What it is. These six projects mean different things by "outbox": a starter that delivers to a broker, a persistence layer, event handlers, or an event stream inside the database. That determines what you will have to write yourself.
  • Platform and Java. The library has to fit your stack without switching frameworks or upgrading the JDK just for its sake.
  • Where it delivers. A library is useless if it cannot deliver to where your services publish.
  • Databases. The outbox table lives in the same database as your business data, so the DBMS is already chosen for you, and the library has to support it.
  • Failures and DLQ. A broker or consumer can be unavailable for hours, and what matters is what happens to an event once retries are exhausted.
  • Polling and fine-tuning. Events within one service are not equal: a payment must go out in a fraction of a second, while an analytics event can wait a minute, and identical settings for all of them either load the database or delay what matters.
  • Consumer-side deduplication. An outbox gives at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are unavoidable, and something has to filter them out.
  • Observability and operations. You need to notice a growing outbox table before your users do, and be able to deal with stuck events without SQL.
  • Maturity and maintenance. All six projects are young or niche, so API stability, releases on Maven Central and the number of maintainers matter more than stars.

Outbox libraries compared by criteria

Criterion Tandem spring-boot-outbox-starter oncebox ekbatan transactional-event boxy
What it is Outbox library: table write + relay to a broker; Spring starters for both parts Spring Boot starter: outbox table + workers; you write delivery yourself (OutboxSink) Spring Boot starter: outbox with broker delivery + consumer-side inbox Replaces Spring Data and JPA with its own JOOQ-based layer; the outbox only covers changes made through that layer, delivery to a broker via Debezium Transactional events for Jakarta EE: table write + asynchronous handlers Event stream on top of an outbox table: partitions, subscriptions and cursors in the database, no broker
Platform and Java Java 17+; Spring Boot, also works without Spring Java 21; Spring Boot Java 17+; Spring Boot Java 25; Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut or no DI; GraalVM native Java 11; Jakarta EE 9+ (CDI, JTA) and Quarkus; Spring not supported Java 17; no framework integration
Where it delivers Kafka; RabbitMQ (tandem-rabbitmq 0.2.0); CloudEvents format Any target via your own OutboxSink (Kafka and REST in the demos) Kafka 3.7+, RabbitMQ 3.12+ (Kafka and Rabbit in the demos) Kafka via Debezium + Kafka Connect; in-process handlers Your own code in the handler (no built-in broker) No broker: consumers read events from the database
Databases PostgreSQL 14+ (MySQL designed but not implemented) PostgreSQL 13+ PostgreSQL 16+, MySQL 8.0.13+, Oracle 23+ PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB Any JDBC database via DataSource (DDL in README) MySQL 8 (schema and stored procedures); PostgreSQL planned
Failures and DLQ Retries with backoff; after 10 attempts the event is blocked; replay/discard via Admin API max-retries, then DEAD status; RecoveryWorker for stuck records Per-event-type retries and backoff, recovery of stuck events, DLQ with REST API For handlers: exponential backoff, EXPIRED status after 7 days Retries, then blocked; unblocked metric The cursor does not advance until the partition is processed
Polling and fine-tuning Adaptive polling interval (10-100 ms by default), optional pg-notify on PostgreSQL; settings shared across the relay Wake-up queue in memory or Redis; batch, retries and lease set per channel (table) Fixed or adaptive polling; batch size, polling, retry count and backoff set separately per event type Debezium reads the table from the database log; background jobs for in-process handlers Polling interval between initial and maximum; shared settings Adaptive consumer heartbeats and lease acquisition
Consumer-side deduplication No; the consumer deduplicates by event id No Yes: effectively-once and at-most-once consumers, Redis cache For in-process handlers: one row per event × handler pair No Subscription cursors in the database
Observability and operations Micrometer, OpenTelemetry, Admin REST API, CLI, Grafana demo Micrometer, health indicator Micrometer, Grafana dashboards, REST API for the DLQ OpenTelemetry tracing MicroProfile Metrics Subscription statistics in tables
Maturity and maintenance 1.0.0-rc.3 from 2026-11-05, API frozen; one main author 0.2.3 from 2026-10-28; one author 2.0.0 from 2026-10-15; one author 1.1.3 from 2026-11-01; one main author 3.4.2 from 2026-10-12; developed since 2021, one author No releases, not published on Maven Central; last commit 2025-08-15

You don't have to write a transactional outbox and inbox in Spring Boot yourself: Java has ready-made libraries. This article compares six young projects that rarely show up in reviews: Tandem, oncebox, spring-boot-outbox-starter, ekbatan, transactional-event and boxy. In short: Tandem and oncebox provide ready-made event delivery from Spring Boot to Kafka; only oncebox covers RabbitMQ and an inbox for consumer-side message deduplication. Below, the libraries are compared against the same criteria. All versions and facts were checked on 7 November 2026.

How we compared

Each library was assessed against the nine criteria in the table below, the same for all of them. Facts come from READMEs, documentation, pom.xml / build.gradle.kts, Git tags and Maven Central, and each one has a source listed at the end of the article. Where the documentation is silent, we say so. More on the approach on the Methodology page.

What a transactional outbox is and how the six libraries differ

The main difference between these libraries is not just their feature set, but what each of them calls an outbox. Before comparing details, it is worth understanding which type each one belongs to.

  • Tandem and oncebox are full outbox libraries (out-of-the-box solutions): you write an event to a table within your transaction, and the library delivers it to Kafka or RabbitMQ.
  • spring-boot-outbox-starter handles the table, queue, workers, retries and recovery. In exchange, the target can be anything: Kafka, REST, a webhook.
  • ekbatan is a JOOQ-based persistence framework: it does not complement but replaces Spring Data and Hibernate, and writes events to the eventlog.events table on every model change. Debezium sends them to Kafka.
  • transactional-event provides transactional events for Jakarta EE: the event is stored in a table together with the transaction and later processed asynchronously by your Handler.
  • boxy is an attempt to turn the outbox table into an event stream with partitions, subscriptions and cursors right in the database, so that a monolith needs no broker at all.

For a typical Spring Boot microservice that has to send events to a broker, only the first three are truly comparable. The other three are worth considering only if their model suits you.

Why ekbatan doesn't fit an existing Spring Data project

ekbatan's limitation matters more than all its other characteristics. According to its documentation, Spring Data JPA can run in the same application, but ekbatan does not integrate with JpaRepository and does not support Spring @Transactional or PlatformTransactionManager: it has its own TransactionManager, and its Action serves as the transaction boundary. An event is written atomically only together with changes made through ActionExecutor. If an order is saved via JPA and the event via ekbatan, these are two separate transactions — exactly the dual-write problem the outbox is supposed to protect against.

So to get an outbox, you have to move your entire data access layer to ekbatan: repositories in JOOQ, models as immutable ekbatan classes, business operations as Actions. In my view, rewriting a layer as fundamental and battle-tested as Spring Data and JPA just for an outbox is an unjustified risk for most projects. The other libraries in this comparison plug into the existing Spring transaction and store the event right next to your usual repository.save(...).

Spring Boot and Java support

In Tandem, Spring is a compileOnly dependency, so the Spring version is determined by your application's BOM.

Library Spring Boot Java Without Spring
Tandem yes 17+ yes, dependency-free core
oncebox yes 17+ no
spring-boot-outbox-starter yes 21 Spring-free core
ekbatan yes 25 Quarkus, Micronaut, plain Java
transactional-event no 11 Jakarta EE 9+, Quarkus
boxy no 17 plain Java only

If your project runs on Spring Boot and Java 21, oncebox, Tandem and spring-boot-outbox-starter all fit.

Outbox for Kafka and RabbitMQ: brokers and databases

Tandem and oncebox support Kafka out of the box. oncebox also supports RabbitMQ 3.12+ with the same starter, API and settings: the broker is selected by the oncebox-kafka or oncebox-rabbit module and the oncebox.outbox.sender.type property. Tandem's RabbitMQ adapter (tandem-rabbitmq) is recent and versioned separately from the library (0.2.0 versus 1.0.0-rc.3). By default Tandem wraps events in a CloudEvents envelope; a custom format is plugged in by implementing a single interface.

spring-boot-outbox-starter has no built-in transport: the demo projects include sinks for Kafka and REST, but in production you write your own. That is a drawback for the typical "send to Kafka" case, but an advantage if you need an outbox for webhooks or external API calls. Channels are isolated from each other: each has its own table, queue and retry settings.

oncebox has the widest database support: PostgreSQL 16+, MySQL 8.0.13+ and Oracle 23+, each as a separate dialect module. On MySQL, the outbox data source must be switched to the READ COMMITTED isolation level: under InnoDB's default REPEATABLE READ, a SKIP LOCKED query takes gap locks, and multiple instances block each other instead of picking up different batches. PostgreSQL and Oracle don't have this problem. ekbatan supports PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. Tandem and spring-boot-outbox-starter work only with PostgreSQL; MySQL support in Tandem is designed but, according to the author, not implemented. boxy currently contains a schema and stored procedures for MySQL only. transactional-event needs just one table from the database, with the DDL given in the README.

Retries, backoff and DLQ

Each library decides differently what to do with an event that cannot be delivered.

oncebox offers the full set: retries and backoff are configured per event type, events "stuck" in IN_PROCESS after an instance crash are returned to the queue without counting the failed attempt, and once attempts are exhausted the event is atomically moved to the DLQ. The oncebox-dlq-api module adds a REST API for the DLQ: view, requeue or delete. The DLQ is disabled by default.

Tandem retries sending with exponential backoff, and after maxAttempts (10 by default) the event is blocked. The blocked.count metric shows the scale of the problem, and the Admin API (tandem-admin, disabled by default) lets you resend or discard the event. It also lets you pause and resume the relay.

spring-boot-outbox-starter moves an event to DEAD status after max-retries attempts, and RecoveryWorker picks up records with an expired lease. There is no API for working with DEAD records, only SQL.

ekbatan, for in-process handlers, retries the call with bounded exponential backoff and moves the notification to EXPIRED if the event is older than the retention window (7 days by default). transactional-event marks an event as blocked once retries are exhausted; metrics count both blocked and unblocked events.

Polling and per-event-type tuning

oncebox is the only one of the six where outbox behaviour is configured separately for each event type. For order-created and analytics-tracked you can set a different batch size, polling strategy, retry count and backoff, and anything not overridden is inherited from the shared defaults block.

This solves a practical problem: events within one service are not equal. A payment or an order status change must go out in a fraction of a second and be retried quickly, while analytics or search events can be sent in large batches once a minute and retried less often. With shared settings you have to choose: either poll the database often for all types at once, or delay important events along with unimportant ones.

oncebox:
  outbox:
    defaults:
      batch-size: 200
      polling:
        type: adaptive
        min-fixed-delay: 250ms
        max-fixed-delay: 1m
        multiplier: 1.5
      max-retries: 3
      backoff:
        delay: 10s
        multiplier: 3.0
    events:
      payment-completed:
        topic: payments
        polling:
          min-fixed-delay: 100ms   # poll more often, the rest comes from defaults
        max-retries: 10
        backoff:
          delay: 1s
          multiplier: 2.0
      analytics-tracked:
        topic: analytics
        batch-size: 1000
        polling:
          type: fixed
          fixed-delay: 1m          # once a minute in large batches
        backoff:
          enabled: false

Adaptive polling is enabled by default in oncebox: while there are no events, the pause between polls grows by the multiplier up to max-fixed-delay, and as soon as events appear it resets to min-fixed-delay. This way the service reacts quickly to an event stream and puts almost no load on the database when idle. According to the calculation in the oncebox walkthrough on DEV Community, that is about 70 polls per idle hour versus 14,400 with a fixed 250 ms pause; this is an estimate based on the scheduling rule, not a measurement. Retries use exponential backoff: with a 10 s delay and a multiplier of 3, retries happen after 10 s, 30 s, 90 s, 270 s.

Tandem also has adaptive polling: the interval stays at 10 ms while a bucket has events and grows to 100 ms when idle, and on PostgreSQL you can enable instant wake-up via pg-notify. But Tandem's settings are shared across the whole relay and change only on restart. spring-boot-outbox-starter configures batches, retries and leases per channel, that is, per separate table, not per event type within one table. transactional-event has shared polling settings for all events, and ekbatan delegates reading the table to Debezium.

Inbox pattern: consumer-side message deduplication

Inbox is the companion pattern to outbox on the consumer side: it stores the ids of already processed messages and prevents a business operation from running twice. It is needed because any outbox guarantees only at-least-once: if the application crashes after sending to the broker but before marking the record in the table, the event will be sent again. So the consumer has to be able to filter out duplicates.

Only oncebox has a ready-made inbox for a Kafka or RabbitMQ consumer. Since version 2.0.0 it has two idempotent consumers: a transactional one, where the receipt record and the business operation are committed together (effectively-once), and a non-transactional one, where the record is committed before the operation (at-most-once, for side effects such as emails that must not be repeated). The optional oncebox-inbox-cache module adds a Redis cache of records. Records are kept until cleanup (oncebox.inbox.clean-up.ttl, 24 hours by default), so a redelivery after that period is no longer recognised as a duplicate. In practice this leads to three rules: the inbox retention period must cover the longest redelivery window (for example, re-reading old Kafka offsets), the cache TTL must not exceed the inbox retention period, and the cache name must be unique per service, otherwise services sharing a Redis instance will treat each other's events as already processed. The consumer uses the same oncebox-starter, with no separate library.

Tandem does not provide an inbox: each event has a unique id, and the consumer writes deduplication by that id. ekbatan, for in-process handlers, creates one record per "event × handler" pair and ignores repeated inserts, but Kafka consumers downstream of Debezium deduplicate on their own. spring-boot-outbox-starter and transactional-event have no inbox. boxy stores subscription positions in the database and, according to its README, protects against duplicates when a lease is handed over between consumers.

Observability and operations

Tandem has the most operational tooling: Micrometer metrics (backlog age, errors, blocked events, worker health), tracing via Micrometer Tracing or OpenTelemetry, an Admin REST API with an OpenAPI contract, the tandem-cli console tool, and ready-made Grafana demos. The author also publishes benchmarks with raw data: a median latency of 13 ms from COMMIT to Kafka acknowledgement at 600 events/s on a 2 vCPU machine that the relay shares with PostgreSQL and Kafka.

oncebox provides Micrometer metrics for outbox and inbox (the oncebox-metrics module), Grafana dashboards in the repository and a REST API for the DLQ. spring-boot-outbox-starter publishes metrics per channel and event type (outbox_publish_total, outbox_queue_pressure) and a health indicator. ekbatan has OpenTelemetry tracing, transactional-event has MicroProfile metrics.

Maturity and maintenance

All six projects have a single main author, so it is worth looking at versions, release frequency and API stability.

  • oncebox 2.0.0 was released on 15 October 2026; it was preceded by 1.x releases. The project has been developed since October 2025.
  • Tandem is a release candidate: 1.0.0-rc.3 from 5 November 2026, with the API frozen until 1.0.0. The project started in July 2026 and had about 390 commits by November.
  • spring-boot-outbox-starter is at version 0.2.3 from 28 October 2026; the project started in August 2026. A 0.x version means the API may still change; 0.2.0 already included a breaking change to internal classes.
  • ekbatan 1.1.3 was released on 1 November 2026; the project has been developed since November 2025.
  • transactional-event is the oldest of the six: developed since 2021, version 3.4.2 from 12 October 2026. It is the only one here under LGPL-3.0; the rest are Apache-2.0.
  • boxy has no releases and is not published on Maven Central (version 1.0-SNAPSHOT); the last commit was on 15 August 2025. The README roadmap (versions planned for August and September 2025) has not been delivered.

Example: outbox in Spring Boot with Kafka

The task is the same for the three starters that send events from Spring Boot: within a transaction, save an order and write an OrderCreated event to the outbox. The examples are taken from the libraries' READMEs and shortened.

oncebox

Dependencies: io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-starter, oncebox-postgresql and oncebox-kafka version 2.0.0; @EnableOncebox on the main class.

oncebox:
  outbox:
    sender:
      type: kafka
    events:
      order-created:
        topic: "orders"

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private final OutboxPublisher outboxPublisher;

    @Transactional
    public Order create(Order order) {
        Order saved = repository.save(order);
        outboxPublisher.publish("order-created", saved);
        return saved;
    }
}

Instead of calling publish, you can put @OutboxPublish(eventType = "order-created") on the method: the return value then becomes the event.

Tandem

Dependencies: the com.codingful:tandem-bom:1.0.0-rc.3 BOM, tandem-spring-producer where events are written, tandem-spring-relay and tandem-kafka where the relay runs.

@Transactional
public Order create(Order order) {
    orderRepository.save(order);
    outboxRepository.insert(OutboxMessage.builder()
        .aggregateId(order.id())
        .aggregateType("Order")
        .type("com.acme.order.created")
        .payload(serialize(order))
        .contentType("application/json")
        .build());
    return order;
}

In Spring, instead of the low-level OutboxRepository, you can use TransactionalOutboxTemplate, the @TransactionalOutbox annotation, or Spring application events.

spring-boot-outbox-starter

Dependency: com.kholodilin:spring-boot-outbox-starter:0.2.3.

@Transactional
public void create(Order order) {
    orderRepository.save(order);
    outboxService
        .eventType("ORDER_CREATED")
        .aggregateId(String.valueOf(order.id()))
        .payload(order)
        .append();
}

@Component
class KafkaOrdersSink implements OutboxSink {
    @Override
    public OutboxPublishResult publish(List<OutboxRecord> batch) {
        // send the batch to Kafka with your own code
        return new OutboxPublishResult.AllSucceeded();
    }
}

Pros and cons

Tandem

  • Pros: instance coordination via leases, Admin API and CLI, detailed metrics and tracing, published benchmarks, the relay can run as a separate container.
  • Cons: still a release candidate; PostgreSQL only; RabbitMQ adapter at 0.x; no inbox; bucketCount cannot be changed after the first deployment.

oncebox

  • Pros: polling (fixed or adaptive), batch size, retries and backoff are configured separately per event type; adaptive polling by default; outbox and inbox in one starter; Kafka and RabbitMQ; PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle; DLQ with a REST API; minimal code — one call or an annotation.

spring-boot-outbox-starter

  • Pros: delivery anywhere via OutboxSink; isolated channels with their own tables and settings; a Redis queue to wake up workers across instances.
  • Cons: you write the broker transport yourself; PostgreSQL only; version 0.x; no API for DEAD events.

ekbatan

  • Pros: events are stored automatically together with the model change, no separate outbox call needed; Spring Boot, Quarkus and Micronaut; GraalVM native image; sharding; distributed jobs.
  • Cons: the main one — the outbox only works if you fully replace Spring Data and JPA with its own JOOQ-based layer; it does not integrate with JpaRepository or Spring @Transactional, so its outbox cannot be embedded in an existing project; requires Java 25; Kafka requires Debezium and Kafka Connect.

transactional-event

  • Pros: the longest history of the six; standard Jakarta EE APIs; a Quarkus extension; works with any JDBC database.
  • Cons: not for Spring; no built-in broker, you write sending in the handler; LGPL-3.0 license.

boxy

  • Pros: an interesting model — partitions, subscriptions and weighted balancing on top of the database, with no broker.
  • Cons: no releases and no artifact on Maven Central; MySQL only; development stopped in August 2025; no framework integration.

Final scores

The article's nine criteria are combined into seven columns: "What it is" and "Platform and Java" are scored together as "Spring Boot integration", and "Where it delivers" and "Databases" together as "Brokers and databases". Each score from 1 to 10 is the author's opinion based on the facts in the comparison table and the sections above; the total is a simple unweighted average of the seven columns. If one criterion matters more to you than the others (for example, the inbox), look at its column rather than the total.

Scores from 1 to 10 across the article's nine criteria, combined into seven columns; the total is an unweighted average
Library Total Spring Boot integration Brokers and databases Failures and DLQ Polling and tuning Inbox Observability Maturity
oncebox 8.8 9 9 9.5 9.5 9.5 8 7
Tandem 7.0 8 6 8.5 7.5 3 9.5 6.5
spring-boot-outbox-starter 5.3 6.5 5 6 6.5 1 7 5
ekbatan 4.7 2.5 5 5 4 4 6 6.5
transactional-event 3.9 1 3 6 4 1 5 7.5
boxy 2.8 1.5 2 3 5 4 3 1

Who should choose what

  • A Spring Boot microservice, Kafka or RabbitMQ. oncebox: a starter, a single publish call, a DLQ and an inbox for the consumer in the same library.
  • Events of different importance in one service: payments must go out instantly, analytics in batches. oncebox: polling, batch size, retries and backoff are set separately for each event type.
  • A service on MySQL or Oracle. oncebox is the only one of the three Spring starters that supports these databases.
  • An outbox for webhooks and external HTTP APIs rather than a broker. oncebox: a starter has NonTransactionalConsumer for this.
  • Jakarta EE or Quarkus. transactional-event.

FAQ

What are the transactional outbox and inbox patterns?

Transactional outbox is a pattern in which a service writes an event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business data, and a separate process sends it to Kafka or RabbitMQ. This way the event is never lost and never sent without the data change. Inbox is the companion pattern on the consumer side: it remembers the ids of processed messages and filters out the duplicates that an at-least-once outbox inevitably produces.

How do I build an inbox and an idempotent Kafka consumer in Spring Boot?

Of the six libraries compared, only oncebox ships a ready-made inbox for Kafka and RabbitMQ: the idempotent consumer wraps processing in a @KafkaListener or @RabbitListener and records the event id in the database. The transactional variant commits the record together with the business operation (effectively-once), the non-transactional one commits it before the operation (at-most-once). With the other libraries, deduplication by event id is written by hand.

Which Spring Boot outbox library supports both Kafka and RabbitMQ?

oncebox supports Kafka 3.7+ (the oncebox-kafka module) and RabbitMQ 3.12+ (oncebox-rabbit). Tandem delivers to Kafka and supports RabbitMQ through a separate tandem-rabbitmq 0.2.0 module with its own version. spring-boot-outbox-starter is broker-agnostic: you write delivery to Kafka or RabbitMQ yourself in an OutboxSink implementation.

Does transactional-event work with Spring Boot?

No. transactional-event is written for Jakarta EE 9+ and requires CDI 3.0, JTA 2.0 and Concurrency Utilities 2.0; there is a separate Quarkus extension. The project has no Spring integration.

Can ekbatan be added to an existing Spring Data JPA project?

Not as an outbox. Spring Data JPA can run in the same application, but ekbatan does not integrate with JpaRepository and does not support Spring @Transactional, and events are atomic only with changes made through its Action and ActionExecutor. A JPA entity change and an ekbatan event will not end up in one transaction, so for an outbox you would have to rewrite the data access layer in JOOQ. On top of that, ekbatan requires Java 25.

Do these libraries need Debezium?

Only ekbatan, if events must go to Kafka: there they are published by Debezium with the project's SMT plugins. Tandem and oncebox send events themselves by polling the outbox table, spring-boot-outbox-starter calls your OutboxSink, and boxy and transactional-event work without a broker.

About the author

Miguel Carvalho. Java and Kotlin developer with 7 years of Spring experience and more than 5 years working on distributed systems with Kafka and RabbitMQ. Active open source contributor.

title: I added a CSV contact importer to a shadcn registry
description:
I build CSVJetty, an embedded CSV importer for React. I’ve published a shadcn registry item that adds a contact-import card and an account-free demo to your project.

The importer handles CSV upload, column mapping, validation, and inline correction. The example expects a name and email, with an optional company field.

The integration source is MIT licensed. The importer interface runs through the hosted CSVJetty service; production use requires an account and public importer key.

Install

In a React or Next.js project with shadcn already configured:

npx shadcn@latest add https://www.csvjetty.com/r/contact-csv-import.json

The registry declares the csvjetty npm dependency and shadcn Card and Table dependencies.

Try it without an account

For a Next.js App Router page:

"use client";

import { ContactCsvImportDemo } from "@/components/contact-csv-import-demo";

export default function ContactsPage() {
  return (
    <main className="mx-auto max-w-3xl p-6">
      <ContactCsvImportDemo />
    </main>
  );
}

Save this as contacts.csv:

Full Name,Work Email,Organization
Alex Chen,alex@example.com,Acme
Sam Rivera,not-an-email,Example Inc

Upload it, match the columns, and correct the invalid email. The demo displays the latest received batch in your browser. It does not save contacts to a database.

You can also try the hosted demo before installing.

Connect it to your application

The installed ContactCsvImport component accepts a public importerKey and an onData callback. That callback is where your application saves the records.

The callback can await your API request. Throwing an error reports a failed save; returning row-level errors lets you identify records your backend rejected.

Your backend still needs to authenticate requests, validate records, and handle repeated deliveries safely.

The registry provides the contact-import integration and preview. Your application supplies persistence.

Source and integration instructions · Callback documentation

If you try it, I’d be interested in where the mapping or correction flow gets confusing.

title: What It Costs to Run AI Agents in Production: A Worked Cost Model for Tokens, Sandboxes, Storage, and Networking
description:
In production, an AI agent’s cost is model tokens plus the infrastructure around them (orchestration services, code-execution sandboxes, networking, storage, and observability), and at moderate scale tokens usually dominate, so prompt caching, model choice, and call count matter more than compute. In the worked model in this guide, 300,000 tasks a month cost about $21,919, of which model tokens are about 96 percent. Control Plane is a platform that runs agent services and their code-execution steps with autoscaling, scale to zero, and billing for the CPU and memory a workload reserves.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Every input in the model is stated so you can swap in your own numbers.

  • Cost formula. Tasks × calls per task × tokens per call × token price, plus infrastructure (compute, networking, storage, observability).
  • Worked result. 300,000 tasks a month at 8 model calls each costs about $21,919, or $0.073 per task, at list prices.
  • Biggest levers. Prompt caching cut the token bill 45 percent. Routing simple steps to a smaller model, fewer calls per task, and shorter outputs come next.
  • Infrastructure. Sandboxes, always-on orchestration replicas, NAT gateways, and trace storage came to about $799 a month, or $0.0027 per task.
  • Control Plane runs agent services and their code-execution steps on AWS, GCP, and Azure with autoscaling and scale to zero, and, where enabled, Control Plane’s Capacity AI adjusts a workload’s reserved CPU and memory between set minimums and maximums based on historical usage.

What does it cost to run AI agent workloads in production?

Monthly cost splits into token spend and infrastructure spend.

Token spend depends on four variables: tasks, model calls per task, tokens per call (input and output), and price per token. Agents run multi-step loops that resend accumulated context, so they use far more tokens per task than a single-turn chatbot.

Infrastructure spend covers the orchestration services that run the agent loop, sandboxes that execute model-generated code, NAT gateways that carry traffic to model APIs, and storage for traces and logs.

Monthly cost = token cost across all calls + sandbox compute + orchestration compute + networking + storage

Worked model: 300,000 tasks per month

This is an illustrative scenario at list prices checked in November 2026. Check current pricing before you budget.

Assumptions

  • 10,000 agent tasks per day, 300,000 per month.
  • Each task makes 8 model calls.
  • Each call sends 6,000 input tokens, of which 4,500 are a repeated prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, context) that is cached, and returns 400 output tokens. Input is held flat for simplicity; real loops grow context with each step, which raises cost, and token counts differ by model tokenizer.
  • The first call in each task writes the cache and the other 7 read it, assuming calls are less than 5 minutes apart (each hit refreshes the 5-minute cache lifetime). A long sandbox run between calls can force a new write. If the prefix is identical across tasks and traffic is steady, most first calls also hit the cache, so this assumption is conservative.
  • Model: Claude Sonnet 5.5 at list prices of $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, $2.50 per million tokens for 5-minute cache writes, and $0.10 per million for cache reads (Claude pricing, prompt caching).
Line item Tokens per month Price per million tokens Monthly cost
Uncached input 3.6 billion $2.00 $7,200.00
Cache reads 9.45 billion $0.10 $945.00
Cache writes 1.35 billion $2.50 $3,375.00
Output 0.96 billion $10.00 $9,600.00
Token total $21,120.00

Without caching, all 14.4 billion input tokens bill at $2 per million ($28,800), plus $9,600 of output, for $38,400. Caching cuts the token bill 45 percent.

Prices are AWS us-east-1 on-demand list prices, applied to both regions in the model: AWS Fargate (Linux/x86) at $0.04048 per vCPU-hour and $0.004445 per GB-hour, NAT gateways at $0.045 per hour and $0.045 per GB processed, and Amazon S3 Standard at $0.023 per GB-month.

Line item Sizing Monthly cost
Code-execution sandboxes 30% of tasks run code for 3 minutes on 2 vCPU and 4 GB = 4,500 sandbox-hours $444.33
Agent orchestration service 3 replicas of 1 vCPU and 2 GB, always on, in each of 2 regions (6 replicas × 730 hours) $216.24
NAT gateways One per availability zone, 2 zones in each of 2 regions (4 gateways × 730 hours) $131.40
NAT data processing About 57.6 GB of model API request traffic (about 24 KB per call; responses add little) $2.59
Trace and log storage 50 KB per task = 15 GB a month, kept 12 months = 180 GB at steady state $4.14
Infrastructure total $798.70

Sandbox hours count execution time only. Fargate bills per second with a one-minute minimum from the start of the image pull, so startup time, warm pools held for latency, and peak concurrency above the average all add cost.

Metric Value
Monthly total About $21,918.70
Cost per task About $0.073
Token share of total 96.4%
Infrastructure per task About $0.0027

The model deliberately leaves out databases, vector stores and embedding calls, observability or tracing subscriptions, load balancers, internet egress to end users, engineering time, and taxes, because they vary too much by architecture to price generically. The storage line prices S3 at rest only; log and trace ingestion and indexing are billed separately and often cost more than storage.

What the model shows

  • Tokens dominate at this scale.
  • Caching the repeated prefix is the single largest saving.
  • Output tokens cost 5 times input tokens, so verbose outputs are expensive.
  • Each model call removed from a task cuts cost roughly in proportion.
  • Sandbox cost scales with execution minutes, so idle sandboxes should sleep.
  • Always-on replicas and NAT gateways are fixed costs, so at much lower task volumes their share of the bill rises.

How do I estimate costs for AI agent infrastructure including sandbox execution, storage, and networking at scale?

Build the estimate from measured traces wherever you can, in seven steps:

  1. Measure tokens per call and calls per task. Pull input and output token counts from your provider’s usage data or trace spans, then multiply by projected task volume. Re-count tokens with the target model before switching, because tokenizers differ.
  2. Separate cached from uncached input. Identify the stable prefix (system prompt, tool schemas, shared context) and count how many calls per task read the cache and how many write it.
  3. Size sandboxes by execution minutes. Estimate the share of tasks that run code, how long each run lasts, and the CPU and memory each sandbox needs.
  4. Count always-on replicas and regions. Multiply replicas by their CPU and memory, by hours per month, and by the number of regions.
  5. Add networking. NAT gateways charge per hour and per GB processed; add internet egress and cross-zone traffic between orchestration, sandboxes, and databases.
  6. Add storage retention. Multiply per-task trace and output size by monthly volume and by the retention period to get steady-state storage.
  7. Add a margin for retries and failed tasks. Size it from your observed failure and retry rates, since agents can retry steps or loop, and plan for provider rate limits, which can force higher usage tiers or queueing at peak.
Line item What drives cost How to measure
Model tokens Calls per task, tokens per call, model price Trace spans, provider usage data
Prompt caching Prefix size, cache hit rate Cache read and write token counts per call
Sandbox compute Execution minutes, vCPU and memory, share of tasks Sandbox runtime logs
Orchestration compute Replicas, CPU and memory, regions Deployment configuration
NAT and networking Gateway hours, GB processed, cross-zone and egress traffic VPC flow logs, billing reports
Storage Per-task data size, retention Log volume metrics
Retries Failure rate, retry depth Error-rate dashboards

How do I cut AI agent costs?

Roughly ordered by typical impact; items 1 and 3 are calculated in the worked model.

  1. Prompt caching. Keep the cacheable prefix stable across calls within a task so later calls hit the cache.
  2. Route simple steps to a smaller model. Parsing, extraction, and formatting steps rarely need a frontier model; reserve the larger model for planning and hard reasoning.
  3. Make fewer calls per task. In the worked model, going from 8 calls to 6 cuts the token bill about 21 percent. Combine steps and detect completion early.
  4. Shorten outputs. At $10 per million output tokens against $2 for input, concise and structured outputs save money on every call.
  5. Batch non-interactive work. Anthropic’s Message Batches API costs 50 percent less than standard API calls, which suits nightly processing, evaluations, and bulk classification.
  6. Let idle sandboxes sleep. Stop or sleep environments between tasks.
  7. Right-size reservations. Match always-on replicas to measured load with autoscaling and right-sizing.
  8. Avoid NAT processing charges where possible. For model APIs reachable through private endpoints, such as Amazon Bedrock over AWS PrivateLink interface endpoints, traffic skips NAT gateway processing, though the endpoints carry their own hourly and per-GB charges. The charge was small in the worked model and grows with data volume.

How much does setting up a production grade LangChain stack cost?

The open-source LangChain and LangGraph libraries are free under the MIT license, so production cost comes from what surrounds them: model tokens, hosting, a database or vector store, and observability.

  • Model tokens remain the largest line item; the framework does not change per-token prices.
  • Hosting for the agent service and its workers, with autoscaling, availability, and security, drives compute cost.
  • Databases and vector stores depend on corpus size, embedding model, and query volume.
  • Observability and evaluation. LangSmith, LangChain’s tracing and evaluation product, has a free tier and paid plans; see LangSmith pricing for current plans and limits.

At the volume in the worked model, a LangChain stack faces the same token bill as any other framework, plus hosting and tooling costs set by your architecture.

What infrastructure do I need to run AI agents securely at scale?

A secure production setup includes:

  • Isolated sandboxes for model-generated code, ideally with microVM isolation, so generated code cannot escape to the host or other workloads. See the best AI agent sandboxes in 2026.
  • Per-agent identity and least privilege, scoped to the services each agent needs.
  • Short-lived credentials through identity federation instead of static API keys.
  • Network egress controls that restrict which endpoints an agent can reach.
  • Audit logs of every action an agent takes.
  • Human approval for destructive or irreversible actions.
  • Autoscaling and multiple regions for availability under spikes and regional outages.

For the full checklist, see how to let AI agents operate production infrastructure safely, and for why agent work should leave local machines, stop running AI agents on developer laptops.

Which platform gives the lowest cost for always-on production workloads?

The cheapest platform depends on your load pattern. Compare platforms on these factors:

  • Billing granularity. Platforms bill provisioned instances, reserved CPU and memory, or per-request consumption at different granularities; unused reservation is waste unless right-sizing closes the gap.
  • Right-sizing. Automatic adjustment of CPU and memory reservations to observed usage prevents chronic over-provisioning.
  • Commitments vs. on-demand. Reserved instances and savings plans lower unit prices in exchange for a term commitment; on-demand keeps flexibility at a higher rate.
  • Scale to zero. Services idle for hours, including staging and low-traffic agent endpoints, should cost little or nothing in compute while idle.
  • Networking and egress fees. NAT, cross-region transfer, and internet egress pricing differ by provider and grow with data volume.
  • Multi-region duplication. Running in two regions roughly doubles always-on capacity, so per-unit price and right-sizing matter more.

Compare total cost across all of these factors.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds. Each workload runs across a Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a named set of locations across one or more clouds.

  • Billing. You pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, with no contracts or minimums, and, where enabled, Capacity AI adjusts the reservation between set minimums and maximums based on historical usage. Egress, storage, observability, dedicated load balancers, and GPUs are billed separately, and Capacity AI does not apply to GPU workloads or to workloads that autoscale on CPU utilization or multiple metrics.
  • Scale to zero. Serverless workloads scale to zero natively; standard and stateful workloads can scale to zero through KEDA, enabled per GVC.
  • Sandboxes. Control Plane Sandboxes give coding agents dedicated environments, sized from 2 to 16 or more CPUs, that sleep when idle and spin back up in under one second. Sandboxes are for building and running agent code during development; production agent services, including their code-execution steps, run as Control Plane workloads. Each workload is isolated with cgroups, namespaces, and restricted syscalls and capabilities, and Sandboxes run in dedicated Kata Containers microVMs.
  • Cloud access without stored keys. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity (UCI) lets a workload call AWS, GCP, and Azure services, such as Amazon Bedrock or Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), through an IAM role or service-account grant instead of long-lived keys in your code, with short-lived, least-privilege credentials at runtime.
  • Operations. Built-in logs, metrics, and traces, and Control Plane’s MCP server, which lets AI assistants operate Control Plane resources with the signed-in user’s permissions. A Cost & Usage view, a billing_viewer role, and a monthly spend alert for billing admins track spend.
  • Availability. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Agent services spread across locations keep running when a zone, region, or provider fails.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure; that applies to the compute share of agent costs, while model tokens are billed by the model provider. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. For how training, inference, and agents fit together, see AI infrastructure in 2026.

FAQ

Short answers on AI agent production costs.

What does it cost to run AI agent workloads in production?

It depends on task volume, calls per task, tokens per call, and model price. In the worked model, 300,000 tasks a month on Claude Sonnet 5.5 cost about $21,919: $21,120 in tokens and $799 in infrastructure.

How do I estimate costs for AI agent infrastructure including sandbox execution, storage, and networking at scale?

Measure tokens and calls from traces, split cached from uncached input, size sandboxes by execution minutes, count always-on replicas per region, then add NAT, egress, storage retention, and a retry margin.

How much does setting up a production grade LangChain stack cost?

The LangChain and LangGraph libraries are free under the MIT license; you pay for model tokens, hosting, a database or vector store, and observability such as LangSmith’s paid plans.

What infrastructure do I need to run AI agents securely at scale?

Isolated sandboxes for generated code, per-agent identity with least privilege, short-lived credentials, egress controls, audit logs, human approval for destructive actions, and autoscaling across regions.

Which platform gives the lowest cost for always-on production workloads?

It depends on load pattern. Compare billing granularity, right-sizing, commitment discounts, scale to zero, networking fees, and multi-region duplication.

What share of AI agent costs is tokens versus infrastructure?

Tokens dominate at moderate scale: 96.4 percent in the worked model. At low volume, fixed costs such as always-on replicas and NAT gateways take a larger share.

How much does prompt caching save?

In the worked model, caching the 4,500-token prefix cut the token bill from $38,400 to $21,120, or 45 percent.

Why are output tokens so expensive for agents?

Output costs 5 times input in the worked model ($10 versus $2 per million), and every call in every task pays it, so concise outputs save money quickly.

Does batch processing reduce agent costs?

Yes, for work that can wait. Anthropic’s Message Batches API costs 50 percent less than standard calls.

How do always-on costs affect agent economics at low volume?

They dominate it. The $347.64 of orchestration and NAT gateway hours in the worked model stays roughly the same at 1,000 tasks a month, so per-task infrastructure cost rises sharply unless idle orchestration services scale to zero and gateway count shrinks.
