title: How to Choose an AI Model Inference Service: Managed APIs vs ML Endpoints vs Serverless GPUs vs Self-Hosted Serving
description:
Choose an inference deployment option by model type (proprietary vs open-weight), traffic shape, latency target, model features, data control requirements, and cost model. Managed model APIs are the fastest way to start, managed ML endpoints and serverless GPU services trade some control for convenience, and self-hosted serving on containers gives the most control over cost, data residency, and portability. Control Plane runs containerized model servers on AWS, GCP, and Azure regions and on your own GPU clusters, with built-in NVIDIA GPUs on Control Plane-managed locations that offer them and no Kubernetes cluster to operate on those locations.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Five deployment options:

  • Managed model APIs: Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), Microsoft Foundry (formerly Azure AI Foundry), and model providers’ own APIs
  • Managed ML endpoints (Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform endpoints, Azure Machine Learning online endpoints)
  • Serverless GPU inference services
  • Self-hosted serving on containers or Kubernetes: vLLM, NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton (formerly Triton Inference Server), or KServe as the Kubernetes serving layer
  • A platform layer that runs your model containers across clouds, such as Control Plane

Decision factors:

  • Model type: a proprietary API model or an open-weight model
  • Traffic shape: steady, bursty, or batch
  • Latency target: interactive or offline
  • Model features: structured output, tool calling, context length, and fine-tuned adapters
  • Data control and residency: where prompts and completions are processed
  • Cost model: per token, per GPU-hour, or reserved capacity
  • Team skills: the operations experience you have to run what you choose

Top inference challenges: latency, GPU cost from low utilization, cold starts, autoscaling on the wrong signal, provider rate limits and outages, GPU capacity, data privacy, observability gaps, and multi-region availability.

Containers vs managed platforms: Running model servers in your own containers gives you full control over the runtime, weights, and optimizations. A platform layer removes the work of operating Kubernetes clusters, autoscaling, and multi-cloud networking while keeping that container-level control.

How Control Plane fits: Control Plane runs containerized model servers such as vLLM as workloads, on Control Plane-managed locations in AWS, GCP, and Azure regions or on GPU clusters you add as locations, and handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security.

How do I choose an AI model inference service for my application?

Start with these seven factors.

Model type

If you need a proprietary model from a provider such as OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google, you call it through a managed model API. If you run an open-weight model such as Llama, Mistral, or Qwen, you can call it per token through a managed API that hosts it, deploy it to a managed ML endpoint, or serve it yourself. Open-weight models give you portability and the ability to fine-tune, quantize, and change versions on your schedule.

Traffic shape

Steady, predictable traffic favors reserved or dedicated compute where GPU utilization stays high. Bursty traffic benefits from services that scale elastically and avoid paying for idle GPUs. Batch workloads, such as nightly embedding jobs, can run on spot or preemptible GPUs and tolerate queuing.

Latency target

Interactive applications such as chat, code completion, and retrieval-augmented search need a short time to first token and steady token output. Dedicated endpoints and self-hosted serving give the most predictable p99 latency. Offline workloads such as summarization pipelines or evaluation runs can tolerate cold starts and queuing.

Model features

List the features your application depends on before you pick a service. Structured output and tool calling vary by API and model, and self-hosted servers such as vLLM enforce JSON schemas through structured outputs (guided decoding). Context length sets KV cache memory, so long contexts need much more GPU memory per request than short ones. Serving many fine-tuned variants is cheapest as LoRA adapters on one base model, which vLLM can serve together on one GPU. Applications that call several models need a routing layer, such as an LLM gateway, for fallback and cost-based routing.

Data control and residency

Regulated industries and privacy-sensitive applications often require that prompts and completions stay in a specific region or in the organization’s own environment. Self-hosted serving and managed ML endpoints with private networking can meet these requirements. Managed model APIs process data on the provider’s infrastructure. Hyperscaler APIs such as Bedrock, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry offer regional processing and private connectivity, and retention terms vary by provider and contract. Check whether cross-region inference routing is on, because it can move requests out of your chosen region.

Cost model

Per-token pricing is simple to budget at low volume but grows with usage. Per-GPU-hour pricing rewards high utilization. Reserved capacity lowers the hourly rate but requires a volume forecast. Include idle GPU time, egress fees, and engineering time to get a true total cost of ownership. For the build-or-rent decision, see the build vs rent GPUs break-even model.

Team skills

Managed APIs need almost no MLOps experience. Managed ML endpoints need moderate DevOps and ML engineering effort. Self-hosted serving needs experience with GPU drivers, container runtimes, model optimization, autoscaling, and incident response. A platform layer needs container and configuration skills without cluster operations.

Decision table

If you need Start with
Fastest integration, proprietary models, minimal operations Managed model API
Custom or fine-tuned models with cloud automation Managed ML endpoint
Elastic GPU scaling for bursty open-weight workloads Serverless GPU inference service
Full control over runtime, weights, data, and cost Self-hosted serving on containers
Container control across several clouds without operating clusters A platform layer such as Control Plane

Can you compare different AI model deployment solutions?

This table compares five inference deployment options across six dimensions, based on each option’s published documentation.

Option What you manage Model choice Scaling and cold starts Cost model Data control Best fit
Managed model APIs (Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, provider APIs) Prompts and application code. The provider runs serving and scaling. A catalog of proprietary and open-weight models, with fine-tuning on some. Automatic, with no cold starts for provider-hosted models; imported custom models can cold start. Rate limits can throttle bursts. Per token, with provisioned throughput options for reserved capacity, billed hourly or on a fixed-term commitment depending on the provider. The provider processes prompts and completions under its retention terms. Hyperscaler APIs offer regional processing and private connectivity. Prototyping, low to moderate volume, and teams without ML infrastructure experience.
Managed ML endpoints (Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform endpoints, Azure Machine Learning online endpoints) Model artifacts, container choice, endpoint configuration, and monitoring. Your own custom, fine-tuned, or open-weight models. Autoscaling on configured metrics. A minimum instance count avoids scale-up delay but adds cost; some services can scale to zero. Per instance-hour while instances run. Runs in your cloud account, with private networking options. Custom models that need predictable latency on cloud-managed infrastructure.
Serverless GPU inference services (on-demand GPU platforms, such as Google Cloud Run with GPUs) Container image and model weights. The provider schedules GPUs and scales. Any model you package in a container, including custom and fine-tuned models. Scales to zero by default, with optional warm instances. Cold starts include image pull, weight loading, and engine warmup. Per second of instance time, including idle time before an instance scales down and any warm minimum instances. Varies by provider. Bursty or unpredictable traffic where cold starts are acceptable.
Self-hosted serving (vLLM, NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton, KServe on Kubernetes) GPU provisioning, Kubernetes or VMs, networking, autoscaling configuration, monitoring, and patching. Any model you can load, with full control over weights, quantization, and runtime. You configure autoscaling. KServe uses Knative, HPA, or KEDA, and plain vLLM needs HPA or KEDA. Warm replicas avoid cold starts. GPU instances plus engineering and operations time. Full control; data stays in your environment. High-volume, latency-sensitive, or compliance-driven workloads with an experienced platform team.
Control Plane (platform layer for containers across clouds) Container image and workload configuration. Control Plane runs compute, networking, scaling, and Day 2 operations; on clusters you add as locations, you run the underlying servers. Any model you package in a container, plus a vLLM template for Hugging Face models. Serverless workloads scale on request concurrency and can scale to zero, and standard and stateful workloads, including GPU model servers, can scale on custom metrics through KEDA, which is enabled on Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a named set of locations across one or more clouds. The vLLM template runs as a stateful workload with a set replica count and caches weights on a volume to shorten restarts. You pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, with no contracts or minimums; the pricing page lists GPU rates per GPU-hour. Runs in the locations you select, on Control Plane-managed compute in AWS, GCP, and Azure regions or on your own clusters. Teams that want container control, Day 2 operations handled, and active-active serving across regions and clouds, with their own GPU clusters as additional locations, without cluster operations.

Many production architectures combine more than one option. A common pattern uses a managed model API for proprietary models and self-hosted serving for open-weight models where cost, data control, or customization matter.

What are common challenges in AI model inference and how can I overcome them?

This table maps each common problem to its cause and a fix.

Challenge Why it happens How to fix it
Latency: time to first token and inter-token latency Prefill on long prompts sets time to first token. Decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth, sets inter-token latency. Network hops add to both. Enable prefix caching for repeated system prompts and retrieved context, use chunked prefill so long prompts do not stall other requests, quantize weights (FP8, AWQ, or GPTQ) to speed decoding, use speculative decoding to cut inter-token latency at low batch sizes, and serve from regions close to users.
GPU cost and low utilization GPUs sit idle between requests or off-peak, and reserved capacity costs the same regardless of load. Right-size GPU types, autoscale on request concurrency or queue depth, and scale idle low-traffic services down. See the best GPU cloud providers.
Cold starts from large model weights Loading multi-gigabyte weights into GPU memory takes time when a new replica starts, on top of image pull and engine warmup. Cache weights on persistent volumes, use quantized models, keep a warm minimum of replicas before expected traffic, and use a fast weight loader such as the Run:ai Model Streamer, which vLLM supports.
Autoscaling on the wrong signal CPU utilization misses the real bottleneck, which is request concurrency, queue depth, or KV cache usage. Scale on request concurrency, waiting requests (vLLM’s num_requests_waiting), or KV cache usage. GPU memory and GPU utilization are poor signals because vLLM preallocates most GPU memory and utilization reads high even at low load.
Throughput under concurrent load Serving one request at a time wastes GPU cycles, and KV cache pressure forces recomputation. Use a server with continuous batching (vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM batch this way by default), size the KV cache for expected concurrency with max model length and an FP8 KV cache, use tensor parallelism within one node only when a model does not fit on one GPU, and add replicas for throughput.
Provider rate limits and outages Managed APIs impose token and request limits, and a single provider is a single point of failure. Retry with exponential backoff, keep a fallback model or provider, and route around unhealthy endpoints. See how to run AI inference across multiple GPU clouds.
GPU capacity and quotas High-end GPUs are often unavailable in a given region or blocked by account quotas. Request quotas early, qualify more than one GPU type per model, and keep capacity in more than one region or provider.
Data privacy and residency Sending prompts to third-party APIs can conflict with residency rules or expose sensitive data. Host open-weight models in your own environment or use managed endpoints with private networking, keep regional processing on, and review each provider’s retention terms.
Model and version management Rolling out new model versions, rolling back bad ones, and running variants side by side adds risk. Version model servers by container image tag and pin model weights to a fixed revision, roll out gradually, and keep the previous version ready for rollback.
Observability gaps Standard monitoring misses tokens per second, time to first token, and KV cache pressure. Export serving-framework metrics and track time to first token, inter-token latency, latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99), token throughput, queue depth, and KV cache usage.
Multi-region availability One region adds latency for distant users and is a single point of failure. Run replicas in at least two regions behind a global endpoint that routes to the nearest healthy one.

For the infrastructure components behind these fixes, see what infrastructure you need to run an inference layer.

Where can I find a cloud friendly deployment platform for AI models?

A cloud friendly inference platform meets five criteria:

  • Runs standard containers. You package your model server as a standard container image and deploy it without rewriting it for a proprietary runtime.
  • Works on more than one cloud. You can run the same workload definition on AWS, GCP, and Azure regions and on your own GPU clusters.
  • Supports GPUs. Your serving framework gets GPU access without manual driver work.
  • Scales on demand signals. Autoscaling follows request concurrency or queue depth instead of generic CPU metrics.
  • Keeps data where you choose. Inference traffic and model weights stay in the regions and clusters you select.

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds. For a wider comparison of hosting platforms, see the best PaaS providers in 2026.

How do containers compare with a managed PaaS for scaling AI infrastructure with predictable costs?

Running model servers in containers yourself gives you full control over the serving framework, weights, quantization, and GPU choice. The cost is operational work, including Kubernetes clusters, GPU drivers, networking, autoscaling policies, certificate rotation, and incident response.

A managed platform takes over that layer. You still bring your container image, and the platform runs compute, scaling, load balancing, and Day 2 operations. The cost shifts from engineering hours to platform fees.

Dimension Self-managed containers Managed platform (Control Plane)
Control Every layer Container image and workload configuration, with infrastructure run by the platform
Cost predictability Varies with utilization, spot pricing, and engineering time Billing follows the CPU and memory a workload reserves, and the pricing page lists GPU rates per GPU-hour, so monthly cost tracks workload configuration
Operational work Cluster management, patching, scaling, and monitoring Control Plane runs clusters, patching, scaling, and monitoring on Control Plane-managed locations

Availability You build redundancy The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane runs containerized model servers such as vLLM as workloads. On Control Plane-managed locations in AWS, GCP, and Azure regions there is no Kubernetes cluster to operate, and teams can also add GPU clusters they already run, including on a neocloud, as locations.

The vLLM template serves one Hugging Face model through vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible API on a built-in NVIDIA A10G or T4, or on your own GPU cluster registered as a location, and caches weights on a persistent volume so restarts skip the download. On Control Plane, serverless workloads scale on request concurrency and can scale to zero, and standard and stateful workloads can scale on custom metrics such as queue length through KEDA, enabled per GVC. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity (UCI) lets workloads call AWS, GCP, and Azure services, such as Amazon Bedrock or Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, through an IAM role or service-account grant instead of long-lived keys in your code, with short-lived, least-privilege credentials at runtime, so an application can combine self-hosted open-weight models with managed model APIs.

Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

FAQ

These questions come up often when teams compare inference deployment options.

Should I use a model API or host my own model?

Use a model API when you need a proprietary model, want to start quickly, or have low to moderate traffic. Host your own model when you need control over data, want to fine-tune or quantize, or when per-token cost at your volume exceeds the cost of dedicated GPU compute.

What is the cheapest way to serve an open-weight model?

It depends on utilization. At high, steady traffic, self-hosted serving on reserved GPUs usually gives the lowest cost per token, and spot GPUs suit batch jobs that tolerate preemption. At low or bursty traffic, a per-token API that hosts the model, or a GPU service that scales down when idle, avoids paying for unused GPUs. Include engineering and operations time in the comparison.

How do I reduce inference latency?

Cut time to first token by reusing cached prompt prefixes and splitting long prompts into chunks. Cut the time between tokens with quantized weights and speculative decoding. Keep warm replicas near users so requests never wait on a cold start.

How do I keep inference running when a model provider has an outage?

Keep a fallback. For managed model APIs, route to an alternative provider or model when calls fail. For self-hosted models, run replicas in at least two regions. On Control Plane, a workload in a GVC with several locations runs active-active, and the workload’s global endpoint uses DNS to route clients to the nearest location where it passes its readiness probes. Every location in that GVC must offer the GPU model the workload requests.

What GPU should I use for LLM inference?

Match GPU memory to model size, context length, and concurrency. Weight memory is the parameter count times bytes per parameter: 2 at FP16 or BF16, 1 at FP8, and about 0.5 at 4-bit, plus headroom for the KV cache, which grows with context length and concurrent requests. A 7 or 8 billion parameter model needs about 14 to 16 GB at FP16 and fits on a 24 GB GPU such as the A10G with moderate context, or on a 16 GB T4 with 4-bit quantization. A 70 billion parameter model needs about 140 GB at FP16, so it runs on four 80 GB GPUs such as the H100 with tensor parallelism, on two 80 GB GPUs at FP8, on one 80 GB GPU only at 4-bit, or on one H200 or B200 at FP8. Control Plane’s pricing page lists NVIDIA GPUs from T4 to B200, subject to availability.

How do I autoscale AI inference workloads correctly?

Scale on request concurrency, waiting requests, or KV cache usage instead of CPU or GPU utilization, which do not reflect inference load. On Control Plane, a vLLM server running as a standard or stateful workload can scale on vLLM’s waiting-request count through KEDA.

Can I run inference across multiple clouds?

Yes. Package the model server as a container and run it in more than one cloud. On Control Plane, one workload definition runs across AWS, GCP, and Azure regions and your own clusters. A GPU workload uses one GPU source per GVC: built-in NVIDIA T4 or A10G on Control Plane-managed regions, or the GPUs on your own clusters added as locations.

How do I handle data privacy requirements for AI inference?

Host models in your own environment or use managed endpoints with private networking and regional processing. Send sensitive data to a third-party model API only when its retention and usage terms meet your requirements.

What infrastructure do I need to run an inference layer?

You need GPU compute, a model server such as vLLM or Dynamo-Triton, a container runtime or a serving layer such as KServe, autoscaling, load balancing, observability, and storage for model weights. For the full breakdown, see what infrastructure you need to run an inference layer.

Is a platform layer worth it compared to managing Kubernetes myself?

For most teams, yes, when engineering time is the constraint. A platform layer removes cluster operations and custom autoscaling setup while you keep control of the model server and weights. The tradeoff is a platform fee in place of engineering hours, and Control Plane customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

title: Why Next.js Navigation Feels Slow Even When the Server Is Fast
description:
I used Next.js for a while before I could explain why clicking a link sometimes did nothing for a moment.

The server was not doing anything especially expensive. The browser already had plenty of JavaScript. Yet the next screen still waited for a network round trip.

The missing piece was the React Server Component payload for the destination route. Understanding when Next.js fetches that payload, and which parts it can reuse, made the delay much easier to explain and fix.

This is the first article in my Next.js performance series. The examples cover the App Router, the older route-level caching model, and the cacheComponents and partialPrefetching options available in Next.js 16.3 and later.

The browser needs more than JavaScript

In a client-rendered application, the browser can render a destination screen as soon as it has the relevant JavaScript. Data may still be loading, but the application can show its own loading UI immediately.

Server Components change what the browser has available. Their implementation stays on the server. The browser receives their rendered output through the RSC payload, alongside references to Client Components and the props those components need.

That payload is a serialized representation of the component tree. It is not simply an HTML document, and it is not the source code of the Server Components.

Here is a small example:

// app/posts/page.tsx
import { LikeButton } from './like-button'

export default function PostsPage() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Posts</h1>
      <LikeButton />
    </main>
  )
}

// app/posts/like-button.tsx
'use client'

import { useState } from 'react'

export function LikeButton() {
  const [liked, setLiked] = useState(false)
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setLiked(!liked)}>
      {liked ? 'Liked' : 'Like'}
    </button>
  )
}

PostsPage is a Server Component even though it has no async, await, or database query. App Router pages and layouts are Server Components by default. The 'use client' directive establishes a client boundary; components imported through that boundary belong to the client module graph.

For navigation, I find it useful to imagine that the browser has part of the destination tree, with spaces that need the server's output. The important question is whether that output arrives before or after the click.

If the required payload is missing, navigation may wait for the server. A prefetched loading boundary or static shell can still provide immediate feedback, so the presence of a Server Component alone does not make every transition slow.

What Link prefetching actually does

Next.js can fetch route data before navigation. In production, a <Link> entering the viewport normally triggers prefetching. The browser can then reuse the payload when the user clicks. Automatic prefetching is disabled in development, so next dev is not a useful way to judge its production behavior.

Before enabling Partial Prefetching, the default behavior differs by route:

Destination Default prefetch behavior
Statically rendered route Prefetch the full route
Dynamically rendered route Prefetch down to the nearest loading.js boundary, when available

prefetch={true} requests a fuller prefetch, including for dynamic routes under the older model. It can reduce the wait after a click, but it also does more server work before the user decides to visit. With Partial Prefetching enabled, the rules change again: default prefetching focuses on the shared App Shell. Next.js Link reference

The basic sequence is:

Link becomes visible
  → fetch reusable route content
  → keep it in the browser's Client Cache

User clicks
  → render the cached content
  → request anything still missing

Moving work before the click can matter more to perceived speed than shaving a few milliseconds off the server render.

Dynamic segments and dynamic rendering are different

The word “dynamic” causes a lot of confusion here.

A folder such as posts/[slug] defines a dynamic URL segment. It does not, by itself, mean that every visit requires request-time rendering. generateStaticParams can provide values that Next.js prerenders.

Dynamic rendering means rendering at request time. In the previous caching model, reading request-specific values such as cookies() or headers() opts a route into dynamic rendering. That can happen deep inside a component tree.

Imagine a mostly static article page with a small personalized control:

Article page
├─ Article title
├─ Article body
└─ Personal controls
   └─ reads cookies()

Without Cache Components or another partial-prerendering setup, that request-specific read affects the route's rendering mode. The title and body may be easy to render, but the route no longer has one completely static response that can serve every request. Cached data and shared layouts can still be reused; “dynamic” does not mean every cache disappears. Next.js previous caching model

Suspense helps only when its fallback is available

Wrapping the personalized control in <Suspense> lets the server stream the surrounding content and fallback before the slow part finishes.

But in the previous model, an ordinary Suspense boundary inside a dynamic page does not automatically turn everything around it into a build-time shell. The browser may still need the first server response before it knows what to render.

Click
  → request the destination payload
  → first response arrives
  → show surrounding content and fallback
  → stream the remaining content

A prefetched loading.tsx boundary can make the initial transition feel immediate. A fallback that exists only in an unfetched destination payload cannot do that yet. This is the distinction I was missing when I thought, “I already use Suspense, so why does navigation still pause?” Next.js instant navigation guide

Network distance makes the difference obvious. While hosting one of my services on Cloudflare, I sometimes saw traffic from Korea reach Los Angeles or Hong Kong. Even a quick server render could not eliminate that round trip.

Read staleTimes as page reuse rules

The experimental staleTimes configuration controls reuse of page segments in the Client Cache:

// Defaults in the previous caching model
const nextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    staleTimes: {
      dynamic: 0,
      static: 300,
    },
  },
}

export default nextConfig

The names are easy to read too literally. The dynamic interval applies to pages that are neither statically generated nor fully prefetched. The static interval also applies to fully prefetched pages. Loading boundaries use the static interval, shared layouts can remain reusable, and browser back/forward navigation has its own caching behavior.

So dynamic: 0 does not mean “Next.js never keeps anything from a dynamic route.” It explains one particular reason an ordinary revisit may request the page segment again. The default changed from 30 seconds to zero in Next.js 15. Next.js staleTimes reference

Cache Components gives the page a reusable shell

With Cache Components, Next.js can prerender a shell while leaving request-specific content behind Suspense boundaries:

// next.config.ts
const nextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
}

export default nextConfig

That gives us a different navigation sequence:

Before the click
  → prefetch the static shell and its fallbacks

After the click
  → show that shell immediately
  → stream request-specific content into it

I now place a boundary around the part that actually needs request-time information, rather than assuming the whole page must wait.

Enabling the flag also changes how the application expresses caching. Reusable work can use 'use cache'; uncached work that should stream needs an appropriate Suspense boundary. Existing applications may need more than a configuration change to adopt this model. Next.js caching guide

I learned that through an awkward migration. With Next.js 16.2 on Cloudflare/OpenNext, I turned the option on and off while working through middleware compatibility, authentication reads in layouts, and transition behavior. I eventually enabled it after changing hosting. That experience made me treat this as an application migration, not a free performance switch.

There is also a lifecycle detail to check. Next.js can preserve recently visited screens with React Activity. Activity hides DOM and preserves state while cleaning up Effects. Code that assumes leaving a route always destroys its DOM may need attention, particularly media elements and other work tied to the DOM itself. React Activity reference

Partial Prefetching shares the shell across URLs

Next.js 16.3 introduced another opt-in flag:

const nextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
}

export default nextConfig

An article list might link to /posts/1, /posts/2, and /posts/3. Those URLs can share the same structural shell even though the article content differs. Partial Prefetching lets Next.js reuse that App Shell across links to the same route pattern, instead of treating each URL as a completely separate prefetch target. Next.js 16.3 announcement

Where we read URL-specific information matters. Awaiting params at the top of a page ties more of the render to that particular URL. Passing the promise down and reading it inside a Suspense boundary leaves more URL-independent UI in the shared shell.

The default prefetch then brings in the shell; URL-specific content can stream after navigation. If a particular link deserves more eager work, prefetch={true} can also prefetch cached content that depends on its URL. It is a tradeoff between earlier work and faster transitions. Adopting Partial Prefetching

Service workers need a separate caching design

I also use Serwist to persist selected resources beyond the browser's in-memory route cache. Static assets are an obvious starting point. Persisting RSC responses is much more sensitive because their representation can depend on request headers, route state, deployment, and authentication.

My original implementation used Next.js response headers to distinguish responses and applied custom cache rules. I would not treat that snippet as a general recipe for other applications. Removing _rsc from cache keys or caching personalized responses without preserving the relevant distinctions can reuse the wrong response.

For most applications, I would first get framework prefetching and the App Shell right, then add a service worker only for a specific offline or persistence requirement. Next.js CDN caching guide, Serwist

A list already contains part of the detail page

The last improvement in my application came from the screen design.

When someone opens an item from a list, the browser already knows its title, thumbnail, and summary. Replacing all of that with a full-page spinner throws away useful information.

For the showcase in my service, I use Intercepting Routes to distinguish two ways of reaching the same URL:

Entry path What the user sees
Navigation from the list Show the cached summary immediately, then fetch the remaining detail
Direct visit or refresh Render the full detail through the normal server route

The intercepted route uses the list's existing client state as initial content. If there is no matching summary, it falls back to a skeleton. The regular route handles server data loading and metadata for direct visits.

Intercepting Routes provide the routing distinction; the shared client state provides the instant content. They do not, by themselves, guarantee a navigation without any RSC request. Next.js Intercepting Routes

Start with the delay after the click

I still like Next.js. These changes came from using it in Comwit, the service I build, and wanting the navigation to feel better.

When a transition feels slow, I now look at three things: what the browser already has, what it still needs from the server, and what it can show while that request is in flight.

A Server Component does not automatically make navigation slow. Waiting until the click to obtain the UI needed for the next screen is what I look for first.

title: Supabase "email rate limit exceeded"? Turn on custom SMTP, then raise the limit
description:
Sign-ups worked yesterday. Today new users never get the confirmation email, and the sign-up or reset call comes back with one of these:

email rate limit exceeded
over_email_send_rate_limit
429 Too Many Requests
Email address not authorized
email_address_not_authorized

Supabase's built-in email provider sends at most 2 emails an hour for the whole project, and only to members of your team. Connect your own SMTP provider and Supabase sends to every address, starting at 30 emails an hour, which you can raise.

I see this a lot in Lovable and Bolt apps on Supabase right when the first real users arrive.

Why it happens

  1. The default email service is still on. It refuses addresses outside the project team (email_address_not_authorized) and sends 2 emails an hour for the whole project, across every sign-up, reset, magic link and invite. Supabase describes it as best effort and not meant for production.
  2. Too many emails to one address. Repeated sign-up or reset attempts trip over_email_send_rate_limit (HTTP 429) for that address. By default the same user waits 60 seconds before another confirmation or reset email.
  3. The custom SMTP limit is still the starting value. After you add custom SMTP, Supabase starts at 30 emails an hour to protect your new sender's reputation, until you change it.

Find the cause

  1. Read the error code returned by the sign-up or reset call. over_email_send_rate_limit and email_address_not_authorized need different fixes.
  2. In the Supabase dashboard, open Authentication > SMTP settings and check whether custom SMTP is enabled.
  3. Open Authentication > Rate Limits and read the limit for emails sent.

Fix 1: connect a real email provider

  1. Create an SMTP account with a transactional email provider and verify your sending domain there.
  2. In Authentication > SMTP settings, enter the host, port, username, password, a From address such as no-reply@yourdomain.com, and a sender name.
  3. Save. From then on, Supabase sends auth emails to every address, not only your team.

Fix 2: raise the limit to fit real traffic

Set the limit for emails sent in Authentication > Rate Limits to cover your busiest hour of sign-ups and resets. Or do it from a script with the Management API:

# Access token from https://supabase.com/dashboard/account/tokens
export SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN="your-access-token"
export PROJECT_REF="your-project-ref"

# Read the current limit
curl -X GET "https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT_REF/config/auth" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN" | jq '.rate_limit_email_sent'

# Set it to your busiest hour of auth emails (replace <emails-per-hour>)
curl -X PATCH "https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT_REF/config/auth" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "rate_limit_email_sent": <emails-per-hour> }'

Keep the per-user wait between emails, so one person can't flood their own inbox.

Check the fix worked

  • Sign up with an address outside your team: the confirmation arrives from your domain.
  • Request three password resets in an hour from different addresses: all of them arrive.

Stop it coming back

  • Switch to custom SMTP before you invite any real users.
  • Add the sending domain's SPF, DKIM and DMARC records at your provider so the emails reach inboxes.

Quick answers

Is the built-in service fine for launch? No. Supabase describes it as best effort, for testing and non-critical projects, with no delivery guarantee.

Does this affect magic links and invites too? Yes. Every auth email, including one-time codes, magic links and invites, goes through the same sender.

Sources: Supabase rate limits, Send emails with custom SMTP, Auth error codes.

title: Eliminating Sub-Millimeter Drift When Printing Barcode Label Grids from the Browser
description:
Anyone who has built an HTML/CSS sheet-label generator for 30-up Avery 5160 sheets or 4×6 direct-thermal shipping labels eventually hits vertical creep: row 1 aligns inside the die-cut border, while row 10 clips 3 millimeters below the perforation.

1. Why CSS Pixels Drift Across Operating Systems

Browser print engines rasterize or paginate DOM layouts through CSS reference pixels (1in = 96px) before handing the spool to the OS print dialog. Two silent mutations commonly ruin physical pitch accuracy:

  • Fit-to-Page Auto-Scaling: Chrome and Edge shrink printable boxes by 94%–97% whenever unprintable printer hardware margins intersect the CSS @page box.
  • Sub-Pixel Rounding Accumulation: An Avery 5160 cell is 2.625 in × 1.0 in with a horizontal pitch of 2.75 in. Rounding fractional CSS flex/grid tracks over 10 rows accumulates enough vertical error to cross the die-cut line.

2. Computing Directly in PostScript Vector Points (72 pt = 1 inch)

Generating native PDF streams client-side in WebAssembly/JavaScript bypasses DOM layout rounding completely. In the PDF coordinate system (origin at bottom-left), physical measurements convert deterministically:

const INCH_TO_PT = 72;
const MM_TO_PT = 72 / 25.4;

// Avery 5160 exact geometry on US Letter (612 x 792 pt)
const topMarginPt = 0.5 * INCH_TO_PT;     // 36 pt
const leftMarginPt = 0.1875 * INCH_TO_PT; // 13.5 pt
const colPitchPt = 2.75 * INCH_TO_PT;     // 198 pt
const rowPitchPt = 1.0 * INCH_TO_PT;      // 72 pt

3. Crisp Code 128 & EAN-13 Quiet Zones on 203 DPI Thermal Heads

Direct thermal printers (Zebra, Rollo, Dymo) print at 203 DPI (8 dots/mm). Rendering a barcode into a PNG canvas first introduces anti-aliased gray edge pixels that thermal printheads dither, causing handheld laser scanners to reject narrow bars. Emitting each Code 128 module as an unstroked filled PDF vector rectangle guarantees sharp 1-bit bar boundaries at any DPI.

For client-side CSV-to-PDF batch generation with zero cloud uploads, see the CSV and Excel barcode sheet builder on LabelQueue, or query exact template pitches programmatically via npx labelqueue-cli demo.

title: スマートグラス元年の前に、「どう見せるか」を設計する
description:
スマートグラス元年の前に、「どう見せるか」を設計する

今朝のXR業界ニュースが面白い。韓国のアイウェア大手Gentle Monsterが、Samsung・Googleと組んだAndroid XRスマートグラスを12月に発売すると発表し、Joaquin Phoenix主演の短編フィルムの予告編も公開した。

ハードウェアのニュースが続くと、つい「デバイスが普及すれば解決する」と考えがちだ。だが、エンジニアとして気になるのはむしろ逆で、スマートグラスが日常の視界に入り込むほど、「目そのものの機能」をどう訓練し、どう可視化するかというソフトウェア側の設計問題が前景化する。弱視（lazy eye / amblyopia）や両眼視機能の調整に課題を抱える成人は少なくない。従来は遮蔽（パッチ）や赤青メガネ、通院訓練が中心で、日常生活に組み込みにくいというUX上の制約があった。

ここで紹介したいのが、Seven Sports が開発した Amblyotube だ。VR上で視覚協調と注意のエクササイズを行うレクリエーション兼教育ソフトウェアで、Meta Quest向けに提供されている。アーキテクチャの面白さは、左右の目に異なる視覚ストリームを同時提示する点にある。YouTubeライクな動画コンテンツをそのまま「視覚のジム」に変換する発想だ。

実装上のポイントを整理すると：

  • 左右どちらの目を対象にするかを選択し、症状の程度に応じたプリセットやLogMAR視力チェックを利用できる
  • 優位眼には調整可能なデジタルブラー、弱視眼にはAI Sharpener（MFBF）が人物を検出して輪郭とハイライトを強調
  • マゼンタのフォーカスキューで両眼の融合（binocular fusion）を促し、立体視の手がかりを訓練

これは臨床の代替ではなく、補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールという位置づけだ。1日30〜40分（最大1時間）、13歳以上が対象。ハードウェアの進化を待つだけではなく、体験の中身を自分で設計できる。そういう選択肢が増えていくことに、少し希望を感じている。

title: Responsive Website Design Service
description:
Responsive Website Design Service: The Architectural Breakdown

In the digital landscape, responsive website design is not merely an option but a necessity. It ensures that your website adapts seamlessly across all devices, from smartphones to desktops, enhancing user experience and driving engagement. However, relying on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often falls short of delivering a truly effective responsive design. Let's delve into why these approaches fail and explore the engineering principles that underpin a successful responsive website design service.

Why Off-the-Shelf Templates and Generic Forms Fail

  1. Lack of Customization: Off-the-shelf templates are designed for a broad audience, which means they can't cater to the specific needs of your business. They often lack the flexibility to incorporate unique branding elements, functionalities, or user experiences tailored to your audience.

  2. Performance Issues: Generic forms and templates are not optimized for performance. They may include unnecessary code, bloated assets, or inefficient practices that slow down your website, leading to higher bounce rates and poorer search engine rankings.

  3. Inadequate Adaptability: While these templates may claim to be responsive, they often fail to provide a truly seamless experience across all devices. They might not account for varying screen sizes, touch interactions, or device capabilities, resulting in a suboptimal user experience.

Three Concrete Engineering Takeaways

  1. User-Centric Design: A successful responsive design prioritizes the user experience. It involves understanding your target audience's behavior, preferences, and pain points. By conducting thorough user research and creating personas, you can design interfaces that are intuitive, accessible, and engaging across all devices.

  2. Performance Optimization: Responsive design

title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now offers a Web Search API
description:
Today, AWS announces the general availability of the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which lets you search the web with a single API call. Web Search on AgentCore has been available as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway. The new InvokeWebSearch API gives applications, custom agent loops, and data pipelines search results with no resources to create.

The API returns ranked results from the Amazon-operated web index behind Web Search on AgentCore. Each result includes a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You can filter each request by domain and publication time, for example to find recent product announcements or check a claim against trusted domains.

You call the API with the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and authorize calls with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). You can call it from your virtual private cloud (VPC) through AWS PrivateLink and log requests as AWS CloudTrail data events. Web Search API queries are billed at $7 per 1,000 queries, the same rate as Web Search through AgentCore Gateway, with no gateway charges.

The Web Search API is available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). To learn more, see Search the web with the InvokeWebSearch API in the AgentCore Developer Guide, the Web Search  page, and AgentCore pricing .

title: How I built a responsive landing page with animated cards in HTML, CSS and JavaScript
description:
I wanted to practice building a landing page from scratch without a template, so I made a dark-themed sports page with tilted cards, a responsive navigation bar, and simple hover animations. Here is how I put it together.

The goal

The page needed three sections, each with a title, a short description, and a call-to-action button. The main challenge was making the cards look dynamic on desktop without breaking the layout on phones.

Structure

I kept the HTML simple: a header with navigation, a main section with a grid of cards, and a footer. Each card is a div with a heading, a short paragraph, and a button.

html

<h2>Train in the gym</h2>
<p>Strength, volume and definition routines for every level.</p>
<a href="#">View routines</a>

Responsive layout

I used CSS Grid for the cards, so they stack on small screens and sit side by side on larger ones:

css

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
  gap: 2rem;
}

Hover animation with JavaScript

For the interactive part, I used a small script that adds a class when the mouse enters a card. The CSS handles the actual movement, which keeps the JavaScript light:

javascript

document.querySelectorAll('.card').forEach(card => {
card.addEventListener('mouseenter', () => card.classList.add('active'));
card.addEventListener('mouseleave', () => card.classList.remove('active'));
});
What I learned

Keeping the CSS and JavaScript separate made the page easier to debug. Animations feel better when they are subtle, and responsive design is easier to test if you check the layout at each breakpoint while you build, not at the end.

I also offer landing pages and simple interactive websites as a freelancer. If you need one for your business or community, you can see my services here: https://www.fiverr.com/s/2pQdqBq

title: How to Succeed as a Solo UX or Product Designer in the AI Era
description:
Over the years, the role of UX designers has continuously evolved with changes in technology, business needs, and user expectations.

In the early days, UX designers primarily focused on creating simple mockups and designing applications for desktop screens. As technology advanced, designers began creating responsive experiences across multiple devices, including desktops, tablets, and mobile phones. This shift required designers to expand their skills and adapt to new design challenges.

As digital products became more complex, UX design expanded into different industries, including B2B, SaaS, healthcare technology, e-commerce, and developer experience (DevEx). Today, UX designers are no longer limited to a single industry or type of product. They have opportunities to apply their knowledge and skills across a wide range of domains.

However, the responsibilities of UX designers often depend on the size and structure of an organization. In small companies and startups, a solo UX or product designer may be responsible for the entire design process, from understanding user needs and conducting research to creating user interfaces, testing designs, and collaborating on product development. In contrast, larger organizations often have dedicated teams or specialists focusing on specific areas, such as UX research, interaction design, visual design, and design systems.

One challenge that often receives less attention is UX documentation and knowledge management. Many designers focus on delivering design solutions and showcasing their work through portfolios, while documenting research findings, design decisions, workflows, and lessons learned receives less priority.

This challenge can be particularly noticeable in small organizations, where limited resources and multiple responsibilities make it difficult to establish consistent documentation practices. Larger and mid-sized organizations may have more dedicated resources, processes, and teams to support UX documentation, although they can face similar challenges.

Now, with the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, the role of UX and product designers is evolving once again. AI creates opportunities for solo designers to work more efficiently, support research activities, improve documentation, explore design ideas, and contribute across different stages of product development.

The question is no longer just how UX designers can create better designs, but how they can adapt their skills, manage broader responsibilities, and use AI effectively to succeed as solo designers in a rapidly changing industry.

This article explores the evolution of UX design, the challenges faced by solo designers, and how AI can help them improve their workflows, strengthen documentation practices, and deliver meaningful user experiences.

UX Fundamentals and Domain Knowledge: Essential Skills for Every UX Designer

A strong foundation in UX design and domain knowledge is essential for every UX or product designer, especially in the AI era.

Understanding the fundamentals of UX design helps designers recognize the importance of user experience, identify user needs, and create intuitive, accessible, and user-friendly applications.

With a solid understanding of UX principles, designers can make better decisions about application layouts, screen sizes, responsive design, color palettes, navigation, and information architecture. These foundational skills also help designers use AI tools more effectively to explore ideas, build prototypes, and develop successful digital products.

However, UX fundamentals alone are not enough. Domain knowledge is equally important. For example, when designing a healthcare application, designers need to understand the purpose of the product, its users, accessibility requirements, privacy concerns, and the specific challenges of the healthcare industry.

Similarly, designers working in SaaS, e-commerce, FinTech, or Developer Experience (DevEx) need to understand the workflows, terminology, user expectations, and challenges specific to those domains.

In the AI era, designers can use AI to speed up design and development activities, but AI cannot replace their understanding of users, design principles, and industry-specific requirements. However designers don't need to be experts in every industry.

The key takeaway is that AI can help designers build products faster, but strong UX fundamentals and domain knowledge help them build the right products for the right users.

From UX Knowledge to Practical Experience: A 40-Day Design Challenge for Beginners

By now, you should have a better understanding of the importance of UX fundamentals and domain knowledge, how UX design has evolved over the years, and how these changes have shaped the way we design digital products and improve user experiences.

But understanding UX concepts is only the beginning. The real learning starts when you apply that knowledge to practical design challenges.

Step 1: Build Your UX Skills Through a 30-Day Design Challenge

Once you understand the fundamentals of UX design and the importance of domain knowledge, the next step is to put your learning into practice.

I recommend starting with a 30-day UX design challenge. Depending on your interests, learning pace, and availability, you can also extend it to 60 days.

The goal is to complete 30 design challenges while developing your problem-solving skills, design thinking, and practical UX knowledge.

Why a design challenge?

  • It helps you develop consistency and discipline.
  • It motivates you to practice UX design regularly.
  • It encourages you to think critically about everyday user experiences.
  • It gives you opportunities to apply user-centered design principles.
  • It helps you build confidence through hands-on experience.

Let's divide these 30 challenges into three stages.

Step 2: Days 1–10 : Improve the Applications You Use Every Day

Start with something familiar: the applications and websites you use in your daily life.

Think about the apps you use for shopping, banking, communication, note-taking, learning, or managing your daily activities.

Your challenge: Choose 10 applications you regularly use and identify opportunities to improve their user experience.

For each application, ask yourself:

  • What is the main purpose of this application?
  • Who are its target users?
  • What works well in the current experience?
  • What challenges or frustrations might users face?
  • How could I improve the experience using UX design principles?

For example, you might use a shopping application regularly but find its checkout process confusing or time-consuming. Think about how you could simplify the process and make it easier for users.

Try to understand the problem before jumping into a design solution.

By the end of these 10 challenges, you will have gained practical experience in evaluating existing applications, identifying usability problems, and proposing improvements from a user's perspective.

Step 3: Days 11–20 : Turn Your Own Ideas Into UX Design Projects

Now that you have practiced improving existing applications, it's time to think about your own product ideas and choose one design tool such as Figma and practice these challenges using this tool. (At the beginning choosing the one tool is enough to practice the skills later you can explore other similar tool like Adobe XD and many more depending on your interest.

Have you ever thought, "I wish there were an application that could help me do this task more easily?"

This is a great starting point for a UX design project.

For example, I often think about having a personalized notepad application that helps me organize meeting notes, capture important discussions, and track action items.

Instead of simply imagining the application, I can turn this idea into a design project using user-centered design principles.

Your challenge: Come up with 10 application or website ideas based on problems you experience or observe in everyday life.

For each idea:

  1. Identify the problem you want to solve.
  2. Understand who might experience this problem.
  3. Define the users' needs and goals.
  4. Explore possible solutions.
  5. Create user flows, wireframes, or prototypes.
  6. Evaluate your design and identify improvements.

You don't need to build a fully functional application for every challenge. Focus on understanding the problem and practicing the UX design process.

By the end of these challenges, you will have more confidence in turning ideas into practical design solutions.

Step 4: Days 21–30 : Explore UX Design in Your Area of Interest

Now it's time to explore a specific industry or domain that interests you.

Domain knowledge plays an important role in UX design because every industry has its own users, workflows, challenges, regulations, and technical requirements.

For example, you might be interested in:

  • Healthcare and medical applications
  • Banking and financial technology
  • Developer tools and cloud-native technologies
  • Education technology
  • E-commerce applications

Your challenge: Choose one domain that interests you and explore 10 applications or tools related to that domain.

Try to understand how these tools work, who uses them, and what problems they solve.

What if you don't have access to these tools?

Some professional applications are not publicly accessible. They may require a paid subscription, an organizational account, or special permissions.

For example, imagine you are interested in designing clinical or medical applications.

Many hospital management systems and electronic health record applications are accessible only to authorized healthcare professionals because they handle sensitive patient information.

As a beginner, you may not have access to these applications.

So, what can you do?

You can explore:

  • Applications that offer free trials or demo environments.
  • Open-source alternatives.
  • Publicly available training environments.
  • Similar applications with accessible features.
  • Product documentation, tutorials, and walkthroughs.

The goal is to understand the workflows, user needs, and design challenges within your chosen domain. Once you have explored these tools, think about how you could improve their user experience.

An important note for beginners:

During these first 30 challenges, I recommend avoiding AI-generated design solutions as much as possible.

Why?

Because this is your opportunity to strengthen your UX fundamentals, critical thinking, research skills, and problem-solving abilities.

You can use learning resources and documentation, but try to analyze problems, develop ideas, and make design decisions independently.

Learn to think like a designer before depending on AI to design for you.

Step 5: Days 31–40 : Learn How to Use AI in Your UX Design Process

Congratulations! By now, you have completed 30 practical design challenges covering everyday applications, your own product ideas, and domain-specific tools.

You have practiced identifying user problems, exploring solutions, and applying UX principles.

Now it's time to take your learning to the next level.

How can AI help you become a more efficient UX designer?

AI can support designers in many ways, from organizing research findings and exploring design ideas to creating prototypes and speeding up repetitive tasks.

But the goal is not to replace your design thinking with AI.

Instead, you should learn how to combine human creativity, UX knowledge, domain expertise, and AI capabilities to solve design problems more effectively.

Your challenge: Complete 10 additional design challenges using AI tools alongside your UX skills.

You can revisit some of your previous projects or choose entirely new design problems.

For each challenge:

  1. Identify the UX problem independently.
  2. Think about how you would approach the problem without AI.
  3. Explore where AI could help you save time.
  4. Use AI tools to support research synthesis, ideation, prototyping, or documentation.
  5. Review and validate the AI-generated outputs.
  6. Compare your workflow with and without AI.

Ask yourself:

  • Did AI help me complete the task faster?
  • Did it improve the quality of my solution?
  • Did it provide useful ideas I hadn't considered?
  • Were any AI-generated suggestions inaccurate or unsuitable?
  • Which design decisions still required my judgment?

Remember, AI can help you work faster, but your UX knowledge helps you decide whether the solution is actually useful, accessible, and user-friendly.

By completing these challenges, you will begin to understand how AI fits into your design process without losing your independent problem-solving skills.

Step 6: Move From Practice Projects to Real-World Open-Source Contributions

After completing these 40 design challenges, you will have built a stronger foundation in UX design, gained practical experience, explored an industry of interest, and learned how to use AI effectively in your workflow.

Now it's time to move beyond personal design challenges and start working on real-world problems.

One of the ways to gain practical experience is by contributing to open-source projects.

Open-source communities give you opportunities to collaborate with developers, maintainers, designers, and users who are working together to improve real products.

You can begin by exploring projects related to your chosen domain and looking for opportunities to contribute through usability reviews, user research, documentation improvements, design proposals, or accessibility enhancements.

You don't need to be an expert to get started. Begin with small contributions, understand the community's needs, and gradually take on more challenging problems.

This experience can help you develop collaboration skills, understand real product constraints, and build a portfolio that demonstrates your ability to solve meaningful user problems.

How to Document Your UX Design Challenges

Now that you have completed your design challenges, the next important step is to learn how to document your design process and decisions.

Documentation is an essential skill for UX designers. It helps you organize your ideas, explain your design decisions, communicate your problem-solving approach, and eventually build strong portfolio case studies.

Start by exploring how well-known companies such as Google and Microsoft document their design systems, design principles, components, and user experience guidelines.

For example, you can explore Google's Material Design and Microsoft's Fluent Design System to understand how established companies create and maintain design documentation.

Every organization has its own approach to documenting design systems, product experiences, and design decisions. By studying these examples, you can learn how to structure documentation for your own applications and projects.

As you document each design challenge, focus on:

  • Problem statement: What problem are you trying to solve?
  • User needs: Who are your users, and what challenges do they face?
  • Design process: What steps did you follow to explore and solve the problem?
  • Design decisions: Why did you choose a particular solution?
  • Design system: What components, typography, colors, and interaction patterns did you use?
  • Testing and improvements: How did you evaluate your design, and what did you learn?
  • Key takeaways: What skills and knowledge did you gain from the challenge?

Remember, good UX documentation is not just about showcasing your final designs. It is about explaining your thinking, decisions, challenges, and learning process.

By developing documentation skills early in your UX journey, you will find it much easier to turn your practice projects into meaningful portfolio case studies and communicate your design experience to future employers and collaborators.

Final Thoughts

Learning UX design is not just about understanding design principles or becoming familiar with design tools. It is about developing the ability to identify problems, understand users, think critically, and create meaningful solutions.

My recommendation for beginners is simple:

First, learn the fundamentals. Then practice independently. Explore a domain that interests you. Learn to use AI as a supporting tool. Finally, apply your skills to real-world projects.

You don't have to complete every challenge perfectly. What matters most is your learning process, consistency, curiosity, and willingness to improve.

The goal is not simply to complete 40 design challenges. The goal is to become a designer who understands why a problem exists, how to approach it, and how to create a better experience for users.

title: Game-Style Feedback for Law Firm Site Forms and Buttons
description:
Press a button in a well-made video game and something happens right away. The character moves, a sound plays, the button glows or the controller vibrates. Players never wonder whether the game registered their input. Game designers treat that instant response as a basic requirement, and players notice at once when it is missing.

Law firm websites rarely get the same attention. A visitor taps "Call now" and nothing seems to happen for a second. They submit a contact form and the page sits there with no sign it worked. On a criminal defense site, the person tapping is often anxious and in a hurry, so a moment of uncertainty can send them back to the search results. This post covers how to bring game-style feedback to the interactive parts of a law firm site.

Respond to every tap within a fraction of a second

Games aim to respond to input within a frame or two. Jakob Nielsen's long-standing guidance on response times puts the limit for feeling instant at about 0.1 seconds. Anything slower and users start to notice the delay.

Google measures something similar with Interaction to Next Paint, one of the Core Web Vitals. It tracks how long the page takes to visibly respond after a user interacts, and Google describes 200 milliseconds or less as good. Heavy chat widgets, tracking scripts and large JavaScript bundles are the usual reasons a law firm site responds slowly.

Start by giving every button a visible pressed state in CSS. That costs almost nothing and tells the user the tap registered even if the next step takes a moment.

Show progress during anything that takes time

Games show loading bars, spinning icons or animations whenever the player has to wait. The player knows the game is working and roughly how long it will take.

On a law firm site, form submission is the main wait. When someone submits a contact form, disable the button, change its label to something like "Sending" and show a small spinner. That prevents double submissions and reassures the user. If the request fails, re-enable the button and explain what happened.

Make errors clear and fixable

Good games tell players exactly what went wrong and how to fix it. A locked door has a symbol showing which key it needs. A failed jump shows where the player fell short.

Form errors on many law firm sites do the opposite. They show a generic message at the top of the form or clear every field after a failed submit. Better practice looks like this:

  • Validate fields as the user leaves them, not on every keystroke
  • Show the error message next to the field it belongs to
  • Explain the fix in plain words, such as "Please enter a phone number with area code"
  • Keep everything the user typed when an error appears

Screen reader users need to hear these messages too. Connect each error to its field and announce status changes in a live region:

<label for="phone">Phone</label>
<input id="phone" name="phone" type="tel" aria-describedby="phone-error" aria-invalid="true">
<p id="phone-error">Please enter a phone number with area code.</p>
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" id="form-status">Sending your message...</div>

Confirm success in a way the user cannot miss

When a player finishes a level, the game makes it obvious with a sound, a screen and often a summary of what happens next. The player is never left wondering.

After a form submits successfully, replace the form with a clear confirmation message rather than a small line of green text. Tell the user what happens next, such as when they can expect a call and from what number. On a defense site, add a reminder not to share case details by email if the firm prefers to discuss them by phone.

The form itself matters as much as the feedback around it, and this guide on designing an intake form a frightened caller will finish covers which fields to ask for and which to leave out.

Test like a game studio

Game studios watch real players and note every moment of confusion. Law firm sites can do a lighter version. Ask someone who has never seen the site to find the phone number and send a message on their own phone while you watch. Note any pause, repeated tap or confused look.

Test on a slow connection as well. Browser developer tools can throttle the network so you see how the site behaves on weak mobile data, which is how many people will reach it.

For more on interface lessons drawn from games, the UX lessons from video game design site collects related articles.

Questions about feedback on law firm sites

Does a pressed state on buttons really matter?

Yes. It is the cheapest way to tell users their tap registered, and it reduces repeated taps that can cause double calls or duplicate form submissions.

How do I measure Interaction to Next Paint?

PageSpeed Insights and the Chrome User Experience Report show field data for INP when a site has enough traffic. Chrome DevTools can measure it during local testing.

Should a law firm site use sound or vibration like games do?

No. Visual feedback is enough on a website, and unexpected sound or vibration would feel intrusive to most visitors.

SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense law firms, one firm per city. It builds defense firm websites, handles SEO for the charges a firm defends, works on visibility in AI search tools and runs SEO audits.

title: React Email Verification States That Explain Themselves
description:
Email verification looks like a small form until you ship it. Then the edge cases arrive: the request is still running, the code is wrong, the link expired, the user clicked resend twice, or the browser came back from a suspended tab.

The UI problem is usually an unclear state model

Many React forms start with three booleans:

const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
const [verified, setVerified] = useState(false);

This is friendly at first, but it can describe impossible combinations. What does loading: true and verified: true mean? Should an old error remain visible while a new request is running? Can the resend button be enabled during a code submission?

The important part are the transitions, not the number of variables. A verification flow should tell the user what is happening and what action is safe next.

Model verification as a small state machine

Start with named states that match product behavior. A TypeScript discriminated union makes the rules visible in the component:

type VerificationState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending" }
  | { kind: "awaiting-code"; expiresAt: number; resendAvailableAt: number }
  | { kind: "verifying"; code: string }
  | { kind: "verified" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string; canRetry: boolean }
  | { kind: "expired" };

Now the UI has a smaller decision surface. An awaiting-code state must carry the timing information needed by the countdown. A verified state does not need an error message. The compiler helps keep these informations together when the flow changes later.

I like this approach because it connects product language to implementation language. “Check your inbox” becomes awaiting-code, while “Your code expired” becomes expired. This makes a confusing email flow a little more clear for both the user and the next developer.

Render states with a discriminated union

Keep rendering close to the state model, but keep side effects in event handlers or a dedicated hook:

function VerificationPanel({ state }: { state: VerificationState }) {
  switch (state.kind) {
    case "idle":
      return <button type="button">Send verification email</button>;
    case "sending":
      return <p role="status">Sending your verification email…</p>;
    case "awaiting-code":
      return <CodeForm expiresAt={state.expiresAt} />;
    case "verifying":
      return <p role="status">Checking the code…</p>;
    case "verified":
      return <p role="status">Email verified. You can continue.</p>;
    case "expired":
      return <button type="button">Send a new code</button>;
    case "error":
      return (
        <div role="alert">
          <p>{state.message}</p>
          {state.canRetry && <button type="button">Try again</button>}
        </div>
      );
  }
}

The UI should not guess from a partially updated collection of flags. It should announce the current state, disable actions that cannot succeed, and preserve focus when an error replaces the form. A status message that appears only visually is not enough; screen readers need a useful announcement too.

Keep resend and expiration explicit

Resend is where many otherwise clean implementations become flaky. Treat it as a separate transition with a server-side policy behind it. The client countdown is useful feedback, but it is not the source of truth.

When the user submits a code, capture the request identity. If an older request finishes after a newer one, ignore the stale result. A simple sequence number works for a small hook:

const requestId = useRef(0);

async function verify(code: string) {
  const currentId = ++requestId.current;
  setState({ kind: "verifying", code });

  const result = await verifyCode(code);
  if (currentId !== requestId.current) return;

  setState(result.ok
    ? { kind: "verified" }
    : { kind: "error", message: "That code is not valid.", canRetry: true });
}

This small guard prevents a slow response from moving a fresh form backwards. It also make the failure behavior much easier to explain in a test.

For temporary test inboxes, a service such as tempmailso can help isolate verification data during development. Do not use an inbox you do not control for real customer accounts, and do not treat a successful test message as proof that production delivery is healthy.

Test the transitions, not just the happy path

Component tests should cover state changes and user-visible consequences:

  1. Sending starts with one click and announces progress.
  2. A successful response renders the code form.
  3. An invalid code keeps the user in a recoverable error state.
  4. A stale response cannot overwrite a newer request.
  5. Resend is unavailable during its cooldown and becomes available afterward.
  6. Expiration offers a clear next action.

This is also where connecting one alert to one rollout is a useful operational idea: make each failure point explainable instead of collapsing several causes into “Something went wrong.” For account flows, proof-first email change flows offer the same mindset from a security angle.

During manual testing, try a tem email, paste a code twice, navigate away while the request is pending, and return after the expiry time. These cases finds the gaps that a single successful test will miss. They are boring checks, but boring checks is exactly what protects a sign-up flow from surprise.

A short shipping checklist

Before shipping, check that:

  • Every visible message maps to one explicit state.
  • Submit, resend, and continue actions have clear disabled rules.
  • Stale responses cannot overwrite current state.
  • Expiration and retry behavior are tested.
  • Status and error messages work with keyboard and screen readers.
  • The server still enforces verification expiry and resend limits.

An explicit state machine does not make email delivery perfect. It does make the product honest about what it knows, what it is waiting for, and what the user can do next. That clarity is a feature worth shipping.
