title: Why a Java pod gets OOMKilled in Kubernetes with a half-empty heap
description:
In short. A container memory limit covers everything the JVM uses, and the heap is only part of it. Metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache and direct buffers live outside the heap, so a pod with -Xmx close to its limit is killed while the heap still has room. Size the limit as heap plus non-heap, check which GC and how many CPUs the JVM really sees, and add a startup probe. jvm-fit does that arithmetic from the manifest before you deploy.

The pod restarts with exit code 137. The dashboard shows the heap at 50 or 60 percent. Nothing in the application log, because the kernel killed the process and the JVM never got to write an OutOfMemoryError. This is one of the most common ways Java breaks on Kubernetes, and the cause is almost always visible in the manifest.

Why is the pod killed when the heap isn't full?

Because the limit is on the container, and the heap is one of several things in it. The JVM also needs memory for:

  • Metaspace: class metadata. Grows with the number of loaded classes, which in a Spring Boot app is a lot.
  • Thread stacks: each thread reserves its own stack.
  • Code cache: machine code produced by the JIT compiler.
  • Direct buffers: off-heap memory used by NIO and Netty-based clients and servers.
  • The GC's own structures and other native memory.

None of that is counted by -Xmx. If the heap is allowed to take 900Mi of a 1Gi container, everything else has to fit in what is left, and it doesn't.

Memory budget
  container limit        1024Mi
  heap max (-Xmx)         900Mi
  non-heap estimate      ~350Mi
  -----------------------------
  needed                ~1250Mi
  over limit by ~226Mi

The JVM does not know it is over budget. It grows into memory it believes it has, the container crosses its limit, and the kernel's OOM killer ends it.

A real run: 51% heap, exit code 137

I reproduced it on a kind cluster with a small Spring Boot service made for the purpose. It keeps a fixed 260Mi in the heap and 140Mi in direct buffers, which is what NIO clients do.

Before After the fix
Memory limit 512Mi 832Mi
Heap setting -Xmx450m sized to leave room for non-heap
Result under the same load OOMKilled, heap at 51% in the last log line 0 restarts, peak 670Mi

"Stable" here means no restarts for a minute after full load, not a soak test. The point is the first column: a heap that was half empty, and a pod that died anyway.

Three container defaults that are easy to get wrong

I wanted the rules in jvm-fit to match what the JVM actually does, so a test starts Temurin 11, 17 and 21 in Docker with different limits and reads back the heap size, CPU count and GC. Three results are easy to get wrong.

Container What you might expect What the JVM does
2 CPUs, 1Gi G1, because there are two cores SerialGC. G1 also needs about 1792Mi of memory
256Mi, no heap flags A 64M heap, 25% of the limit A 126M heap. Small limits have a floor
1Gi with -XX:-UseContainerSupport Roughly the same as without it A heap sized from the host's memory, not the container's

The first one matters most in practice. A service with a 1 CPU limit or a small memory limit runs on a single-threaded collector, and nobody chose that. The app is slow, CPU usage looks low, and the cause is one line in the pod spec.

The other default worth knowing: with no -Xmx and no MaxRAMPercentage, HotSpot gives the heap 25% of the limit. In a 1Gi container that is 256M, and the rest of the memory you pay for sits idle. OpenJ9 behaves differently: the same 1Gi container got a 512M heap.

How much memory should a Java container get?

Work it out as a sum, not a percentage:

  • Start from the heap the app needs, taken from real usage if you have it.
  • Add non-heap. About 350Mi is a typical figure for a Spring Boot service, more if it uses many threads or large direct buffers. This is an estimate, so measure your own app when you can.
  • Set the limit to the sum, with some headroom.
  • Then express the heap as MaxRAMPercentage so it follows the limit when someone changes it. Values above 80 rarely leave enough room.

There is no single correct MaxRAMPercentage. Non-heap memory does not shrink when the limit does, so 75% is comfortable in a 4Gi container and too much in a 512Mi one.

What else to check in the manifest

  • A memory limit exists. Without one the JVM takes a percentage of the whole node.
  • The CPU limit. Below 1 core means throttling; below 2 means SerialGC unless you set a collector yourself.
  • ActiveProcessorCount is not higher than the CPU limit.
  • A startup probe. A liveness probe with a short initial delay kills a JVM that is still starting.
  • Memory request equals the limit, so the scheduler places the pod where the memory really is.

Checking it before deploy

To stop doing this arithmetic by hand, I wrote jvm-fit. It reads the pod spec and the JVM flags together, from plain manifests, Helm charts or Kustomize overlays, and prints the budget and a fix for each finding.

go install github.com/andronaft/jvm-fit/cmd/jvm-fit@latest

jvm-fit scan ./k8s/                            # files and directories
jvm-fit scan ./charts/payments -f values.yaml  # Helm chart
jvm-fit explain JVM007                         # why it matters, how to fix it

It collects flags in the order the JVM applies them (JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, then JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, then the command line), has 12 rules, and outputs text, JSON or SARIF for CI.

What it doesn't do

It is a static check. It does not see how much memory your app really uses, and the non-heap figure is an estimate you can override. Tools like KRR and Goldilocks answer the other half of the question from real usage: they tell you how much the app needs, and jvm-fit checks that the JVM flags fit the limit you chose. Reading live clusters and Prometheus metrics is planned for the next version.

Source and docs: github.com/andronaft/jvm-fit (Apache 2.0) · the measurements: results on real JDKs · the demo: OOMKilled with a half-empty heap

title: How to Upload AI-Generated Images with Go Presigned URLs — Logistics Storage
description:
When a logistics platform stores an AI-generated image, the application server should authorize the upload without carrying the image bytes. That boundary matters more than the storage brand: a presigned URL lets the API authenticate the request, while the worker or browser sends the image directly to object storage. For a multi-tenant system, generate the URL only after validating the tenant-owned bucket and key, and treat the resulting object key as an auditable write decision.

TL;DR: create a presigned upload URL for /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}\, bind the intended Content-Type\ and any other required headers to that request, then issue an HTTP PUT\ with the image bytes. Keep the URL short-lived, never expose storage credentials, and make the object key collision-resistant because this storage surface has no If-Match\ conditional write or object versioning.

Start with the tenant boundary

Suppose a route receives a dispatch ID and an image produced for a delivery exception. The route must establish three facts before it asks storage for a presign: the authenticated principal belongs to the tenant, the dispatch belongs to that same tenant, and the destination key is derived by the server rather than accepted verbatim from the client.

That authorization decision is the real upload control.

For example, a retry from tenant 42 must not be able to reuse a key copied from tenant 17, even when both keys point to valid-looking PNG names. The service should resolve the dispatch from its own database, compare its tenant owner with the caller's tenant, and then construct the path from trusted identifiers. This takes more code than accepting a filename, but it gives the audit record a defensible explanation: the caller was authorized for this dispatch, the server selected this key, and the presigned capability was issued for that exact destination. A storage provider can enforce the byte write; it cannot infer the business relationship between a delivery exception and a tenant.

I prefer a key such as tenant-42/dispatch-9817/images/2026-10-23T14-05-00Z-7f3c.png\. The timestamp is useful in an audit record; the random suffix prevents an innocent retry from silently selecting the same name. A database record should retain the tenant ID, dispatch ID, object key, content type, requesting identity, and the idempotency key used for the create operation. The object store is the byte system, not the business ledger.

This is also where the exactly-once mindset earns its keep. A network timeout after the presign request does not tell the caller whether the authorization was recorded, and a retry must not create a second business attachment. Deduplicate the attachment command in the database, then reuse the accepted key or mark the command for reconciliation. Do not pretend that a presigned URL alone provides exactly-once semantics; it provides a constrained write capability.

The same rule applies to a generated image rather than a camera upload. A model worker can request a presign after it has a tenant-scoped job, but it should not be allowed to choose an arbitrary bucket and path. Authorization first, URL second, bytes third.

For teams that want the storage handoff behind one backend surface, Infrai is a plausible fit at this exact boundary: your service still decides tenant access, while its storage route supplies the presigned capability. The one-key, one-bill model is useful when the same logistics backend already has several backend integrations to operate, but it does not remove the need for an application-owned audit trail.

How do I use presigned URLs for uploading AI-generated images?

The flow has a narrow, useful contract:

  1. Your service authenticates the caller and chooses the bucket and key.
  2. Your service requests a presigned URL from the storage API.
  3. The uploader sends a PUT\ to that URL with the exact content headers used when the URL was generated.
  4. Your service records the intended object and reconciles the result using the storage metadata it can read.

The important detail is header parity. If the presign was generated for image/png\, the upload must send Content-Type: image/png\; changing that header can invalidate the signature or produce an object whose metadata disagrees with the application record. The URL is a capability, so log its request ID and expiry metadata when available, but do not put the URL itself into a long-lived audit record.

Here is the byte-transfer portion in Go. It deliberately accepts the presigned URL as input: the URL-generation request belongs behind your authorization boundary, while this small function can run in a worker without a storage access key.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func uploadImage(presignedURL, imagePath string) error {
    image, err := os.ReadFile(imagePath)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read image: %w", err)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, presignedURL, bytes.NewReader(image))
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("build upload request: %w", err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")

    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload image: %w", err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode < http.StatusOK || resp.StatusCode >= http.StatusMultipleChoices {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        return fmt.Errorf("upload failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, string(body))
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    presignedURL := os.Getenv("PRESIGNED_URL")
    if presignedURL == "" {
        panic("PRESIGNED_URL is required")
    }
    if err := uploadImage(presignedURL, "generated.png"); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The judgment point is the status code, not the absence of a transport error. A successful request should advance the attachment state only after the upload response is successful; an unsuccessful response should retain enough context for a retry or reconciliation job. For large images, stream from an io.Reader\ instead of reading the entire file into memory, while preserving the same explicit method, content type, and response check.

Which storage boundary fits a logistics platform?

The right comparison is not “which service can store a PNG?” All of these can participate in an upload workflow. The practical question is where signing, tenant policy, compatibility, and operations should live.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A direct object-storage integration with a mature ecosystem and broad AWS-native controls Your service owns tenant authorization, key policy, retries, and reconciliation around S3’s presigned request
Cloudflare R2 An S3-compatible object store for teams already operating at the Cloudflare edge Confirm the exact S3 compatibility and the account-level policy model you need; compatibility does not remove application-level tenant isolation
Alibaba Cloud OSS A direct choice for deployments already aligned with Alibaba Cloud regions and tooling Validate regional, identity, lifecycle, and audit requirements against the deployment rather than assuming S3 parity
Infrai storage A plain REST boundary when one backend credential and one billing surface should cover storage alongside other backend capabilities The storage caveats below are material: this is not a public image host or an immutable financial archive

The last row is a workflow choice, not a universal winner. Infrai’s useful distinction here is one key and one bill for backend services, which removes a separate credential and invoice boundary for a platform that already combines storage with other services. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples can also reduce the integration work of a small Go service. I would recommend it to a logistics team that wants a single REST handoff for tenant-authorized private objects and is prepared to keep business authorization and reconciliation in its own database.

Choose direct S3, R2, or OSS instead when your system depends on their provider-specific controls, established cross-region replication, or an existing operations platform that already owns those policies. The documented storage coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS vendors, but not GCS or Backblaze B2, so vendor fit must be checked before migration rather than inferred from an S3-shaped interface.

Where the presign approach stops

Private uploads are a good fit. Permanent public links are not: there is no public or public-read\ ACL, and public_url\ remains null. A client that needs a public image page needs a separate delivery design, not a longer-lived presigned URL.

There is no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through storage history and a compliance archive requiring WORM behavior needs an external control. There is also no If-Match\ conditional write. If two workers must be mutually exclusive, coordinate them with a queue or database lease before either requests a write capability.

Browser-direct uploads deserve another warning. The bucket model contains a cors_rules\ field, but there is no independently exposed route for setting CORS rules. A browser workflow therefore needs its CORS configuration verified in advance; a Go worker-to-storage path avoids the browser policy, but it does not solve authorization by itself.

Lifecycle retention is measured at a minimum of one day, not an hourly cleanup interval, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule. Metadata is not a server-side search index: object listing supports prefix filtering, not arbitrary metadata queries. Finally, trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes, so a trial environment must account for that before a worker treats presign success as deployability.

Here is the smallest provider-specific check I would run after the tenant authorization decision. It calls only the documented presign route, keeps the key in an environment variable, and fails loudly on a non-success response; the exact required headers must remain the same between this request and the later upload.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "net/url"
    "strings"
)

func requestPresign() error {
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    bucket := os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET")
    key := os.Getenv("OBJECT_KEY")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if bucket == "" || key == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("STORAGE_BUCKET, OBJECT_KEY, and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    template := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    presignURL := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(bucket),
        "{key}", url.PathEscape(key),
    ).Replace(template)
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, presignURL, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        return fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry after %q", resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < http.StatusOK || resp.StatusCode >= http.StatusMultipleChoices {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        return fmt.Errorf("presign failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, string(body))
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := requestPresign(); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Roll out with reconciliation, not hope

Start with one tenant-scoped bucket or an equally strict key policy, then make the database command the source of truth for the attachment. Store a short-lived upload state, the chosen object key, and the idempotency key. When the PUT\ succeeds, verify the object through the supported read or head workflow and move the attachment to complete; when it fails or expires, leave a retryable state and record the reason.

Do not automatically retry a completed PUT\ against a new key. That creates duplicate media and turns an ambiguous network result into a data-quality problem. Retry the same business command with the same deduplication identity, and reconcile the known key before creating anything else. The rule is simple: one business attachment, one authoritative key, many observable attempts.

For a logistics system, this boundary is usually enough: the application decides who may write, storage receives the bytes directly, and the ledger records what was intended and what was confirmed. Select the provider whose missing controls are acceptable for your retention and tenancy model, then test expiry, wrong content type, duplicate commands, and cross-tenant key attempts before broad rollout.

Keep the test matrix small and unforgiving.

If your team needs this private, tenant-authorized handoff and wants one backend credential across its services, try Infrai for the presign step and keep the ledger and reconciliation logic in your application. Start with the storage documentation; choose S3, R2, or OSS instead when their provider-specific retention, replication, or archival controls are part of the requirement.

References

The HTTP upload relies on explicit request methods and content headers, while browser-based variants depend on the server’s CORS policy. The provider comparison should be validated against each vendor’s current documentation before an architectural commitment.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS documentation: https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss

title: The Page Looks Ready. Your Browser Test Disagrees.
description:
A user opens a page, sees a button, and clicks it.

Your automated test opens the same page, sees the same button, and fails.

Sometimes the button is replaced a moment later. Sometimes a loading skeleton looks enough like the real component to confuse a selector. Sometimes the browser's address bar changes the available space, and an element moves just as the test tries to click it.

The application might be broken. The test might be broken. Or both might be behaving exactly as designed, just at different moments.

That's what makes modern browser testing frustrating. We build increasingly dynamic interfaces, then write tests as if pages appear all at once and stay put.

A visible page isn't necessarily an interactive page

Consider an app using React Suspense and server-side rendering.

The server sends HTML. The browser displays it. A person looking at the screen thinks the page is ready. But JavaScript may still be loading, data may still be resolving, and React may still be attaching event handlers or replacing parts of the DOM.

Your test finds the Save button and clicks it. Nothing happens. So someone adds a two-second wait.

That seems to fix it, until CI gets a little slower.

The better approach is to test readiness, not elapsed time. Wait for the specific control to become usable or for the application to expose the state that means the interaction can succeed. If a component passes through loading, hydrated, and interactive states, make those states observable.

This guide to testing React Suspense, streaming SSR, and partial hydration lays out the important distinction between slow data, replaced DOM nodes, and lost focus. Those failures can look identical from the outside, but they need different fixes.

A longer sleep is not a diagnosis.

Your selector may be perfectly valid and still be wrong

Now imagine a dashboard with a list of customer accounts.

The test clicks the third row. It worked yesterday. Today, a new account arrives and the list reorders automatically. The third row is now a different customer.

The selector didn't fail. That's worse. It worked on the wrong thing.

Skeleton loaders create another version of this problem. A test sees the container, assumes the content is ready, and attempts to interact with something that hasn't been rendered yet. Virtualized lists make it even trickier because rows may not exist in the DOM until they're scrolled into view.

A useful benchmark plan for dynamic lists, skeleton loaders, and selector resilience suggests measuring more than pass rate. It also looks at how often selectors need rewriting, how many special waits are required, and whether failures explain what actually happened.

That seems like a much better way to compare testing frameworks than clicking the same static login form 1,000 times.

For application tests, I would rather target an account by its stable identifier or accessible name than by its position on the page. And I would rather wait for a meaningful loaded state than assume the disappearance of one spinner proves everything is ready.

Checkout isn't one page. It's a series of handoffs.

Payment flows expose the limits of simplistic browser tests particularly well.

A checkout form might live inside a third-party iframe. Then the provider redirects the user to a 3D Secure challenge. The browser returns to your site, perhaps after a reload, and the application has to recover the original order.

A test that only enters card details and looks for a success message can miss the worst failures.

Was the original payment intent preserved? Did the order remain associated with the correct customer? What happens if someone refreshes during the challenge or submits twice? Could you create a duplicate charge or order?

The guide to testing payment iframes, redirects, and 3DS flows approaches checkout as a state-preservation problem, not just a sequence of clicks.

That's the right mental model. Use a payment provider's sandbox or test environment, exercise the redirect and challenge paths, and verify the backend result. The browser reaching a thank-you page is useful evidence, but it isn't proof that the payment was processed exactly once.

On mobile, even the viewport is moving

Desktop tests have a fairly stable idea of how much screen space is available.

Mobile browsers are different. The address bar expands and collapses. The on-screen keyboard appears. Safe-area insets protect content around notches and system UI. A fixed footer that looked fine in one screenshot can cover the only button a customer needs.

This is where pixel-perfect assertions can become counterproductive.

A practical guide to viewport units and safe-area testing makes a useful point: test whether content remains reachable and the layout responds correctly, not whether every coordinate remains identical after the browser chrome changes.

For a mobile checkout, I'd want to know whether the Pay button stays visible or scrollable into view, whether the keyboard obscures an input, and whether fixed elements overlap important content.

Those are customer problems. A three-pixel difference in an unrelated margin usually isn't.

Visual tests need a review process, not just screenshots

Visual regression testing sounds simple: take a screenshot, compare it with the baseline, and flag differences.

Then your team updates a shared button component and gets dozens of screenshot changes. Some are intentional. Some are real regressions. Someone has to tell them apart.

The more noisy the system gets, the easier it is to approve a change without looking carefully.

A comparison of visual testing tools for design system teams evaluates the parts that matter after a difference is detected: noise control, baseline management, pull-request context, approvals, and ongoing maintenance.

That's the interesting buying decision. Not just whether a tool can find differences, but whether people can review those differences quickly enough to keep trusting it.

Test the transitions, not just the destinations

If I were evaluating a browser testing setup today, I'd make a small collection of deliberately annoying scenarios before writing a large suite.

A page that hydrates after the HTML appears. A list that reorders during interaction. A payment flow that leaves the site and returns. A mobile footer that has to survive changing viewport height. A component update that produces a lot of legitimate visual differences.

Then I'd ask a few plain questions.

Can the tests complete without arbitrary sleeps? When something fails, can we tell whether the app or the test is wrong? How much work does it take to maintain the selectors and review the screenshots?

Passing the happy path matters. But real applications spend a lot of time between states: loading, updating, redirecting, returning, resizing.

That's where customers find bugs.

It's also where your tests need to earn their keep.

title: Why Disabling the Submit Button Isn't Enough: Preventing Duplicate Requests in React & Node.js
description:
Imagine this scenario:

A customer clicks Place Order.

The request reaches your server, the database successfully creates the order, but the response never reaches the browser because of a network issue.

The customer assumes something went wrong and clicks again.

Now you have two orders instead of one.

This is a common reliability problem in web applications.

Disabling a submit button might prevent accidental double-clicks, but it doesn't guarantee that an operation will execute only once.

Let's explore how to handle this properly using React, Node.js, and PostgreSQL.

1. Frontend protection is only the first layer

In React, we often prevent repeated submissions using a loading state:

const [isSubmitting, setIsSubmitting] = useState(false);

async function handleSubmit() {
  if (isSubmitting) return;

  setIsSubmitting(true);

  try {
    await createOrder();
  } finally {
    setIsSubmitting(false);
  }
}

This is useful for improving the user experience.

But there is a problem.

Duplicate requests can still happen because of:

  • Network retries
  • Multiple browser tabs
  • Concurrent API calls
  • Repeated webhook deliveries
  • Client or server failures

Even rapid calls within the same render cycle can observe the same React state before an update takes effect.

The important lesson: frontend protection improves UX, but backend protection ensures data integrity.

2. Understanding idempotency

An operation is idempotent when performing it multiple times has the same intended effect as performing it once.

For example:

POST /api/orders
Idempotency-Key: order-abc-123

If the same request is submitted again with the same idempotency key, the server should recognize that the operation has already been processed.

Instead of creating a new order, it can return the result of the original operation.

This is particularly important for:

  • Order creation
  • Payment processing
  • Subscription activation
  • Inventory adjustments
  • Financial transactions

3. Implementing idempotency in React

We can generate a unique idempotency key using the browser's built-in Web Crypto API.

import { useRef } from "react";

function OrderForm() {
  const idempotencyKeyRef = useRef(null);

  async function createOrder(order) {
    // Generate once for this intended operation.
    if (!idempotencyKeyRef.current) {
      idempotencyKeyRef.current = crypto.randomUUID();
    }

    const response = await fetch("/api/orders", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKeyRef.current,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(order),
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error("Order request failed");
    }

    return response.json();
  }

  // Use createOrder in your submission flow.
}

The key detail is that the same idempotency key must be reused when retrying the same intended operation.

Generate a new key only when the user starts a genuinely new order.

In a real application, you may need to persist the key beyond the component lifecycle if an unfinished operation must survive a page refresh.

4. Protecting the database against duplicate inserts

Frontend protection and idempotency middleware are useful, but concurrent requests can still introduce race conditions if the database isn't protected.

Consider this backend logic:

const existingOrder = await findOrder(key);

if (!existingOrder) {
  await createOrder(data);
}

Looks fine, right?

Not necessarily.

Two requests can execute simultaneously:

Request A                  Request B
    |                          |
Check existing order       Check existing order
    |                          |
Not found                  Not found
    |                          |
Create order               Create order
    |                          |
Success                    Success

Both requests can pass the check before either creates the record.

This is a classic check-then-insert race condition.

A better approach: Database uniqueness constraints

In PostgreSQL, enforce uniqueness at the database level.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX unique_order_request
ON orders (user_id, idempotency_key);

This assumes your orders table contains the corresponding columns.

Now use PostgreSQL's ON CONFLICT functionality:

INSERT INTO orders (
  user_id,
  idempotency_key,
  product_id,
  quantity,
  request_hash
)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5)
ON CONFLICT (user_id, idempotency_key)
DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;

If the insert succeeds, the query returns the new order ID.

If another request already used the same key, PostgreSQL prevents a duplicate insert.

The backend can then retrieve the existing order.

One additional safeguard is important: compare the stored request hash with the incoming request's hash.

If the same idempotency key is reused with different order parameters, return a conflict response instead of silently accepting the changed request.

Database constraints provide protection that application-level checks alone cannot guarantee.

5. What about transactions?

Preventing duplicate orders is only part of the problem.

Creating an order might involve multiple operations:

  1. Create the order.
  2. Reserve inventory.
  3. Update related database records.
  4. Record the transaction.
  5. Send a notification.

If one operation fails halfway through, the system can end up in an inconsistent state.

Database transactions help ensure that related database modifications succeed or fail together.

However, external operations such as sending emails or publishing messages are not automatically rolled back with a database transaction.

For these cases, patterns such as the transactional outbox and idempotent event consumers can improve reliability.

This is an important distinction when designing systems that interact with external services.

6. Test real failure scenarios

A feature working during normal testing doesn't necessarily mean it is reliable under failure conditions.

Here are five scenarios worth testing:

Scenario Expected behavior
Two concurrent requests with the same key Only one order is created
Retry after the original request commits Existing order is returned
Same key with different request data Request is rejected
Failed database transaction No partial order is committed
Two legitimate operations with different keys Both can proceed

These tests provide more confidence than simply checking whether a submit button becomes disabled.

7. The approach I recommend

For reliable applications, multiple layers should work together:

Frontend safeguards improve the user experience and discourage accidental repeated submissions.

Backend idempotency identifies repeated attempts to perform the same operation.

Database constraints protect against duplicate inserts, including concurrent requests.

Transactions and carefully designed side effects help maintain consistency across the entire workflow.

No single layer solves every problem.

The goal isn't just to make an API request succeed.

It's to make sure retries, failures, and concurrent requests don't produce unintended results.

Final thoughts

Building reliable software requires thinking beyond the happy path.

A submit button can be disabled. A network request can fail. A server can process the same operation more than once.

The application should still behave predictably.

A combination of frontend safeguards, idempotency, database constraints, and transaction handling is generally more reliable than depending on any one of them.

What's your approach to preventing duplicate requests in production applications?

Further reading: PostgreSQL INSERT / ON CONFLICT documentation

title: EUDI Wallet Verifier in Spring Boot: OpenID4VP, SD-JWT VC
description:
To accept an EU Digital Identity Wallet in Spring Boot, you build a verifier service that sends a signed OpenID4VP request, receives the SD-JWT VC presentation on a direct_post endpoint, and then checks the issuer signature, key binding, trust list and revocation status before returning a minimal yes or no.

Member states have to make a Digital Identity Wallet available to their citizens by the end of 2026. The duty to accept those wallets falls on relying parties in 2027, and payment providers and banks are named in that group through strong customer authentication and KYC rules, the same regulated corner I covered in my PSD2 and EU banking API guide. If your onboarding team still has wallet acceptance parked under "later", the calendar has stopped agreeing with that.

I spent a few weeks building a verifier in Spring Boot to find out what accepting a wallet credential costs an engineering team in practice. What follows is the wiring: how the request leaves, what comes back, which checks are mandatory, and where the specs leave the decision to you. There is no policy discussion here; the regulation is public. The one thing I will show that bit me is the iss and aud handling in the key binding check, because the verifier URL that looks right in a test environment is not necessarily the string a wallet signs over in production.

How I frame the verifier

A relying-party verifier is a small service that does four things in a row:

  1. Builds an authorization request that names the credential type and the exact attributes you want.
  2. Gets that request in front of a wallet, through a QR code on desktop or a deep link on a phone.
  3. Accepts the presentation the wallet posts back.
  4. Makes a deterministic accept-or-reject decision and writes down why.

The exchange runs on OpenID for Verifiable Presentations (OpenID4VP) and the credential format is SD-JWT VC. The wallet obtained its credential earlier through OpenID4VCI. You never speak OID4VCI as a verifier, but every field you validate was written at issuance by somebody else, so you have to know what that process produced.

Coming from payments, I treat it like a card-acquiring path with no stored cardholder data. It keeps no accounts and no copies of identity documents. A signed claim goes in, signatures and signers are checked, validity is checked, and a minimal result comes out. That shapes the architecture: short-lived sessions, almost no state, an audit trail, and no customer data store.

The flow end to end 

Browser/App        Verifier (Spring Boot)         Wallet            Issuer / Trust infra
    | start KYC           |                          |                      |
    |-------------------->| create session+nonce     |                      |
    |   QR / deep link    | sign request object      |                      |
    |<--------------------|                          |                      |
    |---- open link ------------------------------->|                      |
    |                     |<-- fetch request object--|                      |
    |                     |--- signed JWT ---------->| user consents        |
    |                     |<-- direct_post (vp_token)|                      |
    |                     | verify issuer sig, KB-JWT, nonce               |
    |                     |-- trust list lookup ---------------------------->|
    |                     |-- status list fetch ---------------------------->|
    |<-- result (poll/SSE)|                          |                      |

Two points catch people out. The phone running the wallet is not the browser that showed the QR code, so the answer cannot return through the browser. The wallet calls your backend directly (response_mode=direct_post, or direct_post.jwt when the body is encrypted), and the front end has to poll or subscribe for the result. And the request object is itself signed, so the wallet can check who is asking before the user sees a consent screen. Authentication runs in both directions.

Step one: ask for the smallest set of claims

The query language in OpenID4VP is DCQL, which lets you list credentials and claim paths you need. Selective disclosure is only useful if the verifier actually asks narrowly, and I resist the "request everything, we may need it later" instinct from product teams.

For a standard onboarding journey you usually need legal name and date of birth, and sometimes nationality or country of residence for sanctions screening and jurisdiction rules. Address and document numbers are separate decisions. Every extra attribute lands in your logs, backups and breach-notification scope, which is the practical meaning of data minimisation.

Minimal does not mean minimal at any price. KYC duties under AML rules usually require identifying the customer, verifying identity and, for many products, capturing date of birth and an address, so an over-18 assertion on its own is typically enough for age-gated services but not for opening a regulated account. Whether a given bank can onboard on fewer attributes is a question for its compliance function and its supervisor, not a default I can hand you. What I did was encode that decision as data: one profile per journey, each reviewed by compliance before it ships.

Here is the request builder with all helpers shown, so nothing is hidden. The session record keeps the nonce and the query and never any user data.

@Service
public class PresentationRequestService {

    private static final SecureRandom RANDOM = new SecureRandom();

    private final SessionStore sessions;           // Redis-backed, TTL 5 minutes
    private final RequestObjectSigner signer;      // signs with the key behind our x509 cert
    private final VerifierProperties props;

    public PresentationRequestService(SessionStore sessions,
                                      RequestObjectSigner signer,
                                      VerifierProperties props) {
        this.sessions = sessions;
        this.signer = signer;
        this.props = props;
    }

    public StartedSession start(KycProfile profile) {
        String sessionId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        String nonce = randomUrlSafe(32);
        String clientId = "x509_san_dns:" + props.hostname();

        Map<String, Object> dcql = Map.of(
            "credentials", List.of(Map.of(
                "id", "pid",
                "format", "dc+sd-jwt",
                "meta", Map.of("vct_values", List.of(props.pidVct())),
                "claims", profile.requiredPaths().stream()
                    .map(p -> Map.of("path", p))
                    .toList()
            ))
        );

        Map<String, Object> requestObject = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        requestObject.put("response_type", "vp_token");
        requestObject.put("client_id", clientId);
        requestObject.put("response_mode", "direct_post.jwt");
        requestObject.put("response_uri", props.baseUrl() + "/oid4vp/response/" + sessionId);
        requestObject.put("nonce", nonce);
        requestObject.put("dcql_query", dcql);
        requestObject.put("state", sessionId);

        sessions.save(new VerifierSession(sessionId, nonce, clientId, profile.name(),
                profile.requiredPaths(), Instant.now()));

        String jwt = signer.sign(requestObject);
        sessions.saveRequestJwt(sessionId, jwt);

        String link = "openid4vp://authorize?client_id=" + enc(clientId)
                + "&request_uri=" + enc(props.baseUrl() + "/oid4vp/request/" + sessionId);
        return new StartedSession(sessionId, link);
    }

    private static String randomUrlSafe(int bytes) {
        byte[] buf = new byte[bytes];
        RANDOM.nextBytes(buf);
        return Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(buf);
    }

    private static String enc(String v) {
        return URLEncoder.encode(v, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }
}

KycProfile.requiredPaths() returns something like [["family_name"], ["given_name"], ["birthdate"], ["nationality"]], since DCQL claim paths are arrays of path segments. Profiles live in versioned configuration, one for basic onboarding and one for higher-risk accounts. The profile name goes onto the session so an audit can show exactly which minimisation decision applied. A request profile is a compliance artifact: it sits in Git and goes through review.

Pay attention to the client_id prefix, and note that I now store the full prefixed value on the session. That is the detail behind my earlier remark. The wallet signs the key binding over the client_id exactly as it appeared in the request, prefix included. My first version compared the audience to the bare hostname, which is what I had in configuration, and the check was wrong for every real presentation. Keeping the prefixed string on the session removes the guesswork.

The identity itself comes from an X.509 certificate chain (a relying party access certificate) in the request object's header, and the client_id has to match a DNS name in its SAN. A registrar-linked authority in your member state issues that certificate, and it is why a wallet can show "Acme Payments is asking for these three attributes" instead of a bare URL.

One operational note from the signing side: the request-object key should not sit as a PEM on disk. I put it behind a PKCS#11 interface so the same RequestObjectSigner works against a software keystore in dev and an HSM in production, and signing latency stays a rounding error next to the user's consent tap.

Step two: receiving the presentation

The wallet calls your response_uri with a vp_token. With direct_post.jwt the whole response is a JWE encrypted to a key you published in the request, so a proxy or WAF log in between cannot leak the credential.

The controller stays deliberately thin. Validation belongs in a service you can unit test with fixture credentials.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/oid4vp")
public class ResponseController {

    private final ResponseDecryptor decryptor;
    private final SdJwtVcVerifier verifier;
    private final SessionStore sessions;
    private final VerificationAudit audit;

    // constructor omitted

    @PostMapping(value = "/response/{sessionId}",
                 consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_FORM_URLENCODED_VALUE)
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> receive(@PathVariable String sessionId,
                                                       @RequestParam("response") String jwe) {
        VerifierSession session = sessions.consume(sessionId)   // single use, atomic
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.GONE));

        VerificationOutcome outcome;
        try {
            Map<String, Object> payload = decryptor.decrypt(jwe);
            String vpToken = extractPresentation(payload, "pid");
            outcome = verifier.verify(vpToken, session);
        } catch (VerificationException e) {
            outcome = VerificationOutcome.rejected(e.reason());
        }

        audit.record(session, outcome);
        sessions.storeOutcome(sessionId, outcome.minimised());
        return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of());   // wallet only needs a 200
    }
}

sessions.consume has to be an atomic get-and-delete, implemented with Redis GETDEL. A wallet that retries after a network timeout, or an attacker replaying a captured response, must hit a 410 before any cryptography runs. This is the same idempotency thinking I described in transactional outbox and idempotent consumers for payment systems, applied to identity instead of payments.

That design has a cost worth naming. If the wallet's first attempt reaches you, you consume the session, and then the response is lost on the way back, the retry gets 410 and the user must restart. I accepted that: a restart costs the user one more scan, while a reusable session costs you a replay window. The related race is the TTL. With a five-minute TTL and a slow user on a bad connection, the session can expire between the wallet fetching the request object and posting the answer. I treat that as a normal outcome, return a distinct "expired" reason, and let the front end offer a fresh QR.

Step three: what an SD-JWT VC actually contains

A presentation is a tilde-separated string: the issuer-signed JWT, then zero or more disclosures, then a final key binding JWT (KB-JWT). A disclosure is a base64url-encoded array [salt, claim_name, claim_value]. The issuer JWT holds no values for hidden claims; it holds only _sd, a list of digests. When the user shares family_name, the wallet appends the matching disclosure, and you hash it and confirm the digest appears in _sd.

So you cannot decode the JWT and read the claims. A reader that skips the disclosure step sees an almost empty payload, and a sloppy one might accept it.

My checks, in order, with the reason for each:

  1. Parse strictly. Reject disclosures that match no digest, duplicate digests, and disclosures for claims you never asked for. An unrequested claim is not a free bonus. It means data is arriving outside your declared purpose.
  2. Validate the chain from the x5c header to a trust anchor taken from the EU trusted lists (below).
  3. Verify the issuer signature with the leaf certificate's key.
  4. Check vct against what you requested and exp/nbf against the clock, with a small skew allowance.
  5. Verify the KB-JWT. Its signature must verify under the key in the credential's cnf claim, and it must carry your nonce, your prefixed client_id as aud, a fresh iat, and an sd_hash over the exact presentation string you received.
  6. Check revocation status.

Step 5 proves the person holding the phone is the holder the credential was issued to. Skip it and a leaked SD-JWT becomes a bearer token for someone else's identity.

@Component
public class SdJwtVcVerifier {

    private static final Duration CLOCK_SKEW = Duration.ofSeconds(60);

    private final TrustAnchorProvider anchors;
    private final StatusListClient statusClient;
    private final KeyBindingVerifier keyBinding;
    private final Clock clock;

    public VerificationOutcome verify(String presentation, VerifierSession session)
            throws VerificationException {

        SdJwtPresentation p = SdJwtPresentation.parse(presentation);   // splits on '~'

        SignedJWT issuerJwt = p.issuerSigned();
        List<X509Certificate> chain = X5cChain.from(issuerJwt.getHeader());
        anchors.validate(chain);                                       // PKIX against trust list

        try {
            if (!issuerJwt.verify(new ECDSAVerifier((ECPublicKey) chain.get(0).getPublicKey()))) {
                throw new VerificationException("issuer-signature");
            }

            JWTClaimsSet claims = issuerJwt.getJWTClaimsSet();
            Instant now = clock.instant();
            Date exp = claims.getExpirationTime();
            if (exp == null || exp.toInstant().isBefore(now.minus(CLOCK_SKEW))) {
                throw new VerificationException("expired");
            }
            Date nbf = claims.getNotBeforeTime();
            if (nbf != null && nbf.toInstant().isAfter(now.plus(CLOCK_SKEW))) {
                throw new VerificationException("not-yet-valid");
            }

            Map<String, Object> disclosed = p.resolveDisclosures(claims);   // checks every digest
            if (!session.requiredClaimNames().containsAll(disclosed.keySet())) {
                throw new VerificationException("unrequested-claims");
            }

            Map<String, Object> cnf = claims.getJSONObjectClaim("cnf");
            JWK holderKey = JWK.parse((Map<String, Object>) cnf.get("jwk"));
            SignedJWT kb = p.keyBinding()
                    .orElseThrow(() -> new VerificationException("no-key-binding"));
            keyBinding.verify(kb, holderKey, session, p.presentationForHash(), now);

            statusClient.assertValid(claims.getJSONObjectClaim("status"), chain.get(0));

            return VerificationOutcome.accepted(disclosed,
                    chain.get(0).getSubjectX500Principal().getName());
        } catch (ParseException | JOSEException e) {
            throw new VerificationException("malformed");
        }
    }
}

And the key binding check itself, which is the part I would not leave to a library you have not read:

@Component
public class KeyBindingVerifier {

    private static final Duration MAX_AGE = Duration.ofMinutes(5);
    private static final Duration SKEW = Duration.ofSeconds(60);

    void verify(SignedJWT kb, JWK holderKey, VerifierSession session,
                String presentationForHash, Instant now)
            throws VerificationException, JOSEException, ParseException {

        if (!"kb+jwt".equals(kb.getHeader().getType() == null ? null : kb.getHeader().getType().getType())) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-typ");
        }
        if (!kb.verify(new ECDSAVerifier(holderKey.toECKey()))) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-signature");
        }

        JWTClaimsSet c = kb.getJWTClaimsSet();

        // aud must equal the client_id exactly as sent, scheme prefix included
        if (c.getAudience() == null || !c.getAudience().contains(session.clientId())) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-aud");
        }
        if (!session.nonce().equals(c.getStringClaim("nonce"))) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-nonce");
        }

        Instant iat = c.getIssueTime() == null ? null : c.getIssueTime().toInstant();
        if (iat == null || iat.isAfter(now.plus(SKEW)) || iat.isBefore(now.minus(MAX_AGE))) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-iat");
        }

        // sd_hash covers everything up to and including the last '~' before the KB-JWT
        String expected = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(
                MessageDigestUtil.sha256(presentationForHash.getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII)));
        if (!MessageDigest.isEqual(expected.getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII),
                String.valueOf(c.getClaim("sd_hash")).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII))) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-sd-hash");
        }
    }
}

On clock skew: a phone clock that is two minutes off is not exotic, and the iat window is where it shows up first. I kept the skew at a minute and the maximum age at five, which matches the session TTL, rather than widening either to make a bad device clock pass.

I use Nimbus JOSE + JWT for signatures since Spring Security usually brings it along already. The SD-JWT parsing, digest checking and key binding I wrote myself, a few hundred lines in total. Libraries exist, including the EU reference implementations, and for production I would evaluate one, but writing it once showed me the sharp edges, and the spec's test vectors keep you honest.

Step four: the trust list question

Tutorials tend to skip this, and it is where the "EU" in EUDI becomes an engineering problem. A valid signature only proves somebody holding a private key signed the credential. What you need to know is whether that somebody is an authorised issuer of the credential type you are accepting.

That answer lives in the EU trusted lists. Each member state publishes a signed trusted list (ETSI TS 119 612 XML), and the European Commission publishes a list of lists (LOTL) pointing at them. The verifier must fetch the LOTL, check its signature against pinned signing certificates, follow the pointers to the national lists, check each of those, extract the service entries for the relevant provider types, and turn them into trust anchors for PKIX path validation.

I keep that work entirely out of the request path, in a scheduled loader:

@Component
public class TrustAnchorProvider {

    private final AtomicReference<TrustSnapshot> current =
            new AtomicReference<>(TrustSnapshot.empty());
    private final TrustListFetcher fetcher;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "PT1H", initialDelay = 0)
    void refresh() {
        try {
            TrustSnapshot next = fetcher.fetchAndValidate();   // LOTL -> national lists -> anchors
            if (next.anchorCount() < current.get().anchorCount() / 2
                    && current.get().anchorCount() > 0) {
                log.error("Trust snapshot shrank from {} to {} anchors, keeping previous",
                        current.get().anchorCount(), next.anchorCount());
                return;
            }
            current.set(next);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            log.warn("Trust list refresh failed, serving snapshot {}", current.get().version(), e);
        }
    }

    public void validate(List<X509Certificate> chain) throws VerificationException {
        TrustSnapshot snap = current.get();
        if (snap.isStale(Duration.ofHours(48))) {
            throw new VerificationException("trust-snapshot-stale");
        }
        snap.pkixValidate(chain);
    }
}

The fetcher is where the real effort goes. Each list carries a NextUpdate timestamp and I honour it, so the hourly job usually re-checks and finds nothing new. Cert path validation is done with the JDK's PKIXParameters against the anchor set, revocation checking off for the chain itself because the trust list is the authority, and with the validation time taken from the injected Clock so tests can replay a past date. The signature on each national list is verified before a single entry is parsed. A list that fails its signature is dropped and the previous snapshot of that member state stays in place, rather than the whole refresh failing.

Three decisions are visible in the snippet. Request handling reads an in-memory snapshot and never touches the network, so a slow national server cannot hold up onboarding. A refresh that loses more than half the anchors is rejected and alerted on, since a parser bug or a truncated download should not quietly un-trust a country. And a snapshot older than 48 hours fails closed, because accepting credentials against a trust view you cannot vouch for is the wrong failure direction for a regulated firm.

I also store the snapshot version in each audit record. When a regulator or your fraud team asks why you accepted a credential on a particular date, you can answer with the exact trust data you held at that moment.

Step five: revocation without a privacy leak

Credentials get revoked: a lost phone, a corrected record, an expired residence permit. SD-JWT VC handles this through status references, typically a Token Status List. The credential holds a status claim with a list URI and an index. The list is a compressed bit array signed by the issuer, and you check the bit at your index.

The privacy argument is easy to miss. The list is public and covers a large population, so fetching it tells the issuer nothing about which person you are verifying. That is the point of preferring it to a per-credential online status call.

In practice you cache and respect the list's own time-to-live:

@Component
public class StatusListClient {

    private final RestClient http;
    private final OutboundHostPolicy hostPolicy;
    private final Cache<String, StatusList> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .maximumSize(500)
            .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
            .build();

    public void assertValid(JSONObject statusClaim, X509Certificate issuerCert)
            throws VerificationException {
        if (statusClaim == null) {
            return;   // credential type may legitimately carry no status; policy decides
        }
        JSONObject ref = (JSONObject) statusClaim.get("status_list");
        String uri = (String) ref.get("uri");
        int idx = ((Number) ref.get("idx")).intValue();

        hostPolicy.assertAllowed(uri, issuerCert);   // allow-list before any network call

        StatusList list = cache.get(uri, this::download);   // list signature checked on parse
        if (list.statusAt(idx) != 0) {
            throw new VerificationException("credential-revoked-or-suspended");
        }
    }

    private StatusList download(String uri) {
        byte[] body = http.get().uri(uri).accept(MediaType.valueOf("application/statuslist+jwt"))
                .retrieve().body(byte[].class);
        return StatusList.parseAndVerify(body);
    }
}

Two cautions. The URI comes from inside the credential, so someone who builds a credential, even one that will fail signature verification later, can try to aim your service at an internal address. I verify the chain before fetching anything and limit outbound hosts to an allow-list derived from the issuer's trust list entry. This is the SSRF class of bug discussed in the Spring Boot 4.1 SSRF mitigation write-up. The order matters: never make a network call on the strength of unverified input.

The second is policy rather than code: what happens if the status list cannot be reached? For onboarding to a payment product I fail closed with a short retry, since KYC is a point-in-time control and a retry costs a customer half a minute. For a login-style re-authentication, living with a cached list for longer is a defensible choice.

What the audit record should hold

Compliance will want to know what you checked. I persist the session ID, the request profile name and version, the requested claim paths, the issuer certificate subject, the trust snapshot version, the status list URI with the fetch timestamp, and the outcome with its rejection reason. What I do not persist is the raw presentation, or any claim not required downstream.

The onboarding service downstream sees only the minimised outcome: the claims it asked for and a verification record ID. If your KYC provider needs a date of birth, it gets a date of birth, and the raw credential never leaves the verifier. The same instinct shaped how I handle evidence in DORA and NIS2 policy-as-code on Spring Boot: make evidence a by-product of the control, not a document someone assembles later.

Operating it for real

Some observations from building and load-testing this, informed by years of running trading and market-data systems where verification latency is directly visible:

  • Cost per verification is small. Two EC signature checks (issuer and key binding) plus a chain validation against in-memory anchors. On modest hardware the cryptography is not the bottleneck; the human at the consent screen is. Virtual threads suit the occasional blocking status fetch, and I covered the production details in Java virtual threads in Spring Boot.
  • Trace everything, log little. Carry a trace ID through request creation, response receipt and outcome delivery, and keep claim values out of spans and logs. Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry is where I configured attribute filters for exactly this, and the same discipline applies to observability guardrails for agentic AI backends.
  • Test against more than one wallet. Implementations are still maturing, and I saw differences in how they encode claim paths, pick the key for direct_post.jwt and handle optional claims. Build integration tests around recorded real-wallet responses, not just your own generator, and note that a generator you wrote will agree with your own misreadings of the spec.
  • Keep format support narrow. ISO mdoc credentials (mobile driving licences above all) are also in the ecosystem. Start with SD-JWT VC for the PID, ship, and add mdoc as a second adapter behind the same verify interface when a concrete requirement appears.
  • Plan the unglamorous fallback. Many customers will not have a wallet in year one. Keep the wallet route beside your existing document-and-selfie flow, and have KYC orchestration treat "wallet verified" as one strong signal among several.

Where the standards still bite

This is not settled. DCQL details, status list drafts, and each member state's final attribute and certificate profile are all still moving. The sensible answer is isolation: my verifier exposes a narrow internal interface (start(profile), outcome(sessionId)), and everything protocol-specific sits behind it. When a draft changes I edit one module instead of the onboarding service.

There is also a real build-versus-buy question. A hosted verifier gets you moving sooner and carries someone else's maintenance load. Building gives you control over the trust snapshot, the audit trail and exact data flows, which for a regulated payments company can be the whole argument. Having co-founded a startup that was acquired (I wrote up what that taught me) and built payment-adjacent APIs for OpenBanking PSD2, my bias is to own the decision logic and the evidence, and to rent the commodity parts if you have to.

If you are weighing this for your team, my background across AirAsia-scale platforms (see building microservices at 130 million requests per day) and regulated fintech is on the experience section of this site, and you can reach me via contact if you want to compare notes.

A starting checklist for this quarter

Before the 2027 acceptance obligations bite, I would work in this order:

  1. Pick one onboarding journey and write down the minimum attribute set it needs, agreed with compliance. Turn it into a versioned DCQL profile.
  2. Stand up a verifier against a reference or test wallet environment, with the single-use session store and signed request objects.
  3. Implement strict SD-JWT parsing, including unrequested-claim rejection and key binding.
  4. Build the trust list loader as a background job with stale-snapshot protection.
  5. Add status list checking with an explicit fail-closed policy and an outbound host allow-list.
  6. Write the audit record and review it with your compliance and data protection people before any real user touches it.

Related Articles

  • Open Banking PSD2 API development
  • DORA and NIS2 policy-as-code with Spring Boot and Kubernetes
  • Transactional outbox and idempotent consumers for payment systems

This week, take the one KYC journey you would move to wallets first, write its minimum attribute list as a DCQL query in a Git-tracked file, and run that query against a test wallet to see which claims come back.

FAQ

What is an EUDI Wallet verifier?

An EUDI Wallet verifier is the relying-party service that requests a credential from an EU Digital Identity Wallet, receives the presentation over OpenID4VP, and validates the signatures, trust chain, key binding and revocation status. It returns a minimal outcome to your onboarding system and stores no identity documents.

Do I need to implement OpenID4VCI to accept wallet credentials?

No. OpenID4VCI is the issuance protocol used between the issuer and the wallet. As a verifier you only speak OpenID4VP, but you need to understand what issuance produced, because the claims, x5c chain and status reference you validate were all set at issuance.

How does selective disclosure work in SD-JWT VC?

The issuer-signed JWT carries only _sd digests of the hidden claims. The wallet sends a disclosure ([salt, claim_name, claim_value]) for each claim the user agrees to share, and the verifier recomputes the SHA-256 digest and checks that it appears in _sd. Any disclosure that matches no digest, or that you did not request, should be rejected.

How do I check whether a wallet credential has been revoked?

Read the status claim, fetch the signed Token Status List from the URI it points to, and check the bit at the credential's index. Cache the list according to its time-to-live, verify its signature before use, restrict outbound hosts to an allow-list, and decide up front whether you fail open or closed when the list is unreachable.

title: Building a dual-view Shopify lookbook from the Born Agency case
description:
Campaign imagery can define the identity of a streetwear, eyewear, beauty, accessories, or camera brand. A standard four-column Shopify grid can flatten that identity.

The two usual shopping paths leave a gap. A lookbook can be hard to shop directly, while a collection page can lose the visual character that drew the buyer in.

Ukrainian design studio BY.SHIVA STUDIO, with Polina Prykhodko and Oleksandr BY.SHIVA, addresses that tension in Born Agency | Creative Studio Website. Its brief asks for a custom visual approach with a monochrome base and strong accents, letting the imagery set the tone from the first scroll.

Two other public projects help frame the comparison.

  • NM Art & Design uses warm greys and generous negative space to give objects the attention they would receive in a gallery.
  • Volenta uses a dark B2B layout with Bento cards that make metrics easy to scan.
  • Born Agency combines viewfinder marks, mixed typography, saturated gradients, and a CAROUSEL / GALLERY toggle. The visitor can look through large images or filter a grid within the same interface.

The following sections examine four design decisions and show how to translate them into a Shopify Online Store 2.0 theme, including the complete reference section.

1. Four design decisions in the Born Agency case

Colour system — carbon black with lime and magenta accents

Born Agency starts from carbon black, #1C1C1C, rather than a pure black #000000 canvas. The darkroom-like base supports two separate gradients.

  • Background and cards. Carbon black #1C1C1C with a 1px translucent white line, rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12), creates an exposed hairline grid.
  • Primary action. Electric lime runs from #5AFE41 to #EBF61D. It highlights actions such as the circular CONTACT US ↗ button, the footer's project inquiry panel, and active filters.
  • Atmosphere and navigation. Magenta runs from #FF0046 to #FF006A. The fullscreen menu uses it behind large vertical links for Home, Projects, Services, About, and Contact. It also appears as a red glow in the team portraits.
  • Main text. Pure white #FFFFFF gives the dark canvas strong contrast.

For a Shopify implementation, start with the product images. Keep most of the browse area carbon black and white so the campaign colours can carry it. Reserve magenta for the full-screen menu and collection navigation, and keep lime for circular Shop Now ↗ and Add to Bag ↗ actions.

Hero and imagery — use a viewfinder to label a detail

On the hero and selected work images, the project puts crosshairs and right-angle viewfinder corners around the subject. Small uppercase labels sit beside the frame, including TAILORED TO YOUR REQUEST, ATTENTION TO DETAIL, and REAL TEAM WITHOUT AI AGENTS.

A Shopify lookbook can give its hotspots the same job. On a hero or campaign image:

  1. Use CSS corners to frame a detail such as the sunglasses a model is wearing, the bag they are holding, or the keyboard on a desk.
  2. Put the material, feature, or price next to the frame, for example TITANIUM FRAME · $240 ↗.
  3. Connect the hotspot to the relevant product's Quick Add Drawer if the theme supports that flow.

Brand typography — combine typefaces and small inline images

The project’s brand statement uses several editorial techniques.

  • Change typeface within a sentence. Extra-bold geometric sans-serif carries the main words. A high-contrast italic serif marks an emphasis or a turn in the sentence.
  • Place a small image capsule inside a line. A rounded image or looping texture close to the text height lets the reader shift from words to material details.
  • Use a circular text badge. A phrase such as CREATE · DOMINATE · CREATE · DOMINATE runs around a rotating badge in a corner of the page.

Product and portfolio browsing — two views with a shared filter bar

The PROJECTS page has two levels of navigation. The control on the right switches between the large horizontal CAROUSEL and the multi-column GALLERY. The filter bar divides browsing into four decisions.

  • Sort By. No Filter / Latest / Popular / Featured
  • Content Type. All / Photo / Video / Motion
  • Industry. All / Fashion / Beauty / Food & Beverage / Tech / Automotive / Lifestyle
  • Style. All / Minimal / Bold / Editorial / Surreal / Cinematic / Abstract

On detail pages such as SMITH and FLORA, a fine-line grid puts About, Fields, Tasks, Platforms, Services, Duration, and Team on the left, alongside a large image carousel.

Born Agency pattern Problem it addresses Equivalent for a Shopify store
CAROUSEL versus GALLERY New visitors want to feel the campaign through large images. Shoppers with a product in mind want to scan a grid. Let the same collection switch between a campaign carousel and a three-column shopping grid in place.
Filter by Minimal, Bold, or Editorial Product categories alone can make it hard to browse by aesthetic. Add a Style product metafield alongside category filters. Use it to group styles such as minimalist everyday wear, runway pieces, or technical outerwear.
Fine-line specifications on SMITH and FLORA A visual page can hide details a shopper needs before buying. Put fit, weight, fabric, origin, and model size in a structured grid on the product page.

2. Implement the visual system in a Shopify theme

The reference uses three pieces that can live in a Shopify Online Store 2.0 theme.

1. Set the palette, gradients, and mixed typography

Define the carbon black and both gradients in assets/base.css. The same file can supply classes for the bold sans-serif and italic serif combination and the inline image capsule.

:root {
  /* Born Agency 核心色板 */
  --born-black: #1C1C1C;
  --born-surface: #242424;
  --born-white: #FFFFFF;
  --born-muted: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.62);
  --born-grid-line: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.14);

  /* 双色高饱和渐变 */
  --born-grad-green: linear-gradient(135deg, #5AFE41 0%, #EBF61D 100%);
  --born-grad-pink: linear-gradient(135deg, #FF0046 0%, #FF006A 100%);

  /* 字体组合：宽体粗无衬线 + 高对比衬线 */
  --born-font-sans: 'Syne', 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
  --born-font-serif: 'Playfair Display', 'Instrument Serif', Georgia, serif;
}

/* 混排标题中的斜体衬线强调词 */
.born-editorial-serif {
  font-family: var(--born-font-serif);
  font-style: italic;
  font-weight: 400;
  padding: 0 0.15em;
}

/* 行内微缩胶囊图（Inline Image Pill） */
.born-inline-pill {
  display: inline-block;
  vertical-align: middle;
  width: 2.4em;
  height: 1.15em;
  border-radius: 999px;
  object-fit: cover;
  margin: 0 0.2em;
  border: 1px solid var(--born-grid-line);
}

2. Draw the circular action and viewfinder corners

The circular CONTACT US ↗ action and the four viewfinder corners can be drawn with CSS and pseudo-elements. The corner marks need no separate image assets.

/* 正圆形电光绿渐变主按钮 */
.born-circle-cta {
  width: 116px;
  height: 116px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  background: var(--born-grad-green);
  color: #1C1C1C;
  display: inline-flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  gap: 4px;
  font-family: var(--born-font-sans);
  font-size: 0.75rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  letter-spacing: 0.06em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  text-decoration: none;
  transition: transform 0.25s cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1);
}
.born-circle-cta:hover {
  transform: scale(1.06) rotate(4deg);
}

/* 相机取景框四角准星容器 */
.born-viewfinder-box {
  position: relative;
  padding: 10px 14px;
  background: rgba(28, 28, 28, 0.72);
  backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
  color: #FFFFFF;
  font-size: 0.75rem;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
}
.born-viewfinder-box::before,
.born-viewfinder-box::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  width: 8px;
  height: 8px;
  border-color: #5AFE41;
  border-style: solid;
}
.born-viewfinder-box::before {
  top: 0; left: 0;
  border-width: 1.5px 0 0 1.5px;
}
.born-viewfinder-box::after {
  bottom: 0; right: 0;
  border-width: 0 1.5px 1.5px 0;
}

3. Compare the three Shopify design approaches

Dimension NM Art & Design Volenta Born Agency
Palette Black #000000, warm greys #736E68 and #A29A91, with copper accents Matte black #0B0D0C, forest green #182920, and electric lime #C6FF33 Darkroom carbon #1C1C1C, lime gradient #5AFE41 → #EBF61D, and magenta #FF0046 → #FF006A
Typography Architectural geometric capitals with restrained sans-serif body text Aeonik for the headings, Inter for utility text, and bracketed tags as signposts Extra-bold wide sans-serif mixed with high-contrast italic serif and inline image capsules
Evidence and browsing Generous negative space, artist credentials, and downloadable specifications A 12-column Bento matrix and an 01–04 process. The +63% and 4X figures appear in the design as examples Viewfinder labels, campaign imagery, and carousel and gallery views
Primary action Add to Bag, an Enquire drawer, and a PRO selection folder A single lime action such as Book a Call ↗ or Get Started ↗ A circular CONTACT US ↗ action and filters for browsing by style
Shopify fit Design furniture, lighting, ceramics, homewares, collectors' goods 3D printers, portable power, industrial equipment and tools, and custom B2B wholesale Fashion, eyewear, beauty, fragrance, gaming accessories, and photography equipment

The patterns can work together on the same store. A homepage or lookbook can use Born Agency's hotspots and two views. A performance section can use a Volenta-style evidence matrix. On a detail page, a structured specification table, a PDF download, and a side drawer for enquiries can follow the NM Art & Design approach.
